artigo.texto: AMD Helion Puts CPU Density at the Center of Agentic AI Infrastructure Key Highlights - AMD Helion offers two configurations: a CPU-only rack supporting up to 32,768 sixth-generation EPYC cores and an integrated enterprise design combining EPYC processors with Instinct MI350P accelerators. - The architecture supports independent scaling of CPU-based agent execution and GPU inference resources, potentially improving infrastructure utilization as AI workload demands evolve. - Built around Open Compute Project standards, Helion provides a modular foundation for hardware integration, customization and future upgrades across participating equipment manufacturers. - AMD offers high-density, balanced and high-frequency CPU configurations, allowing system designers to match processor performance and electrical requirements to different agentic AI workloads. - Initial Helion availability is targeted for November 2026, with commercial implementations planned by industry partners. Rack-level power requirements, independent performance benchmarks and deployment economics remain unproven. The next phase of AI infrastructure will require more than expanding GPU capacity. As agentic AI moves toward production deployment, data center operators face a different computing challenge: how to balance the CPU resources needed to execute increasingly complex workflows with the GPU infrastructure that powers AI model inference. AMD's answer is Helion, an open, modular rack-scale architecture introduced October 12 at the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit in San Jose, California. As DCF reported from the event, Helion reflects AMD's expectation that agentic applications will place substantially greater demands on general-purpose computing, requiring infrastructure that can be configured around distinct workloads rather than fixed combinations of CPUs and GPUs. Built around OCP specifications, Helion offers two principal configurations. A CPU-only rack supports as many as 32,768 sixth-generation AMD EPYC processor cores, targeting large-scale agent execution. An integrated enterprise configuration combines EPYC CPUs with AMD Instinct MI350P accelerators to support agent processing and model inference within the same rack. The architecture accommodates both air-cooled and liquid-cooled implementations, giving system manufacturers options for different deployment environments. Helion also extends AMD's rack-scale strategy beyond Helios, its tightly integrated architecture for GPU-intensive AI training and large-scale inference. Where Helios concentrates accelerator performance within high-density systems, Helion emphasizes the distribution of computing resources across the different tasks involved in agentic AI. For data center operators, the distinction raises questions that extend beyond processor selection. How CPU and GPU resources are distributed will affect electrical demand, cooling requirements, network architecture and ultimately the amount of useful AI computing capacity that can be delivered within a facility's infrastructure constraints. Agentic AI Changes the Computing Equation Traditional chatbot-style AI applications generally follow a straightforward computing pattern: a user submits a prompt, a model processes the request on GPUs, and a response is generated. Agentic AI introduces a more complex sequence of operations, extending beyond model inference into software execution, data retrieval, decision-making and coordination across multiple systems. An AI agent may query databases, execute code, retrieve information from external sources, communicate with other agents and evaluate intermediate results before completing a task. These activities introduce substantial general-purpose processing requirements alongside the GPU resources needed for model inference. As the number of agents and concurrent tasks increases, so do the demands on memory, storage, networking, security and workload orchestration. The result is a more heterogeneous computing environment, where adding GPU capacity alone may not improve overall application performance. CPU throughput, memory bandwidth and the ability to coordinate workloads across distributed infrastructure become increasingly important to system efficiency. For data center operators, that changes the equation for allocating computing resources within available power and cooling capacity. AMD sees this diversity of workloads as a central consideration in the design of agentic AI infrastructure. As Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager of Compute and Enterprise AI at AMD, explained: Agentic AI is not a single workload. It spans personal agents, enterprise applications, code execution and complex workflows, each with different compute requirements. To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing AMD EPYC performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power. AMD expects the growth of agentic applications to substantially increase demand for server CPUs alongside GPU infrastructure. During her October 12 OCP keynote, CEO Lisa Su said the company now projects the server CPU market will exceed $200 billion by 2030, a significant upward revision from its earlier $120 billion estimate. While that remains AMD's market forecast rather than an independent measure of future demand, it underscores the company's conviction that general-purpose computing will play a much larger role in AI infrastructure. Two Rack Designs for Different Markets Helion's two principal configurations reflect different approaches to deploying and managing agentic workloads. For hyperscale operators, the architecture emphasizes high-density CPU infrastructure dedicated to agent execution, with model inference handled by separate GPU-accelerated systems. artigo.texto: Nokia relata força contínua impulsionada por IA e expansão de data centers A empresa informou na quinta-feira que as vendas do terceiro trimestre em sua divisão de infraestrutura de rede — unidade que abriga as tecnologias de rede para IA e data centers — subiram 17% na comparação anual A Nokia continua a registrar um forte crescimento vindo de clientes de inteligência artificial e data centers, à medida que a empresa finlandesa capitaliza seu portfólio expandido de produtos para fornecer infraestrutura essencial para a implantação da IA. A empresa informou na quinta-feira que as vendas do terceiro trimestre em sua divisão de infraestrutura de rede — unidade que abriga as tecnologias de rede para IA e data centers — subiram 17% na comparação anual, impulsionadas pela demanda de clientes de nuvem e IA nas Américas. A companhia registrou 1,5 bilhão de euros (US$ 1,68 bilhão) em pedidos de clientes de IA e nuvem no trimestre e continua projetando um crescimento de 12% a 14% nas vendas totais da divisão de infraestrutura de rede para este ano. As vendas de equipamentos de infraestrutura móvel da empresa — seu negócio tradicional de tecnologia e serviços de comunicação móvel — subiram 5% na comparação anual, com Japão, Índia e a região de Europa, Oriente Médio e África apresentando o crescimento mais forte. A empresa ainda espera reportar um lucro operacional comparável do grupo para todo o ano entre 2,1 bilhões e 2,6 bilhões de euros, apesar de prever custos mais elevados de reestruturação e economia de gastos, agora estimados em 1,1 bilhão de euros, ante a projeção anterior de 800 milhões de euros. A expectativa de custos mais altos ocorre no momento em que a Nokia ampliou a escala de alguns de seus programas de reestruturação, acelerando os esforços para simplificar suas operações.

artigo.texto: Nebraska data center leaders talk natural resource protection, responsible development By Macy Byars, Reporter Nebraska Public Media News Oct. 22, 2026, 7:50 p.m. · Three Nebraska data center leaders discussed responsible data center development, water and energy usage and community pushback Wednesday at a renewable energy conference panel. Bringing more data centers to Nebraska is a contentious topic. City council and county board meetings discussing data centers have drawn large crowds of opposition across party lines. The panel covered a few of these common concerns, including water consumption, strain on Nebraska’s power system and community impact. Kearney Mayor Jonathan Nikkila said citizen engagement is an involved process, but it is key to creating city regulations. “I'm really thankful for the citizen push, because if they hadn't pushed us at that moment at that time we wouldn't have been ready. Instead, we were able to set the expectations for what we wanted from that kind of development in our town,” Nikkila said at the Nebraska Wind and Solar Conference panel. “Instead of reacting, we were the ones explaining what we expected from them.” More than a dozen Nebraska counties have placed moratoriums on new data centers as a response to the backlash. But other counties are rethinking zoning rules, possibly to allow for data center construction. Responsible resource management Developers are eyeing the Midwest for its wide swaths of land and access to natural resources – like water. Data centers can use anywhere from thousands to millions of gallons of water per day to cool processing chips. Panelist John Winkler is the general manager of the Papio-Missouri Natural Resources District and a Nebraska Data Center Task Force member. He said Nebraska has strong regulatory safeguards to protect groundwater. “There isn't one data center in Nebraska that's using any aquifer water. Every data center that we have is hooked up to a municipal supply,” he said. Those regulations allow Nebraska NRDs to ask industries for analysis on how they would impact the area’s water. Winkler said he is “very comfortable” with the systems Nebraska has to manage data center water usage. “There's a lot of coordination between not only the local jurisdictions but also the state as well,” Winkler said. “There isn't going to be a user that pops up in the middle of the night that throws a bunch of straws into an aquifer and drains it. It's just not going to happen in the state of Nebraska.” The Nebraska Legislature has also tried to safeguard the cost of energy. Passed last session, LB1261 allows private power developers to generate on-site energy for industrial customers – like data center companies – without interference from Nebraska’s public power sector. The bill was supported by Gov. Jim Pillen. Tax incentives for data centers are also restricted following an executive order signed by Pillen in September. He also appointed the Nebraska Data Center Task Force made up of energy, infrastructure and natural resource management leaders. Data center companies developing large facilities must also provide some kind of “community benefit,” like investing in workforce development or road improvements. Chris Matos, energy market development lead for the central U.S. at Google, said the company is doing what it can to protect natural resources when developing data centers. “Google, as a company, has a corporate goal to return 130% of our water usage nationally,” Matos said. “You see that play out here in Nebraska, actually, with our investments in agricultural water initiatives, where we're helping farmers optimize or reduce their water uses using drift lines.” On Monday, Google announced a $6 million contribution to help Omaha Public Power District customers with their bills, install leak detection sensors and invest in clean energy generation. “It works best when we do it with our utility partners because it offers the right mix, I think, of us being the anchor load for those big investments that are needed – particularly as infrastructure is aging and needs to be replaced with newer, more efficient and cheaper resources – where we can.” Matos said Google has made other significant investments in infrastructure that shield ratepayers from increased energy costs. “We did learn that lesson with OPPD and others where we were realizing that our ramp schedules were off due to delays, and we figured out how to make sure that those costs that were being incurred by OPPD were not shared amongst ratepayers,” he said. Water cooling is 30% more efficient than air cooling, said Matos, but Google does switch to air cooling when surface water supply can’t support operations. Matos said Google’s data centers aren’t using less water for cooling, but the computing power they can get from their current water usage is increasing. “Over the last five years, we've reduced our overhead energy demand by 83%. Now, that hasn't slowed down the demand at the data center – we still draw the same amount of power. It increases what we can do with that compute power,” he said. Energy demand is already a top issue in the state – which panelists say data centers are rapidly requiring Nebraska to push forward on. “We're at that point now where we've used up all of our excess generation capacity that was built back in the late '80s and '90s, and so we're at that point where we need to to build more generation,” Winkler said. Managing negative publicity Nebraska could stand to benefit from the industries, jobs and economic boost that data centers bring. But Nikkila said he tried not to make the community conversation about money. “I think that people, especially in Kearney, would have assumed we were trying to justify real problems for the amount of money that we would potentially get in tax revenue,” he said. “What dollar amount is worth draining our aquifer? artigo.texto: Rondo Energy and Rio Tinto Advance Australia's Largest Thermal Energy Storage Project GLADSTONE, Australia, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rondo Energy and Rio Tinto have started front-end engineering and design on the project for a 360 MWh storage / 30 MW discharge Rondo Heat Battery, supported by a grant from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA). ARENA's funding for the project will be provided in stages, with an initial $3.6 million to complete front-end engineering and design work. Following successful completion of that study, ARENA will provide up to $38 million for deployment. ARENA has also approved up to $33.3 million in conditional contingency support, which would only be made available in defined circumstances to manage specific project risks, including cost overruns and electricity costs. If progressed, the project would be delivered at Rio Tinto's Yarwun alumina refinery near Gladstone, Queensland and would be one of the first large-scale demonstrations of thermal energy storage for industrial process heat globally, and a world-first for the alumina industry. Rondo Heat Batteries use abundant, low-cost midday electricity to charge, storing energy as high-temperature heat in refractory brick, and supplying energy as 24/7 continuous process heat to industry. Typically, the heat is delivered as steam, directly into an industrial facility's steam network. Australia regularly has 4-6 hours of surplus solar-generated renewable electricity in the middle of the day, but industrial facilities need heat 24 hours a day, not just when the sun is shining. By charging when electricity is cheap and abundant and discharging continuously, Rondo Heat Batteries turn short periods of low-cost electricity into 24/7 delivery of low-cost steam. For energy-intensive industries such as alumina refining, Rondo Heat Batteries create a pathway to electrification that addresses both emissions and energy costs. Because the heat battery slots into the existing steam network, the facility's processes run exactly as before — the only thing that changes is the energy for that heat: no longer from fossil fuels, but sourced from low cost electricity instead. The Yarwun study will assess the technical and economic viability of integrating the technology into refinery operations. "This project shows how Australia's abundant energy can become a competitive advantage for industry," said Dr. Kira Rundel, Rondo's Head of Australia. "Heat batteries allow manufacturers to use low-cost electricity to produce the reliable, round-the-clock heat their operations need. Australia's largest heat battery will show how factories can cut emissions without increasing energy costs, helping Australian industry to increase global competitiveness and supporting local manufacturing jobs." Rio Tinto Pacific Operations Managing Director Armando Torres said: "Reducing emissions from alumina refining is complex, particularly when it comes to generating the high-pressure steam needed for our operations. "This study will help us determine whether thermal energy storage can provide a technically and economically viable alternative to fossil fuels for part of Yarwun's steam requirements. "The best way to tackle challenges of this scale is through collaboration between industry, government, and technology partners. We welcome ARENA and Rondo's support as we assess technologies that could help reduce our Scope 1 emissions while maintaining reliable operations at Yarwun." About Rondo Energy Rondo Energy delivers firm heat and power, including combined heat and power (CHP), to heavy industry and provides power solutions and long duration storage to data centers. For industrial heat applications, Rondo Heat Batteries convert 4-6 hours of low-cost electricity into continuous 24-hour, high-temperature heat, delivered as steam or hot air up to 1,000°C. The heat delivered integrates directly with existing industrial equipment and processes, eliminating on-site emissions and running on lower cost energy. Rondo heat storage can integrate with steam turbines to deliver combined heat and power (CHP) for industry, and long duration power-to-power solutions for large energy consumers such as data centers. Built on proven refractory brick as the thermal storage medium, Rondo's platform is engineered for multi-decade operation in the most demanding industrial environments. Rondo Heat Batteries have been delivering firm heat and power at scale since 2023, with operational facilities serving customers in fuels and cement (including steam driving turbines for electricity) in the United States and in Asia. The next unit will come online shortly - a 100 MWh Rondo Heat Battery under construction in Europe for a chemical plant. Rondo is a global company based in California, with teams across North America, Europe, the Middle East, and Australia. Providing heat and power solutions to the alumina industry is an area of focus for the company due to the strong fit of Rondo's technology with the heat and power needs of the alumina industry. artigo.texto: Featured Fairfield council calls meeting to discuss data centers Daily Republic Staff Oct 22, 2026 1 hr ago 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save FAIRFIELD — The City Council called for a special meeting Nov. 10 to discuss data centers and possible moratorium on them. The suggestion came during council updates. A Facebook post surfaced late last week saying Vice Mayor Pam Bertani would bring up the topic. Appointed Mayor Rick Vaccaro initiated the conversation. Bertani noted she had prepared a motion for a moratorium. The item will be discussed at 5 p.m. in the Harry T. Price Memorial Council Chamber, 1000 Webster St. Several people were in attendance to support the idea. None supported the idea of a data center. A proposed project, to be built between Vanden Road and North Gate Road, includes a data center. "I'm here to speak on the moratorium," Monte Hoover said. "I am not against date centers in general." As a longtime business owner, Hoover said he has dealt with many issues over the years, such as permit issues, etc. "Data centers have no requirements," he said. Two One Lake residents, where the data center would be located, also asked the city to consider a moratorium on data center development in Fairfield. One man said he feels Fairfield mirrors the sentiment of most cities that don't want data centers near their homes. Gail Mahoney said there is not enough information on data centers and was concerned one would "suck our water away," especially since living through the drought. "We should not rush in," Robert Myers said. artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- Data from the Tianyancha app shows CATL Chery (Wuhu) New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. has officially registered. Capitalized at 1 billion yuan, the entity is jointly held by CATL and Chery Automobile. Corporate filings indicate this is the second joint venture established by the pair in 2026 focused on battery manufacturing, signaling a deeper integration of their industrial chains. Image Source: Tianyancha App The new company’s business scope spans battery manufacturing, the production and sales of components, and energy storage technical services. It will focus on the R&D and manufacturing of power battery-related products. Back in February 2026, the partners had already registered CATL Chery (Hefei) New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. with a registered capital of 2 billion yuan. CATL holds a 51% stake, while Chery Automobile and Chery Commercial Vehicle collectively hold the remaining 49%. With combined registered capital totaling 3 billion yuan, the Hefei and Wuhu joint ventures appear designed to establish a dual power battery footprint in Anhui province. Image Source: CATL The partnership has deep roots. In 2023, CATL and Chery jointly launched the battery brand ENER-Q, with Chery becoming the first to equip its models with sodium-ion batteries. In April 2026, Chery, CATL, CATL Amperex, and Chery Green Energy signed a strategic cooperation agreement to coordinate on the development of chargeable and swappable models and the rollout of battery swapping networks, aiming to advance a vehicle-energy integration ecosystem. This sustained, multi-tiered collaboration is set to secure a stable supply of core products—including Qilin and sodium-ion batteries—for Chery’s new energy models. The two sides are also jointly pushing the commercial application of frontier technologies like semi-solid-state batteries and battery swapping. Establishing joint ventures between automakers and leading battery makers has become a defining model for deep integration in the new energy supply chain. For Chery, this move locks in battery production capacity and mitigates supply chain volatility, underpinning the sales growth of its new energy lineup. CATL, meanwhile, secures a deeper tie with a key OEM, stabilizing order volume and leveraging Anhui’s industrial cluster advantages to expand its share of the power battery and energy storage markets. As these two major joint venture projects advance, the partners are poised to build synergies in both battery costs and the speed of deploying new technologies.

artigo.texto: Aurubis AG Major integrated copper producer and busbar manufacturer According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Silvered Copper Busbars market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The world market for silvered copper busbars is entering a structurally stronger demand phase as electrification, high-frequency power conversion, and renewable energy infrastructure scale through 2035. Silvered copper busbars—copper conductive bars with a silver coating that lowers surface-contact resistance and resists oxidation—are increasingly specified in battery energy storage systems (BESS), electric-vehicle charging infrastructure, semiconductor and RF equipment, and precision industrial automation. IndexBox projects the market to expand at a compound annual growth rate in the range of 5–8% over the 2026–2035 forecast horizon, with the strongest momentum in BESS and EV charging applications, where adoption is accelerating at 12–18% per year. Premium specifications, including controlled silver thickness above 2 µm, ultra-low surface roughness, and tight dimensional tolerances, command a 20–40% price uplift over standard commercial grades and are capturing a growing share of orders from semiconductor and RF equipment sectors. Supply remains concentrated, with roughly 30–40% of global production capacity located in China, while Europe, North America, and parts of Southeast Asia operate smaller but technologically specialized facilities. Import dependence in several large end-use markets exceeds 50%, and qualification bottlenecks for certified suppliers create lead times of 6–14 weeks for qualified material. This report provides a data-driven view of market size, demand architecture, supply structure, trade flows, pricing logic, and competitive positioning, with a transparent analytical definition of product scope and segmentation. The baseline scenario for the world silvered copper busbars market assumes continued electrification of energy and transport systems, steady expansion of renewable generation and storage capacity, and gradual recovery in industrial automation investment through the 2026–2035 forecast period. Under this scenario, global demand is projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate in the range of 5–8%, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to a materially higher level by 2035. Growth is front-loaded in BESS and EV charging infrastructure, where adoption rates of 12–18% per year outpace traditional industrial automation and power-distribution applications. Premium specifications—controlled silver thickness above 2 µm, ultra-low surface roughness, and tight dimensional tolerances—are expected to capture a growing share of orders, particularly from semiconductor and RF equipment sectors, supporting value growth ahead of volume growth. Supply-side constraints remain a key variable: copper and silver together represent 60–75% of direct material cost, and silver spot price volatility of 20–35% in recent years creates margin pressure on fixed-price contracts. Qualification bottlenecks for ISO- and UL-registered busbar coaters, with lead times of 6–14 weeks for qualified material, may cap near-term upside in fast-growing segments. Trade and tariff complexity, including multiple HS code headings and sector-specific certifications, adds procedural friction across borders. Regionally, Asia-Pacific remains the largest consumption and production center, while North America and Europe show above-average growth in BESS and EV charging applications. The baseline assumes no major demand-destroying recession and a gradual easing of silver price volatility as recycling and thrifting reduce silver usage per part by up to 15–20%. Industrial automation and instrumentation represents a mature but steadily expanding demand base for silvered copper busbars. In this segment, busbars are used in control panels, drive systems, programmable logic controllers, and precision measurement instruments where low contact resistance and oxidation resistance are critical for signal integrity and long service life. Current demand is driven by factory automation upgrades, particularly in Asia-Pacific and Europe, where labor cost pressures and quality requirements favor automated production lines. Through 2035, demand-side indicators to watch include industrial robot installations, PLC and drive shipment volumes, and capital expenditure in process industries such as chemicals, food and beverage, and pharmaceuticals. The segment is gradually shifting toward higher-specification busbars as automation equipment becomes more compact and power-dense, requiring tighter dimensional tolerances and improved surface finish. However, growth in this segment is slower than in BESS and EV charging, and price sensitivity is higher, with buyers often qualifying multiple suppliers to maintain competitive pricing. Replacement demand from aging installed systems provides a stable baseline, while new automation projects in emerging markets offer upside. The segment is expected to maintain its position as the largest single application by share, though its relative weight will decline as BESS and EV charging expand faster. Current trend: Steady growth, with increasing specification of silvered busbars in precision control and measurement equipment. artigo.texto: PALO — Google is looking to expand its Iowa footprint through a new data center campus near Palo. Company leaders outlined the project Thursday during a three-hour town hall at the Palo Community Center. More than 200 people attended the event, which marked the company’s first time speaking publicly about the project since Linn County leaders announced Google’s interest in the site last fall. “This is going to be a journey that we do together,” Google representative Eric Murray told the crowd. “We’ve pledged to work with your leadership and communities, and we’re going to be standing by to address your concerns because we are going to be your neighbor.” Google has operated data centers in Iowa since 2007 when it broke ground in Council Bluffs, and the company has a site under construction in southwest Cedar Rapids. The centers are essentially warehouses that store servers and other equipment that support the internet and artificial intelligence. ‘This is going to be a journey that we do together.’ — Google representative Eric Murray Project basics Google wants to build its new data center campus — dubbed Project Meridian — on a roughly 550-acre site at the intersection of Palo Marsh and Power Plant roads. The land is now in unincorporated Linn County, but the company intends to seek annexation into the city of Palo. The site sits along the Cedar River just south of the Duane Arnold Energy Center, which will provide nuclear energy to the campus. Google officials said the 600-megawatt nuclear plant will be the site’s “anchor power supply,” while the river will be its main water source. Technical program manager Kiran Udayakumar said the campus will use a “climate-conscious,” closed-loop evaporative cooling system where water is drawn from the Cedar River, treated and used to keep the campus cool. That water would be used and recirculated anywhere from four to eight times, he said, before being treated at an onsite wastewater treatment plant and discharged back to the Cedar River once it is clean. Water use will be regulated, per state code, by the Iowa Department of Natural Resources. “Whenever we approach a project, we take into consideration the energy-water-carbon nexus,” Udayakumar said. “At evaporative facilities, we see a 10% reduction in water usage … so here, with a healthy water body and very strong flows, we chose a water-cooled facility.” Total water use will depend on the scope of the project, but Google has pledged to replenish 100% of its nationwide data center water use by 2030 through a five-part water stewardship framework. The company already publicly reports its water use each year, broken down by data center location. The company hopes to begin construction of its data centers in early 2027, Murray said, with Phase 1 operations tentatively slated to begin in mid- to late 2028. The project would be phased over time, with each phase including one data center building. The number of buildings will depend on market demand factors, but the site could hold as many as six. Each facility would be one-story tall warehouses that take up anywhere from 280,000 to 300,000 square feet. What can Cedar Rapids learn from other Iowa cities with data centers? Big names like Google, Microsoft have been in the state for years. Here’s what The Gazette found out. The site is expected to support at least 180 permanent jobs and thousands of temporary construction roles over the course of the project and generate an estimated $170 million in local property taxes over 20 years. Palo leaders already have stated no tax breaks will be given to the company, meaning those funds will go directly to the city, county, school district and other taxing entities. Asked/answered The bulk of Thursday’s meeting was dedicated to answering attendees’ questions — first through a moderated Q&A and then through a set of science-fair style tables people could visit to learn more about specific topics. Most of the audience questions — submitted via digital QR code or on hand-written notecards — revolved around the project’s resource demands and the impact it could have on the surrounding community. Can the Cedar River sustain the water use needed to support the campus? According to Udayakumar, yes. Will the project drive up residential electric bills? No, said Allen Gleckner, a member of Google's Upper Midwest energy team, who stressed that the company pays for all its own energy and the infrastructure needed to supply it. Will surrounding residents be able to hear any sort of hum or other noise from the daily operations? Maybe, but not much. “If you’re standing right by the buildings, you’re going to experience noise that’s like the air conditioner at your house,” environmental health consultant Chris Ollson said. “The good news for you folks is that the city of Palo has an ordinance with a bunch of guardrails.” That ordinance — passed by Palo City Council members in July — outlines maximum noise levels of 55 dBA as measured from the outer wall of any occupied structure in an adjacent area zoned residential, or 65 dBA for areas those zoned otherwise. The code language was similar to that drafted by Linn County as part of its own data center ordinance, which looked to limit sound pollution among other factors. For reference, 55 to 65 dBA is considered to be moderate ambient noise. “If you’re actually in the city of Palo itself or south of that, you’re not going to hear this data center at all,” Ollson said. “If you get closer, I’m not going to say you’re never going to hear it, but it’s not going to be the level of noise where you can’t throw a football around in your yard with the kids or carry on with other normal activities.” Google representatives also fielded questions about road use impacts and traffic, job creation and community partnerships, among other topics. artigo.texto: BYD's Overseas Battery Surge Meets a 350,000-Vehicle Ceiling in Europe Published on 10/21/2026 at 05:11 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD's expansion story is running on two tracks that don't move in step. New figures show its battery installations outside China climbing sharply, while at home the volume and market share both slipped. On the vehicle side, a fresh trade understanding between Brussels and Beijing has put a number on how many hybrids can flow into Europe each year. A tale of two battery markets Data from SNE Research cited in an October 15 report put BYD's overseas battery installations at 39.7 GWh for the period covered — a 66.5% jump on the same stretch a year earlier. That growth stands in contrast to a softer home market, though it says nothing about how many cars BYD is shipping abroad. The distinction matters: a strong battery business does not by itself answer questions about vehicle demand. Inside China, installations reached 106.44 GWh, down 4.3% year on year, with a market share of 18.53%. The domestic share fell 4.04 percentage points. So both the installed volume and the relative position weakened at home, even as the overseas picture brightened — the regional split within the battery unit is widening. Europe sets a hard limit The vehicle business faces a different set of constraints. On October 13, BYD shares came under pressure as investors weighed export prospects and margins after the European Union and China agreed to cap Chinese hybrid imports. Reuters reported an annual ceiling of 350,000 vehicles. On top of that, Beijing plans to cut the export tax rebate for alternative-drive vehicles from 13% to 9%. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? The two measures bite in different places. The import cap limits access to the European market by volume; the lower rebate sits behind the margin concerns that were reported. Neither figure, on its own, allows a specific earnings impact for BYD to be calculated. Malaysia: a partner named, a start date missing In Southeast Asia, BYD is pushing local assembly and distribution forward on several fronts. BYD Malaysia named Inokom in Kulim as its assembly partner on Thursday, a deal covering local assembly from shipped vehicle kits — an extension of BYD's Malaysian activities beyond sales, though not evidence that production has begun. No model has been fixed and no start date confirmed, so the economic contribution remains an open question. Distribution is further along. A new outlet opened yesterday in Rawang, Selangor, operated by BE Autohaus — another BYD site for the BE Group after Setia Alam and Kota Kemuning. BYD Sime Motors runs 45 sales and marketing outlets nationwide, 33 service facilities and 16 body-and-paint centres, so the new location slots into a network covering both vehicle sales and after-sales care. An opening promotion in Rawang runs from 19 to 30 October 2026, with test drives and offers on selected models. BYD at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. Philippines: tariff relief, currency drag On the Philippines, BYD is backing an extension of duty-free EV imports through 2040; under the existing rule the exemption ends in 2028. The terms for imported vehicles therefore remain a key variable for regional expansion. AB Capital Securities also flags a weak peso as a possible risk to import costs and margins — growing sales and a broader dealer network don't erase such pressures on their own. Ayala/BYD sales reached 28,399 vehicles through August 2026, already ahead of the full-year 2025 total. The pieces of BYD's Southeast Asian build-out are tangible but unevenly advanced. In the Philippines, sales sit alongside an unresolved tariff question. In Malaysia, the retail network is growing while local assembly waits on specifics about model and production timing. What counts for investors is not the tally of new locations but whether they turn into durable business. Ad BYD Stock: New Analysis - 21 October Fresh BYD information released. What's the impact for investors? Our latest independent report examines recent figures and market trends.

artigo.texto: Clifford Chance advises Vattenfall on battery storage tolling agreement with Royal Vopak 21 October 2026 Clifford Chance advises Vattenfall on battery storage tolling agreement with Royal Vopak Global law firm Clifford Chance has advised Vattenfall on a tolling agreement with Royal Vopak (Vopak) for a portion of a planned battery energy storage system near Meeden in the province of Groningen, the Netherlands. Under the agreement, Vattenfall will have access to 100 MW / 400 MWh of battery storage capacity, helping to balance fluctuations in electricity supply and demand. Vopak will develop and operate the battery energy storage system, which will have a total capacity of 150 MW and a storage duration of four hours. Commercial operations are expected to begin in the second quarter of 2028. The agreement supports Vattenfall’s goal of contracting at least 1.5 GW of battery capacity across its core markets and Vopak's expansion into electrical energy storage infrastructure. Read more about the transaction here. The Clifford Chance team consisted of associate Niels Kuil, partner Liesbeth Buiter and senior associate Johanneke Butijn. Press contact: Iva Celic

artigo.texto: A explosão da inteligência artificial está acelerando uma corrida global pela construção de data centers, enormes complexos que armazenam e processam os dados que sustentam desde pesquisas na internet até ferramentas avançadas de IA. Mas, para quem vive ao lado dessas estruturas, o avanço tecnológico também tem trazido preocupações. Em uma reportagem exibida pelo Fantástico, moradores do condado de Loudoun, na Virgínia, nos Estados Unidos, relataram os impactos provocados pela expansão dos data centers na região que concentra o maior número dessas instalações no mundo. São mais de 200 unidades e, segundo a reportagem, há 16 anos não passa um único dia sem que algum novo centro de processamento esteja em construção. Considerados a infraestrutura física por trás da inteligência artificial, os data centers dependem de enormes quantidades de energia e água para manter milhares de computadores funcionando sem superaquecimento. À medida que novos empreendimentos avançam, essas estruturas vêm se aproximando cada vez mais das áreas residenciais. Barulho constante e fumaça Entre os moradores afetados estão Lindsay, Greg e Jessica, que vivem em frente a um complexo construído onde antes existia uma área verde. Eles afirmam que a realidade do bairro mudou completamente desde 2022. Segundo os relatos, o empreendimento opera de forma diferente de outros da região porque gera a própria energia, utilizando oito turbinas movidas a gás natural e dezenas de geradores a diesel para emergências. O resultado é um ruído permanente que passou a fazer parte da rotina dos moradores. "Você ouve esse zumbido? É constante", relata uma das residentes. Ela também afirma que, quando os geradores entram em funcionamento, é possível ver fumaça escura saindo das instalações. "E a gente pensa: meu Deus, o que tem nessa fumaça?" Outra moradora afirma que o impacto vai além do barulho. "Quando você sai, sente o gosto de diesel no ar", diz. Uma terceira relatou que precisou deixar a própria casa após os geradores de emergência funcionarem durante 24 horas seguidas. "Eu tive que sair de casa e ir para a casa da minha filha, a uns 25 quilômetros daqui." Preocupação com saúde e energia A reportagem mostra que especialistas também acompanham os possíveis impactos ambientais dessas operações. Um estudo citado pelo programa, elaborado por um pesquisador de Harvard, estima que a poluição gerada por um dos data centers da região pode representar custos de até US$ 99 milhões por ano associados a internações e mortes prematuras. Além das emissões, o crescimento acelerado dos data centers tem aumentado a demanda por energia elétrica. Segundo organizações ambientais locais, a expansão prevista exigirá grandes investimentos em infraestrutura de transmissão e a construção de novas linhas de alta tensão cruzando o estado da Virgínia. Torres de energia dividem moradores Uma das moradoras que lideram a resistência aos projetos é Vicky Woo, que vive na região há mais de duas décadas. Hoje, ela trava uma batalha judicial contra a companhia elétrica local, que pretende instalar uma torre de transmissão a menos de 15 metros de sua residência. "Estamos dentro da área de queda. Se uma torre de 56 metros cai numa tempestade, ela atinge tudo nesse raio. Quem vai assumir a responsabilidade?", questiona. Vicky também marca com fitas rosas as árvores que poderão ser derrubadas para a implantação do projeto. Para ela, o problema não é a existência dos data centers em si, mas a proximidade das estruturas com as áreas residenciais. "A gente não é contra data center. É que esse nunca deveria ter sido construído tão perto das casas." Debate que chega ao Brasil A discussão não se limita aos Estados Unidos. O Fantástico destaca que o Brasil aprovou recentemente o programa Redata, que oferece incentivos fiscais para atrair investimentos em data centers. Pela legislação, as empresas devem utilizar energia renovável ou de baixa emissão e reduzir o consumo de água no resfriamento dos equipamentos. No entanto, questões como distância mínima de áreas residenciais, controle de ruído e emissões atmosféricas ainda não foram detalhadas e dependem de regulamentação futura, segundo especialistas ouvidos pela reportagem. Enquanto governos e empresas discutem o futuro da inteligência artificial, moradores de regiões como Loudoun convivem diariamente com as consequências dessa transformação. "Tenho quatro netos e me preocupo com o futuro. Que mundo eu vou deixar para eles?", questiona uma das residentes. artigo.texto: BEIJING, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI’s strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL’s dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI’s standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery’s depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold, CATL’s seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - “1+X” Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a “1+X” architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns. CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models: Battery Asset Service Partners and Energy Replenishment Service Partners. These models allow partners to participate in battery asset services and energy replenishment, extending their role beyond one-off vehicle sales to ongoing operations. artigo.texto: Data centers have become a major campaign topic in Ohio, as the industry transforms from a tech issue into a political one, with the governor's race now a toss-up. Republican Vivek Ramaswamy told our partners at the Journal News he would sell stock connected to data center industries if elected governor. His opponent, Democrat Amy Acton, says she has already sold her individual stocks. With the midterms just over a week away, the issue is becoming a political test for both candidates. WATCH: Your photos. Your emails. That AI chatbot you ask questions all day. It all lives in a data center. And as AI drives demand for more of them, data centers have gone from a tech issue to a political one. Across Ohio, massive data center projects are fueling debates over electricity, water, and who should foot the bill. And with just two weeks left in the Ohio governor's race, the issue is putting both candidates on the spot. David Niven, a University of Cincinnati political science professor, says the issue presents a particular challenge for Ramaswamy. "I think it does present a problem for Ramaswamy not only because he's spoken out in favor of data centers, but because his background is as a biotech billionaire. It's not particularly easy for him to connect with the average Ohioan who fears that a data center might go up in their community and fears the cost of that in quality of life and utility bills," Niven said. Ohio now ranks among the top states for data centers, with about 240 operating statewide. Both Acton and Ramaswamy say they want more oversight of the industry. Acton's running mate, David Pepper, says ratepayers shouldn't be left holding the bag. "Nobody should have to pay a dollar more on anything because the data centers are moving in. That should be an absolute baseline," Pepper said. Ramaswamy, who has generally been more supportive of the industry, says he's open to regulating resource usage. "I am against you and the people of this state having to pay for them. If you are going to use electricity from the electric grid, you should have to pay for it and bring your own energy," Ramaswamy said. The concerns on the campaign trail are fueled by the advocacy of voters from more rural areas like Wilmington. "Nobody told us that this was going on, the land had been rezoned, that any of this was in the works!" Jessica Sharp said. In Mount Orab, residents have voiced similar frustration. "This is ridiculous!" one resident said. And in Trenton, the opposition has been just as direct. "Right now, I'm a hard no!" Hubert said. Even in urban Cincinnati, residents are raising questions. "The Data Center Coalition of Ohio wants to make Ohio the Silicon Valley of the Midwest. They want to make us the largest data center state there is. And I don't know if everybody wants to co-sign to that," Cincinnati resident Kaylee Baker said. With the Cook Political Report now rating the Ohio governor's race a toss-up, experts say cost-of-living concerns are driving voters. And in a rare moment of agreement, opposition to data centers is emerging as an issue attracting both Democrats and Republicans. "It's been a significant political issue because it's created this sense of unease. Normally folks think about development as a source of great job growth. You build an auto plant and thousands of people are employed. You build a data center; there might be 10 people employed," Niven said. artigo.texto: The Hyderabad-based engineering, procurement and construction company has landed a mandate from a Gujarat utility, pushing it deeper into long-duration energy storage. The order lands next to a strong June quarter, so the real questions now are about margins, execution and how quickly this new line can grow from here. The Nifty 50 closed at 22,687.65, down 0.54%, while the Sensex fell 0.62% to 73,249.39 on Thursday. Following this the Shares of BONDADA ENGINEERING LtdCLOSED at Rs. 275.00, up 0.18 percent on Thursday. The stock touched the intraday high of Rs. 277.00 after opening at Rs. 274.20 before slipping to a low of Rs. 270.00. The company commands a market capitalization of Rs. 3,070.97 crore. Also Read: Havells India Q2 FY27: revenue up 34.6% YoY to ₹6,431.99 Cr; net profit rises to ₹349.22 Cr Bondada Lands a Big Battery Storage Contract Bondada Engineering Limited has received a Letter of Intent from Gujarat Industries Power Company for a 20 MW/120 MWh vanadium redox flow battery storage system. The package covers engineering, procurement and construction, along with ten years of operations and maintenance, at the utility’s 165 MW gas-based power complex in Vadodara. Work must finish within 18 months of the notification of award. The company describes it as India’s largest grid-scale project of its kind. It told BSE on October 22 that neither promoters nor group firms hold any interest in the customer, and that the deal is not a related-party transaction. What the Order Could Mean for Bondada For Bondada, the order opens a door into long-duration energy storage, a different game from its usual renewable EPC work. The ten-year maintenance piece matters too, since it brings recurring service income after construction ends and could steady revenue over time. A marquee project like this may also help when other utilities weigh storage bids. Rivals will likely notice that a listed EPC player now has a reference project to point to. Execution is the catch, because vanadium flow technology is still young in India at this scale. The contract value was not disclosed, so the effect on earnings is hard to size for now. With an 18-month schedule, revenue will probably be booked in stages rather than all at once. The company walks into this phase with decent momentum after a 29.3 percent jump in quarterly profit. Order value, margins and delivery milestones will be the things to watch in coming filings. Any slippage in delivery could dent margins, so timelines deserve as much attention as the headline number. How the Company Performed in the June Quarter Looking at the quarterly results of Bondada Engineering Limited, the company’s consolidated revenue from operations increased by 24.0 percent YOY, from Rs. 557.83 crore in Q1 FY26 to Rs. 691.65 crore in Q1 FY27, but fell 24.3 percent QoQ from Rs. 913.85 crore in Q4 FY26. Bondada Engineering Limited generated 86.8 percent of its revenue from EPC, 7.3 percent from services and 6.0 percent from products in Q1 FY27. In Q1 FY27, the consolidated net profit increased by 29.3 percent YOY, reaching Rs. 53.94 crore compared to Rs. 41.71 crore during the same period last year. Against Q4 FY26, net profit slipped 14.2 percent from Rs. 62.88 crore. The basic earnings per share increased by 37.0 percent and stood at Rs. 4.74 as against Rs. 3.46 recorded in the same quarter of the previous year, FY2026. About Bondada Engineering Bondada Engineering Limited, based in Hyderabad, is an engineering, procurement and construction company focused mainly on renewable energy and infrastructure. It reports three segments: EPC, services and products. The group has 12 subsidiaries, among them Bondada Renewable Energy, Speck Systems, and Bondada Hindupur BESS Projects. Formerly Bondada Engineering Private Limited, it trades on BSE under scrip code 543971 as BONDADA.

artigo.texto: Projeto cria indicador para calcular custo de restauração ambiental e crédito de carbono em Maringá A Câmara de Maringá aprovou em primeira discussão, na sessão desta quinta-feira, 22, um projeto de lei do Executivo que cria o Valor de Referência de Restauração Ambiental e Crédito de Carbono (VRRCC). O indicador será usado como parâmetro técnico para avaliar projetos ambientais, investimentos que reduzam a emissão de gases de efeito estufa e custos de ações de restauração ecológica no município. A proposta atribui ao Instituto Ambiental de Maringá (IAM) a responsabilidade de definir a metodologia de cálculo, estabelecer o valor inicial e atualizar periodicamente o indicador. A medida busca criar uma referência econômica para estimar quanto custa capturar carbono por meio de ações de recuperação ambiental. Custos e estudos científicos De acordo com o projeto, o cálculo do VRRCC deverá considerar os custos médios de restauração ambiental, com base em contratos públicos, atas de registro de preços e composições de custos disponíveis, além de estimativas científicas sobre a capacidade de captura de carbono das ações de recuperação ecológica. O resultado será expresso em reais por tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (R$/tCO₂e), unidade utilizada para mensurar o custo relacionado à redução ou captura de gases de efeito estufa. O IAM terá prazo de 90 dias, contados da publicação da lei, para estabelecer o valor inicial e divulgar a metodologia por meio de portaria, acompanhada de um memorial de cálculo com as fontes e os critérios utilizados. - Entre no canal do GMC Online no Instagram - Acompanhe o GMC Online no Instagram - Clique aqui e receba as nossas notícias pelo WhatsApp Orientar obras e contratações O VRRCC poderá subsidiar estudos técnicos, projetos ambientais e climáticos, análises de viabilidade econômica e avaliações de custo-benefício ambiental em obras, serviços e contratações públicas. O indicador também poderá servir de referência para programas de restauração ecológica, arborização urbana e mitigação das mudanças climáticas, além de auxiliar na análise de tecnologias e materiais com menor impacto ambiental. A proposta prevê ainda que o parâmetro possa justificar a escolha de soluções com melhor desempenho ambiental, mesmo quando apresentarem custo inicial mais elevado. Para isso, o benefício ambiental ou climático deverá ser demonstrado em processo administrativo, respeitando a legislação de contratações públicas. Atualização a cada dois anos O valor de referência será atualizado pelo IAM conforme a variação dos custos de restauração, a evolução dos estudos científicos sobre captura de carbono e os dados obtidos em contratos e projetos ambientais executados no município. A revisão deverá ocorrer sempre que os custos ou parâmetros técnicos apresentarem variação igual ou superior a 10%, quando houver justificativa técnica para mudança e, obrigatoriamente, pelo menos a cada dois anos. O valor vigente e os respectivos parâmetros deverão ser publicados no Diário Oficial do Município em até 30 dias após a edição do ato de fixação ou atualização. O projeto estabelece que o VRRCC terá caráter exclusivamente referencial e orientativo. Portanto, não será uma tarifa obrigatória nem um valor vinculante, e sua aplicação deverá considerar as características de cada caso e a legislação vigente.

artigo.texto: O Piauí deu mais um passo para a implantação de sua política de crédito de carbono. Nesta terça-feira (20), foi realizada, no Centro de Educação Ambiental (CEA), em Teresina, a primeira reunião do Conselho Gestor do REDD+(Redução de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa provenientes do Desmatamento e da Degradação Florestal), iniciativa voltada à redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa provenientes do desmatamento e da degradação florestal. O conselho reúne representantes do poder público, da sociedade civil, da academia, dos povos indígenas, das comunidades quilombolas e tradicionais, da agricultura familiar e do setor produtivo. A proposta é garantir participação social, transparência e segurança na construção do projeto, que poderá gerar recursos para a conservação ambiental e beneficiar as populações que contribuem para a proteção das florestas. O secretário do Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos, Feliphe Araújo, destacou que a implantação do projeto é uma das prioridades da gestão e ressaltou a importância de construir uma política regulamentada, com participação da sociedade. “Queremos proteger nossas florestas e, ao mesmo tempo, gerar recursos para beneficiar as pessoas que ajudam a preservar o meio ambiente. Por isso, é fundamental que esse processo seja construído com diálogo, transparência e participação de todos os setores”, afirmou. Segundo o secretário, o Estado já avançou na elaboração de normas, na regulamentação da iniciativa e na busca de parceiros para viabilizar o projeto. A experiência de outros estados, como o Tocantins, também serve de referência para acelerar as etapas necessárias à implantação da política no Piauí. Feliphe Araújo ressaltou ainda que a preservação ambiental precisa caminhar junto com o desenvolvimento econômico. Ele citou ações de recuperação de áreas degradadas, educação ambiental, fiscalização e prevenção e combate aos incêndios florestais como medidas complementares para reduzir os impactos ambientais. O modelo de Redução de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa provenientes do Desmatamento e da Degradação Florestal (REDD+) poderá viabilizar mecanismos de pagamento por serviços ambientais, com benefícios para povos indígenas, comunidades quilombolas, populações tradicionais e agricultores familiares, além de contribuir para a conservação dos biomas piauienses. A criação e o funcionamento do conselho representam uma etapa importante para consolidar a governança do projeto, assegurando que as decisões sejam discutidas coletivamente e que a política de crédito de carbono seja construída com responsabilidade ambiental e participação social.

artigo.texto: A inteligência artificial depende de uma infraestrutura física capaz de processar grandes volumes de dados continuamente. Por trás de cada consulta a um chatbot, geração de imagem ou aplicação corporativa de IA, existem servidores executando operações computacionais que consomem energia e geram calor. À medida que essas operações se tornam mais exigentes, a densidade computacional dos Data Centers aumenta. Isso significa que mais capacidade de processamento pode ser concentrada em um mesmo espaço, elevando a carga térmica que precisa ser controlada para manter os equipamentos dentro das condições adequadas de operação. O desafio não se resume a evitar o superaquecimento. A infraestrutura precisa acompanhar a demanda computacional, controlar o consumo de energia e manter condições operacionais estáveis, inclusive em ambientes que funcionam ininterruptamente. Por isso, o resfriamento passou a ocupar uma posição estratégica no planejamento e na expansão dos Data Centers. Fabricantes como a LG Electronics desenvolvem soluções de resfriamento para acompanhar essas novas exigências de eficiência e confiabilidade. O que é um chiller em um Data Center? Um chiller é um equipamento de refrigeração que remove calor de um circuito de água ou de outro fluido utilizado no sistema de climatização. Em instalações de grande porte, ele pode integrar a infraestrutura responsável por retirar o calor dos ambientes e dos equipamentos de TI, conforme a arquitetura de resfriamento adotada. Em um sistema tradicional com água gelada, por exemplo, o chiller resfria a água que circula pelo sistema. Essa água absorve o calor em pontos de troca térmica e retorna ao equipamento para que o ciclo continue. Existem diferentes configurações de chillers, que variam conforme a capacidade, o método de rejeição de calor e as necessidades da instalação. A escolha depende de fatores como densidade computacional, condições climáticas, espaço disponível, demanda energética e requisitos de disponibilidade. Em Data Centers de IA, esse dimensionamento ganha importância porque a infraestrutura de resfriamento precisa responder à carga térmica existente e acompanhar possíveis aumentos na capacidade de processamento. Como chillers ajudam a manter a operação dos Data Centers? O resfriamento integra uma cadeia de sistemas que precisam funcionar de maneira coordenada. Se a capacidade de retirar calor não acompanhar a demanda, a instalação pode precisar limitar o desempenho dos equipamentos ou adotar medidas operacionais para preservar as condições de funcionamento. Por isso, o projeto de cooling considera tanto a capacidade térmica quanto a confiabilidade dos componentes, as estratégias de redundância e a possibilidade de expansão. Em instalações críticas, a continuidade do resfriamento é especialmente relevante: uma interrupção no fornecimento de energia, por exemplo, exige que os sistemas retomem suas funções de acordo com os requisitos operacionais do Data Center. Outro aspecto é o consumo energético. A refrigeração representa uma parcela da energia utilizada por essas instalações, embora seu peso varie conforme o projeto, o clima, a carga de TI e as tecnologias empregadas. Melhorar a eficiência do sistema de resfriamento pode contribuir para reduzir a energia necessária à operação da infraestrutura. Quais tecnologias estão mudando o resfriamento de Data Centers? A evolução dos chillers envolve diferentes frentes tecnológicas. Entre elas estão os compressores mais eficientes, sistemas de controle inteligentes, arquiteturas modulares e recursos que aproveitam as condições ambientais para reduzir o trabalho mecânico de refrigeração. O free-cooling é um exemplo. Dependendo da configuração do sistema e das condições externas, essa estratégia permite utilizar o ambiente para auxiliar na remoção de calor, reduzindo a necessidade de refrigeração mecânica em determinadas situações. O resultado depende de fatores como temperatura ambiente, projeto da instalação e regime de operação. Também há avanços nos sistemas de monitoramento e diagnóstico. Com dados operacionais integrados, equipes de engenharia e facilities podem acompanhar o funcionamento dos equipamentos, identificar desvios e avaliar oportunidades de otimização. A inteligência desses sistemas ajuda a transformar o acompanhamento da infraestrutura em uma atividade mais orientada por dados. A modularidade é outra característica relevante, pois permite planejar a capacidade de acordo com as necessidades da instalação e simplificar etapas de implementação e expansão. Para Data Centers que precisam acompanhar a evolução da IA, essa flexibilidade pode facilitar o planejamento de longo prazo. Como a LG está desenvolvendo soluções para esse cenário? É nesse contexto que a LG Electronics apresenta o LG Air-Cooled Centrifugal Chiller (ACC), desenvolvido para aplicações de grande porte, incluindo a infraestrutura de resfriamento de Data Centers. O equipamento combina compressor centrífugo com mancal magnético e operação oil-free, ou seja, sem óleo no sistema de mancais do compressor. Essa arquitetura dispensa a lubrificação por óleo nesse conjunto, característica que integra a proposta tecnológica do equipamento. O ACC também incorpora a tecnologia refrigerant free-cooling, voltada ao aproveitamento de condições favoráveis para auxiliar o processo de resfriamento. A aplicação desse recurso depende das condições ambientais e operacionais, assim como do projeto da instalação. Outro destaque é a capacidade de recuperação após uma interrupção de energia. Conforme as condições de teste informadas pela fabricante, o equipamento pode restabelecer sua capacidade total de resfriamento em até três minutos após o retorno da energia. Esse intervalo deve ser considerado dentro das condições específicas de operação do sistema, e não como uma garantia de retomada integral de todo o Data Center. artigo.texto: COLUMBIA — Columbia's Planning and Zoning Commission met on Thursday to review Columbia residents' responses and feedback on data centers. A total of 142 Columbia residents took the two-hour virtual dialogue. The survey took note of respondents' political parties and ethnicities, but it grouped together a general percentage for the people who show support between the groups using what they called a bridge. While the plans might not mirror the input from citizens, the survey data is still important to take into account, said Patrick Zenner, Columbia's development services manager. "We will be providing back an opportunity for the public to again comment on regulation that we develop, which will hopefully be representative of what their comments were," Zenner said. "It may not be identical, but it will include concepts and ideas." How respondents felt about data centers in Columbia The respondents' viewpoints on data centers in Columbia were split into three categories based on the 23 questions that were asked: ban, permit and incentivize. Forty-three percent of those surveyed said Columbia should ban new data centers outright, even if that means turning away potential jobs and investment, and even if it invites a legal challenge the city might not win. Thirty-nine percent said Columbia should not offer financial incentives but should welcome data centers under strong new standards on utility service terms and pollution, even though no set of standards fully removes the risk to nearby neighborhoods. Eighteen percent said Columbia should incentivize data centers to build in the city as long as data centers meet environmental standards and commit significant investments in Columbia, such as improving city infrastructure or funding local schools. Other findings from the survey A majority of respondents said residents should have a formal role in deciding how data centers operate in Columbia — not just city staff and elected officials. About 88% said they believed residents should not have to pay for the new infrastructure. Around 85% of respondents favored a recycled water requirement, and 79% favored noise limits with independent testing. Sixty-two percent of respondents said the money paid to the city by data centers should first be spent on reducing the effects Columbia neighborhoods experience before any of it is spent citywide. Sixty percent were in favor of safe distance standards, meaning a data center must sit far enough from homes, schools, daycares, hospitals and community centers. It must also meet the city's noise limit at the property line but never be closer than 1,000 feet away. Almost all respondents said there should be full transparency with any written non-disclosure agreement, confidentiality or private commitment between a data center and any city official or employee, including the Water and Light Board. A full list of the questions and responses can be found on the city's website. The next step for data centers in Columbia is for the Planning Commission to conduct a survey over what it has been discussing for the past six months and review the survey results in January.

artigo.texto: AI's Fragmented Regulatory Landscape Becomes a Data Center Design Challenge Key Highlights - Global AI infrastructure expansion faces mounting challenges from fragmented regulatory requirements, power constraints, and supply chain pressures. - U.S. federal initiatives aim to accelerate data center development, but electricity costs, state regulations, and community opposition remain significant obstacles. - The EU AI Act, UN governance initiatives, and competing U.S.-China approaches are creating different expectations for AI infrastructure and its operation. - Data center operators serving international customers must establish clear contractual responsibilities and verifiable controls for security, workload location, data handling, and access. - Delivering usable AI capacity increasingly requires more than energized infrastructure: developers must demonstrate operational readiness, documented controls, and clear compliance responsibilities. AI infrastructure is expanding across a world increasingly divided over how the technology should be regulated. For data center developers and operators, that fragmentation introduces a challenge beyond securing power, deploying compute, and bringing facilities online: ensuring that the resulting infrastructure can support workloads governed by different legal, security, and contractual requirements. The scale of the buildout makes these distinctions increasingly consequential. According to the International Energy Agency, global data center electricity demand rose 17% in 2025, while consumption at AI-focused facilities increased 50%. The agency projects total data center electricity consumption will reach roughly 950 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2030, nearly double its 2025 level of 485 TWh. Even so, grid constraints, equipment shortages, chip availability, and financing challenges threaten to delay projects, leaving substantial uncertainty over how much announced capacity will actually reach service. At the same time, the regulatory environment is becoming more complex rather than more uniform. The European Union is implementing binding AI rules, the United States is pursuing policies to accelerate domestic infrastructure development, and competing international initiatives are taking shape around AI governance and supply-chain security. Although these measures impose very different obligations, their combined effect is to make verifiable operating controls, clear contractual responsibilities, and jurisdiction-specific requirements increasingly important in delivering AI infrastructure. PBS examines how the rapid expansion of AI data centers is intensifying disputes over electricity, water and the costs borne by host communities. U.S. Policy Meets Local Development Constraints In the United States, the Trump administration has made faster data center development a federal policy goal. Its AI Action Plan calls for accelerated infrastructure permitting, a grid prepared to support AI growth, and more secure facilities for sensitive military, government, and intelligence workloads. A July 2025 executive order, Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure, gives federal agencies a more specific assignment: identify ways to expedite reviews and support qualifying data center projects and their supporting infrastructure. Under the order, projects can qualify through several routes, including committed capital expenditures of at least $500 million or an incremental electrical load greater than 100 MW. The order directs agencies to examine environmental review procedures, consider eligible projects for federal permitting schedules, and identify suitable federal land. It also covers supporting infrastructure such as transmission lines, substations, transformers, and switchgear, extending the permitting initiative beyond the data center campus to the electrical systems needed to serve it. These measures create opportunities to accelerate federal reviews, but do not eliminate other applicable approvals or guarantee that a project can proceed. The White House's Ratepayer Protection Pledge, introduced in March 2026, addresses another constraint: who pays for the electricity and grid infrastructure required by large data centers. Participating companies committed to build, bring, or buy the power needed for their facilities, cover required delivery upgrades, and negotiate separate rate structures under which they pay for electricity and infrastructure brought online to serve them, even if actual consumption falls below projections. The pledge remains voluntary, with its practical effect dependent on agreements among developers, utilities, and state authorities. Congress has pursued related legislation. On September 16, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417–3 vote, although the measure subsequently failed to advance in the Senate on September 30. If enacted, the legislation would require state utility regulators to consider standards for assigning the incremental costs of generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades to large-load customers. It would not require states to adopt those standards. The distinction underscores how much responsibility for translating federal energy policy into enforceable arrangements still resides with state regulators and utilities. A separate December 11, 2025 executive order, Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence, targeted the growing patchwork of state AI regulations. It directed the Justice Department to establish an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws the administration considers inconsistent with federal policy, while calling for a legislative proposal establishing a more uniform national framework. Significantly for data center developers, the order specified that such legislation should not preempt otherwise lawful state laws concerning AI compute and data center infrastructure, except for generally applicable permitting reforms.
