artigo.texto: Mercado global de condicionadores de energia para células a combustível: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de condicionadores de energia para células a combustível até 2035, impulsionada pela demanda dos data centers por energia de backup confiável Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de condicionadores de energia para células a combustível, o setor inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de condicionadores de energia para células a combustível entra em uma fase de desenvolvimento acelerado, à medida que a economia do hidrogênio avança de programas-piloto para a implantação em escala comercial. Esses dispositivos especializados de eletrônica de potência, que convertem a saída variável de corrente contínua dos stacks de células a combustível em energia CA estável e compatível com a rede ou em energia CC regulada, tornaram-se viabilizadores essenciais da eficiência, da confiabilidade e da viabilidade econômica dos sistemas. A análise de mercado de 2026 revela uma indústria que vai além das aplicações de nicho em backup e caminha para uma integração mais ampla na geração estacionária de energia, na mobilidade de uso pesado e nos sistemas de energia distribuída. O crescimento é sustentado, em sua base, por metas globais rigorosas de descarbonização, que se traduzem em apoio político concreto e em investimentos na infraestrutura de hidrogênio. Os avanços tecnológicos tanto nos stacks de células a combustível quanto na eletrônica de potência impulsionam melhorias em densidade de potência, eficiência de conversão e durabilidade dos condicionadores de energia, reduzindo assim o custo total de propriedade. O cenário competitivo reúne empresas especializadas em eletrônica de potência, conglomerados industriais diversificados e uma integração vertical crescente por parte dos principais integradores de sistemas de células a combustível, que buscam controlar esse subsistema crítico. O período de previsão até 2035 projeta uma trajetória de mercado fortemente influenciada pela escala de produção, pela padronização de plataformas e pela comercialização bem-sucedida das aplicações de células a combustível de próxima geração. A dinâmica regional será decisiva: a Ásia-Pacífico consolida sua liderança em fabricação e implantação, enquanto a América do Norte e a Europa se concentram em inovação tecnológica e aplicações de alto valor. Este relatório oferece uma análise abrangente e baseada em dados do estado atual do mercado, do equilíbrio entre oferta e demanda, dos mecanismos de preço e das forças competitivas, culminando em uma perspectiva estratégica que identifica os principais desafios e oportunidades para os agentes de toda a cadeia de valor. O cenário de referência para o mercado mundial de condicionadores de energia para células a combustível até 2035 prevê uma expansão robusta, com o índice de mercado subindo de 100 em 2025 para um patamar substancialmente mais alto em 2035. Essa trajetória é sustentada pela aceleração da transição energética global e pelo amadurecimento dos roteiros da economia do hidrogênio nas principais economias. Espera-se que a demanda se acelere sobretudo após 2028, à medida que as implantações de células a combustível ganhem escala em geração estacionária, data centers e transporte de uso pesado. O cenário de referência pressupõe a continuidade do apoio político, incluindo subsídios e mecanismos de precificação de carbono, além da queda dos custos dos stacks de células a combustível e da eletrônica de potência. Os avanços tecnológicos impulsionarão melhorias em eficiência de conversão, densidade de potência e conformidade com a rede, ampliando a bancabilidade das instalações de células a combustível. O cenário competitivo registrará maior integração vertical por parte dos integradores de sistemas e consolidação entre os fabricantes de eletrônica de potência. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico manterá sua participação dominante, liderada por China, Japão e Coreia do Sul, enquanto a América do Norte e a Europa se concentrarão em aplicações de alto valor e inovação tecnológica. A América Latina e o Oriente Médio e África terão adoção gradual, principalmente em aplicações remotas e isoladas da rede. Os principais riscos para o cenário de referência incluem restrições na cadeia de suprimentos de componentes críticos, como módulos IGBT, a expansão da infraestrutura de hidrogênio mais lenta do que o esperado e atrasos regulatórios. Ainda assim, a perspectiva geral permanece positiva, com previsão de taxa de crescimento anual composta (CAGR) de 12,5% entre 2026 e 2035, impulsionada pelo imperativo de descarbonizar os setores de energia e mobilidade. Vetores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Vetores de Demanda - Aumento da demanda por energia de backup confiável em data centers e telecomunicações - Metas globais de descarbonização e roteiros da economia do hidrogênio impulsionando implantações de células a combustível - Avanços tecnológicos que melhoram a eficiência dos condicionadores de energia e a conformidade com a rede - Crescimento do transporte de uso pesado e da infraestrutura de veículos elétricos a célula a combustível (FCEV), que exige eletrônica de potência robusta - Adoção crescente de sistemas de energia distribuída e microrredes para resiliência energética - Incentivos políticos e subsídios para tecnologias de energia limpa nas principais economias Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Custos iniciais elevados dos sistemas de células a combustível e dos condicionadores de energia, que limitam a adoção generaliza

artigo.texto: American Battery Technology Maps U.S. Battery Metals Push With Recycling, Nevada Lithium Key Points - American Battery Technology is pursuing a U.S.-based battery-materials supply chain centered on lithium-ion battery recycling and its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project in Nevada, targeting lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese production. - The company’s Reno recycling facility can process 20,000 metric tons annually, while a proposed southeastern facility would expand capacity to 100,000 tons with a $150 million Department of Energy grant and an estimated $375 million total cost. - Tonopah Flats is projected to have a 45-year mine life, $2.6 billion net present value and 21.8% after-tax internal rate of return. MarketBeat All Access sends real-time alerts on ratings, earnings, and news — $149 a year, locked in for as long as you stay. American Battery Technology NASDAQ: ABAT is advancing a U.S.-based battery-materials strategy built around lithium-ion battery recycling and the development of its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project in Nevada, Chief Financial Officer Alex Flores said during a company presentation. Flores said the company is seeking to build a domestic, lower-cost and environmentally responsible supply chain for battery metals, including lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese. He cited supply-security concerns, logistics costs and environmental risks associated with overseas sourcing as major challenges for the U.S. battery industry. “Our approach is to first close the loop and then fill the loop,” Flores said, referring to the company’s recycling operations and its planned lithium mining and refining operations. Recycling Operations and Expansion Plans American Battery Technology operates a 138,000-square-foot lithium-ion battery recycling facility outside Reno, Nevada, with annual intake capacity of 20,000 metric tons. Operations at the site began in October 2023, according to Flores. The company’s recycling process first dismantles battery packs into modules, cells and sub-cell components. It separates materials including copper, aluminum and steel, while producing a lithium-bearing intermediate known as black mass. In a subsequent refining phase, the company said the material can be processed into battery-grade nickel sulfate, manganese sulfate, cobalt sulfate and lithium hydroxide. Flores said the company currently sees stronger economics in selling black mass than in further refining it into lithium products. He said a federal directive issued on Aug. 27 banned black-mass exports, but American Battery Technology received a license allowing it to export up to $100 million of the material. The company is not selling black mass to China, Flores said, adding that its customers are primarily in South Korea and other OECD countries. American Battery Technology also plans to build a second recycling facility in the southeastern U.S. The proposed site would have annual intake capacity of 100,000 metric tons, representing a five-fold increase from the Reno facility’s capacity. Flores said the project has received a Department of Energy grant equivalent to $150 million and is expected to require total capital expenditures of $375 million. The funding is a grant rather than a loan and carries performance milestones, he said. Tonopah Lithium Project On the mining side, the company is developing its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project near Tonopah, Nevada. Flores said the project encompasses 631 unpatented lode mining claims covering more than 13,000 acres and is based on a claystone lithium resource rather than conventional ore. According to Flores, the project contains 21.3 million tons of accessible lithium hydroxide monohydrate and has a projected 45-year mine life. The company expects the operation to employ more than 200 full-time workers and reach a peak mining rate near 30,000 tons per day. Flores cited the company’s pre-feasibility study, published about a year ago, which estimated an after-tax internal rate of return of 21.8%, net present value of $2.6 billion and production costs of slightly more than $4,300 per metric ton of lithium hydroxide monohydrate. Planned infrastructure includes a surface mine, commercial refinery and a behind-the-meter solar field with battery energy storage. The project has received a $900 million letter of interest from the Export-Import Bank, Flores said. It has also been designated a priority project under the FAST-41 permitting framework. The company has initiated a definitive feasibility study, completed required National Environmental Policy Act baseline studies and submitted results to the Bureau of Land Management. Flores said the Bureau of Land Management approved the company’s mining and refining plan of operations, which American Battery Technology had been developing since November 2022. The company was awaiting a notice of intent from the agency before moving into the environmental impact statement process. Under its expectations for the FAST-41 process, Flores said the company could break ground by the middle of the following year. Financial Results and Domestic Supply Focus Flores said American Battery Technology reported record fiscal 2026 revenue of $21.7 million, up 407% year over year. Cost of goods sold increased 67%, which he attributed to operational efficiencies at the Nevada recycling facility. The company reported cash-basis gross profit of $1.7 million, a non-GAAP figure excluding non-cash items such as depreciation and stock compensation. The company ended the fiscal year with $49.5 million in cash and no debt, Flores said. He also said American Battery Technology has operated a multi-ton-per-year integrated pilot facility that produced battery-grade lithium from Nevada claystone. artigo.texto: Albemarle Corporation One of the world's largest lithium producers According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Lithium Carbonate Powder market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global lithium carbonate powder market is entering a phase of rapid expansion, with demand projected to grow at a double-digit CAGR through 2035. This growth is underpinned by the accelerating adoption of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries in electric vehicles and the surging deployment of stationary energy storage systems. Battery-grade lithium carbonate, which constitutes the majority of consumption, is witnessing tightening supply-demand balances as producers race to qualify new refining capacity outside China. The market is also shaped by a shift toward long-term contracts, regionalization of supply chains, and evolving trade policies. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the market size, segmentation, competitive landscape, and regional dynamics, offering stakeholders a data-driven view of the opportunities and challenges ahead. The baseline scenario for the lithium carbonate powder market anticipates robust growth from 2026 to 2035, with a CAGR of 15.0% in volume terms. This outlook is supported by the continued penetration of electric vehicles, particularly in China, Europe, and North America, and the increasing use of LFP chemistry, which relies on lithium carbonate rather than hydroxide. Stationary energy storage installations are also expected to contribute significantly, as grid operators and utilities invest in battery storage to integrate renewable energy. On the supply side, new refining projects in Australia, Europe, and North America are expected to gradually reduce China's dominance in processing, although project delays and permitting hurdles may keep the market tight in the near term. Prices are assumed to stabilize above historical lows, encouraging investment in upstream and midstream capacity. The market index is forecast to reach 350 by 2035 (2025=100), reflecting a more than threefold increase in market size over the decade. The electric vehicle battery segment is the largest and fastest-growing consumer of lithium carbonate powder, driven by the global shift toward electrification. Lithium carbonate is a critical input for LFP cathodes, which are gaining market share due to their cost-effectiveness and safety. As automakers ramp up EV production and introduce more affordable models, demand for LFP batteries is expected to surge, particularly in China and emerging markets. Through 2035, the segment will be supported by declining battery costs, expanding charging infrastructure, and stringent emissions regulations. Demand-side indicators include EV sales volumes, LFP market share, and average battery pack size. The trend is toward higher nickel chemistries in some regions, but LFP's dominance in entry-level and mid-range EVs will sustain strong carbonate demand. Current trend: Growing rapidly. Major trends: Increasing LFP adoption in mass-market EVs, Government mandates for zero-emission vehicles, Declining battery costs and improved energy density, and Expansion of EV production capacity in China, Europe, and North America. Representative participants: Tesla, BYD, CATL, LG Energy Solution, and Panasonic. The energy storage system segment is a key growth driver for lithium carbonate powder, as grid-scale and residential storage installations expand to support renewable energy integration. Lithium carbonate is used in LFP batteries for stationary storage, which prioritize safety, cycle life, and cost over energy density. The global push for decarbonization and the increasing share of intermittent renewables are prompting utilities and governments to invest in storage capacity. Through 2035, demand will be bolstered by falling battery costs, supportive policies, and the need for grid stability. Demand-side indicators include renewable energy capacity additions, storage procurement targets, and battery cost trends. The segment is expected to grow at a faster pace than EV batteries, albeit from a smaller base. Current trend: Accelerating. Major trends: Rapid growth in grid-scale battery storage projects, Falling costs of LFP batteries for stationary applications, Government auctions and incentives for energy storage, and Increasing renewable energy penetration driving storage demand. Representative participants: Samsung SDI, Fluence, Tesla, BYD, and LG Energy Solution. The consumer electronics segment, including smartphones, laptops, and tablets, represents a mature but stable market for lithium carbonate powder. Lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) batteries, which use lithium carbonate, are prevalent in portable electronics due to their high energy density. Demand in this segment is driven by replacement cycles, device proliferation, and the adoption of new form factors like wearables. Through 2035, growth will be moderate, with demand-side indicators including global device shipments and battery capacity per device. The trend toward higher energy density and faster charging may favor alternative chemistries, but lithium carbonate will remain a key input for LCO and NMC batteries used in premium devices. Current trend: Steady growth. Major trends: Increasing demand for high-energy-density batteries in premium devices, Growth in wearables and IoT devices, Shift toward sustainable and recyclable materials, and Proliferation of 5G-enabled devices driving replacement cycles. Representative participants: Apple, Samsung, Xiaomi, Panasonic, and Murata. Industrial applications of lithium carbonate powder include the production of glass, ceramics, and greases, where it is used as a flux and additive. artigo.texto: From our correspondent in Strasbourg – European industries will be able to count on a greater number of carbon emission allowances to set aside and draw upon when necessary. Today (21 October), the European Parliament and the Council of the EU have reached an agreement on an amendment to the Market Stability Reserve (MSR), the automatic mechanism that regulates the number of CO2 emission allowances in circulation within the European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS). The agreement raises the threshold from 400 to 700 million, above which, from 1 January 2031, excess allowances will be invalidated, with the aim of supporting the stability of the European carbon market. In effect, “the agreement strengthens the MSR’s ability to respond to changing market conditions, including a potential contraction in supply after the mid-2030s, as the overall emissions cap continues to decrease,” states the Council of the EU. In this way, the updated rules enhance the MSR’s capacity to intervene by allowing, where necessary, the release of allowances, thereby protecting European industry from extreme price volatility while at the same time sending “a clear signal to the market through safeguard mechanisms against an oversupply of allowances.” According to the rapporteur for the text, the Democratic Party MEP, Pierfrancesco Maran, Chair of the European Parliament’s Environment Committee (ENVI), the agreement “demonstrates that climate ambition and industrial competitiveness can and must go hand in hand.” Maran expects the current revision of the ETS to demonstrate “to businesses and citizens that Europe can play a leading role on climate issues and strengthen its industry.” Darragh O’Brien, Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment of Ireland – the country currently holding the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU – also argued that, with the agreement between the two sides, the EU has achieved “a balanced outcome on the market stability reserve” which provides European industry with “immediate flexibility, while ensuring price stability and protecting the integrity of the EU carbon market.” Under the rules currently in force, all allowances held in the reserve in excess of the 400 million threshold would have been invalidated. Under the agreement, the limit is raised to 700 million: allowances falling between the two thresholds will therefore not be cancelled, but will remain available in the reserve to help stabilise the market and address imbalances between supply and demand. The agreement amends the European Commission’s initial proposal, which had suggested suspending immediately and indefinitely the mechanism for cancelling excess allowances. This solution would have made it possible to keep an unlimited number of additional allowances in the reserve, creating a buffer to support market stability. The European Parliament and the Council, however, have opted for a compromise solution. The aim, according to the press release, is “to ensure the orderly functioning of the European carbon market and the MSR, to increase long-term market predictability and to align with the EU climate targets for 2040 and 2050.” The threshold should thus maintain a “sufficiently large reserve” to absorb imbalances between supply and demand, while avoiding “the excessive accumulation of allowances in the reserve” that might have resulted from the Commission’s proposal. The co-legislators have also agreed that the cap should be gradually lowered on an annual basis, to “ensure a consistent overall approach.” The next step involves the formal approval of the agreement by the European Parliament and the Council. The amended regulation will enter into force three days after its publication in the Official Journal of the EU and will apply immediately. English version by the Translation Service of Withub

artigo.texto: The Philippines is taking a major step toward building a national carbon market. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered the government to develop a policy framework to guide carbon credit projects, attract investment, and support the country’s climate goals. Under Executive Order No. 127, signed on October 13, 2026, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) will lead the development of the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework. The order also creates an inter-agency committee to guide the process and names the DENR as the country’s main authority for carbon markets. The framework will set rules for carbon projects, credit trading, monitoring, and benefit-sharing. It will cover both voluntary carbon markets and international trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The DENR must submit the proposed framework to the committee for review and approval within 30 days after the order takes effect. The move could help bring more funding to forest protection, clean energy, farming, and other projects that cut or remove greenhouse gas emissions. However, the detailed rules still need to be developed, and the impact will depend on how the system is put into practice. Marcos Orders National Carbon Market Rules Executive Order No. 127 aims to give the Philippines a clearer and more coordinated approach to carbon markets. The government wants the framework to support climate goals while opening the door to investment, funding, and technology. The EO read: “There is a need to formulate a national carbon market framework aligned with international standards, through a whole-of-government approach, to support the achievement of the country’s NDCs (nationally determined contributions).” Carbon markets allow companies and other buyers to purchase credits from projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. One carbon credit usually stands for one metric ton of carbon dioxide equivalent. These credits are based on specific rules and standards. Selling carbon credits can help fund projects that may struggle to secure enough money through other sources. The new framework will establish rules for: - Which projects qualify, - How credits are issued and transferred, - Accepted carbon standards, and - How projects report results. It will also cover environmental and social safeguards and how project benefits should be shared. These rules could support projects in forestry, renewable energy, agriculture, and other sectors. The order does not create a new carbon tax. Instead, it sets the direction for regulating carbon market activities and developing a more coordinated system for carbon projects. DENR Takes the Lead as Agencies Join Carbon Market Committee The order names the DENR as the national authority for carbon markets. It will oversee eligible projects and help ensure they follow national rules and environmental policies. An Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets (IACCM) will coordinate government policy and review the proposed framework. The Climate Change Commission will chair the committee, while the Department of Finance will serve as vice chair. Other members include: - DENR, Department of Energy, Department of Agriculture, Department of Transportation, Department of Trade and Industry, and the Securities and Exchange Commission. These agencies cover areas that can affect carbon projects, from climate policy and land use to energy, transport, business, and finance. Their cooperation will be important because projects may need several permits and must meet different technical and reporting requirements. The committee will review how the framework is applied. It will also approve fair fees for carbon market applications and certifications. Philippines Plans National Registry to Track Carbon Credits The government will establish a Philippine National Carbon Registry, which the DENR will manage. The digital system is intended to record carbon credits and related transactions. It should help regulators track credits and reduce the risk of the same emissions reduction being counted more than once. This matters when credits are sold to different buyers or transferred between countries. If the same emissions reduction is claimed more than once, the climate benefit becomes less reliable. The framework will also set rules for measuring and checking emissions reductions, approving international transfers, and reporting transactions. These requirements could help buyers assess credits and give project developers a clearer process for selling them in eligible markets. However, the registry’s value will depend on how well the government checks project data, tracks credits, and enforces the rules. Opening the Door to International Carbon Trading The framework will cover both voluntary carbon markets and international trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. In voluntary markets, companies and other organizations buy credits to support their climate goals. Eligible projects may include forest conservation, reforestation, renewable energy, farming, and waste management. Article 6 allows countries to work together to meet their climate targets. Under Article 6.2, countries can transfer approved emissions reductions or removals, known as internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs). These transfers require government approval and proper accounting. Countries must follow the rules. This stops the same emissions reduction from counting for more than one climate target. The new framework will set rules for approving international transfers. It will also manage carbon credits. This could help Philippine projects reach international buyers. However, approval under the national framework will not automatically mean that every credit qualifies for every market or buyer. New National Framework Builds on Existing Sector Rules The Philippines is not starting from zero. Several government initiatives have already laid the groundwork for carbon market development. artigo.texto: A inteligência artificial depende de uma infraestrutura física capaz de processar grandes volumes de dados continuamente. Por trás de cada consulta a um chatbot, geração de imagem ou aplicação corporativa de IA, existem servidores executando operações computacionais que consomem energia e geram calor. À medida que essas operações se tornam mais exigentes, a densidade computacional dos Data Centers aumenta. Isso significa que mais capacidade de processamento pode ser concentrada em um mesmo espaço, elevando a carga térmica que precisa ser controlada para manter os equipamentos dentro das condições adequadas de operação. O desafio não se resume a evitar o superaquecimento. A infraestrutura precisa acompanhar a demanda computacional, controlar o consumo de energia e manter condições operacionais estáveis, inclusive em ambientes que funcionam ininterruptamente. Por isso, o resfriamento passou a ocupar uma posição estratégica no planejamento e na expansão dos Data Centers. Fabricantes como a LG Electronics desenvolvem soluções de resfriamento para acompanhar essas novas exigências de eficiência e confiabilidade. O que é um chiller em um Data Center? Um chiller é um equipamento de refrigeração que remove calor de um circuito de água ou de outro fluido utilizado no sistema de climatização. Em instalações de grande porte, ele pode integrar a infraestrutura responsável por retirar o calor dos ambientes e dos equipamentos de TI, conforme a arquitetura de resfriamento adotada. Em um sistema tradicional com água gelada, por exemplo, o chiller resfria a água que circula pelo sistema. Essa água absorve o calor em pontos de troca térmica e retorna ao equipamento para que o ciclo continue. Existem diferentes configurações de chillers, que variam conforme a capacidade, o método de rejeição de calor e as necessidades da instalação. A escolha depende de fatores como densidade computacional, condições climáticas, espaço disponível, demanda energética e requisitos de disponibilidade. Em Data Centers de IA, esse dimensionamento ganha importância porque a infraestrutura de resfriamento precisa responder à carga térmica existente e acompanhar possíveis aumentos na capacidade de processamento. Como chillers ajudam a manter a operação dos Data Centers? O resfriamento integra uma cadeia de sistemas que precisam funcionar de maneira coordenada. Se a capacidade de retirar calor não acompanhar a demanda, a instalação pode precisar limitar o desempenho dos equipamentos ou adotar medidas operacionais para preservar as condições de funcionamento. Por isso, o projeto de cooling considera tanto a capacidade térmica quanto a confiabilidade dos componentes, as estratégias de redundância e a possibilidade de expansão. Em instalações críticas, a continuidade do resfriamento é especialmente relevante: uma interrupção no fornecimento de energia, por exemplo, exige que os sistemas retomem suas funções de acordo com os requisitos operacionais do Data Center. Outro aspecto é o consumo energético. A refrigeração representa uma parcela da energia utilizada por essas instalações, embora seu peso varie conforme o projeto, o clima, a carga de TI e as tecnologias empregadas. Melhorar a eficiência do sistema de resfriamento pode contribuir para reduzir a energia necessária à operação da infraestrutura. Quais tecnologias estão mudando o resfriamento de Data Centers? A evolução dos chillers envolve diferentes frentes tecnológicas. Entre elas estão os compressores mais eficientes, sistemas de controle inteligentes, arquiteturas modulares e recursos que aproveitam as condições ambientais para reduzir o trabalho mecânico de refrigeração. O free-cooling é um exemplo. Dependendo da configuração do sistema e das condições externas, essa estratégia permite utilizar o ambiente para auxiliar na remoção de calor, reduzindo a necessidade de refrigeração mecânica em determinadas situações. O resultado depende de fatores como temperatura ambiente, projeto da instalação e regime de operação. Também há avanços nos sistemas de monitoramento e diagnóstico. Com dados operacionais integrados, equipes de engenharia e facilities podem acompanhar o funcionamento dos equipamentos, identificar desvios e avaliar oportunidades de otimização. A inteligência desses sistemas ajuda a transformar o acompanhamento da infraestrutura em uma atividade mais orientada por dados. A modularidade é outra característica relevante, pois permite planejar a capacidade de acordo com as necessidades da instalação e simplificar etapas de implementação e expansão. Para Data Centers que precisam acompanhar a evolução da IA, essa flexibilidade pode facilitar o planejamento de longo prazo. Como a LG está desenvolvendo soluções para esse cenário? É nesse contexto que a LG Electronics apresenta o LG Air-Cooled Centrifugal Chiller (ACC), desenvolvido para aplicações de grande porte, incluindo a infraestrutura de resfriamento de Data Centers. O equipamento combina compressor centrífugo com mancal magnético e operação oil-free, ou seja, sem óleo no sistema de mancais do compressor. Essa arquitetura dispensa a lubrificação por óleo nesse conjunto, característica que integra a proposta tecnológica do equipamento. O ACC também incorpora a tecnologia refrigerant free-cooling, voltada ao aproveitamento de condições favoráveis para auxiliar o processo de resfriamento. A aplicação desse recurso depende das condições ambientais e operacionais, assim como do projeto da instalação. Outro destaque é a capacidade de recuperação após uma interrupção de energia. Conforme as condições de teste informadas pela fabricante, o equipamento pode restabelecer sua capacidade total de resfriamento em até três minutos após o retorno da energia. Esse intervalo deve ser considerado dentro das condições específicas de operação do sistema, e não como uma garantia de retomada integral de todo o Data Center. artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia O Tianneng Holding Group revelou seu portfólio de baterias multiquímicas em sua Global Alliance Partner Conference 2026 (Conferência Global de Parceiros da Aliança 2026) em Huzhou 20 de outubro de 2026, às 07:27 HUZHOU, China, 20 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — O Tianneng Holding Group revelou seu portfólio de baterias multiquímicas em sua Global Alliance Partner Conference 2026 (Conferência Global de Parceiros da Aliança 2026) em Huzhou, Zhejiang, sob o tema “Liderando o Benefício Ecológico”, reunindo aproximadamente 300 parceiros de todo o mundo. O portfólio abrange quatro vertentes de tecnologia de baterias — chumbo-ácido, íons-lítio, íons-sódio e estado sólido — para aplicações que incluem veículos elétricos de duas e três rodas, veículos de baixa velocidade, força motriz industrial e armazenamento de energia para residências, data centers voltados a IA, usuários comerciais e industriais, além de projetos em escala de concessionária. Parceiros da Argélia, Indonésia, Nigéria, Camboja e Brasil participaram de uma mesa redonda sobre produção local, eletrificação de veículos de duas rodas, armazenamento de energia e transformação da distribuição, concordando que as raízes locais e a sinergia do ecossistema são essenciais. Mi Yue, secretária-geral da New Energy Industry Association for Asia and the Pacific (NEIAAP, Associação da Indústria de Novas Energias para a Ásia e o Pacífico), incentivou a inovação, o reconhecimento mútuo de normas e a colaboração transfronteiriça na cadeia de suprimentos. Guo Kuilong, secretário-geral da Câmara de Comércio da China para Importação e Exportação de Máquinas e Produtos Eletrônicos (CCCME), afirmou que a câmara utilizará sua plataforma para ajudar empresas de novas energias em sua expansão global e promover a cooperação na cadeia industrial para um crescimento mutuamente benéfico. “A incerteza torna os pilares da certeza ainda mais vitais”, disse Zhang Tianren, presidente do Tianneng Holding Group. “O Tianneng Group se concentrará em baterias melhores e soluções de sistema mais abrangentes, impulsionando a pesquisa e o desenvolvimento, a fabricação local e o fortalecimento da marca para construir uma cadeia de suprimentos verde, resiliente e localizada, com parceiros globais.” Sobre o Tianneng Group Fundado em 1986, o Tianneng Group é líder global em soluções de energia verde, impulsionando a inovação em energia para mobilidade elétrica, sistemas de armazenamento de energia e economia circular. Com 21 bases de produção inteligentes, a empresa oferece valor sustentável a mais de 100 países e regiões. artigo.texto: CATL's 58.6% Revenue Surge Exposes a Margin Problem Citi Can't Ignore Published on 10/23/2026 at 03:30 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL still expects global demand for traction and storage batteries to grow 20–30% in 2027, a forecast the company reaffirmed in its own assessment of quarterly results published today. Yet the headline number that matters for investors sits elsewhere: sales are climbing far faster than earnings, and the gap between the two has become the central question hanging over the stock. Shares fell 3.3% in the previous session as the market digested a profit miss that has forced a rethink of how the battery giant should be valued. The debate is no longer about whether CATL can keep growing revenue. It is about whether additional business can be converted into proportionally stronger profit. Storage Volumes Race Ahead The storage battery segment is expanding fastest. Shipments rose roughly 60% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, with storage accounting for about 25% of CATL's total battery volumes. That momentum underpins the company's confident demand outlook, though it leaves unanswered how profitably those extra volumes are being sold. Industry forecasts point to a growing pie. BloombergNEF expects newly installed global energy storage capacity to rise 45% to 188 GW in 2026, driven by solar buildout, storage mandates and subsidy programs. Protectionism is simultaneously complicating market access for Chinese suppliers and shifting supply chains — a reminder that a larger global market does not automatically translate into unrestricted opportunities for CATL. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Revenue and Profit Diverge Sharply Third-quarter revenue climbed 58.58% year-on-year. Net profit, by contrast, advanced just 14.54% to RMB 21.2 billion — against analyst expectations of 41.2% earnings growth. CATL earned more than in the prior-year period but fell well short of forecasts. The divergence is not a reported profit collapse. It is a question of why strong top-line growth failed to flow through to the bottom line. Management attributed the pressure to product mix, a consumption tax and a reduced export tax rebate. The gross margin slipped to 20.69%, down 5.1 percentage points year-on-year and 2.46 percentage points sequentially. Reuters linked Tuesday's disappointment to intensifying competition in the battery market and slowing growth in Chinese car sales. Media reports also pointed to lower-margin energy storage sales and new policy costs weighing on profitability. The shortfall therefore touches several drivers of earnings power and cannot be reduced to the demand environment alone. Cost Sharing Becomes the Pivot CATL is negotiating with customers over how to split the additional costs. The company has not confirmed that any pass-through has already been secured. The demand outlook and the negotiations address separate questions: volume opportunities on one side, the distribution of burdens on the other. UOB Kay Hian expects CATL to pass on part of the tax load through higher battery prices and considers a margin recovery in the final quarter possible. That view rests on the assumption that the company and its customers each absorb half of the tax burden. Additional pressure arrives when the export tax rebate ends on January 1, 2027. Citi Trims Its Target Citi cut its price target for CATL on Wednesday to RMB 479 from RMB 500, citing a lower-than-expected gross margin, higher expenses and impairments. The disappointment, in other words, spans multiple inputs to profitability. A recovery case cannot rest on rising revenue alone. More convincing would be evidence that additional business contributes more strongly to profit — which would require a more favorable product mix, easing cost pressure or less pricing strain. That is a scenario, not a confirmed turnaround. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. SERES Deal Offers a Demand Anchor One concrete data point comes from the long-term cooperation agreement signed roughly two weeks ago with the SERES Group. AITO models will continue to use CATL batteries, and the two companies plan to expand the second phase of the SERES plant to 10–12 GWh annually. Combined, both phases are intended to reach more than 20 GWh of capacity. The agreement supports the case for a longer-term demand base. It does not yet demonstrate improved profitability. What matters for investors is that such partnerships generate not just additional capacity and sales opportunities but economically attractive business. Growth Quality Takes Center Stage If competition remains intense, higher revenue need not bring better earnings. A larger share of lower-margin storage sales could cap any recovery, as could persistent cost burdens, while slowing Chinese car sales deepen the uncertainty. Conversely, should profitability pressure ease, the revenue base could once again drive earnings — growth would become a genuine profit engine rather than a counterweight to margin strain. Until new earnings figures show that gross margin and expenses are moving in a more favorable direction, the recovery thesis remains conditional. Strong top-line growth offers little relief if CATL must permanently accept weaker returns to achieve it. The stock's next move will hinge on the quality of growth rather than its sheer size. artigo.texto: General Motors (GM) used its GM Forward event on Wednesday to put a new battery chemistry at the center of its next wave of mass-market electric vehicles and paired it with an AI-driven push to cut vehicle development time in half. This comes as GM tries to make EVs work for mainstream buyers while spreading its autonomy and AI features across its gas-powered lineup. GM announced its upcoming fourth-generation EV platform will use lithium manganese rich (LMR) chemistry in prismatic cells, which GM calls the world's first production LMR battery. The cells will be made by Ultium Cells, GM's joint venture with LG Energy Solution, in Spring Hill, Tenn. GM says LMR is designed to offer 33% more energy density than lithium iron phosphate (LFP), the widely used low-cost chemistry, at a comparable price. Paired with new drive units and better aerodynamics, the platform should deliver approximately 20% more range per kilowatt-hour. GM said the battery pack is 20% more compact, the vehicle is expected to be 15% lighter and 25% more aerodynamic, and the drive units use 40% fewer parts, cutting complexity. When GM and LG unveiled LMR in May 2025, it was aimed at full-size electric trucks and SUVs starting in 2028. GM now says it plans to use LMR in its "highest-volume EV segments, where range, durability, and affordability matter most." The company didn't give a launch date or models for the new platform. What GM didn't announce was an energy storage system (ESS) play, which some expected. The ESS trade has been buzzing recently as hyperscalers and neocloud firms build out data centers that need backup energy solutions. GM rival Ford pivoted hard into this business, using its EV battery know-how to make a new division, Ford Energy. Back in March, Ultium Cells said it would spend $70 million retooling Spring Hill to build LFP cells for ESS. The move brought back 700 workers who had been furloughed in January. But those cells go to LG Energy Solution Vertech, LG's US storage unit, which packages them for grid-scale and data center projects across North America. Bob Lee, president of LG Energy Solution North America, called Spring Hill "a key hub in our North American ESS manufacturing footprint" — making it more LG's storage business than GM's. GM's own storage work is smaller. It includes a 7.2-megawatt-hour system built by Redwood Materials from around 100 used GM EV packs at a GM plant in Michigan. Outside of batteries, GM said its next-gen central computer debuts on the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. It has 40 times the computing power and 30% less wiring, and it will then roll out to gas-powered full-size SUVs and trucks, three-row crossovers, and fourth-gen EVs.

artigo.texto: PHOENIX (KVOA) -- Federal land managers are reviewing dozens of applications to build massive data centers on public lands across the West, including in Arizona. According to a new interactive map released by the Center for Western Priorities, the Bureau of Land Management is currently considering at least 35 applications tied to data centers and supporting infrastructure. The proposals cover more than 24,000 acres of public land across Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming. The map, which was last updated on Friday, Oct. 16, shows that 17 of these applications are for actual data center campuses, while 13 are for supporting infrastructure like water pipelines and transmission lines. Some of the proposed projects are massive. In Utah, one developer proposed a 9,000-acre project powered by small modular nuclear reactors. Another developer filed 16 proposals across five states, including a 2,520-acre site near Las Vegas. Unlike traditional energy projects, there is currently no established permitting process for building data centers on public land, officials said. On Sept. 24, a group of congressional representatives sent 18 questions to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum demanding answers about public input, with a deadline of Thursday, Oct. 8. "Before even considering putting data centers on public lands, the Trump administration should be obligated to solicit public feedback on this idea," Lauren Bogard, deputy director of the Center for Western Priorities, said. Public opposition to these projects is growing. A Pew Research Center poll found that the share of Americans who believe data centers are bad for the environment rose to 54 percent in September.

artigo.texto: CATL's Buyback Draws a Line in the Sand, But the Margin Fight Is Only Beginning Published on 10/22/2026 at 16:50 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL is putting real money behind its conviction that the market has got it wrong. The battery giant has earmarked a buyback programme worth between 20 billion and 40 billion yuan, with every repurchased share destined for cancellation and a permanent reduction in registered capital. It is a decisive use of the balance sheet — and it has done little so far to arrest the slide. The stock fell another 3.3% on the day the programme drew attention, a reminder that capital returns cannot offset doubts about earnings power. Tuesday's session had already been brutal: shares dropped 4.1% after quarterly profit fell short of expectations, a miss Reuters identified as the trigger for the sell-off. Treating the buyback as a reliable floor would be premature. Its immediate significance lies in how CATL is deploying capital, not in any guarantee about the share price. Growth Is There — Just Not Where It Counts The numbers tell a story of a company expanding faster than it is earning. Revenue for the third quarter of 2026 climbed 58.58%, yet net profit attributable to shareholders rose just 14.54%. For the first nine months, sales advanced 56.19% while cost of sales jumped 61.61%, and operating cash flow retreated 23.60%. That decoupling explains the skepticism. A company does not need to shrink to lose the market's confidence; it only needs additional revenue to arrive at thinner margins, making prior profit expectations look too generous. Gross margin slipped to 20.69%, down 5.1 percentage points year on year, with CATL pointing to product mix as well as changes in consumption tax and export rebates. The quarterly top line came in at 165.22 billion RMB, with attributable net profit of 21.25 billion RMB — a 5.77% decline from the prior quarter. The weakness is not a shortage of demand. It is the price at which that demand is being served. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? A Partnership With Industrial Substance Against that backdrop, CATL signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement with SERES on 10 October. AITO models will continue to use CATL batteries, and the planned second phase of their joint "Plant in Plant" project is designed for annual capacity of 10–12 GWh. That gives the alliance a concrete industrial footing rather than a bare statement of intent — though it is a blueprint, not completed expansion. CATL also unveiled a new generation of batteries for heavy trucks, alongside plans to expand its battery-swapping network, as reported by Reuters. Each of these widens the commercial runway. None of them answers the question investors are actually asking: whether extra volume can be converted into extra profit. The Tax Cliff With a Fixed Date One burden arrives on a set timetable. The value-added tax rebate on battery exports is due to expire on 1 January 2027, and talks with customers over how to split the added cost are still underway. Until that pass-through is settled, part of the hoped-for recovery rests on assumption rather than evidence. Buybacks offer no operational relief here. There is a potential tailwind on the product side. According to the company, shipments of lower-priced storage orders have passed their peak and are set to fall sharply in the final quarter, opening the door to a more favourable mix. That is an opportunity, not a guarantee of margin repair. CATL remains confident on demand, forecasting 20% to 30% growth in worldwide appetite for power and storage batteries in 2027. That outlook argues against the idea of a collapsing end market. Demand and profitability, however, are different creatures — a growing market only helps shareholders if CATL earns adequate returns from it. Analysts Are Repricing the Risk JPMorgan downgraded the Hong Kong-listed shares to "Neutral" and cut its price target from HK$725 to HK$500. The 30% reduction was attributed to profitability in the battery sector fading faster than expected. Reuters also flagged intensifying competition and weakening growth in Chinese car sales as headwinds behind the quarterly figures. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. Those calls are not prophecy, but they make clear that a recovery will need more than fresh growth agreements. Under harsher competitive conditions, additional shipments may come with commercial concessions attached. The buyback does not alter that operational calculus. The shares are earmarked for cancellation and a lower registered capital, which can strengthen the stake of remaining holders — but it does nothing to improve the economics of the underlying business. What would change the picture is a better translation of revenue into profit and cash. A confirmed implementation step on the second phase of the SERES project would be the next tangible catalyst, and the capacity figure alone will not be the measure. What matters is whether it produces economically viable additional business. Should margin pressure intensify further, even the expansion case loses its persuasive force. Until then, the buyback signals resolve — the commercial test is still to come. Ad CATL Stock: New Analysis - 22 October Fresh CATL information released. What's the impact for investors? artigo.texto: Google pagará a quem economizar energia para alimentar data centers com as 'sobras' Gigante da tecnologia está financiando uma das maiores usinas virtuais do país, que remuneraria residências e empresas para ajustar seu consumo quando redes elétricas estiverem sob pressão As empresas de tecnologia estão enfrentando dificuldades para encontrar eletricidade suficiente para abastecer todos os novos data centers de que precisam para a inteligência artificial. Recentemente, elas têm explorado alternativas como reativar antigas usinas nucleares e instalar conjuntos de motores a gás independentes da rede elétrica. Agora, o Google está tentando uma abordagem diferente: pagar, ao menos indiretamente, para que residências e empresas reduzam o consumo de eletricidade em determinados horários, ajudando a liberar energia para os data centers. Nesta quinta-feira, o Google anunciou um acordo com uma empresa chamada Voltus para criar o que é conhecido como uma “usina virtual” na grande rede elétrica da região do Atlântico Médio dos Estados Unidos, conhecida como PJM. A Voltus fornecerá ao Google até 1.070 megawatts de capacidade elétrica quando necessário — aproximadamente o equivalente à produção de um grande reator nuclear. - Após desmatamento ilegal do Google: Finlândia questiona custos ambientais da expansão da inteligência artificial Essa eletricidade não virá de novas usinas. Em vez disso, a Voltus firmará acordos com residências e empresas e oferecerá incentivos financeiros para que reduzam o consumo quando a demanda local por energia estiver elevada ou a rede elétrica estiver sob pressão. Muitas dessas reduções poderão ocorrer automaticamente, por exemplo, por meio de termostatos inteligentes que diminuem o uso do ar-condicionado nos horários de pico durante o verão ou de baterias capazes de fornecer energia temporariamente no próprio local. Cada uma dessas medidas, isoladamente, libera apenas uma pequena quantidade de energia. Mas, ao reunir os efeitos de milhares de empresas e residências, a Voltus afirma que pode disponibilizar, de forma confiável, uma grande capacidade adicional justamente quando ela é mais necessária — e fazer isso em poucos anos. - Tecnologia com visões distintas: Flávio propõe ‘liberdade para inovar’; Lula defende soberania e regulação Embora as empresas de tecnologia provavelmente ainda precisem construir usinas elétricas convencionais para continuar expandindo seus grandes data centers, essa abordagem poderá ser uma alternativa mais rápida, barata e menos poluente no curto prazo. — Realmente vemos as usinas virtuais como uma solução fundamental de curto prazo — afirmou Ellen Zuckerman, responsável pelo desenvolvimento dos mercados de energia para as Américas do Norte e do Sul no Google. — É uma maneira de investir nas comunidades em que atuamos, reforçar nosso compromisso com a energia limpa e, ao mesmo tempo, atender à demanda por capacidade elétrica com rapidez e em grande escala. O Google não divulgou os termos financeiros do acordo com a Voltus, mas afirmou que esse é um dos maiores exemplos, até o momento, de uma gigante da tecnologia pagando por capacidade elétrica dessa maneira.

artigo.texto: When Alexander Olshansky received a call in September telling him that the data center hosting his company's infrastructure in Kyiv had been destroyed by a Russian attack, he made a beeline for the scene. “As I was driving up to the data center, I saw a column of black smoke, a block cordoned off by the police and fire trucks,” recalls Olshansky, president of the Ukrainian domain registration and Web hosting provider MiroHost. The data center was damaged, but Olshansky’s employees had been sheltering elsewhere when the attack happened. Despite the facility’s destruction on September 23, just around one in 20 of MiroHost’s customers were affected. The company had reserved enough computing capacity in Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia to back up its Ukrainian infrastructure in the event of an attack. On supporting science journalism If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today. Other data centers haven’t fared as well. In October Ukrainian drones struck three data centers operated by the Russian technology giant Yandex, disrupting services and damaging artificial intelligence infrastructure. Earlier this year Iranian drones damaged Amazon Web Services facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, causing Web outages across the region. What is inarguable is that, like them or not, data centers are increasingly important parts of our lives, and as such, they’re increasingly seen as fair targets in war. How they are secured is a matter of national—and even international—importance. “I would say 2026 is going to be the first year of drone strikes taking out data centers being a thing,” says Doug Madory, head of international Internet analysis at the cybersecurity company Infoblox. “I just don’t think that anybody had anticipated this as a risk to interrupt service.” Because of their vital role in the economy, data centers are designed with multiple layers of security. These include restricted access to the site, constant surveillance and backup power systems. In the event of fire, suppression equipment keeps flames at bay. But those defenses are mostly focused on stopping bad actors from getting inside or on keeping services running when equipment fails—not on withstanding attacks from the air. “Most data center security standards in the industry focus on physical access restrictions,” says Connor Martin, an international affairs fellow in national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. But protecting facilities against drone or missile strikes is a different challenge—and one the sector must start focusing on. Data centers can seem like sitting ducks from the air because they’re massive, cavernous buildings containing enormously expensive equipment in often remote areas. They “can’t pick up and move,” Martin says. Still, some protection is possible without going as far as installing missile defenses at key data center locations. Peter Judge, senior research analyst at the Uptime Institute, says operators can build shields around vulnerable equipment such as generators and air-handling units and use overhead netting or screens to hinder aerial surveillance. Yet more sophisticated systems might combine radar, cameras and radio sensors to identify approaching drones or aircraft. But if a craft is spotted, what can actually be done is trickier. Aviation laws typically prevent jamming drone signals—scrambling their radio signals—or bringing them down without authorization. Some newer drones don’t transmit radio control signals at all. For his part, Olshansky isn’t convinced physical protection is viable in a war zone anyway. “No fire suppression system is designed for a direct hit by a bomb, missile or drone,” he says. Truly protecting such a facility could mean burying it deep underground, which isn’t feasible. Instead, the industry’s best approach may be in redundancy—distributing services across multiple facilities so that when one is destroyed, another can take over. It works, as MiroHost showed, but it also costs more: Olshansky says his company effectively doubled its available computing capacity to prepare for an attack. Madory points out that cloud providers already offer ways to distribute workloads across different geographic regions. The problem is that many customers don’t bother because of the additional cost and technical complexity. “In theory, you could be resilient, but in practice, a lot of stuff is not,” he says. The recent attacks could change where companies choose to build their data centers, Martin says. The Gulf states have invested heavily in attracting those kinds of instalments, but their proximity to regional conflicts could make future projects harder to justify. Larger countries such as the U.S. and China, meanwhile, have more opportunities to build facilities far from potential conflict zones. But even then, there are no guarantees. As Olshansky says, “It is always better to have two copies of something than just one, even if it is highly protected.”

artigo.texto: Brussels, 21 October 2026 On 20 October 2026, the EU Council and the European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on amending the rules on the invalidation of allowances in the market stability reserve (MSR) for the EU emissions trading system. This targeted amendment of the MSR will increase long-term market liquidity and predictability while protecting industrial competitiveness. The provisional agreement still needs to be confirmed by both institutions before formal adoption. The agreement bolsters the MSR’s ability to respond to evolving market conditions, including any potential market tightness after the mid-2030s as the overall cap on emissions continues to decrease. The updated rules increase the firepower of the MSR for possible future allowance releases to shield European industry from extreme price volatility, while sending a strong market signal with safeguards against allowance surpluses. The MSR is a mechanism created to address imbalances in the carbon market by absorbing excess allowances or releasing them to stabilise prices. This targeted amendment does not alter the overall design of the MSR. A broader review of the ETS, including the rules governing the MSR, is currently underway. In response to European leaders’ call for accelerated action, we reached a balanced outcome on the market stability reserve that provides European industry with immediate flexibility, while ensuring price stability and protecting the integrity of the EU carbon market. The EU is delivering on the ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap. Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Future-proofing the market stability reserve Since the invalidation mechanism began in 2023, over 3 billion allowances have been invalidated and removed from the market, restoring balance between supply and demand and addressing the historical oversupply of allowances accumulated in the ETS. While the Commission proposal provides for the indefinite halt of its invalidation mechanism, the co-legislators provisionally agreed on a balanced compromise: the invalidation mechanism will still be in place, with a higher invalidation threshold of 700 million allowances (compared to the current 400 million threshold) entering into immediate effect, after the proposal is formally adopted. The larger number of allowances will enhance the long-term stability of the EU carbon market and will provide a larger buffer for future market fluctuations, while providing a safeguard against excessive oversupply of allowances The co-legislators also agreed that a gradual decrease of the invalidation threshold should be included in the context of the wider ETS review to ensure a consistent overall approach. Next steps The provisional agreement will now have to be endorsed by the Council and the Parliament. It will then be formally adopted by both institutions following legal-linguistic revision. Background The Commission proposal is one of the short-term measures announced by the Commission to address high and volatile energy prices, as referred to in the March conclusions of the European Council. It is a first, stand-alone amendment to the market stability reserve, which is to be followed by a broader reform of the reserve in the context of the ETS review, currently under discussion within the Council. Source – EU Council EU Commission welcomes political agreement on rules enhancing stability and long-term resilience of EU carbon market Brussels, 21 October 2026 The European Commission welcomes the provisional political agreement reached by the European Parliament and the Council on a targeted amendment to strengthen the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) of the EU’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). Following the Commission’s proposal in April 2026 and delivering on the European Council conclusions last week on 16 October, this swift agreement will help to ensure a stable, well-functioning carbon market in the EU and enhance EU ETS’ resilience to excessive price volatility. As a result, it also makes concrete progress on the implementation of the ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap agreed among EU institutions to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness by the end of 2027. Under the current system, all emission allowances in the reserve above 400 million are invalidated. Thanks to the agreement, the reserve will be able to retain up to 700 million allowances as a buffer to support future market stability and predictability. These new rules will reinforce the reserve’s capacity to operate in the longer term, while preserving the fundamental rules-based design of the system and its environmental integrity. The MSR reduces the supply of allowances to the market when there are too many in circulation and injects allowances when there is scarcity. This agreement sends a clear signal that the EU is committed to a predictable and reliable carbon market, providing greater certainty for businesses, and investments in clean transition. It is a first step towards a wider modernisation of the Market Stability Reserve, for which further reforms have been proposed by the Commission as part of the separate MSR reform and the EU ETS review on 17 July 2026. Next steps Following this provisional agreement, the European Parliament and the Council of the EU will have to formally adopt the text. Thereafter, the amendment of the Market Stability Reserve Decision enters into force upon publication in the Official Journal of the EU. Background First introduced in 2019, the MSR is designed to enhance the resilience of the EU ETS by adjusting the supply of allowances in response to market developments, making the carbon market more resilient to future shocks and price volatility. The MSR contains price volatility by reducing auction volumes during periods of supply surpluses and releasing allowances in periods of scarcity based on predefined rules. The European Commission welcomes the provisional political agreement reached by the European Parliament and the Council on a targeted amendment to strengthen the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) of the EU’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). Following the Commission’s proposal in April 2026 and delivering on the European Council conclusions last week on 16 October, this swift agreement will help to ensure a stable, well-functioning carbon market in the EU and enhance EU ETS’ resilience to excessive price volatility. As a result, it also makes concrete progress on the implementation of the ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap agreed among EU institutions to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness by the end of 2027. Under the current system, all emission allowances in the reserve above 400 million are invalidated. Thanks to the agreement, the reserve will be able to retain up to 700 million allowances as a buffer to support future market stability and predictability. These new rules will reinforce the reserve’s capacity to operate in the longer term, while preserving the fundamental rules-based design of the system and its environmental integrity. The MSR reduces the supply of allowances to the market when there are too many in circulation and injects allowances when there is scarcity. This agreement sends a clear signal that the EU is committed to a predictable and reliable carbon market, providing greater certainty for businesses, and investments in clean transition. It is a first step towards a wider modernisation of the Market Stability Reserve, for which further reforms have been proposed by the Commission as part of the separate MSR reform and the EU ETS review on 17 July 2026. Next steps Following this provisional agreement, the European Parliament and the Council of the EU will have to formally adopt the text. Thereafter, the amendment of the Market Stability Reserve Decision enters into force upon publication in the Official Journal of the EU. Background First introduced in 2019, the MSR is designed to enhance the resilience of the EU ETS by adjusting the supply of allowances in response to market developments, making the carbon market more resilient to future shocks and price volatility. The MSR contains price volatility by reducing auction volumes during periods of supply surpluses and releasing allowances in periods of scarcity based on predefined rules. The Commission tabled its proposal to strengthen the MSR in April 2026, following President von der Leyen’s announcement at the March European Council. This provisional agreement addresses an immediate need to strengthen the resilience of the carbon market by preserving allowances in the reserve, while the broader ETS review provides the opportunity to modernise the MSR’s functioning for the next decade. artigo.texto: A fabricante chinesa de baterias CATL apresentou nesta terça-feira (20) um sistema que permite trocar a bateria de um caminhão elétrico em cerca de cinco minutos, tempo próximo ao necessário para abastecer um veículo a diesel. A novidade busca resolver um dos principais desafios do transporte pesado eletrificado: o tempo que os caminhões precisam ficar parados para recuperar a autonomia. Batizada de Dual-Electric Range Extender, a tecnologia usa duas baterias com funções diferentes. Uma alimenta o veículo durante a maior parte do trajeto. A outra funciona como reserva e permite que o motorista continue rodando quando a carga principal está perto do fim. As informações foram divulgadas pelo site CarNewsChina. Saiba também: - Novo BYD Dolphin Mini cresce, recarrega em 5 min e custa menos de R$ 50 mil - Dá para ter carro elétrico em condomínio sem wallbox? O que diz a lei e quanto custa instalar A troca de baterias em si não é novidade na China. A empresa NIO já soma mais de 100 milhões de trocas em carros de passeio, e a própria CATL já opera uma rede de estações para caminhões. O que muda agora é a bateria reserva, que dá ao motorista uma margem de segurança até a próxima estação. Como funciona a troca de bateria em cinco minutos? O sistema usa uma arquitetura chamada A+B. A bateria principal, instalada na parte inferior do caminhão, pode ser removida e substituída em uma estação de troca. A CATL oferece duas capacidades: 432 kWh e 513 kWh. A segunda bateria é fixa, tem 77 kWh e entra em funcionamento quando a principal está quase descarregada. Segundo a fabricante, essa configuração permite usar a bateria removível até restarem apenas 5% de carga, sem que o caminhão dependa só dela para chegar à estação. Ao chegar a um ponto compatível, o veículo recebe outra bateria carregada, dispensando a espera por uma recarga convencional. A empresa também pretende oferecer as baterias removíveis por meio de contratos de locação. Assim, as transportadoras poderão comprar os caminhões sem arcar com o custo integral desses componentes. Economia pode passar de R$ 345 mil, diz fabricante A CATL estima que a tecnologia possa gerar economia superior a 460 mil yuans, cerca de US$ 68,7 mil ou R$ 345 mil, em três anos de operação, na comparação com caminhões a diesel. O cálculo considera o custo total de propriedade (TCO), indicador que reúne despesas com aquisição, energia, manutenção e uso do veículo. Trata-se, porém, de uma projeção da fabricante. A economia real dependerá de fatores como quilometragem, preço da eletricidade, valor do diesel e condições de operação de cada transportadora. Rede de troca deve chegar a 2 mil estações em 2027 A nova tecnologia faz parte do QiJi, projeto da CATL para criar uma rede de estações de troca de baterias voltada ao transporte pesado. Atualmente, cinco grandes corredores logísticos chineses já contam com a estrutura. Segundo a empresa, os veículos atendidos pela rede acumulam mais de 5 milhões de quilômetros rodados. A previsão é instalar 900 estações até o fim de 2026 e chegar a 2 mil em 2027, cobrindo as principais rodovias chinesas. A meta de longo prazo é alcançar 10 mil pontos. Para garantir a compatibilidade entre diferentes caminhões, a empresa padronizou as baterias removíveis em dois formatos. O módulo de 432 kWh atende veículos com entre-eixos de 3.800 mm, e o de 513 kWh foi desenvolvido para modelos com entre-eixos de 4.200 mm. Durante a apresentação, a CATL também anunciou acordos com 14 empresas, entre elas as operadoras logísticas SF Express, ZTO Express e YTO Express. Os compromissos envolvem um volume inicial de 13 mil unidades. Nova bateria promete mais de 600 km de autonomia Além do sistema de troca rápida, a fabricante apresentou quatro produtos da linha Tectrans II, voltados a diferentes operações de transporte. O principal destaque é a Tectrans II Long-Range, com 760 kWh de capacidade, autonomia anunciada de mais de 600 quilômetros e arquitetura elétrica de 800 volts. Leia também - Scania adianta lançamento de sua linha 2027 de caminhões - Custo ainda é ‘pedra no sapato’ para renovar frota, dizem executivos A empresa também desenvolveu uma bateria mais leve para entregas de curta distância e outra mais fina, para caminhões basculantes. Nesta, a espessura caiu de 860 mm para 580 mm, o que libera espaço para carga. Há ainda uma configuração para caminhões com entre-eixos de 3.350 mm, voltada a operações em regiões montanhosas e áreas portuárias. Metade dos caminhões pesados vendidos na China já é elétrica, diz fabricante Segundo a CATL, a participação dos caminhões pesados elétricos no mercado chinês passou de 5,2% em 2022 para 50,28% em setembro de 2026. A companhia afirma ainda que mais de 430 mil caminhões pesados elétricos em circulação no mundo usam suas baterias, o equivalente a mais de 70% desse mercado. Os números ajudam a explicar a aposta da CATL em soluções para a operação comercial. Para as transportadoras, o desafio não é só ampliar a autonomia, mas reduzir o tempo de parada e tornar a eletrificação economicamente viável. E no Brasil? Por aqui, a eletrificação do transporte de carga ainda está no começo. Segundo a Federação Nacional da Distribuição de Veículos Automotores (Fenabrave), foram emplacados 216 caminhões elétricos no País entre janeiro e setembro de 2026. A troca de bateria já foi apresentada ao mercado brasileiro. Em 2024, a XCMG lançou no País um caminhão elétrico cujo conjunto de baterias pode ser substituído em até seis minutos em uma estação de troca. Não há, porém, anúncio de implantação do sistema da CATL nem da rede QiJi no Brasil. Carregando ofertas...

artigo.texto: SiC Ups Efficiency of Utility-Scale Battery Storage to Over 99% Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are building up behind the grid to help keep up with the rising demand for power driven by everything from electric vehicles (EVs) to AI data centers. By storing excess energy, including from non-constant sources such as solar and wind, they can deliver electricity to the grid during periods of peak demand. They can also supply backup power to facilities such as factories and data centers, helping the latter manage the highly variable power demands associated with AI workloads. But increasing the capacity and performance of these big lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries is only part of the equation. Equally important is maximizing the amount of energy that power electronics can wring out of them. “At utility scale, even small improvements in power-conversion efficiency can have a meaningful impact on battery energy storage system performance and total cost of ownership,” said Sergio Fissore, vice president and general manager of the IPD power division at onsemi. To that end, the company is working with battery-storage supplier Sungrow to integrate its silicon-carbide (SiC) power-module technology into a new utility-scale BESS. Sungrow's PowerTitan 3.0 platform incorporates onsemi's power integrated modules (PIMs), optimized for the three-level inverter topologies widely used in grid-connected batteries. The "hybrid" module combines SiC MOSFETs, used in the high-frequency switching stages to maximize efficiency and power density, with silicon power devices, used in other portions of the design. This dual-material approach balances SiC's higher performance with silicon's cost to improve the “system economics” of energy storage. Compared with the previous-generation platform, the new architecture improves inverter-level efficiency by 0.4%, according to onsemi. It supports power-conversion units rated up to 450 kW, enabling higher-power storage deployments while maintaining high conversion efficiency. Peak efficiency exceeds 99.3%, helping minimize losses and the associated heat in utility-scale systems that convert DC from the battery to AC for grid delivery. In a large-scale BESS deployment, even small improvements in efficiency can make a big impact on both performance and cost, said Fissore. onsemi’s analysis revealed that a 0.4% efficiency boost delivered by the hybrid SiC module could add up to more than 475 megawatt-hours (MWh) of energy savings per year in a 100-MW battery energy storage installation compared to the previous module. These savings can increase the amount of energy available for grid delivery, reduce operating costs, and improve the overall economics of storage assets, according to onsemi. The same characteristics also enable higher overload capability and improved thermal performance, which helps energy storage systems handle the heavy demands of loads such as AI data centers while maintaining reliability. In these situations, the BESS acts as a shock absorber, supplying extra power to the data center during AI power spikes. Chen Peng, general manager of energy storage conversion products for Sungrow's Energy Storage business, said the new architecture would help with the "deployment of higher-performance storage solutions that deliver greater value throughout the lifecycle of energy assets. By integrating advanced technologies and collaborating with strategic partners such as onsemi, Sungrow is accelerating the deployment of higher-performance storage solutions that deliver greater value throughout the lifecycle of energy assets." About the Author James Morra Senior Editor James Morra is the senior editor for Electronic Design, covering the semiconductor industry and new technology trends, with a focus on power electronics and power management. He also reports on the business behind electrical engineering, including the electronics supply chain. He joined Electronic Design in 2015 and is based in Chicago, Illinois.
