artigo.texto: O Ceará abriga a construção de um data center que será o maior do Brasil em operação. Além disso, há outros 10 projetos hiperescala de processamento de dados na região do Pecém. Especialistas que participaram da terceira edição do Atlantic Convergence, em Lisboa, apontam o que está por trás desse boom: energia renovável em abundância e o hub de cabos submarinos de Fortaleza, que representa o segundo ponto de maior conectividade do mundo. Nesse contexto, o Estado caminha para se tornar uma potência global de processamento de dados, avalia o especialista em Transformação Digital e Inteligência Artificial do Banco Mundial, Luciano Charlita de Freitas. "O Ceará já tem histórico de investimentos em infraestrutura digital, um cinturão que cobre todos os municípios e recebe cabos submarinos. Entendemos que o Ceará pode se tornar um exportador global de dados, não só para o mercado brasileiro, mas também para fora do Brasil", lista. A agenda de expansão da geração e distribuição de energia foi desenhada antes do boom dos data centers, o que posiciona o Estado na dianteira, segundo o especialista. "A capacidade instalada de data centers no Estado deve aumentar muito nos próximos anos. O Ceará tem força de trabalho qualificada, conhecimento sobre o negócio e posição estratégica dentro do Brasil para continuar nessa agenda", observa. O Banco Mundial conversa com a gestão estadual para financiar projetos de tecnologia no Ceará. A instituição tem portfólio de US$ 1 bilhão no Brasil e já fez investimentos em Hdrogênio Verde. Data centers menores O Ceará também pode ficar na dianteira no mercado de data centers de menor porte, instalados o mais perto possível dos usuários finais, chamados de edge. Ao contrário dos grandes empreendimentos, esses data centers ficam em regiões periféricas, para permitir o processamento e a entrega de dados de forma mais rápida. De acordo com o CEO da holding de tecnologia e telecomunicações SAMM, Carlos Eduardo Sedeh, "os data centers menores vão permitir, por exemplo, que a população do Ceará tenha acesso a serviços como carros autônomos, inferências, internet das coisas, sensorização e cidades inteligentes". "Tudo isso a partir de data centers descentralizados", frisa. O executivo destaca que o Brasil deve registrar expansão dos pequenos empreendimentos nos próximos anos, em paralelo à atração de projetos em grande escala. "A economia digital está se tornando realidade. A demanda está aumentando muito, não só em telecomunicações, mas também em computação em nuvem e outros serviços", afirma. Segundo Sedeh, o ambiente de negócios criado na Zona de Processamento e Exportação (ZPE) do Pecém é um atrativo para as empresas. "Criar uma ZPE numa área que carece de desenvolvimento e direcionar energia e esforços para trazer as empresas é uma estratégia muito acertada. Não existe investimento dessa magnitude sem investimento do governo e estabilidade jurídica", diz. DE-CIX avalia levar interconexão a Fortaleza O Brasil desponta como um dos mercados com maior demanda por serviços de conectividade e processamento de dados, segundo o CEO do grupo DE-CIX, Ivo Ivanov. A empresa oferece interconexão premium e opera vários pontos de troca de tráfego ao redor do mundo. "No nosso negócio, o Brasil é o mercado com crescimento mais acelerado neste ano. Chegamos a mais de 100 clientes atendidos. Estamos oferecendo a primeira plataforma de interconexão de inteligência artificial do país", afirma. Com operação em São Paulo e no Rio de Janeiro, a empresa estuda levar seus serviços a Fortaleza, que caminha para se tornar o segundo maior mercado brasileiro, segundo Ivanov. "Temos muita vontade de construir do Brasil para o Brasil, e não entregar serviços de fora. Fortaleza está no nosso mapa. Vemos como a inovação impulsiona a infraestrutura e como a infraestrutura precisa ser implantada em todos os lugares", aponta. Ivanov ressalta que, com a crescente digitalização, as instalações devem ficar cada vez mais próximas dos usuários para diminuir o tempo de resposta. Para o executivo, com a chegada de pequenos e grandes data centers, o país deve atentar para a soberania e a proteção das informações processadas. "Dados de organizações e de pessoas que vivem no país devem ficar no país, e não ser enviados para treinamentos nos Estados Unidos ou na Europa. É uma questão de soberania. Também é preciso criar ambiente de inovação. Riscos sempre existem, mas temos de proteger e garantir que sejam mitigados", completa. *A repórter viajou a convite da DE-CIX para a Atlantic Convergence em Lisboa.

artigo.texto: At the OCP Global Summit 2026, we presented a compressor architecture designed around a problem that does not get enough attention: what happens when the cooling plant is not running at peak load. Most data center cooling conversations focus on peak capacity. But most cooling plants spend a significant share of their operating hours nowhere near it. Mild weather, seasonal transitions, and cold-plate supply temperatures rising toward 45°C push the system toward low-lift conditions, where the pressure ratio across the compressor is low but refrigerant flow remains high. This is where conventional compressor architectures lose their efficiency advantage, and where operators quietly burn energy they do not need to. As the industry moves toward air-cooled systems to reduce water dependence, the compressor faces a wider operating envelope than ever before. Conventional two-stage centrifugal compressors lock both impellers to a single shaft speed, and at their design point they perform well. But the fixed speed ratio between stages limits how precisely the pressure split can be optimized, and at low lift near the free-cooling boundary, pushing high refrigerant flow through two compression stages when only one is needed creates parasitic losses at exactly the operating points where the plant spends much of its time. Decoupling the Rotors The architecture we presented takes a different approach. Instead of coupling both impellers to a single shaft, the design uses two independent magnetic-bearing rotors, each driven by its own motor and variable-speed drive. The two stages can run at different speeds, and the second stage can be isolated entirely when it is not needed. This gives operators two distinct operating regions. Under high ambient temperatures, both stages run together with independently tuned speeds, improving stage matching and peak isentropic efficiency by 2% to 3% over a coupled-speed reference. Near the free-cooling threshold, integrated bypass valves switch the system to single-stage operation, eliminating redundant compression work. At representative duty points, this reduces compressor power from 80 kW to 48 kW at the same cooling capacity, a 40% reduction, while improving low-lift efficiency by up to 15% and increasing usable low-lift flow by 70%. At a pressure ratio of 1.6 and 22% of reference inlet flow, the architecture reaches 81% isentropic efficiency without inlet guide vanes, compared with 73% for a coupled-speed compressor fitted with inlet guide vanes. Keeping Cooling Continuous During Mode Transitions For facilities that prioritize refrigerant-pump free cooling backed by mechanical cooling, the transition between modes is where things can go wrong. In liquid-cooled AI environments, even brief interruptions can trigger server thermal throttling or downtime. The risk during a mechanical-to-free-cooling transition is well understood: rapid depressurization can cause stored liquid to flash at the pump inlet, starving flow and creating a transient capacity gap. The independent-speed architecture addresses this by preconditioning the refrigerant in single-stage mode before pump takeover, reducing inlet mixture volume by 78.4% compared with a direct two-stage-to-pump handover. The reverse transition carries its own risk. Conventional compressors require an iterative startup sequence, slowing condenser fans to raise condensing pressure before the compressor can reach its operating envelope. Single-stage startup eliminates that delay: the compressor begins operating at a low pressure ratio and builds capacity before ramping up to the second stage, while also supporting faster restarts after power restoration. Fitting Two Shafts into One Footprint A conventional dual-shaft arrangement would be approximately 25% longer than a single-shaft unit, and in space-constrained air-cooled chillers, that extra length comes directly out of the space available for heat exchangers, fans, and service access. The architecture we developed maintains the axial footprint of a conventional single-shaft compressor by placing outboard magnetic bearings inside volute recesses and combining seals, sensors, and backup bearings into integrated function units, alongside compact motors rated up to 70 kW at 41,000 rpm. At the OCP Global Summit 2026, our compressor technology received the “2026 GW-Scale Open AIDC Excellent Technical Presentation Award,” recognizing its contribution to more efficient and reliable thermal architectures for next-generation AI data centers. From Compressor Innovation to Full-Chain Cooling A compressor is only one part of the cooling system. Clivet brings this core cooling-source technology into a full-chain liquid cooling approach that spans cooling sources, high-capacity coolant distribution units (CDUs), fan walls and terminal units. Designed to prioritize free cooling while retaining dependable mechanical-cooling backup, this integrated portfolio supports scalable thermal management across different climates and AI infrastructure requirements. At this year’s OCP Global Summit, Midea also appeared in the list of participating companies in the NVIDIA MGX ecosystem. The inclusion highlights Midea’s growing role in the broader AI computing infrastructure ecosystem, where effective thermal management increasingly depends on coordination across equipment, systems and industry platforms. As AI facilities move toward gigawatt-scale computing, we see the next step as bringing core cooling innovations together with system-level engineering and open ecosystem collaboration. Building on Midea and Clivet’s “equipment + systems + ecosystem” approach, our goal is to help deliver more efficient, reliable and sustainable cooling infrastructure for the next generation of AI data centers. For more information about Clivet's liquid cooling portfolio for AI data centers, visit www.clivet.com.

artigo.texto: The Kentucky Digital Infrastructure Resource launched on Thursday, Oct. 22, and its leaders say it hopes to educate and provide resources to communities on all data center-related topics. The nonprofit will be able to answer questions on data centers, provide information on a variety of data center topics, and give access to experts for community leaders. “What we found is that there’s a lot of conversation around data center projects and in these communities, but a lot of times, local leaders don’t have access to the information they need from subject matter experts so that they can make good decisions based on the specific needs of their community,” Kerri Richardson, the managing director of KyDIR, said. “This nonprofit is stepping in to convene all of that information and offer that to local leaders, so that they can make good decisions and ask good questions.” Richardson said not only is the resource for local leaders, but it’s also for community members too. “Our metric of success is: Do communities feel better evaluating a data center project that may be approaching them to build a new development? If communities feel that they have the information that they need, that they have good processes, that is the metric of success for these digital infrastructure resources,” Richardson said. The nonprofit was created by Kentuckians and for Kentuckians, so all information will be tailored to Kentucky data center questions. However, Richardson notes that not all data center projects are the same in Kentucky. “Let’s talk about Paducah and the proposal to add a data center to the former site of the gaseous diffusion plant. It’s a much different scenario for Paducah since that is heavy industrial land. It’s been used for heavy industrial a long time, and the federal government is also involved in that,” Richardson said. “That’s a different scenario than perhaps a rural county in another part of the state, or on which a data center project might be entirely new construction. Different scenarios, different energy providers, different local governments and different planning and zoning.” Despite those differences, Richardson said all communities should be able to find advice through the information they have on their site or through a provided expert. “Our hope is that local leaders can contact Kentucky Digital Infrastructure Resource and ask about — I need information about electric use, I need information about land use, I need information about watershed. We can be sort of the convener to help those leaders find the subject matter expert that they might need,” Richardson said. She noted that KyDIR does not advocate for any specific data center project. The organization's website does list companies that financially support it, and one is data center-related. Richardson said each company is either in Kentucky, works in Kentucky or has interest in working in Kentucky. “We want to be very clear about who those supporters are so people can evaluate the information that they’re receiving,” Richardson said. Not only are its supporters from Kentucky, but the nonprofit’s founders have also been directly involved with business in Kentucky, including Bill Jones of Paducah, a former executive at US Bank and former chair of the Kentucky Chamber of Commerce. “The board hopes we'll be that convening agency that can help communities figure that out because they feel that an informed local community is a local community that makes good decisions,” Richardson said. Since the nonprofit was announced Thursday, organization leaders haven’t received much reaction yet, but Richardson said they hope people will appreciate what the nonprofit provides. “I hope that as we begin our work in the state, some of the response will be relief," Richardson said. "Thank goodness that there’s finally one place where we can go to get information, and if we have questions, we can ask further questions. And from a resource that is very clear about who they are and who supports them, because again, transparency is really important here.” KyDIR’s website is live, and visitors can only send speaker request forms. Richardson said the website will continue to grow over time. “We’re going to be adding on information about Kentucky energy use, water use, land use — a lot of different topics that tend to come up frequently when we talk about data centers in Kentucky specifically. This information has been received by our subject matter experts, and sometimes we’re reaching out to other states to see what are your best practices, and we’ll add those to our website,” Richardson said. To learn more, visit kydir.org.

artigo.texto: Amazon presents on data center water resource usage ST. JOSEPH COUNTY, Ind. (WSBT) — Amazon Data Center representatives presented their water usage plan in front of the St. Joseph County Water Resources Advisory Board on Thursday. The presentation from Amazon at the St. Joseph County Water Resources Advisory Board meeting shared their work on topics such as commitment to water, environmental stewardship and construction dewatering regarding their ongoing construction at the New Carlisle data center site. A major topic was how much water would be used, which was addressed early in the presentation, with Amazon presenters saying they are planning to make their water usage as effective as possible They said that, on average, they will use 18 million gallons of water for cooling once construction is complete per year. "This is about less than a golf course annual use, and present about 0.9 percent of the total water produced by town of New Carlisle in 2024, and also we are funding 114 million for water and wastewater infrastructure for development as well as future development in the area," said Pubudu Ranasinghe, Amazon senior water strategy manager. Board president David Jeffers said that while he is satisfied with Amazon only expecting to use 35 to 40 gallons a minute, he was hoping a different answer about what type of cooling system would be used was given. "They're not using a closed-loop system like some data centers are. It's an open discharge once it's the water is heated up. Basically, it gets discharged to the wastewater system," said David Jeffers, St. Joseph County Water Resources Advisory Board president. He added that confirming where the water will be coming from and the protections involved in that were important. "The aquifer that they're taking it from is actually from the town of New Carlisle's water wells. So it kind of gives you, which is which is really overseen by the state of Indiana, so there's oversight on multiple levels of that," said Jeffers. Microsoft was also set to present at the meeting but was unable to attend. They have committed to presenting at the next meeting in January.

By combining residential and utility-scale storage, renewable energy solutions and energy management technologies, the company is building a more flexible and resilient electricity system while supporting Japan’s long-term decarbonization goals. We have also experienced increasingly hot summers, which place additional pressure on electricity demand and reinforce the importance of maintaining a reliable energy system. Events affecting global fuel markets can therefore influence electricity prices, while natural disasters such as earthquakes can interrupt supply itself. These realities have led both businesses and consumers to pay much closer attention to energy security than they did in the past. As dependence on electrification continues to increase across every sector of society, the importance of building a resilient energy system will only become greater. Ultimately, energy has become an essential element of economic stability, industrial competitiveness and everyday life. artigo.texto: IREN Co-CEO Daniel Roberts Says Firm’s Data Centers Carry No Debt As Funding Worries Hit Stock - After recent pressure on the IREN stock, co-CEO Daniel Roberts said that the company's data centers are supported fully by cash, and the company had no debt against assets. - Under recent three-year contracts, customer prepayments cover 45% to 55% of GPU expenses, Roberts said. - IREN's Microsoft agreement covered 96% of GPU expenses, with prepayments at 6%, and non-investment payment-grade customers paid 9%. Shares of IREN Limited (IREN) edged lower in pre-market trading on Tuesday after co-CEO Daniel Roberts said that the company's data centers did not carry any debt. Roberts responded to investors' concern over how the artificial intelligence (AI) cloud providers will fund their expansion. Roberts said on X that IREN has paid for their data center construction in cash so far. Adding to it, he said that the sites can support their own financing once they come online with contracted customers. Robert laid out the process step by step. Customers must first sign multi-year take-or-pay contracts, which require payment whether or not they use the capacity. On recent three-year deals, he said prepayments covered 45% to 55% of the cost of the graphics processing units (GPUs).https://x.com/danroberts0101/status/2112200081034129419?s=20 He added that lenders mostly fund the rest, with the GPUs serving as collateral. Robert added that Iren's Microsoft (MSFT) contract was supported by an A-rated facility at 6% or so. That, plus prepayments, accounts for 96% of the GPU spending. One customer without an investment-grade rating at Iren's McKenzie site in British Columbia was borrowing at a fixed 9%. The loan and prepayment more than pay for the whole cost of the GPU, the co-CEO added. He acknowledged that future debt will price at whatever the market charges. But he said a payback of about 2 years on recent contracts means "a wider spread barely moves the economics." Demand Outruns Build Capacity According to Roberts, customer demand exceeds what IREN can build. The company's 2026 capacity is largely sold out, he added, saying recent 3-year contracts are priced at more than double last year's level. Demand for capacity arriving in 2027 is several times oversubscribed, and discussions on 2028 have begun. The holdup in the industry is not signing deals, he said. Getting GPUs online is the issue, as announced capacity keeps sleeping across the sector. Pressure On Neocoloud Stocks Continue Neoclouds, the specialized AI cloud providers, have been under pressure through the past week. The stock has been down over 20% over the past week. Investors became increasingly worried after debt pressures at CoreWeave (CRWV) and a research firm warned that over 80% of neoclouds might no longer be able to operate independently by 2030. Retail Chatter For IREN Surges IREN stock was down over 4% in pre-market trade, trading at $26. On Stocktwits retail sentiment around IREN remained in the ‘extremely bullish’ zone, with ‘high’ chatter levels over the past day. According to platform data, chatter around IREN has been up over 952% over the past 30 days. One user on Stocktwits said that the IREN stock had erased all of the previous day's gain, and it would need to rise 70% to reach above $46 again.

artigo.texto: CATL Unveils Dual-Electric Range Extension Battery to Accelerate Electric Heavy-Duty Truck Adoption BEIJING, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold, CATL's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns. CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models: Battery Asset Service Partners and Energy Replenishment Service Partners. These models allow partners to participate in battery asset services and energy replenishment, extending their role beyond one-off vehicle sales to ongoing operations. artigo.texto: Trump defende que empresas de data centers paguem "dividendos" às comunidades Donald Trump defendeu que empresas de data centers paguem "dividendos" às comunidades locais para reduzir a oposição popular gerada pelo alto consumo de água e energia dessas instalações de IA. O ex-presidente também exigiu que esses empreendimentos gerem sua própria eletricidade e repassem o excedente à rede elétrica. A pressão pública sobre o setor já levou iniciativas de compartilhamento de recursos por empresas como a Anthropic e por Elon Musk. O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta quarta-feira que as empresas que constroem data centers deveriam pagar um "dividendo" às comunidades onde eles estão localizados, caso queiram que esses empreendimentos sejam bem-aceitos. "Tenho acompanhado o processo de perto e percebi que data centers que eram altamente impopulares em determinada região tornaram-se extremamente populares quando um acordo financeiro foi fechado", disse Trump em uma postagem no Truth Social. Os data centers, que impulsionam o avanço da IA, tornaram-se um ponto de tensão política em comunidades por todo o país, devido às grandes quantidades de água e energia que consomem, com a oposição unindo eleitores de todas as tendências ideológicas. O governo Trump, que priorizou o rápido desenvolvimento da IA para competir com a China, também observou a mudança no sentimento dos eleitores. "Exigi que os novos e grandes -- em alguns casos, gigantescos -- data centers produzam sua própria eletricidade e doem ou vendam qualquer excedente de volta à comunidade local ou à rede elétrica", disse Trump em sua postagem. Trump afirmou em fevereiro que as grandes empresas de tecnologia devem construir suas próprias usinas de energia para seus data centers, a fim de proteger os consumidores do aumento nas contas. A gigante de IA Anthropic e o bilionário Elon Musk apresentaram, nos últimos dias, planos para compartilhar parte dos frutos do boom da inteligência artificial. A criadora dos modelos Claude anunciou no fim de semana que está destinando 5% de suas ações a um novo fundo para o "bem público", enquanto Musk se comprometeu na segunda-feira a doar uma ação da SpaceX para "cada criança nos Estados Unidos", defendendo essas distribuições diretas à medida que o setor em expansão enfrenta o escrutínio público.

artigo.texto: Lead On October 20, 2026, EVE Energy and Chery Automobile unveiled the latest engineering milestones in all-solid-state batteries on the same day. At its Chengdu base, EVE Energy released the “Longquan No. 3 2.0” all-solid-state battery, targeting implantable brain-computer interfaces with a volumetric energy density of 1,045 Wh/L. On the same day, Chery unveiled a roadmap for its “Kunpeng S” all-solid-state battery trial production line at the 2026 Global Innovation Conference, with production scheduled to begin in 2027; a day earlier, its “Rhino” all-solid-state battery pack had just rolled off the line and made its debut. These latest moves by the two companies offer two equally crucial yet distinctly positioned samples for observing the real cadence of China’s solid-state battery transition from technical validation to engineering validation. I. EVE Energy’s “Scenario Wedge”: An Alternative Validation Path Beyond the Automotive Narrative 1.1 Longquan No. 3 2.0 In public communication, EVE Energy’s newly released “Longquan No. 3 2.0” may easily be folded into the broad narrative of “a new breakthrough in all-solid-state batteries,” but its technical positioning calls for a more precise reading. The product adopts an anode-free route and achieves a volumetric energy density of 1,045 Wh/L in a titanium-cased coin cell measuring 23 mm in diameter and 4 mm in thickness, explicitly serving the implantable brain-computer interface segment—a field with extremely stringent demands on volume, safety, and long-term stability. It follows a different product logic from automotive traction batteries: automotive all-solid-state batteries pursue a comprehensive balance of high specific energy, high rate capability, and wide-temperature cycling, whereas the core constraint for implantable medical power sources is to achieve the highest possible volumetric energy density within an extremely small space while eliminating leakage and thermal-runaway risks through a solid electrolyte. 1.2 Longquan No. 4 In March this year, the “Longquan No. 4” 60 Ah all-solid-state battery for traction applications had already rolled off the line and can cycle under a pressure of ≤5 MPa, showing preliminary potential for practical use. EVE’s published roadmap also points to launching an all-solid-state battery 1.0 at 350 Wh/kg and 800 Wh/L in 2026, and advancing a 2.0 product exceeding 1,000 Wh/L in 2028. But the decision to make the implantable brain-computer interface the debut scenario for “Longquan No. 3 2.0” reveals a pragmatic validation strategy: at a stage when large-scale engineering validation of automotive-grade all-solid-state batteries still takes time, first complete the technical loop and manufacturing ramp-up in a niche market with clear scenario constraints, higher cost tolerance, and a greater weighting on safety. The implantable medical segment is far too small in volume to support power-battery-scale capacity, yet it imposes sufficiently rigorous validation requirements on the reliability of the “anode-free + solid electrolyte” scheme under extreme conditions, and its engineering experience can feed back into interface control and packaging processes for later automotive products. EVE Energy also signed strategic agreements with Jingyu Medical and Sichuan Provincial People’s Hospital to forge a chain from R&D to industrialization to clinical application, showing that this is not a mere concept launch but a concrete deployment with clear downstream uptake. Compared with anode-containing routes, the anode-free route is more like an extreme challenge with zero buffer. Anode-free design discards pre-existing anode active material and allows lithium ions to deposit directly on a current collector (such as copper foil) to form the anode. This removes the “buffer layer” of a conventional anode and magnifies the risk to the extreme. Extreme demands for uniform deposition: Without anode material as a backstop, lithium deposition must be even more uniform than in a lithium-metal anode. Any non-uniformity can directly trigger lithium dendrites, pierce the solid electrolyte, and cause a short circuit. Irreversible accumulation of “dead lithium”: Lithium dendrites and volume changes cause the SEI film to repeatedly fracture and re-form, continuously consuming limited active lithium and forming “dead lithium” that can no longer participate in reactions—directly manifesting as rapid decay in cycle life. Some analyses explicitly note that anode-free solid-state batteries are “more technically difficult and pose greater challenges to cycle stability.” II. Chery’s “Manufacturing Readiness”: What the PACK Roll-off and Trial Line Signify Chery has recently disclosed a denser set of information, but several milestones of different natures need to be distinguished. The October 19 debut of the “Rhino all-solid-state battery PACK” rolling off the line means the technology has advanced to the system-integration level—cells are integrated into a pack, involving thermal management, structural safety, and BMS adaptation, a form closer to a vehicle-ready engineering configuration than cell roll-off. The “Kunpeng S” all-solid-state trial production line unveiled at the Global Innovation Conference on October 20, scheduled to begin production in 2027, sets its time anchor on building manufacturing capability. Chery Chairman Yin Tongyue previously laid out the vehicle-installation cadence: hybrid solid-liquid batteries will be installed in vehicles in Q4 2026, and all-solid-state batteries will begin on-vehicle validation in 2027. The trial line addresses whether cells meeting automotive-grade consistency requirements can be produced; the PACK roll-off addresses whether those cells can be safely and stably integrated into a usable pack; and “on-vehicle validation” remains essentially a validation stage, years away from large-scale consumer delivery. artigo.texto: ‘No question’ data centers will be considered critical infrastructure, top House intel Dem says Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., said the AI-focused facilities are going to be even more critical than their traditional data center counterparts because “so much more functionality is going to rely on their health and existence.” The growing web of data centers across the United States that are needed to power artificial intelligence technologies is destined to be deemed critical infrastructure, according to the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee. During an event at the Brookings Institution on Wednesday, Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn. — the powerful House panel’s ranking member — said “I think there’s no question” that data centers will be considered critical infrastructure in the future, adding that “they're going to be even more important than the network data centers that we've been living with for 40 years now because so much more functionality is going to rely on their health and existence.” U.S. critical infrastructure services are currently divided into 16 sectors, which range in size and scope from water and wastewater facilities to IT infrastructure and financial services. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency oversees the security of these sectors, which have been deemed so vital to U.S. interests that their destruction could have national security or other serious repercussions. Although AI data centers already underpin some of the critical infrastructure, they are not yet deemed to be a standalone sector. Ongoing global conflicts, however, have highlighted the importance of these new data centers, with the facilities increasingly becoming military targets. In March, Iran hit Amazon Web Services data centers in the United Arab Emirates and a third commercial data center in Bahrain with drones as Tehran moved to target U.S. tech companies’ regional interests as part of the war. In recent weeks, Russia and Ukraine have also traded strikes on data centers within each country. Himes said securing U.S. data centers will ultimately result in the need for a “robust compute infrastructure,” with technologies likely having to “fragment and disperse” key services so that “critical functions are redundant and protected.” “They haven't had to think in those terms quite yet because this is a new thing,” he added. “But as more and more of the agents, and as more and more of the commercial economy depends on these things, they will start to look more like JP Morgan's resilience centers than they look like today's data centers.” JPMorganChase launched its $1.5 trillion, 10-year Security and Resiliency Initiative last year to help drive investments in industries deemed critical to U.S. national and economic security interests. The firm announced on Monday that it has invested $5 billion in startups over the first year of its effort, although it did not disclose most of the recipients of those funds. AI data center construction has become increasingly controversial, with some Americans and lawmakers criticizing the facilities’ power use and water consumption. Although the House overwhelmingly passed bipartisan legislation, known as the Ratepayer Protection Act, last month that would push the companies building data centers to pay for their electrical use, Himes said the measure “wasn't meaningful or substantive” and noted that it hasn’t been voted on yet in the Senate. Himes said data center backlash is “driven by an eminently solvable problem,” which is addressing the underlying question of, “‘How do we equitably divide up the costs of building the compute?’” He added, however, that continuing data center construction is inevitable, saying that “the experts tell me that the underlying demand for compute still looks infinite, and as long as that is a true fact, the build will happen.”

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no CEO do HSBC alerta que boom da IA não torna todos os data centers bons investimentos Publicado 20/10/2026 • 10:07 | Atualizado há 21 horas KEY POINTS Pexels A inteligência artificial (IA) é uma tecnologia transformadora que merece investimentos, mas os investidores precisam ser criteriosos ao escolher projetos de data centers, segundo o presidente-executivo de um dos maiores bancos do mundo. Em entrevista a Dan Murphy, da CNBC, nesta terça-feira (20), Georges Elhedery, CEO do HSBC, classificou a inteligência artificial como “um importante facilitador para reformular e reinventar todos os nossos negócios e atividades”. “Ela vai devolver muito poder aos nossos colegas por causa do nível de produtividade que proporciona. Portanto, será transformadora, e estamos certamente em uma jornada para adotá-la”, afirmou. Segundo ele, a IA também ajudará a “reformular o banco”. No entanto, ao abordar os investimentos em infraestrutura que sustenta essa tecnologia, Elhedery recomendou cautela, em vez de uma aposta indiscriminada no setor. Leia também: HSBC amplia receita e mantém lucro estável no 1º trimestre, com alta de depósitos e pressão de custos “É preciso ser seletivo”, afirmou. “É necessário avaliar a qualidade dos contratos de locação e os preços estabelecidos nesses contratos. Nem todos apresentam um nível de qualidade que permita sustentá-los com confiança. Alguns podem ser mais desafiadores.” O HSBC foi classificado pela S&P Global, no ano passado, como o sétimo maior banco do mundo e o maior credor da Europa, com ativos próximos de US$ 3 trilhões. Com sede em Londres, a instituição atua tanto no financiamento quanto na operação de data centers. Em seu relatório anual de 2025, o HSBC afirmou que pretende se tornar “o banco líder para ecossistemas de transição de rápido crescimento”, destacando que sua carteira de clientes abrange setores como data centers e inteligência artificial. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Os complexos de data centers abrigam os servidores que sustentam a IA e a computação em nuvem. Nos últimos anos, o setor passou por uma expansão bilionária, impulsionada pela crescente demanda por capacidade computacional. Segundo a consultoria McKinsey, os gastos globais com data centers podem atingir US$ 7 trilhões até 2030. Para financiar a construção dessas instalações, grandes empresas de tecnologia têm recorrido cada vez mais ao crédito privado e à emissão de dívidas. O endividamento relacionado à IA, porém, está se tornando uma fonte de tensão nos mercados financeiros. O custo do capital está aumentando, enquanto empresas acumulam grandes volumes de dívida na corrida para financiar o desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial e a expansão da infraestrutura de data centers. Durante o GZERO Summit, organizado pela LSEG e pelo Eurasia Group em Londres no início deste mês, Mohamed El-Erian, principal consultor econômico da Allianz e ex-CEO da PIMCO, destacou a disputa por financiamento entre governos e empresas ligadas à IA como uma fonte de pressão sobre os mercados de títulos de dívida. Leia também: HSBC impulsiona Bolsas da Europa após elevar meta de rentabilidade “Os governos estão tomando emprestado o que precisam tomar, além de refinanciarem suas dívidas a taxas de juros mais altas”, afirmou. “E temos as grandes empresas de tecnologia que operam em larga escala na nuvem, que captaram US$ 200 bilhões em financiamento por meio de títulos de dívida no ano passado e provavelmente vão captar US$ 1 trilhão dessa forma neste ano. Elas não são sensíveis aos rendimentos. Não são sensíveis aos spreads de crédito, porque estão apostando em algo verdadeiramente transformador.” Os rendimentos dos títulos de dívida emitidos por diversas grandes economias atingiram, em 2026, os níveis mais elevados em várias décadas. O movimento ocorre em meio a preocupações com os elevados déficits públicos e o aumento do endividamento, além dos temores de que a inflação permaneça persistente e os bancos centrais adotem posturas mais rigorosas. No início deste ano, o JPMorgan Chase estimou que a emissão de dívidas relacionadas à inteligência artificial poderá alcançar US$ 4,1 trilhões até o fim da década, à medida que empresas de data centers e outros negócios ligados à IA ampliam os investimentos para expandir sua capacidade. 🔷 Canal 562 ClaroTV+ | Canal 562 Sky | Canal 592 Vivo | Canal 187 Oi | Operadoras regionais 🔷 TV SINAL ABERTO: parabólicas canal 562 🔷 ONLINE: www.timesbrasil.com.br | YouTube 🔷 FAST Channels: Samsung TV Plus, LG Channels, TCL Channels, Pluto TV, Roku, Zapping | Novos Streamings Este conteúdo foi fornecido pela CNBC Internacional e a responsabilidade exclusiva pela tradução para o português é do Times Brasil. artigo.texto: Pará tem potencial para liderar restauração florestal com créditos de carbono Conciliar a produção agrícola com a conservação das florestas, ampliar a restauração de áreas degradadas e transformar a preservação ambiental em oportunidades econômicas estão entre os desafios e as possibilidades para o Pará. Em entrevista ao Grupo Liberal, Leonardo Sobral, diretor de Florestas e Restauração do Imaflora (Instituto de Manejo e Certificação Florestal e Agrícola), destaca o potencial do estado para avançar nessa agenda por meio de incentivos econômicos, do mercado de carbono, da bioeconomia e das concessões florestais para restauração. O especialista também ressalta a importância de valorizar os produtos da floresta em pé e de fortalecer iniciativas que conciliem conservação ambiental, produção sustentável e geração de renda. * Repórter: Jéssica Nascimento Por Liberal Entrevista

artigo.texto: A 35ª edição da Mercopar recebeu, nesta quinta-feira (22), dois painéis do MobiConecta 2026. Os encontros abordaram a infraestrutura digital e as perspectivas para o desenvolvimento regional, com destaque para conectividade, inteligência artificial, data centers e os desafios do setor empresarial. O primeiro painel, intitulado “IndTech: a nova infraestrutura digital do século XXI”, reuniu especialistas e representantes do poder público e da indústria para debater os avanços tecnológicos e os impactos no desenvolvimento das cidades e dos negócios. Antes do debate, foi realizada a assinatura simbólica de um protocolo de intenções entre Caxias do Sul, Balneário Pinhal e o MobiCaxias, com o objetivo de fortalecer a cooperação em infraestrutura digital. A iniciativa considera o município do Litoral Norte ter sido selecionado como ponto de ancoragem do Cabo Submarino Malbec de fibra óptica, ligados à Meta e a perspectiva de implantação de novos data centers no Estado. Conforme o vice-presidente do MobiCaxias, Fabiano Vergani, o documento prevê o intercâmbio de conhecimentos e a identificação de oportunidades conjuntas em tecnologias emergentes. A proposta busca aproximar a Serra Gaúcha do Litoral Norte e impulsionar o desenvolvimento regional por meio do projeto IndTech, que pretende conectar indústrias de diferentes setores por uma infovia. O superintendente de Governança Pública da Prefeitura de Caxias do Sul, Samuel Adami, destacou a intenção de antecipar a revisão do Plano Diretor Municipal para adequar o planejamento urbano à expansão tecnológica. A partir de 2027, o município pretende promover discussões com a sociedade e o setor produtivo para contribuir com a revisão. Ao final do primeiro painel, o diretor-executivo do MobiCaxias, Rogério Rodrigues, falou sobre a realização do MobiConecta 2026 e a importância dos debates para o futuro tecnológico e da infraestrutura regional. Participaram o diretor comercial da Bridia Consultoria e Engenharia de Data Centers, Vicente Brandão; o vice-prefeito e secretário municipal de Planejamento de Balneário Pinhal, Jorge Luis de Souza Fonseca; o superintendente de Governança Pública de Caxias do Sul, Samuel Rodrigues Adami; o CEO da Algcom, Lissandro Gerhardt; e o consultor sênior e fundador da dooop, Danniel Pozza. A mediação ficou a cargo da advogada especialista em Direito Empresarial e Digital e coordenadora do Comitê IndTech da Câmara de Atração e Retenção de Investimentos do MobiCaxias, Andrea Rebechi de Abreu Fattori. Na sequência, o Espaço Conhecimento da Mercopar recebeu o painel “O futuro digital da Serra Gaúcha na visão de quem empreende”, que discutiu desafios, necessidades e oportunidades para o crescimento dos negócios na região. Os painelistas discutiram como as novas tecnologias estão transformando os processos empresariais, da criação ao acompanhamento e à entrega de produtos e serviços. O diretor Executivo da Marcopolo Rail, Petras Amaral Santos, destacou o potencial de expansão da conectividade entre os modais de transporte e a importância de acompanhar as tendências tecnológicas para oferecer soluções que atendam melhor às necessidades dos usuários. O CTIO da Randoncorp, César Augusto Ferreira, ressaltou que a tecnologia é fundamental para sustentar o fluxo de informações. O executivo também destacou a expansão da inteligência artificial sendo o futuro das indústrias. Participaram o diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação (CTIO) da Randoncorp, César Augusto Ferreira; o diretor industrial do Grupo Florense, Felipe Luis Corradi, o vice-presidente do MobiCaxias e fundador e CEO da XPLAY e da FIXER, Fabiano André Vergani; e o diretor-executivo da Marcopolo Rail, Petras Amaral Santos. artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- CATL addressed recent investor concerns over demand for the new energy sector in 2027 in an investor relations filing dated October 20. From the company's vantage point, industry demand that year remains promising. CATL noted that while overall domestic passenger car sales dipped in 2026, the electrification rate is climbing rapidly. So is the average battery capacity per vehicle. As a result, the power battery market for domestic new energy passenger cars still managed positive growth. Image source: CATL Electrification among domestic commercial vehicles is accelerating as well. In Europe, the shift to electric power shows continuity, with a steady stream of competitive new models hitting the market. Meanwhile, the potential for electrification in other regions is gradually unlocking. Data shows domestic power battery installations climbed 17% year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, while sales (including exports) surged 38%—growth driven largely by higher battery capacity per vehicle. The average battery capacity for new energy vehicles hit 69.5 kWh during that period, a 32% jump, with both pure electric and plug-in hybrid models seeing significant gains. Image source: Baidu Stock Tong CATL's response comes against a backdrop of sustained pressure on its stock price. As of October 21, shares had halved from their historical peak. Several brokerages have already trimmed their profit forecasts for CATL for 2027. Adding to the strain are shifts in tax policy: the value-added tax rebate on battery exports was cut from 9% to 6% starting April 1, 2026, and will be eliminated entirely on January 1, 2027. CATL indicated it is in talks with customers to share the burden of these policy shocks.

artigo.texto: A busca por autonomia, segurança operacional e independência da rede elétrica tradicional tornou-se uma prioridade crescente para brasileiros, empresas e produtores rurais. De acordo com um levantamento recente da Descarbonize Soluções, empresa especializada em transição energética, os últimos 12 meses registraram mais de 50 mil consultas relacionadas a soluções de armazenamento de eletricidade no Google, representando um salto anual de 48%. O destaque absoluto da temporada fica por conta dos Sistemas de Armazenamento em Baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês), que ultrapassaram 104 mil buscas e dispararam impressionantes 120% no período. Em termos de volume total, as tradicionais baterias estacionárias mantêm a liderança isolada, acumulando 248 mil pesquisas online. Segundo dados pesquisados pela redação do CenárioMT, o estado de Mato Grosso figura com destaque entre os dez estados brasileiros que mais demonstraram interesse pelo tema do armazenamento avançado de energia (BESS), refletindo a necessidade do agronegócio e das indústrias locais em buscar estabilidade frente aos desafios climáticos e gargalos de distribuição. Fatores econômicos e leilões da Aneel impulsionam o setor O aquecimento do mercado não é impulsionado apenas pelo desejo de autossuficiência, mas também por importantes marcos regulatórios e econômicos. A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) colocou em consulta pública os primeiros leilões voltados especificamente ao armazenamento de energia no país, com licitações agendadas para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. Além disso, um fator histórico mudou o jogo: pela primeira vez, o custo dessas estruturas de armazenamento tornou-se inferior ao das usinas termelétricas a gás. Dados da BloombergNEF apontam que, desde 2022, os investimentos em instalações de porte utilitário caíram mais de 50%, com uma retração de 27% registrada apenas no último ano, tornando a tecnologia comercialmente viável em larga escala. Radiografia do interesse no país O mapeamento das buscas online — realizado entre setembro de 2025 e agosto de 2026 — avaliou os termos mais procurados por estado proporcionalmente à sua população: - Baterias estacionárias: Lideram em volume absoluto com 248 mil pesquisas (+22%). - Bess: Aceleração recorde de 120% e mais de 104 mil buscas. - Bateria para energia solar e kits off-grid: Mantêm crescimento expressivo, com altas entre 22% e 53%. No ranking dos estados que mais buscaram por BESS, Santa Catarina lidera o interesse — embalada por investimentos recentes do BNDES de R$ 280 milhões para a construção de uma fábrica de baterias em Itajaí —, seguida por Distrito Federal e Paraná. São Paulo ocupa o quarto lugar, enquanto Mato Grosso, Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, Goiás, Rio Grande do Sul e Minas Gerais completam o top 10 nacional. Impacto para o agronegócio e grandes setores em Mato Grosso Para o ecossistema produtivo de Mato Grosso, onde a alta performance agrícola exige fornecimento elétrico contínuo para sistemas de irrigação, armazenagem de grãos, aviários e operações logísticas, a adoção de baterias e sistemas BESS representa um divisor de águas. A tecnologia deixa de ser apenas uma alternativa ecológica e passa a funcionar como um seguro operacional estratégico. Ao blindar propriedades e indústrias contra oscilações e quedas de energia na rede de distribuição tradicional, o armazenamento garante previsibilidade, corte de custos operacionais e máxima eficiência para o motor econômico do estado. A redação do portal CenárioMT esclarece aos seus leitores que os dados estatísticos referentes ao crescimento das buscas nacionais por soluções de armazenamento de eletricidade — incluindo o avanço expressivo dos sistemas BESS e das baterias estacionárias no Google entre setembro de 2025 e agosto de 2026 — foram oficialmente enviados à nossa equipe de jornalismo pela Descarbonize Soluções, empresa especializada em transição energética e energia solar. Receba em primeira mão nossas notícias, tendências e exclusivas.

artigo.texto: SPARTANBURG — Spartanburg County Council on Oct. 22 approved a preliminary development agreement for the NorthMark and Valara data center being built on Pine Street after balking at a deal days prior. The deal is in addition to the fee-in-lieu-of-tax agreement council passed in 2025 to lure the project to the area before details of its scope were known by the public and also some of the council members who voted to approve the deal. It was authorized through the county’s recent data center moratorium, which lists a handful of conditions data centers have to meet before they’re approved, including a size restriction of no larger than 65 megawatts. While the 457-megawatt NorthMark data center has already been approved for one permit, it still needs a second to finish the project, which county officials believe puts it under the purview of the moratorium. The vote on the development agreement was 4-1, with council member Jessica Coker not in attendance and councilman Monier Abusaft as the lone no vote. Council members Grant DeShields, Jack Mabry and Paul Abbott voted for it, as did Chairperson Manning Lynch. Mabry, Lynch and Coker are all serving their last terms on council. “Business comes down to people being able to look each other in the eyes and being able to trust what they say to each other,” Abusaft said. “Environmental Protection, what had been talked about before, I did not feel like came out in our final agreement.” NorthMark declined to comment. In some ways, the agreement reflects what the county approved for the AIB data center in the Tyger River Industrial Park and the Jones Road data center. Both of those are 65 megawatts or smaller and neither will produce its own power like NorthMark does with its attached natural gas plant. The agreement requires the company to submit documents showing it complies with performance zoning ordinance rules around light and glare, noise and landscaping. It’s also required to conduct annual community meetings and report annually to the county capital investment made, construction status, water, grid and gas utility demand, employment data and charitable contributions, if applicable. In return, the county agreed to accelerate review of development approvals and not unreasonably withhold them. County officials painted the approval as a preliminary step with more negotiation needed. “This gives us a greater role in what council has control over,” DeShields said. “That’s what we were looking for. This ain’t finalized, but it’s in the negotiation process, and it’s the first draft for approval.” DeShields said the county wants some oversight over water, groundwater, air quality and inspection power, but that finer details would be worked out in the negotiations. Already, the county has asked the state Department of Environmental Services to put an air quality monitor to the east of the NorthMark data center, and DeShields said the county is willing to help cover some of the cost. “We want other counties to look at us and say ‘Spartanburg County got it right,’” DeShields said. “‘They might have stumbled a little bit in the beginning, but in the final product, they brought something together that their citizens are happy with.’” Abusaft, who’s said he believes data centers are safe and has held public safety committee meetings to hear opinions from environmental attorneys, regulators and utility executives, said he believes it would be risky for the county to turn away the industry. But despite his support, he refused to back the first version of the agreement. “It’s long been said that South Carolina is a handshake state,” Abusaft said, adding, “I don’t believe that the spirit of handshake communications have been kept, and I can’t vote for this as it comes now.” He declined to elaborate after the meeting.

artigo.texto: Making Carbon Pay for Ireland’s Energy Transition: What a Modernised Emissions Trading System Could Mean for Ireland’s Energy Supply Could a modernised EU Emissions Trading System help Ireland ensure a more self-reliant and resilient energy supply? In response to rising energy prices and their impact on European industry, the European Commission published a proposal to modernise the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) on the 17 July 2026. Ireland has been severely impacted by the rising cost of energy caused by Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, and the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East. In addition to sparking public protests, the energy crisis has imposed significant costs on industry, the State, and consumers. With this in mind, this blog will explore how a modernised ETS could support Ireland in its energy transition. What is the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS)? The EU ETS is a European Union (EU)-wide carbon market on which carbon emission allowances, each worth the equivalent of one tonne of carbon dioxide, are exchanged via a cap-and-trade system. Under this system, companies must cover their carbon emissions with allowances that have either been freely allocated to them, that have been auctioned off by Member States, or that have been bought from other companies. This creates an economic incentive for companies to reduce their carbon emissions. Each year, the overall cap on allowances is lowered, in theory, driving a gradual reduction in carbon emissions. The EU ETS is the primary decarbonisation policy of the EU’s Green Deal and has proven to be fairly effective. Since is was launched in 2005, the ETA has helped emissions to be cut by around 50%, and since 2013, it has raised over 270 billion euros in auction revenues. Ireland has taken in 1.28 billion euros through EU ETS allowance auctions since 2013. From the 139 million euros raised in 2024 under the scheme, the vast majority (102.3 million euros) has gone to the Department of Transport and been invested in public transport projects. In addition the EU ETS revenue has also funded specific projects in Ireland through EU-level funds. For example, the ETS revenue funded an EU Innovation Fund grand of 39 million euros to the Saoirse Wave Energy Project located in Ireland. For these EU-level funds, the Irish National Contact Point is the Environment and Climate Research and Advisory Unit in the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications (DCEE). Ireland’s energy supply vulnerability Recent geopolitical events have exposed one of Ireland’s strategic vulnerabilities as one of the most import-dependent economies in the EU when it comes to energy, with 80% of its energy supply being imported in 2024. This number can be explained by the fact that Ireland continues to rely heavily on fossil fuels. Of Ireland’s 168.0 TWh energy supply in 2024, fossil-fuel made up for 81.3%. Meanwhile, the country as yet does not produce or harvest much energy of its own. Therefore, to minimise the impact of future energy crises and to render Ireland’s energy supply more independent, policymakers should certainly consider how to foster the country's homegrown energy production capacity. For this, a modernised EU ETS, as proposed by the European Commission could be useful. How a modernised EU ETS could support Ireland’s energy transition In response to the ongoing energy crisis, the European Commission was invited by the European Council to draft a proposal for a review of the EU ETS. The aim of this review is to make the EU ETS a more effective instrument to strengthen independence, innovation and competitiveness in Europe. Its guiding idea is to redirect current expenditure on imported fossil fuel towards investments in the green transition. In the proposition published by the European Commission, two elements are particularly relevant to Ireland’s situation. First, the Commission’s proposal includes provisions to reform the Market Stability Reserve (MSR). The MSR was first established in 2018 as, at that time, carbon prices were considered too low to provide companies with a sufficient incentive to reduce their emissions. A mechanism that invalidates the carbon allowances surplus was thus introduced. Today, however, the opposite problem seems to be the case, as excessively high carbon prices are being passed on to electricity prices, thus increasing costs for businesses and consumers. Therefore, the proposal suggests stopping the invalidation of the surplus, and instead, sets it aside as a buffer that could be used if prices rise unexpectedly in the future. In principle, this reform of the MSR should ensure better market stability and reduce price volatility, which should be of interest to Irish policy makers. Second, the Commission’s proposal introduces a number of measures aimed at improving the use of EU ETS revenue. The underlying principle is that EU ETS revenue should go back to industry to support its decarbonisation efforts. If funds to that effect were already in existence, such as the aforementioned Innovation Fund, the proposal aims to establish an Industrial Decarbonisation Bank (IDB) that will enable investment at a bigger scale. The Commission also considers that there should be better control over the way Member States spend their EU ETS revenues. The revenue should be spent on genuine climate action, which, according to the WWF, is not always the case. How could this benefit Ireland? A modernised ETS with an amended MSR could protect the EU, and thus Ireland, from carbon-price volatility in the allowance market, limiting the extent to which fluctuations in allowance prices contribute to electricity costs. In the longer term, clean energy investments, such as those supported by a modernised EU ETS, can help reduce the impacts of energy crises. artigo.texto: “I think that the ‘what ifs’ on this one are pretty scary,” Amsterdam Ward 4 Alderman Christopher Carpenter said. “So we're going to prohibit them.” The Amsterdam Common Council on Tuesday unanimously adopted a local law modifying city code to prohibit battery energy storage systems in all zoning districts within the city. An ad hoc committee of city officials and staff recommended banning the devices after studying their potential benefits and dangers of the systems. The committee concluded the systems pose serious fire and public safety concerns in the densely populated city. “I've had a pretty strong opinion about this because I don't think the technology is there yet to put it anywhere close to any of our residents in case something bad did happen,” Carpenter said. Safety concerns have plagued the devices following fires at lithium-ion battery facilities in Jefferson, Orange and Suffolk counties in summer 2023. Fire broke out at a facility in Warwick in Orange County for a second time in December 2025. The state has since updated its fire code to introduce stricter safety standards that took effect this year. Amsterdam is the latest among a growing number of communities to ban battery systems citing safety concerns. Battery bans have been enacted by the towns of Amsterdam, Florida and Glen in Montgomery County. The town of Mohawk has a moratorium in place as potential zoning updates are considered. In Fulton County, the towns of Johnstown, Northampton and Perth have either enacted or extended battery moratoriums this year, as did the city of Johnstown while Gloversville banned them outright. Amsterdam enacted a six-month moratorium on industrial solar and battery systems last year to give officials time to study the technology and develop potential updates to city code to regulate them. The moratorium was extended this spring to Jan. 5. City officials on Tuesday adopted another local law ending the moratorium without any changes to existing solar regulations. “Our planning board has the power to judge this more fairly, so we're leaving this the same. We're just lifting the moratorium that's been in place since December of 2025,” Carpenter said. There was an urgency to determine if and how to regulate the devices after officials realized city code didn’t address standalone battery systems when Carson Power sought feedback from the planning board on conceptual plans for a 5-megawatt system at 43 Verbraska Ave. last year. The company informed city officials in May it was instead considering a 12.5-megawatt project at an unspecified site on Edson Street. Mayor Michael Cinquanti supported the decision to prohibit the systems in the city at this stage while acknowledging the need for sources of renewable energy. He hopes the technology will improve over time and win public confidence. “There's a need for a technology, but it just isn't at the stage it needs to be for us to be able to permit it to be present in our city,” Cinquanti said.

artigo.texto: At Humber's Barrett Centre for Technology Innovation (Barrett CTI), a new mobile Electric Vehicle (EV) Battery Assembly System is giving students hands-on experience in a rapidly growing industry, equipping them with the skills and knowledge to work with the technologies that are shaping the future of automotive manufacturing. The new system was made possible through a donation from the RBC Foundation and showcased on October 15, 2026, at the Barrett CTI. Designed specifically to replicate real-world EV battery assembly, students work with two KUKA industrial robots as they move components from storage onto a shuttle. A magnetic planar table transports the shuttle through simulated battery-production stations, where technologies such as 2D and 3D vision systems, robotic grippers and tool changers demonstrate how modern manufacturing comes together. The robots ultimately complete the simulated battery module and return it to storage. "This system represents much more than new equipment. It creates exciting opportunities to prepare our students for careers in the rapidly growing clean energy, electric vehicle, and advanced manufacturing sectors," said Neal Mohammed, director, Barrett CTI. "Our vision is to build on this foundation by integrating emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, and condition monitoring. These advancements will strengthen our training capabilities, support innovation, and help our industry partners develop the skilled workforce they need to remain competitive." The greatest advantage for students is the opportunity to learn across disciplines. The Battery Assembly System brings together robotics, automation, electronics, programming, mechanical engineering, systems integration and quality control into one working environment. Rather than learning individual technologies in isolation, students we will be focusing on the system as part of the curriculum for Humber's Mechatronics degree program and Electromechanical Engineering Technology program and develop the problem-solving skills needed to understand how an entire automated system works, and how to troubleshoot it when something goes wrong. That multidisciplinary approach is already making an impact. Humber students, such as Tete Soto, saw the Battery Assembly System in action by working alongside Barrett CTI technologists. In their third year of Humber's Electromechanical Engineering Technology program, Soto is excited that the Battery Assembly System is being integrated into their learning: "Now we have an idea of how it all comes together. [The Battery Assembly System] is lighting the way for students to learn how to make fully functioning robotic systems." As the system is larger than any capstone project, the learning opportunity will train students to be better prepared for jobs in various engineering fields. Humber students have also been trained to lead STEAM workshops, introducing visiting middle and high school students to the technologies found in the Battery Assembly System. More than 1,200 middle and high school students have encountered the system through tours of the Barrett CTI. RBC Foundation's support of the Battery Assembly System also allows Humber to connect directly with industry. Organizations such as KUKA Robotics, Rockwell Automation, SICK Sensor Intelligence, DMG Mori, Javelin, Pilz, B&R and Weidmuller have contributed their technology, expertise or support and approximately 56 industry and government visitors have already seen the Battery Assembly System during its build phase. The Battery Assembly System is mobile, ensuring its impact can extend beyond the classrooms at Humber. It can be brought into high-traffic spaces for demonstrations, workshops and tours, making advanced EV manufacturing available and accessible. Recently, the Battery Assembly System was showcased at the PAC Global Disruptors Summit in June 2026. "RBC Foundation is committed to fostering innovation and sustainability and is proud to support Humber's Barrett Centre for Technology Innovation with an $800,000 contribution," says Chris Misch, regional vice-president, Toronto Downtown, RBC. "This funding will help advance the mobile Electric Vehicle (EV) Battery Assembly System, a transformative initiative that equips students with hands-on skills in automation, robotics, and clean-energy technologies." "Aligned with RBC's sustainability goals and Humber's leadership in applied learning, the collaboration will help to strengthen Ontario's position in the green economy while empowering the next generation of innovators. Together, we are helping build ecosystems where education, industry, and communities thrive, supporting the progress towards a brighter, more sustainable future for all."

artigo.texto: Both incumbent Rep. Eugene Vindman and Douglas Ollivant, his Republican challenger, say they want to put the brakes on data centers in sensitive areas but have different ideas about how to provide relief to people feeling the sting of higher prices. Vindman, 51, is a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and former legal adviser for the National Security Council. Ollivant, 58, is also a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and served as the director for Iraq on the National Security Council. He was recently diagnosed with an aggressive form of leukemia but chose to stay in the race. The 7th Congressional District includes parts of Prince William, Stafford, Spotsylvania, Culpeper, King George, Madison, Orange, Greene and Albemarle counties and the city of Fredericksburg. U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-7th, and his Republican challenger, Douglas Ollivant, submitted … The Prince William Times asked both candidates to weigh in on three issues ahead of the Nov. 3 election. The economy and rising prices Economic issues, including rising prices for everyday goods and fuel, are the top issue for voters going into this year's midterms, according to several recent surveys. Vindman said lowering costs has been “a top priority” for his office. He said he supports legislation to lower utility bills, provide relief from high diesel prices and lower healthcare prescription costs for military families. “Everywhere I go in Virginia's Seventh District, I hear the same thing: families are struggling to keep up with the rising cost of living. Whether it's filling up their gas tanks, putting groceries on the table, paying their utility bills, or affording health care, hardworking Virginians are being stretched to the breaking point,” Vindman said. Vindman also said he is committed to repealing Republicans’ “Big Beautiful Bill,” which slashed Medicaid funding and raised health-care premiums for people insured under the Affordable Care Act. Ollivant, however, said politicians need to be “more forthright” with the public about how government decisions impact kitchen table issues. “Politicians need to quit treating the public as infants and start leveling with us as adults. Prices are higher and are going to stay that way until the economy recovers and there is broader stability overseas — including Ukraine and Iran,” Ollivant said. Immigration enforcement The 7th District has one of the highest immigrant populations in the state, with 16% of residents having moved there from another country. The Prince William Times asked both candidates whether they support the Trump administration’s immigration policies andwhat should be done differently. Ollivant did not directly criticize President Trump’s approach. He said the country’s immigration laws need to be enforced and questioned adopting any policy that would “allow violent illegal immigrants to prey upon our communities.” He also said immigration officers should be treated better by opponents of the president’s agenda. “Few people put their lives on the line in the same way they do, enforcing our laws and keeping our families safe. They deserve a lot better than the broad brush applied by their detractors,” he said. Vindman, who immigrated to the U.S. from Ukraine as a child, said he opposes the Trump administration’s enforcement tactics. “Americans deserve an immigration system that keeps our communities safe, upholds the rule of law, and respects the dignity and rights of every person,” Vindman said. “As a former prosecutor and 25-year Army veteran, I know we can and must secure our borders without abandoning our values or treating our neighbors with cruelty.” Vindman said he would support reforms to immigration enforcement, such as requiring ICE officers to remove their masks, wear body cameras, issue judicial warrants, and ensure clear constitutional protections. He’d also like the agency to adopt enforceable use-of-force standards and conduct independent investigations when federal agents are accused of breaking the law. “As an immigrant whose family came to this country seeking freedom and opportunity, I believe deeply in the promise of America,” Vindman said. Data centers and electricity The rapid proliferation of data centers has provoked widespread backlash among Northern Virginia residents. It has also caused concerns about how those data centers will get their electrical power. New transmission line corridors and electrical substations have been proposed, some of which will be near homes, schools and businesses. Vindman said he is concerned about data centers being placed near sensitive areas, such as neighborhoods, schools and parks, but stopped short of calling for a moratorium. “Data centers should not be built near national parks, schools, or residential communities, and Virginians should not be stuck paying higher utility bills to support their growth. I firmly believe rural communities should not be forced to shoulder the costs and consequences of transmission infrastructure built to benefit everyone else,” he said. Vindman added that he is “deeply concerned” about the rapid expansion of transmission lines being built to serve data centers. “Hardworking Virginians should not be forced to pay higher utility bills, lose their land, or watch their communities transformed just so billion-dollar technology companies can turn a bigger profit,” he said. Ollivant said he is against data center development on farmland and on battlefields but did not respond to questions about whether he would support slowing data center development.The electrical grid in Virginia needs to be upgraded, Ollivant said, and he would consider “smart solutions” to boost the grid. “We can do a lot of good with advances in technology and economic growth in Virginia. We can't solve any of these problems, much less pay for basic services, without economic growth and technological innovation,” Ollivant said.
