artigo.texto: CATL's Sales Jump 58.58% While Profit Lags — and a 30% Target Cut Shows Why the Market Noticed Published on 10/22/2026 at 18:11 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL can still move batteries in vast quantities. What it is struggling to do is turn that volume into earnings fast enough to satisfy investors. The stock has come under pressure for two straight sessions — down 3.3% today after a sharper slide of 4.1% the previous day — following third-quarter results that missed profit expectations and reignited doubts about the company's pricing power. The sell-off has a clear trigger. Reuters attributed the bulk of the subsequent selling to the earnings miss, with intensified competition in the battery sector and cooling growth in Chinese car sales adding to the gloom. One brokerage responded by slashing its price target by 30% to HK$500, citing a faster-than-expected deterioration in industry-wide profitability. A quarter of two halves Tuesday's release laid bare the gap between top-line momentum and bottom-line delivery. Revenue for the third quarter of 2026 reached RMB 165.22 billion, up 58.58% year on year. Attributable net profit came in at RMB 21.25 billion — 14.54% higher than a year earlier, but 5.77% lower than the preceding quarter, and short of what analysts had pencilled in. Those are not contradictory signals so much as a warning about growth quality. CATL is earning more than it did twelve months ago; it is simply converting each additional yuan of sales into less profit than before. Management pointed to the product mix as one reason unit profit came under pressure. Analysts, according to media reports, flagged a weaker-than-expected gross margin, higher expenses and impairment losses — a cluster of pressures rather than a single culprit. The nine-month picture reinforces the theme. Revenue for the first three quarters of 2026 totalled RMB 442.14 billion with net profit of RMB 64.53 billion. Sales rose 56.19%, but cost of sales climbed 61.61% — outpacing revenue — while operating cash flow fell 23.60%. Costs, in other words, are eating into the benefit of every extra order. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? SERES deal offers volume, not yet proof of profit Against that backdrop, CATL is leaning on its customer relationships to build a case for recovery. On 10 October the company signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement with SERES, under which AITO models will continue to use CATL batteries. A second phase of their joint "Plant in Plant" project is designed for annual capacity of 10–12 GWh. That is a concrete industrial roadmap — but only a roadmap. The capacity expansion has not been completed, and a larger production base would carry limited economic weight if cost trends absorb the extra revenue it generates. Investors would do well to separate the signed partnership from the planned build-out. The same logic applies to the new generation of batteries for heavy-duty trucks unveiled on Tuesday, and to Reuters' report of plans to expand the battery-swapping network. Both widen the commercial runway. Neither answers the question that matters most right now: whether the additional business arrives at an attractive margin. Buyback doesn't change the operating math A share buyback disclosed on Wednesday does little to alter that calculus. The repurchased shares are earmarked for cancellation and a reduction in registered capital — a technical adjustment to the share count that leaves the economics of the underlying business untouched. What would move the needle is evidence that CATL can translate revenue growth back into profit and cash. A confirmed implementation step on the second phase of the SERES project would be the next tangible operational catalyst, though capacity alone is not the test; the question is whether it produces economically viable incremental business. For now, the market is applying a stricter yardstick than it once did. Growth is not in doubt — the demand for CATL's products is plainly there. What is in doubt is the return on it. Until the spread between rising sales and rising costs narrows, and cash generation stabilises, each new partnership and product launch will be judged less on its scale than on what it contributes to the bottom line. artigo.texto: By JENNIFER McDERMOTT A battery system installed in a Buffalo, New York, apartment building will store excess energy when it’s plentiful and power the building when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. The 3.75 megawatt-hour lithium-ion battery system, which can power the Peace Bridge Place affordable housing complex for several days, is among the largest battery systems in a U.S. residential building, manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. said Tuesday. “We want our electric power to be resilient, affordable and available. Distributed battery storage accomplishes all three,” Viridi CEO Jon M. Williams said. “The only thing that has been holding up installations at scale is safety; a lot of the products on the market over the last 10 years have burned things down.” Deploying large batteries that can safely power apartment buildings is an important step toward replacing fossil fuels with renewables, experts say, but they’re uncommon because of the cost and concerns about fire risks. Already, larger batteries are paired with solar and wind projects, and homeowners are using smaller batteries to store excess energy from rooftop solar and for backup power. How batteries help keep electricity flow steady Batteries help maintain a steady flow of power when sources such as solar and wind are not producing. They charge when the sun is shining or when wind is blowing. That energy can then be used when demand is high. Batteries can also store excess electricity from hydropower, and New York is one of the top hydropower-producing states. Buffalo is close to Niagara Falls, where most of the state’s hydropower is produced. When electricity demand is high, Peace Bridge will use the battery. It will get paid by the utility for not drawing from the grid and for sending power back if needed. This helps lower the complex’s overall electricity costs, which benefits residents. The building can use the system during outages, too. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency helped fund the Peace Bridge Place project, as part of its focus on including disadvantaged communities in the clean energy transition. “It goes a long way toward demonstrating the safety and viability of these types of projects,” said NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris. Viridi has manufacturing facilities in Buffalo and Richmond, California, where a state grant assisted with renovations. California Energy Commission Chair David Hochschild said he’s impressed with the company. More than two-thirds of California’s electricity comes from clean energy and batteries get a lot of credit for that, Hochschild said. As electricity demand grows, batteries help ensure the grid is reliable, reduce pollution and contain costs, he added. “I believe the battery industry is the single most important energy industry for the next several decades,” said Hochschild, who co-founded the Electric Innovation Initiative to use electricity instead of fossil fuels more broadly throughout the U.S. economy. Viridi’s system passed a ‘near impossible’ test As large battery fires have garnered attention, some communities have opposed further development. However, the failure rate for batteries has decreased as more are installed, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Viridi spent six years and $10 million figuring out how to make a fireproof container for batteries. Half the cost was for batteries Viridi destroyed during testing. Viridi uses plates, pouches and spacing to isolate each battery cell. If one fails, the energy dissipates instead of spreading to the next battery, so that no gas, smoke, heat or fire escapes the container, Williams said. Jigar Shah, an expert in clean energy financing and deployment, said the Peace Bridge Place system is a milestone in overcoming safety concerns. To ensure nothing would catch fire when used inside a residence, Viridi’s system had to pass a test where the battery was forced to fail while a cheesecloth covered the container. The cheesecloth did not char or ignite, according to the test report record. Viridi announced in April it met stringent Underwriters Laboratories safety standards so its system could be installed indoors without adding additional fire suppression to a building. Shah, who led the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office during the Biden administration, said Viridi is the only company to consistently pass this “near impossible” test. Shah thinks far more U.S. homes will use batteries for backup power by 2030. The U.S. can meet much more electricity demand and avoid costly upgrades to the grid if batteries are strategically deployed, he added. New York and California officials want forward-thinking energy solutions Viridi and Good Carbon Co. chose the Peace Bridge apartments because the all-electric building uses a geothermal system for heating and cooling rather than natural gas and needed additional, resilient power. The electricity demand locally can exceed the available supply, so the utility National Grid supported the endeavor, Williams added. Peace Bridge is considered affordable housing because renters earn no more than 80% of the area’s median income, Good Carbon said. It said energy storage will be an important part of future multifamily housing projects. Viridi has been manufacturing in Buffalo since 2018. A medical research building in the city is using its battery system, too. Viridi’s plant could build enough battery packs in a year to supply energy for about 14,000 average U.S. homes for 24 hours, Williams said. Harris, at NYSERDA, said the state needs more options like this for maintaining a reliable grid and managing costs. Gov. artigo.texto: A TIM defendeu que o leilão da faixa de 6 GHz ocorra em "momento adequado e em linha com a evolução do 5G", discordando do planejamento da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) de realizar a licitação em 2028. O posicionamento foi manifestado pelo diretor de Assuntos Regulatórios da tele, Carlos Eduardo Franco, em audiência pública sobre a frequência de 6 GHz, realizada pela Anatel, em São Paulo, nesta quarta-feira, 21. Embora não tenha citado um ano específico para o leilão, o executivo ressaltou que o certame deve levar em conta a disponibilidade de equipamentos e os investimentos relacionados a outros editais de espectro em execução pelas operadoras. "O ecossistema de 6 GHz ainda está em fase inicial de implementação em escala", pontuou. "Até 2028, deve ser avaliada a evolução efetiva do ecossistema e dos ciclos tecnológicos em andamento. O calendário precisa ser compatível com a evolução tecnológica", acrescentou. Para a TIM, o edital também deve trazer previsibilidade econômica para as participantes do eventual leilão, levando em conta preço mínimo, garantias exigidas, compromissos e retorno esperado. "É recomendável que os parâmetros econômicos sejam conhecidos com antecedência. Maior transparência favorece o planejamento", ressaltou Franco. Data centers O executivo da TIM também sugeriu que o compromisso de investimento em data centers, proposto pela Anatel, seja substituído por obrigações de expansão de cobertura móvel e de redes de transporte em áreas desassistidas. Na semana passada, Claro e Vivo se posicionarem de forma parecida em audiência pública realizada em Brasília. Nesse ponto, Franco ainda disse que a obrigação de aporte em data centers nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste pode sobrepor investimentos privados e políticas públicas. Desse modo, indicou que o melhor caminho seria a priorização de obrigações mensuráveis de redes de telecomunicações. Ele também contestou a eventual criação de uma entidade para administrar os recursos que iriam para os data centers. "O objetivo de reduzir desigualdades regionais é relevante, mas o desenho merece uma avaliação cuidadosa quanto à complexidade e alocação dos recursos do certame", asseverou. Blocos de espectro Na audiência, levando em conta os 700 MHz da parte superior da frequência de 6 GHz, a TIM ainda propôs que o edital preveja três blocos nacionais de 200 MHz e um regional de 100 MHz. "Este desenho preserva os incumbentes e uma alternativa regional, reduz a fragmentação e promove o uso eficiente da faixa", apontou Franco. A consulta da Anatel, contudo sugere apenas dois lotes nacional de 200 MHz, um regional de 200 MHz (dividido em seis regiões) e outro regional de 100 MHz.

artigo.texto: Israel explores nuclear fusion as data centers drive demand for power A new Energy Ministry proposal would fund research into a technology that could eventually transform electricity generation. The recommended plan calls for up to NIS 1 billion over five to seven years, although commercial fusion remains a distant and uncertain prospect. Israel’s growing demand for electricity, driven in part by the expansion of data centers, is prompting the Ministry of Energy to explore a technology that could one day transform power generation. The ministry has proposed a long-term investment program in nuclear fusion, an emerging energy source that promises abundant electricity but remains far from commercial viability. The proposal outlines three possible levels of investment in domestic research and development. The most modest would allocate NIS 50 million to NIS 100 million over five years. A more ambitious program would invest NIS 500 million to NIS 1 billion over five to seven years, while the most expansive option would commit up to NIS 2 billion over a decade and include the construction of an experimental reactor. The ministry recommends the middle option. It would bring together public institutions, private companies and research organizations in joint consortia, with participation from Israeli defense contractors such as Rafael and Elbit. The plan also calls for a regulatory sandbox that would ease certain requirements during experimental work and greater involvement in international fusion research programs. The proposal is intended to help Israeli companies and research institutions develop expertise and become part of a global industry attracting growing investment. However, it remains a policy recommendation rather than an approved government program, and no funding has yet been allocated. The incoming government will ultimately decide whether to prioritize the field and how much public money to commit. Israel already has two startups working in the sector. nT-Tao is developing a compact fusion reactor, while FusionMantle is developing components for fusion systems. The ministry’s proposed program would seek to build on this base by bringing together companies, academic researchers and state-supported facilities. Israel’s defense industry could contribute technologies developed for other demanding applications. Rafael and Elbit, for example, have expertise in high-power lasers, including technologies relevant to laser-based interception systems such as Iron Beam. Such capabilities could prove useful in some areas of fusion research, alongside expertise in vacuum systems and other complex engineering challenges. Elbit and Israel Aerospace Industries also have experience in materials engineering and turning specialized materials into functional systems. The Soreq Nuclear Research Center, which houses a particle accelerator and other research infrastructure, could provide facilities to support development in the field. The government’s proposal reflects an effort to identify where Israel can contribute to a global industry before fusion power becomes commercially established. The country would not need to develop an entire reactor independently to participate. Specialized components, materials, research capabilities and engineering technologies could offer routes into the international supply chain. But the distance between laboratory research and a commercially viable power plant remains considerable. Fusion researchers must overcome difficult physical and engineering challenges before the technology can reliably deliver electricity at a competitive cost. The approximately 417 nuclear reactors operating worldwide generate electricity through nuclear fission, in which heavy atomic nuclei, such as uranium, split and release energy. Fission is an established technology, but it carries challenges involving radioactive waste and the risk of accidents that can release radioactive material. Nuclear fusion works in the opposite direction. Rather than splitting heavy nuclei, it combines light ones. In the most widely studied approach, nuclei of hydrogen isotopes, deuterium and tritium, fuse to form helium and release energy. Fusion powers the Sun and other stars, but reproducing the process in a controlled environment on Earth is exceptionally difficult. Hydrogen nuclei carry a positive electrical charge and repel one another. To bring them close enough to fuse, researchers must create extreme conditions, typically heating fuel to temperatures exceeding 100 million degrees Celsius. At these temperatures, the fuel becomes plasma, an electrically charged state of matter. Maintaining that plasma under the necessary conditions is a major challenge. Researchers must confine it long enough for fusion reactions to occur while managing the enormous heat and energy involved. Different approaches seek to achieve this through magnetic fields, lasers or other methods. The energy balance is another critical hurdle. Fusion reactions can release substantial energy, but a practical power plant must generate more usable energy than the entire system consumes, while operating reliably and economically. In 2022, researchers at the U.S. National Ignition Facility achieved a landmark result when the energy released by fusion reactions exceeded the laser energy delivered to the target. The experiment demonstrated an important scientific breakthrough, but it did not mean that a fusion power plant had achieved net electricity production. The energy required to run the facility and the broader system remained much greater than the energy delivered by the lasers to the target. That distinction helps explain why fusion, despite decades of research, has yet to become a commercial source of electricity. The prospect of a new source of abundant, low-carbon electricity has attracted growing investment, particularly as data centers and AI infrastructure increase demand for power. artigo.texto: [Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.] GM plans lower-cost EVs with new battery chemistry Despite EV sales slump, GM to debut lithium manganese-rich batteries, which will support upcoming SUV Key Takeaways: - General Motors is developing lithium manganese-rich batteries for multiple affordable EVs, including a mainstream battery-powered SUV expected in about three years. - GM's EV sales fell 43% to 82,000 through the third quarter, and GM wrote down more than $11 billion in investments. - GM plans to debut autonomous highway driving on the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028, then expand it to lower-priced models. General Motors Co. is unfazed by the electric vehicle meltdown of the past few years, moving ahead with a new EV program expected to produce a new battery-powered mainstream SUV with about three years. The automaker’s latest effort aims to field multiple affordable EVs in high-volume vehicle segments, GM executives told reporters at an event in New York. At the center of it are batteries leveraging lithium manganese-rich (LMR) chemistry, which offers greater driving range at a lower cost than the technology in GM’s offerings. “Our end goal is profitable EVs,” said Jaclyn McQuaid, GM’s senior vice president for vehicle products. “We see data that says customers who spend time in EVs enjoy the experience.” Staying the course by planning new EV models is a bold move for GM. Under CEO Mary Barra, the company invested $35 billion in electric drive and other technologies to field a lineup that now comprises 12 models. Yet vast majority of car buyers in the U.S. — GM’s biggest source of sales and profit — continue to purchase gasoline-powered models as well as hybrid-electric cars predominantly made by Asian rivals. That dynamic was magnified last year after President Donald Trump and Republican lawmakers slashed federal policies that had pushed carmakers to produce more EVs and incentivized consumers to buy them, including a $7,500 tax credit for EV purchasers. So far this year, GM’s electric vehicle sales have fallen 43% to 82,000 through the third quarter. The company has written down more than $11 billion in EV investments and sold stakes in battery plants to partners LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI. It’s also doubled down on internal combustion with new V-8 engines for its pickup trucks and SUVs. Despite those immediate challenges, the carmaker still sees electric drive as its long-term future that will eventually be embraced by consumers. McQuaid said recent developments with LMR chemistry have made it possible to GM to develop a broad lineup of EV models. Its current EV batteries utilize nickel manganese cobalt chemistry, which offers long driving range but at a high cost. Chinese automakers use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which are cheaper but don’t go as far on a charge. GM said its LMR batteries are designed to carry 33% more energy density than LFP, and by reducing weight, should be able to deliver 20% longer range on every kilowatt-hour of energy. The company is extracting additional cost savings with new battery packs that are lighter, have less wiring and 40% fewer parts than its current models, said GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson. GM is using more AI tools to coordinate between its design, engineering and manufacturing operations to halve the nearly five-year process of developing new models, Anderson said. EVs also represent GM’s opportunity to introduce GM’s latest autonomous driving capabilities, which will debut on the electric Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028 and then be added to lower-priced models, Anderson said. That system will allow drivers to take their hands off the wheel and eyes off the road on highways. The company is working to eventually have its vehicles capable of off-highway autonomous driving, Anderson said.

artigo.texto: Data Centers: Benefits vs Costs and Risks EconoFact The Issue: The dramatic recent surge in investment in data centers in the United States is boosting the economy but at the same time sparking heated opposition. The stark tensions reflect very different viewpoints on the benefits vs the costs and risks of data centers. For their supporters, data centers are providing the infrastructure backbone for the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with a potentially transformative long-term impact on the US economy, well beyond the already significant short-term stimulus to growth. However, critics have raised a wide range of concerns: that the data center boom and the required massive debt financing needed to sustain it could end in a damaging bust; that the promised local benefits of data centers in terms of jobs and tax revenues are exaggerated while the spending on data centers is crowding out other types of investment; that data centers can impose heavy energy and environmental costs on local communities; and that the Artificial Intelligence that data centers are empowering will destroy jobs and even threaten humanity itself. Data center spending is expected to continue at a high level through the end of the decade, although projections vary widely. The Facts: - Data centers are industrial facilities that house the servers, storage and networking equipment that run digital services provided remotely over the internet. Data centers have been around at a small scale since the late 1990s as the internet and cloud computing developed. However, global data center capacity has taken off over the past decade, growing three times from 2015 to 2024, mainly in the United States (see chart). This boom has intensified since the launch of Chat GPT in late 2023 and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence tools by both businesses and households in the US, which has far outpaced the spread of personal computers and the internet in earlier decades. - The recent surge in capacity has been driven by huge investments by the so-called five hyperscalers: Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, Meta and Alphabet [Google]. These companies are spending an estimated $800 billion on data centers in 2026 representing about 9 percent of all U.S. capital expenditures. Modern AI-related data centers are often designed at a massive scale, packing together cutting-edge GPU microprocessors with high-speed interconnects in a single location with large electricity and cooling needs. These mega centers are used to train new AI models such as those offered by Open AI and Anthropic and increasingly to support the use of AI (known as “inference”), which Deloitte estimates at around 2/3 of AI computing needs in 2026, up from one third in 2023. While model training could be accomplished offshore in places with cheap and abundant energy — for instance in the Middle East — inference services need to be near centers of population to minimize delays in real time response by AI applications such as AI agents, fraud detection, and self-driving cars. This means that widespread adoption of artificial intelligence in the United States can't just rely on data centers built in remote locations with abundant cheap energy. - Data center spending is expected to continue at a high level through the end of the decade, although projections vary widely. A report by the International Energy Agency (IEA) provides a baseline scenario with global data center capacity rising from 97 GW in 2025 to 226 GW in 2030, but with three other scenarios ranging from 158 to 305 GW in 2030 (see chart), driven largely by growing AI computing needs. The wide range of uncertainty arises from unresolved questions about the extent to which AI will be widely adopted by businesses and households; whether AI providers can capture monetary returns from the users commensurate with their costs; how quickly the microchips that account for the lion’s share of data center construction costs are replaced by newer, more powerful and more energy efficient chips; and the political resistance to new data center construction. Estimates from a study focusing on the United States, present a central scenario projecting an increase from 57 GW of data center capacity in 2026 to 240 GW by 2032, at a total cost of around $10 trillion. This would represent 3.5 percent of US GDP over 2025-2032, which would be substantially larger than previous surges in infrastructure spending like railroads in the 19th century (2.2 percent of GDP) and the internet in the 20th century (1.1 percent of GDP) (see here). - The recent surge in data center spending has provided a short-term boost to the US economy. A Federal Reserve study used simulations of actual projects to estimate that data center spending on plant and equipment (net of imported components) contributed around 0.20 percentage points to the 2.3 percent US GDP growth in 2025 and is contributing 0.40 percentage points in 2026. (See also these similar estimates based on recent GDP data). The US economy has also benefitted indirectly from the run-up in stock prices of the leading companies providing AI services, which increases investors’ wealth (and therefore spending), partially offset by the crowding out of other types of investment through the competition for funding and the associated increase in long- term interest rates. On the employment front, data center construction boosts US jobs for construction workers and in manufacturing electrical equipment, although the post-construction employment impact is small since running and maintaining data centers requires very few people. There could be a negative impact on jobs displaced by increasing use of AI, although such effects so far seem limited. artigo.texto: [Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.] CATL bets big on electric truck market with new upgrades Offerings include battery upgrades and expanded swap stations Key Takeaways: - CATL is betting on the burgeoning electric-truck market to bolster growth, introducing battery upgrades and planning to open more so-called swap stations. - Electric trucks accounted for just over half of China’s vehicle sales last month, according to First Commercial Vehicle Network. - CATL plans to more than double its e-truck battery-swap stations to 2,000 by 2027 and ultimately operate 10,000 facilities. Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. is betting on the burgeoning electric-truck market to bolster growth, introducing battery upgrades and planning to open more so-called swap stations. The Chinese battery giant launched a slew of upgrades for the packs used in the cargo-hauling vehicles at an event in Beijing on Oct. 20, and said it has secured orders for swap products covering 13,000 units from major logistics companies including SF Holding Co. and China Postal Express & Logistics Co. The e-truck market is expanding rapidly in China, with vehicle sales accounting for just over half of the total last month, according to First Commercial Vehicle Network. CATL — which has seen its stock price slump this year amid concerns about rising competition — is due to release earnings later Oct. 20. The company plans to more than double its battery-swap stations for e-trucks to 2,000 by 2027, with a goal of running 10,000 facilities in the longer term, according to Yang Jun, CEO of CATL’s e-truck battery-swap business. The sites allow drivers to quickly exchange a depleted battery pack for a charged one, rather than waiting for a recharge of an existing unit. E-truck battery products introduced Oct. 20 included rear-mounted ultra-light and ultra-thin packs that can be suitable for weight- or space-sensitive applications. The company added that it will offer flexible battery leasing options for customers to tailor rental periods to their needs. “This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs,” according to a company statement.

artigo.texto: The Milwaukee Common Council unanimously passed a one-year moratorium last week on new data center projects while officials draft new zoning standards. Mayor Cavalier Johnson signed the ordinance the day after the council’s vote. Data center plans are facing public backlash across the state and the country. Milwaukee joins places like Superior, Madison and Wisconsin Rapids that passed their own data center construction moratoriums. Milwaukee’s moratorium comes in response to public controversy after a proposed project to redevelop a vacant Walmart on the city’s north side. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Debate in the city mirrors what’s happening in other communities. Officials say they need time to write rules for projects that affect neighborhoods, utility costs and other issues. But business leaders say a pause may drive economic investment to other places. There are currently 53 data centers around the state, according to the Data Center Map. And at least 19 of varying sizes are in the Greater Milwaukee area. But while developers are moving quickly to build data centers, Milwaukee Common Council Ald. Marina Dimitrijevic told WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” that local government operates at a slower pace to weigh how major changes could affect residents. Before the moratorium, Dimitrijevic said the city had essentially no zoning rules or regulations regarding data center construction. “Government is not set up to move that fast, which is why we have to pause,” she said. “Zoning code has to account for land use; we have to look at how it would affect neighbors, the noise, the possible pollution; the list goes on and on. And I think there are very few Wisconsinites that want to live right next to one of these (data centers).” Dimitrijevic said she had concerns about how the boom in data centers would affect the region’s energy grid and utility costs for constituents. A Pew Research Center survey released in September found 54 percent of Americans believe that data centers would have a negative impact on the environment, up from 39% in January. The survey found half of Americans believe data centers would negatively affect home energy costs. “No one is asking for this, other than the corporations that are seeking to make money off of us,” Dimitrijevic said. But for the businesses hoping to build in Milwaukee and stimulate its economy, a moratorium like the one the city just passed could scare away potential investment, said Dale Kooyenga, president and CEO of the Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce. MMAC opposed Milwaukee’s moratorium. Kooyenga said he thought the data center pause could’ve been worse and that businesses still have opportunities to negotiate with the city, but that such a moratorium is essentially putting up a “we’re not open for business” sign on the city’s front door. “We understand that with any economic development, there’s a back-and-forth discussion, but you should have policies that invite a discussion, and then when you have those discussions, then share with the investor what you need to get to a yes,” Kooyenga said. “We just think (the moratorium) sends the wrong message for a city that really needs more economic development.” Building a new data center can take thousands of workers in construction jobs, from electricians to carpenters to engineers. But once built, the centers themselves host relatively few job openings, up to several hundred. Kooyenga said the years of construction jobs shouldn’t be discounted. And he said the jobs the centers host once operational are typically well above the median wage. Kooyenga said such projects raise significant property tax revenue for the area, which local governments could use to bolster schools, fire departments and other public services. Dimitrijevic said she was more skeptical over the long-term payoff of such projects after the construction is done and the builders have moved on to other projects. “I think we want the same (as businesses and developers) when we want investment in the city of Milwaukee, but we’ve got to do it in a way that serves the many, not just the few,” she said.

artigo.texto: Earlier this year, the German government laid out an ambitious plan: By 2030, it would double the scale of the country’s data center fleet, and quadruple the amount of compute available for running artificial intelligence models. The idea was to minimize Germany’s dependence on the United States for access to AI—a point of concern across Europe—and boost its faltering economy. However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy. As part of its broader climate commitments, the previous German administration voted through the Energy Efficiency Act in 2023. Among other things, it required all new data centers to recycle a portion of the waste heat generated by their computer equipment, ideally into nearby municipal heating systems. It seemed like a no-brainer, says Patrick Graichen, who served as a senior official at Germany’s Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy at the time, before resigning over cronyism allegations. “We need clean heat, and data centers are a source of clean heat,” Graichen tells WIRED. In June, a month before the rules were due to finally take effect, the German federal government walked them back. Data center firms had complained that the requirements made it almost impossible to build in the country; the German Data Center Association characterized an early version of the bill as a “data center prevention act.” Under an amended bill, which will be put to the German parliament for ratification imminently, data center operators would no longer be obligated to reuse waste heat, only to scope out the possibility. Graichen and others have accused the German government of sacrificing climate targets for a chance to ride the AI wave. But countries across Europe find themselves pulled between these same two poles, under simultaneous pressure to cash in on rapid growth in the energy-intensive AI sector—and limit dependence on the US—and to protect the climate. The German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy did not respond to a request for comment. Among data center developers, the chief objection to the original Energy Efficiency Act was the chance it could land them in an impossible bind, obligated to reuse waste heat even when there was no available offtake—whether a municipal heating system or an industry, like greenhouse agriculture. “Some of the things they had to comply with were outside of their control,” says Barbara Smitten, associate director for critical systems at consulting firm Cundall. “It felt that [the burden] was all on the data center.” In the last 18 months, multiple data center proposals have fallen through in Germany: Stack Infrastructure canceled a $3 billion facility in Hesse, and state-owned Komm.ONE withdrew from a project in Baden-Württemberg. Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act. Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says. When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.” Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change. The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten. But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns. As policymakers contend with conflicting ambitions to improve domestic AI capabilities and meet climate objectives, some say the swelling public unease about that trade-off will complicate things yet further in Europe. In the last year, the attitude toward data centers “has switched completely,” claims Graichen. “First and foremost in the US, but the same will happen in Europe.”

artigo.texto: - BAIC will connect models across multiple brands to CATL's battery swap network and open its dealer network to support station construction. - The companies aim to build a battery swap ecosystem serving vehicles in the million level. Beijing Automotive Group, or BAIC Group, has reached an agreement with CATL (HKEX: 3750) to deepen their battery swap partnership, expanding the range of compatible models and using its dealer network to support station construction. The companies have formally signed the agreement, covering vehicle and battery development, swap station network construction, battery energy services and business model innovation, BAIC said in a statement on Thursday. Under the agreement, BAIC will connect compatible models across multiple brands to CATL's Choco swap network and jointly develop nationwide public energy replenishment infrastructure. BAIC will also open its dealer network to support CATL's deployment of swap stations around dealerships. The companies will work with dealers to explore joint station development and operation. The companies plan to consolidate battery swap assets under specialized management, improve operating efficiency through a division of responsibilities, and promote unified swap standards and shared, interoperable networks. Their goal is to build China's first mature battery swap ecosystem serving vehicles in the million level, BAIC said. The statement did not provide a timeline or identify additional models or the number of stations to be built. The agreement builds on an existing partnership. In June 2024, BAIC and CATL signed a deal covering swap-compatible vehicles, battery block development and battery data management. BAIC's electric vehicle brand Arcfox launched the Beta S3 on May 22 this year. Its battery swap version uses CATL's Choco-SEB solution and offers a battery rental option. In August, a battery swap version of the Arcfox Beta T1 also appeared in a vehicle filing catalog published by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). The filing showed that the vehicle and battery could be sold separately. A broader lineup of compatible models could help CATL expand the user base for its swap network. Battery swapping can generate recurring revenue from battery rentals and energy replenishment services, but requires a sufficient vehicle base to support station construction and operating costs. The expanded BAIC partnership comes shortly after CATL secured another partner. Huawei's intelligent automotive technology company Newcool, also known as Yinwang, announced on October 19 that it had joined CATL's Choco swap ecosystem. That partnership will make models using Huawei's Qiankun intelligent automotive solutions compatible with CATL's swap network and connect data and services across vehicles, swap stations and cloud systems. BAIC is also a Huawei partner. The companies jointly developed Stelato, a brand under HIMA (Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance). CATL had built 2,520 swap stations across 200 Chinese cities as of September 29, according to information it previously released. Its long-term goal is to expand the network to 30,000 stations. CATL also plans to build 1,000 highway swap stations in 2026 and 2027, extending its services beyond cities to long-distance travel.

artigo.texto: US-based Peak Energy has closed a $108m Series B funding round to accelerate manufacturing and expand the deployment of its sodium-ion energy storage systems. The company, which produces passively cooled storage technology for grid and data centre applications, said the financing was oversubscribed. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. General Motors Ventures led the round, with Maverick Silicon, Eclipse, Infinite Capital, Xora Innovation and LG Technology Ventures also participating. The new capital is intended to allow Peak Energy to expand domestic manufacturing capabilities and support the fulfilment of more than $1bn in existing customer orders. The company also plans to target the data centre sector, where demand for power and effective storage solutions is increasing. Peak Energy co-founder and CEO Landon Mossburg said: “Peak’s mission from day one has been to lower the cost of energy through safer, simpler, cleaner and more reliable technology. “The investment we announce today will supercharge Peak’s ability to scale and deliver as the world increasingly turns to passively cooled sodium-ion storage to solve our energy needs.” Peak Energy has developed its sodium-ion storage system over the past three years, positioning it as an alternative to lithium-ion batteries for grid-scale uses. According to the company, demand from power producers, utilities and data centres continues to grow. The Series B funding follows a partnership announced in June with General Motors (GM) to jointly develop next-generation sodium-ion battery cells. The collaboration is expected to utilise GM’s battery cell industrialisation expertise in the US. In July, Peak Energy revealed plans for a new 4GW-hour (4GWh) manufacturing facility in Sacramento, California, with production scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. Peak Energy says its storage system aims to lower operating and maintenance (O&M) costs by removing the need for cooling systems, reducing energy waste and requiring no planned maintenance. The system is also designed for minimal noise, zero water use and addresses common causes of battery fires, according to the company. The latest funding is intended to position Peak Energy to meet rising demand from data centre operators and utilities, particularly as requirements for reliable and cost-effective energy storage continue to grow.

artigo.texto: Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy. India is touted as one of the hottest markets for data centers, with several U.S. Big Tech companies investing to set up capacity in the country. But of late, some projects have faced public backlash over the use of water and power resources. Now the Indian government is taking steps to address the situation. Will it work? Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team. The big story Several U.S. Big Tech companies that are spending billions to set up digital infrastructure in India are facing growing public anger over resource sharing and environmental concerns, prompting the government to step in and calm tensions. On Oct. 14, Jitin Prasada, a junior minister for electronics and information technology, announced that India will roll out a policy for data centers, calling the country a "fertile ground for hyperscalers." The minister reportedly said India wants to avoid a situation where consumers have to pay more for power because they have to compete with data centers for supply. Globally, data center companies are facing public backlash as communities raise concerns over electricity, water and land use. India is also grappling with similar issues that pose a threat to its ambitions to host the whole world's data. As per local media reports, Amazon's data center near Mumbai is facing resistance from residents who are worried that the U.S. company's facility would receive priority access to water and electricity during shortages. Meanwhile, environmental activists have been demanding the cancellation of permissions given to AI data centers in Visakhapatnam, where Google is constructing its $15 billion project. Amazon told CNBC that it is committed to being a "good and responsible neighbor," and said it is engaging with the community through educational sessions. They denied using water for cooling and added that their data centers "do not draw electricity from the local distribution network that supplies homes, shops and businesses." The American firm also said it "will be a part of industry consultations with the government to advise on India's data center regulations." Google did not respond to CNBC's request for comments. Experts told CNBC that the government plans to roll out a policy directive to pacify local resistance to some projects across the country. It will also lay down clear approval guidelines that will minimize the risks data center developers face from public pushback and execution challenges, they added. Policy shift The proposed policy indicates a shift in direction from "primarily encouraging the data center investment" to now balancing it with infrastructure readiness and sustainability aspects, Jaspreet Singh, partner at Grant Thornton Bharat, told CNBC. Last week, Niti Aayog, an Indian government think tank, shared a framework for local governments to evaluate data center projects for sustainability and to provide suitable locations, based on grid readiness and water supply availability. It underscored the need to establish guidelines "before constraints emerge," adding that data centers should get faster approvals only in cases where resource readiness, local safeguards and public value are proven. Experts who are part of consultations expect the new policy to lay down clear and consistent rules, which will also help the industry overcome challenges around land acquisition and simplify a fragmented approval process. "India does not have a dedicated national policy for data centers, and it is high time that this gap was addressed," Shobhit Agarwal, chief executive of real estate consultancy ANAROCK Capital, told CNBC. He explained that projects are currently approved under existing environmental and building rules, and every state has its own "variations and incentives." While the Indian government has been enthusiastic in welcoming the hyperscalers to invest in data centers in India, even giving them 20-year tax sops, regional governments are the final decision-makers when it comes to providing land, water and power resources. Nikhil Narendran, a partner for technology at law firm Trilegal, who works with U.S. Big Tech companies, said local governments are proposing data center projects in locations that are already facing constraints in terms of electricity, water and other infrastructure. He added that state governments need to be encouraged to identify locations where reliable electricity, substantial cooling infrastructure, water availability and high-quality connectivity are available, "rather than simply competing to announce large investments." artigo.texto: - EU lawmakers and member states have reached a provisional agreement on changes to the bloc’s carbon market rules. - The deal raises the Market Stability Reserve’s allowance invalidation threshold from 400 million to 700 million. - Formal approval is still required, with the changes aimed at improving liquidity and predictability for industry. The European Union agreed earlier today to increase the buffer for surplus carbon allowances under its Market Stability Reserve, marking a new step in efforts to balance industrial competitiveness with the bloc’s climate objectives. The provisional compromise increases the threshold above which allowances held in the reserve are invalidated from 400 million to 700 million. The change is intended to improve the availability of permits over time and make the carbon market more predictable for businesses. The agreement follows months of debate over how to maintain the carbon market’s role in reducing emissions while responding to concerns about costs and future supply. It must still be endorsed and formally adopted by both institutions before becoming law. A larger buffer for Europe’s carbon market The Market Stability Reserve was established to address a historical oversupply of emissions permits that had weakened the EU carbon market’s price signal. Under the mechanism, allowances can be withheld from auctions when supply is high, while permits held above a defined threshold have been subject to permanent cancellation since 2023. The European Commission says more than 3 billion allowances have been invalidated since that cancellation mechanism began. Raising the threshold would allow a larger stock of permits to remain available within the reserve, providing more flexibility if market conditions tighten. “In response to European leaders’ call for accelerated action, we reached a balanced outcome on the market stability reserve that provides European industry with immediate flexibility, while ensuring price stability and protecting the integrity of the EU carbon market. The EU is delivering on the ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap,” said Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O’Brien. The deal represents a compromise between competing approaches. In its original proposal, the Commission sought to end the invalidation mechanism. The Council’s negotiating position instead envisaged a temporary suspension followed by a higher threshold. The provisional agreement retains the cancellation framework but raises its threshold to 700 million allowances. Industry costs and climate targets remain in focus The changes come amid broader EU efforts to revise emissions trading rules as policymakers weigh high energy costs, industrial competitiveness and emissions-reduction targets. The Commission’s wider ETS review, proposed in July, covers additional elements of the carbon market and industrial decarbonisation policy. The threshold agreement is a targeted adjustment, not a wholesale redesign of emissions trading. Its practical effects will depend on future allowance supply, demand and the implementation of the revised rules. For companies covered by the system, the deal offers a change to the rules governing the reserve, but it does not guarantee lower carbon prices. The EU’s wider challenge remains ensuring that the market supports investment in cleaner production while preserving incentives to cut greenhouse gas emissions. artigo.texto: Chinese EV demand weakens while overseas competition and taxes pressure battery makers while Korean battery firms gain an opening with U.S. ESS orders and automaker diversification The earnings growth of China’s CATL, the world’s number one electric vehicle battery maker, has faltered. The net profit growth rate for the third quarter of this year recorded the lowest in 7 quarters. The slump in the Chinese electric vehicle market and the moves by countries around the world, including the United States and Europe, to keep Chinese electric vehicles in check appear to have had an impact. This is expected to be an opportunity for the domestic battery industry, including LG Energy Solution. While China is being kept in check, domestic companies are continuing a streak of winning orders for energy storage systems (ESS) for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, utilizing their local production lines in the United States. Domestic battery makers are also a strong alternative for major automakers to execute a ‘break away from Chinese batteries.’ According to Reuters and others on Oct. 21 (local time), CATL, the world’s number one electric vehicle battery maker, announced through its third-quarter earnings report the previous day that its net profit recorded 21.25 billion yuan (about 4.2 trillion won, $3.23 billion), up 14.54% from the same period last year. This figure falls significantly short of the net profit growth rate of the second quarter (36.5%) as well as the market forecast of 41.2% compiled by market research firm London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG). It is also the lowest since the fourth quarter of 2024 (13.6%). Third-quarter sales increased by 58.58% year-on-year to 165.22 billion yuan (about 32.8 trillion won, $25.23 billion). Although the growth rate was higher than the second quarter (56.9%), it fell short of the LSEG compiled market forecast of 60.2%. The South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported that CATL’s stock price has been showing weakness after Chinese electric vehicle makers Xiaomi and Li Auto announced last month that they would collaborate with other battery manufacturers. The Chinese battery industry has grown rapidly for several years, driven by domestic subsidies and price competitiveness. However, as indiscriminate facility expansion and excessive competition continue, even the frontrunner CATL is facing checks from domestic companies in the domestic market. Furthermore, as the Chinese domestic automobile market continued its slump for 12 consecutive months until September, major battery manufacturers are staking their lives on expanding overseas exports. The tax reform by the Chinese authorities has also added to the industry’s burden. In order to curb oversupply and cutthroat competition in the battery industry, the authorities ended the lithium-ion battery consumption tax exemption in July for the first time in 10 years and applied a 2% tax rate starting in September. Following the reduction of the export value-added tax refund rate, a complete abolition was confirmed for next year. Nevertheless, the global electric vehicle battery market share of CATL, which expanded its supply to overseas automakers, rose to 39.4% from January to August this year, up from 37.7% in the same period last year. On the other hand, the market share of the second-place BYD dropped from 17.1% to 15.1%. The market foresaw that the blow could spread not only to the industry leader CATL but also to small and medium-sized battery makers. An official from Citigroup analyzed, “If even CATL cannot completely pass on the consumption tax burden to its customers, second-tier companies will also find it difficult to handle.” The moves by global automakers to ease their dependence on CATL are also a threat factor. As major automakers diversify their orders to stabilize supply chains, they are fueling competition to lower unit prices within the market. Investment bank J.P. Morgan recently downgraded its investment opinion on CATL’s Hong Kong stocks to ‘neutral,’ stating that if the profitability of the Chinese electric vehicle industry deteriorates faster than expected, it could affect the demand for CATL battery products. Analysts say that such moves by global automakers to diversify their supply chains will act as an opportunity for South Korean battery companies. The three major domestic battery makers are rapidly converting their existing lines exclusively for ESS to respond to the slowdown in electric vehicle demand. They are intensively targeting the North American ESS market, which is growing rapidly due to the proliferation of AI data centers. LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On are increasing the production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries locally in the United States while simultaneously preparing for the mass production of next-generation products such as solid-state batteries. CATL also plans to expand the proportion of its ESS business, which currently accounts for about 1/4 of its total sales, to half by 2030. In addition, it recently unveiled a next-generation battery for heavy-duty trucks and announced a plan to expand its battery swap network.

artigo.texto: CATL, BYD, and Gotion Expand Production and Supply Chains in Europe and Southeast Asia Since 2023, Holding 56.2% Share Outside China While South Korean Trio Falls to 26.8% and LFP Battery Share Rises to 27.5% Major Chinese battery companies have invested approximately $90 billion in overseas operations since 2023, expanding their penetration of the global market. While the market share of Chinese companies has increased even in the electric vehicle battery market excluding China, the market share of three domestic battery companies, including LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On, has declined. According to the UK Financial Times (FT) on October 21 (local time), major Chinese battery companies such as CATL, BYD, and Gotion High-tech were found to have invested approximately $90 billion in building overseas battery production and supply chains, including in Europe and Southeast Asia, since 2023. The market share gap in overseas markets is also widening. According to market research firm SNE Research, the combined market share of six Chinese companies, including CATL, BYD, Gotion, CALB, SVOLT, and EVE, in the global electric vehicle battery market excluding China from January to August this year was 56.2%, up 12.6 percentage points compared to the same period last year. On the other hand, the combined market share of the three domestic battery companies was 26.8%, down 11.1 percentage points during the same period. Among Chinese companies, the growth of BYD was prominent. In markets excluding China, the total battery capacity of electric vehicles equipped with BYD batteries was 39.7GWh, an increase of 66.5% compared to the same period last year. Its market share also rose from 8.2% to 11.0%. By region, battery installation volume increased by 65.6% in Europe and 138.5% in South America. Conversely, the combined battery installation volume of the three domestic battery companies, LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On, in markets excluding China was 96.5GWh, a decrease of 12.8% compared to the same period last year. In particular, it dropped by 46.5% from 47.4GWh to 25.3GWh in North America. In Europe, it increased by 5.2% from 49.9GWh to 52.5GWh, but this failed to offset the decline in the North American market. Along with the rising market share of Chinese companies, the proportion of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries is also expanding. According to SNE Research, the proportion of LFP batteries in the global electric vehicle battery market excluding China rose by 11.9 percentage points from 15.6% in January to August last year to 27.5% during the same period this year. LFP batteries have relatively low manufacturing costs and are mainly used in entry-level electric vehicles. As Chinese companies have secured high production competitiveness in this area and overseas automakers increasingly adopt LFP batteries, changes are also appearing in the competitive landscape of the global battery market.

artigo.texto: Energia limpa – O Google planeja construir um data center de 780 megawatts em Pine Island, Minnesota, nos Estados Unidos, acompanhado de investimentos em energia renovável e armazenamento. O acordo com a Xcel Energy prevê ampliar a capacidade da rede elétrica além da demanda da instalação, mas ainda depende de aprovação da Comissão de Utilidade Pública do estado. Segundo a CNBC, a empresa financiará a adição de 1.400 MW de energia eólica, 200 MW de energia solar e 300 MW de armazenamento em baterias. A capacidade adicional busca compensar a geração intermitente das fontes renováveis. LEIA: Consumo de água por IA varia conforme servidores e geração de energia Proteção contra a saída antecipada O contrato prevê que o Google pague pelo menos 75% da capacidade acordada, mesmo que utilize menos energia. Se encerrar o compromisso antes do prazo, poderá arcar com até oito anos de cobranças mínimas. “Ninguém quer ter uma grande expansão e depois não ter para onde mandar essa energia e ninguém para pagá-la”, diz Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva da Xcel Energy. “É aí que essas proteções entram.” A iniciativa ocorre em meio à crescente demanda por eletricidade dos centros de dados. A Corporação Norte-Americana de Confiabilidade Elétrica (NERC) aponta essas instalações como principal fator de expansão prevista do consumo na América do Norte na próxima década. Nos Estados Unidos, o envelhecimento da infraestrutura também pressiona o setor elétrico. Centros menores como alternativa Para Jigar Shah, sócio da consultoria Multiplier, empresas poderiam optar por instalações menores em regiões com capacidade disponível na rede, reduzindo custos para os consumidores. “Se você encaixar o crescimento de carga que os centros de dados querem na rede existente, as tarifas de todo mundo caem muito”, afirma. Segundo ele, construir unidades menores exige mais planejamento, mas pode evitar grandes expansões de infraestrutura. Incentivos das distribuidoras David Pomerantz, diretor-executivo do Energy and Policy Institute, observa que as distribuidoras têm incentivos financeiros para investir em novas estruturas. “Quando [as distribuidoras] constroem algo novo, financiam parte desse investimento com recursos de investidores de Wall Street e desfrutam de retornos incrivelmente altos, exorbitantes sobre esses investimentos, tipicamente em torno de 10%”, afirma. Uma alternativa seria os operadores de data centers financiarem melhorias na rede com capital mais barato. Pomerantz, porém, aponta que essa possibilidade gera conflitos com as distribuidoras. Apesar das ressalvas sobre o modelo, Shah avalia positivamente a proposta do Google, que aguarda autorização regulatória. artigo.texto: South Korea's Big 3 Battery Makers Race to Mass-Produce 'Salt Batteries,' Chasing CATL's Head Start South Korea's three major battery makers are accelerating commercialization of sodium-ion batteries, which replace lithium. Using sodium as a raw material, these batteries are seen as a technology that could reshape the next-generation energy storage system (ESS) market thanks to advantages in cost and low-temperature performance. However, China's CATL and BYD have already entered mass production, giving China the early lead. LG Energy Solution has built a sodium-ion battery pilot line at its Ochang Energy Plant in Cheongju, North Chungcheong Province, and is running sample tests for ESS applications at a scale of 30MWh with North American customers. The company aims for first mass production next year. In the early commercialization phase, it plans to target the vehicle auxiliary battery and ESS markets before expanding into affordable electric vehicles. Samsung SDI is developing sodium-ion batteries for uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems at AI data centers and for ESS. It has drawn up mass production plans and will disclose a detailed schedule by the end of this year or during next year. SK On aims to complete prototype development by next year, centered on ESS products, and pursue commercialization in 2028. It is also reviewing the possibility of using the technology in EV batteries. Sodium-ion batteries use sodium, the main component of salt, as a raw material. Unlike lithium, the mining and refining supply chain is not concentrated in a handful of countries, making supply stable and prices cheap. Another highlighted strength is that charge and discharge performance degrades less than lithium-ion batteries in subzero conditions. Energy density, long cited as a weakness, is also improving. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), recently developed products reach energy density of up to 175Wh/kg, approaching lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries at up to 205Wh/kg. Nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries stand at around 255Wh/kg. ESS, where weight and volume constraints are relatively less binding, is the likely first application market. Global sodium-ion battery output last year was less than 1% of lithium-ion battery production, underscoring that the market is still in its early stages. Morgan Stanley expects sodium-ion batteries' share of total battery deployments to rise from 2% in 2027 to 20% in 2030 and 37% in 2035. Annual deployments are projected to reach 830GWh in 2030 and 2.4TWh in 2035, and the analysis estimates that about $800 billion in new investment will be needed by 2035 to achieve this. China is furthest ahead in seizing the market. In April, CATL signed a three-year supply contract for 60GWh with Chinese ESS company HyperStrong and entered a mass production regime. It plans to increase shipments through the end of the year and begin overseas supplies from June next year. BYD is also building a dedicated sodium-ion battery plant. The sense of urgency in South Korea's industry stems from memories of past failures in responding to LFP. The prevailing view is that while Korean companies focused on high-performance NMC batteries, they fell behind in LFP mass production and handed leadership of that market to China. There is a growing sense of crisis that if they are also outrun in sodium-ion batteries, they could lose leadership of the battery industry itself. If sodium-ion batteries are commercialized in earnest, the cost-competition landscape in the ESS market could change. The burden on existing supply chains exposed to lithium price swings would ease, and the economics of long-duration storage facilities could improve. However, a gap with LFP in energy density remains, suggesting it will take considerable time before sodium-ion becomes a mainstream EV battery. Whether South Korea's three companies can move up their mass production timelines is seen as a variable that will determine the supply landscape of the ESS market going forward.

artigo.texto: CATL Tries to Reassure Investors: Next Year's Battery Demand Not as Bleak as Feared, but Shares Still Plunge Nearly 10% CATL (03750.HK), China's battery leader, on the 21st took the rare step of proactively addressing market doubts. Responding to investor concerns about weakening demand in next year's new energy vehicle market and for batteries, the company said "next year's industry demand is still worth looking forward to," emphasizing that the global market size for power batteries and energy storage batteries may not be as bleak as outsiders imagine and still holds solid growth potential. The reassurance, however, failed to reverse the stock's slide. The shares touched an intraday low of HK$371.2 that day and last traded at HK$371.8, down 9.71%, on volume of 5.1631 million shares worth HK$1.964 billion (approximately $250.3 million), extending a run of new lows. CATL's weaker-than-expected third-quarter net profit was the direct trigger for the selloff. Breaking down the fundamentals, the company believes the market's assessment of demand is too conservative. In China, overall passenger vehicle sales have declined this year, but the electrification rate is climbing rapidly, and the battery capacity per vehicle is rising at the same time. Combined, these two forces are keeping shipment growth of power batteries for new energy passenger vehicles in positive territory. The electrification rate for new energy commercial vehicles is also in a rapid ascent. Overseas, the electrification trend in Europe has continuity, with new models continuing to launch and remaining competitive, while electrification potential in other markets may be underestimated. The energy storage business is another bright spot, maintaining solid growth in both China and overseas markets, with demand particularly strong in some overseas markets. Asked about capacity utilization, the company said utilization was at a very saturated level in the first half. In recent years it has accelerated capacity construction in line with market demand, and as new capacity added this year gradually comes on stream, the tightness has eased somewhat. But demand is also continuing to grow, so capacity utilization will remain at a relatively high level going forward and is overall healthy. The change in cash flow that has drawn outside attention is tied to an adjustment in supply chain strategy. The company noted that upstream lithium battery supply chain companies have faced relatively heavy cash flow pressure in recent years, and CATL has proactively adjusted payment arrangements with suppliers since the third quarter, giving priority to supporting partners with R&D capabilities, an innovative spirit and active cooperation in capacity expansion. Measures include shortening payment terms, making prepayments and providing R&D funding support, among others. This approach to supporting the supply chain may continue for some time, with the aim of fostering healthier and more sustainable development across the industry. It will have a phased impact on operating cash flow, but over the long term will not hurt the company's cash profitability, which is expected to return to a relatively healthy level. As for the quarter-on-quarter increase in third-quarter inventory, the company explained that the larger inventory figure is a natural result of business growth. Inventory turnover days have been relatively stable in recent quarters, with no sluggish sales or shipment disruptions, representing normal turnover. By composition, the increase was mainly goods shipped but not yet recognized as revenue, which will gradually be reflected in the company's revenue. In energy storage, the company is shifting from simply selling battery cells and DC-side products to offering AC-side and system-level products. The product mix and formats are richer than before, and the corresponding delivery and revenue recognition cycles have lengthened. In terms of market impact, CATL is a bellwether for the global power and energy storage battery industry, and its read on next year's demand is seen as an important gauge of conditions across the electric vehicle and energy storage sectors. The company's disclosures on capacity, cash flow and inventory in its earnings call and response help investors clarify the line items in its third-quarter report most likely to raise questions. Still, the stock's nearly 10% plunge after the results reflects short-term investors' heightened sensitivity to the profit miss and the phased pressure on cash flow. The strength of the demand recovery and the actual impact of the supply chain payment adjustments will be key focal points as the market re-evaluates the stock.

artigo.texto: Huawei and CATL Partner to Fully Automate EV Battery Swaps, 'Full' in 99 Seconds China's electric vehicle (EV) market has kicked off a race to automate "battery swap" services that replace an entire battery without waiting to charge or discharge. Yinwang (In-One), the automotive technology subsidiary of telecom equipment giant Huawei, CATL, the world's largest automotive battery maker, and Shidai Dianfu, which operates battery-swap services, have formed a partnership aimed at building a system in which vehicles decide on their own whether a swap is needed and complete everything from entering the station to swapping the battery to leaving, unmanned. Huawei disclosed the plan on October 19. At the core of the partnership is connecting Huawei's advanced driver-assistance system "Qiankun" with CATL's battery-swap network "Choco-Swap" at the data level. Information will be exchanged among vehicles, swap stations and the cloud, and the need for a swap will be judged based on remaining battery charge and the user's travel patterns. If a swap is deemed necessary, the vehicle will search on its own for a compatible station, enter it autonomously, adjust its position to align with the swapping equipment, be fitted with a charged battery and then leave autonomously—the envisioned flow. According to CATL, BAIC Group's EV "Arcfox S3 Choco-Swap Edition" can complete the battery swap itself in 99 seconds. However, the total time required, including entering and leaving the station and positioning, has not been disclosed. Huawei plans to make the system available on vehicles that adopt its automotive technology, but it has not touched on which models will be compatible or when the service will launch. Huawei explains that the aim of the collaboration is to realize a power-replenishment experience in which users do not need to think about charging, looking ahead to the era of autonomous driving, and to provide more diverse and convenient swap services. Information on the scale of the battery-swap network is mixed. According to details CATL published in April 2026, it operates more than 1,470 swap stations in 99 cities in China. Meanwhile, according to reports by U.S. EV-specialist media outlet Electrek and others, the network has reached more than 2,520 stations in about 200 cities, with a goal of expanding to more than 30,000 stations in the future. Both sets of figures were provided by CATL, and the differences are believed to stem from different tally dates and definitions. Note: Station counts vary depending on the disclosing party and timing. Total time required, compatible models and service launch timing have not been disclosed. Behind this lies the delay in commercializing all-solid-state batteries, seen as next-generation batteries. CATL Chairman Robin Zeng, speaking at the 2026 Summer Davos (World Economic Forum) in June 2026, rated the technological maturity of all-solid-state batteries on a scale of 1 to 9 and said, "We are currently at stage 4, and mass production will only become possible once we reach stage 9." If the swap network is sufficiently developed, the time spent waiting to charge and the burden of long-distance travel can be reduced without waiting for dramatic improvements in battery performance itself. However, the commercial success of the battery-swap model remains unclear. Tesla began a demonstration project for an automated swap system in 2014 but later withdrew. CEO Elon Musk said at the time that he called on 200 customers to use it, but only about four or five showed interest. He has expressed the view that "charging time" provides users with leisure—time to stretch their legs, go to the restroom or drink coffee during a trip—and takes the position of questioning the superiority of the swap model. Some market participants see the partnership as a move that will shake up the battle for leadership in the battery-swap ecosystem in China's EV market. If Huawei expands the number of vehicles equipped with its driver-assistance technology, CATL's swap network can strengthen its connection with users as a touchpoint that "makes them forget about charging." On the other hand, a design that deeply integrates in-vehicle systems with external infrastructure could become a barrier to entry for other automakers. In the initial phase, when compatible models are limited, investors will likely be watching closely how quickly the partnership is implemented and how utilization rates trend.
