artigo.texto: Why New England doesn't have large AI data centers, and what the region is doing to prepare for them From Bangor to Boston to Bow, New Englanders are buzzing about data centers — which might be surprising considering the region doesn’t have any of the super-sized facilities cropping up elsewhere in the country. There are several reasons for this, so let's dig into the data center landscape in New England today, and how people in the region are planning for the (perhaps unavoidable) arrival of these resource-gobbling facilities. What is a data center? At the most fundamental level, a data center is a building — or even a single room — full of computer servers and other hardware that store and process digital information. Put another way, a data center is a bunch of computers that makes many aspects of modern life possible. These facilities have been around for decades, but until recently they've mostly been "out of sight, out of mind," said Daniel Goetzel, a practitioner in residence at Harvard University's Reimagining the Economy Project. "You weren't looking at multi-football field-size projects that had as much electricity use as cities. You were looking at smaller things that were powering your cell phones," he said. These smaller data centers run on a collection of computer chips known as central processing units, or CPUs, and they make it possible to stream videos, transfer money online or back up documents to the cloud. The newer AI data centers, by contrast, use more powerful chips known as graphics processing units, or GPUs. These chips can run thousands of simultaneous tasks and are used for jobs like training artificial intelligence and running large language models like ChatGPT or Claude. But GPUs are also more energy-intensive to operate, and they get hotter than CPUs. These resource-thirsty chips are powering the colossal new data centers companies are building, and they're fueling community pushback over the facilities' water and electricity demands. Data centers in New England come in all sizes. The largest facility in the region, in Lowell, is about the size of Fenway Park. While people talk about AI data centers and non-AI data centers, the distinction isn't black and white. Many facilities, including some in New England, employ some combination of CPUs and GPUs in their servers. The more important distinction, according to Goetzel, is between data centers designed for training cutting-edge AI models and the ones that do everything else. Data centers for training tend to be massive in scale and use enormous amounts of electricity. They can be located almost anywhere, since the small delay between a request and its answer — known as latency — isn't a big concern. On the other hand, data centers used for AI "inference" — like a query for ChatGPT or a non-AI process — work best when they're near the people or companies using them. "Right now, we're seeing a huge increase in training, which is why you're seeing these massive facilities in rural areas," Goetzel said. "Perhaps in the future, you might see more of a shift to inference, where it's more important to be closer to city centers where this work is being done." Are there data centers in New England? Yes. An exact number is tough to pin down, but there are about 100, according to Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, an industry group. The largest concentration of facilities is in the Greater Boston area, though there are small clusters near other major cities. While some companies house their servers on-site, most data centers in New England are "colocation" facilities. This means private companies — like a bank, biotech firm or television streaming service — pay a third party to house, deliver power to and cool their computer hardware. At the Boston BO2 data center in Billerica, Massachusetts, for example, the company Equinix owns the building and handles power and cooling, but the actual servers are owned by hundreds of companies. Many universities in New England also use colocated data centers. At the Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center in Holyoke, a big room of humming server racks power all sorts of research and data processing projects — including some that use AI — for Boston University, Harvard, MIT, Northeastern, the University of Massachusetts and Yale. Are there AI data centers in New England? This is tricky to answer, since it depends on what is meant by an AI data center. There are no large-scale AI training data centers in the region right now. But there are facilities capable of supporting AI-related functions. How big are New England data centers? The data centers in New England today are relatively small compared to some others across the country. And they're not always easy to spot. Some look like office buildings. And perhaps unbeknownst to shoppers, one sits atop the Macy's department store in downtown Boston. On the large end, the Markley data center in Lowell, Massachusetts, provides 352,000 square feet of building space, making it just smaller than Fenway Park. (It's also about 2.5 times bigger than Market Basket's flagship supermarket north of Boston.) Most data centers in New England, however, tend to be much smaller; the facility in Billerica is more typical for the region with 108,000 square feet. Others, like a facility in Burlington, Vermont that occupies about 39,000 square feet, are even smaller. Another way to compare the size of data centers is by the maximum amount of power they use, which can vary widely. Some New England facilities use less than one megawatt. (A megawatt is about the amount of electricity needed to power 500 homes.) Others, like a data center in Trumbull, Connecticut, use up to 15 megawatts. A few are even bigger. In Massachusetts, a Watertown data center uses up to 19 megawatts of power, and a facility spread across two buildings in Waltham can use just over 38 megawatts. Markley

artigo.texto: Peak Energy Raises $108 Million in Series B Funding Peak Energy, a semiconductor company, has raised $108 million in an oversubscribed Series B. The round was led by General Motors Ventures, with additional participation from Maverick Silicon, Infinite Capital, Eclipse, Xora Innovation and LG Technology Ventures. The Sacramento-based company develops sodium-ion energy storage systems for grid-scale applications. The new capital will support domestic manufacturing expansion and entry into the data centre market. Peak Energy also plans to fulfil more than $1 billion in existing customer orders. The company was formed in 2023 to provide more affordable and safer large-scale energy storage. It utilises a sodium-ion battery-based technology with an innovative passive cooling system to cut costs without the need for traditional active cooling technology. This investment comes on the back of increased demand for electricity infrastructure. Data centres, for example, consume significant amounts of power in servicing AI applications. Storage solutions can ease grid constraints and bolster electricity grid reliability. Passive Cooling Targets Lower Storage Costs Peak Energy’s system is designed to reduce the costs associated with operating and maintaining conventional energy storage installations. Its passive cooling architecture removes the need for energy-intensive cooling systems. The company says this design can lower energy costs by up to 20%. The platform also aims to reduce maintenance requirements and improve operational reliability. Peak Energy says its systems require no planned maintenance. They also consume no water and produce virtually no noise. Safety remains another central part of the company’s approach. Peak Energy says its design eliminates leading causes of battery fires. These features could make its systems attractive to communities near large storage installations. Sodium-ion technology also offers an alternative to lithium-ion batteries. Sodium is an abundant material that could support domestic supply chains. Peak Energy is developing its platform for utility-scale storage rather than consumer electronics. Sacramento Factory Supports Domestic Manufacturing Peak Energy is expanding its manufacturing operations through a new facility in Sacramento, California. The factory is designed to provide four gigawatt-hours of annual manufacturing capacity. Production is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. The facility will help the company increase output as customer demand grows. Peak Energy has secured commercial agreements with Jupiter Power, RWE and Energy Vault. Its existing commitments exceed $1 billion, according to the company. In June 2026, Peak Energy announced a strategic partnership with General Motors. The companies plan to develop next-generation sodium-ion battery cells for energy storage. GM will contribute its experience in domestic battery manufacturing and industrialisation. More News: Blacksmith Raises $66M for AI Code Testing Infrastructure Data Centre Expansion Creates New Growth Opportunities Peak Energy plans to use its latest financing to enter the data centre market. Artificial intelligence growth has increased pressure on electricity infrastructure. Operators require reliable power solutions that enable growth without incurring the high costs. Energy storage to ease the stress on power systems and meet peak demand Peak Energy says its passive cooling system can bring a “competitive edge” to facilities with space, water and safety concerns. Execution will depend on manufacturing progress and successful commercial deployment. General Motors Ventures sees potential in the company’s approach. Its president, Kevin McCabe, highlighted the technology’s potential as a cost-effective solution using abundant, domestically sourced materials. The planned 2027 production launch will be an important milestone for the company. artigo.texto: Saft, a subsidiary of TotalEnergies, is set to inaugurate new solid-state battery production lines at its site in Bordeaux, marking a significant step towards industrial-scale manufacturing of next-generation energy storage technology. The facility will make Saft the first French manufacturer with the capacity to develop and produce solid-state batteries using both sulphide and polymer electrolytes at room temperature. This combination of technologies offers potential applications across several industries, particularly aviation and space. Higher energy density and improved safety Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte found in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid material. According to Saft, this approach offers improved safety and energy density up to 50% higher than that of traditional lithium-ion batteries. The manufacturing process also incorporates dry electrodes, which can reduce carbon dioxide emissions during this stage of production by up to 40%, offering potential environmental benefits alongside improved battery performance. These characteristics make solid-state technology a promising option for applications where safety, compact design and energy density are important requirements. Supporting electrification in aviation and space Saft is targeting the aviation and space sectors, where advances in battery performance could support further electrification. The company has already reached an initial milestone in aviation, delivering semi-solid-state cells for the evaluation of future electric and hybrid aircraft architectures. Solid-state batteries have also attracted significant interest from the space industry, highlighting their potential across demanding applications. Turning research into industrial production The new production lines represent the transition from years of research into manufacturing capability, supporting the development of solid-state batteries for future applications. Cedric Duclos, Chief Executive Officer of Saft, said: “Solid-state batteries are among the most promising innovations to meet tomorrow’s electrification needs. These new production lines mark an important milestone for Saft, as we turn several years of research into real industrial capacity, a statement of our ambition to establish France and Europe as leading players in this strategic technology.” The initiative reinforces Saft’s ambition to help establish France and Europe as key participants in the development and production of solid-state battery technology. artigo.texto: Fundos imobiliários de data centers: nova fronteira O avanço da inteligência artificial (IA) está abrindo novas possibilidades de investimento no mercado imobiliário. Embora a IA seja frequentemente associada ao desenvolvimento de software, sua operação depende de uma estrutura física robusta, que envolve semicondutores, energia elétrica, redes de transmissão, sistemas de resfriamento e data centers. Para investidores e empresários de Araçatuba e região noroeste paulista, essa tendência pode representar uma nova fronteira de diversificação de portfólio e de negócios. Segundo a XP, os fundos imobiliários podem acessar esse mercado por meio da aquisição de data centers operacionais, do financiamento de projetos em desenvolvimento e do investimento em infraestruturas associadas, como subestações elétricas. Nesse modelo, a exposição do cotista é imobiliária: o fundo adquire o imóvel e recebe os aluguéis pagos pelo operador responsável pelo data center ou pela infraestrutura locada. As receitas provenientes de serviços de computação em nuvem, processamento de dados ou outras atividades tecnológicas permanecem com o operador, e não são diretamente apropriadas pelo fundo. Modelos de investimento em data centers Os fundos imobiliários podem atuar de diferentes formas nesse segmento. A aquisição de data centers operacionais é uma das estratégias: o fundo compra um imóvel já em funcionamento, com contratos de locação vigentes e fluxo de caixa previsível. Outra possibilidade é o financiamento de projetos em desenvolvimento, no qual o fundo fornece capital para a construção ou expansão de um data center, assumindo riscos maiores em troca de retornos potencialmente mais elevados. Há ainda o investimento em infraestruturas associadas, como subestações elétricas, que são essenciais para o fornecimento de energia aos data centers e podem gerar renda estável por meio de contratos de locação de longo prazo. Em todos esses casos, a exposição do cotista é imobiliária. O fundo adquire o imóvel e recebe os aluguéis pagos pelo operador responsável pelo data center ou pela infraestrutura locada. As receitas provenientes de serviços de computação em nuvem, processamento de dados ou outras atividades tecnológicas permanecem com o operador, e não são diretamente apropriadas pelo fundo. Essa separação é fundamental para entender o perfil de risco e retorno do investimento. Perspectivas e riscos do setor A perspectiva de expansão dos serviços digitais pode favorecer a ocupação dos empreendimentos e a capacidade de pagamento dos locatários. Com o crescimento do uso de IA, streaming, comércio eletrônico e outras aplicações, a demanda por processamento e armazenamento de dados tende a aumentar, o que pode elevar a taxa de ocupação dos data centers e a estabilidade dos aluguéis. Para investidores do interior paulista, isso pode significar uma alternativa de renda passiva com lastro em ativos reais. Ainda assim, diz a XP, o resultado depende de como cada ativo foi adquirido, da estrutura de financiamento e das necessidades futuras de investimento para manter a infraestrutura competitiva. Data centers exigem atualizações constantes de equipamentos e sistemas de resfriamento, o que pode demandar novos aportes de capital. Além disso, a localização geográfica e a disponibilidade de energia elétrica são fatores críticos que podem afetar a viabilidade do empreendimento. Built to suit: contratos sob medida Já no modelo built to suit, o imóvel é construído ou adaptado de acordo com as necessidades específicas do futuro ocupante. Em contrapartida, o locatário firma um contrato de longo prazo, que deve remunerar adequadamente o capital investido pelo proprietário. Esse modelo é comum em projetos de data centers, pois as exigências técnicas — como piso elevado, refrigeração redundante e segurança física — são muito específicas e difíceis de encontrar em imóveis prontos. Contratos atípicos podem prever prazos extensos, reajustes periódicos pela inflação e penalidades por rescisão antecipada. Quando essas penalidades são elevadas e vinculadas ao saldo de aluguéis até o vencimento, podem desestimular a saída antecipada do inquilino e favorecer o alinhamento entre o prazo contratual e o horizonte de retorno do investimento. Para o investidor, isso proporciona maior previsibilidade de fluxo de caixa e reduz o risco de vacância. Impacto para o noroeste paulista Embora os grandes data centers estejam concentrados em regiões metropolitanas, a expansão da infraestrutura digital pode gerar efeitos indiretos para cidades como Araçatuba, Birigui, Penápolis e Andradina. A necessidade de energia elétrica confiável, por exemplo, pode impulsionar investimentos em subestações e redes de transmissão na região. Além disso, empresas locais de construção civil, manutenção predial e serviços técnicos podem ser contratadas para obras e operações de data centers de menor porte. Para empresários do comércio e da indústria local, a tendência também pode representar uma oportunidade de diversificação de investimentos. Fundos imobiliários que investem em data centers são negociados na bolsa de valores e podem ser acessados por meio de corretoras, com valores mínimos relativamente baixos. No entanto, é essencial avaliar o perfil de risco e buscar orientação de profissionais especializados antes de investir. A fonte não detalhou valores mínimos de investimento, prazos de retorno ou exemplos específicos de fundos. Ainda assim, a sinalização da XP indica que o setor deve ganhar relevância nos próximos anos, acompanhando o crescimento da economia digital. Para o noroeste paulista, o desafio será criar condições de infraestrutura e mão de obra qualificada para atrair parte desses investimentos. artigo.texto: A battle over protecting the electric bills of Xcel Energy residential and small business customers from the costs of burgeoning data centers is set to begin Wednesday before the Colorado Public Utilities Commission. The PUC required Xcel Energy — the state’s largest electricity provider with 1.6 million customers — to develop a “large load tariff,” a set of requirements designed to protect retail customers from the cost of data centers and other high-demand electricity customers. Xcel Energy filed its proposed tariff in April and since then it has been the focus of a debate between environmental and consumer advocates who want even tougher protections and business and data center groups seeking to trim requirements. Hearings on the proposed tariff are scheduled to run for several days beginning Wednesday afternoon. “It’s a big deal,” said Eric Frankowski, executive director of the Western Clean Energy Campaign, a consumer and environment advocacy group. “This determines how data centers are brought into the mix and what it means to every other customer in the Xcel system. “If they get it right then data centers can join the state’s economy and contribute to it and it doesn’t affect customers’ rates,” he added. “If wrong, we are all kind of screwed. Rates will soar; the grid will be stressed.” One controversial element in the proposed tariff is a “speed to market” pathway, which would enable Xcel Energy and a developer to negotiate a confidential contract that would not necessarily have the tariff’s safeguards and would require rapid PUC approval. “The concept is necessary to provide an option for large load customers who require greater commercial flexibility,” Jack Ihle, the company’s vice president for data centers and large loads, said in PUC testimony. But Frankowski said speed to market could “potentially undermine the tariff.” Environmental groups are also worried data centers’ big electricity demands will jeopardize the state’s goal of cutting greenhouse gas emission by 80% over 2005 levels by 2030 and result in data centers relying on natural gas and coal-fired generation. “Load growth stands to raise system costs, increase cumulative greenhouse gas emissions, risk delays of approved retirements of fossil-fuel generation units,” Clare Valentine, a senior policy advisor with environmental law nonprofit Western Resource Advocates, said in a filing. WRA is urging the commission to expand renewable energy options in the tariff. The PUC hearings on data center rates are taking place against the backdrop of a pushback on rapid data center development across Colorado. Eight municipalities and counties have enacted or are considering moratoriums or caps on data centers. Proposed projects have sparked community opposition in Colorado Springs, Brighton and Weld County. Ratepayers need to be protected against those costs.” With business groups arguing for the tariff to do less and consumers and environmental advocates calling for it to do more, Xcel Energy says its approach is a compromise. “The company’s proposals reflect a reasonable and balanced middle ground between approaches that would impose commercially impractical obligations and approaches that would reduce customer responsibility in ways that could unreasonably shift costs and risk to existing customers,” Ihle of Xcel said in a filing. A data center houses a network of computer systems that are used for data storage. They require the use of backup diesel generators and freshwater to keep the computers cool. Those who oppose data centers have cited environmental concerns as their reasoning, while those who support them say they help the U.S. stay ahead technologically of global competitors. Measure DB in Alhambra The measure allows Alhambra residents to decide whether data centers should be prohibited in the city. The measure reads: “Shall an ordinance be adopted affirming the Council-adopted ban on "Data Centers" by amending the Alhambra Municipal Code to again define "Data Centers" and prohibit them in all zones of the City?” Voting “yes” for the measure would prohibit data centers in the city of Alhambra. Voting “no” against the measure opposes prohibiting data centers in Alhambra, which could pave the way to allow them in the city.

artigo.texto: Recentemente, foi publicada a revisão do Corporate Net-Zero Standard da Science Based Targets initiative, a SBTi, trazendo uma mudança relevante para empresas que buscam cumprir metas climáticas com maior integridade. A mensagem é clara: a transição para o net zero não será construída apenas com compensações genéricas, mas com ações de mitigação diretamente conectadas às cadeias de valor das empresas. Esse movimento tem implicações profundas para setores intensivos em embalagens, como alimentos e bebidas, cosméticos, higiene, varejo, e-commerce e bens de consumo. Nesses segmentos, parte expressiva das emissões está no Escopo 3, ou seja, fora das operações diretas da empresa. Elas aparecem na produção dos materiais adquiridos, no transporte, no uso e, principalmente, no fim de vida das embalagens colocadas no mercado. Até aqui, muitas empresas trataram essas emissões com uma combinação de redução interna, compromissos de circularidade e compra de créditos de carbono. Mas a nova lógica da SBTi exige uma pergunta mais sofisticada: se a emissão está associada a materiais e embalagens, qual deve ser o instrumento climático mais coerente para mitigá-la? A resposta tende a colocar a reciclagem no centro da estratégia. Redesign, redução de gramatura, substituição de materiais e modelos de refil são fundamentais. Essas ações reduzem o inventário de emissões e devem ser priorizadas. No entanto, elas não eliminam integralmente as emissões associadas à cadeia de materiais. Mesmo após ganhos de eficiência, continuará existindo uma parcela residual ligada à produção, circulação e destinação das embalagens. É nesse espaço que o crédito de carbono da reciclagem ganha relevância estratégica. Ele não deve ser tratado como uma compensação genérica, desconectada da origem da emissão. Ao contrário: seu valor está justamente em financiar e comprovar uma mitigação climática associada à própria cadeia de valor dos materiais. A reciclagem possui uma característica singular nesse debate. Ela atua sobre o fluxo físico da embalagem. O material pode ser coletado, pesado, classificado, rastreado, destinado a um reciclador e reinserido como matéria-prima secundária. Quando esse processo substitui matéria-prima virgem, há redução mensurável de emissões. Quando é feito com tecnologia, documentação e auditoria, passa a existir lastro climático verificável. Essa conexão entre emissão e mitigação é o que diferencia o crédito de carbono da reciclagem de muitos créditos tradicionais. Uma empresa que emite por embalagens plásticas, metálicas, de vidro ou papel não deveria, por coerência climática, tratar essa emissão exclusivamente com créditos desconectados de sua cadeia de materiais. O instrumento mais aderente é aquele que atua sobre o mesmo problema que originou a emissão: o fluxo de materiais pós-consumo. A tese é simples e poderosa: se a emissão vem da embalagem, a mitigação climática mais coerente deve vir da circularidade da própria embalagem. Essa abordagem também responde a uma demanda crescente por integridade no mercado de carbono. Compradores corporativos não buscarão apenas toneladas de CO₂. Buscarão rastreabilidade, adicionalidade, conexão com sua cadeia de valor e benefícios socioambientais comprováveis. Nesse contexto, a reciclagem tem uma vantagem competitiva: é física, mensurável e auditável. No Brasil, essa oportunidade é ainda maior. O país possui uma das cadeias de reciclagem social mais relevantes do mundo, mas ainda recicla muito menos do que poderia. O valor dos materiais, sozinho, muitas vezes não paga a conta da coleta, triagem, tecnologia, transporte, formalização e remuneração adequada dos trabalhadores da cadeia. O crédito de carbono pode ser o mecanismo financeiro capaz de fechar essa equação. Ao financiar operações de reciclagem rastreáveis, empresas não apenas reduzem emissões associadas ao Escopo 3. Elas fortalecem a logística reversa, ampliam a circularidade, geram renda e transformam resíduos em ativos climáticos. O crédito de carbono da reciclagem, portanto, não é apenas mais uma categoria de crédito. Ele representa uma nova infraestrutura de financiamento climático para a economia circular. É um instrumento que conecta metas de net zero, responsabilidade pós-consumo, inovação em rastreabilidade e inclusão produtiva. No novo ambiente regulatório e reputacional da agenda climática, créditos genéricos tendem a perder espaço para ativos com maior conexão material e maior qualidade de evidência. Para empresas que colocam milhões de embalagens no mercado, a reciclagem deixa de ser apenas uma obrigação ambiental ou uma pauta de sustentabilidade. Ela passa a ser uma ferramenta central de mitigação climática. O futuro do carbono será cada vez mais exigente. E, para as embalagens, esse futuro passa necessariamente pela circularidade. Rodrigo Oliveira é CEO da Green Mining e Vice-presidente da ABELORE

artigo.texto: Nio's Firefly Lands in Bangkok as Battery Upgrade and Self-Driving Economics Face Investor Scrutiny Published on 10/23/2026 at 06:01 | Editorial boerse-global.de Firefly, Nio's budget-focused marque, opened its first standalone overseas location on Monday at the centralwOrld shopping mall in Bangkok, pairing the launch with a revised right-hand-drive model. The Thai beachhead gives investors a physical test bed for a brand whose next product move — a larger battery — is still waiting in the wings. That battery is a 60 kWh pack from CATL, slated for unveiling on 23 October with a claimed CLTC range of 560 kilometers. Firefly marketing chief Pu Yang outlined the plans on 16 October, and the company says the option will be available to both new buyers and existing owners, with upgrade details to follow at launch. Range Figures Only Matter If They Move Metal The distinction Nio's investors need to hold onto is between an enriched product line and actual incremental sales. A battery option that mainly appeals to people who already own a Firefly supports retention but does little for volume. The more meaningful question is whether the added choice pulls in buyers who would otherwise have looked elsewhere. Nio has a solid base to build from. Co-founder and president Qin Lihong said on 17 October that the group's three brands together notched 111,638 retail sales in China during the third quarter of 2026, overtaking BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Audi individually for the first time — including the sub-brands Qin attributed to each. That milestone describes the combined standing of the Nio portfolio in China; it is not evidence of standalone demand for Firefly, nor of any effect from the pending battery. Thailand: Store Open, Factory Still a Question Mark The Bangkok site and the right-hand-drive update are done deals. Local vehicle assembly is not. Nio is reportedly studying the feasibility of manufacturing in Thailand, weighing customer uptake, suitable models and the country's tax structure. No investment decision has been made, so booking a local plant as a settled expansion step would be premature. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Nio? The bull case requires several links to hold together: a compelling product, genuine customer response, and only then firm commitments on deeper local engagement. Product breadth and market presence reinforce each other only when both convert into orders. Li Puts a Price Tag on Driver Assistance Separately, CEO William Li used yesterday's World Intelligent Connected Vehicles Conference to reframe how Nio measures its driver-assistance push, citing willingness to pay and demonstrable safety as the yardsticks. The system has already been deployed in more than 950,000 vehicles — a figure that captures reach, not revenue. That gap is the crux. Broad adoption and a customer's readiness to pay for features are different metrics, and Li's remarks do not establish any contribution to earnings. Investors are left asking how technical penetration turns into durable profit. Goldman's Call Meets a €2.94 Share Price Goldman Sachs analyst Tina Hou took an upbeat view on 9 October, upgrading the stock from Neutral to Buy with a 12-month price target of US$7.00. She pointed to expected volume growth, premium-segment margins and a turnaround in profit and free cash flow — forecasts rather than reported results. The shares trade at €2.94, so the bullish rating has not dispelled uncertainty about the road ahead. Judging driver assistance purely by its installed base would fall short, just as counting new product announcements would miss whether Firefly can win fresh buyers. Two Yardsticks for the Coming Weeks The immediate checkpoint is the 23 October battery reveal, when Nio should clarify how the 60 kWh option is positioned for new versus existing customers. In parallel, the Thai feasibility study stays in view: only a later investment decision would turn a possibility under review into a committed project. For shareholders, the real question is whether future demand can carry the weight — not how many options appear on the price list. artigo.texto: Nio Slips 2% as CATL's Miss Weighs on Chinese EV Stocks, With Firefly's 60 kWh Battery Looming Published on 10/22/2026 at 06:21 | Editorial boerse-global.de Nio shares closed Tuesday with a 2.0% daily decline, but the move had little to do with the company itself. The drop came as Chinese electric-vehicle and battery names in Hong Kong came under pressure following weaker-than-expected quarterly results from battery giant CATL, according to media reports. No fresh operating update from Nio accompanied the slide. A Sector Story, Not a Company One CATL reported 14.5% net profit growth for the third quarter — a figure that fell short of expectations and sent its own stock sharply lower, dragging the wider group of Chinese automakers down with it. For Nio, that distinction matters: the immediate drag originated in the sector, and CATL's disappointment should not be read as a deterioration in Nio's own delivery trajectory. By the same token, Nio's growth offered no protection against the sector-wide selling. Roughly three weeks ago, Nio reported 109,178 vehicles delivered in the third quarter of 2026, a 25.4% increase year over year. That headline figure spans multiple brands, however, folding in ONVO and Firefly alongside the Nio marque — a detail that matters when stacking the company against rival manufacturers. On Saturday, Nio President Qin Lihong said the combined brands had each outsold BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Audi in Chinese quarterly sales, according to media reports. The claim rests on bundled deliveries, not on vehicles carrying the Nio badge alone. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Nio? Firefly Sets the Next Date While the market reacted to the sector backdrop, Firefly has a product expansion on the calendar — one aimed at both new buyers and existing owners, and a different focal point from the recent delivery comparisons. Media reports point to an October 23 launch of a 60 kWh battery option, with a stated range of 560 kilometers under the CLTC standard. Coverage of the battery plan first surfaced on Friday, when the head of Firefly's brand marketing discussed it at a user meetup. Existing Firefly owners are expected to be eligible for an upgrade as well, according to the reports — meaning the rollout would not be confined to prospective customers. For investors, that adds a dimension to the product strategy, though it is not yet evidence of higher revenue. Two Lenses, One Stock The distinction investors face is between two layers. The recent share-price move reflects pressure on Chinese auto stocks; Nio's company-specific news, by contrast, consists of the delivery growth already reported and the announced Firefly expansion. The next hard checkpoint is the planned battery launch — a date on which the announcement can be measured against execution, but not yet proof of additional sales. Nio at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. In a positive scenario, Firefly confirms the variant and explains its rollout clearly, which could shift valuation attention back toward Nio's own product lineup rather than the broader sector weakness. The counterargument carries weight too: even an on-schedule unveiling would only confirm that a product announcement is being delivered. It would not by itself signal stronger demand or improved economics. Sustained pressure on Chinese EV and battery stocks could also drown out any positive reaction, so Nio's short-term share performance need not track the operational significance of the Firefly news. Equating the two risks overreading a product headline. Should Firefly's implementation stall, the expectation would weaken; should sector headwinds persist, even a confirmed launch might not be enough to trigger a re-rating. What Firefly actually announces on October 23 — and which expectations can credibly be drawn from it — is the question that matters. artigo.texto: I’m the Mayor of Lochbuie, Colorado, and my residents are worried about our water supply. So we passed a five-year moratorium on AI data centers. Your town can, too. Like many other parts of the country, our state is facing a serious water-supply problem. Colorado’s water supply depends heavily on mountain snowpack, and our Colorado River system has been overburdened for years. This problem is exacerbated by reduced reservoir levels, population growth, and irrigation-intensive agriculture. At the same time, climate change has led to record heat and droughts. A single large-scale data center, depending on location and available resources, can use as much water as our entire town uses. Meanwhile data center energy use makes climate change worse, further endangering our shared future. Data center emissions are projected to skyrocket by 2035. Water is a finite resource and can’t always replenish fast enough to meet growing demand. We don’t want hyperscale data centers coming into our town and overburdening our already stressed water resources — and polluting our air and groundwater while they’re at it. Big data centers claim they bring jobs to communities. A closer look shows how flimsy these claims are. In reality, data centers create very few permanent jobs. Most data center jobs are temporary construction jobs, and most of those don’t go to local community members. “I do want to see businesses in our community that create jobs, but I don’t see how a data center does that when it takes up so much land and produces so few jobs,” Shannon Donnelly, one of my constituents, told me. “We need a clear, evidence-based understanding of the costs and benefits before we make such big decisions that impact people’s lives.” Shannon is not alone. I heard many comments like these at our town board meetings about water use, noise, and other pollution from data centers. So I wrote up a proposal for a moratorium on AI data centers in Lochbuie. The ensuing public meeting drew more attendees than I had ever seen. They overwhelmingly supported a moratorium, and it passed easily. What happened next reflects another troubling reality about how data centers are encroaching on unwilling communities: Brighton, which borders Lochbuie, announced a proposal for a data center there. A town boundary would not protect our water, air, animals, or residents. “We’ll see the lights and hear the noise,” constituent Desirae Zima told me. “We’ll have to live with the traffic, the infrastructure demands, the industrial equipment, and the potential impacts to water and electricity resources. We will be the neighbors dealing with the impacts to our quality of life.” Fortunately, opposition from Brighton residents was strong enough that the developer withdrew its application for the proposed data center and the city council voted to advance a one-year moratorium on any such construction. It awaits final approval. Our small town reflects communities across the country. According to a recent Gallup poll, over 70 percent of Americans oppose data centers in their local areas. Nearly 500 cities, towns, and counties nationwide have enacted or are considering moratoria on data centers. Congress and the federal government have so far refused to meaningfully regulate the data centers cropping up across the country. So for now, state and local measures like these represent the best tool to protect our communities. Artificial Intelligence has not yet surpassed good old-fashioned human common sense.

artigo.texto: In a recent interview with the Journal-News, Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy was asked about his personal and financial ties to companies involved in the data center industry. According to a financial disclosure statement filed with the Ohio Ethics Commission in April 2026 covering fiscal year 2025, Ramaswamy reported holdings in Prologis, the company developing a data center project in Trenton, along with Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA. The size of the investments was not disclosed beyond the reporting threshold requiring assets to be listed if valued at more than $1,000. The filing reported $1,137.12 in dividends from Apple stock and $20,230 in dividends from Microsoft stock. A May 2026 report from Innovation Ohio argued those investments could create a conflict of interest. The report stated Ramaswamy holds investments across multiple sectors connected to data center development, including semiconductor manufacturers, technology companies that operate data centers, real estate firms that develop industrial properties and infrastructure funds that finance data center construction. "Ramaswamy holds financial positions in every link in that chain, creating a scenario where, as governor, he would be regulating an industry in which he is also a primary shareholder," the report stated. Asked about the investments, Ramaswamy said he was unaware of the specific holdings. "Someone's gonna have to tell me what those are because I'm not aware what they are," he said. He suggested the investments may be held through index funds. "If they're part of generalized index funds, this is a non-issue for me," he said. "I have no interest in having financial interests." When asked specifically about Prologis, Ramaswamy said he did not know he owned stock in the company. "I didn't know I owned that. Thank you for telling me," he said. He later added that he had "never heard" of Prologis. "It might be a speck of dust in a portfolio of biotech and other holdings," he said. "It's sort of an inane proposition if you're in my shoes to think that that would matter." Ramaswamy said an independent manager oversees his investment portfolio and argued that his financial independence would allow him to govern without influence from special interests. "What that allows me to do is to be independent of a lot of special interests," he said. Asked whether he would keep investments in those companies if elected governor, Ramaswamy said he would not. "No. I don't think it would make sense for me to do that," he said. "We're going to follow exactly what the rules say." Ramaswamy said the wealth he accumulated came from biotechnology ventures, not data center-related investments. "If you think about it from a common-sense perspective, my wealth and the way I generated it has nothing to do with data centers; it's been in biotech," he said. "It would be a boneheaded thing to go into this position to pursue wealth. I'm spending immense amounts of my wealth on this campaign, not to make money from it." He also defended what he described as a stringent approach to regulating data centers. "I think it's going to be one of the most demanding sets of requirements anywhere," he said. Ramaswamy pointed to proposals that would require data centers to be built on abandoned industrial sites rather than farmland or near residential neighborhoods, eliminate tax abatements, strengthen environmental standards, prohibit nondisclosure agreements and require tree buffers around campuses. Acton campaign responds Ramaswamy's opponent, Amy Acton, also disclosed investments in companies connected to the data center industry in her 2025 financial filing. Those holdings included Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, Iron Mountain and several semiconductor companies whose products are commonly used in servers, artificial intelligence systems and data center equipment. Virginia Schaus, a spokesperson for Acton's campaign, said Acton sold all of her individual stocks in April 2026 to avoid questions about potential conflicts of interest. According to the campaign, Acton also moved her individual retirement account investments into exchange-traded funds and other diversified funds. "She does not currently own any individual stocks, and as governor, she pledges to not invest in or possess individual stocks," Schaus said. Schaus said Acton has argued that Ramaswamy's holdings create a potential conflict of interest in a recent op-ed published by The Columbus Dispatch. On July 27, Acton announced support for a conditional moratorium on new data center development unless projects meet several requirements, including: - Paying 100% of utility-related costs - Using union labor - Operating without nondisclosure agreements - Supporting local community needs - Complying with Ohio environmental standards - Building on brownfield or industrial sites "If companies cannot meet these rigorous standards, they have no business working in Ohio," Schaus said. The Acton campaign also argues Ohio's long-term tax incentives for data center projects should be scaled back.

artigo.texto: Dan Cox blasts data centers near Adamstown school, vows permanent ban if elected Republican gubernatorial candidate Dan Cox criticized data centers and Democratic incumbent Gov. Wes Moore during a campaign stop at a park near Carroll Manor Elementary School in Adamstown, where construction noise from nearby data centers was as loud as the children at recess. Cox said he has a plan to address data centers if elected, which includes banning them permanently, enacting a temporary freeze while working toward the ban, requiring independent environmental testing, and mandating compensation for property and environmental damage. | MARYLAND VOTER'S GUIDE: 2026 Maryland gubernatorial election "We need immediate statutory relief at a minimum, and as governor, I will issue an executive order and pursue that immediately," Cox said. Cox accused Moore and his administration of fast-tracking permits for data centers and failing to respond to public concerns. He reiterated similar criticisms made during their recent debate, where Moore defended his stance and actions. "It is important that we step in, and it's why I signed amongst the most stringent EOs, executive orders in the country, saying that data centers need to bring their own energy and their power," Moore said during the debate. "They need to make sure they are not polluting our air or our water. Data centers do not get to write the rules. We do." Cox described data centers as a nonpartisan issue and expressed confidence that his position could attract voters across party lines in November. Maryland's early in-person voting period begins Thursday, with voting by mail continuing. Election Day is set for Nov. 3.

artigo.texto: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, instead opting for a shorter-term ban In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, voted against a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city, which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI. Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days. Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi. Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution. SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but earlier Tuesday, a Mississippi federal judge blocked that bid. Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary. The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations. The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development. Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations. The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting. Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country. Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact. "It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said. Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month. A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

artigo.texto: Texas has shut down the web portal for its automated construction permit filing system and suspended construction permits of 17 data center projects. The change came after 404 Media reported that a group of Texans discovered the state had continued to issue construction permits related to data centers despite Governor Greg Abbott calling for a pause in September. On Monday, the watchdog groups FracTracker Alliance and Public Citizen published reports detailing more than two dozen permits issued to Texas data center projects. On Tuesday, the website for STEERS – an application filing system for construction projects run by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) – returned a 404 error. By Wednesday, the site had this message on it: “TCEQ’s electronic filing application used for automatic authorizations has been temporarily shut down to ensure all applications are reviewed by agency staff to determine if they are related to data centers.” Before TCEQ shut the portal down, 404 Media viewed 17 different permits related to data center projects and saw that they’d been moved from “active” to “suspended” in the TCEQ central registry. “STEERS is a portal that TCEQ uses to rubber stamp construction approvals,” Sam Law, a researcher at FracTracker Alliance told 404 Media. “It seems like they forgot about it and the portal has been quietly issuing approvals since the governor’s order for a pause, including for OpenAI and Amazon this Monday and Tuesday.” The 17 suspended permits are related to stormwater construction, an approval that allows construction companies to raise and level ground. It’s a key, and sometimes final, part of the approval process for any construction project in Texas. “Now they’ve taken the unprecedented step of suspending 17 approvals and taking down the whole site as they switch to a more involved human review process,” Law said. “The irony is not lost on me. When fighting the AI data centers build out, it’s nice to have a clear example of how some work is better left to humans.” Law said he reached out to TCEQ and didn’t hear anything from them. The commission also didn’t respond to 404 Media’s request for comment. “I am very concerned that since contractors are accustomed to this automated approval process, they might not be aware of the suspension and continuing construction at some of the largest hyperscale facilities in Texas,” Law said.

artigo.texto: BEIJING: CATL has unveiled its dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. CATL pointed out that competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. "While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilisation, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics," said the Chinese battery manufacturer. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with its self-developed Qiji's strategy of standardisation, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses Qiji's standardised chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold, CATL's switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardised main battery maintains compatibility with the Qiji battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customised for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardisation with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications.

artigo.texto: International carbon market cooperation is gaining ground as more countries sign agreements to trade carbon credits under the Paris Agreement. However, a new report highlights a big challenge: turning agreements into verified emissions reductions. Countries need these reductions to reach their climate goals. The 2026 Article 6 Implementation Status Report, released by the Paris Agreement Article 6 Implementation Partnership (A6IP), found that bilateral carbon market arrangements rose 14% in one year, reaching 113 by July 2026. These arrangements allow countries to work together on projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. The report also found that countries are making progress on approval rules, carbon registries, and emissions tracking. Yet, many governments still lack the systems needed to fully carry out international carbon trading. For carbon project developers and investors, the findings point to a growing market opportunity. More countries are building the rules for cross-border carbon deals, but the pace of actual credit transfers will depend on how quickly they can put those systems into practice. Article 6 Agreements Reach 113 as Global Cooperation Expands The report recorded 113 bilateral arrangements in 2026, up from 99 in 2025. Of these: - 61 were memorandums of understanding (MoUs), - 44 were bilateral agreements, and - 8 fell into other categories, such as declarations or statements of intent. These arrangements provide a starting point for countries to cooperate on emissions-cutting projects and the transfer of carbon credits. However, an MoU or other arrangement does not automatically authorize projects or allow credits to be transferred. The report identified 68 countries taking part in bilateral cooperation: 58 host countries and 10 countries seeking to acquire emissions reductions. Japan remained the leading acquiring country, with 32 agreements. Singapore followed with 29, up from 24 in 2025. Switzerland increased its agreements from 17 to 20, while South Korea rose from 11 to 14. Among host countries, Ghana and Kenya had the highest engagement, each working with five acquiring countries. Indonesia, Mongolia, Senegal, and Zambia followed, each with four partners. These figures show that international carbon cooperation is spreading across regions. They also highlight the growing role of Asian countries in building cross-border carbon markets. More Countries Are Preparing to Authorize Carbon Credits Bilateral agreements are only one part of the process. Countries also need rules for deciding which projects can generate credits for international transfer. Under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, countries can cooperate by transferring internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, or ITMOs. These transfers need government approval and clear records. This stops the same emissions reduction from counting for more than one country’s climate goal. The A6IP report found that 36 countries had authorization arrangements in place, compared with 22 in the 2025 report. Another 56 were developing or considering these arrangements. Tracking systems are also advancing. Sixteen countries had systems in place to track ITMOs, while many others were still developing or considering them. However, only 15 of the 106 countries analyzed had both authorization and tracking arrangements in place. Just 23 had submitted initial reports to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). This gap matters. Countries must know who can approve credit, how to track it, and how to report transfers. This knowledge is key for confident international trading. Actual Carbon Transfers Remain Small The report’s figures show why the growth in agreements should not be mistaken for a mature trading market. By July 2026, countries had transferred 151,566 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO₂e) in ITMOs under bilateral cooperation, according to the report. This is a small volume compared with the number of agreements and projects being developed. It shows that many countries are still building the systems needed to move from policy commitments to completed transactions. The report also tracked progress under Article 6.4, which created the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM), a centralized United Nations system for issuing carbon credits. By the report’s cutoff, host countries had approved 415 activities for transition from the earlier Clean Development Mechanism. Two transitioned programs of activities had generated about 1.11 million Article 6.4 emission reductions (A6.4ERs). These developments show that different parts of the Paris Agreement carbon market are progressing at different speeds. The next challenge is to convert project pipelines and approvals into credits. These credits must follow the rules and be usable for their intended purposes. Singapore and Southeast Asia Build New Opportunities Recent developments in Southeast Asia offer a clear example of how Article 6 cooperation is moving forward. Singapore and Laos signed an implementation agreement in September 2026 and agreed on 58 eligible carbon credit methodologies. The list covers areas such as forestry, agriculture, methane reduction, biochar, and renewable energy. The agreement gives project developers a clearer starting point for preparing eligible projects in Laos. However, the 58 methodologies do not represent 58 approved projects. Individual projects must still meet the countries’ requirements before credits can be authorized for international transfer. Singapore’s network of 29 bilateral arrangements also makes it one of the most active acquiring countries in the report. Its agreements aim to provide access to eligible international carbon credits as the country works toward its climate targets. Indonesia is another important market to watch. artigo.texto: A battery system installed in a Buffalo, New York, apartment building will store excess energy when it’s plentiful and power the building when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. The 3.75 megawatt-hour lithium-ion battery system, which can power the Peace Bridge Place affordable housing complex for several days, is among the largest battery systems in a U.S. residential building, manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. said Tuesday. “We want our electric power to be resilient, affordable and available. Distributed battery storage accomplishes all three,” Viridi CEO Jon M. Williams said. “The only thing that has been holding up installations at scale is safety; a lot of the products on the market over the last 10 years have burned things down.” Deploying large batteries that can safely power apartment buildings is an important step toward replacing fossil fuels with renewables, experts say, but they're uncommon because of the cost and concerns about fire risks. Already, larger batteries are paired with solar and wind projects, and homeowners are using smaller batteries to store excess energy from rooftop solar and for backup power. How batteries help keep electricity flow steady Batteries help maintain a steady flow of power when sources such as solar and wind are not producing. They charge when the sun is shining or when wind is blowing. That energy can then be used when demand is high. Batteries can also store excess electricity from hydropower, and New York is one of the top hydropower-producing states. Buffalo is close to Niagara Falls, where most of the state's hydropower is produced. When electricity demand is high, Peace Bridge will use the battery. It will get paid by the utility for not drawing from the grid and for sending power back if needed. This helps lower the complex’s overall electricity costs, which benefits residents. The building can use the system during outages, too. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency helped fund the Peace Bridge Place project, as part of its focus on including disadvantaged communities in the clean energy transition. “It goes a long way toward demonstrating the safety and viability of these types of projects,” said NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris. Viridi has manufacturing facilities in Buffalo and Richmond, California, where a state grant assisted with renovations. California Energy Commission Chair David Hochschild said he's impressed with the company. More than two-thirds of California's electricity comes from clean energy and batteries get a lot of credit for that, Hochschild said. As electricity demand grows, batteries help ensure the grid is reliable, reduce pollution and contain costs, he added. “I believe the battery industry is the single most important energy industry for the next several decades,” said Hochschild, who co-founded the Electric Innovation Initiative to use electricity instead of fossil fuels more broadly throughout the U.S. economy. Viridi’s system passed a ‘near impossible' test As large battery fires have garnered attention, some communities have opposed further development. However, the failure rate for batteries has decreased as more are installed, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Viridi spent six years and $10 million figuring out how to make a fireproof container for batteries. Half the cost was for batteries Viridi destroyed during testing. Viridi uses plates, pouches and spacing to isolate each battery cell. If one fails, the energy dissipates instead of spreading to the next battery, so that no gas, smoke, heat or fire escapes the container, Williams said. Jigar Shah, an expert in clean energy financing and deployment, said the Peace Bridge Place system is a milestone in overcoming safety concerns. To ensure nothing would catch fire when used inside a residence, Viridi's system had to pass a test where the battery was forced to fail while a cheesecloth covered the container. The cheesecloth did not char or ignite, according to the test report record. Viridi announced in April it met stringent Underwriters Laboratories safety standards so its system could be installed indoors without adding additional fire suppression to a building. Shah, who led the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office during the Biden administration, said Viridi is the only company to consistently pass this “near impossible” test. Shah thinks far more U.S. homes will use batteries for backup power by 2030. The U.S. can meet much more electricity demand and avoid costly upgrades to the grid if batteries are strategically deployed, he added. New York and California officials want forward-thinking energy solutions Viridi and Good Carbon Co. chose the Peace Bridge apartments because the all-electric building uses a geothermal system for heating and cooling rather than natural gas and needed additional, resilient power. The electricity demand locally can exceed the available supply, so the utility National Grid supported the endeavor, Williams added. Peace Bridge is considered affordable housing because renters earn no more than 80% of the area's median income, Good Carbon said. It said energy storage will be an important part of future multifamily housing projects. Viridi has been manufacturing in Buffalo since 2018. A medical research building in the city is using its battery system, too. Viridi's plant could build enough battery packs in a year to supply energy for about 14,000 average U.S. homes for 24 hours, Williams said. Harris, at NYSERDA, said the state needs more options like this for maintaining a reliable grid and managing costs. Gov. Kathy Hochul has made that a priority. “If we don’t need to build generation, we can utilize the grid that we have more effectively, that’s extremely valuable to us,” she said. artigo.texto: Anti-data center, energy expansion groups gather pre-commission meeting Published 9:30 pm Thursday, October 22, 2026 ROWAN COUNTY — Representatives from Down Home North Carolina, Yadkin Riverkeepers and other community groups voiced their concerns on the proposed Rowan County data center, expansions at Duke Energy’s Buck Station and additional data center and energy projects in Davie and Davidson counties coinciding with the proposed state constitutional tax amendments. Over two dozen people gathered in front of the Rowan County administrative building steps before the Oct. 19 County Commission meeting. Down Home North Carolina has hosted multiple press conferences and protests before commission meetings in the past months protesting the proposed data center and Buck expansion; however, this was the first to directly include the Yadkin Riverkeepers. With signs reading “save the Yadkin River” and “people over profit,” speakers from each of the organizations spoke about the environmental and cultural impacts of the various energy and data center related projects on the Yadkin that are underway. County staff and the public filtered through the conference. The speakers primarily called for a two-year moratorium on data center development statewide and restrictions on energy developers like Duke Energy from passing expansion costs onto customer rates. The new Yadkin Riverkeeper Nicole Eastman focused on water quality and quantity impacted by the potential developments. “Hyperscale data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure require large quantities of water to cool the facilities, putting a strain on aquatic life and our drinking water sources,” Eastman said. “This year’s drought and low water levels highlight the vulnerability of water quantity. “Water quality is at risk too. These proposed developments would increase impervious surfaces and stormwater runoff which carries pollutants to nearby streams and rivers and increases the risk of flooding.” Mark Ortiz from Down Home and the We the People party spoke on privacy and safety concerns of the potential data centers. He believes all of the problems people have with data centers and security are connected together, which he explained with the iceberg metaphor. “About 10 percent of the ice occurs above the surface. Ninety percent of it is under the surface,” Ortiz said. “Data centers, the surveillance state, the coming down of people and education, the destruction of the environment, the endless wars, the endless economic bubbles, those are tips. What’s under the surface is one big iceberg.” “What ties all these together is the linkage to a problem that has plagued human civilization since it began. The concentration of power and wealth in ever fewer hands and ever more powerful hands.” Laura Love from the North Carolina AI Data Center Accountability Network reiterated the concerns and opposition to data centers and large-scale developers; however, she also voiced opposition to the two constitutional amendments regarding taxes. “If you do vote for these amendments, you are voting for power to be taken out of the local government and put into the general assembly. You’re voting for the local government to not have the ability to choose what services are needed in the county, how the money is supposed to be spent in the county,” Love said. Catawba College Center for the Environment sociologist Tim Clark expanded on the resource concerns and the impact to surrounding communities based on noise and other factors. Before releasing the crowd to the meeting, Down Home’s Mike Pope urged people to continue opposing the projects and vote against the proposed tax amendments. “We’re here to address our collective, ongoing concern for the construction of data centers and their impact on the health and environment of our community, energy affordability and the rate hikes we’re already seeing from Duke Power. And how the proposed amendments on the ballot this November will affect our community’s ability to grow responsibly for all of us, not just to satisfy corporate greed,” Pope said.

artigo.texto: Emporia voters to decide on data center ban in November EMPORIA, Kan. (WIBW) - Emporia residents will decide whether the city should ban high-impact data centers. The question is on their November ballots. Even if voters reject a ban in the November 3rd vote, city leaders say data center developers won’t go un-checked. It’s an issue driving Emporia voters like Ilea Diaz to the polls. “Me and my wife went out and voted today and checked that, voted yes to ban the data center,” Diaz said. Diaz was among residents speaking against data centers at Wednesday’s Emporia City Commission meeting. “We want jobs, yes, we absolutely want jobs,” Diaz said. “But bring the right jobs, sacrificing too much. Part of the tracks are really close to an elementary school.” City leaders say they are thinking about those issues. The City Commission released 10 pages of development guidelines it would require from any high-impact data center. The guidelines say data centers can still be built, but with major restrictions like companies having to pay their own power and water costs so bills don’t go up for residential customers. “We put together our first draft of guidelines with a legal team to make sure that we were doing things correctly and trying to shore in a lot of the information,” Emporia Mayor Becky Smith said. “And these are just the start of our guidelines but it also talks about noise and making people pay their way.” Mayor Smith said commissioners wanted to draft the guidelines before the vote so people would have a better idea about how development would happen. “There’s a lot of misinformation and a lot of correct information and a lot of rumors,” she said. “So you really need to dog in and trust your sources who you’re hearing from to make sure you’re getting correct information and not just rumors on the internet.” Resident Kathy Lamb isn’t convinced. “This is rural America,” Lamb said. “We live here because we like rural America. And to have it overrun by concrete and pollution and data centers, it’s just not what we want in our town.” One thing they agree on is making your voice heard at the polls. “Go out and vote,” Diaz said. “Go out and vote and be informed when you’re voting,” Lamb said. “You should go to vote,” Mayor Smith said. “Not just about this, you should vote about our governor, and our state representatives and any local issues that you have. This is your time to make your voice known at the poll.” You can see the guidelines HERE. Emporia voters also will decide a separate question to ban battery storage facilities. Copyright 2026 WIBW. artigo.texto: State Reps. John McCravy and Daniel Gibson are preparing legislation that would establish statewide requirements for data center development, including restrictions on water use, electricity generation and costs, noise and proximity to residential areas. The proposed South Carolina Data Center Community Protection Act would establish minimum standards for new data centers while allowing counties and municipalities to impose stricter requirements or reject projects. McCravy, R-Greenwood, said Tuesday the legislation is intended to give local governments a starting point as communities across South Carolina consider data center development. “We’re all for data centers,” McCravy said. “Daniel Gibson and I believe data centers are important for national security, but at the same time, they’ve got to go in the right place.” What would the act do?Under the proposal, new data centers and major expansions would require approval from the South Carolina Department of Environmental Services, the Public Service Commission and applicable local governments. Counties and municipalities would be required to have public hearings and approve projects through recorded votes. Proposed sites would also have to be suitable for heavy industrial use. McCravy said he intends the legislation to require a minimum 5,000-foot separation between data center buildings and equipment and protected properties, including homes, schools, churches, hospitals and residentially zoned land. The preliminary draft reviewed by the Index-Journal specifies 2,000 feet, but McCravy said he has requested a revision. Local governments could require greater separation distances under the proposal. The proposal would also require data centers to use closed-loop cooling systems, which recirculate coolant instead of relying on routine withdrawals from local water supplies. Evaporative and open-loop cooling systems would be prohibited. Data center operators would be required to construct, own or finance new electricity generation sufficient to meet their facilities’ needs. They would also be responsible for costs associated with connecting to the electric grid and providing backup service, with the goal of preventing those expenses from being passed on to existing utility customers. “This would protect our consumers from rate increases because of data centers,” McCravy said. Other provisions would establish noise limits, require public notice and create financial protections for communities if facilities close or are abandoned. Under the draft, normal operating noise would be limited to 20 decibels on the A-weighted scale at the property boundary, while backup generators would be subject to a 50-decibel limit. Property owners within 3,000 feet of a proposed data center would receive a mailed notice. The Department of Environmental Services would be required to have public hearings and provide at least 30 days for written public comments. “We don’t want just secret projects coming in. All of a sudden, you wake up one day and there’s a data center next to you. We don’t want that,” McCravy said. Operators would also have to submit plans and maintain financial guarantees to cover the costs of dismantling abandoned facilities, cleaning up sites and restoring property. Violations could result in penalties of up to $25,000 per violation per day. “We’re trying to put some teeth in the bill,” McCravy said. McCravy said concerns about the potential effects data centers could have on neighboring property values have been among the issues he has heard most frequently from residents. “They have a stigma attached to them that definitely affects property values,” McCravy said. The proposal would not require existing data centers to retrofit their equipment or facilities, but expansions or material changes made if the the legislation becomes law would trigger compliance with the new requirements. Local controlMcCravy said the legislation is not intended to prevent data center development statewide, but to establish protections while allowing local governments to determine whether particular projects are appropriate for their communities. “It does not take away the discretion of local government to decide what’s best for them,” McCravy said. The proposal comes as Greenwood County continues examining data center development through its Ad Hoc Committee for Data Centers. In July, Greenwood County Council voted 4-3 to approve an amendment to Ordinance 2026-19, proposed by Councilwoman Cathy Miller, excluding data centers from all zoning districts and effectively prohibiting their development under the county’s zoning rules. Council also approved a separate one-year moratorium on data center development, giving local officials time to examine potential regulations and the industry’s effects. McCravy said the moratorium gives Greenwood County time to explore its options, including statewide requirements lawmakers may consider during the upcoming legislative session. McCravy said he expects to prefile the legislation in December ahead of the 2027 legislative session. McCravy would serve as the primary sponsor, with Gibson as a co-sponsor. He said other House members have expressed interest in joining the proposal. The legislation has not been introduced or approved by the General Assembly.
