artigo.texto: Ohio Republican Vivek Ramaswamy sat down with journalists from the Dayton Daily News, Springfield News Sun, and Journal-News earlier this month for an unscripted interview about some of the issues at play in this November’s gubernatorial race. We asked the billionaire biotech businessman and former presidential candidate about his plans for public education, taxes, job creation, data centers and more, along with his views on his would-be status as the country’s third richest elected official, according to Forbes. This outlet extended a similar invitation to the Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton, the state’s former health director whom Ramaswamy has roundly criticized for what he sees as shirking opportunities to present her vision for Ohio or debate her ideas. Acton’s campaign agreed this week to schedule an interview with this news outlet; a story will follow. Public education Ramaswamy, who attended Ohio public schools before attending a private Cincinnati-area high school, has campaigned on the premise that Ohio should do more to reward its best teachers. We asked him about this plan. “What I think is we just need greater discretion for principals and superintendents of school districts to be able to pay people who work in their schools, when they do a great job, to give them the opportunity to be rewarded for it,” Ramaswamy said, before turning his attention to the matter of teachers’ starting salaries in Ohio. “More broadly, I’ve also said the starting salary of teachers should be higher than what it is today. By some measures, (it’s) $38,000 a year for entry-level first-year teacher salary. I don’t think that’s enough to attract the best of the next generation into the profession,” he said. When asked about how much he’d like to raise teachers’ starting salary, Ramaswamy said his administration would look into it. He said, “I think it’s got to be something that’s relatively meaningful to make this a more compelling profession for young people to want to go into.” Ramaswamy added that he believes too much of public school funding goes toward aspects of the education system outside of the classroom, and said he wants to prioritize in-classroom instruction. Here are information and tools to help you cast an informed ballot. He went on to say that he believes teachers are “heroes, not magicians,” and said he believes that parents should be asked to take more accountability for their children’s education. “If the kid doesn’t show up at school and they’re chronically absent, there has to be some matter of accountability for the parent,” he said. “I think our public schools can also do a better job of setting standards and expectations for the family and for the parent, which I think will make it easier to set up our teachers for success in the classroom.” This outlet asked Ramaswamy about his stance on teacher unions, which he said he wanted to eliminate throughout his 2024 presidential campaign. He responded: “I’ve never, in this particular race, I’ve not proposed any of those changes, but what I do intend to look at is on a holistic basis, how are we going to improve education?” His wealth Forbes recently reported that, if elected, Ramaswamy would become the third richest public official in the country. His current net worth of $2.3 billion has more than doubled since March 2025, and it ranks only behind President Donald Trump and Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker among current elected officials. This fact has been used against Ramaswamy on the campaign trail, with Acton quick to say his status makes him inherently disconnected from the average Ohioan. When this outlet asked him if he was sympathetic about a voter being uncomfortable voting for a billionaire, here’s what Ramaswamy said: “I think what I am deeply sympathetic to is that families are struggling to get ahead and costs have risen faster than wages, and families are struggling to make ends meet when, in fact, they should be doing more than make ends meet, they should be getting ahead.” He said he had that experience growing up in what he described as a middle class family. “Having had that upbringing, I have seen the full arc of the American dream,” Ramaswamy said. “That’s the place I come from to say, the more we celebrate success and upward economic mobility, the more of it we will get. The more we villainize upward economic mobility, the less we will get for Ohioans.” Beyond that, Ramaswamy considers the line of attack hypocritical, given Acton’s decision to run alongside David Pepper. Pepper, who would become lieutenant governor if Acton is elected, inherited significant wealth from his father John Pepper, the former CEO of Procter & Gamble, Signal Ohio reports. “I would say shame on my opponent for resorting to this kind of identity politics — and it is a kind of identity politics, it’s co-mingled with other forms of identity politics,” he said. “Shame on her for leaning into that while actually being a person who picked a lieutenant governor as her first hire who was a trust fund multimillionaire who did not earn his wealth but inherited it. artigo.texto: BEIJING, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold, CATL's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns. CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models: Battery Asset Service Partners and Energy Replenishment Service Partners. These models allow partners to participate in battery asset services and energy replenishment, extending their role beyond one-off vehicle sales to ongoing operations. artigo.texto: Tianneng revela portfólio de baterias multiquímicas e impulsiona ecossistema de novas energias localizadas AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 20 de outubro de 2026 HUZHOU, China, 20 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — O Tianneng Holding Group revelou seu portfólio de baterias multiquímicas em sua Global Alliance Partner Conference 2026 (Conferência Global de Parceiros da Aliança 2026) em Huzhou, Zhejiang, sob o tema “Liderando o Benefício Ecológico”, reunindo aproximadamente 300 parceiros de todo o mundo. O portfólio abrange quatro vertentes de tecnologia de baterias — chumbo-ácido, íons-lítio, íons-sódio e estado sólido — para aplicações que incluem veículos elétricos de duas e três rodas, veículos de baixa velocidade, força motriz industrial e armazenamento de energia para residências, data centers voltados a IA, usuários comerciais e industriais, além de projetos em escala de concessionária. Parceiros da Argélia, Indonésia, Nigéria, Camboja e Brasil participaram de uma mesa redonda sobre produção local, eletrificação de veículos de duas rodas, armazenamento de energia e transformação da distribuição, concordando que as raízes locais e a sinergia do ecossistema são essenciais. Mi Yue, secretária-geral da New Energy Industry Association for Asia and the Pacific (NEIAAP, Associação da Indústria de Novas Energias para a Ásia e o Pacífico), incentivou a inovação, o reconhecimento mútuo de normas e a colaboração transfronteiriça na cadeia de suprimentos. Guo Kuilong, secretário-geral da Câmara de Comércio da China para Importação e Exportação de Máquinas e Produtos Eletrônicos (CCCME), afirmou que a câmara utilizará sua plataforma para ajudar empresas de novas energias em sua expansão global e promover a cooperação na cadeia industrial para um crescimento mutuamente benéfico. “A incerteza torna os pilares da certeza ainda mais vitais”, disse Zhang Tianren, presidente do Tianneng Holding Group. “O Tianneng Group se concentrará em baterias melhores e soluções de sistema mais abrangentes, impulsionando a pesquisa e o desenvolvimento, a fabricação local e o fortalecimento da marca para construir uma cadeia de suprimentos verde, resiliente e localizada, com parceiros globais.” Sobre o Tianneng Group Fundado em 1986, o Tianneng Group é líder global em soluções de energia verde, impulsionando a inovação em energia para mobilidade elétrica, sistemas de armazenamento de energia e economia circular. Com 21 bases de produção inteligentes, a empresa oferece valor sustentável a mais de 100 países e regiões. artigo.texto: Facing widespread public opposition to the prospect of large, noisy and extremely power-hungry data centers springing up all over the place, Google and its Big Tech competitors have deployed the PR pros to tell the world: “Hey, we get it.” “Early public consultation is increasingly a very important part of the process,” Devi Thomas, Google’s global head of community development and engagement, told the Associated Press this week. “We have done as much as we can to make sure communities are involved early on.” Someone might want to pass that message to Devi’s colleagues in Finland, where the tech giant has been forced to halt work on two planned data centers after cutting down some 1,300 acres of forest before completing mandatory environmental assessments. In September, Donald Trump aired his frustrations over Google’s investments in Finland over Truth Social, railing against calls for regulation on AI and data center expansion. It took a month for Google to deliver a compelling demonstration of why some of those pesky regulations exist in the first place. Par For The Course The debacle unfolding in Finland’s forests demonstrates exactly why so many Americans are uncomfortable with the idea of one of these facilities being built in their backyard. In September, Google announced a €13 billion ($15 billion) investment in Finnish digital infrastructure, promising thousands of jobs, environmental restoration, and economic growth. In a press release, the company specifically hailed its operations in Finland as a model for “responsibly building AI infrastructure.” But in the municipalities of Muhos and Otanmäki, Google’s subsidiary had already felled hundreds of hectares of woodland, uprooting an estimated 400,000 trees. The topsoil was removed, roads were constructed and drainage channels were bored. Vast, muddy expanses of exposed earth now lie where pristine forests once stood. Then on Thursday, regulators reported that roughly five miles of drainage ditches at Muhos had already been dug without the required advance notification, and referred the project to the police for inspection amid concerns over excess metals being released into nearby waterways. Finland’s Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) had already ordered Google to halt further work in early October until all the necessary environmental assessments were finished. But what good is an environmental review if a company with such extraordinary wealth, power and will has already stripped away the environment it was supposed to assess? Our Bad, I Guess Facing public scrutiny by Finnish authorities and the press, Google’s country director Antti Järvinen delivered a statement in which he said officials were fully aware of the company’s activities, but said Google “takes full responsibility for what has happened.” “All decisions were made based on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time,” he told the Finnish media. “I am extremely sorry that we are in this situation. I want to apologize for that.” A Google spokesperson told Newsweek, “We have operated in Finland for 15 years and have always worked to meet or exceed zoning, environmental, health, and safety requirements. After receiving the LVV letters on 6 October, we stopped preparatory works at Muhos and Kajaani and have submitted a formal response to LVV confirming this. We look forward to maintaining an active, open dialogue with all authorities to strengthen our partnership with Finland and local organizations.” The company is now waiting for the LVV’s verdict before construction continues, and says it will plant new trees across 130 hectares of land in the meantime. Whether the Finnish public will consider that anything other than a token gesture before the tech behemoth goes ahead as planned is another matter. Then there’s the question of electricity, of which any data center in Finland and beyond needs a lot to function. To power its expanding Finnish operations, Google signed a 22-year deal with Fortum to buy up to half the output of the Loviisa nuclear power plant, which generates around 10 percent of Finland’s electricity. The agreement should help keep the plant operating until 2050—a genuine benefit—but the scale of Google’s energy demands raises obvious questions about the national grid and whether consumers will ultimately pick up some of the bill. Such concerns sound remarkably similar to those expressed by Minnesotans. Google’s proposed Pine Island data center could leave ordinary electricity customers facing roughly $1 billion in net costs, according to the state attorney general’s office. The utility company claims it would deliver $1.1 billion in net benefits. Sounds like the kind of disagreement that should be settled before the lights turn on, not after. A Pew Research Center survey conducted last month found that 60 percent of Americans would be uncomfortable with a new data center operating in their area. Fifty-four percent think the facilities are mostly bad for the environment, and half believe they’re bad for household energy costs. Is it really any wonder? Trust Is Earned Trump has a point about red tape. Excessive bureaucracy can smother investment and delay projects that would benefit businesses and communities alike, and there’s plenty of it worth cutting. The AI revolution isn’t going away, either. America should absolutely seek to lead it, and its companies deserve support in developing the infrastructure that will underpin economic growth and the digital transformation that awaits. But we’re not talking about a local housing development skirting a local planning permission process or your neighbor building an outhouse in his back garden without permission. These are gigantic industrial developments that can fundamentally reshape communities, consume extraordinary quantities of electricity and water, and permanently alter the environment. artigo.texto: A U.K. homeowner planning a battery and solar installation asked if they could sign up for Octopus Go's cheap overnight rate without owning an electric vehicle. The replies pointed to a reassuring answer for standard Go users — but also a painful catch for anyone hoping to switch between tariffs to maximize savings. Here's what to know The uncertainty started in a Reddit thread on r/OctopusEnergy, where the poster said Octopus had not given a consistent answer as they got ready for a battery-and-solar upgrade. The poster wrote, "I'm about to get a 32kwh battery installed plus solar, but don't currently have an EV." Users replying to the thread said they had not seen much enforcement around EV ownership on standard Octopus Go. One commenter wrote, "I've been on and off Go for 5 years and not had any issues. No EV, just as house battery," and another claimed, "You be fine, no one checks for Octopus Go." A separate reply noted that even if regular Go works without an EV, leaving later may be expensive because of a newer fee: "If you do get away with it you are locked into Go for 12 months as it has an exit fee now." For homeowners thinking about battery storage to unlock cheaper off-peak rates, EnergySage can help compare home battery storage options, including competitive installation estimates. EnergySage has teamed up with electrification brand Qmerit to help homeowners get the best price on home battery storage solutions. More background Adding battery storage is one of the best ways to protect your home during outages, save money on energy, and gain more energy independence. Pairing a battery with rooftop solar also gives homeowners more control over when they buy power from the grid and when they use or export their own electricity. The thread also drew a line between the standard Go plan and Intelligent Octopus Go. One person said they had received an email about disabled smart charging and added that the Loyal version of IOG would need a linked car or charger within seven days. Another commenter clarified the distinction, writing, "That's IOG. The OP is on about regular Go." What can be done? Anyone using a battery to lower electric bills may want to check switching rules and exit fees before choosing a tariff. As one commenter put it, "Ideally you want to be on Flux during the Spring/Summer to make the most of the export rate and Go in Winter." People in the discussion also pointed to software as a way to squeeze more value from battery storage. The original poster said, "I'll probably look at Agile Outgoing and combine it with Axle events, then let PredBat handle it all," while another commenter mentioned Wonder Watt's "Wonder Batt" beta for people who are not comfortable with Home Assistant. For households that want backup power without committing to a full-house system, Pila is another company offering strong battery backup options. Pila's plug-and-play batteries are priced at a fraction of what a whole-home backup system would cost. artigo.texto: Baterias podem reduzir em até 50% os cortes de geração e já começam a impactar o cálculo do curtailment Estimativa do ONS indica potencial de recuperação de energia e receitas em um mercado que registrou R$ 6,5 bilhões em perdas em 2025. Os leilões de dezembro podem impulsionar investimentos em armazenamento O avanço dos sistemas de armazenamento em baterias pode transformar a gestão dos cortes obrigatórios de geração de energia no setor elétrico brasileiro. Segundo o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), a tecnologia pode reduzir esses cortes entre 40% e 50%, dependendo dos resultados dos leilões de armazenamento previstos para dezembro. Essa perspectiva é relevante em um mercado em que o desperdício de capacidade produtiva gera perdas bilionárias para geradores e aumenta os riscos para investidores. Em 2025, os cortes na geração solar e eólica resultaram em prejuízos estimados em R$ 6,5 bilhões, segundo a Volt Robotics. Cerca de 20% da energia potencial dessas fontes não foi aproveitada, equivalente a 4.021 MW médios. O estudo identificou 16 dias em que o sistema operou próximo ao limite inferior de segurança devido ao excesso de oferta, em comparação com apenas um caso em 2024. O problema persistiu em 2026. Segundo a STEMIS, com base em dados do ONS, os cortes de geração eólica e solar totalizaram 29,3 TWh entre janeiro e setembro, 16,3% acima do mesmo período do ano anterior. Esse volume representou 21,6% da geração de referência das usinas analisadas. Aproximadamente 69% dos cortes ocorreram devido ao excesso de oferta em relação à capacidade do sistema. Os dados de agosto reforçam a gravidade do cenário. Segundo a FSET, os cortes representaram 26,6% da geração de referência das usinas eólicas e 32,8% das solares, os maiores índices de 2026 até o momento. A recorrência dessas restrições impacta as projeções financeiras de empreendimentos que dependem da energia efetivamente entregue para cumprir contratos e gerar receita. "Durante muito tempo, o principal desafio do setor era ampliar a capacidade de geração. Agora, estamos diante de uma situação em que há energia disponível, mas nem sempre conseguimos aproveitá-la. Para o gerador, isso significa perder receita sobre um investimento que já foi realizado. O armazenamento começa a mudar essa equação porque cria a possibilidade de aproveitar parte da produção que seria cortada e disponibilizá-la em outro momento", afirma Gustavo Sozzi, CEO da Lux Energia, empresa especializada em comercialização e gestão de energia. Na prática, as baterias armazenam eletricidade durante períodos de alta produção e baixa demanda, liberando-a quando o consumo aumenta ou há necessidade de potência. Em usinas solares, parte da energia gerada nas horas de maior sol pode ser armazenada para uso no início da noite, quando a geração diminui. Esse mecanismo reduz o descompasso entre produção e consumo, uma das principais causas dos cortes de geração no país. Essa possibilidade também impacta os cálculos de rentabilidade dos projetos. Além do volume potencial de geração e do preço contratado, investidores agora consideram a frequência dos cortes, a localização da usina, o custo de instalação das baterias, a capacidade de armazenamento e as oportunidades de remuneração pela disponibilidade de potência. A viabilidade ainda depende das condições de conexão, das regras operacionais e da diferença de preços entre os horários de carregamento e de descarga. "O armazenamento não pode ser analisado apenas como uma solução tecnológica. É uma decisão econômica que precisa considerar quanto de energia está sendo perdida, quanto desse volume pode ser recuperado e qual será a remuneração obtida. Uma bateria mal dimensionada pode aumentar o investimento sem trazer o retorno esperado. Por isso, o histórico de cortes e a estratégia comercial precisam fazer parte da análise desde o início", explica Sozzi. O interesse do mercado é evidente nos primeiros leilões brasileiros para contratação de baterias de grande porte. Segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), foram cadastrados 6.091 projetos, totalizando 296.807 MW de potência, um recorde para o setor. No entanto, esse volume representa apenas manifestações de interesse, sem garantia de habilitação ou contratação de todos os projetos. Os leilões estão agendados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026, com uma disputa para sistemas de fabricação nacional e outra para os demais projetos elegíveis. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início de suprimento em agosto de 2028. Os requisitos técnicos incluem potência mínima de 30 MW, fornecimento por quatro horas e disponibilidade para atender aos comandos operacionais do ONS. O tema avança junto a mudanças regulatórias. Em 6 de outubro, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL) aprovou nova regra para organizar os cortes obrigatórios de geração, estabelecendo critérios para sua distribuição entre diferentes fontes. A regulamentação prevê a participação progressiva da geração hidrelétrica nos cortes por sobreoferta e busca ampliar a previsibilidade da operação. No dia seguinte, a agência abriu consulta pública sobre o custeio dos sistemas de armazenamento contratados como reserva de capacidade, incluindo a metodologia de rateio dos encargos entre agentes de geração. A redução dos custos internacionais também impulsiona o debate. Segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA), os preços médios globais dos sistemas de armazenamento em baterias caíram, em 2025, para cerca de um terço dos valores de 2020. Apesar dessa queda, o investimento ainda requer planejamento financeiro, especialmente devido aos custos de conexão, manutenção, degradação dos equipamentos e incertezas sobre receitas futuras. "Estamos começando a incorporar uma nova variável ao planejamento energético. Não basta avaliar quanto uma usina consegue produzir ou quanto uma empresa paga pelo megawatt-hora. artigo.texto: A battery that lasts 25 years, barely loses capacity and can’t catch fire. Sounds like the dream, right? That’s the pitch behind flow batteries, and it’s why more Australians are curious about them. If you’ve been searching “flow battery home Australia 2026”, you’re not alone. But here’s the honest answer: for most homes, flow batteries aren’t ready yet. The only home flow battery once sold in Australia is gone. The companies working on new models are still testing. And none of them qualifies for the federal battery rebate. That doesn’t mean the technology is a dud. It just means it’s probably not your next upgrade. So let’s look at what flow batteries are, how they stack up against lithium, and who might actually want one right now. Quick summary - Flow batteries offer long life, minimal degradation and very low fire risk, but they’re bigger and less efficient than lithium. - No grid-connected home flow battery is currently on sale in Australia, and none qualify for the Cheaper Home Batteries rebate. - For now, they mainly suit off-grid properties with space to spare. What is a flow battery? Think of a regular battery as a sealed lunchbox. Everything’s packed inside, and once it’s full, that’s all it can hold. A flow battery is more like two water tanks hooked up to a pump. The energy is stored in liquid electrolytes kept in separate tanks. When you charge or use it, pumps push those liquids through a cell stack, where the chemical reaction happens. The neat part? Storage and power are separate. As Electrek explains, bigger tanks mean more storage (kWh), while bigger cell stacks mean more power (kW). There are two main types you’ll hear about in Australia: - Vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) use vanadium in both tanks. Australia has substantial vanadium reserves, so this is the type most local companies are backing. - Zinc-bromine flow batteries were made locally by Redflow, the Brisbane company behind the ZCell home battery. Expert tip Flow battery specs list two numbers. A 5kW/30kWh unit can run up to 5kW of appliances at once and store 30kWh in total, so check both against your household’s needs. Why are flow batteries so appealing for homes? Because they fix the two things people worry about most with lithium. - They last. Vanadium flow batteries can deliver 20 to 30 years of service with little or no degradation. Lithium batteries slowly lose capacity as they age. - They don’t burn. The electrolyte is water-based, so, as Australian Flow Batteries puts it, there’s no thermal runaway to design around. - They can be fully drained. Discharging a flow battery all the way doesn’t shorten its life, unlike many other battery types. - The electrolyte can be reused. Vanadium electrolyte can be recovered and reused at the end of the battery’s mechanical life. Expert tip Long life only pays off if you stay put. A battery that outlasts two lithium systems is worth most to homeowners planning to stay 15 years or more. Flow battery vs lithium: how do they compare? Here’s how a vanadium flow battery stacks up against a typical lithium home battery: So what does that efficiency gap mean in real life? For every 10kWh of solar you store, a flow battery gives back around 7.5 to 8kWh. A lithium battery gives back closer to 9kWh. Day after day, that adds up. Expert tip Compare batteries on their cost per kWh delivered over their whole life, not just the sticker price. Lifespan, efficiency and degradation all change the real cost. Can you buy a home flow battery in Australia in 2026? Not easily. For years, Redflow’s ZCell was the only residential flow battery available in Australia. Then Redflow went into voluntary administration in August 2024 after failing to raise funds, and ceased trading on 18 October 2024 when no buyer was found. VSUN Energy, part of ASX-listed Australian Vanadium, has spent years working on a grid-connected home flow battery. By its own admission, it doesn’t yet have a residential-ready product. What it has done is supply a 5kW/30kWh vanadium flow battery for an off-grid home in regional Western Australia. Meanwhile, Perth-based Australian Flow Batteries has taken delivery of a 5kW/13kWh Volterion unit to gather real-world data and help build the case for flow battery certification and standards in Australia. Expert tip If anyone offers you a home flow battery, ask three things: is it on the CEC approved list, who installs and services it locally, and what happens to your warranty if the supplier leaves Australia. Why aren’t flow batteries eligible for the battery rebate? This is the big one. The federal Cheaper Home Batteries Program takes around 30% off the cost of an eligible battery, but only if it’s on the Clean Energy Council’s approved product list, according to the Clean Energy Regulator. And right now, the Clean Energy Council says its program only assesses lithium-based batteries. No listing, no rebate. That means a flow battery starts well behind a discounted lithium battery on upfront cost, before you even get to size and efficiency. Our battery rebates guide explains what you can claim on eligible batteries. Expert tip Before paying a deposit on any home battery, check the exact model on the CEC approved list. If it isn’t there, you won’t get the federal discount. Who should consider a flow battery now? For a typical suburban home with rooftop solar, a rebated lithium battery is still the practical choice in 2026. But a flow battery might be worth a look if: - You’re off-grid or on a rural property and need storage you can cycle hard every day for decades. - You have plenty of space, like a shed or plant room, for a larger unit. - Fire safety is a top priority and you want to avoid lithium chemistry altogether. - You’re happy to pay more upfront, without a rebate, in exchange for a much longer life. Expert tip Off-grid buyers should ask for a full system design, including backup generation. A flow battery is only one part of a reliable stand-alone power system. Wh

artigo.texto: Around 150 people gathered in University of Illinois Springfield’s Brookens Auditorium Oct. 21 to learn more about the environmental impacts of data centers. Mary Willis, assistant professor of epidemiology at Boston University School of Public Health, discussed federal policies that sped up development and various environmental concerns stemming from the gigantic buildouts that typically require public utilities to run non-stop. Willis cited a federal executive order from July 2025 as a cause of the country’s data center proliferation. “Data centers are simply reshaping U.S. electricity demand, which really leads to a bunch of questions related to air pollution. First, we’ve got the additional need for electricity, which yields additional fossil fuel generation on the grid. There are coal-fired power plants that were unretired specifically with the data centers in mind,” Willis said. “If we are stressing the electrical grid more, we’re at a higher risk of blackouts; and blackouts have a whole host of health effects associated with them as well.” Local blackouts are usually caused by storms damaging transmission and distribution lines, which is what happened in Gary, Indiana, in August – much of the city had no power for two weeks. “It’s worth remembering that we have a decent number of blackouts per year and it’s been increasing over time largely due to storms, but there’s also other components of stressing this aging electrical grid that we really should keep in mind,” Willis said. But assuming a region’s electrical infrastructure can support a hyperscale data center, concerns then extend to how it’s being backstopped. “A lot of these sites have some sort of backup generator, either gas turbines or diesel backup generators, which yields diesel particulate matter or other types of particulate matter,” she said. “Literature shows that increased levels of fine particulate matter are associated with everything from increased rates of stillbirth to mortality across the life course.” That’s not to discount the considerations of noise and impacts to nearby water systems. Newer data centers are promoting the idea of “closed-loop” systems, which require less water but are more energy-intensive and require additional cooling chemicals called refrigerants. “The water that (a) data center is using can go back into the community with some sort of proprietary chemicals potentially in it,” Willis said. “This part of the literature, what is in data center fluid, is really just not as well-described as, say, this water stress component.” She also pointed out how it’s advantageous for both developers and communities to figure out how to lower water use and decrease dependence on expensive fossil fuel power. “We also are in an interesting scenario where a lot of the things that are problems with data centers also don’t benefit the data center – no one wants to be using millions of gallons of water because that’s expensive,” she said. “There’s probably a lot of engineering solutions that could be brought into the forefront that could get rid of a lot of our problems that we have. It’s not necessarily perfect, but getting rid of some of the excess water usage, improving the efficiency of how it’s interacting with the grid. “There’s a lot of things here that actually truly benefit the company that also would have co-benefits for the community and population,” Willis said. Attendees asked about negotiating community benefits agreements, what might happen if the AI boom is actually a bubble, and whether there should be concerns over electronic waste. Addressing community benefits agreements, Willis mentioned how sites with prime location to utilities might have negotiating power to get the best development deal possible. “Where the county would be a really viable spot for a data center – the community has a lot of power in those scenarios sometimes,” she said. Willis also provided insight into how the lack of knowledge surrounding data centers provides an opportunity for citizen science, even locally, such as to see how the approved CyrusOne data center project might impact people near the site. “It’s remarkable how many generators are on that particular (project) and that they even got that far,” she said. “There aren’t a lot of great examples of people being able to pre-think about a cohort study – a cohort study being you recruit people in the community and follow them forward in time – the best sort of evidence you can get.” She pointed out how other counties and municipalities in Illinois, including Bloomington and Morgan County, have advisory questions on the November ballot related to data center development. “Are these perfect? Definitely not, but are they a starting point? I think it’s a much better starting point than having nothing,” Willis said.

artigo.texto: The Accidental Activists of Data Center Alley These would-be rebels in Northern Virginia joined the fight against data centers mostly to stop the encroachment on their homes and exclusive private communities. I am hiking on a nature park that cuts through 45 miles of Northern Virginia, crisscrossing grassy terrain, wetlands, wooden bridges, and goldenrod, and then a dozen promontories offering the most unnatural of sights—windowless, hulking block-long data centers and their attendant transmission lines and substations. I heard “the hum” of the centers before I saw them; their sound resembled a horde of cicadas on meth. I felt nervous, and somewhat overwhelmed, as I counted roughly 20 of them in just the two miles I walked on the Washington and Old Dominion Railroad Trail in Loudoun County. Here is the country’s thickest concentration of data centers—233 centers in all, over 3 percent of the county’s overall land mass. Data Center Alley, as it’s called, is a harbinger of what is to come in this country if tech hyperscaling continues unchecked. But Loudoun County is not only an example of tech infrastructure running amuck. It’s also an example of a semi-successful battle to press pause. The week I visited in September, local activists had just secured a significant victory when the county’s Board of Supervisors voted 7–1 to impose a 12-month pause on board action for data centers and electrical substations. It was one win for the broader opposition, who were cross-partisan, unlikely dissidents in their 50s and 60s, who joined the fight mostly to protect their own homes and exclusive private communities. Some of them even refused to say a bad word about AI, claiming the fear of data centers in popular imagination was “overblown,” even though they themselves had been organizing against them as they encroached on their homes. One of these accidental activists is Jessica Medeiros, 55. I met her in front of her home, in the Oak Trail Square development in Sterling. She works with juvenile offenders by day, as a pretrial officer in nearby Prince William County. In her off hours, she is just another empty nester of two grown children, hanging with her boyfriend, enjoying frequent outdoor runs in the area and five-times-a-day walks with her dog. Well, that was before the gargantuan blue Vantage VA2 data center at the end of her street, four city blocks long and wide, rose up. That Vantage VA2 center happens to be one of the worst ones out there. For one thing, it isn’t connected to the electrical grid, meaning its energy comes from on-site or nearby power plants. These plants are primarily powered by natural gas; the VA2 center uses gas turbines and backup emergency diesel generators. This reliance means that such hubs risk being louder than normal, filthier than normal, and ultimately worse for the environment than normal. As a case in point, on the morning we met, Medeiros pointed out where the soot from the day usually falls. More and more developers have sought power plant equipment like turbines and generators to elide regional power grids, which are now stressed under the data center’s electricity requirements. To me, these data centers are a physical embodiment of both the decline of the rule of law and the rise of the tech oligarchs. They are, of course, part the national conversation around AI and have become a center of the activism against it. In the first half of 2026, the Data Center Watch project by AI security company 10a Labs found that at least 75 data center projects worth $130 billion were disrupted by local groups in the first quarter and at least 45 projects worth $68 billion in the second. The Data Center Opposition Report found that 640,000 people are in anti-data center Facebook groups in the United States. Gen Zers have joined groups like New Jersey’s Climate Revolution Action Network, or CRAN. “To me, this center…is just indicative of what is happening in our country, because the money and the power are taking over the lives of citizens,” says Medeiros, a petite blonde who describes herself as having the energy of a puppy, with the swift gait of a runner, despite a recent foot injury. She was rapidly walking around the perimeter of a building that looks like a post-lobotomy IKEA. It has got the same cheerful cobalt exterior but no furniture, customers, or meatballs inside, only racks and heat. “Last week, Trump eliminated the, what was it? Oh yeah, the emissions level requirements for these power plant. For people like us, that basically screws us. We don’t have those protections anymore.” (The Trump EPA had recently exempted data centers from publicly disclosing their emissions.) Medeiros and her neighbor Greg Pirio, 75, a government contractor who specializes in foreign aid, are two of a number of neighbors who have thrown themselves into protesting the Vantage plant, attending community meetings and town halls, doing press, creating systems for monitoring noise and air quality, and petitioning their local representatives. But the center has also taken its toll, they say, on their bodies. Both have gone to doctors and Pirio twice to the ER, with extremely dry eyes that they believe were caused by the plant. (After an hour, my own eyes were throbbing, and I was blinking for tears to relieve the irritation.) For more vulnerable people in the area, the effects have been even worse. According to Medeiros and other neighbors, one family’s four children have all developed respiratory problems as a result. Medeiros’ voice is a rasp, now, as well, which she attributes to the centers. They aren’t just imagining things. A recent report, “Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers,” modeled emissions from data center electricity and on-site generator usage, projecting health risks and costs particularly in host communities. artigo.texto: Chicago-area households are about to get a clearer picture of where energy-hungry data centers are connecting to the grid — but they will not get the added protection PJM had sought during power emergencies. Here's what to know According to Fox News, on Oct. 12, PJM Interconnection planned to activate a new "Large Load Registry." The grid operator, which oversees Chicago and a large swath of the Midwest and East Coast, will require utilities to identify single-site customers with exceptionally high electricity use, including factories and data centers. With those reports, PJM hopes to spot major new sources of demand earlier instead of being surprised after the system is already under strain. The operator has said a surge in electricity-hungry data centers is a key reason the region could run into a supply crunch beginning in 2027. The registry was only part of PJM's original proposal. It also sought tougher requirements for major new power users, including a rule that would have forced them to line up additional electricity or face being among the first customers curtailed during emergencies. FERC rejected the most disputed parts of that broader plan, saying PJM had overreached by trying to shape how states and local utilities prioritize shutoffs and how rates would apply to those customers. More background For Illinois households, the outcome is mixed: PJM will gain better insight into where very large new electric loads are being added, but residents lose a proposed protection that could have put data centers ahead of homes in line during emergency shutoffs. For homeowners concerned about utility bills as grid strain increases, upgrading heating and cooling equipment is one of the clearest ways to cut costs and guard against rising energy prices. Palmetto can help homeowners understand their HVAC options and reduce their energy bills with newer, more efficient HVAC systems and heat pumps, while its Comfort Plan network can help connect you with vetted installers and efficient heating and cooling solutions for your home. If supplies tighten, PJM still cannot cut power to data centers and other major new users before homes, hospitals, or schools. The power to make that decision remains with state officials and local utilities. In comments to Utility Dive, FERC Commissioner David Rosner said noncritical data centers should be shut off before ordinary customers during an emergency, Fox News reported. At the same time, he said state regulators should write those rules, underscoring a wider debate over who should be protected first as electricity demand climbs quickly. What can be done? The clearest change that is still happening is the registry itself. PJM should get earlier notice about new factories or data centers that could add stress before the 2027 crunch it has warned about. Households can also focus on the part of the energy equation they control most directly: home efficiency. In the second half of this transition, many residents will be looking for ways to lower their own bills, and the Palmetto Comfort Plan includes $0-down options that can lower heating and cooling costs by up to 50%. Palmetto Comfort Plans also include 12 years of free maintenance, which can make an efficient HVAC or heat pump upgrade easier to manage over time. To achieve the same goal, homeowners can pair solar panels with electric appliances, including efficient HVAC systems, to push utility costs even lower. artigo.texto: 3D printing could improve large-scale renewable energy storage October 21, 2026 By University of Waterloo Media Relations University of Waterloo researchers develop a new electrode design that could make redox flow batteries more effective for storing wind and solar energy Talking Points Researchers at the University of Waterloo have developed a 3D-printed electrode that enhances the efficiency and safety of redox flow batteries (RFBs), which are crucial for storing renewable energy from sources like wind and solar. Led by Dr. Maxime van der Heijden, the team utilized natural structures to redesign a key battery component, improving liquid movement and chemical reactions. - The new electrode design increases performance by 52% using triply periodic minimal surface geometries. - RFBs use water-based electrolytes, making them safer than traditional lithium-ion batteries. - This innovation supports large-scale energy storage, addressing the intermittent nature of renewable energy sources. This advancement is significant as it could lead to more efficient energy storage solutions, essential for integrating renewable energy into the electrical grid and ensuring a stable power supply for communities. Researchers have created a 3D-printed electrode that could help make it easier and safer to store large amounts of renewable energy generated by wind and solar farms. Led by University of Waterloo professor Dr. Maxime van der Heijden, the research team drew inspiration from natural structures to redesign a key component of redox flow batteries (RFBs), a technology that can store electricity for later use. The new design helps battery liquid move more efficiently, allowing the chemical reactions that store and release energy to occur more effectively. Redox flow batteries work differently from the lithium-ion batteries commonly found in phones, electric vehicles and many energy-storage systems. These batteries use water-based electrolytes rather than the flammable materials found in lithium-ion batteries, making them a potentially safer alternative for large-scale energy storage. Redox flow batteries are a complementary technology to lithium-ion batteries for large -scale energy storage applications. Their water-based electrolytes make them a safer option for storing renewable energy at the scale needed to supply, for example, communities and the electrical grid with continuous renewable energy. “Instead of storing energy in solid materials, they store energy in liquid electrolytes held in external tanks,” said van der Heijden, a chemical engineering professor at Waterloo. “The amount of stored energy can be increased simply by using larger tanks, making them well-suited for large-scale renewable energy storage and grid applications.” That flexibility could become increasingly important as more electricity comes from renewable sources. Wind and solar power are intermittent, as they do not always produce electricity when it is needed, creating a need for technologies that can store excess energy and return it to the grid later. Researchers used 3D printing to create porous RFB electrodes, enabling precise control over their structure and fluid flow. “With 3D printing, we can design the internal structure of an electrode in ways that are difficult to achieve using conventional manufacturing,” said van der Heijden. “That gives us much greater control over how the liquid moves through the battery and reaches the surfaces where the energy-storing reactions take place.” A key innovation was the use of triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) geometries, complex, repeating three-dimensional shapes that can resemble structures found in nature. The researchers tested several TPMS designs and found that one known as the “diamond” geometry worked best, increasing performance by 52 per cent. They then used a digital light-processing 3D printer to produce the porous structures, which were heat-treated to form conductive carbon electrodes capable of carrying electricity. The team successfully tested the electrodes in laboratory flow cell experiments and in a working vanadium redox flow battery, demonstrating that the 3D-printed designs can function in an operating battery. The proof of concept could help pave the way for more efficient redox flow batteries designed for large-scale energy storage. Future research will focus on increasing the electrodes’ surface area, improving manufacturing methods and exploring advanced design tools to create even more effective electrode structures. —————————– The study, Enhancing Mass Transport in Redox Flow Batteries with 3D-Printed Triply Periodic Minimal Surface Electrode Structures, appears in the Journal of Energy Storage.

artigo.texto: Nvidia weighs $4.5bn AI data-center push in Indonesia A proposed investment in Batam could expand Indonesia's AI capacity, but analysts warn of the strain data centers place on water and power JAKARTA, Indonesia (MNTV) – Nvidia is exploring a $4.5 billion investment to build data-center infrastructure in Batam, Indonesia, and expand the country’s artificial intelligence capacity, the Indonesia Business Post reported. Coordinating Economic Affairs Minister Airlangga Hartarto said the government was prioritizing the digital economy to help reach a 6% growth target in 2027. Indonesia currently has 600-700 megawatts of operational data-center capacity, with a further 1.3 gigawatts in the pipeline, representing an estimated $15-20 billion in potential investment. Such projects, he said, require ample land, reliable electricity and adequate water. Those requirements have drawn scrutiny. Timothy Wong, head of research at DBS Group, said Indonesia needed to rethink its approach given how much electricity and water the facilities consume. “Data centers are very intensive users of electricity and water, and the Indonesian government actually needs these resources for its population,” he said. A DBS colleague, Amit Sinha, said AI projects must plan for power, cooling, water and community impact, pointing to options such as renewable energy, closed-loop liquid cooling and recycled water.

artigo.texto: - The launch comes as Li Auto shifts its batteries from CATL to in-house developed ones produced by its joint venture with Sunwoda. - The Lianshan system covers batteries, electric drive units and the charging network. Li Auto (NASDAQ: LI) has launched its in-house developed electric powertrain technology system named Lianshan, covering batteries, electric drive units and charging network. The company pledged two lifetime guarantees — against battery self-ignition and against fire after collisions — as it seeks to ease consumer safety concerns while expanding the use of its in-house batteries. The Chinese automaker announced the system at its Power Day electric technology event on Tuesday. It said the Lianshan battery, Lianshan electric drive and charging network are all developed in-house, and that it will take care of "everything about electricity." Under the Lianshan battery guarantee program, if a vehicle self-ignites due to quality problems with the original battery and meets scrapping criteria, Li Auto will compensate the owner with a new vehicle of the same configuration. If a battery catches fire following a collision or chassis scraping and the vehicle is scrapped, the company will cover the gap between the vehicle damage insurance coverage amount and the actual insurance payout. The program is subject to eligibility conditions. The launch comes as Li Auto accelerates the switch of its models' batteries from CATL (HKEX: 3750) to in-house developed batteries, which are produced by a 50-50 joint venture it established with Sunwoda (SZSE: 300207) in 2025. In January, Li Auto delayed some Li i6 deliveries due to insufficient battery supply and encouraged order holders to switch to versions equipped with Sunwoda batteries, offering an additional 2-year or 40,000-kilometer battery warranty extension. Sunwoda EVB was sued in December 2025 by Vremt, a Geely-affiliated company, which sought 2.31 billion yuan in damages, alleging quality problems with the battery cells it had delivered. The Lianshan electric drive uses a proprietary patented CAR119 cast aluminum rotor material, adding more than 15 kilometers of pure electric range in urban driving and more than 8 kilometers on highways. Li Auto also restructured the power module so that current flows directly to the chip, adding another 30 kilometers of range and freeing up 24 millimeters of headroom. The next-generation electric drive system will deliver more power and range without increasing in size, it said. artigo.texto: Yankton County is going to take its time to study the economic and environmental effects of electrical energy storage facilities. During its regular meeting on Tuesday, the Yankton County Commission approved temporary Zoning Ordinance No. 23, which imposes a 12-month moratorium on these types of facilities in the county and directs the “Planning Commission, zoning staff, emergency management officials, fire departments, highway officials, and other appropriate advisors to study such facilities, conduct public proceedings and recommend permanent zoning regulations.” According to this ordinance, “Upon the effective date of this temporary zoning ordinance, no application for a building permit, use permit, zoning or rezoning permit shall be accepted by Yankton County, or its offices, specifically for electrical energy storage facilities exceeding a capacity of 1 (megawatt hour), nor shall any permit be issued for the same.” Energy storage systems for electricity generation use electricity — or some other energy source, such as solar-thermal energy — to charge an energy storage system or device, which is discharged to supply, or generate, electricity when needed at desired levels and quality, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. According to Yankton County’s temporary ordinance regarding these systems, commercial- and utility-scale electrical energy storage facilities are an emerging land use not presently addressed with sufficiently specific siting, fire protection, emergency response, environmental protection, road use, financial assurance and decommissioning standards in the county’s zoning regulations. Batteries (electro-chemical) are one of the five types of energy storage systems for electricity generation in commercial use within the United States. “The reason I brought this to the commission is that we do have a company that is interested in putting in an electrical energy storage facility — a battery storage facility,” Yankton County Commissioner Ryan Heine said. “It’s not really well covered in our zoning. There’s been some toss-around of exactly where and how this should be permitted under our zoning. None of the places really work out good. Rather than trying to let this muddle through, we’re just going to put a clear hold on it.” He said this “hold” imposed by the temporary ordinance on electrical energy storage facilities will allow the Yankton County Planning Commission to work on a permanent ordinance on this topic. “We just want to put this in so that we have our zoning code done right and clear,” Heine said. “That’s to the benefit to our community. That’s also to the benefit to any businesses that are going to be putting in a facility like this. They know exactly what the ordinances are, and we can hopefully make a good, clean ordinance that addresses real problems and that also tries to open our county up for real opportunity.” About the temporary ordinance, Yankton County Commissioner Wanda Howey-Fox added that, “just for clarification, we need to do it as an emergency,” addressing meeting attendees and online viewers. Heine said the “emergency part is simply because we do have a business that’s looking at” potentially installing an electrical energy storage facility in Yankton County. “We do have lots of questions around it,” he said. “I like these emergency ordinances only if they’re kind of specific, so that’s why I’m trying to be very specific. I don’t want to be inadvertently affecting other things. … We don’t want to inadvertently make problems for other things … that we shouldn’t be concerned about. “The emergency part of this is simply because we do have questions and we do have a business interested in this, and we want to get it cleared up so that we have a clear field for them to start on,” he said. “An ordinance like this also definitely puts some fire for our zoning committee to get it done.” While he acknowledged that the temporary ordinance says 12 months, Heine said he hopes a permanent and “proper zoning ordinance” can be prepared by the Yankton County Planning Commission much sooner than that, adding that the permanent ordinance will eventually replace the temporary one. “I really hope it’s something fast,” Heine said. “Two to three months would be great. They could do it in two to three months.” He said electrical energy storage facilities present “a few new safety things” that Yankton County has not considered before in its zoning. “We also want to make sure that we are also in a good alignment with the (South Dakota Public Utilities Commission),” Heine said. “There’s a size of things where we don’t want to intrude on things. We don’t want to create an issue for, say, someone who has battery storage for their solar farm or their solar panels on their farm or something like that of personal use. There are sizes to make sure that we are in a good place for that. “There’s also making sure that we’re … making a good law that does not inadvertently have negative effects,” he said. “I like to make sure that we make good laws like that. As I’ve always (said) a lot to the Planning Commission and in general is to not rely entirely on setbacks because setbacks are a poor way of regulating a real problem. If there’s a real problem, let’s make a real regulation to address it, but only address real problems.” Tom Glanzer, NorthWestern Energy’s community relations manager for South Dakota and Nebraska, spoke to the Yankton County Commission about the county’s temporary ordinance on electrical energy storage facilities. “I appreciate your comments, Commissioner (Heine), on doing this sensibly,” Glanzer said. “What we’re here to do is just to explain a little bit where we’re at with it and why we’re interested in battery storage.” He said NorthWestern Energy respects Yankton County’s responsibility to protect public safety, landowners and the community through responsible zoning and permitting standards. “However, even a temporary 12-month blanket m

artigo.texto: Amazon is reversing its plan to expand its data center footprint in Virginia—forgoing its $427 million plan to build data centers on George Washington University’s Virginia campus it had signed an application for in February. The company will donate roughly 25 acres of the property to Loudoun County for community facilities instead. The agreement, dubbed “Project Potomac Promise” by Loudoun County Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall, calls for Amazon to withdraw its data center site plan, abandon legal action to pursue development on the property, and work with the county to rezone the remaining land for mixed-use development—with housing as the predominant use. Amazon will also contribute $5 million to the county’s affordable housing efforts through the Loudoun County Affordable Housing Trust Fund. “My goal was to disallow data centers or infrastructure that could support data centers on this property,” Randall said in a press conference alongside Amazon Web Services data center delivery vice president Joshua Weissman. “Through our collaborative, respectful conversations, Amazon has agreed to forego its proposed application for data centers, and of note, forego any legal action to realize data center development on this site.” Weissman told Fortune in a statement “Loudoun will be a focus for Amazon’s Built Together commitment we announced a few weeks ago, which includes tuition assistance for community colleges and local project funding.” Amazon has a long history in Virginia’s “data center alley,” where the highest concentration of data centers in the world is located. The company launched its Northern Virginia cloud region in 2006, and according to Weissman, invested more than $63 billion with more than 3,400 Amazon employees in Loudoun County itself since 2011. Amazon had announced in 2023 it intended to invest an additional $35 billion in data center campuses across the state by 2040. Loudoun County also reported there were approximately 233 existing data center buildings, representing about 56.5 million square feet of space in the county. Data centers generated approximately $1.2 billion in real and personal property tax revenue in fiscal 2026, or 39% of the county’s overall budget. A land donation worth $65 million Under the agreement, Amazon is dedicating approximately 25 acres along Route 7 to Loudon County, with a stated fair market value of about $65 million. The land is intended to accommodate a community arts center and an indoor sports and recreation facility. Randall said the county would organize public meetings to solicit residents’ input on the redevelopment. She said she expects the rezoning process to take about a year—even under a “fast-track” schedule. “What we’ll probably do is focus first on the indoor sports arena,” she said, “and focus more on the community arts center first as the rezoning process is going through.” How Amazon’s plan unraveled In February, GW president Ellen Granberg announced the university had sold the campus, but did not initially identify the buyer or disclose the purchase price. The university said the transaction would help support its “long-term financial health.” A significant portion of the proceeds were marked for an endowment supporting the university. In March, the university’s student newspaper, The GW Hatchet identified Amazon Data Services as the buyer, who purchased it for $427 million. “It just came as a sudden announcement one day that they had sold the property, and that they couldn’t disclose the buyer because there was some kind of a confidentiality agreement,” former GW professor Ellen Scully-Russ previously told Fortune. “But of course, a student newspaper did their due diligence, and by the end of the day, they knew who it was, and they knew the price, and they communicated that to the community.” In late July, Amazon filed a site plan for a proposed data center development. Named “Bridgefield Tech Center,” the proposal called for four two-story data center buildings totaling more than 800,000 square feet. However, in April, Algonkian district supervisor Juli Briskman called for county staff to examine the potential effects of the proposed development. Briskman said the purchase price of $427 million—roughly four times the assessed property’s value—and the property’s zoning status made it reasonable to expect Amazon to pursue data center construction. But by July, Briskman challenged the prospect of adding another large data center. “Replacing the George Washington University campus with four massive data center buildings would be a profound loss for our community,” Briskman said in a press release. “The site offers a generational opportunity for education, research, housing, and other forms of economic development that could directly benefit Loudoun residents. I strongly oppose this proposal and will fight it every step of the way.” Amazon eventually decided to pursue a deal with Loudoun County and abandon its data center investment. “There was not a moment where it was decided that this was a bad idea,” Weissman said. “We just heard from the community. We partnered with Loudoun, and we just decided this was just the right thing to do.”

artigo.texto: Sitka planners vote down data centers for now By Anna Laffrey Daily Sitka Sentinel As data center developers show interest in Alaska, city leaders are taking steps to keep data centers out of Sitka until proper local protections are in place. At their regular meeting Wednesday night Planning Commission members recommended in a 4-0 vote that Sitka define data centers in city zoning code, and for now prohibit data center development in any zone. The commission’s recommendation will go to the Assembly for consideration. Commissioners agreed Wednesday that data centers should not be allowed as a conditional use in any zone of Sitka because the city’s conditional use permitting standards are inadequate for determining whether these facilities – housing rapidly evolving technologies – could harm local people, nature or resources. Commission member Wendy Alderson said that if Sitka allows data centers to be permitted as a conditional use in any zone, it may have its “hands tied” into approving a facility that meets the existing legal requirements for a standard conditional use permit. “I'd be happy to revisit this when we know a little bit more about the effects data centers will have on small coastal communities," Alderson said Wednesday, before the vote. "For now, I don't support them as a conditional use permit anywhere in Sitka." Commission member Jacquie Foss echoed that sentiment: “I am not opposed to data centers being a conditional use, however, I do not think we have the appropriate conditions in our code to do that at this time." “Until we can have conditions that address energy consumption, impacts to air quality and potentially impacts to our broadband capability, I don't know,” Foss said before the vote. The commission members agreed Sitka should define data centers in code so the city can identify and properly respond to any future proposals to develop a data center here. At the beginning of the meeting, city staff explained that without any definition in city code, data centers could be permitted in Sitka in the same way as a self-storage facility, or another similar development type. Commission member Robin Sherman emphasized that, without a definition in zoning code, “there is significant uncertainty around whether and where a data center might be allowed, and whether and how it could be permitted in Sitka.” By the Sentinel's count 16 members of the public testified at the meeting, and 11 submitted written comments before the meeting. Six speakers Wednesday said Sitka should ban data center development because of the potential that they would compete for Sitka's limited fresh water and hydropower supplies, harm quality of life, the environment, or public safety. Other considerations included neighborhood character, other uses of any zoning district in Sitka, and air, noise and other pollution. Ten people expressed concerns about data center development, and urged caution and restriction, but did not explicitly ask for a ban. Many said they don’t believe data centers would ever provide real benefit to the Sitka community. Sustainability Commission Chair Aurora Taylor explained Wednesday that the commission was first to take up efforts to control data center development here. “We are seeing across Alaska, and specifically in Southeast, an increase in data center interest from outside parties,” Taylor said in a presentation to the Planning Commission. She noted that communities like Petersburg have been caught flat-footed by proposals for data center development in pre-existing buildings, given that many municipalities have not defined data centers in zoning code. “As the Sustainability Commission, who has an interest in energy and water usage, we really wanted to get ahead of this," Taylor said. "We really wanted to prevent any kind of development that didn't have community approval or community input." At a meeting Oct. 5 Sustainability Commissioners unanimously recommended that Sitka keep data centers from being allowed outright in any zone by defining data centers in city code, and determining the zones in which data center development is allowed. City sustainability coordinator Bri Gabel spoke at the planning commission meeting, urging Sitkans to get involved in charting the future of energy usage in the community by taking the Sitka Community Renewable Energy Strategy survey at www.cityofsitka.com/SCRES Gabel noted energy usage as a key concern related to data centers. "When it comes to energy usage, we do have a really good opportunity right now to give input on how energy is used in Sitka via this survey," Gabel told those present for Wednesday's meeting. "That is the document that will help the city and the Planning Commission and the Sustainability Commission to actually determine how energy gets used in Sitka," Gabel said. Gabel told the Sentinel today the city is seeking 300 survey responses and currently has just about 150 responses. • This story originally appeared in the Daily Sitka Sentinel.

artigo.texto: Perhaps one of the most salient topics in Suffolk over the last couple years has been that of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) facilities. These facilities hold lithium batteries capable of harnessing energy and dispersing it to the grid in times of blackouts or grid strain due to high electricity usage, particularly during the summer months. The State has been keen to roll these facilities out, with proponents arguing they’re necessary for sustaining the grid while broader concerns are addressed. Opponents say the technology is too new and firefighting capabilities have not yet evolved to combat lithium fires. At present, there is no conventional method of extinguishing these fires. Letting them burn themselves out is the only option, and that process can take days or weeks depending on the size of the fire. A proposed site on Weeks Avenue in Manorville has caused Senators Anthony Palumbo (R-New Suffolk) and Dean Murray (R-East Patchogue) to urge Governor Kathy Hochul (D-Hamburg) to pause the plans on this facility. The proposed facility is a 150MW lithium-ion storage facility developed by Key Capture Energy (KCE) on a 4-acre portion of a 13-acre light industrial site. It’s adjacent to a LIPA switchyard. “When it comes to the question of safety at these BESS facilities, there are simply too many important questions that have yet to be answered and I’m not willing to move forward without those answers and gamble with the safety of my constituents,” said Senator Murray in a statement. “God forbid a fire does break out at this massive facility, our firefighters need more of a plan than, “let it burn”, which is the state’s official policy for such fires.” Local officials have even more reason to call for the brakes on BESS facilities after a 5MW facility in Wainscott caught fire in 2023. Contamination of at least three wells has been linked to that fire. The County announced in early October that the developer of that facility, NextEra Energy, has suspended operations at two East End locations. “Following the battery energy storage system (BESS) fire in East Hampton and the subsequent contamination of the area’s drinking water, I believe it is prudent to pause further construction of battery storage facilities in Suffolk County,” said Senator Palumbo in a statement. “That pause should last until a thorough review is completed, and safety measures are strengthened to better protect the region’s drinking water and Long Islanders.” KCE is the same developer that pitched a 79MW facility in Hauppauge, which led to vocal opposition from the community, a Town Council-led ban on large-scale BESS facilities in the Town of Islip, and the ascension of the Hauppauge Fire Department to be a de facto regional leader on the issue. While KCE, based in Houston, Texas, is the developer behind the project, the State is involved in the project through funding and contracting. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) chose the Manorville project, while Governor Hochul selected this site as one of eight BESS projects as part of her initiative to deploy 6,000MW of energy storage across the state by 2030. The Town of Brookhaven has no blanket moratorium on BESS facilities. KCE is also behind a 50MW, LIPA-contracted facility in Shoreham on the grounds of the former nuclear site. A large-scale, 110MW plant in Holtsville (Savion Energy) continues to face zoning issues, while a separate, 79MW plant is also proposed in Holtsville (Rhynland). Savion Energy is also exploring large-scale facilities in the Setauket-Port Jefferson Station area. Another 1.9MW facility in Patchogue, developed by Agilitas Energy, is slated to come online by the end of this year or early next year. A 100MW Medford facility has also been proposed by AES. Seven towns – Babylon, Huntington, Islip, Riverhead, Smithtown, Southampton, and Southold – have extended their moratoria on these facilities until large concerns have been addressed.
