artigo.texto: A First Nation community in Canada is using a data center to preserve its heritage The Wiikwemkoong First Nation in Canada is using a data center to help preserve its heritage The Wiikwemkoong First Nation in Canada is using a data center to help preserve its heritage. The data center on the Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory in rural Ontario stores digital files, including Anishinaabe language videos. Chief Tim Ominika emphasizes the importance of protecting the community's language and data. The idea of digital sovereignty has gained momentum in places like Europe, where leaders are wary of the widespread influence of American Big Tech. For the Wiikwemkoong First Nation and other Indigenous communities, it is also about asserting authority over their own information after historically being excluded from its collection and use by colonizers. WIIKWEMKOONG UNCEDED TERRITORY, Ontario (AP) — For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have passed down their traditions and culture through oral storytelling. Now, a Canadian Indigenous community is using a data center to help preserve its heritage. The Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory in rural Ontario installed a small data center as it modernized its recordkeeping systems. Among the digital files it holds are video recordings of Anishinaabe speaking their native language. “Our language is one of the biggest things that most First Nations across the country are losing,” said Wiikwemkoong Chief Tim Ominika. “We will have our knowledge keepers, our language speakers who may be moving on to the spirit world, but their legacy is still going to be protected for many years to come by having our own data systems in place and protecting that.” The idea of digital sovereignty has gained momentum in places like Europe, where leaders are wary of the widespread influence of American Big Tech. For the Wiikwemkoong First Nation and other Indigenous communities, it is also about asserting authority over their own information after historically being excluded from its collection and use by colonizers. About the size of a single-car garage, the data center installed last year also stores the community's corporate documents, health data for residents, and security camera footage. “The purpose of all of this is having the ownership, access, control and possession of our information,” Ominika said. It’s about preventing anyone else from “having authority or setting their guidelines on what they could do with our data.” The First Nation has been transferring all its information from a Microsoft data center in Toronto, about 190 miles (305 kilometers) south, said Michael McCormick, the community’s chief technical officer. Other Indigenous communities have been taking an interest Wiikwemkoong is on the eastern end of Manitoulin Island in Lake Huron, an area that attracts visitors with its rugged wilderness, extensive waterways and Anishinaabe cultural offerings. The reserve prides itself on being Canada’s only “unceded territory,” because it never signed a treaty surrendering its land. The data center, which underpins a modernization of Wiikwemkoong’s administrative services, also has paved the way for new public safety infrastructure, including a drone fleet and a network of surveillance cameras. A backup data center on the mainland and public Wi-Fi transmitters are also planned for the community of about 4,000 people. The chief declined to disclose how much is being spent on the projects. Improvements to data storage gained urgency after a flood in 2022 resulted in the loss of some of its digital records, which had been scattered in various offices. “That information is very important to us. And in order to protect it, keep it safe, we said ’Why can’t we not look at developing and creating and implementing our own data sovereignty program?'” Ominika said. Wiikwemkoong’s upgrade program is among the first for Indigenous communities in Canada that include First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Delegations from other Indigenous communities in Ontario and neighboring Manitoba have come to check out the project, McCormick said. The chief said he has to explain to visitors that their data center is not like the giant ones relied on by artificial intelligence companies that require vast amounts of land and water. Wiikwemkoong's data center sits in a secure bunker next to the administrative office, accessed by a facial recognition scanner. Its four racks of computer servers are cooled by a pair of fans — not water — and it has “a relatively small carbon footprint,” McCormick said. In the U.S., a few Native American tribes like the Navajo Nation have for years been operating their own data centers for local infrastructure services. Wiikwemkoong's data center is believed to be the only one on Indigenous territory in Canada, but McCormick said other Indigenous leaders are increasingly savvy about control of their data. The Chiefs of Ontario, which represents 133 First Nations in the province, held a data sovereignty conference earlier this year that included a panel on AI and data centers. For generations, Indigenous communities worldwide have had no say in how information on them has been collected, interpreted and held by governments, researchers and institutions, said Carmen Jones, director of research and data management for the Chiefs of Ontario. “As more information is collected and stored, it is critical that First Nations determine how that data is accessed, managed, and used,” she said. The technology has addressed some issues — and raised new ones Amid the island's natural splendor, the community faces its share of problems that community leaders hope the technology can help address. Since installing the data center, McCormick’s team has added 700 surveillance cameras around the community, and a dozen drone docking stations on the administrative office’s rooftop housing a fleet of DJI drones. artigo.texto: French battery maker Saft has opened new battery production lines in Bordeaux to advance solid-state technology for electric aircraft and space applications. The TotalEnergies subsidiary inaugurated the lines on October 19, turning years of research into manufacturing capacity. The company said solid-state batteries can offer up to 50 percent higher energy density than conventional lithium-ion batteries, alongside improved safety. Those potential gains are particularly valuable in aviation, where battery weight and performance are central considerations for electrification. The facility gives Saft the capacity to develop and produce batteries using both sulfide and polymer electrolytes at room temperature. According to the company, it is the first French manufacturer with this combination of capabilities. Solid electrolytes offer safety and density gains Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte used in conventional lithium-ion cells with a solid material. The electrolyte allows ions to move between the battery’s electrodes during charging and discharging. Replacing the liquid component offers a route to safer, more compact batteries. Saft identifies increased energy density as another major advantage, citing potential improvements of up to 50 percent over classic lithium-ion technology. The Bordeaux production lines span polymer semi-solid and sulfide solid-state technologies. Their inauguration follows more than a decade of research, innovation, and industrial development, according to the company. More from Energy See All “Solid-state batteries are among the most promising innovations for meeting tomorrow’s electrification needs,” said Cedric Duclos, Saft’s chief executive officer. “These new production lines mark an important milestone for Saft, as we turn several years of research into real industrial capacity, a statement of our ambition to establish France and Europe as leading players in this strategic technology,” he added. The dry electrode process The manufacturing approach also addresses emissions associated with making battery electrodes. Saft said its batteries use a dry electrode process that cuts carbon dioxide emissions from that production stage by up to 40 percent. That figure applies specifically to the electrode production stage, rather than the battery’s entire manufacturing process or lifetime emissions. The new lines represent a step toward industrializing the technology. Saft’s announcement focuses on building the capability to develop and produce these batteries, with aviation and space as target sectors. Both industries want improvements in safety, performance, and energy density. Saft says solid-state technology has attracted significant interest from the space industry and is also seen as important to aviation electrification. Aircraft battery cells enter evaluation Saft has already delivered semi-solid-state cells to Safran for the evaluation of future electric and hybrid aircraft architectures. The delivery builds on a partnership announced at the Paris Air Show in June 2025 to develop high-voltage battery systems for aviation. Most of the cells are destined for Safran’s System Test Center in Niort, France. The facility handles much of the validation and integration work needed to develop battery systems for electric and hybrid-electric propulsion. Evaluation of solid-state cells and batteries is expected to begin next year. For now, the delivered semi-solid-state cells provide an earlier milestone as the partners assess battery technologies for future aircraft.

artigo.texto: BYD’s new Seagull EV is now its cheapest electric car in China with 5-minute Flash Charging, and starts at under $10,000. BYD’s second-generation Seagull EV price and range The all-electric hatchback is BYD’s smallest, most affordable EV in China. Sold as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini in Europe, the UK, and other global markets, the Seagull is among the world’s top-selling EVs. For its second generation, BYD upgraded it with more interior space, its new Blade Battery 2.0 and 5-minute Flash Charging technology, and a few added premium extras. The new Seagull EV is now on sale in China, starting at just 62,900 yuan, or about $9,500. That’s with BYD’s “Super Trade-in” promotion. Regular prices start at 65,900 yuan ($9,900), which is still less than its predecessor. The first-gen Seagull EV normally cost 69,900 yuan ($10,500) without incentives. BYD’s new Seagull EV is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000), without a trade-in. The second-generation Seagull is 425 mm longer and has a 150 mm longer wheelbase than its predecessor. It now measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. It also gains another seat thanks to the added space, with room for five passengers. Unlike the current model, which is front-wheel-drive, the new Seagull switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) that its predecessor offered. To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system. Inside, BYD overhauled the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a two-spoke steering wheel, a redesigned center console with smart storage, and added physical buttons. All variants include the DiLink 150 smart cockpit and BYD’s 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system. Buyers can upgrade to the optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance. The upgraded system uses a roof-mounted LiDAR to offer ADAS features, including City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking. The front seats now include heating, ventilation, and massage functions. BYD added a few other premium extras, including ambient lighting, a 50W wireless phone charger, and smart storage. Top comment by CMG30 Small battery plus extremely fast charge equals a surprisingly useable cheap car. With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the new battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. A full recharge, or 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes 12 minutes to charge from 20% to 97%. The new Seagull EV is available with two BYD Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh, providing CLTC ranges of 320 km (199 miles) and 420 km (261 miles), respectively. After launching in China, BYD is expected to introduce the larger, upgraded version overseas, likely as the second-generation Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

artigo.texto: CATL bets on battery swapping for heavy trucks with Tianxing II CATL unveils its Tianxing II heavy-truck range and argues for battery swapping on long-haul routes, while the Qiji station network remains to be built. CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited), listed in Shenzhen and Hong Kong and described as the world's largest maker of batteries for electric vehicles, unveiled its Tianxing II (å¤©è¡II) heavy-truck range on October 20, 2026. The group used the occasion to defend battery swapping as the preferred route to electrifying long-distance freight. The principle is simple: rather than recharging the battery while the truck sits idle, the haulier replaces it at a station with a full one in a few minutes. The battery sector is also driving projects in Europe, such as the construction of battery parks in Bydgoszcz by Tavion. A range tailored to different markets The range also carries an international name, Tectrans II, and varies by market. The version for the global market emphasizes very high-power charging, while the Chinese presentation, led by Gao Huan, chief technology officer of CATL's passenger car and commercial vehicle division for China, puts swapping first. CATL's heavy-truck swapping offer is called Qiji (éªéª¥) and covers swap blocks, stations and a cloud platform. The Chinese range includes batteries mounted behind the cab, suited to converting diesel trucks, and batteries placed under the chassis, including a very large-capacity version aimed at long-distance haulage. It also features a new two-battery configuration. In this setup, a large swappable battery, leased rather than purchased, provides most of the traction, while a small fixed battery, permanently installed on the truck, takes over when the large battery is nearly empty. According to information relayed after the event, leasing of the large battery would be billed on energy charged, with no unit price published to date. CATL says this configuration is already in production and that commitments covering a significant number of vehicles have been signed. Arguments put forward by the company CATL justifies its choice on physical grounds: faster charging requires higher currents, which generate more heat, so swapping would be the only route to maximum refueling efficiency. This is the company's position; it also sells a global version based on very high-power charging, and it does not reflect an industry consensus. In support of swapping, CATL cites a total cost of ownership, meaning the combined purchase and operating costs of a vehicle, lower than diesel's, as well as operating savings. These estimates rest on mileage assumptions specific to CATL, and the savings announced have changed from one presentation to another, on different bases. Deployment requires building a network of stations. Yang Jun, head of CATL's swapping business and CEO of Qiji Energy (æ¶ä»£éªéª¥), the group's heavy-truck swapping subsidiary, oversees this activity. Qiji's technology relies on "under-chassis" swapping, while Qiyuan Green Power (å¯æºè¯å¨å), an operator of swapping networks, favors "rear-mounted" swapping, with the battery behind the cab. CATL is becoming the top shareholder of Qiyuan Green Power, whose seller is China Power International Development, a subsidiary of the state-owned group State Power Investment Corporation.

artigo.texto: Flatiron Energy wins two battery storage contracts in the Bronx NYSERDA selected Blue Spruce Storage and Palladium Storage among eight lithium-ion projects totaling about 950 MW in New York State's first bulk energy storage solicitation. Flatiron Energy says the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) has awarded contracts to two of its large-scale battery storage projects, Blue Spruce Storage and Palladium Storage. Both projects, located in the Bronx, were selected in New York State's first solicitation dedicated to bulk energy storage. They are among eight lithium-ion projects chosen through a process the company describes as highly competitive. Elsewhere in the state, smaller storage installations are also emerging, such as the one in Buffalo, while in Germany an 840 MWh project at Bertikow has entered construction. Eight projects totaling about 950 MW According to the announcement, the eight selected projects would add about 950 MW of energy storage capacity to the state's electric grid once fully operational. Flatiron says it sited Blue Spruce Storage and Palladium Storage to support the reliability of New York City's grid. The company adds that the projects are meant to help ensure power is available during periods of high demand and reduce reliance on fossil-fueled peaking units. Doreen M. Harris, president and CEO of NYSERDA, congratulated Flatiron Energy. She highlighted the role the two projects will play in providing capacity to New York City's electricity network during peak periods. In her view, the projects are critical to improving grid reliability, reducing costs for ratepayers and deploying clean energy to meet the state's growing power needs. A 6 GW storage target by 2030 The awards fit into New York State's plan to deploy 6 GW of energy storage by 2030. Across the eight selected projects, NYSERDA estimates the inaugural solicitation will generate more than $1.6 billion in private investment. The agency also estimates the creation of more than 500 short- and long-term jobs. Juliana Mandell, Chief Commercial Officer at Flatiron, said the company was proud to have two projects selected in the first solicitation. She describes the awards as an important milestone for the company, which plans to develop the projects alongside NYSERDA and local partners. All NYSERDA-supported storage projects will be held to New York's fire safety standards, covering first-responder training, safe siting and comprehensive emergency response plans. Flatiron plans for both projects to be operational before the end of 2030, subject to required permits, local approvals and safety requirements. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 %

artigo.texto: A divided City Council voted Monday to hold a public hearing on whether to temporarily pause construction of data centers in Fayetteville, and then voted to continue developing an ordinance to regulate them. The dueling votes—both 6-4—highlighted a dispute among the council that dates back to April: Should the city block construction of data centers while the council develops regulations for the controversial facilities? Or should the city forgo a data center moratorium, giving data center developers opportunity to start projects before regulations limiting them take effect? The debate has at times turned contentious, as it did so again Monday, and has unfolded with heightened public interest, packed meetings, and protests at City Hall. Moratorium on the Way? The council first approved a motion by Councilmember Shaun McMillan to schedule a public hearing to consider a temporary ban on data center developments and direct staff to create a moratorium ordinance. The six councilmembers in favor: McMillan, Malik Davis, Stephon Ferguson, Lynne Greene, Antonio Jones, and Brenda McNair voted for it. The four against: Mayor Mitch Colvin, Mayor Pro Tem Derrick Thompson, D.J. Haire, and Deno Hondros. “The public is simply demanding that we move at the speed of trust,” McMillan said. “Our authority to adopt a data center moratorium is written plainly in state law under General Statute 160D-107. We knew that on April 13. That was 190 days ago. More than 50 North Carolina communities, including Cumberland County right next door, have already used this general statute and that moratorium. So the question is no longer whether or not we can execute a moratorium, it’s when we will.” In April, McMillan successfully lobbied the council to move forward with a moratorium. But two weeks later, the council pumped the brakes and passed a 120-day pause on considering a moratorium. The Cumberland County Board of Commissioners passed a data center moratorium, which expires in December, as it considers an ordinance. City Council OKs Effort to Revise Data Center Ordinance On Monday, moments after McMillan’s moratorium motion passed, Thompson made a motion to advance the city’s data center ordinance. He proposed accepting a handful of revisions recommended by Nick Tosco, an attorney and partner with Raleigh-based firm Poyner Spruill, who reviewed the city’s proposed ordinance. “I would like to move that into a motion so we can have some protections for now,” Thompson said, though his motion only proposed revising the proposed ordinance—not enacting it. But the council—and the public—did not receive Tosco’s recommendations ahead of the meeting, and technical problems with computer monitors in the chamber prevented councilmembers from seeing them during his presentation. Thompson revised his motion to instead ask City Attorney Lachelle Pulliam to work with Tosco and city staff to incorporate his recommendations into the proposed ordinance and add it to the agenda for the council meeting on Monday. The motion passed, with Colvin, Davis, Haire, Hondros, McNair, and Thompson supporting it. Ferguson, Greene, Jones, and McMillan opposed it. McMillan called the proposal “foolish.” “For us to make changes this morning, based on information that we just got less than two hours ago, would kind of be, in my opinion, foolish,” he said. “What we just voted to do was to give ourselves some time to make all of these changes that are going to be tighter, more thorough with analysis, and there’s no need to rush to do anything today based on what we just voted to do together,” he added. Colvin said the council has been considering both a moratorium and an ordinance at the same time. “There will be two parallel tracks with the two motions, right, that you are doing both—there’s a public hearing held to hear this ordinance,” he said. “There’s a draft ordinance that we heard tonight and have been hearing for the last four or five months. That’s what was presented tonight. That’s what’s being revised. There’s always been two parallel tracks.” In August, the council debated proposed data center regulations that generally allow data centers on land zoned for industrial use, allow some in commercial areas with permission and restrictions set by the City Council, and prohibit them from residential areas. Those that adjoin residential areas would have to take steps to mitigate noise and other negative impacts on neighbors. A 7-3 vote directed city staff to bring a revised ordinance back to the council by late October. ‘A Solid Foundation’ Andrew Mansell, a senior assistant to the city manager, presented that revised draft on Monday. It incorporated feedback gathered at public forums and from data center operators, the Fayetteville Public Works Commission (PWC), N.C. Department of Environmental Quality, and the Conservative Energy Network, he said. “Council has been studying this for eight months now and has not done a vote yet—at all,” Mansell said. “We put together what we heard, compared to the draft category by category, which you just heard, and our read is that the draft is a solid foundation but a number of points raised by the experts and by the community can be carried into it.” The proposed ordinance sets noise limits and facility setbacks from property lines, requires coordination with PWC and a utility impact statement that addresses power and water usage, and sets emissions and appearance standards. Tosco recommended that the city fold data centers into its existing zoning districts to comply with state law and court decisions, treating them similar to warehouses or freight terminals. Setting specific equipment setbacks and buffer requirements for only data centers could set the city up for legal challenges, he said. He also said state law favors free use of land and rejects blanket bans on unlisted uses—which the city’s proposed ordinance does. artigo.texto: CATL apresenta bateria de extensão de autonomia elétrica dupla para acelerar a adoção de caminhões pesados elétricos AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 21 de outubro de 2026 PEQUIM, 21 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A CATL apresentou hoje a inovadora bateria de extensão de autonomia elétrica dupla e a mais recente geração de solução de troca de baterias para serviço pesado, visando acelerar a eletrificação do transporte rodoviário de cargas. A competição no setor de caminhões elétricos pesados está indo além das especificações técnicas, focando-se no valor ao longo de todo o ciclo de vida do veículo. Embora a troca de baterias tenha tornado o reabastecimento de energia mais rápido e previsível, as preocupações com a utilização da bateria, os custos operacionais e o valor residual do veículo continuam afetando a economia das frotas. Para lidar com esses desafios, a CATL combina sua bateria de extensão de autonomia elétrica dupla com a estratégia da QIJI de padronização, nova infraestrutura e um ecossistema comercial completo, reunindo a troca de baterias e a colaboração em toda a indústria para acelerar a eletrificação de caminhões pesados. Uma abordagem de dupla eletrificação para a extensão da autonomia A bateria de extensão de autonomia elétrica dupla da CATL combina dois sistemas de baterias independentes, porém complementares. A bateria principal utiliza o sistema padronizado de baterias intercambiáveis montadas no chassi da QIJI para maximizar a eficiência. Um sistema de extensão de autonomia instalado atrás da cabine, atualmente equipado com uma bateria de 77 kWh capaz de carregamento 3C, fornece energia de reserva. Em conjunto, os sistemas mantêm o fornecimento ininterrupto de energia e oferecem redundância para condições operacionais exigentes. - Redundância de energia de sistema duplo Em caminhões convencionais de troca de baterias, os motoristas frequentemente retornam para uma troca com capacidade não utilizada porque relutam em deixar a bateria descarregar completamente. A energia de reserva da bateria de extensão de autonomia aaumenta a profundidade de descarga (DOD, depth of discharge) da bateria principal de aproximadamente 70% para mais de 95%, permitindo que ela seja devolvida com menos de 5% de estado de carga (SOC, state of charge). Nesse ponto, a tecnologia de comutação contínua da CATL transfere o fornecimento de energia para a bateria de extensão de autonomia aem milissegundos, mantendo uma fonte de alimentação contínua e estável. - Arquitetura “1+X” e atualizações independentes O sistema usa uma arquitetura “1+X”. Uma bateria principal padronizada mantém a compatibilidade com a rede de troca de baterias QIJI, enquanto a bateria de extensão de autonomia pode ser personalizada para condições específicas, com opções que incluem densidade de energia ultra-alta, resistência a baixas temperaturas para climas frios ou potência ultra-alta. Os dois sistemas de baterias podem ser desenvolvidos e atualizados independentemente para atender aos seus respectivos requisitos técnicos e operacionais. - Leasing flexível e gestão de ativos de baterias A bateria de extensão de autonomia de bordo, de propriedade independente, permanece com o veículo como um ativo durante toda a sua vida útil, reduzindo a dependência do acesso imediato a uma estação de troca. A bateria principal pode ser alugada de acordo com a demanda sazonal de frete, ajudando as frotas a reduzir os custos de aluguel durante os períodos de menor movimento e a gerenciar os ativos de bateria com mais flexibilidade. Essa arquitetura combina os benefícios da padronização com configurações flexíveis dos veículos, tornando os caminhões elétricos pesados mais práticos e economicamente viáveis em uma gama mais ampla de aplicações. QIJI constrói um ecossistema compartilhado de troca de baterias A QIJI complementa essas melhorias com uma estratégia de três pilares de padronização, nova infraestrutura e um ecossistema comercial completo. O objetivo é acelerar a eletrificação de caminhões pesados com um ecossistema de cadeia de valor cocriado por todas as partes interessadas, onde os benefícios são compartilhados coletivamente. - A padronização apoia uma adoção mais ampla Para acomodar uma gama mais ampla de modelos de caminhões e condições operacionais, a QIJI introduziu os blocos de troca de bateria padronizados de 260# (432 kWh) e 300# (513 kWh) juntamente com o bloco existente de 75#. O sistema permite a troca de baterias em apenas cinco minutos, com uma taxa de sucesso de 99,99% na primeira tentativa, ajudando as frotas a minimizar o tempo de inatividade e a manter a eficiência operacional. A QIJI também foi pioneira em um modelo de bateria como serviço (BaaS), no qual os clientes pagam pela energia líquida carregada, em vez da energia descarregada. Isso permite que os clientes retenham o valor da energia recuperada por meio da frenagem regenerativa, reduzindo em até 20% os custos de aluguel de baterias por kWh para usuários de planos básicos. As opções flexíveis de leasing de baterias permitem que os clientes adaptem os períodos de aluguel às suas necessidades, desde a troca de veículos usados até a demanda sazonal. Isso minimizará os custos de ociosidade e oferecerá opções mais flexíveis para períodos de inatividade fora de temporada, ajudando ainda mais as frotas a gerenciar os custos operacionais. - A nova infraestrutura melhora a eficiência dos recursos A QIJI visa fazer melhor uso de quatro recursos críticos no transporte de carga de longa distância: tempo, terreno, capacidade de carga útil e eletricidade da rede. A troca rápida de baterias reduz os tempos de espera, enquanto o layout eficiente das estações atende a mais veículos na mesma área. A capacidade da bateria é dimensionada de acordo com as necessidades de transporte, e o carregamento centralizado e coordenado permite um melhor aproveitamento da eletricidade da rede. artigo.texto: Lithium ions in battery electrolytes do not always remain isolated. Research from Columbia University shows they often form clusters without anions. It revealed a structural feature that challenges long-held assumptions about lithium-ion battery chemistry. The study combines machine learning simulations with experimental validation to examine the atomic-scale structure of these electrolytes. Its findings could guide electrolyte designs for higher-capacity, faster-charging, and longer-lasting batteries. The research was co-led by Richard Friesner of Columbia’s Department of Chemistry and Alexander Urban, Lauren Marbella, and Daniel Steingart of Columbia Engineering. Lithium ions form unexpected clusters Electrolytes are crucial to battery performance and help drive the formation of the solid electrolyte interphase, a protective film on the battery anode. This film influences battery lifespan and safety, but understanding how electrolyte structure affects its formation has remained difficult. To investigate that structure, the researchers used machine-learning force-field technology from Schrödinger, Inc., with additional support from the New York Structural Biology Center. The approach let them simulate battery electrolytes more accurately and at a larger scale. The simulations revealed that up to 40% of lithium ions in standard battery electrolytes form multi-ion clusters. Clustering became more prevalent at higher salt concentrations, challenging the assumption that lithium ions remain predominantly isolated in solution. More from Energy See All “We discovered lithium ions in batteries actually group together into clusters in the absence of anions, and that these clusters are what drive the creation of the protective film on the battery’s surface,” said Friesner, William P. Schweitzer Professor of Chemistry. Experiments support the simulations The team compared its simulations with a wide range of condensed-phase experimental data. Strong agreement between the two supported the physical reality of the predicted lithium clusters. Theoretical analysis came from the Columbia and Schrödinger teams, while Columbia Engineering contributed the experimental work. “While the most novel aspect of the paper is the theoretical simulations, the experimental work confirming the results was essential and extremely difficult to execute,” added Professor Friesner. Friesner, who is also a co-founder and member of Schrödinger’s board of directors, emphasized the importance of combining computational predictions with experimental confirmation. “Predicting this unexpected chemistry computationally and confirming it experimentally demonstrates that we can accurately model the hidden atomic details of batteries,” he said. Clues to protective film formation Quantum chemical calculations indicated that the multi-lithium clusters have particularly favorable reduction potentials. These results suggest that the clusters are key intermediates in forming the solid electrolyte interphase. That connection gives researchers a clearer basis for investigating how electrolyte chemistry influences the protective film and, in turn, battery performance. The findings provide a foundation for designing next-generation electrolytes with improved performance, stability, and charging rates. Those improvements remain potential applications of the research, rather than demonstrated battery gains reported in the supplied material. “It’s a reminder – and an exemplary example – of how advances in AI-driven simulation need to be coupled closely to experiments,” Friesner said. “Ultimately, that will allow us to accelerate our progress in solving problems in biology and materials science, including making better, longer-lasting batteries,” he added. Gates Ventures provided funding for the research. The study was published in the Nature journal.

artigo.texto: Almost everyone agrees that data centers should pay their fair share — even data center developers. The newest proposal out of Congress poses the question: What’s fair? Congress has put forward its most aggressive proposal yet to protect electricity prices from massive new data center developments. The bipartisan permitting reform bill would allow utilities to charge data centers more than other customers for using the grid and would let states charge data centers more on top of that. “I think policymakers are seeing an opportunity for a good deal to take place here between extremely wealthy technology companies and regular everyday consumers, where the technology companies put many tens of billions of dollars into the power system to pay for the upgrade and keep the costs off of everybody else,” said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies, a firm that focuses on integrating clean energy into the power grid. The bill errs on the side of “over-collection,” Gramlich said, meaning data centers could pay more than their impact on the system and effectively subsidize other customers. Trending So far, major data center developers seem to be on board — though as negotiations continue things could change. “There are many devils in the details,” Gramlich said. “Regulators at the state and federal levels will have a lot of work to do.” The data center provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would change a longstanding federal policy that allows utilities to charge customers only one of two costs: the general “embedded” costs of operating on the energy grid or the “incremental” cost of any grid upgrades necessary to serve a new project. Utilities usually only charge customers the embedded cost of operating on the grid, Gramlich said. Incremental costs are difficult to calculate and can vary widely based on the kinds of grid upgrades that are needed at the time a new customer is coming onboard. Data centers, cryptocurrency miners and other “high-density computing facilities” would be subject to both of those costs together under the bill. Awhite paper created for utility company Exelon Corporation earlier this year found that data centers could still shift costs onto other customers if they were only charged the “incremental” costs without the continued embedded cost charges. The bill would also require data centers and similar facilities to provide financial guarantees before the grid is upgraded and to continue paying grid costs even if they abandon projects early. The bill also notes that states could charge data center customers extra, beyond the incremental and embedded grid costs, using the proceeds as rebates for others on the grid. It also tells states they could choose which projects can connect to the grid first based on how much extra money they’re willing to spend to subsidize other customers. The idea of data center developers paying for the cost of upgrading the grid for their projects has been widely embraced; several of the data center provisions in the permitting bill seem directly related to President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge. But past attempts to avoid shifting data center costs onto the general public have included only voluntary commitments. The permitting bill would turn that directive into law. Despite the new potential costs, the data center and AI industries have been quiet and moderately supportive of the permitting reform bill, highlighting the support for energy and infrastructure projects from the bill as a whole. Staci Pies, senior vice president of government affairs and policy at Incompas, an AI infrastructure association, said data center companies have “been very clear” that they will bear appropriate costs. “They’ll contribute their fair share of whatever kind of incremental infrastructure costs are necessary in order to increase and upgrade the grid,” she said. But, she added, the costs and analysis “needs to be transparent” — particularly if states decide to charge data centers above the embedded and incremental costs. “In some instances data centers are going to say ‘we’re willing to live by this additional charge so long as it’s transparent and we understand the implications.’ And in other instances, they may not,” she said. OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta didn’t respond to requests for comment on whether they supported the bill’s data center provisions. Lobbying disclosures show the Data Center Coalition spent $480,000 on lobbying between July and September, including on the permitting reform bill. Michele Nellenbach, vice president of federal affairs at the Data Center Coalition, said the organization was still reviewing details of the bill and noted members were “investing hundreds of billions of dollars in the U.S. annually to build America’s digital infrastructure.” Some progressives have aired concerns that the bill as a whole would amount to a giveaway for data centers because of the easing of environmental laws and the provisions to limit legal challenges to projects. At the same time, there’s been concern that the proposed changes amount to overcharging data centers for grid connection. Travis Fisher, director of energy and environmental policy studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, wrote the bill’s data center provisions risk “shifting costs in the opposite direction,” which, he says, might be necessary to counter the opposition to AI infrastructure developments. Over the course of the last year, data center development has faced an incredible rise in political pushback. Communities across the country have rallied against the centers being built in their backyards out of fear of higher utility costs, pollution and other concerns. Russia prides itself on its digital advances — from an extensive e-commerce services sector to ambitious plans for developing artificial intelligence. But now, some of the key data centers at the heart of its technical prowess have been knocked out by Ukrainian drone attacks in the 4 1/2-year-old full-scale invasion, suffering damage that could take a long time to repair. Ukraine this month hit three main data centers belonging to tech giant Yandex, one for Russia’s biggest bank, Sberbank, and one for social media platform VKontakte, the country's equivalent to Facebook. While Yandex, Sberbank and VKontakte are coy about the damage, people and businesses across Russia have reported widespread interruptions to cloud services. Banking, e-commerce, geolocation and ride-hailing services, as well as Alisa, Yandex’s virtual assistant, and multimodal AI chatbots all have suffered lasting disruptions. The fallout even spread to Russia’s judicial system, reportedly forcing arbitration courts to cancel or postpone sessions and cutting database access. Most experts predict repairing the damage could take months, if not years. Some warn that Moscow’s aspirations to become a leader in AI development could be significantly set back. “This effectively sets Russia far behind in the AI race,” said Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society activist group. Data centers have been hit by both sides in the war Data centers are the latest targets of aerial campaigns waged by both sides against each other’s vital infrastructure. Russian missiles and drones have pummeled Ukraine’s power grid and other key sites, part of Kremlin efforts to weaken morale and resistance. Moscow stepped up those attacks as winter approaches, taking advantage of a shortage of U.S.-supplied Patriot interceptors, whose stockpiles have been drained by Washington's war with Iran. Ukraine retaliated with waves of drone attacks against Russian oil refineries, triggering a massive fuel crisis and bringing the war home to millions of civilians. U.S. President Donald Trump has blamed the attacks for higher global oil prices, which have escalated largely due to the U.S. war in Iran. Earlier this month, Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import diesel oil, shocking Ukraine and its allies. Ukraine also hit huge warehouses for Russia's top online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon. Kyiv's attacks on Russian data centers closely followed Moscow’s recent strikes on data centers in Ukraine, which disrupted the internet and TV broadcasts. On Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones hit a Yandex data center in Sasovo in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company’s three supercomputers. A data center in Kaluga was hit a day later and the one in Vladimir was struck Oct. 11. The data center and AI hub for Sberbank was hit Oct. 14 in Balakovo in the Saratov region, and four days later, Kyiv struck a data center in St. Petersburg serving VKontakte. Data centers are vulnerable While oil refineries and warehouses are easy prey, data centers are even softer targets — massive buildings packed with servers and supporting power and cooling infrastructure. Lasting damage can result from a drone carrying a relatively light load of explosives. The vulnerability of data centers was exposed by Iran, whose drones hit two Amazon Web Services data centers in the United Arab Emirates and one in Bahrain. AWS said last month it was unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted at two of them. Yandex has run drills for an accident that could incapacitate one of its six data centers, but it was caught unprepared when its three key facilities were hit over four days. It wasn’t immediately clear why air defenses near the sites had failed. “The problem in Russia is that they’ve got to cover a big country with air defense and they don’t have enough,” said Nick Reiners, senior geotechnology analyst at Eurasia Group. Russia’s efforts to build a ‘sovereign internet’ backfire Ukraine has stored critical data on servers in allied European countries, helping limit the damage from Russian attacks. But Moscow’s strict digital sovereignty policy requires all data storage at home, making it extremely vulnerable. “Because all the infrastructure and all the data is located inside Russia, it’s relatively easier to take down,” Reiners said. Klimarev predicted the data center attacks could encourage many top Russian companies to move data abroad, while the authorities could ease their efforts to tighten internet controls to minimize the damage. “Paradoxically, the strikes on data centers have saved the Russian internet from isolation, as they will now have to move computing assets, most likely, to Europe,” Klimarev said. “It’s quite likely that many Russian businesses are now roaming the European market to rent computing assets.” Russians are vexed by service disruptions Yandex dominates digital life in Russia and many former Soviet nations. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that its Board of Directors (the "Board") has declared a monthly cash dividend of $0.2708333 per share of the Company's outstanding 13.00% Series D Cumulative Redeemable Perpetual Preferred Stock. The record date for both dividends is October 31, 2026, and the payment date is Tuesday, November 10, 2026. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors, and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. Through its wholly owned subsidiary Sentinum, Inc., Hyperscale Data owns and operates a data center at which it offers colocation and hosting services for the emerging AI ecosystems and other industries. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, Ault Capital Group, Inc. ("ACG"), is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. Hyperscale Data currently expects the divestiture of ACG (the "Divestiture") to occur in 2027. Upon the occurrence of the Divestiture, the Company would be an owner and operator of data centers to support high-performance computing services, as well as a holder of the digital assets and the third wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. The Divestiture will occur through the voluntary exchange of the Series F Preferred Stock for shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock of ACG (collectively, the "ACG Shares"). The Company reminds its stockholders that only those holders of the Series F Preferred Stock who agree to surrender such shares, and do not properly withdraw such surrender, in the exchange offer through which the Divestiture will occur, will be entitled to receive the ACG Shares and consequently be shareholders of ACG upon the occurrence of the Divestiture. artigo.texto: What India’s Forest Rights Act Can Teach Us About Data Centers Vaishnavi Patil / Oct 22, 2026 In 2025, the Andhra Pradesh government allotted 480 acres to support a $15 billion project to build a 1GW Google-Adani data center campus near Visakhapatnam. That allotment has since grown to 601.4 acres across three sites — Tarluvada (266.6 acres), Adavivaram (160) and Rambilli (174.8). The capacity appears to have grown as well, with clearance papers showing approval for 2.51GW. Despite encroaching upon the eco-sensitive zone of the Kambalakonda sanctuary and being in proximity to the Mudasarlova reservoir, the project was granted environmental clearance in just nine days. Since then, protests against this project have intensified. Vizag is not alone. Across India, as in the world at large, planned data center projects are drawing increasing dissent from local communities, who bear the real socio-ecological costs and do not foresee the promised gains of an AI future trickling down to them. States have begun to deploy policy instruments to address public concerns. However, solutions that only consider better engineering or cleaner impact metrics miss the point. This is not just a technical problem, it is also a problem of governance. A data center is a claim on land and its resources, and therefore a claim on people. Its policy, thus, must be anchored primarily in the politics of place, because scratch the surface and you will find data centers to be fundamentally a land rights issue. And India has a rich and unique history of articulating and fighting for land rights. No legal instrument represents this history better than the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, better known as the Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006. It recognizes land and resource rights of forest-dependent communities, defined in its preamble as those “who have been residing in such forests for generations but whose rights could not be recorded.” In this age of data colonialism, critical resources are being extracted from communities to power a global digital system that directs the flow of value elsewhere. The FRA legacy provides us with the working grammar to confront this new form of colonialism and reaffirm pre-existing rights of communities. The grammar can be unpacked in three important rights articulated in the FRA — the right to land, right to resources, and right to development. Right to land (individual and collective rights) In the Vizag campus, two hundred of the 480 acres of the project belong to around 50 Dalit farmers of Tarluvada village. The land was given to landless Dalit farmers in the 1970s through a special program. This program is another example of the Indian state’s attempts to correct historical injustices, especially considering that a 2012 state survey revealed that 68% of Dalit households in Visakhapatnam district still do not own land. And yet, the Dalit community states that they were not consulted when the decision was made. They say that the Open Category (OCs) and Other Backward Classes (OBCs) negotiated the surrender of their land, with evidence of land-pooling and acquisition processes being used to put further pressure on them. They believe that the dominant castes withheld details from them and targeted Dalit lands specifically. It is exactly these types of power asymmetries in land and livelihoods that the FRA combats. By allowing land-dependent communities to collectively claim rights, the FRA sets an important precedent. It expands not just the definition of customary land rights but also the process for making claims. Under Section 3(1)(a), people can claim individual or collective forest rights for land they occupy and cultivate. Claims begin in the gram sabha, not the revenue department, and oral testimony and customary knowledge are permissible evidence. The Act restricts itself to forest land. However, its methodology of making individual and collective claims can be adopted more broadly. If applied to data centers, it would translate into allotment of land only after land claims are formally recorded so that structured negotiations happen with actual right-holders. Public consultation should also be mandated for data centers above a defined threshold. But how do you define that threshold? In Vizag’s case, due to the lack of categorization of data centers in the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) notification of 2006, clearances were processed for each site separately under Category B2 instead of assessing the whole project under Category A. As the Notification does not mandate public consultation for B2 projects, no hearing was conducted. Such obfuscation can be avoided if data center policies mandate cumulative assessments of projects and the EIA notification is amended. But more importantly, public consultation around data centers should draw on the FRA’s model of deliberation through local institutions. As rights under the FRA are place-based, claims and grievance redressal processes are triggered at the village level. If communities could lodge individual and collective claims to the land and resources on which they directly depend, and utilize them to demand accountability, consultation would follow regardless of the project category. If the state continues to insist on opening its land to tech conglomerates, granting rights to land-dependent marginal groups will allow them to protect their livelihoods more effectively. Right to resources (use/management rights) Hyperscale data centers cannot function without existing IT infrastructure. They are also resource-intensive, requiring an uninterrupted supply of power to run servers and freshwater to cool them. This naturally makes urban areas like Vizag attractive for data center clustering. artigo.texto: Fox ESS has introduced Power Cube, an all-in-one residential energy storage system combining an inverter and batteries in a compact, stackable design. Announced in Melbourne on 20 October 2026, the system is designed to simplify installation and allow households to expand their storage capacity as their energy needs change. The launch follows a SunWiz announcement which, according to Fox ESS, ranked the company first in Australia for installed energy storage capacity in the first half of 2026. Power Cube integrates key components into one system, with the aim of reducing installation time and associated costs. Its modular EQ5500 batteries offer storage capacities from 10.92 kWh to 49.14 kWh across two to nine modules. “Power Cube has been designed with the Australian market in mind,” said Brooks Richard, Managing Director of APAC & Middle East at Fox ESS. Richard said the system’s capacity options were designed to suit a range of Australian household energy needs, while its integrated design aimed to simplify installation. System features According to Fox ESS, Power Cube includes: - Power options: CEC-approved single-phase models from 5–12 kW, with three-phase models from 5–15 kW planned for release. Both ranges support up to 200% PV oversizing. - Installation options: A compact, integrated design with an IP66 rating for indoor and outdoor installation. - Backup capability: An integrated gateway with 63A on-grid full-home backup support. - Battery protection: Inter-cell insulation and an aerosol unit in each battery module, providing protection at cell and pack level. - Integrated heating: Designed to help maintain battery performance in colder conditions. - Monitoring and connectivity: Fox Cloud 2.0 with AI functionality, real-time monitoring and remote configuration, alongside Wi-Fi, LAN and Bluetooth connectivity. Power Cube comes with a 10-year product warranty. Its modular design allows households to select an initial storage capacity and expand it as their requirements change. Ends. artigo.texto: CATL Unveils Dual-Electric Range Extension Battery to Accelerate Electric Heavy-Duty Truck Adoption BEIJING , Oct. 20, 2026 /CNW/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold,CATL 's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns.CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models:Battery Asset Service Partners andEnergy Replenishment Service Partners . These models allow partners to participate in battery asset services and energy replenishment, extending their role beyond one-off vehicle sales to ongoing operations. artigo.texto: The AI industry has a problem with bragging. Companies are announcing enormous new data centers to power the AI boom. Some promise facilities bigger than anything the industry has built before. There's just one problem: Most of these projects may never happen. Bernstein Research analyzed thousands of planned US data centers and concluded that only about 35% of the announced capacity is likely to get built. That's roughly 170 gigawatts of data center capacity out of a total of almost 500 gigawatts. The rest? A significant chunk of it belongs to a category the industry has a wonderfully dismissive name for: "Bragawatts." These are ambitious announcements, often from newcomers with little experience building data centers, that have a slim chance of becoming reality. "Press releases are cheap…concrete is not," Bernstein analysts wrote in a research note. Bernstein began its analysis with more than 7,000 data center projects across North America, drawing on information from Aterio, a company that tracks construction through satellite imagery, permits, and other records. The analysts narrowed that to more than 5,000 projects (partly by excluding those already canceled). Then they assessed the chances of these remaining projects being completed. The analysts considered factors such as whether construction had started, whether electricity was available, and whether the companies involved had successfully built data centers before. The results revealed a striking divide. The 'bragawatt brigade' Experienced operators including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta landed at the top. Bernstein gave these companies perfect scores of 5 out of 5 for their development credentials. Other data center specialists, such as Digital Realty, Equinix, and CoreSite, got top marks, too. O'Leary Digital, associated with celebrity investor Kevin O'Leary, ended up at the bottom, with a credibility score of 0.35 out of 5, according to Bernstein. His company has announced 15 gigawatts of data center projects, and Bernstein estimates that only 489 megawatts, or about 3%, will actually materialize. "Sorry, Kevin," the analysts wrote. Although the term "bragawatts" has been doing the rounds in the data center industry lately, it's unclear who coined it, Bernstein analyst Madison Rezaei told me. "I wish I could take credit for that," she said. "I believe I originally heard it from an Equinix executive, but I don't think he owned it either." She said that while some ambitious newcomers could succeed, they haven't yet demonstrated they can deliver. "It's not that all of these guys are sort of terrible and not going to deliver, but we just have lower confidence because we don't know them," Rezaei said. O'Leary Digital responds O'Leary Digital disputed Bernstein's assessment, saying the research doesn't account for substantial work that occurs before construction begins. While acknowledging that O'Leary Digital is a young company, CEO Paul Palandjian said the team has decades of experience building major infrastructure projects and that its proposed 15 gigawatts of capacity would be built in stages over several years. The company said it has secured binding agreements covering about 11,000 acres in Utah and 13,000 acres in Alberta, obtained a 30-year development agreement in Utah, and made progress on planning, engineering, and permits at both sites. It also said the projects would generate their own electricity. The company said its early development work is funded, additional capital is committed to reaching key milestones, and experienced engineering and construction partners are involved. "We would rather be judged on milestones than on a model," Palandjian said. 'An announcement in search of a project' Other low scorers in the "bragawatt" brigade included Vermaland and Joule Capital Partners, according to Bernstein analysis based on Aterio data. Joule has announced 50 data center projects with a combined capacity of 11.7 gigawatts. Bernstein estimates that only about 11% of that capacity will actually get built. Almost all of Joule's planned capacity remains at the announcement stage, with little evidence of construction progress or of major customers committing to use the facilities, Bernstein wrote in a July note to investors. The analysts gave Joule a credibility score of 2.05 out of 5, placing it among the lowest-ranked developers in its database. "An announcement in search of a project," the analysts wrote. Vermaland has announced plans for a massive data center project in Arizona. Bernstein estimates that only 4% of its proposed 2.2 gigawatts of capacity will get built. The company is primarily a landowner, not a data center developer. Its proposed $33 billion La Osa project near Eloy had already been sharply scaled back amid local opposition and without construction approval. In late August, regulators formally rejected the project. Even before that, the analysts gave Vermaland a credibility score of 0.75 out of 5. Joule and Vermaland didn't respond to emails seeking comment this week. A yawning gap for data centers Sergio Toro, CEO of Aterio, sees similar patterns in his firm's voluminous, detailed data. Aterio's tracking shows that roughly 30 to 40 gigawatts of new data center capacity get announced each month. Yet only about 7 gigawatts begin construction each month, while 2 to 3 gigawatts actually start operating. This leaves a yawning gap. Many announced projects get withdrawn before construction begins — and before real money has been spent. "They just make the announcement, but they didn't get their approvals. Or they make multiple filings in multiple locations to see which one gets selected," Toro told me. "That's why we track with satellite if there's real movement on the ground or not." Indeed, Bernstein analysts wrote recently that the amount of "stranded" data center capacity has surged. These are projects that are either canceled, delayed, or not approved. artigo.texto: HADLEY — A stand-alone battery energy storage system will be allowed at a Breckenridge Road gravel pit, despite concerns about the location being in the town’s aquifer protection district and growing unease from those who live in the neighborhood. In a 4-0 vote with one member absent, the Planning Board Tuesday approved the site plans, the solar project special permit and a business use in aquifer special permit for ZP Battery Devco’s 5-megawatt system. The eight-battery system will be placed by the company in a nearly 5-acre gravel pit site located above the Zatyrka Park playground. Board members indicated they had to approve the siting in the agricultural zoning district and aquifer protection district, as grandfathered under previous town zoning, after the Worcester company filed a lawsuit in Hampshire Superior Court. That lawsuit arose after the board rejected previous plans in January 2025, and the company has argued the board’s decision was legally untenable and “unreasonable, arbitrary and capricious.” While Planning Board member Mark Dunn said he couldn’t in good conscience vote in favor of the project due to the potential damage to the aquifer should there be an accident involving the batteries, he was warned by his colleagues that the special permit needed four votes. Another failed vote would lead to further litigation. “Under duress, I will vote yes,” Dunn said. “This has been a tough one, but we are where we are,” said Board Chairman James Maksimoski. The Planning Board began the new hearing over the summer on what is a nearly identical proposal from Zero-Point Development. Since then, the board raised concerns over whether the state would allow it to reject the project under the Dover Amendment, which exempts certain land uses from local zoning based on their impact on public health, safety and the environment. Part of that argument stems from the fact that more than half of the energy to be stored by the battery won’t come from renewable energy sources. Several residents joined the call, asking questions about what avenues exist for neighbors to stop the project. “Any issue of toxic discharge into the aquifer protection area is a problem,” said Greg Owen, of Breckenridge Road. Brian Carroll, also of Breckenridge Road, said residents need to reach out to state legislators and tell them that small communities shouldn’t be subsidizing the energy needs of those in the Boston area. “These are being built, like with the Quabbin, for the cities to have energy when they need it,” Carroll said. Kristi Nelson, of Sylvia Heights, asked if there is a way to appeal the decision. Planners said the decision will be filed soon and abutters will be notified when that happens. Planning Board Clerk William Dwyer said there didn’t appear to be a legal basis to deny the latest application, explaining that three of the four grounds which the board used to turn down the project have been undermined by the state with its modified regulations. A final reason for rejecting the project, Dwyer said, would be if such a system could pose risks to the aquifer, a possibility the developer denied. The town now has to meet the burden of proof that there is a threat. “Now, we’re in the untenable position of having to prove they will harm the aquifer, which we cannot do,” Dwyer said. Those who live near the site had also asked the Planning Board to reopen the hearing, which was closed last month, so they could offer input, contending that neighbors and abutters were unaware of the project until seeing posts on social media. Town counsel, though, told planners the board had no basis for reopening the public hearing. The hearings on the project were legally advertised. In other business, the board approved new signs for The Home Depot, 350 Russell St., including ones that will go on the store’s facade, and for Hadley Pointe, the 20 North Maple St. nursing home and rehabilitation center.

artigo.texto: American Battery Technology is pursuing a U.S.-based battery-materials supply chain centered on lithium-ion battery recycling and its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project in Nevada, targeting lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese production. The company's Reno recycling facility can process 20,000 metric tons annually, while a proposed southeastern facility would expand capacity to 100,000 tons with a $150 million Department of Energy grant and an estimated $375 million total cost. Tonopah Flats is projected to have a 45-year mine life, $2.6 billion net present value and 21.8% after-tax internal rate of return. American Battery Technology reported fiscal 2026 revenue of $21.7 million, held $49.5 million in cash and had no debt. 3 Stocks to Benefit From China's Rare Earth Export Ban on U.S. American Battery Technology (NASDAQ:ABAT) is advancing a U.S.-based battery-materials strategy built around lithium-ion battery recycling and the development of its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project in Nevada, Chief Financial Officer Alex Flores said during a company presentation. Flores said the company is seeking to build a domestic, lower-cost and environmentally responsible supply chain for battery metals, including lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese. He cited supply-security concerns, logistics costs and environmental risks associated with overseas sourcing as major challenges for the U.S. battery industry. "Our approach is to first close the loop and then fill the loop," Flores said, referring to the company's recycling operations and its planned lithium mining and refining operations. Recycling Operations and Expansion Plans American Battery Technology operates a 138,000-square-foot lithium-ion battery recycling facility outside Reno, Nevada, with annual intake capacity of 20,000 metric tons. Operations at the site began in October 2023, according to Flores. The company's recycling process first dismantles battery packs into modules, cells and sub-cell components. It separates materials including copper, aluminum and steel, while producing a lithium-bearing intermediate known as black mass. In a subsequent refining phase, the company said the material can be processed into battery-grade nickel sulfate, manganese sulfate, cobalt sulfate and lithium hydroxide. Flores said the company currently sees stronger economics in selling black mass than in further refining it into lithium products. He said a federal directive issued on Aug. 27 banned black-mass exports, but American Battery Technology received a license allowing it to export up to $100 million of the material. The company is not selling black mass to China, Flores said, adding that its customers are primarily in South Korea and other OECD countries. American Battery Technology also plans to build a second recycling facility in the southeastern U.S. The proposed site would have annual intake capacity of 100,000 metric tons, representing a five-fold increase from the Reno facility's capacity. Flores said the project has received a Department of Energy grant equivalent to $150 million and is expected to require total capital expenditures of $375 million. The funding is a grant rather than a loan and carries performance milestones, he said. Tonopah Lithium Project On the mining side, the company is developing its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project near Tonopah, Nevada. Flores said the project encompasses 631 unpatented lode mining claims covering more than 13,000 acres and is based on a claystone lithium resource rather than conventional ore. According to Flores, the project contains 21.3 million tons of accessible lithium hydroxide monohydrate and has a projected 45-year mine life. The company expects the operation to employ more than 200 full-time workers and reach a peak mining rate near 30,000 tons per day. Flores cited the company's pre-feasibility study, published about a year ago, which estimated an after-tax internal rate of return of 21.8%, net present value of $2.6 billion and production costs of slightly more than $4,300 per metric ton of lithium hydroxide monohydrate. Planned infrastructure includes a surface mine, commercial refinery and a behind-the-meter solar field with battery energy storage. The project has received a $900 million letter of interest from the Export-Import Bank, Flores said. It has also been designated a priority project under the FAST-41 permitting framework. The company has initiated a definitive feasibility study, completed required National Environmental Policy Act baseline studies and submitted results to the Bureau of Land Management. Flores said the Bureau of Land Management approved the company's mining and refining plan of operations, which American Battery Technology had been developing since November 2022. The company was awaiting a notice of intent from the agency before moving into the environmental impact statement process. Under its expectations for the FAST-41 process, Flores said the company could break ground by the middle of the following year. Financial Results and Domestic Supply Focus Flores said American Battery Technology reported record fiscal 2026 revenue of $21.7 million, up 407% year over year. Cost of goods sold increased 67%, which he attributed to operational efficiencies at the Nevada recycling facility. The company reported cash-basis gross profit of $1.7 million, a non-GAAP figure excluding non-cash items such as depreciation and stock compensation. The company ended the fiscal year with $49.5 million in cash and no debt, Flores said. He also said American Battery Technology has operated a multi-ton-per-year integrated pilot facility that produced battery-grade lithium from Nevada claystone. The company is now pursuing strategic partners and long-term commercial offtake agreements as it seeks to expand its role in the North American battery-materials supply chain. artigo.texto: Savannah council workshops data center ordinance, emphasizing resident input SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - Savannah city council gathered Thursday to discuss where and how data centers will be allowed in the city. Council passed a moratorium on data centers months ago, with the intention of implementing an ordinance. The city does not currently have an ordinance for “hyper-scale” centers. Mayor Van Johnson said data centers are common in the city already, but not ones measured in acres. “There’s a data center in this building, we have data centers in our offices, in our homes,” Johnson said. Council discusses resident input Nick Palumbo, District 4 Savannah alderman, spoke about the approach council should take toward data centers. “I encourage us to please be as deliberative as possible, be as selective as possible, and the work to decommission them as diligent as possible,” Palumbo said. After Thursday’s workshop, Johnson said council decided residents need to be part of the decision-making process. “Understanding where in the city they could be, where they are already, where we would not want them to be, but I think most importantly, creating a mechanism by which the city has the ability to have residents come speak to their council before it’s approved,” Johnson said. Johnson said the process would involve residents and city council directly, turning data center proposals into special-use permits. City manager cites existing infrastructure Savannah City Manager Jay Melder said right-sized data centers are critical infrastructure for the city. “We have data centers here in Savannah that have been for decades, they serve hospitals, schools, governments, businesses, we need to be able to account for it, this ordinance is gonna let us do it,” Melder said. Melder said multiple city departments have put effort into the ordinance and said many agencies are involved in the discussions. “This is getting ahead of the issue, we don’t have a project that’s been proposed, this is about getting ahead of the issue so we’ve got our ducks in a row,” Melder said. City council said it is working to include residents in each discussion before making a decision. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.
