artigo.texto: Microsoft abandona projeto de centro de dados no Reino Unido A Microsoft desistiu de um centro de dados no Reino Unido que estava a ser construído pela Nscale, depois de atrasos no acesso à eletricidade terem impedido a entrada em funcionamento das instalações. Neste artigo encontras: A decisão representa um revés para a Nscale e surge numa altura delicada para a empresa, que prepara uma oferta pública de ações este mês. A saída da Microsoft poderá aumentar as preocupações dos investidores sobre a capacidade da empresa para executar os seus projetos. Microsoft deixa projeto da Nscale devido a atrasos Segundo um porta-voz da Nscale, a Microsoft abandonou o plano para utilizar o centro de dados. O principal obstáculo terá sido a dificuldade em garantir a ligação à rede elétrica necessária para colocar o local a funcionar. O acesso à energia tornou-se um dos maiores desafios para os operadores de centros de dados. A expansão dos serviços de computação na nuvem e da inteligência artificial está a aumentar rapidamente a procura de eletricidade e de novas infraestruturas. Porque este projeto era importante Os centros de dados são fundamentais para alojar serviços cloud, aplicações empresariais e ferramentas de inteligência artificial. Sem energia suficiente, mesmo uma instalação concluída pode ficar impossibilitada de operar à capacidade prevista. Para a Nscale, perder um cliente de grande dimensão como a Microsoft pode afetar a perceção sobre o projeto e levantar dúvidas quanto aos prazos de outros empreendimentos. Não foram divulgados detalhes sobre o valor do contrato nem sobre os próximos passos para o local. Possível impacto na oferta pública da Nscale A notícia surge pouco antes da oferta pública planeada pela Nscale. Embora o impacto final dependa das condições do mercado e dos restantes ativos da empresa, os atrasos e a saída da Microsoft poderão pesar na avaliação atribuída pelos investidores. O caso também mostra como a falta de capacidade energética pode travar a expansão da indústria tecnológica. A procura por centros de dados continua a crescer, mas os projetos enfrentam cada vez mais limitações relacionadas com licenças, redes elétricas e disponibilidade de energia. O que acontece agora Ainda não foram reveladas novas datas para a entrada em funcionamento do centro de dados nem foi indicado se a Nscale procura outro cliente para as instalações. A Microsoft, através da Azure, que também enfrenta pressão para cortar custos, não apresentou até ao momento detalhes públicos adicionais sobre a decisão. - A Microsoft deixou o projeto de centro de dados da Nscale no Reino Unido. - Os atrasos no acesso à eletricidade terão estado na origem da decisão. - A saída poderá afetar a oferta pública planeada pela Nscale. - O episódio reforça os desafios energéticos associados à expansão da inteligência artificial. artigo.texto: - The initial models are under development, with launches planned for next year. - The first model will reportedly come from Dongfeng and Huawei's Epicland brand, expanding vehicle coverage for the Choco swap network. Huawei's automotive technology company Yinwang, or Newcool, and CATL (HKEX: 3750) have tentatively set an initial lineup of 5 battery swap models for launch in 2027, according to a media report. Newcool, CATL and the battery maker's battery swap operator are developing the vehicles, LatePost reported on Tuesday, offering further details on the initial scope of their partnership. Newcool reiterated the core provisions of the 3 parties' strategic cooperation agreement to the outlet but declined to comment on the model count or launch plans. Those details have yet to be officially confirmed. Cailian reported earlier today that the first model would come from Epicland, a brand jointly developed by Dongfeng and Huawei, with a launch planned for 2027. The specific model has not been disclosed. The 2 reports add details on the product lineup and timeline to the newly announced battery swap partnership. The strategic cooperation framework agreement announced on October 19 did not identify specific models or launch dates. Under the agreement, Newcool is joining CATL's Choco swap ecosystem to help adapt partner models using Huawei's Qiankun intelligent automotive solutions for compatibility with the battery swap network. The partnership also includes Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES), CATL's battery swap operator. The 3 parties plan to integrate data and services across vehicles, battery swap stations and cloud systems, using real-time battery conditions and users' travel patterns to anticipate energy needs and proactively arrange battery swaps. Under the plan outlined in the earlier statement, vehicles would autonomously locate and enter stations, position themselves for a fully automated 99-second battery swap, and then drive away. Additional partner models would help CATL expand the user base for its battery swap network. The business can generate recurring revenue from battery rentals and energy replenishment services, but requires sufficient vehicle volume to support investment in stations, battery inventories and operations. CATL had built 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 Chinese cities as of September 29, according to information it previously released. Its long-term goal is to expand the network to 30,000 stations. The company also plans to build 1,000 highway battery swap stations between 2026 and 2027, extending the network beyond cities to support long-distance travel. Newcool took over Huawei's former intelligent automotive solution business and supplies automakers with systems for smart driving, smart cockpits and vehicle control.

artigo.texto: Ever since we broke the news that a huge data center might be built in downtown San Diego, local Democrats have been insisting its time to pump the breaks. Thursday morning, San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria posted a photo of himself signing an executive order that temporarily bans data centers on X. “San Diego is putting clear rules in place before we allow data centers in our city,” he wrote. San Diego Councilmembers Sean Elo-Rivera, Joe LaCava and Kent Lee gathered outside City Hall later that day announcing the proposal of a new city law that would place requirements on data centers built under their jurisdiction. “We need more than a pause. We need laws in place to protect us from a tidal wave of harm,” Elo-Rivera said, citing his concerns that such projects raise utility bills for residents, and pollute the air and water. The data center that sparked all this, if ever built, would be erected on federal land owned by the U.S. Navy on a site referred to as NAVWAR. The lawmakers acknowledged their actions Thursday wouldn’t be enough to halt what’s being explored by private developer, Manchester Financial Group. “The city can’t stop this project on its own. Congress can,” Elo-Rivera said. He urged San Diego’s congressional delegation to urge the Navy in writing to rule out a data center on the proposed redevelopment site of their 70 acres near the Midway District. “Data centers… are the physical manifestation of so much we hate that is happening in the world right now,” Elo-Rivera said. “We will no longer sit idly by.” Ex-County Contractor’s Husband Ensnared in Criminal Case The criminal case against the ex-chief operating officer of a former county contractor just expanded to include her husband. Jeff Knox, who is married to former Harm Reduction Coalition of San Diego COO Amy Knox, entered not guilty pleas Thursday to 15 felony charges. The charges against Jeff Knox include receiving stolen funds and embezzlement from the Harm Reduction Coalition. He’s also accused of stealing, filing false tax returns, mortgage fraud and knowingly receiving vacation packages that his wife secured to be auctioned off to support a different nonprofit she once helped lead. An attorney for Amy Knox argues the charges against her husband are “thin and nonexistent.” Refresher: Amy Knox is accused of spending public money on everything from plastic surgery to purebred dogs, allegedly forging an invoice to the county and mortgage fraud among other things. She has also pleaded not guilty to all charges. The county in June 2025 canceled its contracts with the Harm Reduction Coalition to deploy an opioid overdose reversal drug and test drugs for deadly fentanyl. South County Report: National City’s Cannabis Dilemma Since National City leaders voted to legalize recreational cannabis sales in the city five years ago, they haven’t seen the return on investment that they’d hoped. Now, city leaders are grappling with how to turn things around. In many other California cities, like Vista in North County, legalizing weed sales proved to be lucrative, but so far, National City hasn’t had that experience. In fact, it’s been quite the opposite. So far, two cannabis companies have sued the city and sales have been sluggish, something city leaders weren’t really anticipating. The rise in illegal cannabis sales statewide is a contributing factor. National City also crafted its rules so that dispensaries were required to open in a relatively out-of-the-way part of town. That definitely didn’t help. Rather than allow new cannabis business, city leaders are grappling with how to help the ones that already exist. Read the South County Report here. Mayor Todd Gloria has pushed back hard on the effort, calling it a “mistake.” Should the Council approve the measure without a supermajority, Gloria may attempt to veto it. Councilmember Henry Foster didn’t seem deterred by the pushback. “If the mayor wants to veto, good luck, veto. But I think we have a very good shot at getting six votes,” Foster said. San Diego Police Department Chief Scott Wahl has also tried to rally support for Flock. In a statement, he wrote that removing the Flock system will “make it harder for our officers to solve crimes, find suspects and deliver justice for victims.” “We’re gonna do what we need to do even if it means the police chief needs to go and retire early,” Foster said during the rally. artigo.texto: Data centers are the latest trail sign on a path of madness I keep cracking up at these so-called leaders and tech executives that keep trying to sell the rest of us on data centers and AI. They just do not get it at all. There are two primary factors that they, and business leaders all throughout recent history have failed to course correct on. First on the data centers, I can default to the famous line, “It is the economy, stupid.” More specifically the wealth and resource gap that has become such a drain on our economic growth and prosperity. We are getting close to ancient Roman secession of the plebs territory with how bad things have gotten. Over the last 50 or so years we have regressed from needing a reasonably well-paying fulltime job to achieve financial stability to a decade or so ago needing the same fulltime job plus a side hustle to achieve the same results. Now, not only do you need your fulltime job and side hustle but also must learn the ins and outs of day trading in order to achieve basic financial stability in modern times. All because we have this backwards idea that investors who simply throw money at a company should be treated anywhere near as well as the workers who are actually making that company run. And data centers are just the latest trail sign on that path of madness. As for AI, it is the extreme lack of guardrails businesses and governments have put on technology in the last few decades. My favorite comparison I have come up with is this: The harnessing and weaponization of atomic energy has killed less people than the creation and evolution of the cellphone. One is far deadlier than the other on paper, but there are few guardrails for cellphone use. Anthony Smith, Loveland Lest we forget, the UN remains our best hope Oct. 24 is United Nation Day, the date in 1945 when 51 nations, hoping for world peace and international cooperation after six years of war, founded our international organization. Alas, after 81 years and now with 193 members, those hopes almost seem irrelevant. The Security Council is crippled by the big powers veto threat, the General Assembly continues as a sounding board for the world’s conflicts, the World Court’s decisions can be ignored, but the specialized agencies, amid tensions, keep on with their vital work regarding health, agriculture, weather, labor, air and maritime traffic, education, finance, postal matters and other areas which encourage a functioning world. In spite of its weaknesses in 2026, the United Nations remains our best hope. Lest we forget. Richard Rush, Loveland

artigo.texto: Can larger batteries safely power residential buildings? A project in New York aims to show how A battery system that stores excess energy when it’s plentiful will power an apartment building in Buffalo, New York, when the grid is strained and electricity is costly A battery system that stores excess energy when it’s plentiful will power an apartment building in Buffalo, New York, when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. Buffalo-based battery storage manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. say the lithium-ion battery system is connected to the electric grid for Peace Bridge Place. Viridi says the 3.75 megawatt-hour system can power the building for several days. It's among the largest of these systems in a U.S. residential building. A battery system installed in a Buffalo, New York, apartment building will store excess energy when it’s plentiful and power the building when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. The 3.75 megawatt-hour lithium-ion battery system, which can power the Peace Bridge Place affordable housing complex for several days, is among the largest battery systems in a U.S. residential building, manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. said Tuesday. “We want our electric power to be resilient, affordable and available. Distributed battery storage accomplishes all three,” Viridi CEO Jon M. Williams said. “The only thing that has been holding up installations at scale is safety; a lot of the products on the market over the last 10 years have burned things down.” Deploying large batteries that can safely power apartment buildings is an important step toward replacing fossil fuels with renewables, experts say, but they’re uncommon because of the cost and concerns about fire risks. Already, larger batteries are paired with solar and wind projects, and homeowners are using smaller batteries to store excess energy from rooftop solar and for backup power. How batteries help keep electricity flow steady Batteries help maintain a steady flow of power when sources such as solar and wind are not producing. They charge when the sun is shining or when wind is blowing. That energy can then be used when demand is high. Batteries can also store excess electricity from hydropower, and New York is one of the top hydropower-producing states. Buffalo is close to Niagara Falls, where most of the state’s hydropower is produced. When electricity demand is high, Peace Bridge will use the battery. It will get paid by the utility for not drawing from the grid and for sending power back if needed. This helps lower the complex’s overall electricity costs, which benefits residents. The building can use the system during outages, too. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency helped fund the Peace Bridge Place project, as part of its focus on including disadvantaged communities in the clean energy transition. “It goes a long way toward demonstrating the safety and viability of these types of projects,” said NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris. Viridi has manufacturing facilities in Buffalo and Richmond, California, where a state grant assisted with renovations. California Energy Commission Chair David Hochschild said he’s impressed with the company. More than two-thirds of California’s electricity comes from clean energy and batteries get a lot of credit for that, Hochschild said. As electricity demand grows, batteries help ensure the grid is reliable, reduce pollution and contain costs, he added. “I believe the battery industry is the single most important energy industry for the next several decades,” said Hochschild, who co-founded the Electric Innovation Initiative to use electricity instead of fossil fuels more broadly throughout the U.S. economy. Viridi’s system passed a ‘near impossible’ test As large battery fires have garnered attention, some communities have opposed further development. However, the failure rate for batteries has decreased as more are installed, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Viridi spent six years and $10 million figuring out how to make a fireproof container for batteries. Half the cost was for batteries Viridi destroyed during testing. Viridi uses plates, pouches and spacing to isolate each battery cell. If one fails, the energy dissipates instead of spreading to the next battery, so that no gas, smoke, heat or fire escapes the container, Williams said. Jigar Shah, an expert in clean energy financing and deployment, said the Peace Bridge Place system is a milestone in overcoming safety concerns. To ensure nothing would catch fire when used inside a residence, Viridi’s system had to pass a test where the battery was forced to fail while a cheesecloth covered the container. The cheesecloth did not char or ignite, according to the test report record. Viridi announced in April it met stringent Underwriters Laboratories safety standards so its system could be installed indoors without adding additional fire suppression to a building. Shah, who led the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office during the Biden administration, said Viridi is the only company to consistently pass this “near impossible” test. Shah thinks far more U.S. homes will use batteries for backup power by 2030. The U.S. can meet much more electricity demand and avoid costly upgrades to the grid if batteries are strategically deployed, he added. New York and California officials want forward-thinking energy solutions Viridi and Good Carbon Co. chose the Peace Bridge apartments because the all-electric building uses a geothermal system for heating and cooling rather than natural gas and needed additional, resilient power. artigo.texto: China's CATL third-quarter profit growth slowest in nearly two years as competition intensifies Synopsis CATL reports slower third-quarter profit growth as intense competition in China’s EV battery market weighs on earnings. Net profit rises 14.5% to 21.2 billion yuan, below estimates, while revenue grows 58.6%. CATL also unveils new heavy-duty truck batteries and plans to expand its battery-swapping network. The third-quarter net profit growth, which follows a 36.5% rise in the second quarter, is the slowest in nearly two years Revenue climbed 58.6% year-on-year to 165.2 billion yuan, undershooting forecasts for a 60.2% increase, after growing 56.9% in the previous quarter. The EV battery specialist on Tuesday unveiled a new generation of batteries for heavy-duty trucks and announced plans to expand its battery-swapping network CATL, which broadened supplies to overseas automakers, accounted for 39.4% of global EV battery usage in the first eight months of the year, up from 37.7% a year earlier, while second-ranked BYD's share slipped to 15.1% from 17.1%, industry data showed CATL's share of China's power battery installation market fell to 40.9% in September from 49.8% in January, while BYD increased its share to 21.1% from 17.4%, according to industry data. While China's domestic auto market extended a 12-month downturn in September, exports continued to support industry growth as manufacturers expanded abroad. CATL expects energy storage to contribute half of its global revenue by 2030, up from about a quarter currently, Reuters reported in June. (You can now subscribe to our ETMarkets WhatsApp channel)

Veja o resumo da notícia - O avanço da inteligência artificial impulsiona a demanda por data centers, que se tornam uma nova frente para fundos imobiliários. - Fundos podem investir em data centers por meio de compra, sale and leaseback, built to suit, CRIs ou desenvolvimento de projetos. - Contratos longos e atípicos aumentam a previsibilidade da receita, mas não eliminam riscos de crédito e obsolescência tecnológica. - A qualidade do ativo é definida por fatores como preço de aquisição, disponibilidade de energia e flexibilidade para usos futuros. O avanço da inteligência artificial aumenta a necessidade de capacidade computacional, mas essa expansão depende de uma base imobiliária intensiva em energia, conectividade e sistemas de resfriamento. Nesse cenário, os data centers em fundos imobiliários ganham espaço como uma nova frente de investimento, ao lado de outros ativos alternativos como os FIIs de logística. A renda vem do aluguel do imóvel, não dos serviços de tecnologia. Data centers em fundos imobiliários: diferentes estruturas de entrada A exposição pode ocorrer pela compra de um data center estabilizado, por operações de sale and leaseback, por contratos built to suit, pelo financiamento de obras com certificados de recebíveis imobiliários (CRIs) ou pelo desenvolvimento de novos projetos. Os fundos também podem adquirir infraestrutura associada, como subestações elétricas. Cada estrutura combina de forma diferente risco de construção, energização, ocupação, crédito e necessidade de capital. Contratos longos aumentam a previsibilidade Como os ativos são altamente especializados e muitas vezes desenhados para um único ocupante, contratos atípicos e de longo prazo ajudam a alinhar o investimento ao período necessário para recuperar o capital. Reajustes por inflação e multas de saída podem proteger a receita. Ainda assim, um contrato extenso não elimina o risco do inquilino nem garante que o prédio continuará competitivo diante da evolução tecnológica. Energia e flexibilidade definem a qualidade do ativo O preço de aquisição, a disponibilidade de energia, a conexão à rede, a eficiência do resfriamento e a capacidade financeira do operador são variáveis centrais. A especialização que torna um data center valioso para determinado cliente também pode restringir usos alternativos e elevar gastos futuros de modernização. Por isso, o crescimento da IA favorece a demanda, mas não substitui a análise imobiliária, contratual e de crédito de cada operação. artigo.texto: Falling battery prices highlight Africa’s energy storage investment gap Battery prices are falling, but investment in energy storage across Africa is struggling to keep pace. The latest ESI Africa Industry Insights: Energy&Storage Volume 5 (2026) (https://apo-opa.co/3UANmwN) examines the gap between increasingly affordable technologies and the financing, regulation and infrastructure planning needed to support deployment. According to BloombergNEF, stationary battery pack prices fell to around US$70/kWh in 2025, a 45% year-on-year decline. Yet of the US$13.84 billion in energy transition investment Africa attracted in 2025, tracked by Electron Intelligence, just US$666 million, less than 5%, went towards storage and flexibility. For Nicolette Pombo-van Zyl, Editor-in-Chief of ESI Africa, storage has become essential to energy development. “It is now the part that decides whether a project gets financed, whether a grid stays stable after sunset and whether the clean energy already being generated is actually used. The industry's challenge is that capital, regulation and data have not yet caught up with that reality,” says Pombo-van Zyl. Understanding storage economics and infrastructure needs The publication examines battery storage economics, including South African modelling that places lithium iron phosphate ahead of competing chemistries for stationary applications. It also considers how deployment scale, degradation in hot climates, financing costs, import tariffs and freight affect project viability. Emerging battery technologies and their potential implications for Africa’s mineral value chains feature alongside cybersecurity risks and long-duration storage solutions. The volume also examines Africa’s expanding distributed solar market. According to Ember, approximately 26GW of solar was installed across Africa between 2023 and 2025, with only a quarter accounted for in utility-scale and off-grid figures. Improved registration and data could help planners understand this growth and its impact on electricity networks. Connecting investment with delivery The African Infrastructure Elites section highlights the growing role of storage in renewable energy financing, featuring developments including Scatec’s Obelisk project in Egypt and Mulilo’s Hartebeesfontein battery storage project. “Battery prices have done their part. What happens next depends on decisions that sit with regulators, utilities and financiers around how storage is valued for the services it provides, how it is protected as connected infrastructure, and how quickly projects are prepared to the point where capital can move. Those are solvable problems, and the sector already has the tools to solve them,” says Pombo-van Zyl. Published in partnership with Envusa Energy, NOA Group and Lyra Energy, the Energy&Storage Volume is available for free download to subscribers and non-subscribers. Download the volume (https://apo-opa.co/3UANmwN) These challenges will also inform discussions at VUKA Group’s C&I Energy + Storage Summit Johannesburg, taking place on 28–29 October 2026 at The Maslow Hotel, Sandton. The Summit brings together commercial and industrial energy users, developers and financiers to explore storage investment, energy procurement and cost certainty. Find out more about the Summit (https://apo-opa.co/3UaUmA7) Distributed by APO Group on behalf of VUKA Group. Since 1996, it has delivered technical developments and industry analysis through print, digital and multimedia channels, connecting industry professionals with information, expertise and solution providers. https://apo-opa.co/47xPQio About the C&I Energy + Storage Summit: The C&I Energy + Storage Summit brings together commercial and industrial energy users, project developers, investors, financiers and technology providers to explore practical energy solutions, investment opportunities and strategies for greater energy security and cost certainty. https://apo-opa.co/3UaUmA7 About VUKA Group: VUKA Group connects people and organisations with information and opportunities through leading conferences, exhibitions and media publications across Africa. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Entrelinhas de Mercado: Energia vira gargalo para data centers e limita avanço da IA, diz Márcio Aguiar, diretor da Nvidia para a América Latina Publicado 20/10/2026 • 21:43 | Atualizado há 9 horas KEY POINTS A disponibilidade de energia se tornou um dos principais obstáculos para ampliar data centers e a capacidade de processamento de inteligência artificial, afirmou Márcio Aguiar, diretor-executivo da divisão Enterprise da Nvidia para a América Latina, em entrevista ao programa Entrelinhas de Mercado, do Times Brasil – Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC. “O grande gargalo da expansão de um data center, da expansão de um poder computacional é: tem energia suficiente para isso?”, disse Aguiar ao apresentador Júnior Gornelli. Segundo ele, as limitações do setor mudam conforme a tecnologia avança e já envolveram a oferta de GPUs e de memória. Para enfrentar a demanda crescente, a companhia busca otimizar o software e aumentar a eficiência dos servidores, reduzindo consumo de energia e espaço físico. O executivo explicou que a Nvidia também desenvolve CPUs, DPUs e tecnologias de conexão entre equipamentos, além das placas gráficas pelas quais é mais conhecida. “O foco tem sido sempre ao máximo otimizar o uso do software, no sentido da atualização do software para que ele consuma menos energia e traga mais poder de processamento ao cliente final”, afirmou. Aguiar citou a evolução da infraestrutura: a Nvidia já oferece um rack com 72 GPUs e anunciou outro que, segundo ele, deverá reunir 544 GPUs no mesmo espaço físico em cerca de dois anos. A concentração de capacidade exige soluções de refrigeração e aproxima a empresa de fornecedores especializados. Leia também: Nvidia vira termômetro da IA e sustenta aposta do mercado; entenda “A gente começa a atrair também mais próximos de nós empresas que têm especialização na parte de refrigeração”, explicou o executivo, ao descrever o crescimento do ecossistema ligado aos data centers. Na adoção de inteligência artificial, a recomendação de Aguiar é não investir automaticamente na GPU mais avançada. Ele defende que as companhias avaliem seus softwares, suas necessidades de processamento e a infraestrutura já disponível antes de definir novos investimentos. “Comecem pequeno, pensem grande, comecem pequeno”, aconselhou. Segundo ele, o primeiro passo é reunir uma equipe para conduzir a transformação e testar aplicações que possam demonstrar o retorno do investimento. O executivo afirmou que cerca de 80% do trabalho da Nvidia com seu ecossistema envolve educação e orientação. A companhia procura mostrar que a inteligência artificial não se restringe às grandes empresas e que projetos podem começar com equipamentos de gerações anteriores. Leia também: EXCLUSIVO: IA entra na era dos milhares de agentes autônomos, diz diretor da Nvidia para América Latina “Faz o teu benchmark, porque quem define a arquitetura de hardware são os softwares”, destacou Aguiar. Ele acrescentou que GPUs adquiridas há cinco ou seis anos continuam sendo oferecidas por empresas que comercializam capacidade de processamento na nuvem. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Sobre robôs humanoides e veículos autônomos, Aguiar afirmou que a Nvidia pretende fornecer a capacidade computacional dessas máquinas, em vez de se tornar uma fabricante de robôs próprios. Para ele, a expansão da inteligência artificial ainda está em estágio inicial. “A gente vai ser sempre o cérebro de tudo isso”, disse o diretor, ao explicar o papel da empresa no desenvolvimento da chamada IA física. Leia também: Nvidia quer ensinar robôs a entender o mundo real; veja como Aguiar mencionou aplicações que vão além da robótica, como previsões meteorológicas, planejamento urbano, produção e distribuição de alimentos. Na avaliação dele, o processamento de grandes volumes de dados amplia as possibilidades de pesquisa e de tomada de decisões. “O intuito não é você simplesmente sair comprando só o que há de melhor”, ressaltou. Para o executivo, o objetivo é combinar ferramentas diferentes que efetivamente agreguem valor às operações das empresas. Aguiar relembrou que a Nvidia identificou novas possibilidades para suas GPUs em 2012, quando pesquisadores utilizaram plataformas originalmente voltadas a games em uma competição de classificação de imagens. A partir dali, a companhia intensificou o desenvolvimento de hardware e software para aplicações de inteligência artificial. Leia também: EXCLUSIVO CNBC: CEO da Gecko Robotics destaca parceria com Nvidia para ampliar segurança de robôs com IA “O hardware por si só […] não adianta”, explicou o executivo, ao destacar que os programas precisam estar preparados para aproveitar o processamento das placas. Após 16 anos na Nvidia, Aguiar afirmou que não imaginava a dimensão atual da transformação tecnológica. Segundo ele, a orientação da empresa é desenvolver soluções a partir das necessidades dos clientes e continuar abrindo mercados. Leia também: Nvidia supera projeções e segue à frente da concorrência na corrida pela inteligência artificial “O foco sempre foi abrir novos mercados e nunca focado em disputar mercado”, afirmou. artigo.texto: CATL Unveils Dual-Electric Range Extension Battery to Accelerate Electric Heavy-Duty Truck Adoption BEIJING , Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold,CATL 's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns.CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models:Battery Asset Service Partners andEnergy Replenishment Service Partners . These models allow partners to participate in battery asset services and energy replenishment, extending their role beyond one-off vehicle sales to ongoing operations. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. ("ACG"), is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. On December 23, 2024, the Company issued one million (1,000,000) shares of a newly designated Series F Exchangeable Preferred Stock (the "Series F Preferred Stock") to all common stockholders and holders of the Series C Preferred Stock on an as-converted basis. The Divestiture will occur through the voluntary exchange of the Series F Preferred Stock for shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock of ACG (collectively, the "ACG Shares"). artigo.texto: Lake Placid passes moratorium on battery energy storage systems Advertisement Lake Placid passes moratorium on battery energy storage systems LAKE PLACID, N.Y. — The Lake Placid Village Board of Trustees passed a new local law on Tuesday night, enacting a one-year moratorium on battery energy storage systems. The battery energy storage systems, more commonly known as BESS, are designed to stabilize electrical grids by providing steady power from renewable sources, which can sometimes be inconsistent. Many of the facilities also use lithium-ion batteries, which can create fire risks. Advertisement Lake Placid is the latest of several towns across the country to put the brakes on development, at least for now. The one-year moratorium will pause any potential construction until the village is prepared to pass stronger safety regulations. Ticonderoga, Ellenburg and Chestertown have also imposed short-term bans.

artigo.texto: Freeport meeting highlights data center impacts FREEPORT, Ill. (Rockford News First) - As data center development expands across Illinois, residents gathered Thursday at the Freeport Public Library to learn how these facilities could impact their communities. The discussion, hosted by the Environmental Study Group and Northwest Illinois Bird and Nature Alliance, focused on electricity costs, water consumption, pollution and potential regulations. “We’re seeing that these larger data centers can drink up to five million gallons a day,” Jizelle Torres, Prairie Rivers Network Climate and Energy program assistant, said. The concerns are also hitting close to home. Monarch Energy is exploring a large data center development in Rockford, while Stephenson County officials are considering how to regulate future projects. “We know that data centers are popping up all over the place, sometimes without public scrutiny and attention,” Deborah Lischwe, Freeport Environmental Study Group co-chair, said. Beyond local decisions, advocates are pushing Illinois lawmakers to pass the proposed POWER Act, which would introduce water-use protections and measures to prevent data center energy costs from falling on residents. “With the energy, we want to make sure that data centers are actually bringing their own energy and want to make sure that energy is clean,” Torres said. The legislation has not passed. State lawmakers could revisit data center regulations during the fall veto session beginning November 17. Copyright 2026 Rockford News First. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Battery technology is emerging as a critical driver of India’s electric vehicle (EV) market. Due to the increasing popularity of EVs, technological developments in battery science and production costs have become more important in relation to vehicle affordability and performance, and creation of domestic EV supply chain. Over the past few years, an increasing trend of registration of EVs in India has taken place starting from 0.456 million units in FY22 to 2.536 million units in FY26.The focus is now extending beyond EV sales to the development of a broader battery ecosystem. Investments in cell manufacturing, alternative battery chemistries, critical mineral processing and battery recycling are strengthening different parts of the value chain. In addition to government schemes like the ACC Production Linked Incentive, efforts to build domestic manufacturing capabilities have been strengthened. Hence, batteries are becoming increasingly important not just for the development of India’s EV industry, but also for the country's clean mobility and energy storage ambitions in general. Source: Vahan Dashboard, Note: * - Till August 2026 Batteries form a considerable part of the total cost associated with electric vehicles, implying that battery costs and innovations are fundamental factors determining the cost and adoption of EVs. Global lithium-ion battery pack prices fell to an all-time low of Rs. 9,413.28 per kWh (US$ 108 per kWh) in 2025, reflecting an 8% decline compared to 2024, according to reports published by BloombergNEF. This fall in the cost of lithium-ion batteries is because of overproduction, increasing competition, and the use of cheaper battery technologies like LFP batteries. The Indian EV battery market is also forecasted to witness significant growth, increasing from Rs. 23,707.52 crore (US$ 2.72 billion) in 2025 to Rs. 1.50 lakh crore (US$ 15.90 billion) by 2034, which translates into a compound annual growth rate of 21.70%. It becomes vital for India to build its own domestic capability along the battery value chain to facilitate its burgeoning EV market. There is growing focus on developing a domestic battery ecosystem through investments in cell manufacturing, battery components, and battery recycling. The PLI scheme for batteries, through the ACC, has helped develop domestic manufacturing of batteries, with at least 10 manufacturers planning their battery manufacturing capacity to about 178 GWh in the next five years. A layered set of policies is trying to pull India's battery ecosystem in the same direction: cheaper cells, more of them made domestically, and a system for recovering critical minerals once batteries reach the end of their life. Apart from the aggregated production capacity of the battery manufacturers, what is more pertinent for India is the battery chemistry and technology options that are trending, and the reasons behind the selection of these technologies being different from the rest of the world. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries have started gaining popularity all over the world due to cost savings and safety benefits of such technology. It was also stated that in the year 2025, the usage of LFP batteries in global EV batteries constitutes 55% of all the batteries. In addition, LFP batteries are 40% less expensive than NMC batteries. This makes the use of LFP batteries even more pertinent considering the fact that affordability of the batteries is very important in making the EVs affordable. India is developing its battery cells manufacturing capacity as a part of the Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cells (ACC). As of February 2026, at least 10 manufacturers have announced their production capacities of 178 GWh in the subsequent five years' period, helping to create the Indian battery industry. India is exploring the opportunities of sodium-ion battery technology as a part of its energy storage and battery innovation ecosystem. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has conducted the assessment of the global sodium-ion battery market and its potential for applications in India in the framework of the India-UK ASPIRE programme. The use cases for sodium-ion technology include stationary battery storage and selected mobility applications. The ACC PLI Scheme, budgeted at Rs. 18,100 crore (US$ 2.43 billion) aims to create 50 GWh ACC manufacturing capacity in India. Battery recycling becomes an important element of the ecosystem of critical minerals and clean energy in India. Within the framework of the National Critical Mineral Mission, the Government of India has approved a Rs. 1,500 crore (US$ 158.93 million) scheme to support recycling of critical minerals recovered from sources such as lithium-ion batteries. As of April 2026, 58 companies have become eligible for the scheme, taking the pledged recycling capacity to 850 KTPA and investments to around Rs. 5,000 crore (US$ 529.77 million). India's battery ecosystem is expected to gain further momentum, supported by the continued growth of EV adoption and expanding domestic manufacturing capacity. EV registrations reached 25.36 lakh units in FY26, while the ACC PLI Scheme is supporting the development of 50 GWh of domestic Advanced Chemistry Cell manufacturing capacity. Initiatives from the government such as PM E-DRIVE, investment in critical minerals and recycling of batteries have helped strengthen various sections of the battery value chain. Investments in cell production along with advances in new technologies like sodium-ion batteries and development of a recycling ecosystem are helping create an integrated industry in the field of batteries and energy storage in India. India's EV registrations increased from 4.56 lakh units in FY22 to 25.36 lakh units in FY26, reflecting the rapid expansion of electric mobility in the country. artigo.texto: JSU forum examines health, water and economic effects of data centers Researchers and residents discussed air pollution, water use and tax revenue tied to data centers in Mississippi JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT) - Jackson State University held a community forum Thursday to inform residents about data centers and their impact on the community. The JSU Mississippi Urban Research Center presented findings showing 17 data centers in the Jackson metro area and 24 across the state. University officials said data centers have a public health impact, including air pollution that leads to health issues. Melinda Todd, associate director of research at the Mississippi Urban Research Center, said she is concerned about the heath disorders tied to the centers. “My concern is the health impact, what’s being emitted into the air, respiratory disorders, neurological disorders, cardiovascular disorders, impacting a person’s sleep, insomnia,” Todd said. Panelists said data centers require large amounts of water to cool their systems, which affects fresh water used by the public. Dr. Talya Thomas, associate professor in the department of urban and regional planning, said the forums serve an educational purpose. “Understanding what they are, understanding the relevance and importance... if they feel like the data centers are affecting the community, then hopefully this forum can shed light on data centers and what they really mean,” Thomas said. Claudia Robinson, a library employee, said she wants more clarity on protections for residents. “If this technology is going to be here, how is it protecting people? I don’t see much emphasis on how it’s protecting people and not only our health but also our taxes,” Robinson said. University cites economic impact JSU officials said data centers also bring increased tax revenue that funds schools, infrastructure and health care. artigo.texto: Itália desponta como importante polo de data centers no sul da Europa A Itália vem se consolidando como um mercado de data centers de destaque na Europa, à medida que cresce a demanda por superinteligência, computação em nuvem e infraestrutura digital, segundo informações de inteligência de mercado da Administração de Comércio Internacional dos Estados Unidos. O país se apoia em sua localização, que liga a Europa, o Norte da África e a Ásia, além de conexões submarinas de cabos em expansão, imóveis industriais acessíveis e necessidades crescentes de computação em SI, observou o órgão. O mercado italiano tinha um valor de aproximadamente €7,5 bilhões em 2025 e deve crescer de forma substancial. O Observatório de Data Centers do Politecnico di Milano estima o investimento em cerca de €25 bilhões no período de 2026–2029, enquanto a Associação Italiana de Data Centers prevê que a capacidade nacional possa superar 1 GW até 2028 e chegar a 2 GW até 2031, ante cerca de 287 MW em 2024. Milão lidera a capacidade, enquanto Roma desempenha um papel complementar Milão continua sendo o principal polo, representando cerca de 68% da capacidade instalada de data centers na Itália. A Lombardia oferece infraestrutura de fibra existente, proximidade de grandes clientes corporativos, terrenos industriais, um ecossistema tecnológico maduro e conexões com redes europeias. Essa concentração, porém, também pressiona a infraestrutura elétrica, o uso do solo e os processos de licenciamento. Roma atua como um mercado complementar, dada sua proximidade com instituições governamentais e com a infraestrutura digital do setor público, com o Polo Estratégico Nacional e programas mais amplos de transformação digital gerando demanda por infraestrutura de computação segura e hospedada no país. Governo passa da estratégia à implementação Os data centers têm sido tratados pelo governo italiano como infraestrutura estratégica. A estratégia nacional de data centers do MIMIT busca atrair investimento estrangeiro, simplificar os procedimentos de autorização e posicionar a Itália como um polo digital europeu e mediterrâneo. Ao longo de 2026, o governo passou da estratégia à implementação, por meio de reformas no licenciamento, medidas para o sistema elétrico e a designação de grandes projetos como de relevância estratégica nacional. A disponibilidade de energia continua sendo a maior restrição estrutural do mercado. Em 2026, o governo adotou legislação para tratar dos custos de eletricidade, da competitividade industrial e da integração dos data centers ao sistema elétrico, reconhecendo que o desenvolvimento de data centers é indissociável do planejamento nacional de energia e da rede elétrica. Oportunidades para investidores dos EUA Para os investidores dos EUA, a Itália oferece a oportunidade de participar da próxima fase da infraestrutura europeia de SI e nuvem, ao mesmo tempo que ganham exposição ao corredor digital do Mediterrâneo. As oportunidades mais fortes devem surgir em campi de hiperescala preparados para SI, empreendimentos com energia garantida, reurbanização industrial de áreas já ocupadas, infraestrutura de conectividade e nos sistemas de energia que dão suporte aos data centers, segundo o órgão de comércio.

artigo.texto: Redata inaugura nova corrida pela infraestrutura digital no Brasil A política de incentivo pode contribuir para fortalecer a posição do Brasil como protagonista regional de infraestrutura digital. Por Roberto Murakami* – Nos últimos meses, o mercado de tecnologia esteve na expectativa pela aprovação do Redata, que traz incentivos fiscais para o segmento de data centers no Brasil. Em primeiro lugar, porque existe uma demanda crescente pela ampliação dessas infraestruturas, corroborada por levantamentos como o IDC Black Book Live Edition 2025, apresentado pela Brasscom (Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais), que projeta R$ 736,6 bilhões em investimentos em inteligência artificial entre 2026 e 2029 no país. Nesse contexto, a política de incentivo pode contribuir para fortalecer a posição do Brasil como protagonista regional de infraestrutura digital. Em um painel de que participei, no primeiro semestre deste ano, a convite da Japan House São Paulo, sobre o papel estratégico da infraestrutura de conectividade na nova economia digital, ouvi Marcos Vinícius Peigo, cofundador e CEO da Scala Data Centers, falar sobre o Redata e ressaltar que o Brasil tem duas grandes oportunidades: garantir a soberania digital, com infraestrutura para processar suas próprias cargas de dados, e se posicionar como um hub global de processamento de dados e inteligência artificial. Em suas palavras, o país conta hoje com disponibilidade energética e capacidade de expansão, mas essa vantagem não será permanente. Isso porque o mundo já avança em soluções como pequenos reatores nucleares capazes de gerar centenas de megawatts, o que pode reduzir as diferenças competitivas. A consolidação do Brasil como plataforma soberana e um polo global de infraestrutura para IA depende de decisões imediatas para remover barreiras à competitividade, o que incluía a aprovação integral dos incentivos fiscais federais e estaduais. A oportunidade é agora e precisa ser capturada com urgência, Peigo enfatizou. É justamente diante desse cenário que surge uma questão que considero cada vez mais relevante: o que muda no papel das empresas que fornecem tecnologia, integração e serviços para o segmento de data centers? A resposta passa, antes de tudo, por uma mudança de perspectiva. Os fornecedores de tecnologia deixam de ser apenas parte da cadeia de aquisição de equipamentos e passam a ter a oportunidade de atuar como parceiros estratégicos na construção dessa infraestrutura. Com a redução da carga tributária sobre determinados equipamentos de data centers, o Redata tende a favorecer novos investimentos, mas a disponibilidade de hardware, por si só, não resolve os desafios de uma expansão dessa magnitude. Projetos voltados a cargas de inteligência artificial exigem capacidade de processamento, armazenamento, conectividade, segurança e, principalmente, eficiência energética cada vez maiores. Nesse contexto, fabricantes, integradores e provedores de serviços terão de contribuir não apenas com produtos, mas com arquiteturas capazes de combinar desempenho, escalabilidade e eficiência operacional. Esse movimento também abre espaço para uma atuação mais consultiva dos fornecedores. À medida que energia, conectividade e capacidade computacional se tornam ativos estratégicos para a economia digital, será necessário ajudar empresas e operadores de data centers a tomar decisões sobre onde investir, como dimensionar sua infraestrutura e como prepará-la para uma demanda de IA que tende a crescer rapidamente. O Redata, portanto, deve representar mais do que um incentivo fiscal: pode ser o catalisador de uma nova etapa de expansão e sofisticação do ecossistema de tecnologia no Brasil. Para os fornecedores, a oportunidade está justamente em participar dessa transformação desde o planejamento dos projetos até sua operação, contribuindo para que o capital que chegar ao setor se converta efetivamente em infraestrutura digital capaz de sustentar a próxima fase da economia baseada em dados e inteligência artificial. *Roberto Murakami é VP das unidades de negócio de redes e Telecom da NEC na América Latina

artigo.texto: AI data centers boost Arizona construction jobs: Here’s why BuildStrong Academy offers free training as demand for skilled labor grows PHOENIX (AZFamily) — Artificial intelligence is affecting industries from healthcare to education to commerce, and now attention is turning to construction and skilled labor in Arizona. Signing up for a skilled labor class is getting harder as demand for workers continues to climb. Jordan Gil, 39, is one of many aspiring carpenters and electricians looking for a new career path. “I’ve been waiting to find something to work with my hands and develop a career and learn some skills and I found info online and seen a couple videos,” Gil said. “There’s a lot of work out here — everything from new construction and remodels,” Gil said. Demand for workers remains strong The need for construction workers is out there, according to Becca Haro, operations manager at the BuildStrong Academy in Phoenix. Haro said the construction industry in Arizona remains strong, with job openings for skilled laborers. She said that is encouraging amid fears about AI eliminating jobs across the labor market. “Everybody is scared that robots and computers are going to take over — but from my perspective and from what I see in the industry, I think this is actually creating a great opportunity — especially for us in Arizona,” Haro said. Data centers drive need for labor Haro said as AI continues to grow, more data centers will be needed across the state, and building them requires a strong skilled labor workforce. “I think people forget — there’s only so much you can automate or use AI for but when it comes to swinging hammers and using drills and wiring buildings, it still takes a human body to do,” Haro said. The BuildStrong Academy offers nine-week classes for free. The classes are paid for by companies and businesses that need skilled workers. For more details, visit https://homebuilding.academy. artigo.texto: Report: Iowa data center boom carries billions in economic impact Cedar Rapids and Palo will account for about a third of state’s capacity CEDAR RAPIDS, Iowa (KCRG) - Iowa is emerging as a national heavyweight in data centers. A new report says the state is on track to triple its data center operations by 2031. The Common Sense Institute study finds companies have already invested about $15 billion dollars into the state’s economy building and equipping data centers across Iowa, and have announced another $38 billion through 2031. A big share of that activity is clustered within Linn County, with QTS and Google data centers in development in Cedar Rapids, and another Google data center proposed in Palo. Linn County on its own accounts for roughly a third of Iowa’s total capacity. Des Moines and Council Bluffs are the other major data center locations statewide. Compared to the Midwest, Iowa currently ranks second for data center capacity, behind Indiana. Data center jobs Statewide, those projects are expected to more than triple total data‑center capacity by 2031 and support nearly 13,000 jobs from construction and initial equipment purchases. Existing data centers already support an estimated 12,600 Iowa jobs. Announced sites would push that to about 29,600 by 2031. The report says many of those jobs are outside tech — construction, electricians, truck drivers, retail workers and more. RELATED: Cedar Rapids businesses see boost from data centers Average pay in the industry that includes data centers reached about $126,000 in 2025, nearly double the statewide average. Energy demands Analysts warn the growth comes with big resource needs. At typical usage, the combination of existing and planned data centers in the state would take up nearly half of the electricity capacity the state averaged in 2024. Utilities are planning new natural‑gas plants and battery storage to keep up. READ MORE: Surging electricity demand from AI data centers puts Iowa at an energy crossroads Copyright 2026 KCRG. artigo.texto: HiTHIUM launches 8-hour batteries and a sodium-ion solution in Canada The stationary storage manufacturer announces its entry into the Canadian market with 4-hour and 8-hour lithium-ion systems and a 4 MWh sodium-ion unit designed for very cold climates. HiTHIUM, an energy storage solutions provider, has announced its entry into the Canadian market. The manufacturer says it ranks among the top two players globally for energy storage components. It reports having surpassed 200 GWh in cumulative delivered capacity and focusing exclusively on stationary energy storage technologies. A local presence in Canada According to Mizhi Zhang, HiTHIUM's President of Global Business, Toronto will serve as the main hub for Canadian operations. The company has subsidiary offices in British Columbia and Alberta, as well as operating sites in Quebec, Yellowknife and Fort Smith. Battery storage is drawing other players internationally, as with Viridi and Good Carbon installing a 3.75 MWh storage system in Buffalo, Trina Storage supplying 196 MWh to the AEJ Nozu project in Japan, or Leader Energy breaking ground on a 100 MW storage project in Malaysia. HiTHIUM says installed storage capacity in Canada is expected to double between 2025 and 2027. The country's total wind, solar and storage capacity would be on track to reach 50 GW by 2035. The company offers 4-hour and 8-hour solutions for utility-scale projects. It also unveils a 4 MWh sodium-ion solution that supports durations of 2 to 8 hours and targets very cold climates, such as Northern Canada. Two lithium-ion storage durations The 4-hour solution relies on the "âPower" 6.25 MWh container, built on HiTHIUM's own 1175 Ah cell. According to the company, most Canadian projects are currently designed around this 4-hour unit. It allows wind, solar and baseload output to be shifted to later peak times. The 20-foot container can be placed back-to-back and side-to-side, which would reduce projects' overall footprint. HiTHIUM also presents what it describes as the first native 8-hour solution based on lithium-ion technology. This 6.9 MWh BESS (battery energy storage system) uses 1300 Ah cells and has a 25-year lifespan, according to the manufacturer. It targets issues such as curtailments and industrial segments requiring zero downtime, such as AI data centers. A fire test conducted with UL Solutions HiTHIUM worked with UL Solutions at the start of 2026 on an independently conducted, extreme fire test of its 6.25 MWh block's intrinsic safety systems. A container was subjected to 24 hours of extreme combustion conditions, with its doors opened for maximum thermal spread, while neighboring containers were placed 15 cm away. Only the passive safety systems were enabled. According to HiTHIUM, the tested container remained structurally intact, with no thermal propagation across containers. The temperatures of cells in adjacent containers stayed below safety thresholds. Jordan Hebbert, HiTHIUM Senior Manager of Canada, says operational data from North American and European projects shows systems outperforming the company's guarantees, without detailing that data. artigo.texto: CATL has launched a dual battery system for electric heavy trucks that pairs a swappable main pack with a fixed range extender, so fleets can use far more of each battery before swapping. Agreements covering 13,000 units were signed at the launch. The main battery uses Qiji Energy’s standardised swappable packs mounted on the chassis, and a 77kWh extender capable of 3C charging sits behind the cab. With that backup on board, drivers can raise the main pack’s depth of discharge from around 70% to more than 95% and arrive at swap stations below 5% charge. CATL says power switches to the extender within milliseconds. The extender can be tailored for higher energy density, cold weather or high power, and it stays with the truck while the main pack can be leased to match seasonal demand. Qiji has also added standardised 432kWh and 513kWh blocks, and it says a swap takes five minutes. “The combination of the dual-electric range extension battery and Qiji’s battery swapping system offers the best solution for heavy truck electrification,” said Jesse Yang, Chief Executive of Qiji Energy. CATL plans 900 truck swap stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 across China. The design depends on that network, though. In Europe, truckmakers are focusing on megawatt charging instead, so the model may not travel easily. Why this matters: - CATL moves beyond cells. Battery leasing, swap stations and pay-per-net-energy pricing turn CATL into an energy service operator, earning recurring revenue while easing the residual value concerns that deter fleets from electric trucks. - Standard blocks set the interface. Swap packs standardised across multiple truckmakers could make CATL’s format the de facto standard for China’s heavy trucks, deepening truckmakers’ reliance on its ecosystem. - Regional infrastructure models diverge. China’s build-out of swap corridors contrasts with Europe, where truckmakers have backed megawatt charging, suggesting heavy truck electrification could follow different infrastructure paths by region.

artigo.texto: Rubix Battery Builds Solar Storage for the Real World By James Mast, Managing Partner, Rubix Battery | Severe weather, aging infrastructure, and increased demand are causing more frequent power outages. What’s more, the outages are becoming longer. It’s no wonder that savvy home and business owners are looking for solar options to keep their lives running. Increasing solar adoption also means needing energy storage. The U.S. energy storage industry is installing more and more solar batteries each year. According to the Solar Energy Industries Association, solar and battery storage accounted for 70% of all new electricity-generating capacity added in the first half of the year, and the S&P Global reports that U.S. utility-scale battery storage capacity surpassed 55 GW by the end of Q2 2026. Homeowners want more control over their energy. For solar installers, it creates a need for battery systems that are reliable, scalable, and straightforward to install. Rubix Battery is a U.S.-based energy storage manufacturer specializing in high-reliability LiFePO4 solar battery systems. Built with hands-on experience in solar and off-grid installations, Rubix develops storage solutions around the practical demands installers encounter in the field. Built by Installers, for Installers Rubix Battery was founded on a simple but important belief: battery storage should work well on paper and on the job site. The installer-first perspective was integral in creating features like enclosed wiring compartments, magnetic covers, modular stacking, and closed-loop inverter communication. That means cleaner wiring and simpler setups. Rubix also includes integrated safety components and designs that eliminate the need for additional racking or complicated installation work. Rubix created a product line designed to give installers greater flexibility while giving customers dependable energy storage that can grow with their needs. Inside Rubix’s Impactiv Balancing™ Technology For many installers, a simpler solar battery setup is one thing, but Rubix wanted to go further. Rubix wanted to create batteries that work well after the installation, too. Every Rubix Battery uses Impactiv Balancing™ technology, a cell-balancing system designed to maintain more consistent voltage across the battery pack, balancing cells at up to 20 times the speed of passive balancing and add up to 30% more battery life. Traditional passive balancing dissipates excess energy from higher-voltage cells as heat. Rubix’s Impactiv Balancing™ system instead transfers energy from higher-voltage cells to lower-voltage cells, with additional dissipative balancing when a cell reaches a critically high voltage. The translation for installers? Effective cell balancing is an important part of maintaining battery performance, capacity, and long-term reliability. The Rubix Energy Storage Product Lineup Rubix offers two primary battery platforms designed for different system requirements: the modular Stack Series and the high-capacity R-Series. Rubix Stack Series Solar Batteries Rubix Stack Series solar batteries are modular LiFePO4 energy storage systems designed for residential and light commercial applications. Each Rubix Stack Series battery module delivers 5.12kWh of energy storage, scalable up to 32 batteries in parallel for a maximum system capacity of 163.84kWh. Key specifications: - 5.12kWh per battery - 24V/200Ah or 48V/100Ah configurations - Up to 7 batteries per stack - Up to 32 batteries in parallel - Maximum system capacity of 163.84kWh - 6,000 cycles at 80% depth of discharge - LiFePO4 chemistry - Impactiv Balancing™ Technology - Closed-loop communication with compatible inverters - No external racking or exposed cabling - 10-year warranty Rubix R-Series Solar Batteries Rubix R-Series solar batteries provide higher-capacity storage for demanding applications, including off-grid, agricultural, and larger energy systems. Each Rubix R-Series battery module delivers 14.336kWh of energy storage, scalable up to 32 batteries in parallel for a maximum system capacity of 457kWh. Key specifications: - 14.336kWh per battery - 24V/560Ah or 48V/280Ah configurations - Up to 4 batteries per stack - Up to 32 batteries in parallel - Maximum system capacity of 457kWh - 4,500 cycles at 80% depth of discharge - LiFePO4 chemistry - Impactiv Balancing™ Technology - Closed-loop communication with compatible inverters - No external racking or exposed cabling - 10-year warranty Solar Storage Built for the Next Install With the Stack Series and R-Series, you can have reliable energy storage for everything from compact residential systems to high-capacity off-grid applications. Rubix Battery gives installers a scalable approach to energy storage. The LiFePO4 chemistry, Impactive Balancing™, modular architecture, and installer-focused design are built around the realities of modern solar installations. To learn more about battery specifications, find an installer or distributor, or connect with the Rubix team, visit the Rubix Battery website. Tags: BESS, products, Rubix, storage

artigo.texto: A small town east of the Cascades declared an emergency over data centers this week, at a time when many Oregonians are increasingly concerned about their rapid growth. The declaration wasn’t meant to crack down on data centers, but to urge the state to stop impeding them. In response to Gov. Tina Kotek’s pause on data center permits through July, the Umatilla City Council voted on Tuesday to declare an emergency “due to the threat of widespread financial loss” over new data center developments. Local governments across Oregon appear sharply divided on what amounts to a statewide data center moratorium. In Eastern and Central Oregon, where many of the state’s largest data centers have been built, local officials say they feel blindsided and are worried about lost revenue. But in Hillsboro, Oregon’s major tech hub, city officials have embraced the push to slow and regulate these developments. This comes during rising national and local backlash against data centers, which are hubs of much of the internet — hosting websites, streaming platforms, business operations and artificial intelligence. “Governor Kotek directed DEQ to pause certain air and water permits within the agency’s administrative authority because Oregonians have made it clear they expect thoughtful, responsible decisions about data center development,” Kotek’s office said in a statement. A recent poll commissioned by OPB showed that nearly two-thirds of likely Oregon voters favored a temporary ban on data centers, and both major gubernatorial candidates have come out in favor of a moratorium. An earlier survey by a Kotek-appointed data center committee also found widespread opposition to new data centers. The Oregon Legislature is expected to address data center regulations after it convenes in January. Until then, local debates are setting the stage for the political battles to come. Eastern Oregon pushes back More than a dozen massive data center campuses have cropped up along the Columbia River in the Lower Umatilla Basin in recent years. Most belong to Amazon, which has multi-building hyperscale data center complexes in Boardman, Umatilla and Hermiston, and outside city limits in Morrow and Umatilla counties. On Tuesday, the Umatilla City Council decried Kotek’s directive telling environmental regulators to temporarily stop issuing environmental permits to data centers. Councilors argued that Kotek’s move could force the city to forgo millions of dollars in tax revenue from data center companies. They hope to use an emergency declaration as a springboard to get Kotek to reverse her decision, rally other data center communities to their cause or even take further legal action. “(The) City should not be required to wait until investments are abandoned, jobs are lost, or essential services are compromised before taking action,” Umatilla City Manager Dave Stockdale wrote in a report to the City Council. As with many public meetings in Eastern Oregon, Tuesday’s Umatilla City Council meeting was sparsely attended. Two people testified to voice concerns over data centers, while a third resident supported the council’s emergency declaration. Umatilla resident Mary Cahill wondered whether her town had become too reliant on funding from the data center industry. “I understand if we’re not growing, we’re dying, and maybe I should crawl back under the rock I came out of,” she told the City Council. “But I’m concerned (over) how much money we’ve been spending.” City staff, however, painted a picture of data centers as a source of revenue — not expense — for the community. Rural leaders say Kotek’s moratorium has cut into their budgets Small governments in rural areas typically give data center operators 15-year tax breaks under Oregon’s Enterprise Zone program. But while companies forgo property taxes, they still pay other fees that have helped small towns fund new city buildings, services and infrastructure. Kotek’s moratorium has paused data center construction, so cities and counties aren’t getting those fee payments. Umatilla is set to lose out on more than $2.5 million in annual tax payments, $12 million in water infrastructure improvements and contributions to the bond that’s funding the construction of a new police station, staff there calculated. Hermiston officials are also grappling with the financial costs of a pause in data center development. “Total devastation,” is how Hermiston City Manager Mark Morgan described the impact on that neighboring rural city, where Amazon operates two hyperscale data center campuses. “This move has cost Hermiston residents approximately $550 million in lost future anticipated local fee revenue,” Morgan said by email. After the news of the moratorium, Amazon canceled plans for multiple new data center developments it had planned in Hermiston, Morgan said. Morrow County Commissioner Gus Peterson called Kotek’s data center moratorium “executive overreach.” “I’m not a fan of executive decisions that really ought to be legislative ones,” he said. In Central Oregon, the city of Prineville has also become home to a handful of hyperscale data centers. Apple and Meta, the parent company of Facebook, each operate hyperscale campuses in Prineville. Mayor Steve Uffelman said those companies pay fees that “far exceed what we would collect in property taxes.” “It has been a godsend for our community that was trying to recreate itself from a timber town,” Uffelman said. “Now we are a viable, active, productive community.” He said he was blindsided by Kotek’s decision, and that her office hadn’t reached out to Prineville city officials. “I was very unhappy at the shallowness of the thought going into the decision by the governor,” Uffelman said. “Because the data centers, contrary to the public sentiment, have been amazingly beneficial to communities such as the city of Prineville.” Hillsboro moves in step with Kotek’s moratorium In Hillsboro, where data centers have smaller footprints and the regional ec
