artigo.texto: India’s Downstream Battery Storage Manufacturing Capacity Reaches 86 GWh Only 21.6% of India's battery manufacturing capacity is operational October 22, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights India’s operational battery energy storage manufacturing capacity is heavily concentrated in downstream manufacturing, which accounts for 92% of the total, while cell manufacturing represents just 8%, according to Mercom India’s recently released Energy Storage Manufacturing Ecosystem Report. India’s downstream battery storage manufacturing capacity, including battery packs, containers, and integrated energy storage systems, stands at approximately 86 GWh. The gap between cell and downstream manufacturing capacity highlights the country’s dependence on imported battery cells, materials, and specialized equipment. Only 21.6% of India’s combined operational and planned battery storage manufacturing capacity is operational. The remaining capacity comprises projects under construction or announced. Most identified cell manufacturing capacity has yet to become operational. “India’s battery manufacturing industry is expanding rapidly, but domestic cell production is still at an early stage. While downstream manufacturing has grown much faster, enabling companies to assemble battery systems domestically, the industry continues to rely on imported cells and materials. A large amount of cell capacity is under construction or announced, but the real challenge will be converting that capacity into stable commercial production,” commented Raj Prabhu, CEO at Mercom Capital Group. Manufacturing Capacity and Pipeline India’s existing cell and downstream manufacturers accounted for 47% of identified capacity across operational and planned facilities, while new entrants accounted for 53%. Lithium-based chemistries dominated manufacturing capacity across both cell and downstream manufacturing segments. Converting planned capacity into commercial production remains a challenge, particularly for cell manufacturing. Geographic Distribution Gujarat accounted for 51% of India’s battery storage manufacturing capacity under construction, followed by Maharashtra. Together, Gujarat and Maharashtra accounted for 71% of battery storage manufacturing capacity under construction. Competitive domestic manufacturing will require consistent production quality, competitive costs, and sufficient capacity utilization. “Manufacturers will need to achieve competitive costs, consistent quality, strong yields, and sufficient utilization, and that will be much easier with a clear demand trajectory and better visibility on how quickly storage deployment will scale. India has a significant opportunity to build a competitive battery manufacturing ecosystem, but demand and supply need to develop in parallel,” Prabhu said. Battery Costs and Import Dependence Battery systems accounted for more than half of utility-scale energy storage project capital expenditure in the second quarter of 2026, with cells representing a substantial share of battery system costs. Cell pricing and sourcing remain important to project economics and domestic manufacturers’ competitiveness. Despite the expansion of downstream manufacturing, India continues to depend on imported cells, materials, and specialized equipment. The gap between operational cell and downstream capacity highlights the need for an integrated domestic battery supply chain. Government Support Government programs support the development of domestic battery cell manufacturing capacity. The production-linked incentive program for advanced chemistry cell manufacturing has allocated ₹181 billion (~$1.91 billion) to support 50 GWh of manufacturing capacity, plus an additional 5 GWh for niche technologies. Among projects receiving active support under the program, 6.4 GWh of manufacturing capacity is operational, while another 28.6 GWh is under construction. The government’s viability gap funding program also mandates a 20% local-content requirement for supported projects. Eligible downstream components and services can satisfy this requirement without the use of domestically manufactured battery cells, limiting its direct effect on demand for domestic cell production. Manufacturing Outlook Further expansion will depend on storage deployment and the conversion of planned manufacturing capacity into commercial production. Manufacturers need visibility into project awards, storage deployment, and equipment demand to support long-term investment in cell manufacturing. Competitive costs, consistent quality, higher manufacturing yields, and adequate capacity utilization will remain important as new facilities begin operating. “For domestic manufacturing to continue expanding, manufacturers need clear long-term visibility on storage deployment, project awards, and equipment demand before committing large amounts of capital to new cell plants. That visibility is critical to supporting capacity expansion, maintain utilization, and improve cost competitiveness. Domestic manufacturers will ultimately need to compete on cost, quality, reliability, and supply availability as more capacity comes online,” said Prabhu. Mercom India’s Energy Storage Manufacturing Ecosystem Report assesses India’s stationary battery storage manufacturing sector, from materials and cells to packs, containers, power electronics, and integrated battery energy storage systems. The report covers operational and planned capacity, technology trends, supply-chain dependencies, demand, government policies, localization opportunities, and manufacturing challenges. It also provides an outlook through 2030. For the complete report, visit: Energy Storage Manufacturing Ecosystem Report.

artigo.texto: Spartanburg County weighs new rules for data center development Officials discuss changes to zoning ordinance as residents push back on Pine Street project SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - Spartanburg County officials are considering new standards for data center development as they work to establish rules for future projects. The county’s Land Use Committee discussed potential amendments to the Performance Zoning Ordinance, known as the PZO, during a meeting Tuesday at Cleveland Park’s event space. The discussion followed months of research and visits to other parts of the country to examine how other jurisdictions regulate data centers. The county’s planning and development director led a discussion comparing data center regulations in nearby counties and other states. Potential new standards Proposed changes could address the size and type of data centers, their equipment and their proximity to existing homes. Other potential standards include setbacks and buffers, noise mitigation, and measures to manage the effects of electricity and water use. Land Use Committee Chair Grant DeShields said regulating data centers requires balancing competing interests. “The complication of trying to regulate data centers in a proper way that we don’t alienate new data centers from coming here, but at the same time protect our legacy landowners that live here and the people and the citizens that we already have that enjoy peaceful neighborhoods,” DeShields said. DeShields said the county’s current moratorium on data center development is temporary and that establishing permanent regulations is a priority. “There are not data center specific regulations at all. That was the reason for the moratorium to begin with,” DeShields said. County staff also are considering whether to restrict where larger data centers can be built. One option is an overlay district that would designate specific areas for the facilities. The PZO governs development in the county’s Southwest Planning Area, an unincorporated area near Duncan, Lyman, Reidville, Greer and Woodruff. The rest of the county, including the Pine Street corridor, is governed by a separate ordinance, the Unified Land Management Ordinance, or ULMO. DeShields said any changes to the PZO would apply to the entire county, including areas governed by the ULMO. The Valara data center site along South Pine Street falls under the ULMO. The project has faced legal challenges over its classification as a “minor development.” DeShields said the county is working to address potential environmental impacts at the Valara site through a community development agreement. He said the agreement includes environmental studies and monitoring requirements, separate from the broader zoning changes under consideration. Resident reaction Spartanburg County resident Lisa Weir attended Tuesday’s meeting and said she was encouraged by the discussion. “I feel like they are understanding the necessity to put guardrails around or fences around what’s happening with the data centers,” Weir said. Weir said she appreciated hearing about standards used in other areas, including a jurisdiction in Pennsylvania that she said requires buffers of 500 to 1,000 feet between data centers and other properties. She described the county’s current land-use ordinance as “very complicated” compared with those in other communities. But she questioned why the discussion had not happened sooner. “This meeting could have taken place about a year ago,” Weir said. Weir cited the Pine Street site’s proximity to schools, including E.P. Todd, Pine Street School and the South Carolina School for the Deaf and the Blind, as a primary concern. She urged more residents to join opposition to data center development without additional regulations. “I would appreciate if many more people of Spartanburg would mobilize and get involved in it. Because it is imperative that we do this,” Weir said. “It won’t be an immediate thing that we see. But it will have long-term health effects down the line. For everyone.” What’s next Tuesday’s discussion was not a final vote on new data center regulations. County staff must continue developing the proposed amendments before they can proceed through the formal review and approval process. City staff said they plan to discuss recommendations to the planning commission sometime in November. Feel more informed, prepared, and connected with FOX Carolina. artigo.texto: CPQD integra projeto de R$ 68,6 milhões para fabricar células de baterias Iniciativa liderada pelo SENAI prevê planta semiindustrial de baterias de íons de lítio para mobilidade elétrica e armazenamento de energia. O CPQD participa de um projeto de R$ 68,6 milhões voltado à produção nacional de células de baterias de íons de lítio, utilizadas em veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Conduzida pelo Instituto SENAI de Inovação em Eletroquímica (ISI-Eletroquímica), a iniciativa prevê a implantação de uma planta semiindustrial para fabricação de componentes, testes de processos produtivos e desenvolvimento tecnológico em parceria com a indústria. O CPQD atuará na avaliação do desempenho e do comportamento das células produzidas, utilizando sua experiência em ensaios laboratoriais para verificar requisitos técnicos de qualidade, segurança e confiabilidade. Planta semiindustrial terá produção de células de íons de lítio A infraestrutura será instalada no ISI-Eletroquímica e contemplará diferentes etapas do processo produtivo, desde a preparação dos materiais utilizados nos eletrodos até a fabricação de componentes, montagem das células e formação eletroquímica. A unidade permitirá produzir os primeiros lotes em escala pré-industrial e validar procedimentos de fabricação. Também será utilizada para desenvolver tecnologias em colaboração com as empresas participantes, considerando as necessidades de aplicação dos componentes. CPQD fará avaliação técnica das baterias A atuação do CPQD no projeto está relacionada à experiência acumulada pela instituição em pesquisas sobre baterias e sistemas de energia. O centro de pesquisa desenvolveu infraestrutura laboratorial para avaliação desses dispositivos ainda no período de expansão da telefonia celular no Brasil. Ao longo dos anos, participou de projetos envolvendo tecnologias de armazenamento de energia com empresas como Embraer, Marelli, CETEP, CPFL e PHB Eletrônica. Essa experiência será aplicada à análise técnica das células fabricadas na nova planta, fornecendo informações para o aperfeiçoamento das soluções desenvolvidas. “O desafio é criar condições para que o Brasil avance em uma cadeia industrial estratégica, com capacidade para produzir, testar e aperfeiçoar tecnologias utilizadas em diferentes setores da economia”, afirma Gustavo Sinzato, gerente de Soluções em Energias Renováveis do CPQD. Projeto reúne empresas de energia e indústria automotiva A iniciativa conta com a participação de empresas de diferentes segmentos industriais, entre elas Petrobras, WEG, Stellantis, Volkswagen, Marcopolo, Arkema, CBA e Grupo Moura. A colaboração envolve instituições de pesquisa e representantes da indústria interessados no desenvolvimento de tecnologias para mobilidade elétrica e armazenamento de energia. Entre os objetivos estão a ampliação da capacidade brasileira de fabricação de componentes e o desenvolvimento de processos que possam ser utilizados na cadeia produtiva de baterias de íons de lítio. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: Over the course of a sometimes contentious, sometimes awkward hour, the two candidates for Wisconsin governor sparred over taxes, data centers and abortion in the only debate of their general election campaign Wednesday night. Both Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democrat, and U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican, declined on several occasions to attach specific numbers to their policy proposals, instead offering broad assurances that taxes would be cut while priorities would remain well funded. From their opening remarks onwards, both repeatedly criticized one another’s records, as each sought to appeal to voters in what is expected to be a close race largely defined by concerns over the economy and rising costs. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. “Taxes have went up every single year that David Crowley has been county executive. You know what he’s going to do as governor,” Tiffany said in his opening remarks, when asked about his strong support for the policies of President Donald Trump. Asked about rising taxes in Milwaukee County, Crowley said he was proud of his bipartisan achievements — including one deal that increased the county sales tax — and accused Tiffany of selling out Wisconsin. “This is about having a governor who’s going to work for you, someone who’s going to invest in your future, or someone who’s going to work for the billionaires that are bankrolling their campaign or doing exactly what Donald Trump wants them to do,” he said. Crowley, a moderate Milwaukee Democrat running as a pragmatic dealmaker, and Tiffany, a staunch conservative from the Northwoods running as a common-sense everyman, both said they’d restructure taxes but offered few specifics. Tiffany said he would return the state’s projected $3 billion surplus to voters directly, and eventually said it would be through a combination of income tax and property tax reductions, and a 10 percent tax cut for families earning less than $150,000. “I would prefer not to do it as a one-time check because people don’t plan their futures based on one-time checks,” he said, referring to a failed deal out of the Legislature that included rebate checks. “So I want to see long-term tax reductions that … people are going to benefit from not just next year, but in the future, also.” He did not offer specifics when asked how he would make up for lost tax revenue, but said it would derive from a growing economy. “There is enough money in Madison to be able to backfill those things that we need to,” he said. Crowley was even more vague on his plans for restructuring taxes. Asked whether he would create a new tax bracket for Wisconsin’s highest earners, Crowley first pointed to Tiffany’s vote for Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included tax cuts for America’s highest earners. Then he called for a holistic change to the state tax system, including changing how the state distributes money to local communities. “Do you have a number and a percentage?” asked Matt Smith, a reporter with WISN-TV and one of the debate moderators. “What I have is … that we have to make sure that we’re working with the state Legislature to make sure that we’re creating a fair and taxable system that works for all income earners,” Crowley responded. Some overlap among contentious policy differences Unsurprisingly, Crowley and Tiffany disagreed on many issues. Tiffany said he would mandate that local, county and state law enforcement coordinate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, while Crowley said that local law enforcement should not enter into detainer agreements, and that ICE should be banned from wearing masks. Tiffany said he would support researching medicinal marijuana, while Crowley has called for full legalization of both medicinal and recreational cannabis, which he argued could bring in revenue to cover healthcare costs. There were some areas of overlap. Both said that they would not end the private school voucher system, and Tiffany said he would consider raising the income cap for which students can participate. Crowley said that the voucher system, which was developed in Milwaukee, should not be expanded, and that more money should go toward public schools. “But I don’t think that you can just abruptly shut down this program,” he said. “As of this moment, we are not in a position to push all of these children towards any of our public schools.” They sparred over data center development, although they agreed on the broad strokes of putting restrictions on developments. Tiffany said he would require any proposals to follow certain conditions, including ensuring that utilities don’t go up, not converting farmland and offering local communities control. He accused Crowley of flip-flopping on the issue of repealing tax incentives for tech companies to site their developments in Wisconsin. “I have been consistent over the last year, that we are not going to pay those subsidies to these companies. He just came around in the last week when he figured out that’s where the public is,” Tiffany said. “I will not put my finger to the wind when making decisions like this.” Crowley responded that he has long been “open to reforming the sales tax incentives that these data centers have been getting,” and that he would sign a bill to repeal those incentives, which were written into the 2023 state budget by the GOP-held Legislature and signed by Gov. Tony Evers. Crowley also said that he supports pausing existing developments while a statewide environmental review is conducted. artigo.texto: Grassroots coalition opposes proposed Mammoth Cave-area data center Residents cite sinkholes and endangered cave shrimp in fight against project What This Story Is About - A coalition of residents near Mammoth Cave is organizing to oppose a proposed data center they say would be built on land riddled with sinkholes and inhabited by an endangered cave shrimp species. Why It Matters - The project would sit near Angie Herald’s farm, and residents say it threatens the sinkhole-laden land, an endangered species, and the quiet character of the area. What Happens Next - The coalition’s next meeting is Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 5:30 p.m. at the Water Mill Restaurant, where members plan to continue organizing committees to build their case. For Context - Cave City Mayor, Dwayne Hatcher, declined to comment, citing ongoing litigation over the city’s data center moratorium. BARREN COUNTY, Ky. (WBKO) - A grassroots effort is growing to oppose a possible data center near Mammoth Cave. People who live closest to the proposed project say they are not going to back down. Angie Herald has spent nearly her whole life on the farm. “We’ve lived on this farm around 100 acres and we’ve lived there. Well, I’ve lived there almost all my life. I have a business. My dad has a business,” Herald said. A company wants to build a data center just across the railroad tracks from her property. Herald said the latest site plans put the project in her backyard. Neighbors form coalition Neighbor, Jessie Crabtree, helped form a coalition of concerned residents with one goal: stop the project entirely. “I mean, this is Angie’s home. Look at the property. It’s beautiful. Her home’s beautiful. It’s just peaceful. It’s quiet. I can’t even imagine a data center being there,” Crabtree said. The group says it has identified 37 sinkholes on the proposed site. Members are also pointing to an endangered species as part of their case. “We have two strategies. One is the cave shrimp, which is the 2025 cave animal of the year for the United States. And it’s an endangered species. It only lives only in Mammoth Cave in eight underground basins,” Crabtree said. Coalition builds support Crabtree said nearly 40 people showed up to the coalition’s first meeting. The group is now forming committees to continue building its case. “This is their home, their farmlands and so forth. And they spoke up and each one told their own story,” Crabtree said. The next coalition meeting is Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 5:30 p.m. at the Water Mill Restaurant. WBKO reached out to Cave City Mayor, Dwayne Hatcher. He said, “No comment,” citing ongoing litigation over the city’s data center moratorium. Reaction online has been mainly against the data center. However, some commenters say they don’t oppose data centers as long as utility costs don’t rise. Others say they would support one if it’s properly regulated. Copyright 2026 WBKO. artigo.texto: Weltec Biopower Launches Battery Storage Offering for Its 25th Anniversary The German biogas plant builder will present its new Weltec Battery Hub division in Hanover from 10 to 13 November, alongside biomethane projects in Spain and bioenergy plans in Australia. Weltec Biopower, a German biogas plant manufacturer based in Vechta, celebrates its 25th anniversary in 2026 and is expanding into battery-based electricity storage. The company will present its new offering, called Weltec Battery Hub, at the EnergyDecentral trade fair in Hanover from 10 to 13 November 2026, at booth H09 in Hall 25. The segment is also drawing interest from oil majors, as shown by TotalEnergies subsidiary Saft, which has launched solid-state battery production lines in Bordeaux. Weltec will also showcase its biogas and biomethane technologies, as well as slurry and digestate treatment. A storage offering backed by engineering services According to the company, Weltec Battery Hub centres on the supply of battery storage systems. On request, Weltec also supports customers with project development and planning for permit applications. Engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) services can be provided within the same framework. The group says customers can thus obtain both storage technology and implementation support from a single provider. Applications cited include industrial use, integration with solar photovoltaic and wind installations, and electricity trading. The systems could also contribute to peak shaving and microgrid stabilisation. 450 plants delivered in 27 countries since 2001 Weltec Biopower says it has delivered more than 450 bioenergy plants in 27 countries since its foundation in 2001. Its projects span Europe, the United States, South America, Asia and Australia. The company highlights its stainless steel technology and modular design, which allow it to adapt its plants to different feedstocks and site conditions. The portfolio includes stainless steel tanks, control systems, hygienisation solutions and feedstock shredding systems. Weltec also offers Weltec Blue Water, a slurry and digestate treatment process. According to the company, it reduces their volumes by around half while recovering water suitable for discharge, and is already in operation in several countries. Projects in Spain and Australia Among current projects, Weltec cites a biomethane plant north of Madrid, expected to generate up to 60 gigawatt-hours of renewable energy per year. That output would meet the needs of around 11,700 households, the company says. Weltec is also building a bioenergy plant for a vegetable processor in Queensland, Australia. Once fully developed, the plant could supply electricity to around 31,000 households, according to the company. At EnergyDecentral, its teams will detail these projects, services covering combined heat and power (CHP) units, mechanical equipment and biological processes, and options for the continued operation and future development of existing plants. Weltec Biopower is a member of the American Biogas Council, the Renewable Energy Association and the Biogasrat dezentrale Energien.

artigo.texto: Doug Jones campaigns in Eufaula, cites farming, health care, data centers Democratic gubernatorial nominee visits Barbour County ahead of Nov. 3 election EUFALA, Ala. (WTVM) - Alabama gubernatorial candidate Doug Jones made a stop in Eufaula as part of his campaign trail. Jones is the Democratic nominee running against Republican nominee Tommy Tuberville. Jones stopped in Barbour County as part of a push to reach rural communities. In a sit-down interview, Jones emphasized issues including affordability, health care and data centers. Agriculture and farming Jones said for rural areas like Eufaula and Barbour County, there are three pain points he hopes to address, including farmers and the agriculture business. He said farmers don’t want bailouts, they want markets. “They want to be able to sell their commodities and do it at a fair price so that they can make a living for themselves and their family,” Jones said. “So we are going to try to do everything we can and there are some programs we got that can help them I think with their costs of doing things help bring those costs down and put money back in their pockets.” Rural health care Jones said he hopes to improve rural health care. Jones believes the first step is expanding Medicaid. “I want to expand eligibility for Medicaid and work with the legislature to try to find the funding and I think we can find the funding,” Jones said. “That’s an investment in people and that’s an investment in the economy. If we did that it would be one of the biggest economic drivers this state has ever seen, billions of dollars that would be coming into the state.” Data centers Jones’ third biggest push, especially in rural Alabama, is calling for a one-year moratorium on data centers to examine their effects, come up with guardrails and get rid of tax abatements. “Nothing right now is on the books. Nothing about the tax abatements or eliminating them. Nothing about what these companies are going to be required to put back into communities,” Jones said. “The main thing is we need to get a moratorium, get the guardrails on there, and let every communities decide for themselves.” Jones said if elected as Alabama’s next governor, he plans to continue to hold town halls like the one in Eufaula as part of his push for transparency in government. artigo.texto: Over half of Indiana counties now restrict data centers The number of Indiana communities pausing or outright banning data center development has grown. About thirty communities had enacted some form of ban in July. Now, that number has increased to at least 50 counties — or over half — across the state. That’s according to the Indiana University Environmental Resilience Institute, which tracks the local regulations. The collected data shows 32 counties have passed moratoriums, 14 regulatory ordinances, and in four communities data centers are not permitted. At least one county — Marshall — has made that ban permanent. Read More: Madison County commissioners extend data center moratorium for full year “What we’re seeing that’s new but not really surprising since July is an increased number of moratoria, and also several of those moratoria becoming permanent decisions, whether that is a ban on data center development or an ordinance like an updated zoning code or other local policy,” said Therese Dorau, Assistant Director for Climate Policy and Implementation at the Institute. Some counties approved a limited time for temporary bans. Data centers are large facilities that house the computer servers behind cloud computing, streaming services and artificial intelligence. Because those servers run constantly and generate significant heat, the facilities can draw enormous amounts of electricity and water. Indiana lawmakers created policies to lure large data center developers to the state, including laws that enable tax breaks and other incentives. That has attracted large technology companies like Google, Amazon and Meta. These developments have drawn opposition in communities around Indiana and across the U.S. due to concerns about electricity, water and land. Critics have also questioned environmental impacts like noise and air pollution, as well as whether the economic benefits such as long-term jobs will actually benefit local communities. Some data projects are making moves to connect to the electrical grid. Earlier this month, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approved a $737.3 million plan by Central Indiana utility AES Indiana to power a 390-megawatt Google data center project in Monrovia. The companies said Google will cover 100% of the costs, but critics are concerned that $74 million in transmission upgrades will be passed to customers. The IU institute created an updated resource with information about what science and research says about some of these topics. “In my opinion, a responsible use of a moratorium is to take a pause. It’s not to make a permanent decision, but really, it’s a way to say we’re going to put a timeframe on which our government is going to do more in-depth research about what is right for our community,” Dorau said. artigo.texto: There are now 170 megapacks in place alongside the onshore converter station for Ørsted’s Hornsea 3 Offshore Wind Farm, near Norwich, Norfolk. Each is the length of a classic Routemaster London bus but weighs the same as five buses. The system, known as Iceni after the Norfolk-based warrior tribe of the Roman era, will have a capacity of 600 MWh (and a 300 MW power rating). This is equivalent to the daily power consumption of 80,000 UK homes. The Iceni team comprises specialists from Ørsted, Hitachi Energy, Knights Brown & Tesla working together on this first-of-its-kind project. What makes this BESS unique is the split layout of the site with the two areas, separated by the Hornsea 3 Onshore Converter station, linked by 18 x 33 kV cables, each over 600 meters in length. In addition, the shared grid connection point with Hornsea 3 has added additional technical complexity over a stand-alone connection point to the National Grid. The project is now in the final stages of the mechanical and electrical installation, with the 33 kV cross-site cables currently being installed and terminated. The first stage of commissioning and testing is well underway, and preparations are being made for energization of the BESS Transformer. When completed, the battery energy storage system will be one of the largest in Europe. Beatrice d’Eufemia, Project Manager for Iceni BESS at Ørsted, said: “It’s a milestone moment for Ørsted that construction is now complete on our first large-scale battery energy storage system in the UK. “The system will make the best use of renewable energy produced in the UK as when electricity generation exceeds demand, the excess can be stored and then used when demand is greater, helping balance the grid, and lower electricity costs for everyone.” Richard Swann, Construction Manager for Iceni BESS at Ørsted, said: “It’s a real testament to the hard work, dedication and cooperation of the team from many different organizations that the construction has been completed successfully.” David Shillabeer, Head of Transmission & Distribution, at Knights Brown, said: “Reaching this milestone is a significant achievement for everyone involved in the Iceni project. Delivering a battery energy storage system of this scale has required close collaboration between Ørsted, Knights Brown and the many other organizations that have contributed to its success. “Beyond the engineering, the scheme has enabled us to invest in local people, develop skills and create opportunities across Norfolk and the wider region. We are proud to have played our part in an important project that will support the UK’s transition to a more resilient, low-carbon energy system, while leaving a positive legacy for the communities in which we work.”

artigo.texto: Partners with Muehlbauer Group for Production Equipment SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- QuantumScape Corporation (NASDAQ: QS), a global leader in solid-state lithium-metal battery technology, today announced a planned 100 megawatt-hour (MWh) capacity cell production line to meet demand for solid-state batteries from markets including AI data centers, aerospace and defense. To develop this line, QS has partnered with Muehlbauer Group, a leading German automation and manufacturing technology company, as an ecosystem provider of cell assembly equipment. QS is currently demonstrating scalable production of solid-state batteries using its highly automated Eagle Line pilot facility in San Jose. Muehlbauer evaluated the Eagle Line processes and developed design enhancements to bring the technology to mass production; engineering work on higher-throughput processes and equipment for the new line is underway. Start of cell production is targeted for 2028. "We are excited to welcome Muehlbauer to the QS ecosystem,” said Dr. Siva Sivaram, president and CEO of QS. "Muehlbauer is an experienced and respected global player in manufacturing automation and battery equipment, and they’ve shown top-tier system integration capability, impressive engineering depth, and the scalability mindset necessary to bring our groundbreaking technology to the gigawatt-hour scale. They join a world-class ecosystem of technology partners as we bring solid-state batteries into mass production.” "The Eagle Line proved to us that QuantumScape’s solid-state technology is ready to scale to the next level,” said Josef Markus Mühlbauer, CEO of Muehlbauer Group. "We have been working on-site with QS in San Jose to develop a scale-up plan built on the foundation of the Eagle Line. With decades of experience in turning innovative technologies into scalable production processes, we are proud to be a preferred partner within QuantumScape’s ecosystem and to contribute our expertise to the mission of revolutionizing energy storage and enabling a more sustainable future.” About QuantumScape Corporation QuantumScape is on a mission to revolutionize energy storage to enable a sustainable future. The company’s next-generation solid-state lithium-metal battery technology is designed to enable greater energy density, faster charging and enhanced safety to support the transition away from legacy energy sources toward a lower carbon future. For more information, visit www.quantumscape.com. About Muehlbauer Group With around 4,500 employees at 40 locations worldwide and 45 years of experience, the Muehlbauer Group has developed into one of the most advanced suppliers of complete production solutions. The company has achieved a leading position in the semiconductor industry with its unique die sorting technology and serves 90% of worldwide demand for RFID. More than 90,000 machines and systems have already been installed worldwide, and the Group specialises in high-precision, high-speed assembly systems, even in cleanroom environments. For more information, visit www.muehlbauer.de. artigo.texto: Peak Energy Raises $108 Million to Expand Sodium-Ion Battery Manufacturing The funding will support domestic manufacturing, customer orders, and expansion into the data center market October 23, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights Peak Energy, a sodium-ion battery manufacturer, has raised $108 million in an oversubscribed Series B funding round led by General Motors Ventures to expand its sodium-ion battery manufacturing operations. Maverick Silicon, Infinite Capital, Eclipse, Xora Innovation, and LG Technology Ventures also participated in the funding round. The company, which develops passively cooled sodium-ion battery energy storage systems, will use the funds to expand domestic manufacturing, fulfill more than $1 billion in existing customer orders, and enter the data center market. “We spent a lot of time looking at the growing power requirements around AI infrastructure, and it became clear that energy storage is going to be an increasingly important part of the solution. Peak is taking a differentiated approach to sodium-ion, with a focus on the full system from chemistry and design through manufacturing and deployment at scale,” said Kenneth Safar, Managing Director at Maverick Silicon. “The combination of strong technical progress, growing customer engagement and a large end market gives Peak an opportunity to build a defining platform in energy storage. We’re excited to support the team as they scale.” The funding follows the company’s announcement of a partnership with General Motors in June to jointly develop sodium-ion battery cells for energy storage applications. The partnership will also draw on General Motors’ U.S. battery cell industrialization expertise to support Peak Energy’s manufacturing plans. In July, Peak Energy announced a 4 GWh battery manufacturing facility in Sacramento, California. The facility is scheduled to begin production in the first quarter of 2027. In 2024, the company secured $55 million in a Series A funding round led by Xora Innovation, Temasek’s Early-Stage deep-tech investing platform. This round also involved investors, including Lachy Groom, Tishman Speyer, TechEnergy Ventures, Doral Energy-Tech Ventures, DETV-Scania Invest, and existing investor Eclipse and strategic partner TDK Ventures. According to Mercom’s 1H 2026 Funding and M&A for Energy Storage report, VC funding for energy storage companies in 1H 2026 totaled $1.6 billion across 51 deals, representing a 6% YoY decline compared to the $1.7 billion raised across 36 deals in 1H 2025.

artigo.texto: New Update 00:00/ 00:00 Bondada Engineering Limited, a Hyderabad-based engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) company, has received a Letter of Intent (LOI) from Gujarat Industries Power Company Limited (GIPCL) for the development of a 20 MW/120 MWh Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Energy Storage System (VRFB BESS) at GIPCL’s 165 MW natural gas power plant complex in Vadodara, Gujarat. The project includes a 10-year operations and maintenance (O&M) contract. The project marks a significant milestone in Bondada Engineering’s expansion into advanced energy storage technologies. According to the company, the project is India’s largest grid-scale Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Energy Storage System, further strengthening its position in the rapidly growing battery energy storage sector. The scope of work includes the engineering, procurement and construction of the 120 MWh VRFB-based energy storage system, along with operations and maintenance for 10 years. The project is scheduled for completion within 18 months from the receipt of the Notice of Award (NOA). Dr. Bondada Raghavendra Rao, Chairman & Managing Director Said “This project marks an important step in our expansion into advanced energy storage solutions. As India increases its renewable energy capacity, energy storage will play a key role in ensuring reliable and efficient power supply. We are pleased to work with GIPCL on this project and look forward to strengthening our capabilities in long-duration energy storage while contributing to India’s clean energy goals.” Vanadium Redox Flow Battery technology is gaining attention for its potential in long-duration energy storage, offering the ability to store and discharge energy over extended periods. The Government of India has set a target of deploying approximately 236 GWh of battery energy storage systems by 2030, highlighting the scale of infrastructure development required to support the country’s energy transition. The GIPCL project complements Bondada Engineering’s existing renewable energy EPC portfolio and reflects the company’s strategy to expand into emerging infrastructure segments. With capabilities across renewable energy, telecom infrastructure and other EPC sectors, the company is looking to participate in the development of next-generation energy infrastructure. Building on its experience with the 100 MWh Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Energy Storage System project for NTPC Renewable Energy at Khavda, Gujarat, this new 20 MW/120 MWh project for GIPCL further strengthens Bondada Engineering’s presence in long-duration energy storage. Through these projects, the company aims to expand its capabilities in advanced energy storage technologies and contribute to the development of a more reliable, sustainable and resilient power ecosystem in India.

artigo.texto: Can Evaporative Cooling in Data Centers Still Make Sense? Evaporative cooling is hard to defend on water-use grounds, but some operators still choose it for its lower upfront cost, higher efficiency, and dry-climate performance. Water use has surged to the top of the list of community concerns around new data center development. In many markets, it now rivals power demand as a flashpoint for residents and local officials evaluating new facilities. Stories about data centers consuming enormous volumes of water circulate widely in neighborhood forums and on social media and have become a common argument against new construction, especially in drought-prone regions. The concern is not unfounded. According to a report by Media Analytics Ltd., a data center with a 1 MW IT load using evaporative cooling can consume roughly 20,000 to 50,000 gallons of water per day. At that rate, a 10 MW facility could use 200,000 to 500,000 gallons per day, a 100 MW site could consume 2 million to 5 million gallons per day, and a 1 GW facility could use 20 million to 50 million gallons per day, depending on design and operating conditions. With numbers like that, the obvious question is: why would any operator still choose evaporative cooling? The answer is that while evaporative systems are water-intensive, they still offer meaningful advantages in cost and energy performance under the right conditions. Evaporative cooling remains widely used because it can reject large amounts of heat more efficiently than dry cooling alone. In a typical setup, heat from the data center is transferred to water circulating through a cooling tower or a similar heat-rejection system. As a portion of that water evaporates, it carries heat away, and the remaining water is collected and recirculated. It is the same basic principle the human body uses when sweat evaporates and cools the skin. The tradeoff, of course, is water consumption. The Tradeoff: Water Savings vs. Energy Efficiency Matt Green, CEO of HVAC firm Brucker, said one reason open-loop evaporative systems remain in the market is simple: first cost. “Now, there are some reasons why open-loop cooling still exists, and it’s really driven in many cases by upfront first cost, so an open cooling tower is going to be less expensive [than a closed-loop system],” he said. Green estimates that an open-loop system can cost 60% to 70% less upfront than a closed-loop alternative with comparable heat-dissipation capacity. That difference is largely driven by the amount of copper, aluminum, and other materials required in a dry cooler used in a closed-loop design. Over the life of the system, however, Green argues that the economics shift. In data centers with long operating hours, he said, closed-loop systems have a lower total lifecycle cost than evaporative cooling systems once water use and ongoing operating expenses are factored in. Brendan Mark, CEO of Capture H2O, a cooling and heating water treatment provider, makes the case from the other side of the ledger. He argues that evaporative cooling retains an important advantage in energy efficiency. “Water-cooled systems, as opposed to closed-loop air-cooled systems, are about 25% to 40% more efficient from an energy perspective,” he said. “So, there’s a tradeoff. Yes, you are using less water, but you are using more energy.” That tension between water and power is central to the debate. A closed-loop system may sharply reduce evaporation, but it typically requires more fan power and can be less effective at rejecting heat during extreme conditions. Evaporative systems, by contrast, can deliver better thermal performance with lower energy use, particularly when ambient conditions favor evaporation. Ashlesa Mohapatra, quality manager at ServerLIFT LLC, which makes equipment for moving data center hardware, said operators should evaluate the full design picture before choosing a cooling architecture. That includes the facility’s power profile, capital budget, climate, and long-term operational impacts. “You should look at the amount of power that your data center is taking,” Mohapatra said. “You should look at how much money you’re willing to invest in worn-out hardware due to the evaporative systems that you’re installing.” Mohapatra also noted that while the cooling water is not in direct contact with IT hardware, water-based systems still introduce maintenance considerations and mechanical wear that should be accounted for in total cost calculations. Mohapatra estimates evaporative cooling can use 10% to 35% less electricity during peak summer conditions than closed-loop alternatives, though the exact savings depend on climate and system design. For that reason, she does not treat the choice as absolute. Closed-loop systems are strong on water conservation, but evaporative systems can still make sense when energy efficiency is the higher priority. Green is more skeptical. In his opinion, if an operator has the space and can absorb the higher upfront cost, there is little reason not to move to closed-loop systems. “If you’ve got the space and you’ve got the additional capital that you can spend upfront to get the return on investment over the life cycle of the product, [non-closed-loop] technology really should not be used in this application,” he said. He also argues that many companies stick with evaporative technology because it is familiar. “A lot of individuals stick with what they know because it’s worked in the past, and they don’t want to absorb a perceived risk of changing technologies on something that’s been proven to work for them,” Green said. Mark, however, defends evaporative technology on performance grounds. “In a closed-loop system, you’re literally blowing air over a set of tubes that has some sort of fluid running through it,” Mark said. “That tube is not going to be able to reject the heat as effectively as evaporative cooling.” Climate and Geography Change the Equation Mohapatra takes a more situational vi

artigo.texto: Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. O Brasil acaba de transformar em lei uma política de incentivos para ampliar a instalação de data centers no país. O Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) chega em um momento de forte crescimento da demanda por capacidade computacional, impulsionada pela inteligência artificial, e encontra um país com atributos importantes para disputar esses investimentos, entre eles uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável com possibilidade de expansão a custos competitivos. A oportunidade é evidente, mas empreendimentos que concentram centenas de megawatts de demanda contínua também exigem pensar em como o sistema elétrico brasileiro será capaz de absorver essa nova carga sem comprometer a expansão do sistema nem implicar custos aos demais consumidores. Um dos pontos de atenção do Redata está na exigência de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão. A regulamentação dirá o que cabe nessa segunda categoria, mas a possibilidade de incluir o gás natural traz uma contradição importante. O gás natural entra nessa discussão por uma questão de operação. Data centers funcionam 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana, com uma carga praticamente constante e exigências elevadas de continuidade do fornecimento. Ao mesmo tempo, a expansão do parque elétrico instalado no país tem se dado principalmente por meio de fontes variáveis, como solar e eólica. Essa combinação de demanda firme e oferta variável aumenta a necessidade de flexibilidade do sistema elétrico, hoje atendida em parte justamente pela geração térmica despachável a gás. O processo depende ainda da expansão das redes de transmissão. Tais reforços podem levar de cinco a dez anos, enquanto um data center pode ser implantado em prazo muito menor, da ordem de um ano e meio. A discussão sobre flexibilidade, portanto, não pode ser separada das condições da rede e do planejamento de sua expansão. O estudo do Instituto E+ Metodologia Integrada para Transição Energética e Desenvolvimento Industrial no Brasil, prestes a ser concluído, simula a entrada de data centers, projetos de aço de baixa emissão e processamento de terras raras no sistema elétrico entre 2029 e 2039. O estudo mostra que a capacidade da rede é determinante para a localização e a escala desses investimentos. Além de geração disponível, é preciso que a infraestrutura elétrica tenha capacidade para atender a nova carga no ponto em que ela será conectada. Nas simulações, Campinas apresenta melhores condições para grandes data centers em conexões à rede de 500 kV, enquanto, em Fortaleza, a estrutura de 230 kV oferece as condições mais favoráveis analisadas. Em níveis inferiores de tensão, a capacidade para receber grandes cargas diminui. No Pecém, a concentração de projetos eletrointensivos pode levar diferentes empreendimentos a disputar capacidade de conexão antes da entrada em operação das obras de expansão previstas para a rede. A expansão da transmissão, por sua vez, pode demorar muito além do prazo de implantação de um data center, o que torna a capacidade de conexão uma variável cada vez mais relevante para a localização e o cronograma desses investimentos. A contratação de energia deve assegurar adicionalidade, contribuindo para ampliar a oferta de energia limpa e competitiva necessária ao atendimento da nova demanda. A entrada da dessas cargas requer expansão da oferta de baixa emissão e dos recursos de flexibilidade, sem que os custos sistêmicos associados a esses empreendimentos recaiam sobre os demais consumidores. Por fim, o Redata acerta ao associar incentivos à instalação de data centers no país a contrapartidas em pesquisa e desenvolvimento, capacidade computacional para o mercado brasileiro e eficiência no uso de recursos. Mas a escala do consumo elétrico exige que a política pública olhe também para a produtividade energética. Afinal, a atração de data centers precisa caminhar junto com o planejamento elétrico de uma maneira favorável à sociedade brasileira como um todo. Os incentivos devem contribuir para ampliar a oferta de energia limpa e competitiva, assegurar capacidade de rede e gerar valor para o país, preservando as vantagens energéticas que tornam o Brasil atraente para esses investimentos. Clauber Leite é diretor de Energia Sustentável e Bioeconomia do Instituto E+ Transição Energética.

artigo.texto: O crescimento do consumo de energia no Paraguai, que já vem reduzindo o excedente da hidrelétrica binacional de Itaipu destinado ao Brasil, poderá ganhar uma nova demanda com a instalação de um data center anunciado nesta semana pelo governo dos Estados Unidos. O empreendimento começará a operar em 2027 e poderá alcançar 280 MW no longo prazo, potência que, se utilizada continuamente, equivaleria a quase 25% da energia da parcela paraguaia recebida pelo Brasil em 2025. O projeto se insere em um movimento já considerado nos estudos de planejamento energético brasileiro. A usina binacional, que tem 14 mil MW de potência instalados, tem a geração de energia dividida de forma igual entre Brasil e Paraguai. O país vizinho, porém, historicamente não utiliza toda a capacidade disponível, e o Brasil é obrigado a comprar o excedente por um preço acordado entre as alas diplomáticas de seus respectivos governos. Após décadas de estagnação, o consumo de eletricidade no Paraguai tem crescido, ancorado, principalmente, na chegada de data centers voltados para mineração de criptomoedas, atraídos pelo baixo preço da energia. Segundo dados do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), entre 2023 e 2025, o fornecimento de Itaipu ao Paraguai aumentou 32%, enquanto a energia da parcela paraguaia destinada ao Brasil caiu 53%. O anúncio feito pelo governo dos Estados Unidos marca um novo momento dessa expansão do consumo de energia do Paraguai. A americana Crusoe divulgou nesta quinta-feira, 22 de outubro, detalhes da parceria com a paraguaia Araico para desenvolver o empreendimento. A primeira etapa deverá entrar em operação em meados de 2027, com expansão até 106 MW de capacidade de tecnologia da informação (TI), cerca de 10% da energia excedente de Itaipu enviada ao Brasil ano passado. No longo prazo, a empresa prevê a possibilidade de ampliação até os cerca de 280 MW, ou 23,5% do total exportado em 2025. “Esse montante é pequeno, mas pode ser o começo de um novo negócio para Itaipu, o que, naturalmente, pode aumentar a utilização pelo Paraguai dessa energia, com implicações para o Brasil”, disse Luiz Barroso, CEO da PSR, à MegaWhat. Para Barroso, a atração de novos data centers poderá, no longo prazo, levar o Paraguai a utilizar toda a sua parcela da produção de Itaipu, eliminando o excedente atualmente destinado ao Brasil. Brasil já considera redução no planejamento Segundo dados do MME, o volume de energia da parcela paraguaia comercializado no Brasil caiu de 22,203 milhões de MWh em 2023 para 12,973 milhões de MWh em 2024 e 10,455 milhões de MWh em 2025. No mesmo período, o fornecimento de Itaipu ao Paraguai aumentou de 19,515 milhões de MWh para 25,768 milhões de MWh. A geração total da hidrelétrica passou de 83,879 milhões de MWh em 2023 para 72,879 milhões de MWh em 2025. Segundo o presidente da EPE, Thiago Prado, a redução do excedente destinado ao Brasil já é considerada nos estudos de planejamento. Ele citou como exemplo a decisão de revitalizar inicialmente apenas um dos dois bipolos do sistema de transmissão em corrente contínua que transporta a energia de Itaipu entre Foz do Iguaçu (PR) e Ibiúna (SP). A modernização completa das conversoras do Bipolo 1 foi priorizada, enquanto a decisão sobre uma intervenção equivalente no Bipolo 2 ficou condicionada à evolução da demanda paraguaia e à disponibilidade de energia para o Brasil. Embora o Brasil hoje tenha uma sobra estrutural de energia, a eletricidade de Itaipu contribui com o atendimento dos picos de consumo, no fim do dia, quando não há geração solar. Por isso, a redução do envio de eletricidade do Paraguai contribuiu com a contratação do leilão de reserva de capacidade (LRCap) de março, voltado para termelétricas e hidrelétricas, e também vai ter reflexos na demanda do certame de baterias previsto para dezembro. Quanto custa a energia de Itaipu Pelo Tratado de Itaipu, assinado em 1973, Brasil e Paraguai têm direito a metade da energia produzida pela hidrelétrica. A legislação brasileira, por sua vez, determina que a energia seja destinada às distribuidoras das regiões Sul, Sudeste e Centro-Oeste. Em 2026, a energia da hidrelétrica tem representado cerca de R$ 220/MWh nos reajustes das distribuidoras, abaixo do custo médio de aquisição do país, estimado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) em R$ 342/MWh neste ano. O aumento do consumo no Paraguai, portanto, tem potencial de pressionar as tarifas de energia dessas distribuidoras para cima, mas o impacto efetivo depende de uma série de questões, incluindo o preço de contratação dos leilões. Por outro lado, o encerramento do acordo tarifário firmado entre Brasil e Paraguai tem potencial para reduzir as tarifas. Desde o fim do pagamento da dívida contraída para construção da usina, em 2023, há expectativas de redução da tarifa da usina, mas isso tem esbarrado nas negociações com o Paraguai sobre a compra da energia excedente. A revisão do Anexo C do Tratado de Itaipu, que estabelece as bases financeiras e de prestação dos serviços de eletricidade da hidrelétrica, deveria ter sido concluída até dezembro de 2024, mas o prazo não foi cumprido. As negociações foram suspensas pelo Paraguai em abril de 2025, após denúncias de espionagem envolvendo a Agência Brasileira de Inteligência (Abin), e retomadas posteriormente. Em 2024, os países chegaram a um acordo tarifário, válido até 31 de dezembro de 2026. O entendimento estabeleceu que, a partir de janeiro de 2027, o Paraguai deverá contratar toda a potência necessária ao seu consumo e que a tarifa de Itaipu deverá refletir apenas os custos estritos de operação, sem despesas discricionárias. Também ficou prevista uma mudança na comercialização da energia paraguaia não consumida internamente, que poderá ser vendida livremente no mercado brasileiro, em substituição ao atual modelo de cessão. artigo.texto: STACK data center projected to generate $48 million in revenue Pittsylvania County, Va. (WSET) — The proposed STACK data center project in Berry Hill is drawing opposition from Danville and Pittsylvania County residents concerned about its potential impact on the community. A protest in Danville on Monday highlighted concerns about the development’s projected energy use, water consumption and possible noise. The project is expected to include 21 buildings and use up to 3,000 megawatts of power. Plans call for the development to span approximately 3,000 acres at the megasite off Berry Hill Road. Residents have questioned how the project could affect utility bills and the environment. SEE ALSO: Data centers become midterm minefield as candidates scramble to answer voter backlash Vic Ingram, chairman of the Regional Facility Authority, pushed back against some of those concerns, saying residents should not expect higher utility bills because of the development. When asked about concerns over water use and the environment, Ingram criticized the information circulating among opponents. “What’s propaganda? You know, I think it was like seven folks. I didn’t see anybody that I knew that lived in this area,” Ingram said. “The propaganda by those protests, as well as what you read on social media, is in part generated by people that just really don’t know.” Meanwhile, Pittsylvania County’s director of economic development says the project is now expected to generate $48 million in revenue, with that figure projected to increase. The project’s first building is expected to be fully operational by 2028.

artigo.texto: New certification program supports flexible system configurations and helps reduce complexity when modular installations undergo certification and code authority review. - The certification addresses modular DC energy storage systems that connect evaluated subsystems, including power conversion systems. - Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database for verification by code authorities. - Evaluations address electrical safety, communication and interoperability between the system and identified subsystems. NORTHBROOK, Ill., October 20, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--UL Solutions (NYSE: ULS), a global leader in applied safety science, today announced a new certification pathway designed to help manufacturers of modular direct current (DC) energy storage systems, used for backup power for critical infrastructure and grid-scale energy storage, bring systems to market with greater flexibility and clearer documentation for installation reviews. An energy storage system captures energy so it can be stored for later use and provides electricity to the grid or to a building's wiring system. A battery energy storage system can help save energy by reducing the number of times electricity must be converted from one form to another, including conversion between alternating current (AC) and DC. It can also simplify the connection to solar panels, backup generators and other equipment. Many of these systems use a modular design, allowing manufacturers to combine different components for a project. However, confirming that those components work safely together can make certification and installation reviews more complex. The new certification program offers manufacturers an alternative to seeking a full matched-assembly system listing at the outset. When a compatible subsystem is identified, the resulting certification documentation can provide manufacturers, developers and code authorities with information about the evaluated configuration. "Modular energy storage designs require a clear way to demonstrate how the system and its critical subsystems work together," said Wesley Kwok, vice president and general manager of the Energy and Industrial Automation group at UL Solutions. "This certification program gives manufacturers, developers and code authorities documented information about evaluated system combinations while supporting a more flexible approach to DC energy storage system design." Through the new certification program, UL Solutions evaluates the DC energy storage system with each identified subsystem to applicable requirements of UL 9540, the Standard for Energy Storage Systems and Equipment. The evaluation addresses electrical, communication and interoperability between the system and its evaluated subsystems. Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database under the DC energy storage system certification category, allowing code authorities to verify evaluated combinations.

artigo.texto: A Greenvolt celebrou um acordo para a venda de dois projetos de armazenamento de energia em baterias na Polónia, à sociedade A&R Investments, por 391,5 milhões de euros, segundo um comunicado ao mercado. Na nota, divulgada pela Comissão do Mercado de Valores Mobiliários (CMVM), a empresa informou que a sua subsidiária Greenvolt Power “celebrou um acordo para a venda de dois projetos de armazenamento de energia em baterias na Polónia, com uma potência total de 400 MW [megawatts] e uma capacidade de armazenamento total de 1,6 GWh [gigawatts/hora], à A&R Investments, um veículo de investimento sediado em Malta”. De acordo com o comunicado, o valor da operação ascende a 391,5 milhões de euros, dos quais 311,5 milhões de euros correspondem a um valor fixo e até 80 milhões de euros a um pagamento adicional, “cujo montante dependerá do momento em que os projetos obtenham a autorização para prestar serviços de equilíbrio à rede elétrica”. Segundo a empresa, “os projetos Ełk e Turośń Kościelna, situados no nordeste da Polónia, já se encontram construídos e têm, cada um, 200 MW de potência e 800 MWh de capacidade de armazenamento”. A Greenvolt indicou ainda que estes projetos “têm receitas contratadas a longo prazo, através de contratos de 17 anos no mercado de capacidade polaco, a partir de 2028, e de um contrato com a Statkraft” para gestão das baterias e “venda da sua flexibilidade nos mercados de eletricidade”. A empresa referiu que a conclusão da operação está prevista até ao final de 2026, sujeita à verificação das condições habituais. “Esta venda enquadra-se na estratégia de rotação de ativos da Greenvolt, que consiste em vender integralmente a maioria dos projetos que desenvolve, realizando o valor criado e reinvestindo o capital em novos projetos, e em manter os restantes projetos detidos a 100%”, rematou.

artigo.texto: Publicidade As vendas da Tesla na Europa dispararam em setembro de 2026, indicando que a montadora de veículos elétricos de Elon Musk segue ganhando espaço em uma região onde concorrentes chineses também avançam rapidamente. Os novos emplacamentos de carros da Tesla – usados como sinal de vendas – saltaram 72,5% na comparação anual, para 68.776 unidades, nos mercados da União Europeia, Reino Unido, Islândia, Liechtenstein, Noruega e Suíça, segundo a Associação Europeia de Fabricantes de Automóveis (ACEA). O ritmo acelerou de forma clara em relação a agosto, quando o aumento havia sido de apenas 4% – mês que costuma ser mais fraco para registros, já que muitas concessionárias na Europa fecham nas férias de verão do Hemisfério Norte. O avanço sugere que consumidores europeus continuam aderindo à Tesla apesar da concorrência mais intensa, sobretudo de marcas chinesas. No mesmo recorte, a ACEA informou que montadoras chinesas registraram altas expressivas. Os emplacamentos da BYD quase dobraram, em salto de 99%, para 49.953 veículos. A SAIC Motor avançou quase 24%, para 41.987 unidades, e a Leapmotor teve alta superior a quatro vezes, para 14.594 veículos. Em contraste, grupos tradicionais europeus mostraram desempenho mais fraco: a Volkswagen registrou queda de 2,9%, para 308.474 unidades, e a Renault recuou 0,7%, para 114.726. O desempenho da Tesla ocorre enquanto a empresa busca ampliar aprovações para seu sistema de direção assistida Full Self-Driving (FSD) na União Europeia. Em abril de 2026, a Holanda foi o primeiro país do bloco a autorizar o sistema em funções como mudança de faixa e navegação em torno de veículos e objetos. Segundo a própria Tesla, o FSD não torna o carro totalmente autônomo e deve ser usado com o motorista totalmente atento. Desde então, países como Lituânia, Estônia e Dinamarca reconheceram a autorização holandesa, permitindo que a Tesla disponibilize o FSD nesses mercados enquanto autoridades europeias avaliam um pedido para expandir a autorização para todo o bloco. Em setembro, o mercado europeu de veículos 100% elétricos a bateria cresceu quase 60%, segundo a ACEA. Os emplacamentos de híbridos subiram 5,3%, enquanto as de híbridos plug-in avançaram 24%. No total, os registros de automóveis de passageiros aumentaram 10% na Europa como um todo e 9,3% na União Europeia, com alta de 9% na Alemanha, 12% na França e 9,8% na Itália. Fonte: Dow Jones Newswires. artigo.texto: Equinix abre cinco centros para testar resfriamento líquido em data centers Unidades na Europa, Ásia e Oceania permitem testar infraestrutura de IA em operação; empresa prevê novos centros em 2027. A Equinix anunciou a abertura de cinco centros destinados à validação de infraestrutura de IA com resfriamento líquido. Localizadas em Frankfurt, Londres, Paris, Osaka e Sydney, as instalações permitem que empresas avaliem servidores, sistemas de refrigeração e cargas de trabalho de IA antes de ampliar sua capacidade computacional. Denominada Equinix Enhanced Performance Innovation Centers (EPIC), a rede funciona dentro de data centers ativos da companhia. Os ambientes foram desenvolvidos para atender à demanda por equipamentos de alta densidade, incluindo plataformas com GPUs e CPUs utilizadas em aplicações de treinamento e inferência de IA. A iniciativa também prevê a participação de fabricantes de equipamentos e parceiros tecnológicos na avaliação de configurações de infraestrutura, com acompanhamento das equipes técnicas da Equinix. Centros funcionam dentro de data centers ativos As cinco unidades estão instaladas nos data centers LD5, em Londres; PA10, em Paris; FR6, em Frankfurt; OS3, em Osaka; e SY5, em Sydney. Nesses ambientes, os clientes poderão avaliar diferentes configurações de resfriamento líquido e sua integração com servidores, sistemas elétricos e demais componentes necessários à operação de equipamentos de alta densidade. Os testes serão realizados em condições operacionais, permitindo verificar o comportamento das soluções antes de sua adoção em instalações de maior porte. As atividades incluem a execução de cargas de trabalho de inteligência artificial e a identificação de requisitos técnicos relacionados à operação e manutenção da infraestrutura. Segundo a Equinix, as configurações disponíveis e os fabricantes participantes poderão variar entre os centros, de acordo com as características de cada instalação. O programa também permitirá que equipes corporativas trabalhem com especialistas da companhia e fornecedores de equipamentos durante a avaliação das tecnologias. Empresa amplia programa de validação de infraestrutura O EPIC dá continuidade a iniciativas de testes desenvolvidas pela Equinix desde 2022, quando a companhia anunciou sua primeira Co-Innovation Facility, destinada à avaliação de novas tecnologias em colaboração com parceiros. Em 2024, a empresa lançou os Solution Validation Centers, voltados à validação de arquiteturas de infraestrutura e ambientes distribuídos. O novo programa concentra essas atividades em sistemas de resfriamento líquido e processamento de alta densidade. A Criteo está entre as empresas que utilizaram ambientes de validação da Equinix para avaliar tecnologias de refrigeração antes de ampliar sua infraestrutura distribuída de inteligência artificial. Segundo Matthieu Blumberg, vice-presidente sênior de Engenharia de Infraestrutura, Segurança e TI Interna e CISO da Criteo, a companhia realizou testes para compreender os requisitos operacionais do resfriamento líquido antes de incorporá-lo aos seus ambientes de processamento. A experiência foi apresentada pela Equinix como exemplo de utilização de seus recursos de validação. Novas unidades estão previstas para 2027 A Equinix pretende ampliar a rede de centros EPIC em 2027, mas ainda não divulgou a quantidade de novas instalações nem os países que receberão as próximas unidades. Segundo Brian Stein, vice-presidente sênior de Produtos e Serviços de Infraestrutura da companhia, o programa busca permitir que as empresas testem e validem configurações de resfriamento líquido antes de iniciar projetos de maior escala. Os ambientes poderão ser visitados por empresas interessadas mediante contato com a equipe comercial da Equinix. A companhia também disponibiliza informações sobre o programa em seu site. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: Trending LORDSTOWN – In a unanimous opinion, the Ohio Supreme Court ruled Tuesday that Lordstown officials were within their rights to stop processing the site-plan review requested by a Bristolville 25 developer, which was the first step toward obtaining a permit to construct four three-story data centers and ancillary structures in an area of the Trumbull County village zoned for industrial use. Last year, village officials imposed a moratorium after Bristolville 25 had issued a permit request with the village planning/ zoning office. Mayor Jackie Woodward said she learned of the court’s decision Tuesday. “This is a pretty significant victory not only for Lordstown but all the municipalities in Ohio who want to maintain the ability to decide and do what is best for their local communities. This sets a precedent for other communities dealing with the same situation with data centers. It allows each community to decide what they want and what is best for their local area.” The court’s decision indicates that Lordstown does not have to complete a site-plan review for a proposed data center that was submitted days before the village imposed a moratorium on data centers. In November 2025, Lordstown passed an ordinance banning data centers within the corporate boundaries. In January 2026, the village repealed the total ban and replaced it with a six-month moratorium on data center construction, which was set to expire July 4. Before its expiration, the council extended the moratorium through the remainder of 2026. Bristolville 25 initiated the first step in October 2025 under Lordstown's codified ordinances to construct the data centers and was notified the next day by the village planning and zoning administrator that a ban on data centers was pending before the village council. Two weeks later, the village council adopted the ban, which it later converted to a moratorium on data centers. Bristolville sought a writ of mandamus from the Supreme Court to compel the village to follow its site plan review process and act upon it under the village's pre-moratorium ordinances. The company argued the village must follow the zoning law in effect on the day the company submitted its plan, which at that time did not prohibit data centers. The court ruling stated that Bristolville's arguments may have prompted a duty for the village to act on the request had the company completed all the steps required to apply for a zoning permit. Because the company had not completed the required preliminary steps to apply for a permit, the village was under no obligation to consider its proposal. Bristolville purchased land from BHGH Properties in February 2025 to construct the data center complex. Under village law, an applicant for a zoning permit for new construction must undergo a site plan review overseen by the village zoning and planning office. Village officials submit a final site plan review for approval by the village's planning and zoning commission. If the commission approves the site plan, then a developer can file for a zoning permit. No construction can begin until a zoning permit is issued. Bristolville delivered its draft site plan to begin the permitting process in October 2025. The village planning and zoning administrator responded, notifying Bristolville about the pending ban, and stated the office could not begin the site plan review until the village council decided on the ban. Bristolville responded by asking the planning and zoning office to proceed because, at that time, data centers were still permitted under village law. Village Solicitor Matt Ries, who reviewed the draft site plan, notified Bristolville that the village officials were proceeding with the site plan, but indicated that, based on the newly enacted ban, the proposal would likely be prohibited. Once the ban was transformed into a moratorium, the village suspended any further review of Bristolville's plan. While the moratorium was in effect, the village's obligations to conduct site-plan reviews or to act on any application for a permit for data-center construction were suspended. Bristolville said the company then asked the Supreme Court to order the village to move forward with the review. Because it submitted its site plan for review before the moratorium, Bristolville argued that the village had a legal duty to proceed with the review. The court stated that Lordstown does not have a duty to act on the request, "unless the moratorium is unenforceable as to Bristolville's submission." Late last year, village council pulled back on its ban on data centers and in January approved temporary moratorium instead. Solicitor Matt Ries has said the originally ban was scheduled to take place in December 2025 but the 180-day moratorium was approved in January, which would give the village or any municipality an opportunity to study the environmental pollution concerns. Ries has said under a Lordstown ordinance, a company has to operate within the permit with what was approved as a site plan review. He said courts favor moratoriums over bans because they are temporary. Village residents have expressed concerns that any large-scale data center would strain Lordstown's energy and water systems, drive up utility bills and bring other complications. At the time company officials said the proposed facility by Bristolville 25 Developers LLC was to be built on 133 acres in both Trumbull and Mahoning counties, employing 120 full-time employees with an average wage of over $84 an hour. artigo.texto: Press Release / photo provided in by County Press Release The Riley County Board of County Commissioners adopted a resolution October 15 extending the temporary moratorium on the development of data centers and battery energy storage systems in unincorporated Riley County. The moratorium, originally established May 18, 2026, suspends the acceptance of land use petitions for these types of developments while the County considers potential regulations and standards. The original moratorium was scheduled to expire November 12, 2026. Under the resolution, the receipt, review, and approval of certain Conditional Use Permits, Special Use Permits and Building Permits for data centers and battery energy storage systems in unincorporated Riley County will remain suspended for applications submitted after the resolution’s effective date. No final decisions have been made regarding new regulations. The extension provides additional time for the County to review potential standards and determine whether changes to existing land development regulations are appropriate. The resolution takes effect following adoption and publication in the County’s official newspaper. The resolution’s stated expiration date is May 14, 2027.

Spanning the runtime, network, data and infrastructure layers, this integrated security approach helps customers run autonomous AI agents securely at enterprise scale.
