artigo.texto: - Bridge Michigan held its inaugural Issues Summit on Wednesday at Marygrove Conservancy in Detroit - Panels drew from the newsroom’s yearlong reporting initiative, Bridge Listens, and were moderated by Bridge reporters - Topics included health, education, the environment, the economy and affordability Bridge Michigan held its inaugural Issues Summit on Wednesday afternoon, bringing together civic leaders, policymakers and subject-matter experts to discuss some of the most pressing issues in the state. Held on the campus of Marygrove Conservancy in Detroit, the event was also livestreamed for an online audience that included a watch party at Alpena Community College. Bridge journalists moderated panels about education, healthcare and data centers. More than 375 people attended the event either in person or virtually. The summit grew out of Bridge Michigan’s yearlong Bridge Listens initiative, which asked readers what issues matter most to them in this election year. “For 15 years, Bridge Michigan has been working to make Michigan better through our high-quality, nonpartisan journalism and public engagement,” Katy Locker, CEO of Center for Michigan, said to kick off the summit. Related: “We believe good information matters, listening matters and Michigan needs more spaces like this one, where people with different perspectives can come together for thoughtful, respectful conversations about the issues shaping our future.” With Election Day two weeks out, the summit included panels and discussions about the political races, policies and candidates that will help shape the future of Michigan and the country. Senior Capitol Reporter Lauren Gibbons, who has covered the US Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, gave her insight on the race of national significance that has set campaign fundraising records. “I keep telling people, everyone is asking, and this is most likely going to be a toss-up race,” she told Stephen Henderson, founder and executive advisor of BridgeDetroit and host of “Michigan: We Need to Talk.” Capitol Reporter Simon Schuster spoke on stage with Henderson about the race between Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican US Rep. John James to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Senior Health Reporter Robin Erb moderated a panel focused on why healthcare costs are climbing and how consolidation and drug prices are affecting coverage. “We all remember the game of tug-of-war as a kid,” said Dr. Deidre Hurse, a public health researcher and medical educator. “And we have families that are just trying to be healthy. They’re trying to get their kids to school. They’re trying to go to work, and opposing them is a complicated health system that isn’t giving them the grace to be healthy.” Capitol Reporter Jordyn Hermani moderated a panel on how affordability challenges shape Michigan’s economic outlook, from housing costs to wages to the ways the state can start addressing the issues. Senior Environment Reporter Kelly House facilitated a discussion about one of the most controversial topics that will play a factor in races up and down the ballot: Data centers. And Education Reporter Isabel Lohman moderated a panel about how Michigan can build a 21st-century workforce when its K-12 foundation is struggling. Venessa Keesler, president and CEO of Launch Michigan, said the state is capable of fixing its education system. “But we have to be really honest about the fact that Michigan starts and stops and starts and stops and starts and stops and we let politics come in. We make policy competitive and not collaborative. And who pays for that is our kids.” Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan.

artigo.texto: Graco Announces Technology Partnership with ABB to Bring High Torque ETM Technology to Data Center Cooling This license agreement positions ABB and ETM to address a fast-growing, mission-critical cooling market where efficiency, reliability, and energy consumption are increasingly important to data center economics MINNEAPOLIS--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 21, 2026-- Electric Torque Machines (ETM), a wholly owned subsidiary of Graco Inc. (NYSE: GGG) and owner of patented Transverse Flux Motor (TFM) technology, today announced that ABB has signed a license agreement covering the use of ETM’s technology in data center cooling towers and heat rejection systems. The agreement builds on a successful collaboration between ABB and ETM in industrial applications to capitalize on one of the fastest-growing areas of global infrastructure. As artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and high-density data centers accelerate demand for thermal management, cooling performance is becoming increasingly important to energy use, operating cost, reliability, and the ability to support higher-density computing. ETM’s TFM architecture is built for applications that need high torque, low speed, and efficient direct drive. By reducing mechanical complexity, TFM-based systems can help customers create cooling solutions that are simpler, use fewer drivetrain components, and are better suited to the reliability demands of modern data centers. The agreement creates a path to participate in a multi-year infrastructure buildout where differentiated motor performance can become a competitive advantage. “This is an exciting opportunity to bring a differentiated motor technology from Graco’s ETM business into one of the most important infrastructure markets in the world,” said Mark Sheahan, Chief Executive Officer of Graco Inc. “ABB’s decision to expand its relationship with ETM reflects confidence in the technology, the team, and the commercial opportunity ahead. Together, we can help customers simplify cooling systems, improve reliability, and convert thermal management from a cost challenge into a strategic advantage for the next wave of data center growth.” “ABB continually evaluates technologies that can deliver meaningful value to customers through improved efficiency, reliability, and ease of operation,” said Jesse Henson, President, NEMA Motors, ABB. “Our work with ETM has shown the potential of direct-drive motor systems, and we are pleased to expand that work into cooling applications where performance and uptime matter.” “Data center cooling is one of the most dynamic opportunities in the electric motor industry,” said Justin McMahon, Global Business Line Leader, ABB. “Combining ABB’s market reach with ETM’s TFM technology gives us the opportunity to develop next-generation motor solutions for mission-critical cooling and thermal management systems while helping customers improve resiliency, simplify maintenance, and support the efficient expansion of large-scale cooling capacity.” “The best validation of a technology platform is when a partner expands the relationship after working with it firsthand,” said Jeffrey Weiss, President of Electric Torque Machines. “ABB has worked closely with ETM to leverage TFM technology in industrial applications, and this agreement moves that work into a high-growth market where direct-drive performance can make a real economic difference. We believe TFM can help redefine what customers expect from motor systems in cooling towers and other critical infrastructure.” Under the license agreement, ABB and ETM will develop TFM-based products for data center cooling towers, heat rejection, and related thermal management applications, with the companies targeting the first installations in data center environments by the end of 2029. ABB and ETM will continue collaborating on product development, application engineering, customer qualification, and market development. The opportunity brings together complementary strengths: ABB’s scale, channel access, and customer relationships, and ETM’s motor technology, in a market where performance, reliability, and energy efficiency are increasingly central to data center operating economics. About GRACO Graco Inc. supplies technology and expertise for the management of fluids and coatings in both industrial and commercial applications. It designs, manufactures and markets systems and equipment to move, measure, control, dispense and spray fluid and powder materials. A recognized leader in its specialties, Minneapolis-based Graco serves customers around the world in the manufacturing, processing, construction, and maintenance industries. For additional information about Graco Inc., please visit us at www.graco.com. About ABB ABB is a global technology leader in electrification and automation, enabling a more sustainable and resource-efficient future. artigo.texto: Follow-on Order Brings Orders from INNIO Data Center Customer to 1.72 GW, Further Strengthening INNIO's Data Center Backlog and Revenue Visibility - Customer also signs long-term full maintenance agreement for first 500 MW, expanding INNIO’s recurring services base. MUNICH--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 22, 2026-- INNIO N.V. (Nasdaq: INIO) today announced a 620 megawatt (MW) follow-on order from a leading developer and operator of mega-scale data center campuses in the U.S. Together with the customer’s 1.1 gigawatt (GW) order announced in July 2026, the new order brings cumulative orders from the customer to approximately 1.72 GW, further strengthening INNIO’s order backlog and visibility into future revenues. “This follow-on order, coming just months after the customer’s initial 1.1 GW order, underscores the strength of customer demand and continued confidence in INNIO. Our containerized Jenbacher solutions deliver what data centers need most: fast deployment, high power density, fuel efficiency, and the performance to support demanding AI workloads,” said Dr. Olaf Berlien, President and CEO of INNIO. “Repeat orders of this scale, combined with long-term service agreements, strengthen our backlog and expand the services base that underpins our business model,” added Dr. Berlien. All 620 MW will be delivered as containerized Jenbacher J624 solutions, enabling standardized installation and accelerated deployment. The 620 MW equipment order was booked in September 2026. In line with customary confidentiality practices in the data center industry, the customer’s name is not disclosed. Separately, the customer has signed a long-term full maintenance agreement covering the first 500 MW of the previously ordered capacity. The agreement includes all spare parts and labor through a major overhaul and supports long-term equipment availability and performance, and extends INNIO’s recurring services revenue across the equipment lifecycle. A major overhaul gives the gas engine a second operating lifecycle, restoring reliability and performance by renewing key components. artigo.texto: Sensata Technologies Introduces Ultrasonic Flow Sensors Designed for AI-Driven Data Center Cooling Systems - FL Series uses ultrasonic technology to deliver highly accurate, non-intrusive flow monitoring for data center liquid cooling systems. - Designed for data center liquid cooling applications, the FL Series provides continuous visibility into coolant flow to support effective thermal management and system performance. - An IP65-rated, non-intrusive design, low pressure drops and no moving parts support reliable, low-maintenance operation. SWINDON, United Kingdom--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 22, 2026-- Sensata Technologies (NYSE: ST) today announced the launch of its FL Series Ultrasonic Flow Sensors, a non-intrusive flow-monitoring solution for liquid cooling systems in data centers and other industrial applications. Supporting flow rates up to 400 liters per minute, the FL Series provides visibility into coolant flow to help operators identify potential issues and protect the uptime of critical computing infrastructure. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261022536039/en/ Sensata Flow Sensors As data centers support increasingly demanding computing and AI workloads, owners and operators need cooling systems capable of keeping Graphic Processing Units (GPUs) and other critical equipment operating at peak performance. Maintaining accurate coolant flow is central to achieving that goal: too little flow can lead to overheating and reduced equipment performance, while excessive flow can waste energy and decrease cooling efficiency. Key benefits of the new FL Series include: - Flow measurement accuracy of up to ±1% of full scale to support precise cooling-system monitoring and control. - Support for a wide range of cooling applications, including coolant distribution units (CDUs), chillers, HVAC systems, and industrial cooling equipment, with flow rates up to 400 liters per minute. - Simple integration with digital and analog outputs compatible with Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs), building management systems, and other control platforms. - Reliable, low-maintenance operation supported by an IP65-rated design, non-intrusive ultrasonic sensing, no moving parts and low pressure drop. “As AI and high-performance computing place greater demands on data center infrastructure, effective cooling is becoming increasingly critical,” said Alice Martins, EVP and President of Industrials at Sensata Technologies. “Sensata brings capabilities across the data center environment, from thermal management to electrical protection and power management. The FL Series builds on that broader portfolio, giving customers reliable flow data to help them manage cooling performance and keep critical systems operating reliably.” Designed for primary and secondary cooling loops, the FL Series is purpose-built for coolant distribution units (CDUs), chillers, HVAC systems and a range of industrial cooling environments. The platform is compatible with deionized water and glycol mixtures commonly used in liquid cooling systems. Customers can select from a range of housing materials, connection types and communication protocols, with integrated temperature sensing available as an option. Ultrasonic sensing enables the FL Series to provide stable flow measurements across varying coolant conditions, including the presence of bubbles. This gives operators more dependable cooling data to help identify potential flow issues earlier, support proactive maintenance and reduce the risk of unplanned downtime. The FL Series expands Sensata’s data center portfolio and strengthens its position as a grid-to-chip engineering partner supporting AI and high-performance computing. Across thermal management, electrical protection, and power and peak management, Sensata is helping customers address critical infrastructure needs across the data center environment. About Sensata Sensata Technologies is a global industrial technology company striving to create a safer, cleaner, more efficient and electrified world. Through its broad portfolio of mission-critical sensors, electrical protection components and sensor-rich solutions, Sensata helps its customers address increasingly complex engineering and operating performance requirements. With more than 16,000 employees and global operations in 13 countries, Sensata serves customers in the automotive, industrial, aerospace, defense and commercial equipment markets. artigo.texto: UL Solutions Introduces Certification Pathway for DC Energy Storage Systems, Simplifying Reviews of Modular Installations New certification program supports flexible system configurations and helps reduce complexity when modular installations undergo certification and code authority review. - The certification addresses modular DC energy storage systems that connect evaluated subsystems, including power conversion systems. - Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database for verification by code authorities. - Evaluations address electrical safety, communication and interoperability between the system and identified subsystems. NORTHBROOK, Ill.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 20, 2026-- UL Solutions (NYSE: ULS), a global leader in applied safety science, today announced a new certification pathway designed to help manufacturers of modular direct current (DC) energy storage systems, used for backup power for critical infrastructure and grid-scale energy storage, bring systems to market with greater flexibility and clearer documentation for installation reviews. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261020793648/en/ Modular DC battery energy storage systems can be configured with different components to meet project needs. The new UL Solutions certification pathway evaluates identified system combinations for electrical safety, communication and interoperability. An energy storage system captures energy so it can be stored for later use and provides electricity to the grid or to a building’s wiring system. A battery energy storage system can help save energy by reducing the number of times electricity must be converted from one form to another, including conversion between alternating current (AC) and DC. It can also simplify the connection to solar panels, backup generators and other equipment. Many of these systems use a modular design, allowing manufacturers to combine different components for a project. However, confirming that those components work safely together can make certification and installation reviews more complex. The new certification program offers manufacturers an alternative to seeking a full matched-assembly system listing at the outset. When a compatible subsystem is identified, the resulting certification documentation can provide manufacturers, developers and code authorities with information about the evaluated configuration. “Modular energy storage designs require a clear way to demonstrate how the system and its critical subsystems work together,” said Wesley Kwok, vice president and general manager of the Energy and Industrial Automation group at UL Solutions. “This certification program gives manufacturers, developers and code authorities documented information about evaluated system combinations while supporting a more flexible approach to DC energy storage system design.” Through the new certification program, UL Solutions evaluates the DC energy storage system with each identified subsystem to applicable requirements of UL 9540, the Standard for Energy Storage Systems and Equipment. The evaluation addresses electrical, communication and interoperability between the system and its evaluated subsystems. Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database under the DC energy storage system certification category, allowing code authorities to verify evaluated combinations. UL 9540 testing covers electrical, electrochemical, mechanical and other types of energy storage technologies used in systems intended to supply electrical energy. Its evaluation framework includes charging and discharging, protection, controls, communication between devices and other system-level considerations. Learn more about UL Solutions energy storage system testing and certification services at UL.com/services/energy-storage-system-testing-and-certification. About UL Solutions A global leader in applied safety science, UL Solutions Inc. (NYSE: ULS) transforms safety, security and sustainability challenges into opportunities for customers in more than 110 countries. UL Solutions delivers testing, inspection and certification services, advisory offerings and software solutions that support our customers’ product innovation and business growth. The UL Mark serves as a recognized symbol of trust in our customers’ products and reflects an unwavering commitment to advancing our safety mission. We help our customers innovate, launch new products and services, navigate global markets and complex supply chains, and grow sustainably and responsibly into the future. Our science is your advantage. artigo.texto: Tesla Gigafactories for cells & packs A new lithium battery energy storage system manufacturer opened a site in the United States in September and intends to serve the commercial, industrial and utility-scale markets, according to Solar Power World. NeoVolta Power, a joint venture between the lithium brands NeoVolta and PotisEdge, unveiled a 4-GWh manufacturing facility in Pendergrass, Georgia, located roughly an hour northeast of Atlanta. The site is designed to support solutions that are compliant with foreign entity of concern rules and eligible for domestic content treatment for U.S. project developers. NeoVolta CEO Ardes Johnson spoke with the publication after the factory opening about the outlook for domestic battery storage manufacturing. Johnson said NeoVolta began in 2018 as a residential battery storage company founded by Brent Willson in La Jolla, California, shipped its first system in 2019 and listed on Nasdaq in 2022. For several years, he said, the business focused on selling home battery systems such as the NV14 through certified solar installers. That changed when the residential storage market contracted sharply after federal incentive changes, he said. The pullback made clear that a broader footprint was needed across residential, commercial, industrial and utility-scale segments, and that the company needed to move from selling equipment to manufacturing it domestically. Johnson described NeoVolta today as a U.S. energy storage manufacturing platform, with the path from a garage-built residential unit to a gigawatt-hour-scale line in Georgia as the central story of its growth. The Pendergrass facility is about 210,000 square feet on the I-85 corridor in northeast Georgia and is operated through NeoVolta Power, the joint venture with PotisEdge, a LONGi Green Energy company. The first production line has a 4-GWh capacity at full run rate, with a second line intended to move toward 8 GWh as orders warrant. Johnson said manufacturing at the site goes beyond final assembly. NeoVolta Power has its own battery management system, storage energy management system and intelligent cell contact system, a combination he described as the real differentiator rather than mechanical integration alone. The intelligent cell contact system sits directly on the battery pack with voltage and temperature sensors on every cell, which Johnson said can detect a failing cell minutes before a safety event, confirm a thermal event within about a minute to trigger suppression and identify degradation trends months in advance. He described the design as more automatable and lower cost than the wire-harness approach still common in the industry. The battery management system draws on electric-vehicle-grade heritage and handles cell- and pack-level monitoring, active balancing and full protection, according to Johnson. The energy management system is the layer that allows the systems to participate in grid services such as frequency regulation and arbitrage rather than only storing energy passively. When cells arrive in Pendergrass, he said, the work performed there is the engineering value-add: integrating cells with proprietary hardware and software into a finished, grid-ready pack and container, built and tested on NeoVolta's own equipment. Johnson said the company faced many challenges that required careful thought and solutions. NeoVolta had no prior large-scale manufacturing experience, having focused entirely on residential storage, which is why the Pendergrass venture was structured as a partnership rather than a solo build. PotisEdge brought equipment installation, commissioning and ramp-up expertise that NeoVolta lacked in-house, he said. While the plant is highly automated, the company is staffing up engineering, facilities, operations and supporting talent to scale efficiently. The policy environment around foreign entity of concern rules has also been complex, Johnson said, given that NeoVolta Power's manufacturing partner has ties to a Chinese parent company. The joint venture had to be structured carefully, with NeoVolta holding the controlling interest including all board seats, to stay compliant, and he noted that the rules are still being finalized by the IRS, which complicates planning. The domestic cell supply chain is not yet mature, Johnson said. U.S.-made cells are not abundantly available at the volume or price point needed, so Chinese-sourced cells have bridged the gap in the near term even as non-foreign-entity-of-concern content requirements rise each year toward 2030. He also cited the operational and financial lift of a first-of-its-kind ramp: commissioning a new line, hiring and training a production workforce, converting pipeline into signed binding contracts and financing through a mix of equity, debt and project-level financing, all while the legacy residential business was contracting. Johnson said the U.S. is in the early stages of a real onshoring shift that is likely to happen in stages rather than overnight. Most U.S. manufacturers, NeoVolta included, still rely on imported cells, first from China and moving toward Southeast Asia and eventually toward domestic cell production as capacity comes online, he said. He pointed to the SK On agreement as an illustration: 9 GWh of U.S.-manufactured LFP cells from 2027 to 2031, under a framework that could scale to 18 GWh. Cells are only one part of the value chain, according to Johnson, and other components also matter for differentiation. He said many manufacturers still treat the DC block as little more than a container of batteries with cells and a basic battery management system, while NeoVolta engineers its battery management, energy management and intelligent cell contact systems directly into the DC block. Products such as NVAPEx therefore carry power electronics and controls, including cell-level safety monitoring, active management and grid-facing intelligence, rather than functioning as a passive box of cells.

artigo.texto: “We want to be absolutely clear: Earl Warren Showgrounds will not consider a data center on this property,” said Earl Warren Showgrounds CEO Ben Sprague on Wednesday. This announcement comes after the months-old data center company Global Stack U.S.A. reached out to Earl Warren Showgrounds through the California Department of Agriculture. The company has been reaching out to state owned fairgrounds across California with a pitch to build shipping-container-sized data centers inside parking structures with helipads on top. Their claim is that these centers will aid in emergency preparedness and help generate year-round revenue for fairgrounds. Sprague said that the company requested the showgrounds to sign a Memorandum of Understanding, which he declined. He did have “Global Stack” listed under his CEO report on meeting agendas for the previous two board meetings; his report was not given at either meeting. “Global Stack U.S.A.” is listed on the agenda for the next board meeting on Thursday, October 29, which was released on Monday night. On Wednesday, the showgrounds issued a press release stating that there will be no data centers built on the property. “No such project is being pursued, nor will it be.” “The reference to Global Stack on previous Board agendas was included solely as part of the CEO’s routine reporting of outside inquiries,” the showgrounds said in a statement. “It did not represent a proposal initiated, endorsed or under consideration by Earl Warren Showgrounds.” Sprague said that “our focus remains on preserving and strengthening the Showgrounds as a community asset, supporting agriculture and equestrian activities, recreation, public gatherings and emergency preparedness for generations to come.”

artigo.texto: Data centers need water to stay cool and functional, and lots of it: The larger facilities can consume as much water a day as a town of 50,000 people, and because much of the cooling involves evaporation, freshwater is often preferred. That raises serious questions about the environmental impact of the cloud compute we use to run AI queries, host photos and videos, stream music, and all the rest. Researchers are trying to get a handle on what the impacts on water usage actually are. In a new study published in Environmental Science & Technology, researchers led by a team from the Carnegie Institution for Science in the US mapped the location of the 9,347 currently identified data centers worldwide. When the local water conditions of all these sites were analyzed, the team found that around 25 percent of data centers are in areas where there's a water gap during at least one month of the year – that's when water demand outstrips supply. Based on climate models and 3 °C (5.4 °F) of average global temperature rise from 1900 levels, the number of water-stressed data center locations would rise to 33 percent within as little as 10 years, the researchers found. "These facilities are not landing in empty landscapes," says environmental scientist Lorenzo Rosa, from the Carnegie Institution for Science. "They are landing on top of the water supply of cities and farms." While electricity can be spread across long distances through a power grid, the same can't be said for water. It typically needs to be sourced locally, which means the local conditions at sites chosen for data centers really do matter. Water typically gets pulled from lakes, rivers, and aquifers – which can all vary seasonally in terms of the water they supply. "The energy footprint of data centers has been quantified in detail because electricity is metered and reported," says Rosa. "Water scarcity is measured locally, inconsistently, and often not at all." "So, we built the map because it did not exist." The map showed that 41 percent of global data centers are competing directly with cities and municipalities for their water, while for another 28 percent of sites the primary water use is for agriculture. For 523 facilities – that's a little over 5 percent of the total – there are already water gaps for at least 9 months of the year. There were differences in terms of climate change impact too. Most data centers pushed beyond the water gap threshold by temperature rises would be in the US, the modeling showed, while in countries such as the UK and Germany there wouldn't be much change. "Data centers typically have the financial capacity and institutional priority to secure water supplies whenever water is available," write the researchers in their published paper. "As a result, the primary risk may not be to data center operations themselves but to other water users within the same basins." The researchers note that information on data center water usage remains limited – the giant tech companies involved are reticent to share the exact level of demand these facilities are putting on our natural resources. More accountable reporting would definitely help, which might require intervention from regulators and governments. There is some positivity from the researchers at the end of their paper, though, pointing to efforts to use wastewater and treated seawater in place of freshwater, as well as improvements in data center heat management. What's clear is that changes are needed before the data center water drain gets worse. "The extent to which water-stress exposure translates into operational impacts for data centers themselves or into measurable consequences for other water users remains an open question to address," write the researchers. "Ensuring data center long-term viability will require siting and governance choices that account for local hydrological limits." The research has been published in Environmental Science & Technology. This article was fact-checked by Rachel Garner and edited by Fiona MacDonald. While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human. If you spot a mistake, please let us know.

October 22, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey Bondada Engineering has announced that the company has received a Letter of Intent (LOI) from Gujarat Industries Power Company (GIPCL) for the EPC package for the development of a 20 MW/120 MWh Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Energy Storage System (VRFB BESS), including 10 years of Operations and Maintenance (O&M), at GIPCL's 165 MW natural gas power plant complex in Vadodara, Gujarat. “The award reflects GIPCL's confidence in the Company's engineering capabilities, project execution expertise and experience in delivering large-scale renewable energy infrastructure projects. It also marks an important milestone in the Company's strategic expansion into advanced energy storage technologies,” the company stated. It further highlighted that while the Government has set an ambitious target of deploying approximately 236 GWh of Battery Energy Storage Systems by 2030, the current installed capacity is around 9.3 GWh. This highlights the immense growth opportunity in the Indian energy storage market, driven by the rapid expansion of renewable energy capacity and the increasing need for grid stability, the company stated. “With this landmark order, Bondada Engineering has secured India's largest grid-scale Vanadium Redox Flow Battery (VRFB) BESS project, demonstrating the Company's ability to adopt and execute energy storage projects involving advanced Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES) technologies. This achievement further strengthens Bondada's position in the rapidly expanding BESS sector, complementing its existing renewable energy EPC portfolio,” asserted the company. artigo.texto: Mundo Corporativo BYD Energy Storage Acelera Expansão da Rede Global BESS Pós-Venda SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — A BYD Energy Storage desenvolveu uma rede abrangente de serviços pós-venda em uma estrutura de vários níveis: operação e manutenção de estações, centros de projetos, centros regionais e sede global. A BYD Energy Storage opera nove centros de O&M de 2.500 metros quadrados em todo o mundo. Ela conta com uma rede de serviços de pós-venda em diversos países como China, Chile, África do Sul, Reino Unido, Estados Unidos, Austrália, Japão, Polônia e Oriente Médio. Novos centros de serviços serão inaugurados na África do Sul e na Bulgária em 2027 para expandir ainda mais sua presença global de serviços. Os centros desempenham funções essenciais, como armazenamento e gestão de peças de reposição, reparo e manutenção de baterias, alocação regional de peças de reposição, reciclagem de baterias e treinamento de engenheiros contratados localmente. Os centros regionais da BYD Energy Storage estão em total conformidade com os requisitos regulamentares locais, oferecem treinamento estruturado para a força de trabalho e viabilizam uma resposta local rápida. A equipe de serviços profissionais é composta por mais de 200 engenheiros de campo e mais de 100 especialistas em P&D. A empresa aplica SLAs de serviço padronizados: resposta em até 24 horas, chegada ao local em até 48 horas e solução de problemas em até 7 dias. A rede global de serviços da empresa alcança uma ampla cobertura. Ela forma uma rede de suprimentos multiponto que garante a entrega rápida de peças de reposição em todo o mundo. Além disso, com suas linhas de produção locais, as equipes de operação e manutenção integram recursos regionais para oferecer serviços locais de reparo de baterias, fornecendo aos clientes globais um suporte pós-venda rápido, conveniente e localizado. “Nossa presença global de serviços é adaptada às nossas implementações de BESS em rápido crescimento. “O suporte pós-venda confiável sustenta a operação estável de longo prazo dos ativos de armazenamento de energia”, comentou He Dehong, Chefe de Serviço Pós-Venda Global da BYD Energy Storage. Guiado por sua visão de capacitar o setor global de armazenamento de energia com serviços digitais e inteligentes, o sistema global maduro de O&M da BYD Energy Storage apoia fortemente sua crescente presença no armazenamento de energia em baterias. A empresa liderou as remessas globais de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), superando 60 GWh em 2025, e entregou, ao todo, mais de 650 projetos de armazenamento de energia, contando com serviços pós-venda padronizados e localizados que garantem a operação confiável dos ativos. artigo.texto: NAVASOTA — Joie Miller moved to rural Grimes County to raise her daughter hunting, fishing and spending time with her grandparents on their 100-acre ranch. Then Elon Musk announced he was constructing the world’s largest building a little more than a mile from her in-laws’ property. The Terafab semiconductor factory, which Musk has projected will be 50 times larger than the Pentagon, will produce computer chips for artificial intelligence. As construction kicked off, trucks rumbled past their property day and night. Big chunks of ash rained down. Miller, 31, started investigating, joining the ranks of outraged rural Texans who have seen wide open spaces suddenly sold off to support the state’s rapacious growth. The more she dug, the more Miller, a born-and-raised Republican, came to blame the party that’s run the state her whole life. “You just look around and think, are things better or worse, and if they’re worse, who has been in charge?” she said. Rural Republicans have long been the floodwall that’s held back hopes of a blue wave big enough to flip Texas. While they make up less than one-fifth of the electorate, rural voters turn out and vote red at such high rates they’ve reliably undercut Democratic gains in cities and suburbs. In what’s shaping up to be a razor-tight midterm election, Republicans are counting on these votes more than ever to hold onto Texas’ powerful statewide offices. But some rural voters are revolting, angry over the sudden proliferation of data centers, massive power lines and other physical manifestations of the state’s relentless development. Miller said she’s planning to vote Democratic for the first time in her life. “The Republican Party doesn’t seem to care about us right now,” Miller said. “They do this every single time, where they say they’re going to fix a problem, despite having had decades to fix it, and I think a lot of us are sick of it.” As early voting kicks off, the rural Republican firewall is showing its first real cracks since the Obama era, the last time a statewide Democrat broke 25% of the rural vote. James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominees for U.S. Senate and governor, are polling north of 30% in rural Texas, with Talarico hitting 42% in a late-September Fox News survey. But it will take a lot of Joie Millers to change Democrats’ fate. When he nearly bested Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018, Democrat Beto O’Rourke won a narrow majority of non-rural counties but was undone by Cruz’s 75% share in rural Texas. O’Rourke would have had to swing the rural margin 15 points in his favor to have changed the outcome, a Texas Tribune analysis found. This cycle, Democrats are proposing a marriage of convenience to frustrated moderates, open-minded independents and disenchanted MAGA populists, asking them to put aside culture war differences in the face of shared causes, like data centers. “If Democrats break through in rural Texas, it will be because Republican leadership was caught flat-footed by a new issue,” said Ali Zaidi, a Democratic political consultant who oversaw rural outreach for Mike Collier’s 2018 and 2022 lieutenant governor races. “Because on the fundamentals — low taxation, business climate, conservative values — they’ve got those locked down and there’s nothing a Democrat can do to explain that away.” “It’s hard enough to get people to trust me” On a recent Tuesday afternoon, half a dozen people gathered in a conference room in Corsicana, an hour southeast of Dallas, in dusty boots and business suits. They came armed with binders and printed dossiers, meticulously laying out their investigations into the data centers that are popping up across their communities. They’d documented persistent noise pollution, diminished air quality, spiking electricity bills and ignored pleas for help from the state. These diehard Republicans were meeting with Hinojosa, they said, because they didn’t know where else to turn. Over the course of an hour, she didn’t ask for their vote. Instead, she gave them what every voice in the wilderness really wants — undivided attention. “Talk to me like a dummy,” she said, as she put on her glasses to review their findings. “I can tell you’re in deep, and I’m sorry you had to get so educated on this.” When Hinojosa, an Austin state representative, signed on to face three-term incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, it seemed like a suicide mission. A fundraising juggernaut, Abbott began the year with over $100 million in his campaign account and a record of smashing his Democratic opponents by double digits. But few expected the data center curveball, least of all Abbott, who vowed last year that Texas would become the “epicenter of AI development.” In the face of rural rage, Abbott backtracked, temporarily pausing new projects and recommending the Legislature enshrine what he says are the toughest guardrails in the country on water and power usage. That has put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said communities that reject data centers will end up “backwards and poor.” At Hinojosa’s roundtable discussion in Corsicana, the attendees said they still blamed Abbott for what they described as violent incursions on their tranquil way of life. “But didn’t he fix it?” Hinojosa asked with a cheeky smile. “Greg Abbott has enticed them,” Michael Ellis said with vitriol, referring to data center developers.“He didn’t fix anything.” Ellis, 70, and his wife live less than a mile from a new data center going up in Navarro County. They’re worried their quiet patch of countryside will soon have lights shining on it around the clock, with noise, air pollution and the possibility of accidents that could endanger the neighbors. Abbott’s initial support of data centers is “disqualifying” to Ellis. He worries the recent executive orders are election-year pandering, and Abbott will roll the red carpet back out if he’s reelected. artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Central Georgia Electric Membership Corp. will deploy up to 50 MW of small-scale, customer-sited energy storage in partnership with Base Power, the organizations said last week. - Set to begin in 2027, the deployment marks Base Power’s first utility partnership outside its home state of Texas, Base and CGEMC said. CGEMC will charge the batteries when wholesale power prices and members’ energy demand are low and discharge during periods of peak demand, helping to stabilize the grid across its 14-county territory southeast of Atlanta. - The batteries will add capacity to a CGEMC system that could see substantial large-load growth in the coming years. Multiple data center projects are proposed or under development in its territory, including a 240-MW Equinix campus near Hampton. Dive Insight: Base Power operates as a retail energy choice provider in Texas and the Illinois zone of the PJM Interconnection, and as a direct partner for public power entities in parts of Texas. The company says its fleet has more than 750 MWh of capacity spread over 30,000-plus homes. Base is one of several companies that provide deeply discounted home battery subscriptions via energy choice retail frameworks in restructured markets or utility partnerships in regulated markets. In both scenarios, Base installs and maintains relatively large residential backup batteries at little or no direct cost to the homeowner. When the grid is up and running, Base or its utility partners charge and discharge the batteries to shave demand peaks, mitigate price spikes and tap energy arbitrage value. During outages, Base says each 39.2-kWh battery can provide up to 36 hours of backup power. Base’s partnership with CGEMC marks its first outside Texas and one of its first in a regulated utility market. Base is also partnering with El Paso Electric, a vertically integrated utility serving parts of far west Texas outside the deregulated Electric Reliability Council of Texas market, on a resilience-focused pilot program. While that means the company and its utility partners target different value streams, the core business proposition — using distributed batteries to reduce power supply costs — remains the same, company spokesperson Gabriel Federman said in an email. “In Texas, that means addressing transmission and energy costs through peak-shaving and arbitrage. In Georgia, the main value is in transmission and reducing capacity obligations,” Federman said. “However, the core principles and the value of distributed storage [are] consistent across markets.” Both transmission-scale energy storage and customer-sited distributed batteries deliver benefits at the wholesale level, according to an analysis published in September by the consultancy ICF. Distributed BESS offers additional value in alleviating distribution grid congestion, boosting local resilience and allowing utilities to defer grid upgrades, ICF said. Unlike vertically integrated utilities that earn a regulated rate of return on infrastructure spending, member-owned rural electric cooperatives like CGEMC and not-for-profit municipal power utilities like Base Power partner Austin Energy have strong incentives to minimize wholesale power costs and avoid expensive system investments. Regardless of local market structure, they’re tapping distribution-connected energy storage for help — from networked residential batteries to multi-megawatt installations at substations or industrial sites. George Weaver, CGEMC president and CEO, framed the utility’s partnership with Base Power as a win for members themselves and the grid they pay to support. The 50-MW deployment will “add flexible local capacity to support our electric system while giving participating members greater peace of mind through dependable backup battery power,” Weaver said in a statement.

artigo.texto: Key Takeaways - Energy storage additions headed for a record in 2026 and 2027 - Local battery supply chains grow as activity shifts from China The global energy storage market – led by China and US – is seeing new growth centers emerge. This year, India will add 26 times more batteries than last year and Australia will almost double its annual addition, contributing to the global 45% year-on-year growth in gigawatts in 2026 being projected by BloombergNEF in its latest forecast. The record will be followed by yet another one in 2027 – when energy storage additions top 200 gigawatts – as several more markets scale deployment. Drivers of growth include rising solar penetration, storage-pairing mandates and fiscal incentive programs. Meanwhile, protectionist policies are reshaping regional battery-storage supply chains – promoting local component production and restricting Chinese imports. Chinese equipment suppliers are increasingly drawn to new markets with fewer restrictions as a result. Cumulative storage capacity grows 10-fold to 3 terawatts or 11 terawatt-hours in 2036 from 2025 levels. High of 2026 Energy storage deployment is set for another record in 2026 by adding 188 gigawatts (GW) or 535 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage projects, 62% of which are installed in China, the US and Australia, according to BloombergNEF’s latest outlook. China is surprisingly strong given the phaseout of a major policy last year which mandated energy storage for renewables build. The transition to different revenue and business models led to uncertainty in the market this year, but new supportive policies are reinforcing the country’s lead. These include a firming requirement for standalone solar and wind projects and a renewed 300GW deployment target by 2030. The US maintains strong build, supported by preserved tax credits and accelerated by on-site energy storage demand from data centers. Meanwhile, India leapfrogs peer markets as tender-driven annual additions top6GW this year from a few hundred megawatts last year. Beyond the UK, Germany and Italy, which led European build last year, a myriad of countries emerge in the gigawatt-scale addition this year, including Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, France, Greece, Netherlands and Ukraine. Global annual additions grow 11% year-on-year in gigawatts in 2027 to 209GW/638GWh, as deployment broadens beyond today’s largest markets. Spain, the United Arab Emirates, Chile and Japan accelerate build, supported by power market fundamentals, diversified revenue stacks and utility-led procurement activity. By2036, the growth engine shifts to emerging regions such as Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia and other European countries. Sodium-ion batteries are increasingly gaining traction amid the recent increase in material prices for lithium iron phosphate materials. Sodium-ion battery storage has a lower fire risk and can operate across a wide temperature range, reducing the need for liquid cooling and auxiliary energy use. Despite these advantages, limited manufacturing scale and cost competitiveness pose hurdles to adoption for sodium-ion batteries as well as other non-lithium long-duration energy storage. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is expected to be the primary chemistry for energy storage over the next decade due to its cost competitiveness, high cycle life and supply chain dominance. Battery-storage supply chains reset Several markets are scrutinizing supply chains much more closely and mandating more localization, complicating market entry for Chinese equipment suppliers. The US leads these efforts with tariffs and incentives for domestic battery storage production and use in projects, while restricting the use of equipment reliant on supply chains involving China. Similar concerns on cybersecurity and supply-chain security are guiding policies across the European Union and Japan. With these barriers, Chinese equipment providers are tapping into markets with fewer restrictions, such as the Middle East, Latin America and Sub-Saharan Africa. Protectionist policies are also in place in other countries, such as South Korea, India and Brazil, although their measures are not as stringent as the ones in the US. Pairing with renewables Globally, energy storage installations co-located with renewables, particularly solar projects, are gaining more traction. By the end of 2025, as much as 69GW/196GWh of energy storage projects had been paired with299GW of solar. Growing volume of solar electricity curtailment and price cannibalization in key markets such as the US, Australia and Chile continue to drive additions. Despite an expiring policy mandate for co-location of batteries with renewable energy projects in China, nine other countries including India, Mexico, and the Philippines, have also implemented regulatory or auction-linked mandates. Deployment of renewable-plus-storage projects is seen remaining robust over the next few years.

artigo.texto: Trending There has been some delay in the electrical infrastructure for a proposed data center campus near Allenwood. Recently, the Union County Commissioners told PNK Group, the New York City-based developer of three proposed data centers, to stop construction of an electrical substation that would serve them, according to Pennlive.com. Commissioners' in a cease-and-desist letter Wednesday said the board had not received the required approvals before starting work, which can continue in terms of safety aspects. The so-called "Allenwood Project" is considered by the developer to be a necessary transmission investment to help PPL Electric Utilities safely and reliably serve growing demand for electricity by accommodating a new customer connection. Work permitted is what is needed to secure the site, protect the environment and comply with safety requirements. The developer has 30 days to confirm in writing that all non-protective construction activities have ceased and the county is prepared to seek legal recourse if the developer does not abide by the terms. The substation work is adjacent to a 478,000 square-foot building in the Great Stream Commons business park north of Allenwood, part of which is to be retrofitted into a data center. It appears a stormwater retention basin is being relocated and a modified access road will be built as part of the substation construction, the cease-and-desist letter states. That letter is a follow up to one the commissioners sent Oct. 9 advising PNK Group that three days earlier it had denied its request for approval of the substation because of a lack of information. The commissioners told PNK Group since it contends the substation is an integral component of a larger unified development of which the proposed data center campus is a part, they cannot evaluate the submission for it independently. Commissioners say a piecemeal review of one component without full information regarding the scope, design, use, intensity and impact of the project as a whole would not protect the interests of other property owners, Pennlive reported. The commissioners suggested PNK Group not resubmit an application for the substation until the Gregg Township supervisors act on an amendment to the zoning ordinance that will determine where data centers could be built in that municipality. That vote is anticipated next month. The issue with the construction of the substation is between the county and the developer which has obtained a building permit from the township. PPL has revealed its preferred route for a 230KV transmission line to provide power for the data centers. PNK Group is paying all costs of the 6.8-mile line that will extend from a substation in the Elimsport area to the business park with costs to be determined. The transmission investment is projected to help PPL Electric Utilities safely and reliably serve growing demand for electricity by accommodating a new customer connection. The utility said it has received input from property owners, local officials, businesses and residents that has helped it to better understand local priorities, identify potential concerns and refine the route to minimize community and environmental impacts where practical while continuing to meet the project's objectives. The transmission line would support growing energy needs including a new customer connection, specifically a data center. PPL says its "Customer Protection Framework" helps ensure large-load growth occurs responsibly while protecting affordability, reliability and transparency for the customers and communities it serves. The current preferred route, pending regulatory approval, will include building approximately 6.8 miles of new double-circuit 230 kV transmission line in Lycoming and Union counties. The line will begin at the existing Elimsport substation, near Elimsport Road, and extend largely southeast for about 6.8 miles to a new customer facility near Route 15. The transmission structures will be constructed of steel with a dark brown protective coating and are designed to be stronger and more weather-resistant. Based on preliminary engineering, the monopole structures will likely range from about 90 to 180 feet, with an average height of around 140 feet. Actual pole heights will be determined during final engineering. Safety for customers, communities and employees is a top priority to the utility which is committed to minimizing disruption as much as possible in any future construction. Construction will include: • Installation of environmental controls and access roads. • Clearing of any trees in the new right-of-way. • Installation of new steel transmission structures. • Creation of temporary work pads and pull pad used to install new conductors. • All temporarily disturbed areas will be restored upon completion of the project. • Construction of the project is anticipated to begin in late 2027 and conclude by the end of 2029. "PPL Electric is committed to keeping landowners, communities and stakeholders informed throughout the project," officials with the utility said in a statement on PPL's website. "We will continue engaging with municipal leaders, property owners and community members as planning and engineering work progresses." A second informational open house will be held from 6 to 8 p.m., Oct. 28 at Warrior Run Area Social Hall, 196 White Deer Ave., Allenwood for area residents to review the preferred route. The project team will be available at information stations to discuss the project and answer questions one-on-one. There is no formal presentation, set agenda or large group question and answer session. To submit a question or comment about the project, email allenwoodproject@pplweb.com.

artigo.texto: Littleton and Brighton are joining a growing number of communities seeking to halt data center development to give staff time to develop zoning regulations and catch up with the rapidly growing technology. Littleton and Brighton both unanimously advanced moratoriums on data center applications Tuesday following a growing number of community concerns about the developments and their potential impacts. Recommended Stories Littleton unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on first reading, and Brighton gave final approval to a one-year moratorium. A number of residents in both communities spoke against data centers, citing concerns including water usage, noise, heat, energy consumption, environmental impacts and quality of life. In both meetings, staff said the moratoriums would allow time to study the impacts of data centers and integrate regulations into zoning codes that do not specifically address data centers in a comprehensive manner. “The purpose of the moratorium is to analyze the various land uses related to data centers,” Littleton City Attorney Reid Betzing said. “To find out if they are appropriate and, if they are, where they are appropriate.” Brighton’s moratorium comes as a proposed data center project that faced considerable public backlash was withdrawn. The proposal called for a 2.5 million-square-foot data center campus in northeast Brighton composed of eight two-story buildings. According to 9News, the application was withdrawn shortly before the council approved the moratorium on first reading Oct. 6. Brighton’s moratorium suspends the acceptance, processing and approval of applications while the City Council determines what regulations may be appropriate to mitigate impacts on the community. Littleton Councilmember Pam Grove said much of the concern is centered on hyperscale data centers, which use significantly more energy than smaller facilities. Grove said she is aware of six state bills that may be introduced on the topic of data centers, ranging from outright bans to environmental protection regulations. Littleton and Brighton join communities including Denver, Larimer County and Broomfield that have passed moratoriums for similar reasons. Aurora is also considering a moratorium following public backlash over a proposed data center development. 9News contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: As emissões de gases de efeito estufa do Brasil recuaram 6% em 2025, atingindo o menor patamar em oito anos, segundo dados do Sistema de Estimativas de Emissões e Remoções de Gases de Efeito Estufa (Seeg), do Observatório do Clima. O resultado foi impulsionado pela queda do desmatamento em todos os biomas, especialmente na Amazônia e no Cerrado. Esta é a terceira redução anual seguida (-12,7% em 2024 e -7,5% em 2023), que somadas resultam em queda de 26% nas emissões brutas no período, revertendo o ciclo anterior — entre 2019 e 2022 o país registrou uma alta expressiva do desmatamento. “Os últimos três anos reverteram uma tendência de mais de uma década de crescimento de emissões”, disse David Tsai, coordenador do Seeg e gerente no Instituto de Energia e Meio Ambiente (Iema), em coletiva de imprensa realizada nesta quarta-feira (21). As emissões brutas somaram 2,06 bilhões de toneladas de CO2 equivalente no ano passado. A maior parcela vem da mudança do uso do solo (39%), que é a conversão da vegetação nativa em outros usos, como agropecuária e urbanização — ou seja, desmatamento. A agropecuária foi o segundo maior emissor (30%), seguida de energia (21%, inclui transportes), resíduos (5%) e processos industriais e uso de produtos (5%). O Seeg também calcula a quantidade total de remoção de carbono, que foi de 650 milhões de toneladas de CO2 equivalente em 2025. Assim, as emissões líquidas do país (emissões brutas descontadas as remoções) totalizaram 1,41 bilhão de toneladas no ano. As remoções ocorreram no setor de mudança de uso da terra e florestas, que abrange duas atividades: crescimento de vegetação secundária e remoção de carbono por áreas protegidas (vegetação mantida em terras indígenas e unidades de conservação). De onde veio a queda A redução nas emissões brutas foi puxada pela forte desaceleração do desmatamento, observado em todos os estados e biomas brasileiros, principalmente na Amazônia e no Cerrado. Enquanto o setor de uso da terra reduziu significativamente suas emissões, os demais setores apresentaram estabilidade ou alta. Resíduos tiveram o maior crescimento proporcional, com alta de 3,6%, associado ao crescimento populacional e ao descarte em aterros e lixões e no tratamento de efluentes. Já energia registrou alta de 1,2% nas emissões, impulsionada pelo setor de transportes (com maior consumo de diesel e gasolina) e pela geração de eletricidade, cujas emissões subiram 6% devido ao acionamento de termelétricas a gás. As emissões da agropecuária permaneceram praticamente estáveis, com queda de 0,1% — o aumento de 6,45% da agricultura foi compensado pela redução nas emissões da pecuária. O segmento de processos industriais e uso de produtos também ficou estável, com leve variação positiva de 0,2%. “É um resultado bem positivo em nível nacional, em função da redução das emissões de uso da terra, e mostra a importância e a efetividade não só de continuar controlando o desmatamento, mas iniciar, de fato, medidas contundentes nos outros setores”, disse Tsai. O Brasil está em processo de regulamentação do seu mercado de carbono, que vai estabelecer um limite para as emissões de setores poluentes da economia. No Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), cada empresa recebe cotas (os CBEs). Quem emite menos que sua cota vende o excedente, e quem emite mais compra cotas ou créditos (os CRVEs). Estamos no rumo das metas? Segundo análise da equipe do Seeg, o ciclo de quedas recente permitiu ao Brasil recuperar o atraso causado pela disparada de emissões de anos anteriores. O país ficou, assim, mais próximo de cumprir as metas estabelecidas em sua contribuição nacionalmente determinada (NDC, na sigla em inglês) no âmbito do Acordo de Paris. O limite de emissões líquidas para 2025 era de 1,32 bilhão de toneladas de CO2 equivalente, correspondente a uma redução de 48,4% em relação a 2005. O Brasil não conseguiu cumprir a meta do ano. O resultado de 1,41 bilhão de toneladas de emissão líquida ficou 6% distante do objetivo. Para 2026, a estimativa do Seeg é que as emissões líquidas do país somem 1,22 bilhão de toneladas de CO2 equivalente. O cálculo considera os dados mais recentes de desmatamento do Prodes (Programa de Monitoramento dos Biomas Brasileiros por Satélite) e uma projeção linear das emissões dos demais setores, baseada na tendência dos últimos cinco anos. “Isso nos coloca na zona onde deveríamos estar para cumprir a meta de 2030”, disse o coordenador do Seeg. A meta brasileira para 2030 é de limite de 1,2 bilhão de toneladas. O Observatório do Clima avalia, no entanto, que essa trajetória será ameaçada em uma eventual mudança de governo.

artigo.texto: Taunton City Council unanimously approves data center ban TAUNTON, Mass. (WJAR) — The Taunton City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to ban data centers amid discussion of a proposed facility at an industrial park in the city. City Hall was packed as opponents turned out for the vote, with residents raising concerns about potential environmental impacts and strain on the local power grid. “I found out, like most people via Facebook, because I wasn’t given a letter,” said Taunton resident Willembert VanBruniswaardt. He also accused data center companies of misconduct. “We’ve seen these data center companies perform all kinds of, frankly, criminal actions. I’m not going to sugarcoat it,” he said. In a letter to Mayor Shaunna O’Connell, property owner VMD Industrial requested an exception to the ban. Asked about the property owner’s warning that the decision could cost it a multimillion-dollar deal, O’Connell said business development must be balanced with residents’ needs. “We always support business, but it has to be done the right way,” she told NBC 10 News. “I know the priority of the council and my priority is to protect the resources that our residents rely on every single day.” The Planning Board said Tuesday night that the John Hancock Road property did not qualify for an exception because no permit application was pending. City leaders said the proposed facility could not be grandfathered in without an existing application. “I’m glad people were here tonight to hear the actual facts, because when people believe the gossip and, you know, crap that’s on Facebook or whatever social media, it starts problems,” O’Connell said. Officials said the ban has no expiration date and would remain in place unless changed through another zoning hearing. - ALSO READ: One year after near-fatal stabbing, Former Fall River Mayor William Flanagan eyes 2027 run The council also approved a moratorium, which officials said would provide additional legal protection if the ban is challenged. Despite the unanimous vote, VanBruniswaardt remained cautious. “I would not describe this as a win. I would describe this as we scored a goal. artigo.texto: Trending When a city plans something big, it should not check driver’s licenses at the door. That is what happened Monday night in Woodward. The City Council cancelled its regular meeting and instead held what it called a "community conversation” in the Woodward-Granger High School auditorium. The notice required attendees to show a photo ID with a Woodward address or a piece of mail with their name and Woodward address before they could enter. Security officers and police were there to oversee the screening of IDs. I was there as president of the Iowa Freedom of Information Council and was turned away. So was a rural Dallas County resident interested in data centers. A KCCI reporter saw at least two others who were refused entry. Inside, Mayor Todd Folkerts and three Microsoft officials announced that the company had closed on the purchase of about 600 acres in the Woodward Eco Business Park, on the city’s south side, for a data center campus. About 200 residents listened for 90 minutes. Folkerts said the council would need to approve a development agreement and a site plan before the project could proceed. Fewer than a majority of the five council members attended, so the gathering likely falls outside Iowa’s open meetings law. Legal or not, the residency screening was a mistake. It treated a regional decision as a private family matter. Consider what a data center brings. Microsoft’s representatives told the crowd a closed-loop cooling system would spare the city’s water supply and buying electricity from a wholesaler would protect residential rates. Those are promises about water and electricity, and neither resource stops at a city limit. New power lines would cross farm fields. Construction trucks would use county roads. Storm water runs downhill without regard to annexation maps or city boundaries. A farm family just outside town will live with the data center's lights, noise and traffic as surely as any resident of Main Street. That farm family pays property taxes, too -- just not to the City of Woodward. Iowa law already recognizes that a city’s choices reach past its borders. Section 354.9 of the Iowa Code allows a city to review subdivision plats as far as two miles beyond its city limits, giving the city a voice over how its rural neighbors’ land is developed. On October 12, Woodward denied those same neighbors a seat in the auditorium. The venue underscored that point. Woodward-Granger High School belongs to the Woodward-Granger Community School District, which has its central offices in Granger and reaches into Dallas, Boone and Polk counties. Taxpayers in Granger and the surrounding countryside helped pay for that auditorium. The city used the school district's building and then told people without a Woodward address to stay outside. Iowa’s local governments cooperate all the time. Chapter 28E of the Iowa Code allows cities, counties and other public bodies to share services and work together for mutual advantage. The Legislature has directed the courts to interpret that law liberally. Twelve central Iowa cities, utilities and water districts, including the Xenia Rural Water District, formed Central Iowa Water Works under a 28E agreement to plan the region’s drinking water together. Metro Waste Authority grew out of a 28E agreement among Des Moines-area governments dating to 1969. Polk County and its cities fund emergency management jointly through another 28E agreement. None of these partnerships asks a neighbor for proof of address before letting the person listen to a discussion of matters of mutual concern. A residents-only rule divides communities. It turns the city limit into a wall, as if the people on the far side have no stake in what happens on the near side. This also invites the same treatment in return. If Granger, Madrid or Dallas County someday puts a landfill on Woodward’s doorstep, Woodward residents will want to attend meetings where such a development is discussed. They should get in. Everyone else should, too. Monday’s rule was also unneighborly. Picture a farmer who plans a hog confinement on his fence line and invites only his own household to hear the details. The people downwind would not call that a community conversation. They would call it a snub. I told KCCI the requirement that only Woodward residents could attend Monday's information session “erodes the trust and confidence” in Woodward city government. And the damage spreads beyond Woodward. Woodward still has time to fix this. The development agreement and site plan still need council approval. The council will have to take these up at regular, properly noticed meetings that are open to anyone who wants to attend. Woodward officials should invite the Dallas County Board of Supervisors, the Woodward-Granger school board and nearby townships to hear the plan. It should publish what Microsoft has said about water, power and traffic. Woodward’s neighbors will live with this data center. They deserve to hear about it, ask about it and argue about it in the same room as everyone else. A project this large deserves the widest audience -- not the narrowest. Randy Evans is the executive director of the Iowa Freedom of Information Council. He can be reached at DMREvans2810@gmail.com.

artigo.texto: - Bridge Michigan held its inaugural Issues Summit on Wednesday at Marygrove Conservancy in Detroit - Panels drew from the newsroom’s yearlong reporting initiative, Bridge Listens, and were moderated by Bridge reporters - Topics included health, education, the environment, the economy and affordability Bridge Michigan held its inaugural Issues Summit on Wednesday afternoon, bringing together civic leaders, policymakers and subject-matter experts to discuss some of the most pressing issues in the state. Held on the campus of Marygrove Conservancy in Detroit, the event was also livestreamed for an online audience that included a watch party at Alpena Community College. Bridge journalists moderated panels about education, healthcare and data centers. More than 375 people attended the event either in person or virtually. The summit grew out of Bridge Michigan’s yearlong Bridge Listens initiative, which asked readers what issues matter most to them in this election year. “For 15 years, Bridge Michigan has been working to make Michigan better through our high-quality, nonpartisan journalism and public engagement,” Katy Locker, CEO of Center for Michigan, said to kick off the summit. Related: “We believe good information matters, listening matters and Michigan needs more spaces like this one, where people with different perspectives can come together for thoughtful, respectful conversations about the issues shaping our future.” With Election Day two weeks out, the summit included panels and discussions about the political races, policies and candidates that will help shape the future of Michigan and the country. Senior Capitol Reporter Lauren Gibbons, who has covered the US Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, gave her insight on the race of national significance that has set campaign fundraising records. “I keep telling people, everyone is asking, and this is most likely going to be a toss-up race,” she told Stephen Henderson, founder and executive advisor of BridgeDetroit and host of “Michigan: We Need to Talk.” Capitol Reporter Simon Schuster spoke on stage with Henderson about the race between Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican US Rep. John James to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Senior Health Reporter Robin Erb moderated a panel focused on why healthcare costs are climbing and how consolidation and drug prices are affecting coverage. “We all remember the game of tug-of-war as a kid,” said Dr. Deidre Hurse, a public health researcher and medical educator. “And we have families that are just trying to be healthy. They’re trying to get their kids to school. They’re trying to go to work, and opposing them is a complicated health system that isn’t giving them the grace to be healthy.” Capitol Reporter Jordyn Hermani moderated a panel on how affordability challenges shape Michigan’s economic outlook, from housing costs to wages to the ways the state can start addressing the issues. Senior Environment Reporter Kelly House facilitated a discussion about one of the most controversial topics that will play a factor in races up and down the ballot: Data centers. And Education Reporter Isabel Lohman moderated a panel about how Michigan can build a 21st-century workforce when its K-12 foundation is struggling. Venessa Keesler, president and CEO of Launch Michigan, said the state is capable of fixing its education system. “But we have to be really honest about the fact that Michigan starts and stops and starts and stops and starts and stops and we let politics come in. We make policy competitive and not collaborative. And who pays for that is our kids.” Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan.

artigo.texto: It was deju vu all over again on Tuesday night when the Little Rock City Board of Directors failed on a 4-4 vote to pass a six-month moratorium on data center projects. The board took up this issue in August, when some members tried to pass an 18-month moratorium. But the board made the same vote, with the same directors voting the same way. Six votes are needed to pass an ordinance. The ordinance being considered Tuesday would have given the city time to set up restrictions and regulations relating to water, noise, emergency infrastructure, zoning regulations and monitoring relating to data center projects. The urgency to pass an ordinance comes at a time when Google is planning to build a $1 billion data center at the Port of Little Rock. Both measures were sponsored by Director Kathy Webb, and at both meetings, Jay Chesshir, head of the Little Rock Regional Chamber, came in like a relief pitcher to finish the deal, appearing to scare away anyone considering voting with the “yes” contingent with threats that a moratorium could mean legal trouble for the city. One of the “no” votes came from Webb’s friend, Director Capi Peck, who was listed in the agenda handout as a co-sponsor of the moratorium ordinance. After Peck voted against Webb’s 18-month moratorium back in August, she took heat on social media for her action. Webb seemed to be expecting a different outcome this week. In a text exchange earlier in the day, she was asked if she thought the measure would pass. “I think so!” she wrote back. “Four sponsors including me.” After the meeting, Webb said the vote caught her by surprise. “It was a shock,” she said. “It was not expected.” She said she thought she had five votes going into the meeting and was hoping to peel off one of the at-large directors. Asked if she was done with trying to get a moratorium passed, she said possibly, but that she had made a promise when the board passed an ordinance regulating data centers in June to make improvements to that measure. “I keep my promises,” she said. A half-dozen citizens spoke in support of the passage of the ordinance, with one person speaking against it. Then came time for the directors to speak. Peck confirmed she was a co-sponsor – giving Webb credit for the lion’s share of the work – and said she had read over the measure and marked it up several times. In the end, though, she said she still found it to be “pretty technical.” She then invited Brad Jordan, director of Planning and Development for the city, to the microphone, asking him if his department could handle everything that would be required to implement the ordinance. “Whatever we’re asked to do, we’ll do it and we’ll do it well,” he said. He went on to say that getting it done in such a short period of time would be challenging. “It means for the next year, we’ll be doing this,” he said. Director Dean Kumpurus, instead of immediately giving his thoughts, invited Chesshir to speak, a move that brought a few grumbles from the crowded chamber. Chesshir also spoke against the 18-month moratorium. Chesshir’s main argument was that most of what was covered in Webb’s legislation would already be dealt with by one of several local, state or federal agencies, such as the state health department and the Arkansas Division of Environmental Quality, as well as the federal Environmental Protection Agency. To pass an ordinance that conflicts with those agencies would be to invite “legal and litigation risk,” Chesshir said. In all, Directors B.J. Wyrick, Virgil Miller Jr. and Andrea Lewis joined Webb in voting for the measure, while Directors Lance Hines, Kumpuris and Joan Adcock joined Peck in voting against it. Director Antwan Phillips abstained.
