artigo.texto: Candidates challenging Rep. Higgins weigh in on SpaceX, carbon capture, data centers Meet the candidates for Louisiana’s 3rd Congressional District LAKE CHARLES, La. (KPLC) - Meet the five people challenging Rep. Clay Higgins for his seat in the U.S. House, representing parts of Southwest Louisiana and Acadiana. NOV. 3 ELECTION: - Early voting locations and what’s on your ballot - Key races to watch in Louisiana and across the country in the 2026 election This year’s Congressional races have been a rollercoaster for voters across the state. Voters in Louisiana’s 3rd Congressional District were originally supposed to choose their next representative through separate party primaries back in May. That changed in April, when the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Louisiana’s congressional map. The ruling didn’t target District 3 directly, but Governor Jeff Landry suspended primary elections for all six of Louisiana’s U.S. House seats while the state redrew its map. Because of the compressed timeline that followed, Louisiana reverted to its older “jungle primary” system for Congress this cycle, meaning candidates from every party run against each other on the same ballot, rather than in separate party primaries. That’s why Republican incumbent Clay Higgins, Republican challenger Kate Cotten, Democratic nominee John Day, Priscilla Gonzalez and Caleb Walker, and Tia LeBrun are all on the same Nov. 3 ballot. If no candidate wins more than 50% of the vote on Nov. 3, the top two finishers will meet in a runoff on Dec. 12. We requested an interview with Rep. Higgins for this story. His office did not make him available. Here’s where the five participating candidates stand on four issues shaping the district right now: - The $100 billion SpaceX Starbase Louisiana spaceport planned for Vermilion Parish - Proposed carbon capture projects and the related fight over eminent domain - The rapid growth of data centers statewide, and - The use of non-disclosure agreements by Louisiana elected officials. Kate Cotten (R) Background Cotten runs Cotten’s Downtown, a family hamburger restaurant in Lake Charles. She first worked at Cotten’s at 12 years old, when she started helping her father. She says she’s been a registered Republican her entire life. Cotten entered the race later than most of the field; she says she decided to run specifically because of how the primary rules changed. “The decision was made to put all the qualifying Democrats on the November ballot against Clay Higgins, an incumbent Republican in a red state,” Cotten said. “With the people only voting party lines, I saw that as an opportunity for him to perhaps win outright because their vote would be split so much... I think it’s important that if Republicans win, that it’s a fair race.” SpaceX Cotten says she doesn’t have enough information yet to take a firm position on the incentive package Louisiana offered SpaceX, but she’s skeptical of the promised benefits. “I would really need to see more research that proves that development like that results in positive impacts for our coast and our community,” Cotten said. “I’ve yet to see anything that showed that. Promises, yes, but hard evidence that shows we...” She added: “Any time that these projects are launched, there is a cost to the environment and we need to just be upfront and honest about it.” Asked what she saw as the district’s biggest opportunity among the issues discussed, Cotten pointed to SpaceX. “I would imagine SpaceX would be the biggest opportunity as it’s one of the newer things, and when a product is new, there are opportunities, chances to get in on the ground floor,” she said. “But again, due diligence must be done and how it’s going to affect us.” Carbon capture and eminent domain Cotten said she isn’t familiar enough with carbon capture specifically to take a position. On the broader question of whether companies should be able to use eminent domain to acquire land for CO2 pipelines, she’s the only candidate in the field who stopped short of supporting a ban. “Anytime that you take a right away from an American, I have a lot of hesitation,” Cotten said. “I think it’s something that should be decided on a case-by-case basis. And any sort of a widespread ban I’m hesitant to support.” Data centers Cotten said she opposes shifting the cost of new power infrastructure onto ratepayers, if that’s how the billing structure actually works. “What I’ve heard is that a customer’s rate is based on the usage in that area and that these data centers were going to result in higher bills for the customers,” she said. “If that’s how it works exactly, I absolutely don’t support that.” She declined to answer what conditions she’d want attached to a data center project in the district. NDAs Cotten opposes the use of non-disclosure agreements for most government economic development deals, with one caveat. “I don’t support it outside of maybe proprietary information for their line of business,” she explained, referring to NDA’s commonly used in private business deals. “But when it has to do with pricing transparency and maybe tax breaks, things of that nature, I don’t support NDAs... It’s imperative that we be transparent about these deals.” She named NDAs as the field’s biggest risk: “If it’s not technology related to their line of business, why shouldn’t the public know what sort of a tax break someone got?” John Day (D) Background John Day, a Lake Charles Democrat, has spent roughly 30 years working in healthcare, insurance and the private sector. He says that background shaped his decision to run. Day was endorsed by the Louisiana Democratic Party, but since there was no primary, he is one of several Democrats vying for the seat. “I started running because I thought I could do a better job than Clay Higgins,” Day said. “I was disgusted and embarrassed.” But asked why voters should choose him, Day pointed to his career expertise in insurance and healthcare as some of the many reasons he’s qua

artigo.texto: ARC Capital compra data center em sua estreia na Europa Transação de 100 milhões de francos em Genebra deve ser seguida por outras quatro aquisições A brasileira ARC Capital fez na Suíça a primeira operação de sua plataforma europeia. Acaba de comprar um data center de 9,7 megawatts, com licenças para chegar a 20 MW, ao lado do aeroporto de Genebra e próximo à Organização Europeia para a Investigação Nuclear (CERN). Trata-se de um negócio de 100 milhões de francos suíços (cerca de R$ 609 milhões). A gestora já desembolsou 65 milhões francos, sendo 10 milhões em equity e 55 milhões em dívida. Os 35 milhões restantes virão também de dívida e a ARC deve ficar com cerca de 40% do cheque final após reunir coinvestidores na transação. “Seguimos o modelo de atuação do Brasil, com capital proprietário e chamando coinvestidores, e também como financiadores”, diz Vinícius Senger, o sócio da ARC responsável pela operação na Europa. O data center adquirido foi operado no passado pela IBM e vendido a uma família suíça, que contratou a CBRE para a manutenção. “Não tinha nem poeira”, diz Senger, que está fechando o contrato com o novo ocupante. A operação nasceu de uma parceria firmada no início do ano com a Gira Power, plataforma de Wissam Anastas, ex-head de infraestrutura do Deutsche Bank. Ele é minoritário no equity e atua na prospecção de ativos e captação clientes. Outros quatro data centers estão em negociação avançada e vão ficar sob a mesma holding. Ainda este ano, a ARC deve fechar a aquisição de um ativo na Alemanha e os outros três, que ficam na Noruega, França e Suécia, no primeiro trimestre de 2027. Senger se mudou para Londres há quase dois anos e desde então analisou com o time local, composto por sete pessoas, mais de 450 negócios em 20 países do continente. São quatro teses principais de investimentos por ali. A primeira é a de data centers de médio e grande porte e a segunda é o NAV finance, em que a ARC dá crédito a outras gestoras com garantia nos ativos de seus fundos. A terceira é a de defesa, que financia empresas com contratos com governos de rating AAA e dificuldade de acesso a capital de giro, num momento de alta nos gastos do setor. Um banco italiano, por exemplo, não financia empresa fora da Itália, e a ARC entra com invoice finance. A quarta, batizada de sniper shot, seriam operações com prazo curto e com gatilho de eventos específicos, que não se enquadram no perfil das outras teses mas no perfil de estruturação da casa. Para o executivo, a ARC tem competitividade nas transações pela flexibilidade de cheque - enquanto os grandes grupos de operações estruturados focam apenas operações bilionárias - e agilidade na concessão. “Não falta capital na Europa, mas falta flexibilidade. A gente consegue fazer um desembolso em quatro ou cinco dias”, diz. Até meados do ano que vem, a ARC deve investir cerca de 500 milhões de euros (R$ 2,8 bilhões), considerando as tratativas mais avançadas no momento. Desse montante, cerca de 150 milhões de euros devem ir para a tese de defesa, com o restante entre NAV finance e data centers.

artigo.texto: During the European Union-Montenegro Investment Conference, power utility Elektroprivreda Crne Gore signed four memorandums of understanding: with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and companies Qair, Akuo Energy, and Mantel Capture. The EU – Montenegro Investment Conference (AIM 2026), titled From Partnerships to Projects, was held on October 20–21 in Portonovi. It brought together representatives of European institutions, international financial organizations, investors, and leading companies. The memorandum of understanding between state-owned power company Elektroprivreda Crne Gore (EPCG), state-owned coal mine Rudnik Uglja Pljevlja, and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) establishes a framework for cooperation on the Pljevlja energy transition project, according to EPCG. Battery installation planned within the mining complex Planned activities include the development of a solar power plant with a battery energy storage system (BESS) on the site of the former mining complex, as well as solutions for district heating and thermal energy storage. The memorandum was signed by Nikola Madžgalj, Executive Manager of the Department for Legal Affairs at EPCG, Rudnik Uglja Pljevlja (RUP) CEO Nemanja Laković, and EBRD’s Managing Director for South‑Eastern Europe Grzegorz Zieliński. The signing was attended by Minister of Energy and Mining Admir Šahmanović and Executive Manager of the Department for Development and Investments at EPCG Ivan Mrvaljević. Laković: Two projects prepared in less than two years Nemanja Laković stressed that Rudnik Uglja Pljevlja, through new investments, business diversification, and partnership with the Government of Montenegro and the EU, strives to secure a sustainable future for the company and the economy of the Pljevlja region. “Regarding the energy transition, we have developed two projects in less than two years. We have the 62 MW Grevo solar power plant and a 2.2 MW small hydropower plant on the Ćehotina River,” Laković explained. Additional development directions include new industrial and commercial activities, including the production of personal protective equipment, construction operations, an asphalt facility, and investment in the timber industry, considering that 60% of Montenegro’s forests are located in the municipality of Pljevlja. Partnership with Akuo Energy for solar, wind, and BESS development The term sheet between EPCG and France-based Akuo Energy envisages cooperation on the development of solar parks, wind farms, and BESS. The goal of the cooperation is to increase renewable energy capacity and enhance the stability of the power system, EPCG said. The document was signed by Akuo CEO Bruno Bensasson. Of note, the company is expanding its activities in Southeastern Europe, with investments ahead in Montenegro, Greece, Kosovo*, North Macedonia, and Serbia. Akuo is developing a portfolio of 1.3 GW of green energy projects in the region, dominantly solar and wind. Qair and EPCG to focus on solar power plants EPCG also signed a term sheet with the company Qair Montenegro, laying the foundations for joint development, financing, construction, and management of solar power plant and wind farm projects in Montenegro, with a focus on photovoltaic plants. Louis Blanchard, CEO of Qair International, signed the document on behalf of the company. Of note, the French company signed a grid connection agreement for its Rudine solar power plant in February 2025 and received a construction permit in July of this year. Cooperation with Mantel Capture on CCS project The memorandum of understanding with US-based Mantel Capture opens opportunities for cooperation in the field of carbon capture and storage (CCS) technologies. The focus will be on the potential application of such solutions at the coal-fired power plant Pljevlja and the possibility of reducing emissions. The MoU was signed by co-founder and CEO Cameron Halliday. “Power generation is a growing focus for Mantel as utilities look for practical ways to reduce emissions while maintaining reliable energy supply,” Halliday said. Šahmanović: Results of reforms are increasingly turning into concrete investments According to Admir Šahmanović, Minister of Energy and Mining, Montenegro is entering a new phase of energy development, in which the results of implemented reforms are increasingly turning into concrete investments, new production capacities, and international partnerships. “Our ambition is not only to produce more electricity, but for energy to become the basis for industrial development, new technologies, and better-paid jobs,” he said. Total value of energy projects under implementation exceeds EUR 800 million The minister noted that an investment cycle worth EUR 463 million has been launched since 2025, while the total value of energy projects under implementation exceeds EUR 800 million. As a significant example, he highlighted the establishment of a joint venture between EPCG and UAE-based Masdar. The initial projects include the development of 150 MW of solar capacity, Šahmanović added. Speaking on the panel Strengthening Energy Resilience: Investments in Renewable Energy Sources, he pointed out that the energy transition today cannot be viewed solely as a matter of replacing conventional sources with renewables, but as one of the largest economic and industrial transformations of the modern world.

artigo.texto: Local business owners trained by OpenAI share thoughts on $20 billion data center Business owners say early skepticism has eased as OpenAI answers community questions SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - Small business owners who took part in a training session with OpenAI are sharing their thoughts on the company’s $20 billion data center project planned for Effingham County. OpenAI says the training is one of the ways it is giving back to the community as it prepares to build the data center. Business owners describe early skepticism The agreement between Effingham County and OpenAI drew opposition from hundreds of people when it was first announced. Tim Long, who runs True North Legacy Group and Savannah Honor Flights, took part in Thursday’s training. He said his neighborhood was skeptical when they found out about the deal. “That caused us to engage more and figure out, ask those questions, talk to us about their water supply, electricity and all that stuff, what does it mean for us as a community? And I’ve been really satisfied with what we’re hearing and seeing,” Long said. Long said fear surrounding the data center campus can stem from rumors. “I think it’s the fear of the unknown, and what I’ve seen is this data center is going to be done differently,” Long said. OpenAI says it wants community input Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s chief of financial operations, took part in Thursday’s small business training. She was unable to speak with WTOC. OpenAI spokesperson Aaron McLear said the company wants more community engagement on how it can be a good partner. “That’s our guiding light on this entire project, we want to make sure that the community benefits from having this data center,” McLear said. Another business owner says he’s a ‘big fan’ of data centers Geoff Thatcher, owner of design firm Creative Principals, said he toured data centers 20 years ago. “I’m a big fan of data centers,” Thatcher said. Thatcher said he believes the county should embrace the future and its role in it. “I’m a design firm, I have two kids at Savannah College of Art and Design, and a lot of people say to me ‘ohh AI is going to put me out of business,’ I always respond to them and say ‘no, AI’s only going to put you out of business if you don’t learn how to use it,’” Thatcher said. Thatcher said he believes the data center will go on to help the world. Long said he remains more cautious in his outlook, but events like the small business training have made him more optimistic. “If you will and so time will tell, for sure, the check’s in the mail, but the answers to the questions that we’ve asked have sufficed,” Long said. $2 million grant announced for Atlas Park Effingham County and OpenAI also announced a $2 million grant for Atlas Park. The funds will go toward a trail system for walking and biking. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Franklin County panel addresses data centers, but residents question transparency FRANKLIN COUNTY, Va. (WDBJ) - The Franklin County Board of Supervisors held a panel discussion on data centers this week. No vote was taken and no project is currently on the table. The board described the session as an opportunity for people to learn more about what is and is not true about the experience of having a data center in the county. Panelists who work with data centers regularly were brought in to speak to supervisors. Afterward, some residents said the real story is whether anything discussed will change how the board moves forward, and whether the board will be transparent about its decisions. What other localities learned The panel walked supervisors through what other localities have learned from hosting data centers, including water limits and tax deals. Mecklenburg County, which has had a Microsoft data center for 20 years, said it should have asked for more. “Today, the environment is much more favorable to put much more leverage on the locality against the data center,” said Alex Gottschalk, Mecklenburg County administrator. “Our tax rate would be much higher.” Water supply concerns raised The Western Virginia Water Authority said the water source is key, and groundwater will not get the job done, at least not at the scale that would make a deal worthwhile for the county. “Groundwater is just not a reliable source in this part of Virginia for large scale industrial activity,” said Michael McEvoy, executive director of the Western Virginia Water Authority. “We can supply about a million gallons a day. It wouldn’t be a really big data center.” Resident says comparison is unbalanced Franklin County resident Christine Sizemore said the panel was not balanced. She said Mecklenburg County’s experience would not be Franklin County’s experience, based on where Summit View Park is located. “Their data centers are in an industrial park that is away from communities, away from residential areas, which is not the case here,” Sizemore said. Common ground on transparency Gottschalk and Sizemore agreed that more transparency would be beneficial. “I would strongly suggest that the priorities be set out in that community and all the needs be articulated and then the potential funding sources for those needs be identified,” Gottschalk said. “A data center may be among them. It may not be among them. I think that’s a choice that should be reserved for each locality to make on their own.” Copyright 2026 WDBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: President Donald Trump is calling for data centers to pay for their own power and pay dividends to local communities — a stark change for the president less than two weeks before the election and as opposition to data centers is growing. In Memphis, Tenn., where the City Council was weighing a temporary moratorium on data centers on Tuesday, ultimately voting against the move, attendees used fiery language to describe their feelings. “Lives are at stake and blood is on your hands,” council meeting attendee Tikeila Rucker said. "Supporting a pause on data centers is a vote for reaffirming your dedication to the people of Memphis, not the billionaire class," said attendee Amber Sherman. It’s a scene playing out across the country as Americans raise concerns that data centers, which provide the computing power for artificial intelligence, will drive up electric bills and consume massive amounts of water. Now the president is pitching a new solution. He wrote early Wednesday morning that new data centers are “mandated by me to make their own electricity and give or sell any excess back to the local community.” He added: “If companies want to make their data centers popular, they should pay a ‘dividend’ to the community.” It was not immediately clear how the president’s demand could be implemented. Trump’s social media post marks a shift in tone for the president, who previously criticized data center opponents as wanting to “end up being backwards and poor,” as he said at a rally earlier this month in Ohio. “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio,” he said. “You can’t just turn it off. They’ll go to China.” Todd Eisenstadt, research director at American University Center for Environmental Policy, said data centers are an easy target. He said there’s been a growing uneasiness with data centers tied with a more existential fear over the development of artificial intelligence. A new Washington Post-ABC-Ipsos poll found 66% of Americans oppose construction of new data centers and also disapprove of the president’s handling of AI. “Perhaps the wind has shifted and this is a defining issue of the election,” Eisenstadt told Spectrum News. “And he’s on the wrong side of it. So, he’s trying to swim the other way here at the last minute.” The number of data centers has exploded. Estimates show there are at least 3,000 nationwide.

After holding off on data center-related stocks since our last Micron buy five weeks ago, we are nibbling on the power company GE Vernova into Thursday's sell-off. AI-related semiconductors and industrial stocks are getting hit hard as investors grow increasingly concerned about the source of capital to support the data center buildout. It's less about demand for AI products and more about how these investments will be funded as cash flows get used up and debt-related financing becomes less attractive to investors. But after steering clear of the group for so long, we are dipping back in with GE Vernova and upgrading our rating to a 1 again to play for a bounce here, with demand for intelligence and AI applications continuing to strengthen. artigo.texto: CATL shares drop 11% as new battery tax bites, full-quarter hit still to come CATL (SZSE: 300750, HKEX: 3750) closed down 11.41% at HK$364.80 (c. $46.48) in Hong Kong on October 21, 2026, after the battery maker's third-quarter profit slipped from the quarter before. Net profit attributable to shareholders was 21.25 billion CNY (c. $3.16 billion) for the three months to September 30, up 14.54% from a year earlier but down 5.77% from the second quarter. Sales kept growing much faster than profit. Revenue rose 58.58% to 165.22 billion CNY (c. $24.59 billion), yet gross margin fell to 20.69%, from 23.15% in the second quarter and 25.80% a year earlier. That is CATL's lowest quarterly margin since the fourth quarter of 2022. Advertisement – Continue scrolling for more Part of the squeeze is a new tax. China resumed a 2% consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries and four other battery types on September 1, 2026, and the rate doubles to 4% on September 1, 2027. CATL's taxes and surcharges line reached 3.54 billion CNY (c. $526.7 million) in the first nine months, up from 1.84 billion CNY a year earlier. Almost all of that rise landed in one quarter. Third-quarter taxes and surcharges were 2.21 billion CNY (c. $329.5 million), against 597 million CNY (c. $88.8 million) a year earlier, after a first half of 1.33 billion CNY. The third quarter carried only one month of the new tax, so the fourth quarter will be the first to bear it in full. Advertisement – Continue scrolling for more On the earnings call on October 20, CFO Zheng Shu said the tax is built into the product price, so CATL cannot pass it on to carmakers until prices are renegotiated. Those talks are still under way, and management said the outcome differs by customer and by timing. Asked how much of the cost CATL would carry itself, the company said it was too early to say. Export rebates are the second hit. The VAT rebate on exported batteries was cut from 9% to 6% on April 1 and will be scrapped on January 1, 2027. CATL said the cut barely showed in second-quarter results because revenue is booked some time after shipment, so it came through more fully in the third quarter. CATL's revenue growth of 56.19% for the nine months roughly matched the 57.6% rise in China's power and storage battery sales, to 1,681.7 GWh. The result came in below forecasts. Bernstein had expected quarterly net profit of 22.9 billion CNY (c. $3.41 billion), Goldman Sachs 24 billion CNY (c. $3.57 billion) and CLSA 25 billion to 26 billion CNY. It called this a redistribution of profit along the chain rather than an ordinary price war, with CATL hit first and smaller battery makers hit harder. The Hong Kong shares had already fallen 6.58% to HK$411.80 on October 20, so the two sessions took about 17% off the price. In Shenzhen, the A shares fell more than 12% on October 21 and now sit more than 50% below their record high of May 7, 2026. An executive said CATL began shortening payment terms and paying some suppliers in advance in the third quarter, and that this could weigh on cash flow for a while. On October 10 it signed a long-term agreement with SERES (HKEX: 9927), whose AITO models have all used CATL batteries, to expand their plant-in-plant battery project at the SERES Super Factory to more than 20 GWh a year. That network added Huawei's Yinwang as a partner on October 19. Storage is the bright spot CATL keeps pointing to. Mesa Grande Band Tribe completes first public clean energy installation Solar and batteries power three tribal facilities Systems cut costs and ride out grid outages Stock video by Los Muertos Crew via Pexels Oct 20, 2026 Mesa Grande Band Completes First Public Clean Energy Installation on Reservation The Mesa Grande Band of Diegueno Mission Indians, working with the Solar Electric Light Fund, has finished installing solar and battery storage systems at three Tribal facilities on the Mesa Grande Reservation in San Diego County, California, according to the Tribe. The project represents the first public clean energy installation on the reservation and advances the Tribe's long-term effort to strengthen energy sovereignty. Solar panels and batteries now serve the Tekamuk, Hallyeyaaw and Golden Eagle administration buildings. The three structures function as civic and community hubs, supporting Tribal government, housing services, cultural and educational programming, food distribution and emergency response. The solar systems are sized to cover the three facilities' present electricity needs while leaving room for future growth. Combined, they are expected to produce roughly 60 MWh of solar electricity each year and to reduce the Tribe's electricity costs by at least $16,780 annually. The battery storage allows the administration buildings to keep running independently of the electric grid during outages, which the Tribe describes as common in the rural community. Curtis La Chusa, chairman of the Mesa Grande Tribal Council, commented that electricity is often taken for granted and tends to go unnoticed until service is lost, while noting that power interruptions are a regular reality at Mesa Grande. He said outages there can last for days at a time, disrupting the services the Tribe provides to its members. The installation builds on more than two decades of Tribal efforts to expand access to reliable, affordable clean energy. Grid electricity did not reach the reservation until the 1950s, and some homes remain off the grid today, relying on small generators for basic household needs. Over the years Mesa Grande has pursued residential solar, renewable energy planning and workforce development. Four Tribal members with prior solar installation training were employed on the project. Bob Freling, executive director of the Solar Electric Light Fund, the nonprofit that facilitated the project, said reliable and affordable energy gives communities room to invest in future priorities. He indicated that lower energy costs and stronger resilience can free up resources while providing a sustainable foundation for growth, and that the organization looks forward to seeing how clean energy helps Mesa Grande meet its goals. The clean energy work coincides with the Tribe's start on a long-term plan for new housing and community infrastructure. The plan calls for 1,500 new homes to address housing affordability and supply shortages that have historically limited how many members can live on Tribal land. The development would include the first new housing built on the reservation since 2005. La Chusa said Mesa Grande has a bright future ahead, describing the effort as beginning with enabling Tribal members to return home and providing the spaces and services needed for them to thrive. artigo.texto: Denton City Council members unanimously voted Oct. 13 to adopt development code amendments related to data center zoning restrictions, their proximity to homes and required environmental protections. The details The Denton Development Code updates are intended to prevent facilities from impacting neighboring homes and businesses, keep land use standards up to date with current data center trends, protect water supplies and prevent surface water and groundwater contamination, Assistant Planning Director Angie Glass said at the meeting. They also act as a stopgap while the city considers a moratorium, a temporary pause on accepting and processing new applications. “[These amendments protect] us more while we're going through the moratorium phase,” Councilmember George Ferrie said. Updates to the code for data centers include: - Restricting data centers from being constructed anywhere in Denton to zoning districts labeled as light industrial, heavy industrial and public facility, all three of which require a special use permit - Restricting water cooling methods to closed-loop or free-air systems - Requiring water and wastewater demand studies with their initial application - Expanding the minimum setback from residential zones from 100 feet to 300 feet - Prohibiting any light spillover into residential property lines - Requiring approvals from the Texas Public Utility Commission and Electric Reliability Council of Texas prior to placement on a City Council agenda for consideration The amendments apply to the two previously permitted data centers in Denton if they expand or modify their sites in the future, along with new data center developments within city limits. The city rejected a new data center application in early October because it did not meet all of the city’s initial submission requirements, Glass said. City Attorney Mack Reinwand said parts of that application could potentially be reviewed under the prior standards. What’s next The council will hold the second public hearing and the first reading of the proposed data center moratorium Oct. 27. The first public hearing was held Sept. 22. City Council is required to hold two public hearings before it can vote on passing the moratorium. The earliest council members can vote on implementing a moratorium is at their Dec. 1 meeting. If the resolution passes, all new development and permitting for data centers in Denton city limits will be halted effective immediately, according to previous reporting.

artigo.texto: CATL has unveiled its Dual-Electric Range Extender architecture, a system designed for heavy electric trucks that combines a main swappable pack with a fixed backup battery. The proposal aims to reduce fleet downtime and position battery swapping as an alternative to conventional charging in road freight transport. How the swappable pack and the 77 kWh reserve work ð The system uses a main pack available in two capacities, 432 or 513 kWh, which can be depleted to 5 percent of its charge before going to a swap station. There, the replacement is completed in about five minutes, a time that avoids long waits at charging points. The fixed backup battery, at 77 kWh, also allows the truck to be moved to the station or to cover short journeys when the main pack has already been removed. CATL expects 900 swap stations in 2026 and 2000 in 2027, with 13,000 initial orders and estimated savings of more than $68,700 over three years compared with diesel. Five minutes to change the battery and three years to recoup the investment â¡ The idea sounds good on paper: stop for five minutes, change the pack and continue on the route. The fine print appears when one asks who builds those 2000 stations and with what money. Meanwhile, the calculation of $68,700 in savings over three years invites the question of whether it includes the coffee at the stops, because the haulier crossing half the country looking for a swap point may not have time to check.

artigo.texto: China’s CATL, BAIC target 1 million cars with new battery swap network The companies will also cooperate on infrastructure construction and new business models, among others [BEIJING] Contemporary Amperex Technology Co Ltd (CATL) and Beijing Automotive Group (BAIC) will develop a battery-swapping system, with the aim of servicing one million vehicles, as the battery giant looks to grow what is seen as a long-term revenue stream. BAIC will bring compatible models in multiple brands into CATL’s Choco-Swap network, as well as open its dealership network to support the deployment of battery-swapping stations, the Chinese battery giant said on Thursday (Oct 22). The companies will cooperate on vehicle and battery development, infrastructure construction, battery management and new business models, it said, without disclosing a timeline for the one-million-vehicle target. BAIC’s total new-energy vehicle sales were around 390,000 in 2025. The deal underscores CATL’s intensifying effort to make battery swapping a larger part of China’s electric-vehicle market, and diversify earnings beyond the one-time nature of selling a single battery pack to a carmaker. Battery swapping is currently faster than recharging, but CATL’s efforts to build a network face hurdles including costly investments in stations and spare batteries, and reluctance from automakers that have to standardise their vehicle architecture to accommodate swapping. Competition is intensifying in China’s battery market as domestic car sales cool. CATL’s shares tumbled this week after it reported slower-than-expected quarterly profit growth. The agreement with BAIC follows a separate partnership announced on Monday between CATL, its battery-swapping subsidiary, and Huawei Technologies’ automotive technology business. artigo.texto: A Vertiv, empresa global de infraestrutura digital crítica, anunciou o lançamento do Vertiv SmartAisle 3, uma solução modular para Data Centers que integra backup de energia, gerenciamento térmico, monitoramento e distribuição de energia em uma única arquitetura. Disponível na Argentina, Chile, Peru, Uruguai, Paraguai, Brasil e Bolívia, a solução pode ser configurada para suportar até 120 kW de carga total de TI. O Vertiv SmartAisle 3 combina racks, sistema de alimentação ininterrupta (UPS), gerenciamento térmico, monitoramento e segurança física em uma solução integrada. Sua arquitetura incorpora Inteligência Artificial (IA) e recursos de autoaprendizagem projetados para dar suporte à operação do sistema e ao gerenciamento de energia. Entre esses recursos, a solução pode monitorar as condições operacionais e ajustar a temperatura de acordo com o ambiente. Essas funcionalidades podem ajudar a alcançar economia de energia de até 20% em comparação com sistemas sem recursos de IA, mantendo as condições operacionais definidas para a infraestrutura. “Aplicações intensivas em dados estão levando mais organizações a avaliar como podem expandir ou modernizar sua infraestrutura sem adicionar complexidade operacional desnecessária”, afirmou Felipe Vasco, diretor de Aplicações de Tecnologia da Vertiv Latam. “O Vertiv SmartAisle 3 reúne energia, gerenciamento térmico, distribuição e monitoramento em uma arquitetura modular que pode se adaptar a diferentes requisitos de capacidade e implantação. Isso é feito incorporando recursos de monitoramento e controle essenciais para dar suporte às operações de infraestrutura”, completou. A solução inclui um sistema flexível de distribuição de energia por barramento, projetado para simplificar a distribuição elétrica dentro do ambiente modular e reduzir a complexidade associada ao cabeamento no local. Também incorpora cabeamento integrado, sensores na parte frontal e traseira dos racks e recursos de monitoramento centralizado para supervisionar variáveis como temperatura, umidade e status das portas. O Vertiv SmartAisle 3 inclui, ainda, um painel de controle com tela sensível ao toque de 15 polegadas e a opção de upgrade para uma tela local de 95 polegadas na porta. Isso proporciona maior visibilidade das condições operacionais, além de dar suporte ao monitoramento e à solução de problemas do sistema. A solução pode simplificar o gerenciamento dos sistemas de monitoramento e controle ambiental, ajudando a reduzir o ciclo de falhas operacionais em até 75%. Além disso, os principais componentes são integrados e testados em fábrica antes da instalação no local. O Vertiv SmartAisle 3 faz parte do portfólio de soluções modulares integradas da Vertiv e pode dar suporte a diversas aplicações em setores que incluem bancos e serviços financeiros, governo, educação, infraestrutura de Edge e outros ambientes que exigem energia, refrigeração e monitoramento integrados em uma solução modular. artigo.texto: Offshore Data Center e Kalypso miram gás encalhado para computação offshore A Offshore Data Center LLC firmou uma parceria com a Kalypso Offshore Energy com o objetivo de ajudar proprietários de gás offshore a monetizar reservas encalhadas, subutilizadas e subvalorizadas por meio da geração de energia para computação de IA no mar, segundo o World Oil. As duas empresas avaliarão instalações recém-construídas, bem como a reutilização de infraestrutura offshore existente, incluindo estruturas ociosas selecionadas, para computação modular de borda e de inferência. Art Schroeder, fundador e diretor-presidente da Offshore Data Center, observou que muitas plataformas no Golfo da América estão programadas para descomissionamento, embora algumas possam ainda manter vida estrutural útil. Ele afirmou que as empresas pretendem colaborar com operadores e reguladores, junto com a Kalypso, para explorar a instalação de data centers modulares em ativos existentes adequados, gerando nova receita a partir de recursos offshore e potencialmente adiando determinados gastos com a Obrigação de Aposentadoria de Ativos. A instalação da geração de energia e da computação próximas aos recursos de gás offshore tem como objetivo encurtar a cadeia tradicional, na qual o gás é convertido em energia e depois enviado a um data center em terra. A Offshore Data Center está reunindo parceiros como a Horton do Brasil, cujos projetos de casco semissubmersível, segundo as empresas, poderiam ser até 50% mais leves, com estabilidade aprimorada. De acordo com as empresas, isso permitiria que a construção na costa do Golfo dos Estados Unidos competisse com estaleiros na Coreia, na China e em Singapura. Parceiros da Offshore Data Center também fornecem sistemas de resfriamento em circuito fechado destinados a reduzir substancialmente as cargas de resfriamento dos data centers. A Kalypso liderará o trabalho de cabos submarinos que ligam as instalações à rede elétrica, às redes de comunicação e à costa. Isso abrange o desenvolvimento de rotas, a engenharia, a instalação e a conexão de cabos de fibra óptica, de energia e umbilicais, além de suporte de reparo, operações e manutenção. Owen Rataj, diretor da Kalypso Offshore Energy, afirmou que um data center offshore é tão bom quanto os cabos que o conectam, e que fibra de baixa latência até a costa, conexões de energia confiáveis e capacidade de reparo e manutenção próximas aos ativos são o que transformam uma plataforma offshore em capacidade de computação utilizável.

artigo.texto: - O PiauÃ realiza primeira reuniÃ£o do Conselho Gestor do REDD+ no CEA, em Teresina, para avanÃ§ar na polÃtica de crÃ©dito de carbono. - O encontro reÃºne representantes do poder pÃºblico, sociedade civil, povos indÃgenas e comunidades tradicionais para discutir a polÃtica ambiental. - A iniciativa busca reduzir emissÃµes de gases de efeito estufa e beneficiar comunidades que preservam o meio ambiente. - O secretÃ¡rio do Meio Ambiente destacou a importÃ¢ncia do diÃ¡logo e da participaÃ§Ã£o social na construÃ§Ã£o da polÃtica de crÃ©dito de carbono. - O REDD+ tambÃ©m visa viabilizar pagamentos por serviÃ§os ambientais e associar preservaÃ§Ã£o Ã economia local. O Piauí avançou na implantação da política estadual de crédito de carbono com a realização da primeira reunião do Conselho Gestor do REDD+, nesta terça-feira (20), no Centro de Educação Ambiental (CEA), em Teresina. A iniciativa busca reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa provocadas pelo desmatamento e pela degradação florestal, além de criar mecanismos para beneficiar comunidades que contribuem para a preservação ambiental. O encontro foi aberto pelo secretário de Estado do Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos, Feliphe Araújo. O conselho reúne representantes do poder público, da sociedade civil, da academia, dos povos indígenas, das comunidades quilombolas e tradicionais, da agricultura familiar e do setor produtivo. A proposta é garantir participação social, transparência e segurança na construção da política, que poderá gerar recursos para a conservação das florestas e beneficiar populações envolvidas na proteção dos biomas piauienses. Política prevê benefícios para comunidades Feliphe Araújo destacou que a implantação do projeto é uma das prioridades da gestão estadual. Segundo o secretário, a política precisa ser construída com regulamentação, diálogo e participação dos diferentes setores da sociedade. “Queremos proteger nossas florestas e, ao mesmo tempo, gerar recursos para beneficiar as pessoas que ajudam a preservar o meio ambiente. Por isso, é fundamental que esse processo seja construído com diálogo, transparência e participação de todos os setores”, afirmou. De acordo com o secretário, o Estado já avançou na elaboração de normas, na regulamentação da iniciativa e na busca por parceiros para viabilizar o projeto. A experiência de outros estados, como o Tocantins, também é utilizada como referência para orientar as próximas etapas. REDD+ busca reduzir emissões e preservar florestas O REDD+ é um mecanismo voltado à redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa associadas ao desmatamento e à degradação florestal. A iniciativa também pode viabilizar pagamentos por serviços ambientais, com benefícios para povos indígenas, comunidades quilombolas, populações tradicionais e agricultores familiares. Além da política de crédito de carbono, o secretário ressaltou a importância de associar a preservação ambiental ao desenvolvimento econômico. Entre as ações complementares citadas estão a recuperação de áreas degradadas, a educação ambiental, a fiscalização e a prevenção e o combate aos incêndios florestais. A primeira reunião do Conselho Gestor representa uma etapa na organização da governança do projeto. A estrutura busca assegurar que as decisões sejam debatidas coletivamente e que a política estadual seja desenvolvida com responsabilidade ambiental e participação social.

artigo.texto: Warrick County weighs new data center rules as Alcoa ‘Project Alloy’ draws closer WARRICK CO., Ind. (WFIE) - A massive data center could be coming to Warrick County, and the company behind it isn’t an outsider — it’s Alcoa, a business that has operated in the county for decades. The project, known as “Project Alloy,” is a proposed data center eyed for roughly 700 acres of Alcoa-owned land near the company’s power plant. Warrick County Commissioners, county legal counsel and representatives of Warrick County Economic Development met with the development team on October 16 in a closed executive session — a meeting allowed under Indiana’s Open Door Law for interviews and negotiations with an industrial or commercial prospect. County officials say the discussion was preliminary and informational. No vote was taken, no nondisclosure agreement was signed, and no commitment was made. “I find it kind of exciting that it’s not somebody coming from outside here. It is here. They are Warrick County. They live and work here. They have a vested interest in the success of the county, not just the success of the data center, but the success of the people that live here,” said Warrick County Commissioner Sarah Seaton. What We Know About Project Alloy Based solely on information the development team provided to the county, officials say Project Alloy includes a letter of intent to develop roughly 700 acres of Alcoa-owned land, with only a fraction of that acreage expected to be built out and the rest left undeveloped as separation from surrounding properties. The development team says it has an existing relationship with a prospective end user and told the county there will not be any adverse effects on existing Alcoa or Kaiser operations. The project remains in the due-diligence stage. According to the county, Alcoa’s evaluation will address environmental conditions, water supply and cooling, electrical demand and grid impacts, threatened and endangered species, geological and mine-subsidence risk, drainage and floodplain conditions, traffic, noise, lighting, air emissions, and fire protection needs. More fully developed plans aren’t expected for county review until sometime in the first half of 2027, according to the development team. The county is not paying for those studies, and officials say they have not been told who will conduct them or what methods will be used. The county says it will ask the development team to share completed studies with the public if it moves forward with permits. Commissioners emphasize that none of this information has been independently verified. The county has not determined whether existing water, electric, road or public-safety capacity is sufficient, whether taxpayers or utility customers would bear additional costs, or whether the project would deliver the tax revenue, jobs or other economic benefits the development team has described. A New Rulebook, Regardless of Project Alloy’s Outcome Separately — and for months before Project Alloy became public — the Warrick County Commissioners and Area Plan Commission have been developing a permanent data center ordinance. Officials say the ordinance isn’t written around any single project; it’s meant to establish standards for any data center that might propose to locate in the county, including, but not limited to, Project Alloy. Earlier this year, the Area Plan Commission formed a committee to study data center development, drawing on input from residents, county officials and other stakeholders, and reviewing ordinances adopted in other jurisdictions. The draft ordinance would create a new “Data Center Overlay” (DC-O) zoning district. Under the proposal, a data center could only be built on property zoned both general industrial (M-2) and DC-O — and getting that DC-O designation would require a site-specific rezoning approved by elected county commissioners, not an administrative board. The ordinance also specifies that a data center cannot be approved through a special exception or similar process that bypasses that legislative vote. The draft includes specific numerical standards, including: - Noise: Operational sound from a project could not exceed 55 decibels (dBA) at a neighboring home or residential zoning boundary — roughly comparable to normal conversation — with stricter limits for tonal noise. - Lighting: Exterior lighting would be capped at 0.5 foot-candle at a neighboring residential boundary and limited to “warmer” bulb temperatures to reduce glare and light pollution. - Setbacks and buffers: Data center buildings would need to sit at least 300 feet from homes or residential zoning, with intensive outdoor equipment — generators, transformers, battery storage — set back at least 500 feet. A landscaped buffer of at least 100 feet would be required near residential property. - Water use: The ordinance would ban “once-through” cooling systems for routine operations, require water-efficient cooling technology, and require developers to disclose and cap peak-day water demand. - Decommissioning: Developers would be required to maintain a decommissioning and restoration plan, reviewed at least every five years, along with financial assurance to cover removal and restoration costs if a project shuts down or is abandoned. If a project fails to move forward, the ordinance is designed to return the property to its prior zoning. “Is it a good fit not just for the county, but for their specific site? Is it a good fit for the neighbors in the area? What is it going to do to local roads, traffic and things like that? And it gives us the ability to say, no, this probably isn’t going to work well for us, or we think we have found one that might,” Seaton said. How Residents Can Weigh In The ordinance remains a draft, and officials stress no final decision has been made. The public will get two formal chances to respond: - Area Plan Commission public hearing: November 2, 2026, 6 p.m., Friedman Park Event Center - Commissioners

artigo.texto: Demanda de data centers impulsiona vendas da WEG no exterior no 3º tri Mercado externo respondeu por 62,5% da receita da companhia, que produz geradores de energia e motores para sistemas de ventilação e refrigeração A demanda por equipamentos destinados a data centers contribuiu para o crescimento dos negócios da WEG no exterior no 3º trimestre de 2026. Segundo balanço divulgado nesta 4ª feira (21.out.2026), a fabricante brasileira registrou aumento nas vendas de geradores de energia e equipamentos industriais, principalmente na América do Norte. O mercado externo respondeu por 62,5% da receita da companhia, a maior participação de sua história. Eis a íntegra do relatório (PDF – 306 kB). A WEG registrou lucro líquido de R$ 1,67 bilhão no período, alta de 0,9% em relação ao mesmo trimestre de 2025. A receita operacional líquida somou R$ 10,86 bilhões, crescimento de 5,7% na comparação anual. Desse total, R$ 6,79 bilhões vieram do mercado externo, avanço de 8,3% em relação ao ano anterior. A demanda por data centers beneficia duas áreas de atuação da companhia. A divisão de geração, transmissão e distribuição de energia fornece geradores utilizados como fonte de eletricidade de reserva para essas instalações. Já a área de equipamentos eletroeletrônicos industriais atende à demanda por motores e sistemas de automação, que são utilizados em ventilação e refrigeração, necessários para controlar a temperatura dos equipamentos de processamento de dados. No segmento de geração, transmissão e distribuição de energia, a receita no mercado externo atingiu R$ 2,49 bilhões, alta de 24,1% em relação ao 3º trimestre de 2025. A WEG destacou o desempenho dos geradores Marathon, nos Estados Unidos, destinados principalmente ao fornecimento de energia de reserva para data centers. Esses equipamentos são produzidos por uma divisão da empresa norte-americana Regal Rexnord, adquirida pela WEG em 2024. As vendas de transformadores para reforço da infraestrutura elétrica dos Estados Unidos também contribuíram para o resultado da companhia no exterior. A divisão de equipamentos eletroeletrônicos industriais registrou receita externa de R$ 3,75 bilhões, crescimento de 1,1% na comparação anual. Segundo a companhia, houve continuidade da demanda por motores elétricos de baixa tensão e produtos de automação, com destaque para sistemas de ventilação e refrigeração para data centers, além dos setores de óleo e gás e mineração.

artigo.texto: A chegada de um data center a Belém coloca a capital paraense no centro de uma discussão que vai muito além da instalação de servidores. Enquanto novos projetos ampliam a capacidade de processamento de dados na Amazônia, a Região Norte ainda convive com gargalos de conectividade, custo de acesso e presença desigual de redes de fibra óptica. Dados da TIC Domicílios 2025 mostram que 17% dos domicílios do Norte permanecem sem acesso à internet. Entre os lares desconectados, 43% apontam o preço como principal motivo para não contratar o serviço. Outro indicador ajuda a dimensionar a distância em relação ao restante do país: 62% dos municípios nortistas possuem rede de transporte por fibra óptica, contra 78% na média nacional. É nesse cenário que Belém deve receber o BEL1, projeto anunciado pela Elea Data Centers. A estrutura terá capacidade inicial de 7,5 MW e operação prevista para o segundo trimestre de 2027. A instalação amplia a capacidade local de processamento de dados, mas, sozinha, não resolve os obstáculos que ainda limitam o acesso à economia digital na região. O que um data center muda na infraestrutura digital? Data centers são estruturas que concentram servidores e equipamentos responsáveis por armazenar, processar e distribuir grandes volumes de informações. Eles sustentam serviços em nuvem, plataformas digitais, sistemas empresariais, aplicações de inteligência artificial e uma série de operações que dependem de processamento contínuo de dados. Ter esse tipo de infraestrutura mais próximo pode reduzir distâncias percorridas pelas informações e beneficiar determinadas aplicações. Esse efeito, porém, depende de como o data center estará conectado a operadoras, provedores, empresas, universidades e instituições públicas. Na prática, a instalação do BEL1 não significa que a internet residencial ficará automaticamente mais rápida, que o preço dos planos cairá ou que municípios do interior passarão a ter conexão de melhor qualidade. Esses resultados dependem de outras etapas da infraestrutura digital, como expansão das redes de telecomunicações, atuação dos provedores locais, disponibilidade de fibra e investimentos em conectividade até o usuário final. Norte ainda está abaixo da média nacional em fibra óptica A desigualdade na infraestrutura aparece também na presença das chamadas redes de transporte, responsáveis por conectar redes locais a estruturas de maior capacidade. Segundo o Estudo Estratégico de Infraestrutura, publicado pelo Ministério do Planejamento e Orçamento com dados da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel), 62% dos municípios do Norte contam com esse tipo de conexão por fibra óptica. No conjunto do país, a proporção é de 78%. Em outras regiões, como o Sul, chega a 92%. A diferença mostra que a expansão da economia digital na Amazônia depende de investimentos que vão muito além dos grandes centros urbanos. Para que serviços digitais avancem de forma mais ampla, a infraestrutura precisa chegar também a cidades do interior e a territórios onde ainda existem limitações de acesso. Data center pode abrir espaço para pesquisa e inovação A presença de capacidade de processamento local também pode criar novas possibilidades para universidades, empresas e projetos que dependem de grande volume de dados. O professor e pesquisador Marcus Braga, da Universidade Federal Rural da Amazônia (UFRA), afirma que instituições da região já trabalham com inteligência artificial aplicada a problemas locais. “Nossas universidades já fazem pesquisas de IA aplicada, com soluções para problemas reais, coordenadas por profissionais amazônidas, com DNA do Norte, e com alta capacidade de contribuir com o desenvolvimento sustentável da nossa região”, afirma. Para Braga, uma aproximação maior entre universidades e empresas pode favorecer projetos de pesquisa, estágios e novas possibilidades de inserção profissional. “Esse encontro permite pensar em tecnologia a partir de questões amazônicas e valorizar quem já busca soluções para elas”, acrescenta. Novos projetos também pressionam demanda por profissionais A implantação de um data center envolve diferentes áreas, como construção civil, instalações elétricas, telecomunicações e segurança. Depois de entrar em operação, a estrutura também exige profissionais ligados à tecnologia, manutenção e gestão. Isso não significa, porém, que a chegada de um empreendimento desse porte represente automaticamente uma grande geração de empregos. A quantidade de vagas dependerá do avanço do projeto, do modelo operacional adotado e das contratações efetivamente realizadas. O movimento, no entanto, reforça a necessidade de formação de profissionais preparados para trabalhar em setores ligados à tecnologia, infraestrutura digital, inteligência artificial e processamento de dados. BEL1 terá capacidade inicial de 7,5 MW O BEL1 foi anunciado pela Elea Data Centers para Belém e deverá ser instalado próximo à subestação de alta tensão de Miramar. O projeto prevê capacidade inicial de 7,5 MW e possibilidade de expansão em etapas futuras. Segundo a empresa, a estrutura será preparada para atender cargas relacionadas à inteligência artificial e à computação em nuvem. A Amazônia já tem pessoas criando negócios, produzindo conhecimento e contando suas próprias histórias. “Ampliar a infraestrutura digital é uma oportunidade de dar mais alcance a esse trabalho e de fazer com que os próximos avanços da tecnologia também gerem oportunidades para a população da região”, finaliza Thaís Marçal, diretora de Relações Institucionais da Elea.

artigo.texto: Martin city leaders discuss regulations to get ahead of any potential data centers MARTIN, Tenn. (WBBJ) - The city of martin is getting ahead of a possible data center. City leaders held a meeting to set regulations before any project involving the construction of a data center is even proposed. They recommended capping noise at 60 decibels day and night, requiring 30 foot setbacks for small data centers, and 75 to 100 feet for hyperscale centers, keeping buildings mostly hidden from view, and limiting driveway access. The ordinance passed unanimously. “The regulations I’ve been working on for communities would define what a data center is and then would set up additional requirements, additional buffer from the nearest residential structure,” explained Donny Bunton, Martin city planner. If no regulation was put in before the proposal, it falls under general industrial use requirements, which are not as restrictive and do not include a buffer for the nearest residential structures. artigo.texto: Trending WHEELING - A preliminary draft of proposed amendments to the city of Wheeling’s Planning and Zoning code to include rules and regulations specifically for data centers was reviewed by city leaders on Tuesday night. Members of the Rules Committee of Wheeling City Council met at length prior to Tuesday night’s regular council meeting to discuss the proposed draft. Officials stressed the comprehensive document, currently 15 pages in length, is still a work in progress. However, several language tweaks and suggestions for changes were offered during Tuesday night’s session, and city leaders proposed the latest version of the draft be posted on the city’s website today in order to give the public the opportunity to review it and provide input to council members as the proposed amendment moves forward. "Put it out to the public with the understanding that this is a working draft," Councilman Dave Palmer noted. "That way, we can be contacted with suggestions from the public, listen more to ideas that are out there, and see if we thought we missed anything. It’s going to change. But I think we do have to get it out there to the public." The discussion comes in the wake of concerns by city leaders and the public over the past several months about the looming development of a new data center in the Wheeling neighborhood of Warwood. The former Centre Foundry & Machine Company property was acquired last year by the Silicon Foundation, an energy and artificial intelligence compute infrastructure company with international roots which plans to develop a new data center and energy technology campus at the Warwood location. Mayor Denny Magruder and other city leaders thanked Wheeling City Solicitor Rosemary Humway-Warmuth for working to put together the proposed zoning amendments, along with help from Building and Planning Director Brenda J. Delbert, City Clerk Jessica Holloway and others. This included research stemming from within the city’s own existing codes to municipalities around the country that have addressed similar situations. "I know some folks thought that we weren’t working on this, but those folks who have been working on it I think have been doing so for more than three months," Magruder said. "I think it’s a good move in the right direction." The city has already developed a memorandum of understanding with Silicon Foundation in which the company agrees not to apply with the state to expand and become what is considered a high-impact data center. Vice Mayor Jerry Skavounakis, chairman of the Rules Committee, said there was no previous example in the state of West Virginia on which legislation specific to municipal planning and zoning for data centers could be based. "There’s not a template that she was able to use," the vice mayor said. "There isn’t one. This is something she had to do from scratch. "I know you put a lot of time and effort into this, and I appreciate it," he told the city solicitor. The planning and zoning amendments to include language pertaining to data centers would first require a permitting process. A special use permit application would have to be submitted and approved, and the application process alone would involve a considerable list of requirements. Permitting requirements address a checklist of issues related to the site plan, a utility impact review, anticipated electrical demand and expected peak demands, adequate electrical service without unreasonable burden to city services and public utilities, daily maximum water demands and consumption, wastewater discharges, description of proposed cooling and water conservation measures, location and specifications of backup generators, anticipated air emissions, anticipated noise-producing equipment, proposed storm water management, noise levels and other issues. "There’s a list of things that they have to provide the city," Councilman Ty Thorngate said. "I think that is, to me, the most important thing in this." The application fee alone is currently set at $5,000, according to the proposed language. A surety bond must be provided by the applicant, as well. Currently, the surety bond is set at $75,000, but Humway-Warmuth noted this can be increased. "This is in case that applicant does not fulfill what they are required to fulfill," she said. "We’re not wed to that amount. It may be something you may want to modify - that’s at your discretion." The applicant must also cover the cost for industry experts the city will hire as consultants to review their application to make sure the company is meeting the requirements, to make any recommendations and to assure that industry standards are being met. "This allows us to use experts within this field, rely upon them, and then pass the cost off to the application - which would be the proposed data center, not the citizens," Sklavounakis said. Proposed language also includes potential fines for violations, but city officials noted that financial punishment would not likely have much of an impact on a company involved in data center development. "The big issue isn’t just the fines, we want to make sure that if they are doing stuff that they’re not supposed to be doing, we can revoke their permit in addition to the fines," Sklavounakis said. "If this data center wants to come here, the first thing they’re going to have to do is they have to get a permit. They’re not going to be able to operate without a permit." Humway-Warmuth noted the basic framework of the draft was based in part by language developed more than two decades ago when wireless communication boomed across the country and cell phone towers and infrastructure came to the city. The city created wireless telecommunication-specific ordinances to address issues related to these developments and several tweaks have been implemented in the city over the years, as well. The data-center language is expected to be described in city zoning codes related to industrial zoned properties, such as the Warwood locat

artigo.texto: Ørsted, a global leader in offshore wind energy, has finished construction of its first large scale UK battery energy storage system (BESS). This is the latest milestone along the path to it becoming fully operational. There are now 170 megapacks in place alongside the onshore converter station for Ørsted’s Hornsea 3 offshore wind farm, near Norwich, Norfolk. Each is the length of a classic Routemaster London bus but weighs the same as five buses. The system – known as Iceni after the Norfolk-based warrior tribe of the Roman era – will have a capacity of 600 MWh (and a 300 MW power rating). This is equivalent to the daily power consumption of 80 000 UK homes. The Iceni team comprises specialists from Ørsted, Hitachi Energy, Knights Brown, and Tesla working together on this first of its kind project. What makes this BESS unique is the split layout of the site with the two areas, separated by the Hornsea 3 onshore converter station, linked by 18 x 33 kV cables, each over 600 m in length. In addition, the shared grid connection point with Hornsea 3 has added additional technical complexity over a stand-alone connection point to the National Grid. The project is now in the final stages of the mechanical and electrical installation with the 33 kV cross site cables currently being installed and terminated. The first stage of commissioning and testing is well underway, and preparations are being made for energisation of the BESS transformer. When completed, the BESS will be one of the largest in Europe. Beatrice d’Eufemia, Project Manager for Iceni BESS at Ørsted, commented: “It is a milestone moment for Ørsted that construction is now complete on our first large scale BESS in the UK. The system will make the best use of renewable energy produced in the UK as when electricity generation exceeds demand, the excess can be stored and then used when demand is greater, helping balance the grid and lower electricity costs for everyone.” Richard Swann, Construction Manager for Iceni BESS at Ørsted, added: “It’s a real testament to the hard work, dedication, and co-operation of the team from many different organisations that the construction has been completed successfully.” David Shillabeer, Head of Transmission & Distribution at Knights Brown, concluded: “Reaching this milestone is a significant achievement for everyone involved in the Iceni project. Delivering a BESS of this scale has required close collaboration between Ørsted, Knights Brown, and the many other organisations that have contributed to its success. Beyond the engineering, the scheme has enabled us to invest in local people, develop skills, and create opportunities across Norfolk and the wider region. We are proud to have played our part in an important project that will support the UK’s transition to a more resilient, low-carbon energy system, while leaving a positive legacy for the communities in which we work.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. artigo.texto: Milton Cunha detona Virginia como Rainha de Bateria: "Catastrófico" Em entrevista a Blogueirinha, carnavalesco criticou desempenho da influenciadora e comentou a relação dela com a comunidade da Grande Rio O carnavalesco e comentarista Milton Cunha, 64, criticou o desempenho de Virginia Fonseca, 27, como Rainha de Bateria da Grande Rio durante participação no "Blogueirinha Entrevista", exibido pelo Multishow na última segunda-feira (19). Ao avaliar o samba da influenciadora, ele usou palavras como “catastrófico” e “terrível”. Durante a conversa, Milton também comentou a presença de celebridades em postos de destaque no Carnaval e afirmou que quem chega a uma escola de samba precisa respeitar a comunidade. “Qualquer pessoa que chegar na escola de samba tem que chegar na humildade, no sapatinho, por ali ser um território de comunidade”, declarou. Ao falar sobre Virginia, Milton relembrou a apresentação da influenciadora na quadra da Grande Rio, quando David Brazil teria pedido que ela mostrasse o samba no pé. “Os problemas da Virginia começaram no dia da apresentação dela na quadra. Quando o David Brazil disse: ‘Samba, Virginia’... Aí ela faz aquele passo dela e o queixo de todo mundo [foi para o chão], ‘o que é isso?’, e tal. Ali a gente já viu que não tinha samba no pé”, afirmou. Questionado por Blogueirinha sobre a possibilidade de Virginia aprender a sambar, o carnavalesco disse que também esperava que ela se aproximasse das pessoas que representaria na escola. “Além de esperança de aprender, esperança de que ela virasse íntima daquela gente que ela iria representar. Isso não vem. Aí chegam os ensaios técnicos, aí loucura em cima de loucura porque ela não consegue compreender qual é a estrutura do desfile”, avaliou. Em seguida, um integrante da plateia pediu que Milton definisse o samba da influenciadora. “Catastrófico, terrível, absurdo, impossível ritmicamente, é melhor não”, respondeu ele. O comentarista também comparou a experiência de Virginia com a de outras personalidades que ocuparam o posto de rainha de bateria. Ao citar Paolla Oliveira, ele afirmou que a atriz demonstrou envolvimento com a escola desde o início da trajetória na Grande Rio. “Ser rica e famosa não funciona na quadra da escola de samba”, disse Milton, ao comentar a relação entre celebridades e as comunidades das agremiações. Ele também afirmou que a responsabilidade pela escolha de personalidades para esses cargos não é apenas de quem os ocupa. “A responsabilidade é de quem a convida”, declarou. Virginia Fonseca deixou o posto na Grande Rio Virginia anunciou que deixaria o posto de rainha de bateria da Grande Rio em uma publicação nas redes sociais feita em agosto deste ano. No texto, a influenciadora agradeceu à escola pela oportunidade e afirmou que procurou se dedicar à função. “Não poupei esforços para entregar o meu melhor. Então, venho com o coração apertado e cheio de verdade, me despedir do posto de rainha de bateria da Grande Rio. E antes de qualquer palavra, quero agradecer ao Carnaval e à Grande Rio por me permitirem sentir essa magia de perto. É uma experiência única viver o maior espetáculo da terra”, escreveu. Ela também destacou o acolhimento recebido na agremiação e reconheceu as exigências do cargo. “A Grande Rio sempre me tratou como uma verdadeira rainha. Ali, me senti em casa, amada, protegida e, acima de tudo feliz. Entre vaias e aplausos, a gente caminhou junto, de mãos dadas e com muita coragem dos dois lados”, afirmou.

artigo.texto: The European Commission announced a provisional political agreement between the European Parliament and the Council on a targeted amendment to strengthen the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) of the EU’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). This agreement follows the Commission’s April 2026 proposal and aligns with the European Council’s 16 October conclusions. The timely nature of this agreement is instrumental in ensuring a stable, well-functioning carbon market within the EU, thereby bolstering the EU ETS’s resilience to excessive price volatility. “This agreement is an important deliverable in making the ETS fit for the future and a strong response to the calls of EU leaders last week. It will strengthen market stability and predictability over the next decade, enhance EU industry and competitiveness, and give businesses greater certainty to invest. It will also support industrial decarbonisation by reinforcing the resilience of the EU ETS against future shocks and excessive price volatility,” stated Wopke Hoekstra, Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth. This development represents significant progress toward implementing the ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap, which aims to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness by the end of 2027. Under the existing framework, all emission allowances in the reserve exceeding 400 million are rendered invalid. However, under the new agreement, the reserve will retain up to 700 million allowances as a buffer to promote future market stability and predictability. The new regulations will strengthen the reserve’s long-term operational capacity while upholding the system’s fundamental rules-based design and environmental integrity. The MSR works by reducing allowance supply when there is an excess and injecting allowances during periods of scarcity. This agreement clearly signals the EU’s commitment to a predictable, reliable carbon market, providing greater certainty for businesses and stimulating investment in a clean energy transition. It also marks an initial step towards broader modernisation of the Market Stability Reserve, as outlined in further reform proposals the Commission will present during the EU ETS review on 17 July 2026. Next, the European Parliament and the Council will formally adopt the text. The amendment to the Market Stability Reserve Decision will then take effect upon publication in the Official Journal of the EU.
