artigo.texto: Danville’s busy council race, with nine candidates for four seats and two more in a special election, is coming to a close. One, if not the last, forum before the Nov. 3 election was held Oct. 16. Three incumbents and three challengers shared their thoughts on the top issues the city is facing during the event at Bible Way Cathedral. Housing, poverty, data centers and ensuring that the region’s growth reaches all areas of the city were topics that rose to the top of the discussion, hosted by the Danville-Pittsylvania Chamber of Commerce. Incumbents James Buckner, Bryant Hood and Danny Marshall answered the same set of questions as challengers Lonnie Jones, Shakeva Frazier and Dustin Whittle. Incumbent mayor Alonzo Jones, incumbent Gary Miller and challengers Tony Howerton, Shelby Irving and Jasmine Lipscomb were absent. Nine of the candidates are running for four seats. Marshall and Lipscomb are running in a separate special election to finish the remaining two years of Del. Madison Whittle’s term after Whittle, R-Danville, was elected to the General Assembly last year. In February, the city council selected Marshall to fill Whittle’s seat until the special election Nov. 3. The six candidates answered questions from a moderator at the event. They were mostly aligned on the top issues the city is facing, though there were mixed feelings on data center development. How do data centers fit into Danville’s growth? Data centers are shaping up to be a big factor in the city’s future, some candidates said. Marshall mentioned the Microsoft data center in Mecklenburg County, about an hour east of Danville, that has generated significant revenue that Mecklenburg has put toward schools and property taxes. “They built a new high school and middle school completely with cash, no money borrowed,” Marshall said. “Not only has the school system benefited, but also the property tax in Mecklenburg County is going to be 32 cents per $100. We’re paying twice that much here.” Danville could see similar benefits from the proposed Stack Infrastructure AI data center campus, which would be built at the Berry Hill megasite. The megasite is in Pittsylvania County, but it’s jointly owned by the city and county, so Danville would reap tax benefits from the anticipated $100 billion project. “They [Stack] told me the amount of money they would spend, and I said, ‘Say again?’” Marshall said. “$100 billion with a B. The taxes that is going to generate for Pittsylvania County and for us is just going to be phenomenal.” For context, Buckner shared that the city’s annual budget is $347 million. “Let that sink in for a minute,” he said. “What that new investment is going to look like, what we can do with it for shared prosperity, for programs that need funding, things we can do to improve our city. … It’s a heck of a start if you ask me.” Hood said that “fear of the unknown” shapes many people’s opinions about data centers, and he’d like to see more research and community outreach done to answer resident questions. The city should communicate the information it has about data centers to “every church, every community center, every barbershop.” He said that the tax revenue could go a long way toward reducing poverty, but “if we can get to the point of getting everybody educated on what they are and how they work, I think that’ll do us more justice than anything.” Frazier said she was more hesitant about data centers, because she doesn’t want to see a big investment create greater wealth disparity. She saw this happen with the Caesars Virginia casino, which opened in 2024 and contributes millions of dollars a year to city revenue through state gaming taxes. “When we voted [on the casino], they gave us a promise that things would be cheaper here, that we will be able to afford what we have,” Frazier said. “I know people who were put out of their homes because landlords took advantage of that thing [the casino]. They were able to raise the rent.” Frazier said the city needs to gather more resident input and find out if it’s something residents support. “I’m for growing, I’m for prosperity, but at what cost?” she said. “Can we find something that benefits everyone, or can we at least have time to catch up with what we have going on so we can all understand?” Whittle said he’s done a lot of research about data centers since he began his campaign, and reading about new technology alleviated his concerns about water and energy usage. He said his biggest concern now is vetting a data center developer to make sure they’re honest and trustworthy. Soaring housing demand Each of the city council candidates mentioned Danville’s growing need for housing, especially affordable housing and workforce housing. A housing summit earlier this month revealed that pent-up housing demand in the city calls for nearly 4,000 rental units and 1,300 owned units. The city has added several hundred new apartments and homes since 2023, but major jobs announcements in recent years have exponentially increased the housing need. Microporous, a lithium-ion battery separator manufacturer coming to the Berry Hill megasite in Pittsylvania, plans to create about 2,000 new jobs. And data center developer Stack Infrastructure is moving forward with plans to build an AI data center campus, also at the megasite, that would create about 2,500 jobs. Buckner, Marshall and Hood all said they’d like to see the city loosen up some of the barriers to new home construction. “There’s more than one piece to the puzzle, but one of the biggest things we can do is reduce some of the red tape when it comes to developers coming in to build housing for our workforce,” Buckner said. “We need to build entire neighborhoods. … We’ve got so much red tape and so much in place to prevent us from moving forward with housing the way we need to move forward.” Buckner, who is a Realtor and the board chairman for Third Chance Housing, a local nonprofit that focuses on homelessness prevention, h

artigo.texto: Vídeo: minas de carvão de Criciúma podem abrigar data centers; empresa italiana visitará a região Prefeito afirma que empresário do setor de mineração conhecerá o potencial das estruturas Por Rafaela Custódio Atualizada 2 min de leitura As minas de carvão desativadas de Criciúma e da região carbonífera poderão ganhar novas utilidades, incluindo o armazenamento de data centers. Uma empresa italiana demonstrou interesse nas estruturas subterrâneas e enviará uma missão ao Sul de Santa Catarina no fim de novembro para conhecer as instalações e avaliar possibilidades de investimento. A informação foi divulgada pelo prefeito de Criciúma, Vagner Espindola, ao Portal Engeplus. Segundo o prefeito, a iniciativa faz parte de uma estratégia para diversificar a economia do município, com foco em tecnologia e inovação, aproveitando áreas que hoje enfrentam restrições para novos empreendimentos em razão do passivo ambiental deixado pela mineração. “Porque a grande virada de chave, na realidade, da cidade de Criciúma, ela está voltada para a tecnologia, para a inovação”, afirmou. Espindola destacou que as áreas afetadas pela atividade carbonífera representam um desafio para o desenvolvimento urbano e econômico, principalmente em razão das restrições impostas pela Ação Civil Pública (ACP) do Carvão. “O que nós temos é a herança de um passivo ambiental. E é este passivo ambiental que hoje, ele praticamente sentencia grandes glebas de terras da nossa cidade e que estão impedidas, por conta da ação civil pública do carvão, de edificar qualquer construção. Então, nós ficamos muito amarrados por conta dessa ação civil pública”, declarou. O prefeito relatou que conheceu uma experiência semelhante durante uma viagem ao norte da Itália, neste ano. Na ocasião, a comitiva conheceu uma empresa de mineração de calcário que, conforme Espindola, encontrou novas possibilidades de uso para antigas áreas subterrâneas de extração mineral. “Mas, quando a gente ergue um pouquinho a cabeça e sai de Criciúma, a gente consegue encontrar ali ferramentas para a gente fazer essa inversão das matrizes econômicas. A prova disso, quando nós fomos agora, este ano, para o norte da Itália, e lá nós conhecemos uma empresa de mineração de calcário, que, quando esvaiu-se toda a extração daquele mineral, deu-se para as cavas subterrâneas, as minas, uma nova utilidade. Hoje, essas cavas subterrâneas, elas servem de armazenamento de data centers, armazenamento de champanhes, vinhos e até maçãs”, contou. A partir da apresentação das características das áreas da região carbonífera, o empresário responsável pela empresa demonstrou interesse em conhecer as estruturas locais. artigo.texto: FRANKLIN COUNTY, Va. – Franklin County officials and residents heard from a panel of economic development, utility, water and local government speakers during a public work session on data centers. The panel was intended to explain data center trends, best practices and planning considerations, as county leaders weigh future policy. Board of Supervisors member Lorie Smith said the county has no current proposals before it. “We as a board, we don’t have any current proposals in front of us or anything,” Smith said. “What we acknowledge very clearly is that … we need to get our heads around what’s going on in the data center world.” The discussion comes after county records showed talks with Crusoe AI about Project Flash, a proposed data center at Summit View Business Park. The project was later stopped, prompting questions about the site’s future and whether another proposal could come forward. Panelists discussed the potential economic benefits of data centers as well as considerations such as water, energy and noise. Curry Roberts of Parkway Strategies LLC said data centers support many aspects of modern life. Alex Gottschalk, Mecklenburg County administrator, said communities should decide what they want from a development site before determining whether a data center is a good fit. Residents who spoke with 10 News said the discussion gave them more information but left them with questions. Franklin County resident Vicki Drew said she was still concerned about noise. She also said she learned that some data centers recycle water or use air cooling. Donna Hodges raised concerns about water and energy use amid drought conditions in Virginia. Resident Wayne Mize said data centers could be important, but should come with safeguards, including water recycling and the ability to generate their own power. Board leaders said the session was informational—not an announcement of a project or a vote.

artigo.texto: Politics & Government Fire Safety Concerns Raised Over Bridgewater Battery Storage Plan An expert for the applicant Rockland APV said a modeled battery fire would stay within safety setbacks at the proposed site. BRIDGEWATER, NJ — Fire safety concerns were raised at Bridgewater's most recent review of a proposed battery energy storage project at 760 East Main St. The Bridgewater Township Zoning Board of Adjustment held a special meeting on Tuesday, where board members focused on what could happen if a fire broke out at the site. The application, from Rockland APV, Bridgewater Energy LLC, is looking to construct a battery energy storage system(BESS) on the 7.13-acre tract at the southwest corner of East Main Street and Polhemus Lane. Find out what's happening in Bridgewaterfor free with the latest updates from Patch. At the meeting, Leonard Ganesh Deonarine, a fire and safety expert who had testified previously at the Aug. 3 meeting, returned to address the board. Deonarine told the board he was there to explain a plume dispersion analysis prepared by Jensen Hughes using testing on the Trina Storage equipment proposed for the Bridgewater site. Find out what's happening in Bridgewaterfor free with the latest updates from Patch. He said the equipment was set on fire in testing by a third party, and the resulting gas data was then used in a computerized model that examined nearby buildings and whether people could be exposed if a fire occurred. "We combined the modeling report of toxic gas release against the surrounding structures and facilities where people might be exposed to the toxic gases produced if the equipment caught fire," Deonarine said. He said the analysis focused on carbon monoxide and hydrogen fluoride and on two acute exposure guideline levels published by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Level 1, he said, would involve irritation without disabling effects. Level 2 would involve more serious exposure. Deonarine testified that in a flaming event, carbon monoxide at the Level 2 threshold extended 60.5 feet from a container, while hydrogen fluoride extended 4.6 feet. He said the nearest residence shown in the report was about 560 feet away. He also said the applicant’s emergency plan uses a 200-foot safety perimeter for unprotected people, based on NFPA 855. Board members questioned him about strong winds, calm weather, nearby workers and whether neighboring properties would need to be evacuated. Deonarine said the modeling used prevailing wind direction and that, under the study and the emergency plan, people more than 200 feet away would not need evacuation for this scenario. Major Battery Fires Bridgewater officials also spent part of the recent hearing examining how the facility would be handled in a fire and whether lessons from major battery fires elsewhere have been addressed in the design proposed for the township. Deonarine compared the Bridgewater proposal with battery storage fires in Surprise, Arizona; Warwick, New York; Gateway in San Diego; and Moss Landing, California. Deonarine said the proposed Trina storage containers for Bridgewater have features that older systems did not, including ventilation, remote monitoring, gas venting, signage required by current code and a decommissioning plan. The testimony also stated that the applicant would provide annual training for fire personnel at its expense. Deonarine said firefighters should not open or investigate the inside of a battery storage container during an incident. "It's not a firefighter's job," he said, comparing it to asking firefighters to open electrical equipment inside a substation. He also said current planning calls for responders to keep their distance, protect the public and allow the fire to burn itself out or let the installed suppression system work. Board members questioned the witness about the 2019 Surprise, Arizona fire and whether a similar event could happen here. The fire being referred to broke out at an APS McMicken Battery Storage Facility in Surprise, Arizona in April 2019, according to Azfamily.com. Four firefighters were severely injured when they opened a door to the building, which created an explosion, throwing the firefighters into a fence. Deonarine said the Arizona installation differed in battery chemistry and lacked protections now cited in testimony, including automatic ventilation and remote monitoring. When asked whether opening doors in an enclosed installation contributed to an explosion there, Deonarine said, "your description is accurate. It's the buildup of gases with automatic ventilation. You don't get the buildup of gases and this new equipment has exhaust fans and ventilation has deflogration systems built into it." artigo.texto: Africa is struggling to translate falling battery prices into increased investment in energy storage, with financing constraints, regulatory uncertainty and infrastructure planning gaps slowing deployment, according to the latest ESI Africa Industry Insights: Energy & Storage Volume 5 (2026). BloombergNEF data shows stationary battery pack prices fell to approximately $70/kWh in 2025, a 45 per cent year-on-year decline. However, of the $13.84 billion in energy transition investment attracted by Africa during the year, only $666 million, less than 5 per cent, was allocated to storage and flexibility, according to figures tracked by Electron Intelligence. Nicolette Pombo-van Zyl, editor-in-chief of ESI Africa, said energy storage had become a critical factor in determining whether projects secure financing, electricity grids remain stable after sunset and renewable energy generation is effectively utilised. She said capital availability, regulation and data collection had yet to keep pace with the growing importance of storage in Africa’s energy development. The publication examines the economics of battery storage, including South African modelling that identifies lithium iron phosphate (LFP) as a leading option for stationary applications. It also explores how project scale, battery degradation in hot climates, financing costs, import tariffs and freight charges influence investment viability. Emerging battery technologies, their potential impact on Africa’s mineral value chains, cybersecurity risks and long-duration storage solutions also feature in the report. The volume highlights the need for better data on Africa’s expanding distributed solar market. According to Ember, approximately 26 GW of solar capacity was installed across the continent between 2023 and 2025, with only around a quarter captured in utility-scale and off-grid figures. Improved project registration and data collection could help policymakers and grid operators better understand solar deployment patterns and their implications for electricity networks. The publication’s African Infrastructure Elites section highlights storage projects increasingly shaping renewable energy financing, including Scatec’s Obelisk project in Egypt and Mulilo’s Hartebeesfontein battery storage project. Pombo-van-Zyl said the next phase of market development would depend on regulators, utilities and financiers establishing appropriate ways to value storage services, protect connected infrastructure and prepare projects for investment. She added that these challenges were solvable using existing industry tools and approaches. -OGN/TradeArabia News Service

artigo.texto: Google planeja data center – O Google planeja construir um data center de 780 megawatts em Pine Island, Minnesota, nos Estados Unidos, acompanhado de investimentos em energia renovável e armazenamento. O acordo com a Xcel Energy prevê ampliar a capacidade da rede elétrica além da demanda da instalação, mas ainda depende de aprovação da Comissão de Utilidade Pública do estado. Segundo a CNBC, a empresa financiará a adição de 1.400 MW de energia eólica, 200 MW de energia solar e 300 MW de armazenamento em baterias. A capacidade adicional busca compensar a geração intermitente das fontes renováveis. LEIA: Quanto de água uma pergunta ao ChatGPT realmente consome? Proteção contra a saída antecipada O contrato prevê que o Google pague pelo menos 75% da capacidade acordada, mesmo que utilize menos energia. Se encerrar o compromisso antes do prazo, poderá arcar com até oito anos de cobranças mínimas. “Ninguém quer ter uma grande expansão e depois não ter para onde mandar essa energia e ninguém para pagá-la”, diz Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva da Xcel Energy. “É aí que essas proteções entram.” A iniciativa ocorre em meio à crescente demanda por eletricidade dos centros de dados. A Corporação Norte-Americana de Confiabilidade Elétrica (NERC) aponta essas instalações como principal fator de expansão prevista do consumo na América do Norte na próxima década. Nos Estados Unidos, o envelhecimento da infraestrutura também pressiona o setor elétrico. Centros menores como alternativa Para Jigar Shah, sócio da consultoria Multiplier, empresas poderiam optar por instalações menores em regiões com capacidade disponível na rede, reduzindo custos para os consumidores. “Se você encaixar o crescimento de carga que os centros de dados querem na rede existente, as tarifas de todo mundo caem muito”, afirma. Segundo ele, construir unidades menores exige mais planejamento, mas pode evitar grandes expansões de infraestrutura. Incentivos das distribuidoras David Pomerantz, diretor-executivo do Energy and Policy Institute, observa que as distribuidoras têm incentivos financeiros para investir em novas estruturas. “Quando constroem algo novo, financiam parte desse investimento com recursos de investidores de Wall Street e desfrutam de retornos incrivelmente altos, exorbitantes sobre esses investimentos, tipicamente em torno de 10%”, afirma. Uma alternativa seria os operadores de data centers financiarem melhorias na rede com capital mais barato. Pomerantz, porém, aponta que essa possibilidade gera conflitos com as distribuidoras. Apesar das ressalvas sobre o modelo, Shah avalia positivamente a proposta do Google, que aguarda autorização regulatória. artigo.texto: Natural Power has provided technical due diligence support to ENERTRAG in connection with the financing of the Les Sablons battery energy storage system (BESS) project in France, which has now reached financial close. Located in Vendeuil in France’s Hauts-de-France region, Les Sablons is a 39 MW/117 MWh lithium-ion phosphate (LFP) battery energy storage project. The project is one of the first three-hour duration BESS projects in France and is designed to support the integration of renewable energy and provide additional flexibility for the French electricity system. Construction of Les Sablons is already underway, with a target commercial operation date of spring 2027. Natural Power was commissioned by ENERTRAG to undertake a comprehensive technical due diligence review to support the financing of the project. The assessment covered key technical and contractual aspects of the development, including permitting, grid connection, the EPC and O&M contracts, the route-to-market contract, and the technical inputs to the financial model. Julien Teixeira, Senior Technical Adviser BESS at Natural Power, commented: “Les Sablons is an important project in the development of France’s BESS market, combining three-hour storage duration with co-location alongside significant wind generation. We are pleased to have supported ENERTRAG through the technical due diligence process and to have contributed our BESS expertise to the financing of the project. Reaching financial close represents an important milestone for Les Sablons and demonstrates the continued development of bankable, grid-connected energy storage projects in France.” The role of energy storage in building resilience and reliability into the grid is becoming ever more important, and our team of experts in energy storage technology, consenting, contracting, construction, energy analysis, and asset management has already supported more than 25 GW of energy storage projects globally. For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. Energy Global’s Autumn 2026 issue The Autumn issue of 2026 is available now! The new issue begins with a regional report on Asia Pacific, looking at the region’s transition from building capacity to building systems. The issue also explores topics such as offshore wind foundations, solar maintenance, training the new workforce, inspection & maintenance, and more! With insights from experts such as Everllence, BW Ideol, EM&I, Watson Farley & Williams, and many more, make sure to check out this issue now.

artigo.texto: TotalEnergies subsidiary Saft launches solid-state battery production lines in Bordeaux Saft opens solid-state battery production lines in Bordeaux, mainly for aerospace. The company claims energy density up to 50% higher, without mentioning any use in road vehicles. Saft, a TotalEnergies subsidiary, is inaugurating new production lines for solid-state batteries at its Bordeaux facility. The batteries are primarily intended for aerospace applications. Saft does not mention any potential use in road vehicles. In the broader storage market, other players are announcing projects, such as Flatiron Energy, which wins two battery storage contracts in the Bronx, and Envision, which commissions a 125 MWh storage system for OCP in Morocco. Production lines designed for two technologies Saft describes itself as the first French manufacturer to produce self-developed solid-state batteries using both sulphide and polymer electrolytes at room temperature. The group cites aerospace as a key application area, where gains in safety, performance and energy density are "particularly valuable," according to a statement. In aviation, Saft has already recently delivered semi-solid-state cells in collaboration with its partner Safran. According to Saft, the new lines in Bordeaux, a European aerospace hub, can accommodate several technologies: polymer-based semi-solid-state batteries and sulphide-based solid-state batteries. The facilities operate explicitly at room temperature. However, the company remains vague about the batteries themselves, stating only that they will be particularly safe and compact. Energy density and production emissions The batteries' energy density would be up to 50% higher than that of conventional lithium-ion batteries, according to Saft. The manufacturing process relies on a dry electrode method, which is expected to reduce COâ emissions in production by up to 40%. Saft CEO CÃ©dric Duclos says: "Solid-state batteries are among the most promising innovations for meeting tomorrow's electrification needs. These new production lines mark an important milestone for Saft, as we turn several years of research into real industrial capacity, a statement of our ambition to establish France and Europe as leading players in this strategic technology." A two-player French market and a refocused joint venture France has another producer of already commercialised solid-state batteries, Blue Solutions, part of the BollorÃ© group. Its technology is based on lithium-metal-polymer (LMP). Blue Solutions is currently being restructured, however, after issues arose with the batteries in serial applications, particularly in buses. Saft is also a shareholder in the joint venture Automotive Cells Company (ACC), which it owns with Stellantis and Mercedes-Benz. ACC produces nickel-based cells and modules in France, which currently primarily benefit Stellantis. The Douvrin site was originally supposed to be supplemented by two additional plants in Germany and Italy. The joint venture is now focusing solely on the ramp-up phase at its only cell factory in France, and the other two major projects have been scrapped. In the European research project SUBLIME, the company focused on sulphide-based solid-state batteries with other players starting in 2023. In the TALISSMAN project, it is working with partners to develop lithium-sulphur batteries for electric vehicles.

artigo.texto: Colunistas convidados escrevem para a editoria de Opinião do GLOBO. Brasil tem vantagem para operar data centers verdes Infraestrutura física precisa de energia, e 90% da eletricidade brasileira é gerada por fontes renováveis Atualizado Quando fazemos um Pix, pagamos uma compra com cartão, chamamos um carro por aplicativo ou assistimos a uma série, colocamos em movimento uma extensa infraestrutura digital. São milhões de operações cotidianas que dependem da geração, transmissão, armazenamento e processamento de dados. É essa engrenagem que sustenta a nova economia digital, movida a dados. Embora falemos em “nuvem”, a infraestrutura é física. As informações são processadas em data centers que funcionam 24 horas por dia e demandam uma capacidade computacional sem precedentes. Essa infraestrutura necessita de energia, e é aí que o Brasil possui vantagens únicas. Aproximadamente 90% da eletricidade brasileira é gerada por fontes renováveis. Em outros grandes mercados, como os Estados Unidos, as fontes renováveis representam cerca de 25% da geração elétrica. Enquanto outras economias precisam descarbonizar sua infraestrutura digital, o Brasil já oferece capacidade computacional com baixa emissão de carbono. Para aproveitar essa oportunidade, precisamos corrigir uma percepção equivocada: a ideia de que data centers necessariamente consomem grandes volumes de água para refrigerar suas máquinas. Segundo levantamento da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC), mais de 95% dos data centers em operação no país usam soluções que dispensam o consumo contínuo de água na refrigeração. Na maior parte dessas instalações, o resfriamento é feito a ar ou por sistemas de circuito fechado. A comparação mais simples é com o radiador de um automóvel: o sistema é preenchido inicialmente, e o fluido circula continuamente para transportar o calor. Circulação de água não significa consumo de água. Essa característica não surgiu por acaso. Durante a primeira grande expansão do setor, entre 2010 e 2014, o Sudeste enfrentou uma grave crise hídrica. A insegurança no abastecimento levou operadores e projetistas a adotar sistemas capazes de funcionar sem depender do consumo contínuo de água, elevando o custo por demandarem mais energia para funcionar. Essa limitação transformou-se em vantagem competitiva. Estudo da Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (TIC) e de Tecnologias Digitais — com apoio da ABDC e revisão técnica da Fundação Apolônio Salles de Desenvolvimento Educacional — estimou que o setor respondeu por apenas 0,003% do consumo de água do Brasil em 2022. Isso não dispensa planejamento, licenciamento ambiental ou fiscalização. Na verdade, aponta para a necessidade de o debate público considerar as tecnologias efetivamente empregadas no país, sem importar automaticamente problemas de outros mercados. A aprovação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center permite que a inteligência artificial abra uma nova fronteira para o Brasil. O treinamento de modelos, as análises maciças e outras cargas computacionais não precisam estar próximas do usuário final. Podem ser processadas onde houver energia renovável, conectividade, capacidade técnica e segurança jurídica. O Brasil entra num seleto grupo de países capazes de ofertar capacidade computacional, transformando energia renovável em serviços digitais de alto valor agregado. A ABDC estima em até R$ 1,58 trilhão o potencial de investimentos diretos até 2030. Essa expansão movimenta construção civil, engenharia, energia, telecomunicações, equipamentos, pesquisa, inovação e formação profissional. O país acaba de dar um passo para ser um dos grandes fornecedores mundiais de infraestrutura digital sustentável. *Renan Lima Alves é presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC), Luis Tossi é vice-presidente, e Leonardo Santos é diretor de comunicação da ABDC

artigo.texto: HOUSTON, Texas (KTRK) -- Advocacy groups say a state agency kept issuing data center permits after Gov. Greg Abbott directed a halt to all approvals last month. On Sept. 21, Abbott wrote a letter directing the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt all permits sought by data centers. But watchdog groups Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance found data showing TCEQ approved 35 different permits in the last month. A map released by the groups showed the locations of those approvals. Kathryn Guerra, TCEQ Watchdog Campaign Director for Public Citizen, described the permits as "specifically authorizations that allow those data centers to construct, to clear the land, to grade the land, to do excavation things that they need to do to begin the construction of those sites." TCEQ disputed the characterization, writing that the approvals "are stormwater general construction Notices of Intent (NOI) and are automated authorizations," not operational permits. But Guerra said the agency has since suspended 17 data-center-related permits after the groups released their findings. "The TCEQ took the unprecedented step of suspending 17 authorizations that it issued to data centers, despite, you know, sort of refuting the fact that they had issued them. So I think that that speaks to the fact that that was the TCEQ's error. They should not have been permitted," Guerra said. "The state's website refers to these as permits, and the state and federal code also refer to these as permits, and so we very much believe that the TCEQ dropped the ball and continued issuing these authorizations despite the governor's order." TCEQ's website showed its electronic reporting system is now temporarily shut down. The governor's office said in a statement that "TCEQ has not taken and will not take any proactive actions related to the approval of data center permits." Guerra said real change is still needed. "If the TCEQ and the governor's office want to play word games, you know, that's fine," Guerra said. "Texans are tired of games when it comes to data centers. And what they need are real protections and real laws in place."

artigo.texto: Bondada Engineering Limited has received a Letter of Intent (LOI) from Gujarat Industries Power Company Limited (GIPCL) to develop a 20 MW/120 MWh Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Energy Storage System (VRFB BESS) at GIPCL’s 165 MW natural gas power plant complex in Vadodara, Gujarat. The project includes a 10-year operations and maintenance (O&M) contract. Bondada Engineering said the project is India’s largest grid-scale vanadium redox flow battery storage installation. The contract expands the company’s work in energy storage and adds to its renewable energy engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) portfolio. The scope covers engineering, procurement and construction of the 120 MWh battery storage system, followed by operations and maintenance for 10 years. Completion is scheduled within 18 months from the receipt of the Notice of Award. Dr. Bondada Raghavendra Rao, Chairman and Managing Director of Bondada Engineering, said the project marks an important step in the company’s expansion into advanced energy storage technologies. He noted that storage systems would play an increasingly important role as India adds renewable energy capacity and works to maintain a reliable power supply. Vanadium Redox Flow Battery technology is used to store electricity and release it when required, making it suitable for long-duration energy storage applications. Such systems can support grid stability and help manage fluctuations in renewable power generation. India’s energy transition is expected to drive demand for storage infrastructure. The government has set a target of deploying approximately 236 GWh of battery energy storage systems by 2030, creating opportunities for companies involved in storage project development, equipment supply and system integration. The GIPCL project follows Bondada Engineering’s work on a 100 MWh Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Energy Storage System for NTPC Renewable Energy at Khavda, Gujarat. The two projects strengthen the company’s experience in the deployment and maintenance of flow battery systems. Bondada Engineering operates across renewable energy, telecommunications infrastructure and other EPC segments. The company said its expansion into long-duration storage forms part of its strategy to participate in emerging energy infrastructure markets and support India’s growing requirements for reliable and sustainable electricity. Bondada Engineering Limited is a Hyderabad-based engineering, procurement and construction company with operations across renewable energy, telecommunications infrastructure and other engineering sectors. The company provides infrastructure development and related services to support India’s energy and connectivity requirements.

artigo.texto: Greenvolt Group, through Greenvolt Power, has agreed to sell two battery energy storage projects in Poland to A&R Investments. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to the fulfilment of the usual conditions applicable to transactions of this nature. A&R Investments is Malta-based investment vehicle that oversees, controls and manages a diversified portfolio of private and public investments, both directly and through external fund managers. The projects covered by the agreement are the stand-alone BESS in Ełk and Turośń Kościelna, both located in north-eastern Poland. Each project has a power capacity of 200 MW and an energy storage capacity of 800 MWh, enabling it to discharge at full power for approximately four hours. Both projects were completed in Q3 2026 and have obtained the required permits for use, helping to enhance flexibility in the Polish electricity system and support the integration of renewable energy. Ełk and Turośń have each secured 17-year capacity market contracts in Poland, starting in 2028. Under these contracts, each asset receives a fixed payment for making 85% of its rated capacity available to the system. Both projects are also covered by a 10-year tolling agreement, which will optimise the batteries and trade their flexibility in the power markets. “We have one of the largest battery storage pipelines in Europe, have built strong expertise in developing these assets and will continue investing in this sector. The need for storage capacity and flexibility is growing rapidly, and this transaction confirms that high-quality BESS projects meet a clear market need and attract investor interest”, said João Manso Neto, CEO of Greenvolt Group. “These projects represent an important addition to our portfolio and an opportunity to invest in large-scale battery storage assets in Poland. Their scale and role in providing flexibility to the electricity system make them valuable assets in a market where storage is becoming increasingly important”, said Christian Buhagiar, Director at A&R Investments. “Ełk and Turośń demonstrate Greenvolt Power’s ability to take complex, large-scale battery storage projects from development to completion. Poland is a strategic market for us and a key driver of our growth in Central Europe, where we will continue to deliver projects that meet the evolving needs of the energy system,” said Weronika Nowak, CEO of Greenvolt Power. Greenvolt Power has a BESS pipeline of approximately 4.6 GW across its markets. The sale of Ełk and Turośń forms part of Greenvolt’s asset rotation strategy, which foresees the sale of approximately 70–80% of internally developed projects, enabling the Group to realise value from its development activities and recycle capital into new investment opportunities.

artigo.texto: The all-electric BYD Denza N8 has been spotted without camouflage at a factory staging area in China. The five-seat SUV has a 205-litre front trunk and rear seats that recline to 146 degrees, according to details Denza recently disclosed. The electric N8 is distinct from the plug-in hybrid Denza N8 launched in 2023. It measures 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide and 1,820 mm tall, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase. The six-seat Denza N8L shares that wheelbase but is 50 mm longer, at 5,200 mm. Denza N8 gets a 205-litre frunk Denza says the 205-litre front trunk has two-layer storage, a drainable structure and separate wet- and dry-item compartments. The rear seats recline to a maximum angle of 146 degrees. Denza has also listed three exterior colours: Aurora Green, Deep Space Blue and Sunlight Orange. The three-motor AWD version produces 890 kW Regulatory data reported by CarNewsChina lists two rear-wheel-drive versions with motor outputs of 320 kW and 370 kW. An e3 tri-motor all-wheel-drive version combines a 270 kW front motor with two 310 kW rear motors, for a total rated output of 890 kW, or approximately 1,193 hp. We reported details of the N8’s tri-motor configuration in July. Battery capacities and range The N8 is offered with LFP Blade batteries supplied by BYD subsidiary FinDreams Battery, with reported capacities of 105.792 kWh and 130.15 kWh. Its published CLTC range figures are 800 km, 840 km, 970 km and up to 1,003 km, equivalent to estimated WLTP ranges of around 648 km, 680 km, 786 km and 812 km, respectively. Earlier reporting associated the 1,003 km figure with the 130.15 kWh battery in our August on the N8’s regulatory specifications. Denza has promoted second-generation Blade Battery technology and Flash Charging for the N8, claiming a five-minute quick charge and a nine-minute full charge. These remain manufacturer claims, not independent charging-test results. A roof-mounted LiDAR sensor is visible on the photographed vehicles. Its presence alone does not indicate which driver-assistance functions each version will offer. October 26 has been rumoured as the launch date after an interior image reportedly surfaced with that date.

artigo.texto: ARCHBALD — Silence fell over an otherwise raucous, standing-room-only crowd Wednesday as Archbald Borough Council voted to unanimously deny the Wildcat Ridge Data Center Campus. After intently listening to the roll call vote, residents sprung to their feet, roaring with applause and jubilantly waving yellow signs with “DENY” printed in bold black letters. The energized audience of data center opponents spent more than a minute celebrating the denial of Brooklyn-based Cornell Realty Management’s conditional use application to build 14 data centers on the mountainside above Archbald’s Eynon and Sturges sections. As the cheers started to trail off, shouts of “Thank you!” spread through the Borough Building’s third-floor gymnasium, which served as a makeshift council chambers to accommodate the overflow crowd of at least 175 who anxiously awaited a decision on Lackawanna County’s largest proposed data center campus. Council’s unanimous decision was the culmination of nine public hearings and about 26 hours of oftentimes-heated testimony and cross-examination since January surrounding a proposal for 14 two-story data centers, each 80 feet tall with 202,340-square-foot footprints, across 574.2 acres along Business Route 6 and extending up Route 247, or Wildcat Road. Council President Louis Rapoch, Vice President Joseph Altier III and council members Larry Marchetti, Madonna Munley, Lisa Osborne, Erin Owen and Larry West all voted to deny Wildcat Ridge’s 777-page conditional-use application. Though Wednesday’s vote concludes a saga that first began in January 2025 when representatives for the data center campus attended a council work session to tout a $2.1 billion investment, the decision could face an appeal in the Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas. Wildcat Ridge Attorney Edmund J. Campbell Jr. declined to comment on the decision or whether his client intended to appeal when asked after the meeting. ‘Consequences cannot be undone’ Throughout the past year, the Wildcat Ridge Data Center Campus has emerged as one of Lackawanna County’s most controversial data center proposals, with concerns largely fueled by its plans to use 588 backup diesel generators to power its data centers during an outage, as well as its significant water and electricity use, totaling just over 3.3 million gallons daily in the summer while requiring 1.6 gigawatts of electricity. Residents and local elected officials have widely opposed the development, and speakers reiterated that stance Wednesday as they urged council to deny the application. Meg Nudelman fought back tears as she thanked council members for their “willingness to endure this process and give our community a full and thoughtful hearing.” “Throughout these hearings, we have heard assurances of compliance, promises of litigation and explanations of what can, could, or would be done, but assurances are not a substitute for evidence,” the borough resident said, pointing out the cumulative effects of other proposed data centers. “Pennsylvania’s Municipalities Planning Code requires decisions grounded in the ordinance and the evidence, not assumptions — let me repeat that: the evidence, not assumptions. If the record fails to establish any required approval criteria, that failure cannot simply be overlooked.” The community deserves a decision grounded in law, supported by evidence and protective of residents, Nudelman said. “Once these buildings are constructed, the consequences cannot be undone,” she said. Lackawanna County Commissioner Bill Gaughan, a vocal data center opponent, compared artificial intelligence to Mary Shelley’s “Frankenstein” in his remarks to council. “It was the story of a brilliant scientist who became so consumed with what he could create, that he never stopped to consider what he should create. When his creation escaped his control, the consequences were devastating,” Gaughan said. “Two centuries later, I wonder if we’ve learned anything because tonight we’re being asked to help build the engine of something that even the people inventing it admit they may not fully understand: artificial intelligence — a technology that could transform medicine, cure diseases and accomplish extraordinary things, but also a technology that could eliminate millions of jobs, concentrate unimaginable power in the hands of a few corporations and fundamentally alter what it means to be human.” Archbald has a choice, Gaughan said. “We cannot decide, and you cannot decide the future of artificial intelligence, but we can decide whether this valley, this community and these families must be sacrificed to power it,” he said. “We do not have to build a machine simply because someone else figured out how to turn it on and make billions of dollars on it.” ‘Just dumb’ Almost exactly one year ago, Tamara Misewicz-Healey and her husband, Justin Healey, formed the Stop Archbald Data Centers movement. On Wednesday, the parents of three young children both addressed council, pressing them to deny the application. Misewicz-Healey gained party status at Wildcat Ridge’s first hearing, allowing her to cross-examine every witness presented by the developer and elevating her as a central figure in Archbald’s data center resistance movement. “Here we are, listening to hours and hours of testimony that doesn’t provide the proof that they were required to, and do you know why they’re coming on so strong with fear tactics? Because they know if this hits the court, they lose,” she said. “We are in the right. This is reckless. This is damaging to health, and it’s just dumb.” She asked the crowd how many have experienced anxiety and depression over the past year. Hands shot up throughout the gym. “We’re already struggling physically, mentally, financially. We don’t have money, yet we’re paying for the borough to have all these hearings, and we’re paying for our own lawyer. artigo.texto: Qnetic inicia testes de baixa velocidade do sistema de armazenamento por volante de inércia Pulsar em Xangai A Qnetic, sediada em Sacramento, iniciou os testes de baixa velocidade do seu sistema de armazenamento de energia por volante de inércia em seu centro de tecnologia em Xangai, na China, segundo a pv magazine USA. O protótipo, chamado Pulsar, dá continuidade à arquitetura de armazenamento mecânico da empresa e deve ter capacidade inicial de 200 kWh, expansível para 500 kWh na mesma plataforma, o que permitiria armazenamento de quatro horas a uma taxa nominal de descarga de 125 kW. Os volantes de inércia armazenam energia como movimento cinético em rotores que giram em alta velocidade. O excedente de eletricidade acelera o rotor a altas velocidades e, quando a energia é necessária, um gerador converte a energia cinética de volta em eletricidade enquanto desacelera o rotor. Os defensores argumentam que a tecnologia poderia desafiar os sistemas de armazenamento de energia baseados em baterias, que atualmente dominam o armazenamento em rede para renováveis. A Qnetic informou em setembro que o Pulsar havia concluído seus primeiros 100 ciclos contínuos de carga e descarga sem falhas nem degradação de capacidade. Em testes separados, o motor do sistema produziu 130 kW de potência com 97,3% de eficiência em velocidades acima de 11.000 rpm. A empresa montou uma fábrica e sede em Sacramento, onde planeja produzir em baixo volume unidades comerciais do Pulsar. O Pulsar será avaliado em um programa-piloto pelo Sacramento Municipal Utility District, dentro de uma iniciativa de redução de riscos conduzida pelo Electric Power Research Institute. A Qnetic pretende iniciar o piloto no primeiro semestre de 2027. Michael Pratt, cofundador e diretor-executivo da Qnetic, disse à pv magazine USA que a abordagem da empresa visa resolver deficiências das baterias de íons de lítio, em especial as taxas de ciclagem e a degradação ao longo do tempo. Ele afirmou que, quando o conceito estava sendo formulado, há cerca de cinco anos, os sistemas de íons de lítio conectados à rede em contêineres estavam apenas entrando no mainstream, e era evidente que as baterias eram caras demais, enquanto a degradação continuava sendo o principal problema. Pratt observou que a necessidade de integrar renováveis indicava o armazenamento em baterias como a melhor opção disponível na época. Ele disse que, desde então, investimentos substanciais foram feitos para melhorar a química das baterias, mas a vida útil em ciclos e a vida útil em calendário continuam sendo questões fundamentais. Acrescentou que as baterias de íons de lítio normalmente completam um ciclo por dia e se enfraquecem ao longo da vida útil, enquanto os volantes de inércia podem ciclar repetidamente na rede sem perder capacidade. Disse também que ninguém vinha reunindo todas as peças necessárias para o armazenamento em rede. Historicamente, os volantes de inércia fornecem alta potência para aplicações de curta duração, medidas em minutos ou segundos, incluindo energia de reserva para telecomunicações e data centers, potência de transição até a partida de geradores a diesel e controle de precisão em experimentos de energia de fusão. O objetivo da Qnetic é produzir volantes de inércia adequados ao armazenamento em rede de maior duração. O desempenho de quatro horas, embora no limite da longa duração, ainda atende a muitos requisitos das concessionárias, e as unidades de volante de inércia podem ser agrupadas em bancos acionados por períodos mais longos, com taxas de descarga variáveis para atender à demanda. As unidades em escala de rede já implantadas são enterradas no subsolo, com a maquinaria de controle acessível por uma cúpula exposta. Pratt posiciona os volantes de inércia como mais seguros que as baterias de íons de lítio em termos de risco de incêndio, embora as altas velocidades do rotor ainda exijam salvaguardas contra uma desmontagem rápida não programada. Ele disse que medidas como manter o motor abaixo da velocidade máxima nominal do rotor evitariam tais eventos. A fabricante concorrente Amber Kinetics desenvolveu uma versão de suas unidades de 32 kW para implantação acima do solo em contêineres marítimos de aço. Pratt reconhece que o armazenamento mecânico enfrenta seus próprios obstáculos de desenvolvimento para alcançar capacidades maiores e economias de escala. A arquitetura do Pulsar inclui um rotor de fibra de carbono girando no vácuo sobre mancais magnéticos sem contato, praticamente eliminando o atrito. O rotor é mantido afastado do eixo central com tecnologia semelhante à dos trens de levitação magnética, e o conjunto fica em um contêiner cilíndrico de aço. Um objetivo central é reforçar o rotor compósito de fibra de carbono, já que um rotor mais resistente pode girar mais rápido e armazenar mais energia cinética. Com a configuração atual, uma iteração adicional da fibra de carbono permitiria elevar a capacidade para 500 kWh. Pratt disse que as economias de escala são fortes, com a duplicação do tamanho físico rendendo oito vezes a capacidade potencial de energia no mesmo envelope, e que um rotor resistente aliado a grande escala são as chaves para um sistema de baixo custo. Pratt também citou limites práticos para a ampliação por meio do tamanho, observando que a empresa está desbravando novos caminhos com rotores compósitos fabricados por enrolamento filamentar, que não costumam ser produzidos com mais de cerca de dois metros e meio de diâmetro. Ele disse que o plano é ciclar a unidade intensivamente, corrigir eventuais falhas e então seguir para os primeiros pilotos. Pratt disse que as tecnologias fundamentais por trás do Pulsar são maduras e estão em operação, e que, além de fabricar um rotor de fibra de carbono maior, a Qnetic está focada na integração de sistemas e na otimização de controle, e não em engenharia e pesquisa originais. artigo.texto: EUA planejam usar energia da Itaipu para data centers Parceria com Paraguai visa construção de estrutura de computação com energia da hidrelétrica. O governo estadunidense anunciou nesta quarta-feira (21) que vai construir uma estrutura de computação de inteligência artificial por meio de uma empresa privada e em parceria com o Paraguai, cuja energia será abastecida pela hidrelétrica binacional de Itaipu, na fronteira entre Brasil e Paraguai. O Departamento de Estado dos EUA informou que o negócio de serviços de computação em nuvem será voltado para clientes da América Latina e estadunidense por meio da empresa de tecnologia digital norte-americana Crusoe e a paraguaia Araico, que desenvolve projetos de energia e infraestrutura. A primeira fase da instalação começa em meados de 2027, de acordo com o órgão estadunidense. No início da semana, o vice-secretário de Estado dos EUA, Christopher Landau, reuniu-se com o presidente paraguaio, Santiago Peña, e com o ministro das Relações Exteriores, Rubén Ramírez Lezcano, para discutir cooperação econômica e estratégica, sobretudo nos setores de tecnologia, minerais críticos, infraestrutura fluvial e logística. A usina é administrada em conjunto pelo Brasil e pelo Paraguai. A energia produzida pela hidrelétrica é estabelecida por um tratado assinado em 1973, que prevê a cada país o direito a 50% da energia gerada. Em novembro de 2025, os EUA manifestaram interesse em comprar a energia excedente da usina, hoje destinada ao Brasil, para abastecer data centers. Em maio deste ano, o secretário de Estado dos EUA, Marco Rubio, afirmou que a energia poderia impulsionar projetos de inteligência artificial norte-americanos.

artigo.texto: Park City officials received input on Tuesday about the future of workforce or otherwise income-restricted housing at an open house intended to address the municipal government’s detailed development rules. The crowd’s written comments were some of the noteworthy opinions expressed at the event, held at the Park City Library. The input comes as the municipal government pursues ambitious housing developments in an effort to create options for people priced out of Park City’s resort-driven real estate and rental markets. More than 50 people attended the open house, including Mayor Ryan Dickey, at least two Park City councilors and several members of the Park City Planning Commission. The crowd spoke to municipal staffers and studied poster boards covering topics like transportation and historic preservation. The crowd placed sticky notes on the boards with brief comments about the topics. The anonymous housing notes were broad and did not address the individual projects that are under consideration. Some of the comments included: - “Affordable housing limit to employees who work in the city limits.” - “Limit (building) height as per code — no exception.” - “As a taxpayer + full time resident I want affordable (housing) to be prioritized for individuals/families who work for the community (1st responders, teachers, health care workers, snowplow drivers, municipal employees etc … Use (affordable housing) to help our community focused people — not have taxpayers subsidize retail/profit centers.” - “City owned land must be for local workers!” A station described potential housing-related amendments that could be made to the municipal Land Management Code, the document that outlines development rules. Possibilities included streamlining the process and providing incentives for certain smaller projects. It also addressed living quarters for the seasonal workforce, including, as an example, establishing “regulations for single-room occupancy (or dormitory-style housing).” For decades, Park City leaders have considered housing, saying there are benefits like increased socioeconomic diversity and decreased commuter traffic. The municipal government is currently pursuing two ambitious projects with a large portion of income-restricted housing. The proposals in Bonanza Park and at Clark Ranch, just off the S.R. 248 entryway, have separately spurred organized opposition. Crowd addresses data centers, drones The crowd at the open house also provided written comments about the future of wireless facilities in the community, a broad topic that also covered what were described as “small-scale data centers.” A poster board described possible amendments to the Land Management Code, including a section of the text that said: “Respond to emerging technologies, including battery energy storage systems, small-scale data centers, autonomous vehicles, drone delivery robots, and advanced air mobility vehicles.” The written comments were generally opposed to the possibilities. They included: - “No flying drones or deliveries.” - “No drones!” - “No data centers in city limits.” - “Require any data centers or related uses to meet strict noise reduction requirements.” - “Drones in residential areas should require a permit and times permitted.”

artigo.texto: - President Donald Trump said data center companies should pay a "dividend" to local communities. - In a Truth Social post, Trump said the payments could boost the controversial projects' popularity. - Data centers have sparked widespread public backlash, worrying some investors. In a Truth Social post early Wednesday, Trump urged companies to "MAKE DEALS," but did not provide details on how much money they should return to communities or individuals where data centers are being built. "I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck," he wrote in the post. There's been a growing backlash against data center construction across the US, with some saying the projects are noisy, raise electricity bills, and compromise the general quality of living. Data centers are becoming an increasingly important issue in next month's midterm elections, and some politicians have shifted how they talk about the projects in recent months. Data Center Watch, a research project run by 10a Labs, found that in the first quarter of this year, at least 75 data center projects were delayed or canceled due to local opposition. Some companies have already started trying to placate unhappy locals with money or discounts. This summer, Elon Musk's SpaceX offered eligible Memphis residents a 50% discount on its Starlink internet service, tied to its growing AI build-out in the city. NorthPoint Development opted for a pure cash incentive and said it would pay every household in a Pennsylvania township $10,000 if it got permission to build a data center, the Wall Street Journal reported last month. In his Wednesday post, Trump also referenced one of his previous efforts: having tech companies cover their power costs when they build data centers to help keep local electricity prices flat. Several tech leaders agreed to do so in March, when they signed the "Ratepayer Protection Pledge," which mandates that companies provide or pay for the power generation and electricity needed for their AI projects, among other commitments. Trump closed his Wednesday post by saying that building data centers under his newest stipulations would be "GREAT FOR THE U.S.A."

artigo.texto: Lancaster County Data Center Task Force holds first meeting By Maddie Ames , Reporter Oct. 20, 2026, 10 p.m. · The Lancaster County Data Center Task Force met for the first time Tuesday afternoon. The group of 12, with one member missing, discussed goals, current regulations and heard from community members. “The Lancaster County Data Center Task Force will evaluate the size, siting, and setbacks of data centers in existing zoning classifications and assess potential impacts on energy use, water consumption, noise levels, visual impact, and other considerations contained in the amendment proposed by the applicant,” David Cary, the city’s Planning Department director, said. Board members range from Lincoln Chamber of Commerce CEO Jason Ball members and John Hansen, the president of the Nebraska Farmers Union to John McNally, the governmental affairs manager for Nebraska Public Power District. There’s also five community representatives who were selected by the Lancaster County board. The group will work by consensus, setting recommendations that everyone can live with, as Cary put it. He said a roll call vote is a fallback if the group gets stuck at any point. The group ran through current zoning regulations, which allow for data centers for industrial zoned parcels. Right now, a data center is not a defined use or specifically regulated under current zoning regulations. There was also talk of other community regulations and moratoriums. The group talked about Lincoln’s current permissions that allow for data centers in office, commercial or industrial zoning districts. More than a dozen Nebraska counties have approved moratoriums on data centers in the past few months. Gov. Jim Pillen also signed an executive order last month restricting tax incentives for data centers and appointed a 17-member data center task force. Cary also brought up defining what the sizes are of large and small data centers. “So I would say maybe give some focus to how to define a data center and large versus small data center considerations as we go into the next meeting of this group,” Cary said. This meeting comes after the Lancaster County board halted plans to vote on a potential moratorium after learning that Bold Education — or Bold Nebraska, a political advocacy group founded by Nebraska Democratic party chair Jane Kleeb — had applied for a zoning code text amendment that would address the issue. “We've been studying data center issue for about two years now with different communities and experts across the country, and looked at the concept of moratoriums or the trend of moratoriums,” Kleeb said. “And (we) started to get concerned because you know we think moratoriums might be great in a short-term sense, but if you're not putting good policy in place, then you're just kind of kicking the can down the road.” She added that from an advocate's perspective, it can lead to large corporations like Google or Meta sneaking in and meddling with good policies behind closed doors. “We really wanted to see a strong data center ordinance that maybe other counties could then start to look at because some counties don't have the resources that Lancaster does,” Kleeb said. In the past year, there’s been a string of purchase options taken out by data centers in Lancaster County. There’s Monolith and Stark Power data centers just outside of Hallam in southern Lancaster County. And there’s the Google data center near Interstate 80 and North 56th Street that is operating, but still under construction. Arevia Power of Nevada — a solar and data center developer — optioned over 500 acres of land in Northwest Lincoln. Those options were brought up by community members during the 15-minute public comment period. Nate Tederman of Malcolm raised concerns over deciding what happens to land nearby his family’s residence. “I would say let the community of Malcolm vote on this,” Tederman said. “It's not anybody that's going to be living. You guys aren't the ones that are going to be living right next to this thing. It's going to be me, my family, and the people back here.”

artigo.texto: Shanghai Composite ends down 22 points as CATL sinks Published on 10/21/2026 at 13:20 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS Battery earnings set the tone - Shanghai Composite finished at 3,713 points on October 21, down 22 points or 0.6 percent. - CATL fell 12.0 percent after third-quarter profit growth slowed to 14.5 percent. - Nanwei Software and Aisino each gained 10.0 percent among the strongest Shanghai stocks. - The Financial Street Forum concludes on October 22, 2026, with its closing ceremony in the afternoon. The Shanghai Composite closed at 3,713 points on October 21, 2026, down 22 points or 0.6 percent, Xinhua reported. The decline followed weaker earnings signals from battery maker CATL. CATL fell 12.0 percent after third-quarter profit rose 14.5 percent year over year, below market expectations, Morningstar reported. Why did the Shanghai Composite fall? Corporate earnings concerns weighed on the market, while weak domestic demand added pressure. Xinhua said batteries, energy metals and education stocks were among the biggest decliners, while pork and culture and media shares led gains. CATL's weaker margin and profit outlook intensified selling across the battery supply chain. Winners and losers in the Shanghai Composite Closing movers on October 21, 2026, according to Fisco: - Nanwei Software up 10.0 percent: communication and software shares strengthened. - Aisino up 10.0 percent: software shares outperformed. - Changchun Yidong down 9.0 percent: automobile shares weakened. - Fuyao Glass down 7.2 percent: auto-related shares came under pressure. The index opened higher then retreated The Shanghai Composite opened at 3,741 points, up 0.14 percent, before reversing lower, JRJ reported. By the close, 1,979 stocks had risen and 3,360 had fallen across the mainland market, according to Eastmoney. What comes next for the Shanghai Composite The Financial Street Forum continues through October 22, 2026. Its closing ceremony is scheduled for the afternoon in Beijing and will focus on global financial cooperation and coordinated governance, the Shanghai Stock Exchange said. artigo.texto: More than 30 community members took to Virginia Beach Town Center Tuesday night to call on lawmakers to enact a statewide data center moratorium. Chesapeake Climate Action Network partnered with several organizations to march as part of a two-week tour across the commonwealth. Tuesday’s event was the only stop in Hampton Roads. The demonstrations call for pausing all data center development across the state to allow time to establish protections for public health, environmental and economic protections. Data center development has exploded in recent years, with advocates arguing the growth is in response to people consuming an equally growing amount of data due to technological advancements. Northern Virginia alone has become a global hub for the facilities to the tune of roughly two-thirds of the world’s data centers. That growth has downsides, though. Hyperscale data centers can require roughly 100 megawatts of power and consume up to 530 million gallons of water per year to operate. Facilities of various sizes can also have effects on neighboring communities’ air quality, groundwater and noise pollution. According to Catherine Setaro, Hampton Roads field manager with Virginia League of Conservation Voters, those downsides are unacceptable for Virginia residents, and developers who profit off the facilities’ unchecked growth need to be leashed. “Big tech has had a free pass in Virginia for too long, which is why we’re dealing with more of these industrial facilities than anywhere else in the country,” Setaro said during the rally. “Virginians are fed up. They are tired of a system where big tech can do whatever they want without consequence, cashing in while Virginians bear the cost.” While data center growth has thus far been limited in Hampton Roads, smaller facilities that consume fewer resources still exist in places like Virginia Beach. The Chesapeake City Council blocked a developer’s proposal to build 350,000-square-foot data center last year after outcry from residents. Several localities are now researching what regulating data centers could look like. This summer, Chesapeake enacted an 8-month moratorium and restricted where they can be placed and Virginia Beach enacted a 1-year moratorium. At the state level, Gov. Abigail Spanberger issued an executive order in September shedding by-right approval of large data center projects and instead requiring local approval. For Chesapeake resident Linda Tindell, that doesn’t mean the threat of Hampton Roads residents seeing a data center in their community has gone away completely. As she stood in Fountain Plaza wearing an elephant costume alongside her pet donkey named Darla, Tindell said she’s one of many Chesapeake residents concerned about future development at the former Frank T. Williams farm in southern Chesapeake. The 4,000-acre property was recently sold to a private investment firm called Praetorian Fund with no disclosed purchase details and some residents are wary it could become a future site for data center development. Tindell, a Republican, said reining in data centers in something that crosses party lines. She said she wants to protect her community from facilities that could impact nearby ecosystems and farms that are home to animals like Darla. “People are showing up. It’s a nonpartisan issue,” said Tindell, adding that Darla is an independent and has yet to cast her ballot. “Environmentally, it’s too aggressive. It’s too much too fast.” Michael Jamieson is another concerned Chesapeake resident. He loves hiking and spending outdoors in places like the Great Dismal Swamp. However, if data centers are allowed to continue their expansion, he said those ecological gems will be tainted by the time his daughter grows up. He said he wants to do something about it so his daughter’s future hikes in Chesapeake remain protected. “It comes down to the natural environment that’s going to be harder to experience,” Jamieson said. “For me, it was important that my daughter see her dad come out and talk and actually do the things he talks about at home, not just yell at the TV.” Devlin Epding, 757-510-4037, devlin.epding@virginiamedia.com

artigo.texto: North Elba's town board voted unanimously Tuesday to approve a one-year moratorium on battery energy storage systems, freezing construction, installation and even review of any such project anywhere in town while officials scramble to close gaps in local zoning rules. The vote lands squarely in the middle of two pending Ray Brook solar-farm applications that would pair roughly 25 megawatts of power generation with battery units, leaving their fate uncertain just as developers push forward with permitting. Town officials say they hit pause after realizing their zoning had gaps when it comes to energy projects, according to WCAX. North Elba Town Supervisor Rick Preston told the station he doesn't believe the town will consider individual battery applications going forward, adding plainly: “We don't see a battery energy storage system being suited for North Elba or the village of Lake Placid. We just don't have the acreage for it.” The newly enacted local law prohibits the construction, establishment, installation, review or approval of any battery energy storage system while it remains in effect, according to a public notice posted by the town of North Elba. Two Ray Brook Proposals Now in Question The moratorium arrives as North Elba weighs two separate solar-plus-storage applications in Ray Brook. One proposal, pitched by ClearPath Energy, would place a solar farm and battery storage system on roughly 50 acres of private property off Pendergast Road, according to the Daily Gazette. Citizen Portal described this same ClearPath proposal as two adjacent community solar-plus-storage arrays beside FCI Ray Brook, totaling about 24,000 panels and approximately 40 megawatt-hours of battery capacity. The other proposed Ray Brook solar farm, which Preston said is unlikely to advance, sits too close to a municipal water-supply tank for comfort, per the same Daily Gazette account. It remains unclear whether the ClearPath project could be exempt from the moratorium given its current stage in the permitting process, the newspaper's report notes — a question town officials have not resolved. Part of a Wider Adirondack Pattern North Elba's move follows similar moratoriums already adopted in the Adirondack towns of Champlain and Ticonderoga, per WCAX's reporting. But the trend reaches far beyond the Lake Placid area. According to the Adirondack Explorer, roughly one-fifth of the Adirondack Park's 101 towns and villages have passed battery-storage moratoriums this year alone, with 21 municipalities filing local laws since January 1 that delay construction for periods ranging from six months to a full year. Town boards across the region have repeatedly framed these pauses as necessary to gather more information on the public and environmental safety of the technology, the Adirondack Explorer reports. The scale of the slowdown is significant: testimony from William Acker cited by the outlet put the number of municipalities with active moratoriums above 100, delaying more than one gigawatt of battery storage projects statewide. New York has set a goal of bringing 6 gigawatts of energy storage online by 2030, a target that becomes harder to hit as local governments hit pause one by one. Towns Split Between Bans and Narrow Carve-Outs Some Adirondack municipalities have gone further than a temporary freeze. Fort Ann, Gloversville and Forestport have banned battery energy storage systems outright, according to the Adirondack Explorer. Accounts of neighboring St. Armand's action differ: the Adirondack Explorer reported in one piece that the town passed a one-year moratorium on building battery systems following a public hearing in Bloomingdale, while a separate Adirondack Explorer report states St. Armand is repeating its process after failing to evaluate the local law under the State Environmental Quality Review Act. The Daily Gazette, meanwhile, described St. Armand's June action as a moratorium covering batteries over 600 kilowatt-hours. Not every Adirondack town has slammed the door. The Adirondack Park Agency has already permitted a 10-megawatt, four-hour battery storage system in Northampton — described by the Adirondack Explorer as the park's first large-scale project, consisting of two five-megawatt AC systems with six lithium-ion batteries each. That approval came even as more than 160 people packed a local firehouse before Northampton's own town board separately passed a one-year moratorium on further projects. Ticonderoga's six-month moratorium, passed in March, was nearing its end as officials considered another six-month extension, and Hadley's moratorium was also on the cusp of expiring with a renewal in the works, per the same outlet. Local Capacity to Vet Complex Projects a Recurring Concern Part of the hesitation reflects a broader resource gap. Local Authorities Having Jurisdiction often lack the resources or expertise to evaluate critical battery storage permitting documents, which contain technical data that drives important siting requirements, according to the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority. NYSERDA guidance also discusses peer review and fire-code requirements for these systems. For North Elba, the moratorium buys time rather than settling the matter. Preston has said the pause gives the board a year to study impacts and revise its code, and town officials have stressed it is not intended as a permanent solution. Whether the Ray Brook proposals ultimately move forward, get rejected, or wait out the year in limbo remains an open question the town has yet to answer.

artigo.texto: General Motors and LG Energy Solution are pushing to locally produce in the United States a next-generation battery with higher energy density than existing low-cost batteries. The strategy targets both price competitiveness and driving range. If carried out, it is expected to become the world’s first commercial production of lithium manganese-rich (LMR) prismatic batteries. Cleantechnica reported on Oct. 19 local time that their joint venture Ultium Cells plans to retrofit its Spring Hill plant in Tennessee to produce next-generation LMR prismatic battery cells. LMR batteries are designed to balance cost and energy density by increasing the share of relatively inexpensive manganese in the cathode material. GM set a goal of boosting energy density by 33 percent at a cost similar to lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. Higher energy density allows more power to be stored in the same weight or space, which is favorable for extending electric-vehicle driving range. GM plans to keep high-nickel batteries for vehicles that prioritize long-distance driving, while using LMR as a new option that balances price and performance. It plans to apply LMR to future electric pickup trucks and large sport-utility vehicles (SUVs). The Spring Hill plant is already producing pouch-type battery cells. It also began producing LFP battery cells for energy storage systems (ESS) from June this year. The plan is to add LMR prismatic cells to diversify battery chemistries and formats. The plant retrofit is scheduled to begin late this year and be completed in 2028. The expansion is expected to create about 500 new jobs. At the time of the announcement, the plant workforce stood at about 1,200. Ultium Cells projected the total investment, including switching to LFP production and building LMR facilities, will reach $1.0 billion by 2030. The start date for mass production of LMR and the timing for its application to finished vehicles have not yet been decided. A key issue is whether GM and LG Energy Solution can deliver the targeted performance and costs in commercial production.
