artigo.texto: A combination of San Diego politicians, labor groups and housing advocates gathered in front of City Hall on Thursday to voice opposition to a potential data center a local developer is considering as part of a 70-acre redevelopment project at Naval Base Point Loma Old Town Campus. “I’ve seen many projects in my time,” San Diego City Council President Joe LaCava said. “What we don’t need is a resource-guzzling data center in the middle of our city.” Executives at the Manchester Financial Group have emphasized that a possible data center is simply one of a range of options the company has on the table to reshape about 60 acres of the property on the site straddling Pacific Highway, home to Naval Information Warfare Systems Command (NAVWAR). “We’re committed to getting the project done for the Navy, and I would be neglecting them if I didn’t look at every single idea that comes up,” company president Ted Eldredge told the Union-Tribune on Wednesday. “That’s why we’re looking at all these different alternatives, and the data center was one that came up.” But data centers have become a red-hot political issue across the country and the mere suggestion of the potential construction of a facility in an urban area of San Diego has sparked pushback. San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria signed an executive order Thursday to direct city staff to advance a temporary moratorium on new data center development within the city limits. “San Diego is a city of innovation, and I want us to continue leading in the technologies and jobs of the future,” Gloria said in a statement that was released at about the same time the rally was held. “But we cannot allow a rapidly expanding industry to get ahead of the rules needed to protect our residents.” The proposal will be placed on on the City Council docket Monday. The order establishes a working group of up to 15 stakeholders to develop recommendations for water and electricity demand and potential impacts on utility bills, housing and neighborhoods. Another provision directs the mayor’s government affairs team to develop or support legislation from the impacts of data centers — including those located on state or federal property outside the city’s land-use authority. “Here’s the hard truth about NAVWAR,” Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera told the crowd of a few dozen. “NAVWAR is federal land. The city can’t stop this project on its own.” He and others want San Diego’s federal delegation to take action. “First, immediately urge the Navy in writing to rule out a data center,” Elo-Rivera said. “And second, and most importantly, introduce legislation when the new Congress convenes in January holding leased military land to the same standards that we’re putting forward in San Diego today.” Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed into law multiple bills passed by the state Legislature to address data center concerns. The new legislation intends to make sure large electricity users are responsible for meeting the costs associated with their energy demand, while protecting existing customers from sudden cost shifts. Average residential electricity rates in California have grown faster than inflation, and according to the Public Advocates Office, San Diego Gas & Electric’s rates have jumped 97% in the past 10 years. Southern California Edison’s average residential rate has climbed 101% and Pacific Gas & Electric’s has risen 69% during the same time frame. Among the new laws is Senate Bill 886, authored by Sen. Padilla, D-San Diego, that directs the California Public Utilities Commission to establish tariffs or rules governing interconnection of data centers to the electric grid. But Assemblymember Chris Ward, D-San Diego, said bills passed in Sacramento have not gone far enough. “I think that we are realizing how fast this is coming at us,” Ward said after speaking at the rally, “and we have to get ahead of stricter regulations that are going to guarantee that communities will not lose out.” The Manchester group has floated the idea of a 400-megawatt data center developed by a prospective tenant on the site. But Eldredge told the Union-Tribune, “We’re not married to that megawattage,” adding that any possible facility is dependent on market conditions and the project’s feasibility. “I don’t have all the answers yet,” he said. “There is the potential that it doesn’t work.” For perspective, a data center proposed to be built in Imperial County is designed for 330 megawatts of capacity. Expected to cover about 1 million square feet, the Imperial Valley Data Center would be the largest data center in California. But the project is currently on hold after a Superior Court judge brought up environmental concerns. Others worry that housing development will end up getting short shrift at the NAVWAR project. “NAVWAR is a transit-oriented site,” said Council President Pro Tem Kent Lee, chair of the city’s Land Use and Housing Committee. “It’s adjacent both to the Old Town Amtrak station and the Old Town Transit Center. It must be utilized for mixed-use development with homes not only for San Diegans, but especially to support our many military and veteran families.” A spokesperson for Manchester Financial declined to comment about Thursday’s news conference. Data centers have come under scrutiny following the recent surge in artificial intelligence. The facilities house the massive racks of computer systems required to train generative AI models and chatbots emanating from the cutting-edge technology. Proponents say AI and its accompanied infrastructure create new jobs and will eventually transform almost every segment of the economy — and society at large. But critics, among other concerns, worry that electricity- and water-hungry data centers will strain resources. Within San Diego County, the Poway City Council earlier this month approved an ordinance that bans large, third-party data centers used for artificial intelligence applications throughout the city. artigo.texto: MECOSTA COUNTY — Electric vehicle battery maker Gotion and Green Charter Township have reached a settlement agreement in a multi-million dollar federal lawsuit, ending plans for a proposed $2.4 billion battery plant in Mecosta County. Gotion sued the township in March 2024 for nearly $24 million in damages following a breach of contract claim. Under the agreement, Gotion will drop the lawsuit, walk away from the project entirely and return the acquired development land to the Michigan State Land Bank. In exchange, the state of Michigan will drop its demand for Gotion to repay more than $24 million in grant funding used to buy the property. Green Charter Township must repay $160,000 related to a drafted fire contract amendment along with $1 in damages. All remaining counts in the lawsuit are dismissed with prejudice, meaning they cannot be refiled in the future. All parties agreed to terminate all existing project agreements and drop any claims against each other. The settlement ends litigation that cost Green Charter Township hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal fees. First proposed in 2022, the Chinese-owned company’s project was billed as the largest economic development effort in Northern Michigan history, promising to bring 2,300 jobs to the area. The project faced local and statewide opposition over environmental concerns and alleged ties to the Chinese Communist Party. The pushback led to a recall of the entire Green Charter Township Board in November 2023. Following the election, the new township board rescinded previous contracts agreed to by the former board. Township Supervisor Jason Kruse said at the time that the board had the legal right to take those steps, stating the former board signed the agreement in haste before the recall and that no properly executed development deal existed. By fall 2024, the Michigan Economic Development Corp. pulled more than $175 million in approved tax incentives. The agency sent a letter to Gotion stating the company had abandoned the property, noting no work had occurred at the site for at least four months. In January, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel ordered Gotion to repay more than $23 million in distributed grant money, prompting Gotion to state it would surrender the land rather than repay the funds.Gotion declined to comment on the settlement until the agreement is officially finalized. The Michigan Attorney General’s Office has not responded to requests for comment. Both Green Charter Township and Gotion were also reached ot to for comment but both parties declined, stating they could not comment until the agreement was finalized.

BAIC Group and CATL Deepen Battery-Swapping Cooperation The two companies will collaborate on vehicle and battery development, station deployment, asset integration and unified industry standards. - On October 22, BAIC Group and CATL signed an agreement to comprehensively deepen their cooperation in the battery-swapping business. - The cooperation will cover vehicle and battery design and development, battery-swap station construction, battery energy services, product promotion and business-model innovation. - BAIC Group and CATL will work to promote unified battery-swapping standards, interoperability between networks and the sharing of battery-swapping infrastructure. - The two companies will also promote the professional integration of battery-swapping assets and use a division-of-labor model to improve operational efficiency. - BAIC Group will open its dealership network to support station deployment. CATL's Choco-Swap business will identify suitable dealership locations for new stations and explore jointly operated projects with BAIC Group's dealer teams. Choco-Swap is CATL's official English brand name for its standardized passenger-vehicle battery-swapping solution. catl.com - The cooperation aims to integrate BAIC Group's sales channels with CATL's energy network and provide users with a broader range of energy-replenishment options. AiMoga Robotics Launches MOBO, Its First Consumer Humanoid Robot The family companion robot supports more than 20 languages and is now available for global pre-order. - On October 21, 2026, Chery Group's AiMoga Robotics unveiled MOBO, its first consumer-grade humanoid robot designed for family companionship, at a global launch event in Wuhu, Anhui province. - Standing 0.9 meters tall, MOBO features 22 degrees of freedom, enabling it to walk and use body movements during interactions. - Designed to serve three generations within a household, MOBO can answer children's questions, tell stories and support English-language interaction. It can also chat with elderly users and provide customized reminders. - The robot supports interaction in more than 20 languages. Family-member recognition and long-term memory allow it to maintain personalized conversations over time. - MOBO combines spatial perception, multimodal interaction, decision-making, memory and motion control. Its capabilities include locating objects, performing tasks and navigating around people in social environments. - AiMoga Robotics has recorded global sales of more than 3,000 robots. Its products and services are present in more than 60 countries and regions and cover over 100 application scenarios.

artigo.texto: What Effingham County can expect if AI data center comes to town: Lessons from Abilene, Texas ABILENE, Texas (WTOC) - Effingham County could soon be home to one of the largest AI data centers in the country. To show what having an AI data center next door actually looks and sounds like, WTOC traveled to Abilene, Texas — the town already living with one. What sits eight miles outside Abilene is Stargate — an 875-acre campus and the first campus of OpenAI’s broader AI infrastructure effort, developed by Crusoe with cloud capacity from Oracle. It is already operating. Project Camellia is different — it is a future campus OpenAI itself is designing for Effingham County, with power delivery planned in phases between 2028 and 2032. PREVIOUS COVERAGE In two days in Abilene, two themes emerged: thousands of workers to build it, and the strain they put on housing, roads, water and power. Housing and workers To build Stargate, between 5,000 and 9,000 temporary workers poured into the area, residents and city officials said. The city didn’t have enough housing — or roads built for the extra traffic. Residents and city officials say the influx caused rental rates and cost of living to double, even triple. Many homes were turned into rental properties to house the workforce. The shortage led to dozens of RV parks in and around Abilene to house workers. “They were coming into town and filling up everything available and really pretty quick,” said Scott Senter, of Better Homes and Gardens Realtors. “We kept hearing, oh they’re going to have to build more and we need to build more. That meant more people. It’s impossible to get ready for that kind of influx of people in your community.” Abilene Mayor Weldon Hurt acknowledged the pinch, but said it is temporary. “As the construction nears and the count of our temporary workers goes down, the housing bubble will adjust itself and the pricing will adjust back down,” Hurt said. “But it is a pinch right now, we’re not denying that.” Traffic and deadly crashes Residents say between 4 and 5 p.m. around the site and on the highways is the worst time to drive. During a recent city council meeting, one city leader noted traffic crash fatalities have increased — something many residents blame on the wave of workers. “About 30% in Taylor County and that’s due to the increase of traffic, I mean the traffic has increased tremendously,” Hurt said. “It is so packed on the roads typically. It’s like Dallas — if you’ve ever been there, Dallas traffic is... awful,” said Abilene resident Gretchen Spoon. Hurt said he understands the frustration over traffic and construction, but calls it the price of progress — pointing to a surge in tax revenue he says will benefit the city long term. Water and power Water and power are the two biggest questions in Effingham County. In Abilene, the mayor says water fears haven’t played out — and OpenAI says the Effingham design is meant to follow the same model. Both campuses use the same idea — closed-loop cooling that recirculates water instead of losing it to evaporation. WTOC previously reported Camellia would use about 30,000 gallons a day from treated surface water. In Abilene, the mayor says once the system is charged, use drops to just a few thousand gallons a year. “So they’re not water hogs. They require a lot of power, but they are on the grid,” Hurt said. “If there’s a demand for power from ERCOT, they have to reduce their intake too. So, they’re on the grid just like we all are.” Hurt added many new data centers have on-site power, noting: “We have an abundance of gas in this region. And so they’re going to take advantage of that gas to generate power with gas power generators.” On power, both campuses plug into the grid — in Abilene it is ERCOT, where Stargate must cut back when demand spikes. In Effingham, WTOC previously reported Camellia would draw up to 3,210 megawatts at peak from Georgia Power. OpenAI says Camellia is designed for offsite power generation, with no diesel backup generators after completion, plus vegetative buffers and noise monitoring. artigo.texto: Hermantown, Google reach decommissioning agreement ahead of data center vote Hermantown residents, city officials split on decommissioning plan HERMANTOWN, Minn. (Northern News Now) - Ahead of a city council vote next Monday that could clear the way for Google to begin developing its data center in Hermantown, residents are learning more about what will happen when the data center is no longer needed. A Google representative speaking at a city council meeting earlier this week announced that the company has developed a decommissioning agreement in response to city and resident feedback. City officials say the agreement provides reassurance about the future of the project site. Some residents remain unconvinced. Residents raise long-term concerns Sarah Lofald lives in the area about a mile and a half from the project site. She says she is concerned the data center is being built for immediate tech needs with little focus on the long term. “The lifespan of anything within technology is shortening every year,” Lofald said. In response to that concern from residents, Hermantown Economic Development Director Chad Ronchetti says the city initiated the decommissioning agreement with Google. “It provides protections,” Ronchetti said. Under the agreement, if the site goes unused, Google will need to keep buildings maintained and file a plan to either repurpose the site or clear it. Ronchetti says the city’s preference is for reuse. “It keeps the site productive, it keeps it active and it keeps it on the tax rolls,” Ronchetti said. Resident skeptical of reuse plan Lofald is skeptical another company will need the roughly 1.7 million square feet of building space. “Finding that one in a million industry that is looking for a space in northern Minnesota, on this kind of a property, that fits within light manufacturing—that’s a needle in a haystack,” Lofald said. Ronchetti believes it’s worth a shot before simply clearing the site. The buildings will need to be removed if they sit empty for three years. “I understand that skepticism. That’s why we have the decommissioning option,” Ronchetti said. However, removing the buildings would still not be a win in Lofald and other residents’ eyes. For many, the environmental damage cannot be undone. “Once a wetland is destroyed by industry, there’s no way to bring it back,” Lofald said. The decommissioning agreement would be a 50-year agreement. Google did not respond to a request for an interview. artigo.texto: Fairfield County residents raise concerns about potential data centers near Jenkinsville Jenkinsville, S.C. (WACH) — Fairfield County residents voiced concerns about the potential for data centers in the Jenkinsville area during a community meeting Thursday, raising questions about environmental impacts, rising costs and the effects on quality of life. The meeting comes as Fairfield County remains under a 12-month moratorium on data centers. County officials say there are no current plans for a data center in the area, but they are gathering public input as they consider regulations that could govern future development. For residents in western Fairfield County, the discussion focused on what a potential data center could mean for the area's future. Jenkinsville Mayor Gregrey Ginyard urged residents to remain alert as the area prepares for major changes associated with a pair of nuclear reactors. After the moratorium is over they can simply put a data center up because it's already zoned that way," Ginyard said. County officials said Thursday's meeting was intended to gather public input for a possible ordinance that would establish safeguards if a data center is approved in the future. County Administrator Vic Carpenter said an ordinance could require facilities to recycle water, use reclaimed wastewater where feasible and pay for the infrastructure needed to support their operations. One participant emphasized the importance of educating residents about the facilities and their potential benefits and drawbacks before additional public meetings are held. "I said in one of my questions today here, making sure that we're also educating people on what data centers are, what are the pros, the cons of everything that we need to know," candidate for Jenkinsville County Council Kennedi Bates said. "So when we come into these town halls, that we are prepared. We are prepared to ask questions." The meeting was initiated by Jenkinsville Council Member Carl Bell. Local leaders said Thursday's gathering was the first of three planned community meetings. The next meeting is scheduled for Jan. 7 in Ridgeway.

artigo.texto: Redata amplia incentivo a data centers, mas capacidade local não elimina risco operacional Novo regime tributário busca atrair infraestrutura de nuvem e inteligência artificial para o Brasil, enquanto empresas reforçam importância de redundância, segurança e continuidade 20.10.2026 A criação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, o Redata, abre uma nova etapa para a expansão da infraestrutura digital brasileira. Instituído pela Lei nº 15.504/2026, sancionada em 15 de setembro, o regime estabelece incentivos tributários para instalação, modernização e ampliação de centros de processamento de dados voltados a serviços como computação em nuvem, processamento de alto desempenho e inteligência artificial. Serviços e Informações do Brasil A medida surge em um cenário de forte dependência de infraestrutura localizada fora do país. Segundo diagnóstico do Ministério da Fazenda, cerca de 60% das cargas digitais brasileiras são atualmente atendidas por serviços prestados no exterior. Serviços e Informações do Brasil Regime exige contrapartidas O Redata não prevê apenas incentivos fiscais. As empresas que aderirem ao programa deverão cumprir compromissos relacionados ao mercado interno, pesquisa, desenvolvimento e sustentabilidade. Entre as exigências está a disponibilização mínima de 10% da capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados beneficiada pelo programa para o mercado brasileiro. Serviços e Informações do Brasil Também estão previstos investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento no país e critérios relacionados ao uso de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. Segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, o regime contempla ainda requisitos de eficiência hídrica e compromissos específicos para o suprimento energético das operações. Serviços e Informações do Brasil Mais infraestrutura pode ampliar opções para empresas Para companhias que contratam serviços de nuvem, a expansão da capacidade instalada no Brasil pode aumentar as alternativas de fornecedores e permitir maior diversificação da infraestrutura. Isso, porém, não significa automaticamente redução de custos ou aumento de disponibilidade. Na avaliação da ITGLOBAL.COM, empresas precisam observar não apenas onde os dados estão hospedados, mas também como o ambiente foi estruturado. Entre os critérios estão governança dos dados, redundância, segurança, disponibilidade contratada e capacidade de recuperação diante de falhas. Resiliência depende de arquitetura A presença de mais data centers no país não elimina a necessidade de planejamento de continuidade. Estratégias de Disaster Recovery, definição de objetivos de recuperação e distribuição de cargas entre ambientes diferentes continuam relevantes, especialmente para aplicações críticas. “A ampliação da capacidade de data centers no Brasil é um avanço importante para o mercado, mas a disponibilidade de infraestrutura não garante, por si só, a continuidade das operações”, afirma Peter Jilinski, diretor regional da ITGLOBAL.COM. Segundo ele, a confiabilidade depende da forma como os ambientes são estruturados e dos mecanismos de recuperação previstos. Escalabilidade e previsibilidade também entram na decisão Outro ponto de atenção para gestores de TI é a capacidade de ampliar recursos conforme a demanda. Escalabilidade, previsibilidade de custos, suporte, segurança e conformidade devem ser analisados em conjunto no momento de escolha de um provedor. Com isso, o Redata pode ampliar a oferta de infraestrutura local, mas a decisão empresarial continuará dependendo de fatores que vão além da localização física dos servidores. Brasil tenta reduzir dependência externa O governo federal apresenta o regime como parte de uma estratégia de atração de investimentos em infraestrutura digital e fortalecimento das cadeias tecnológicas ligadas à indústria 4.0. A legislação também busca estimular atividades relacionadas a computação em nuvem, inteligência artificial e outros serviços intensivos em processamento de dados. Serviços e Informações do Brasil Para o mercado corporativo, o avanço da capacidade nacional pode significar mais opções. artigo.texto: VOLUSIA COUNTY, Fla. — The Volusia County Council voted 6-0 Tuesday to stop large-scale data centers in unincorporated areas because of concerns about water resources, infrastructure capacity and local environmental impacts. According to the county’s agenda, large-scale data centers are defined as facilities with an anticipated monthly peak load of 50 megawatts or more. Under the decision, the county cannot accept, process, review, approve or issue applications or development approvals for projects above that threshold. “We beat this horse pretty good. I think it’s time to put it to rest,” said David Santiago, District 5 representative on the Volusia County Council. The facilities do not fit the county’s environment, Volusia County Chair Jeff Brower said. “They just don’t work in Volusia County because of the way our aquifer is structured,” Brower said. “We believe it endangers the aquifer. It uses a lot of water.” Developers can still apply for projects under 50 megawatts, but Brower said they would go through a rigorous review process. He said county staff would review a project first, followed by a zoning and regulation committee, before the council votes on it. “I was concerned with 20 megawatts and above, but I think we have that protection written into this ordinance,” Brower said. Suzanne Scheiber, founder and president of Dream Green Volusia, said she supports the ban on large-scale data centers and remains focused on their potential impacts. “Imagine that amount of industrial waste. Where are you going to put that?” Scheiber said. “It’s going to turnover, and then you also have the noise level that’s caused. Even if they used reclaimed water, for example, there is a turnover of that as well.” The ban applies only to unincorporated areas of Volusia County. Cities and towns within the county will decide how to handle data center proposals within their limits.

artigo.texto: Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL) has issued an advisory introducing updated requirements for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and co-located Renewable Energy Generating Stations (REGS) used for charging. The guidelines specify minimum energy storage discharge durations, connectivity conditions, and commissioning timelines to improve the efficient utilisation of the Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) grid. Under the revised framework, connectivity applications are classified into different categories based on their eligibility and application timelines. Projects falling under the Right of First Refusal (RoFR) category will be subject to a minimum BESS discharge duration of two hours. This requirement applies to existing connectivity grantees and eligible applicants who submitted applications under Regulation 5.2 or Regulation 5.11(a) up to February 21, 2026. Applicants under the RoFR category must also comply with the applicable conditions for co-located renewable energy generation and inverter capacity. Depending on the option selected, developers may be required to apply for co-located REGS under Regulation 5.2 or ensure that the total connected rated inverter capacity remains within their granted connectivity limits at all times. These provisions are intended to maintain compliance with approved transmission connectivity arrangements. For applications outside the RoFR category, CTUIL has prescribed a minimum BESS discharge duration of four hours. The same requirement applies to standalone BESS projects located at renewable energy pooling stations. The higher storage duration is intended to support better utilisation of available transmission infrastructure and improve the operational efficiency of energy storage installations. Although applying for co-located REGS may not be mandatory for every non-RoFR applicant under Clause 1(1) of Annexure IV of the General Network Access (GNA) Regulations, CTUIL has encouraged developers to install matching renewable energy generation capacity equivalent to the BESS energy storage rating in megawatt-hours (MWh). For standalone BESS projects at pooling stations, however, applications for co-located REGS under Regulation 5.2 remain mandatory. Developers must also ensure that inverter output stays within the permitted connectivity limits. CTUIL has further advised that the capacity of co-located renewable energy generating stations used for charging should match the BESS storage capacity. These charging facilities must be commissioned either from the start date of BESS connectivity or within 36 months from the date of the in-principle grant or firm start date, whichever is later. Developers may also draw electricity from the national grid to charge their storage systems, subject to the availability of transmission margins. The advisory also provides a transition mechanism for pending applications that do not currently meet the four-hour storage requirement. Applicants with under-process standalone BESS or non-RoFR projects may seek an increase in energy storage capacity in MWh without changing the overall installed power capacity in MW. Such requests can be raised during Connectivity and Medium-Term Open Access System (CMETS) meeting discussions. Developers choosing to upgrade their projects must submit the required eligibility documents under Regulation 5.2(h) within two months of the advisory’s publication or the relevant approving CMETS meeting, whichever is later. The upgraded projects must also comply with applicable land requirements, financial conditions and scheduled commercial operation date (SCOD) regulations. Through these measures, CTUIL aims to establish clearer storage requirements for different connectivity categories while supporting efficient transmission planning and the integration of renewable energy and battery storage projects into India’s power grid. artigo.texto: Cloverleaf data center plan amendments approved; vote for project approval still to come Piedmont’s proposed Cloverleaf data center campus moved a step closer to a final decision after a tense City Council meeting that included a heavy police presence and continued public backlash. The meeting focused on revised master design conditions for the project, also referred to as Project Open Sky. At least a dozen police cruisers were in the parking lot as the council discussed the rules and conditions that would govern the data center campus, rather than voting on the building itself. Among the revisions, the plan would cap the data center campus’ water use at 75,000 gallons a day, excluding fire suppression. It also would require a water study paid for by the developer to ensure the project does not harm the residential water supply or the city’s master plan goals. City Council members said the data center campus would require about 6 miles of new sewer line. One councilmember said the data center campus would have to adhere to stricter standards than an event center that was previously approved. The council also approved an amended motion stating that Frisco Road, which borders the data center campus, cannot be closed. Councilman Schlomach read criteria he said his vote will be based on, including whether the data center is compatible with surrounding land use, whether it poses a risk to public health and safety, and whether it will tax city resources. Schlomach said the rule of law must apply to everyone equally and compared the “collective private property philosophy” that he said has been displayed in meetings by some residents as fascism. Some residents reacted with anger and profanity in the parking lot, directing it toward the councilman in protest. City Council approved the amendments to the revised master plan. The next hearing for a vote to approve the Cloverleaf data center project is scheduled for Nov. 12. Piedmont is also considering another data center proposal from Beltline Energy. That plan was tabled two weeks ago while several issues are addressed, including additional studies, landscaping requirements, and stronger compliance provisions. Beltline’s proposed data center master design plan is set to go before the Piedmont City Council on Monday.

artigo.texto: A company behind Wyoming’s artificial intelligence data-center boom has launched a $105 million fund for Yellowstone National Park. In a Monday announcement, officials touted the donation as the largest private gift in National Park Service history. But the contribution is also raising questions about the role of private philanthropy as data-center development transforms the rural West. Funneled through the official nonprofit partner of the park, Yellowstone Forever, the donation from energy giant Tallgrass, a Blackstone Inc. portfolio company, is intended to fund research and conservation; develop a new visitor education center at Norris Geyser Basin; and expand opportunities for students and families to experience and learn about Yellowstone, according to Yellowstone Forever CEO and President Lisa Diekmann. As U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum posed for pictures at Yellowstone’s Old Faithful Inn on Monday alongside Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon and representatives of Tallgrass and Blackstone, officials didn’t discuss the environmental impact of AI data centers. Instead, they touted what the donation would do for the park. “More than 120 years ago, President Theodore Roosevelt laid the cornerstone of Yellowstone’s iconic gateway, enshrining the promise that our National Parks exist for the benefit and enjoyment of the American people,” Burgum said in a press release. “This historic $105 million investment honors that legacy, bringing together the best of American enterprise and conservation to expand access to Yellowstone and inspire the next generation to experience America’s great outdoors.” But across the country, only about 11 percent of Americans support the construction of an AI data center in their communities, according to recent polling from the University of Massachusetts Amherst. Brian Childers lives about three-and-a-half miles from a Microsoft AI data center south of Cheyenne — near the separate Tallgrass facility that’s under construction. He’s hard of hearing, he says, but he still can’t escape a constant, overwhelming hum. Birds have left his property, he said, and at night the sky never quite gets dark. He said the gift to Yellowstone feels like the companies are trying to buy goodwill from politicians and the public. “I’m glad (the park) got the money, but if these things are going to impact the people around southeast Wyoming, (the corporations) need to be paying a premium on the electricity they use so that the people don’t have to pay extra,” Childers told Mountain Journal in an interview. Colorado-based Tallgrass manages more than 10,000 miles of pipelines and, with Google as a partner, is developing a 2.7 gigawatt AI data center near Cheyenne, Wyoming. Matt Sheehy, brother of Montana Republican U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy, led the company from 2019 until earlier this year. Tallgrass is also a subsidiary of Blackstone, the largest financier of data centers in the world and major financial backer of Tim Sheehy’s former company Bridger Aerospace. The National Parks Conservation Association, Park County Environmental Council, Wild Montana and the Greater Yellowstone Coalition all declined to comment on the donation. On social media, however, an uproar ensued. “Putting the wolves in charge of the sheep,” one person commented on Yellowstone’s Instagram post, joining a slew of detractors. Tax dollars only cover the basics of Yellowstone National Park’s operations, according to Yellowstone Forever’s Diekmann, who said she hopes the gift will inspire further donations. America’s first national park still has a large need, she added: Yellowstone has a $1.2 billion backlog of maintenance that this donation will not address. In an interview, Mountain Journal asked Diekmann about how closely Yellowstone Forever examined the public pushback to data centers and their ecological consequences elsewhere in Wyoming and across the country in their decision to move forward with the donation. “We are focused on mission-aligned programs,” she said. “I think that the business of Blackstone and Tallgrass and their commitment to the communities in which they work is very important. And this is reflected in this donation.” Tallgrass officials declined an interview. But in an emailed statement, the company touted its contributions to the Wyoming economy, including some of the nation’s largest carbon sequestration technology. “We’ve always believed that energy from Wyoming should create opportunities for Wyoming, and that means more than the jobs we provide and the taxes we pay,” the company said. “It means being a force for good across the entire state, not just in the specific communities where we operate. Our investment in Yellowstone is one way we’re acting on that belief.” Blackstone also declined to comment. In the Yellowstone press release, however, the company lauded its donation. “This historic gift reflects our belief that infrastructure investment can and should be a force for good, helping us invest in Yellowstone’s future and the growth of the communities that surround it,” Sean Klimczak, global head of infrastructure for Blackstone, said in the statement. Experts say there might be more at play. “This falls right into that category of philanthropy designed to win over stakeholders who might be unhappy with you,” Thomas Lyon, a professor of business and sustainability at the University of Michigan who focuses on greenwashing, told Mountain Journal. Donations from data centers across the country are increasingly common, according to reporting from Spotlight PA. They often run in the millions of dollars. In one instance, locals pushed back on a proposal to give every household in Hazle Township, Pennsylvania, $10,000 if officials approve an Amazon data center. Some called it a bribe. Southeast Wyoming, like Phoenix and Northern Virginia, is rapidly becoming a hub of data-center development. artigo.texto: Battery technology company HoriZn opens new headquarters at The Press in Foxton Battery technology company HoriZn officially opened its new headquarters at The Press in Foxton with a warm welcome from CEO Jane Hunter, a ribbon-cutting ceremony and a tour of the facilities. The company has moved from Chesterford Research Park, where it spent the last five years as Superdielectrics, the operating name since being founded in 2014, and hiring its first employees in 2021. In 2025, Jane Hunter took over as CEO to deliver an ambitious growth plan following the successful launch of its field-tested prototype Faraday 2, Superdielectrics’ next generation aqueous polymer battery storage prototype. The new name aligns the business with its key scientific breakthrough – zinc batteries for power management globally. With ‘Zn’, the periodic symbol for zinc, at its heart, the name reflects the role the element plays in the company’s next stage of growth as it drives towards its first battery deployment at a customer site, and then on to manufacture – possibly at an adjacent warehouse at The Press. “It’s very exciting to be officially opening the site under our new trading name today,” said Jane, addressing the guests gathered at the new unit. “Today is a lot more than a new building and corporate identity, it’s about celebrating how far we’ve come and what we’re doing in the next few months. “We have new ideas, foundational research and a shared belief that innovation can solve some of the world’s most pressing technological challenges.” Jane noted that the company’s success is now such that “talent is knocking at our door with people who want to contribute to something new and groundbreaking – we’re building a completely new product and bringing a new technology to market and that’s the spirit for this new chapter of our business”. The CEO paid tribute to fellow Australian, CTO Dr Shelley Brown, who arrived at the company this time last year. “I want to thank everyone who has participated, especially the founders and shareholders,” Jane continued. “The potential is enormous but it has required patience and I thank you for that. The current team has been sprinting since Shelley and I started and it has involved hard work. The creativity and dedication has taken our breath away. It’s been a fun process but it’s been done in a heart-stopping time frame.” HoriZn’s internationally patented technology is based on a novel separator which uses advanced material innovation, providing charging and discharging capability, intrinsic safety advantages, including no risk of thermal runaway (which causes fires) and tolerance of the abnormal operating states at data centres. The battery uses widely available raw materials with no critical minerals and more straightforward recyclability than most current commercial batteries. The company has just completed a fundraise which will help it build Faraday 3, its high-power test battery, for commercial deployment trials - ahead of the commercialisation of its internationally patented Faraday technology. The first benchtop prototype suitable for AI data centres will be ready next month, with a second due for commercial trials early next year: if all goes to plan, a pilot will be built to support larger customer deployment, very possibly at The Press. This new type of battery – suitable for high power stationary rather than on-the-move smartphone or EV use – boasts increased speed, safety (it’s water-based, so no battery fires), high power performance and life cycle, all at a lower cost. The batteries solve one of the big concerns about AI – HoriZn’s Faraday option uses far less energy and is far more reliable than alternatives. It doesn’t (in layman’s language) conk out with the fluctuations of AI demand – “the power drawdown pattern”, as Jane calls it, of “extremely high compute and sudden drop-off”. On a tour of the new labs conducted by Dr Brown, we meet some of the team. First up is Dr Wes Buxton, principal scientist and responsible for developing HoriZn’s zinc-based chemistry platform. It is this platform that scientist Dominic Overland has built upon to “invent the polymer power cell”, explains HoriZn’s tour guide, technical programme director Dr Rudolf Dreyer. Dr Buxton looks rightly proud as he holds up the lab-scale battery cells - which he and the team continue to refine, with the current patented polymer being entirely novel and the result of years of R&D effort to achieve exciting electrochemical performance in HoriZn’s optimised battery chemistry, specifically for high power buffering applications. Next up is Dr Zach Parr, head of strategic projects and another polymer chemist - he explains the IP sensitivities limit around what can be said about the technology on display. However, like Dr Buxton, Dr Parr looks rightly proud as he holds out a sample of the polymer membrane in his gloved hand – explaining the general properties that make it unique to the battery field and explaining the path to scaled production. We move out of the component chemistry laboratory into the space reserved for pack and power electronics development. On display are the previous generation of packs – Faraday 1 and 2. Ben Whitehead, head of pack and deployment, joined from the automotive battery industry two weeks ago. Together with his colleague and principal mechanical engineer, Devam Sanghavi, they explain the evolution to the Faraday 3, emphasising the substantial step up in the number of cells incorporated, more sophisticated design spanning module and pack levels, and significant improvement in performance specification. The challenge is not simply to develop a better cell, but to integrate the technology into a complete battery system that can ultimately be manufactured and deployed at scale. artigo.texto: MILWAUKEE – Milwaukee County Executive and Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley and Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany made their last-ditch appeal to voters in their first and only televised debate, less than two weeks before the Nov.3 midterm election. The two candidates running to be Wisconsin’s next governor sparred over policies including affordability, data centers and education in the highly anticipated debate at Marquette University Oct. 21. The race generated national attention when Crowley upset frontrunner democratic socialist Rep. Francesca Hong in the Aug. 11 partisan primary. Both major parties and individual donors have poured millions into a race that will determine who gets to lead one of the most closely contested states in the country for the next four years. The two candidates for governor wasted no time attacking one another in the debate hosted by WISN-12 News. Tiffany, of Minocqua, tried to distance himself from President Donald Trump while hammering Crowley on raising taxes. Crowley, from Milwaukee, appealed to Wisconsin over why he is the right choice for the state, drawing on his past record passing bipartisan legislation in Milwaukee County. In the latest Marquette Law School Poll on Sept. 30, Crowley holds a three-point lead over Tiffany among likely voters, but the race remains a toss-up with a 4.8% margin of error. Ben Wikler, former chair of the Democratic Party of Wisconsin, stood in for Crowley at the press conference following the event. Affordability Both candidates cited affordability as a top priority and laid out their plans to lower costs for Wisconsinites. Tiffany said he would end Gov. Tony Evers’ 400-year-veto for school funding increases, which can raise property taxes if not offset by state funding. He also said he wants to eliminate taxes on tips and overtime and reduce taxes on middle-income families who make $150,000 or less by 10%. Tiffany was quick to criticize Crowley over his role in the passage of Act 12, a bipartisan bill that increased the state’s shared revenue program and eliminated a property tax via a 2% sales tax hike. “[Crowley] said that he believed higher taxes are not a burden when he nearly doubled the sales tax,” Tiffany said. “That was the one year property taxes went down. He raised the sales tax instead. Taxes went up every single year. You know what he’s going to do as governor.” Crowley, who led the passage of Act 12, has used this as an example for how he will work across the aisle as governor. Crowley did not directly answer a question over whether he would create a new tax bracket for Wisconsin’s highest earners. Instead, he pointed to Tiffany's support of President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and ending the war in Iran, which he said “raised record” gas prices. Regular gas prices in Wisconsin are nearly $2 more per gallon than one year ago, and diesel is up by nearly $3. “Tiffany had the ability to lower costs for families just at the gas pump. He voted to protect the war in Iran and we’ve seen our diesel and gas prices skyrocket,” Crowley said. Tiffany voted against five House resolutions directing Trump to end the war in Iran, the last one on March 5. He was not present for the Sept. 15 roll call vote that prompted Trump to remove hostilities and U.S. armed forces. The two candidates answered questions over what they would do with the state’s $3 billion budget surplus. Tiffany said the state should return “all of that to the taxpayers” through long-term tax relief. Crowley provided a more extensive answer, saying he would funnel the money to education, childcare and healthcare for working families. Crowley’s campaign released a policy plan for Wisconsin renters in early October along with a student renters’ Bill of Rights, calling for a cap on rent increases and longer notice before evictions for all Wisconsin residents. Tiffany claimed rent increases frequently result from utility rate hikes. He said as governor, he would halt utility rate increases. “I think we need to build a growing economy here in Wisconsin where we don't have to worry about that, where we make sure people get good jobs,” Tiffany told The Daily Cardinal. “[Renters] may not realize [increases are] a result of their utility bill… the landlord oftentimes has it included.” Trump and election integrity Tiffany, while he had typically aligned with President Donald Trump in Congress, has recently tried to distance himself from the president, particularly on the war in Iran and certifying the 2020 presidential election. He previously voted against ending the war and certifying former President Joe Biden’s 2020 presidential win, but has since gone back on both. Meanwhile, Crowley’s campaign has tried to highlight that connection. “We’ve always had free and fair elections,” Crowley said. “It is very clear that he is working for Donald Trump.” When asked why he voted to overturn the 2020 election, Tiffany pointed to private election donors like Mark Zuckerberg. He added that a Dane County Clerk allowed people to declare themself indefinitely confined, which was another reason he voted to overturn the election. Tiffany said Crowley is too focused on what he is against rather than what he is for. “While my opponent, you can see early on in the debate, is consistently focused on being against Donald Trump, I’m for Wisconsin,” Tiffany said. Both Tiffany and Crowley said they would certify the 2028 election as governor, no matter the winner. Tiffany declined to answer whether he would eliminate the Wisconsin Elections Commission, saying they need to first explore viable alternatives to the commission. “We may have to keep the Wisconsin Elections Commission,” Tiffany said, adding it depends on a willing legislature. artigo.texto: Data-center companies are ponying up to find out which communities will resist them the least. Startup Hamlet has parsed tens of thousands of city council meetings by scraping local governmentsâ video recordings, tagging comments as friendly or hostile to a potential project. CEO Sunil Rajaraman told Semafor that a large fund that finances data centers and a data-center developer are among its paying customers, looking for whiffs of a moratorium. âWhere there might be more favorable political viewsâ may well determine where future projects get built, Rajaraman said. Investors backing these projects are also obvious customers for a real-time feed into Americansâ growing antipathy toward data centers. The appetite for such data shows the lengths to which the tech industry is going to find where projects are most likely to go through, in the face of a national groundswell of anti-data center activism that has turned community sentiment into a financial risk. Other Hamlet customers include real estate developers, political action committees, and retailers, Rajaraman said. The company on Tuesday launched new rankings for where cities and counties stand on a host of hot-button issues (ranging from zoning laws to pickleball), and a portal for people to look up what their elected officials have said. (Among large local governments, Corpus Christi, Texas ranked No. 1 in speakersâ opposition to data centers.) âThis is public sphere data,â Rajaraman said. âThe data needs to be out there so America can make better decisions.â

artigo.texto: President Donald Trump is calling for data centers to pay for their own power and pay dividends to local communities — a stark change for the president less than two weeks before the election and as opposition to data centers is growing. In Memphis, Tenn., where the City Council was weighing a temporary moratorium on data centers on Tuesday, ultimately voting against the move, attendees used fiery language to describe their feelings. “Lives are at stake and blood is on your hands,” council meeting attendee Tikeila Rucker said. "Supporting a pause on data centers is a vote for reaffirming your dedication to the people of Memphis, not the billionaire class," said attendee Amber Sherman. It’s a scene playing out across the country as Americans raise concerns that data centers, which provide the computing power for artificial intelligence, will drive up electric bills and consume massive amounts of water. Now the president is pitching a new solution. He wrote early Wednesday morning that new data centers are “mandated by me to make their own electricity and give or sell any excess back to the local community.” He added: “If companies want to make their data centers popular, they should pay a ‘dividend’ to the community.” It was not immediately clear how the president’s demand could be implemented. Trump’s social media post marks a shift in tone for the president, who previously criticized data center opponents as wanting to “end up being backwards and poor,” as he said at a rally earlier this month in Ohio. “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio,” he said. “You can’t just turn it off. They’ll go to China.” Todd Eisenstadt, research director at American University Center for Environmental Policy, said data centers are an easy target. He said there’s been a growing uneasiness with data centers tied with a more existential fear over the development of artificial intelligence. A new Washington Post-ABC-Ipsos poll found 66% of Americans oppose construction of new data centers and also disapprove of the president’s handling of AI. “Perhaps the wind has shifted and this is a defining issue of the election,” Eisenstadt told Spectrum News. “And he’s on the wrong side of it. So, he’s trying to swim the other way here at the last minute.” The number of data centers has exploded. Estimates show there are at least 3,000 nationwide.

artigo.texto: O governo dos Estados Unidos anunciou um acordo entre a americana Crusoe e a paraguaia Araico para desenvolver uma infraestrutura de computação de alto desempenho no Paraguai, abastecida com energia da hidrelétrica de Itaipu. A previsão é que a primeira etapa do empreendimento entre em operação em meados de 2027. O anúncio foi feito pelo Departamento de Estado americano nesta quarta-feira, 21 de outubro, durante a divulgação dos resultados da visita do vice-secretário de Estado Christopher Landau ao Paraguai, realizada entre os dias 19 e 21 de outubro. Segundo o governo americano, o projeto poderá representar um dos maiores investimentos privados da história do Paraguai. O comunicado, no entanto, não informa o valor previsto para o empreendimento, sua capacidade de processamento ou a demanda de energia elétrica. A infraestrutura deverá atender clientes de serviços de nuvem dos Estados Unidos e da América Latina. O Departamento de Estado não detalhou as condições de fornecimento da energia de Itaipu nem informou a existência de um acordo específico com a hidrelétrica. A parceria foi anunciada durante uma missão comercial liderada por Landau em Assunção, voltada à ampliação dos investimentos americanos no Paraguai e à identificação de oportunidades em tecnologia, minerais críticos, infraestrutura hidroviária e logística. Além de Itaipu, cooperação nuclear Além do investimento em infraestrutura de computação com energia de Itaipu, os governos dos Estados Unidos e do Paraguai anunciaram o início de negociações para um acordo de cooperação no uso pacífico da energia nuclear. O instrumento, conhecido como 123 Agreement, estabelece a estrutura jurídica necessária para que empresas americanas possam exportar equipamentos e materiais nucleares civis relevantes ao Paraguai, observadas as exigências de segurança nuclear e não proliferação. O comunicado também informa que a Uranium Energy Corp (UEC) anunciou um investimento de US$ 12 milhões para desenvolver uma de suas concessões de urânio no Paraguai. Os anúncios integram uma agenda mais ampla de cooperação econômica e de segurança entre os dois países, discutida durante encontros de Landau com o presidente paraguaio, Santiago Peña, e o ministro das Relações Exteriores, Rubén Ramírez Lezcano.

artigo.texto: ZTE Launches M8000 Micro-Module Data Center for AIDC Deploy ZTE launches ZXEDC M8000 Intelligent Computing Micro-Module at Data Center World Asia, offering a scalable IT POD for AI-driven data centers. October 22, 2026 Sponsored by ZTE Singapore City, Singapore, October 20, 2026 — ZTE Corporation (0763.HK / 000063.SZ), a global leading provider of integrated information and communication technology solutions. ZTE has officially launched the new-generation integrated IT POD solution, ZXEDC M8000 Intelligent Computing Micro-Module, at Data Center World Asia, Asia’s premier data center event. Addressing industry pain points driven by the AI computing boom, soaring rack power density, uncertain business iteration, and the transition from air cooling to liquid cooling-the solution delivers a high-density, scalable and evolvable intelligent computing foundation for data center clients worldwide. The M8000 integrates enclosed cold aisle, liquid-cooled racks, network racks, coldplate liquid cooling CDU, secondary-side piping, high-voltage DC, intelligent busbars, thin-sheet air wall, monitoring, lighting, cabling and fire linkage into one unified solution. It supports high-density deployment of AI servers, flexible power distribution, switchable air/liquid cooling and scalable capacity. Compatible with general-purpose and AI computing hybrid deployment, it enables one-time deployment with long-term evolution. - Key Product Highlights High-Density Deployment and Flexible Evolution — Rack power ranges from 20–60kW per rack, with a peak of 250kW per rack. The racks are decoupled from the frame, supporting full racks and special-form-factor racks. On-site air-to-liquid cooling retrofits are available at later stages. Standardized, productized components allow fast on-site assembly and shorter delivery timelines. Flexible Cooling and Power, Low Carbon — Adopting an air-and-liquid shared-source architecture, the CDU pairs with thin-sheet air walls with dual cooling sources for dynamically adjustable air/liquid cooling ratio. The solution maximizes free cooling, delivering a PUE as low as 1.15 across all regions. The 800V HVDC combined with intelligent busbars enables flexible in-row power supply for racks, achieving up to 98% power supply efficiency. System-Level Liquid Cooling Safety with UL Certification — It is the industry's first solution to obtain UL system-level leak-proof certification. Full-chain leak protection covers CDU, liquid-cooled racks, liquid-cooled servers and switches. Equipped with leak detection and automatic liquid replenishment to mitigate leakage risks. Intelligent O&M for Cost and Efficiency Optimisation — Unified control of air and liquid cooling, integrated cooling & power management, and automatic optimisation via AI algorithms reduce cooling CLF energy consumption by over 10%. Backed by the iDCIM management platform, it delivers end-to-end visibility of power and cooling systems and simplifies O&M for intelligent computing infrastructure. - Customer Benefits Protect Capital Investment — One architecture supports three generations of IT hardware upgrades, avoiding large-scale retrofits during computing capacity expansion and safeguarding customers' infrastructure investment. Guaranteed Business Reliability — Full-chain liquid cooling safety protection delivers stable operating environments for high-power AI clusters. Lower Operating Expense — Free cooling coupled with AI optimization cuts energy consumption and reduces PUE. - Reference Case In 2025, ZTE won the bid for 666 IT modules for a computing center project in the Yangtze River Delta for a leading Chinese internet enterprise. 345 sets of M8000 IT PODs have been successfully delivered. Adopting the architecture of single-row racks plus single-row thin-sheet air walls, the solution uses factory prefabrication and skid-mounted transportation for on-site hoisting. It only took one month from PO issuance to site arrival, efficiently supporting rapid rollout of large-scale intelligent computing clusters. The ZXEDC M8000 Intelligent Computing Micro Module solution is built for high-density air-liquid hybrid AIDC scenarios, helping customers across Asia Pacific and globally build efficient, reliable and low-carbon AI computing foundations rapidly.

artigo.texto: SUFFOLK, Va. — Suffolk City Council voted unanimously, 8-0, to approve an ordinance temporarily prohibiting data centers in the city as leaders consider how to manage future development. Mayor Michael Duman said the city will not accept data center applications during the moratorium. “At this particular time, we will not be accepting any applications for data centers whatsoever,” Duman said. The ordinance also establishes a definition of a data center, describing facilities that house computer servers and equipment used to process and store data. Timothy Wheels, a Suffolk resident who owns a technology company specializing in artificial intelligence and website development, was the only person to speak before the council vote. Wheels said the fast-changing technology industry presents challenges for local governments trying to establish rules for data center development. “It's not much type of governance because all this is new,” Wheels said. He said he supports the moratorium because it gives the city time to prepare for the growing use of artificial intelligence. “I'm in favor because it buys us time to come up with a plan, to come up with a strategy to prepare ourselves on how we use AI,” Wheels said. The decision comes as communities across Hampton Roads weigh the potential benefits and impacts of data center development. Earlier this week, residents from across the region gathered in Virginia Beach to call for a statewide pause on data centers. Chesapeake and Virginia Beach city councils also halted data center expansion earlier this year. Supporters of data center development say the facilities can bring investment, tax revenue and construction jobs to local communities. In Suffolk, city leaders have not specified how long the moratorium will remain in effect. For now, the ordinance puts data center applications on hold as the city considers its approach to future development. Click here to see how we use AI at WTKR News 3.

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta quarta-feira (21) que pretende exigir que novos e grandes data centers instalados no país – “em alguns casos gigantescos” – produzam a própria eletricidade e repassem o excedente à comunidade local ou à rede elétrica, por meio de doação ou venda. A medida evitaria aumentos no preço da energia elétrica e poderia até levar a uma queda “substancial” nos custos, escreveu Trump na rede Truth Social. O líder norte-americano acrescentou que outros elementos do processo também deveriam seguir a mesma lógica de contrapartidas para as regiões que recebem esse tipo de empreendimento. Leia também: Tarifas de Trump sobre aço podem frear os data centers e afetar a rede elétrica, diz analista Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. artigo.texto: KUALA LUMPUR: Gentari Sdn Bhd and BYD Malaysia Sdn Bhd are exploring the deployment of BYD Flash Charging technology as the country's electric vehicle (EV) market continues to expand. Both companies signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore this prospect today. The collaboration will assess opportunities to develop high-power charging infrastructure supported by battery energy storage systems (BESS), with the technology capable of delivering about 400 kilometres of driving range in as little as five minutes for compatible vehicles under optimal conditions. Under the MoU, the companies will identify suitable charging locations, including key intercity corridors connecting major population centres. They will also evaluate power infrastructure requirements, technical and commercial feasibility, project development opportunities and potential operating models. The partnership will also explore opportunities in renewable energy generation and energy storage, combining Gentari's clean energy expertise with BYD's energy storage and technology capabilities. Malaysia recorded 53,537 new EV registrations in the first nine months of 2026, an increase of 98.8 per cent from the corresponding period last year. The growth comes as the government works towards establishing 30,000 public EV charging points nationwide by 2030. Gentari, the clean energy solutions company wholly owned by Petroliam Nasional Bhd (Petronas), currently operates more than 600 EV charging points in Malaysia. It provides access to about 18,000 charging points across Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and India through its Gentari Go Roaming Hub. Gentari group chief executive officer Sushil Purohit said the next phase of EV adoption will depend on the quality, convenience and reliability of charging services, beyond charging speed alone. He said BYD's expertise in EVs, batteries and high-power charging technology, combined with Gentari's experience in developing and operating charging networks, will provide a foundation for strengthening Malaysia's EV charging ecosystem. BYD vice-president and Asia Pacific auto sales division general manager Liu Xueliang said Malaysia was an important market for the company as it expanded its advanced charging technology into international markets. He said the collaboration would explore how BYD Flash Charging could support a faster and more convenient charging experience for Malaysian EV users. BYD Malaysia managing director Jacob Ma said the partnership was an important step towards building a more comprehensive EV ecosystem in the country. He added that a seamless ownership experience is essential to encouraging more consumers to switch to electric vehicles. The MoU was signed by Purohit and Ma in Shenzhen, Guangdong, China, on Wednesday. Representatives from both organisations, including Petronas and Gentari executives, as well as BYD Group chairman Wang Chuanfu were present.

artigo.texto: JEFFERSON CITY — A St. Louis leader warned that communities without large data centers may not be viable in the future while speaking at a summit on Missouri’s energy future on Thursday. Greater St. Louis Inc. CEO Ron Kitchens said communities with data centers are already pulling population from cities that don’t have them. “This is the railroad coming and deciding to come through some communities, and other communities that they don't go through cease to exist,” Kitchens said. “This is Route 66 when the interstates came in and those communities and those businesses died because they weren't on the trade routes. Hyperscale data centers are the same exact opportunity for communities.” Data centers dominated the conversation through the day as politicians, utility executives and other stakeholders gathered in Jefferson City to discuss infrastructure and changes in the state that could affect utilities. The summit is hosted by Missouri’s Public Service Commission, which regulates monopoly utilities. In slideshow after slideshow, speakers displayed charts showing how massive data centers have reworked Missouri’s landscape. They pointed to spiking demand for electricity, increasing state economic growth and in Montgomery County, the home of multiple new hyperscale projects, increasing local tax revenue. This was the third Power MO summit, and speakers largely struck a celebratory tone as they reflected on how much had changed since they launched the annual meetings. “Today, two years later, we've made significant progress securing our energy future and creating a more prosperous state,” said Missouri Public Service Commission Chair Kayla Hahn. State leaders celebrated multiple new hyperscale data center projects that began work this year, with Amazon and Google centers in Montgomery County and Nebius in Independence. “Over the course of 45 days, we announced three data centers and over $40 billion into the state,” said Michelle Hataway, Missouri Department of Economic development director. “That's huge … that is unbelievable, life-changing opportunities for these communities.” But with unprecedented growth, conference speakers said the state’s existing infrastructure needs major updates. “We're at a pivotal moment with our infrastructure,” said Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe. “It's aging while our communities and industries are demanding more from it.” Hahn said electric growth is skyrocketing after it had been flat for 15 years. “We haven't needed to plan significant new generation, transmission, for the last 15 years,” Hahn said. “So this is a significantly different environment that we're operating in than we had in the past.” Hahn said Missouri will have to build new power plants to meet that skyrocketing growth. Multiple speakers said generating electricity from a diversity of sources would be the most reliable and affordable. “It's important to have an all of the above portfolio in energy right now,” Kehoe said. “If you want to be a competitive state, it can't just be one thing or the other.” Nuclear power in particular, Kehoe said, could be key. Ameren Missouri recently released a new long-range plan for power plants that doubled the amount of new power it planned to generate, with more reliance on natural gas power plants than previous plans. “The fact of the matter is we have to build, and we're gonna have to build fast,” said Rob Dixon, vice president of regulatory and legislative affairs at Ameren Missouri. Kehoe acknowledged the opposition to many data center projects, including the hyperscale builds along Highway 70 in Montgomery County. He said each project needs to be right for the community it tries to build in. And Kehoe added there is a limit to how many projects will realistically move to Missouri. “At the end of the day, these are not going to be QuikTrips, there are not going to be one of these on every corner,” Kehoe said. “Missouri might get a look at a dozen or so. So it's a limited conversation, but it's something that will be well warranted.” Kehoe also said he expects the state legislature to put more guardrails around data centers in the upcoming Missouri legislative session.

artigo.texto: One day after announcing Amazon reached a deal with Loudoun County to withdraw its proposal to build data centers on The George Washington University campus in Ashburn, Virginia, and with the county poised to consider pausing new data center applications for one year, the tech giant says it has made recent changes to facilitate trust, cooperation and community buy-in for future data center development in Northern Virginia. “Just this week we marked our 20th anniversary of operating data center infrastructure here in Virginia, as part of our Amazon Web Services footprint,” said Shannon Kellogg, vice president of public policy at Amazon. The company’s second headquarters — HQ2 — is located in Arlington. Yet, this week, Loudoun County leaders applauded Amazon for where the company decided not to build four new data centers. Loudoun County has long been considered “the data capital center of the world.” Recently, with community concern about energy and water consumption connected to data centers, Loudoun and several other counties in the commonwealth, as well as nationally, have been considering a pause on data center construction. Kellogg said since 2010, Amazon has invested over $190 billion in Virginia, including infrastructure and compensation — more than half in Northern Virginia. “So far, we’ve invested $63 billion in Loudoun County, creating 10,200 jobs,” Kellogg said. “In Prince William, we’ve invested $38 billion, creating over 6,100 jobs.” Yet, large groups of residents in Loudoun and Prince William counties are concerned about the visual impacts, noise related to data centers, increased power demand and loss of developable land for other purposes. Back in August, Ann Williams joined a group of other Loudoun County residents in pushing back on the proposed data center campus: “I don’t know when you can say we have enough. We just have enough.” ‘There has to be a transparent process’ With the recent scrutiny on the potential drawbacks of data center construction, Amazon has taken steps to demonstrate the company’s “good neighbor” efforts. Earlier this month, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said the tech giant would no longer require government officials to sign a nondisclosure agreement before a data center project becomes public. Loudoun County Supervisor Juli Briskman said she’s never been asked to sign an NDA, and that dropping the requirement for that type of NDA alone stops short of full transparency. “I would rather see no NDAs between the developer, the land use attorneys, and the end user,” she said. “If they really want to make sure they’re fully transparent, then it’s no NDAs between the organization and local officials. It’s no NDAs between the organization and an economic development director,” she said. “And I would say also it should be no NDAs between the land use attorneys and the developer who is bringing that proposal in front of a board of supervisors, right? That would be full transparency in my mind.” Kellogg said the decision to no longer require nondisclosure agreements is part of Amazon’s attempt to enable residents to learn about the project sooner. “That allows for the government partners that we’re working with, and ourselves, to be very transparent and to answer questions early on that are coming from the communities,” he said. On the decision to not move forward with data centers on the GW campus in Loudoun County, and instead donate land for a new community arts center and indoor sports facility, Kellogg said: “We had purchased that site, evaluated it, but ultimately decided after listening to a lot of community feedback and feedback from government partners that it wasn’t going to be a site that we wanted to develop with data centers.” “This something that we do,” Kellogg said. “We listen, get feedback, and then determine how we want to move forward.” While Briskman said she appreciates the company’s proposal, she said she’s skeptical it was born entirely out of good faith. “I have a feeling that it came about because they ran into a buzz saw, finally, in Loudoun County, and that buzz saw was me bringing several initiatives to challenge what they thought was by-right status for data centers,” Briskman said. “The other part of it was the community. The community is speaking out louder and louder every day about not wanting any more data centers and not wanting any more electrical infrastructure.” But Kellogg said there are common misrepresentations about data centers residents should be aware of when it comes to energy and water use. “For 96% of the year, we don’t use any water,” Kellogg said. “We only have to use water on the hottest days of the year.” “There’s a trade-off between energy use and water use,” Kellogg said. “If we were not to use any water at all during the hottest days of the year, we’re using air cooling for the bulk of the year, then we would likely be using more energy to cool those systems.” Amazon hasn’t shared independently verified data or studies to verify its daily water usage in Northern Virginia. According to Amazon, the company withdrew 2.5 billion gallons of water for data centers in 2025 and its data centers are more water-efficient than the industry average. Through public records and information obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests, the Virginia Mercury reported in June that local governments in Virginia promised Amazon at least 19.6 million gallons of water a day. That’s enough water to fill about 29 Olympic-sized swimming pools every day. Get breaking news and daily headlines delivered to your email inbox by signing up here. © 2026 WTOP. All Rights Reserved. artigo.texto: Google derruba 400.000 árvores para construir data center na Finlândia e gera revolta Big tech não concluiu avaliações de impacto ambiental obrigatórias antes de começar obras em duas cidades, segundo órgão do governo A Autoridade Finlandesa de Licenciamento e Supervisão ordenou que o Google interrompa imediatamente as obras de dois novos data centers no país, após a empresa desmatar ilegalmente cerca de 400 mil árvores. A suspensão das obras nas cidades de Muhos e Otanmäki ocorreu porque a big tech não concluiu as avaliações de impacto ambiental obrigatórias antes de começar a retirar a vegetação. O desmatamento causado pela empresa afetou 330 hectares em Muhos, no norte do país, onde 250 mil árvores foram derrubadas. Em Otanmäki, outras 150 mil árvores foram removidas. A retirada da vegetação e da camada superficial do solo deixou muitas áreas cobertas por lama, provocando o vazamento de água barrenta para riachos e para o rio Oulujoki. A destruição das florestas já afeta diretamente os animais e as comunidades locais: o desmatamento expulsou espécies nativas, como o pica-pau-de-três-dedos, e fez com que lobos da região passassem a invadir áreas urbanas de alguns vilarejos. Além disso, moradores relatam contaminação dos riachos locais e transtornos causados pelo barulho constante das máquinas. Posicionamentos Em resposta à decisão, o Google confirmou a paralisação das atividades e declarou que cumprirá rigorosamente as exigências das autoridades finlandesas. O diretor da empresa no país, Antti Järvinen, pediu desculpas pelo desmatamento, alegando que a equipe atuou com base no entendimento legal que possuía na ocasião. A multinacional comprometeu-se a plantar árvores em 130 hectares na região de Muhos, medida classificada por ecologistas como insuficiente para reparar os danos causados. Por outro lado, porta-vozes da Associação Finlandesa para a Conservação da Natureza (SLL) criticaram duramente a conduta da empresa, classificando a ação como “pura arrogância”. Mais de 93 mil pessoas já assinaram uma petição exigindo regulamentações mais rígidas para data centers e a criação de taxas para compensar a população local pelos danos ambientais. O escândalo atinge o alicerce de um projeto de investimento de € 13 bilhões do Google voltado para a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) no país nórdico. A Finlândia vinha se posicionando como um polo atrativo para data centers devido ao seu clima frio, que reduz custos com resfriamento de máquinas. Além disso, a estabilidade geopolítica e abundância de terras também atraem investidores do setor. Mesmo com o primeiro-ministro finlandês, Petteri Orpo, vendo esses investimentos como prioridade máxima para a economia, o incidente foi descrito por ele como um “banho de água fria”. O escândalo pode se tornar um dos temas centrais das eleições gerais finlandesas programadas para abril.
