artigo.texto: The European Commission has selected 77 projects to receive funding under the Innovation Fund call for proposals announced in December 2025. The total amount of funding is €3.4 billion, drawn from revenues generated by the European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS). These projects come from various EU countries and span a range of sectors – from energy-intensive industries and ‘green’ energy to reducing the use of fossil fuels in aviation and shipping. This was reported by the European Commission. The spectrum of decarbonisation The winning projects span 23 countries in the European Economic Area. The list includes technologies of various types and scales. These include projects in the following sectors: - energy-intensive sectors — steel, cement and chemicals, as well as the production of advanced decarbonised fuels; - manufacturing – this refers to equipment in the clean technology sector. Specifically, this includes heat pumps and electric vehicle batteries, as well as critical raw materials; - renewable energy – the use of wind, solar and hydro power; - mobility – reducing the use of fossil fuels in aviation, road transport and maritime transport. The cumulative environmental impact of implementing all 77 projects is a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions of 290 million tonnes over the first ten years. This is equivalent to a reduction in CO₂ emissions of approximately one tonne every second for a decade. "These projects demonstrate that European innovators are turning climate ambitions into industrial leadership. By reinvesting revenue from the EU Emissions Trading System into clean technologies, the Innovation Fund is helping companies enter the market, reduce emissions and strengthen Europe’s competitiveness,” emphasised Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commissioner for Climate Action. The winners of the competition were selected across five categories: Large-scale general decarbonisation – 12 projects totalling €1.58 billion. The funding will be directed towards low-carbon fuels and emissions management in industry, particularly in the ferrous metallurgy and chemical sectors. General medium-scale decarbonisation – 17 projects totalling €458 million. This group includes projects relating to chemical products, oil refineries, the maritime sector, glass, ceramics and building materials, cement and lime, bioenergy, cast iron and steel, as well as hydrogen. General small-scale decarbonisation – 20 projects totalling €124 million. The projects presented here are from the critical raw materials processing sector, the pulp and paper industry, the construction sector, oil refining, the chemical and hydrogen industries, and so on. Clean technology manufacturing – 12 projects worth €895 million aimed at the production of solar panels, batteries for electric cars, heat pumps, electrolysers and rare-earth magnets. Pilot projects – 16 initiatives totalling €394 million. In addition, 84 projects, although they did not receive funding, did pass the evaluation process. This may therefore help them to secure funding for their implementation from other sources – whether private or public. It should be noted that Ukraine’s National Emissions Trading System has not yet been approved. There is currently one ministerial bill and three parliamentary bills, each of which proposes different options, including the use of funds generated by the NETS. A detailed comparison can be found in this article by EcoPolitic.

artigo.texto: Florence County Board approves data center moratorium, ends Flock camera use Board votes unanimously on both measures Tuesday night FLORENCE, Wis. (WLUC) — Florence County’s 20-year Comprehensive Plan came into question at Tuesday night’s county board meeting because of the potential of proposed data centers in the county. The current 20-year plan, required by Wisconsin State Statutes, establishes land use goals and policies for the unincorporated areas of the county. Moratorium resolution Florence County Board Chair Chad Hedmark says he is concerned about the long-term use of large buildings built for data centers. “Long term I’m concerned about a large building that isn’t used later on. If they were to build something and doesn’t need this one, who winds up with that, that problem and it would be a problem,” Hedmark said. Battery Energy Storage Systems, or BESS, refers to devices that charge or collect energy from the electric grid or generation facility. That energy is stored and then discharged at a later time. The Florence County Zoning Committee did not contemplate the potential impacts of data centers and BESS at the writing of the initial 20-year Comprehensive Plan, leading to the proposed moratorium resolution. In a previous zoning committee meeting, the decision was made to recommend a moratorium on land uses for the development of data centers. That resolution was put to a vote at the Florence County Board meeting. With the board’s unanimous “yes” vote, the resolution passed. The resolution will give the zoning committee up to 18 months, and potentially longer if needed, to revise the Florence County 20-year plan and allow more time to review and revise the county’s zoning regulations and land use policies regarding data center development. Flock camera discussion The board also discussed Flock cameras during the meeting. Florence County currently has two active Flock cameras. After discussion with those in attendance, the board voted on discontinuing the use of Flock cameras. With another unanimous “yes” vote, Florence County will turn the Flock cameras off, and bags will be put over them until they are removed. artigo.texto: A Finlândia estima que um quarto de milhão de árvores que ocupavam os 330 hectares de floresta perto da cidade de Muhos, na zona rural do norte da Finlândia, foram derrubadas pelo Google. Segundo reportagem do The Guardian, a empresa de tecnologia devastou ilegalmente toda a área para construir um centro de dados – levando consigo até mesmo a camada superficial do solo. Com 145 novos centros de dados em diferentes fases de planejamento, a Finlândia se encontra na vanguarda da mais recente investida das empresas de tecnologia. Além de sua relativa estabilidade geopolítica e geológica e da abundância de terras, o clima frio a torna especialmente atraente para a economia de custos de energia. Ainda de acordo com o jornal britânico, no início deste mês, a Autoridade Finlandesa de Licenciamento e Supervisão (LVV) ordenou ao Google que interrompesse temporariamente as obras em Muhos e em outro local a cerca de 100 km a sudeste, na vila de Otanmäki, após a empresa não ter concluído as avaliações de impacto ambiental necessárias antes do desmatamento da área. A notícia provocou indignação generalizada e um debate nacional sobre qual papel, se houver, o país deve desempenhar na corrida global para construir data centers e acompanhar o rápido desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial. Na semana passada, o diretor da Google na Finlândia, Antti Järvinen, pediu desculpas pelo desmatamento, mas afirmou que a empresa agiu “com base no melhor entendimento que tínhamos da legislação na época”. Muhos e Otanmäki fazem parte de um projeto de infraestrutura de IA de € 13 bilhões do Google, que atraiu críticas de Donald Trump, que preferiria que os centros fossem construídos nos EUA e pediu publicamente que a empresa reconsiderasse. É o maior projeto desse tipo já realizado no país nórdico. O governo finlandês, que implementou profundos cortes de gastos, incentivou o investimento. No mês passado, quando os planos do Google foram anunciados, o primeiro-ministro do país, Petteri Orpo, afirmou que atrair investimentos era uma “prioridade máxima” e que “o valor da economia de dados vai muito além do investimento direto”. Ele disse que o acordo com o Google “traria benefícios duradouros para ambas as partes”. Além das 250.000 árvores derrubadas em Muhos, Annala estima que outras 150.000 árvores foram derrubadas em Otanmäki. Como as árvores foram derrubadas ilegalmente, a madeira dos dois locais não pode ser vendida para fábricas de processamento de madeira. A medida também gerou questionamentos sobre o motivo pelo qual as fontes de energia renováveis da Finlândia estão sendo usadas para abastecer corporações internacionais. Mais de 93 mil pessoas assinaram uma petição exigindo maior regulamentação dos centros de dados e uma taxa para compensar as comunidades locais pelos danos ambientais. Hanna Halmeenpää, presidente do conselho da SLL, disse ter ficado incrédula ao descobrir a violação da lei cometida pelo Google. “A princípio, não consegui acreditar”, disse ela ao The Guardian. “Nunca ouvi falar de nenhuma empresa que tenha feito algo assim na Finlândia.” Ela afirmou que o sistema depende muito da confiança, da qual acredita que o Google se aproveitou. “Eles compraram uma vasta área de terra e simplesmente começaram a desmatá-la, assim, sem mais nem menos”, disse ela. “É pura arrogância e é inacreditável.” A rapidez dos acontecimentos chocou o país, disse ela. “Muitas pessoas estão assistindo ao noticiário e se perguntando: ‘O que está acontecendo agora? O que podemos fazer a respeito? E precisamos mesmo aceitar todos esses projetos de data centers na Finlândia?’” ‘Para a Finlândia, não há benefícios’ Jussi Kangasharju, chefe do departamento de ciência da computação da Universidade de Helsinque, afirmou que, embora os centros de dados gerem um número limitado de empregos, potencialmente impulsionando a economia local, os benefícios em nível nacional são mínimos. “Na verdade, para a Finlândia, não há benefícios”, disse ele. “São empresas internacionais que atendem clientes internacionais. A Finlândia arrecada muito pouco imposto corporativo. Os centros de dados, em última análise, trazem muito pouco benefício para outros, exceto para o próprio operador do centro de dados.” Com a legislação ainda em processo de atualização, há uma corrida para iniciar os projetos o mais rápido possível. Alguns defendem a criação de um órgão centralizado para coordenar os projetos de centros de dados, em vez de deixar grande parte da tomada de decisões a cargo dos municípios, que provavelmente priorizarão as necessidades imediatas da área local. Alteração na fauna e flora Em Otanmäki, o impacto na natureza e na vida cotidiana dos moradores é sentido de forma intensa. Quando as árvores foram derrubadas, os lobos que ali viviam vieram para a vila, disse Anni Ranta, de 53 anos, cuja família mora ali há gerações. Antiga vila mineira, a região é conhecida por seus elementos de terras raras. A família de Ranta mora no centro da vila, ao lado da torre triangular de uma igreja e de um antigo bar que está vazio há anos. A floresta tranquila costumava se estender por quilômetros a partir da vila. Agora, o som das obras ao lado do terreno desmatado onde será construída a usina do Google ecoa pelo local. Leia Também: “Tivemos lobos entrando na aldeia porque todos os animais selvagens saíram da floresta”, disse Ranta. “Eles fugiram. O que me preocupa em relação aos centros de dados também é o barulho, porque este é um solo rochoso. Mesmo quando estamos aqui conversando”, acrescentou, batendo os pés, “parece um tambor.” Tamanha é a sua oposição à chegada do Google que ela está pensando em se mudar. Ela também teme que o centro de dados possa tornar a vila um alvo para a Rússia, com quem a Finlândia compartilha uma longa fronteira. “Eu não os quero aqui”, disse ela sobre o Google. “Não os quero na Finlândia de jeito nenhum. Não gosto da ideia de IA e do mundo mudando, e da maneira como está mudando. Está acontecendo rápido demais, cedo demais.”

During an interview with The Daily Sun, a departing city staff member said all five commissioners knew about a proposed data center in North Port, previously under a non-disclosure agreement, months before public meetings about it. All five commissioners have said, and maintain, that they learned about the data center and NDA around the time residents did. Despite their denials, Ray stuck to her guns. ‘POLITICALLY INCONVENIENT’ North Port’s Development Services Director Alaina Ray is leaving the city, in November after joining in 2021, because she does not feel safe anymore. Ray said she’s received due to threats and harassment. Ray said she planned on retiring in North Port, but is instead moving out of state for her next gig. She would not say where she is going for safety reasons. Ray said she was being followed, harassed and threatened by some. The harassment started after the data center conversations began. When data centers were discussed in North Port hundreds attended the meetings. The vast majority spoke in opposition of one being built in town. Due to the threats, Ray is scared to leave her home on her own. During an interview, Ray said that every commissioner knew about a proposed data center by February. Data centers, and a moratorium on their building in North Port, was first discussed in public on July 21. She also said commissioners knew about the NDA beforehand as well. “Sorry if that’s politically inconvenient for anyone,” Ray said. BARBARA LANGDON Vice Mayor Barbara Langdon said she will miss Ray’s work behind the scenes. Ray, she said, has been effective at working with developers, getting them to do things they are not required to do for builds. “I hope this is not the first in a series of defections,” Langdon said. “I can honestly say that before Alaina’s departure, we have the strongest staff we have ever had.” Langdon condemned the treatment of Ray. “It’s unacceptable. It’s hateful,” Langdon said. “This has got to stop. It’s not who we are. It’s frightening, actually. Langdon said it is not the first time someone has felt the wrath of some residents. She cited one person who provided more “balanced” comments on data centers, at previous meetings, being attacked online. Regarding what Ray said, Langdon said she is sure whatever Ray said, she believes to be true. She does not think Ray would lie. Langdon said she knew about the data center “maybe a week, or week and a half before that (first) meeting.” “We were caught flat-footed just like tons of municipalities across the United States,” she said. “We find out about stuff, a lot of times, when the community does.” DAVID DUVAL “The whole situation is upsetting,” Commissioner David Duval said about Ray’s alleged harassment issues. He said it’s not just about the city nor Ray. “Whether I agree with the city manager, or Alaina Ray, or staff, I will speak and then I will vote. But you don’t ever hear me harassing someone. I feel bad for Alaina in that way,” Duval said. He said a number of public comments, at the meetings about data centers, said “we know where you live and we will never forget.” Duval noted how threatening that sounds. As for Ray’s accusations, however, Duval said: “I cannot speak for the other commissioners but for myself that’s just not true.” “I’m not saying she’s a liar, but I’m not sure what she’s referring to,” Duval said. Duval expressed frustration with the way the data center issue transpired. The project was under an NDA and no commissioners signed it, he said. “I felt that I, as a commissioner, was purposely held out of the loop,” Duval said. DEMETRIUS PETROW Commissioner Demetrius Petrow was frustrated with Ray’s comments. He feels as though commissioners must be involved with projects as big as the proposed data center. Steps have been taken by commissioners to scrap NDAs altogether, and to have projects of certain types come before them before approval. A new Unified Land Development Code passed in 2024 allowed projects to bypass the commission and get administrative approval as long as no rules were being broken. Even if some developments that come through cannot legally be denied, per state laws that some argue neuter home rule, commissioners recently agreed certain projects should still come their way. “I’m very upset,” Petrow said. “We’re playing games that are almost childish. This is not right...I think it’s a blatant, false accusation. I was not aware of any of this stuff. Maybe some commissioners did know about this but I did not.” Petrow said if there are commissioners who do know, Ray should name them. He said he was not one of them. “If I was lying, the city could easily provide proof (with public records.) I don’t hide anything,” Petrow said. Petrow noted commissioners had heard about the NDA in December, but they were unsure of what kind of project it was. “If she’s referring to that, then you have to be really stupid to think that was the point that we were all informed,” Petrow said. Petrow said he learned about the data center June 25, in a one-on-one meeting with City Manager Jerome Fletcher, a little over a month before the first public meeting about it July 21. artigo.texto: Ferguson residents submit petition signatures to stop Emerson campus data center project FERGUSON, Mo. (First Alert 4) - Residents submitted 1,401 signatures to the Ferguson city clerk Thursday as part of a referendum petition opposing the redevelopment of the former Emerson campus. It was one month ago that the Ferguson City Council voted to approve a package of tax breaks and incentives for the redevelopment, after a previous attempt failed. Tiffany Bezayiff, a supporter of the petition, was there to turn in the signatures to the city clerk Thursday. “It meant a lot. It meant that the people spoke. They got to hear their voices,” Bezayiff said. “It felt really good to actually get this over the finish line. A lot of us put in a lot of time and effort all across the community and all different wards, all age ranges. We’ve really pushed hard.” Bezayiff and other residents are part of a group supporting a referendum petition that seeks to reserve approval of the ordinance for the former Emerson campus redevelopment, specifically opposing the data center component and the language in the agreement. “We’re told it’s a closed loop system that our water rates won’t increase. Then explain to me why in the bill, does it say they’ll only use reasonable efforts? The language should reflect what they’re saying,” Bezayiff said. “There’s also no protections against the noise. There’s no accountability measures. We want answers, and so far, no one’s been able to answer that to us.” If determined sufficient, the referendum could force the city council to reconsider the ordinance or put it to a public vote. “They’ll vote no. Overwhelmingly,” Bezayiff said. “It’s very important that many of us are involved instead of just four people who voted to pass this ordinance and this bill. Four people making the decision for almost 20,000 people just doesn’t seem right,” Mildred Clines said. Clines, another supporter of the petition, said resident involvement was important because residents felt unrepresented. “The community has been almost speaking with one voice saying we don’t want this data center built in Ferguson. My street runs right into that campus. It’s in my backyard at the bottom of my street. But what I’m trying to press upon everybody is that it’s not just going to affect Ward 3. It’s going to affect all of Ferguson and even the surrounding areas,” Clines said. Clines said the group was going door-to-door and throughout the community. “We received hardly no pushback from anybody in the community. You had a few, but overwhelmingly the majority said they don’t want it. And they want an opportunity to decide and to speak and to vote on it,” Clines said. Bezayiff said the group needs roughly 1,054 or 1,055 validated Ferguson resident voter signatures for the petition to qualify. “We do have a buffer there. So we just need to wait to see what the city clerk has to say. We will have a certain amount of time to go out and recoup the difference if there’s any gap. So we’re just kind of waiting for that process to take place,” Bezayiff said. The plan would turn the former Emerson campus into a tech hub, including expanding beyond the one data center currently on the campus to up to 300 megawatts. The agreement approved by the city council provides the developer up to $1.5 billion in tax breaks, while the developer makes payments to the city and a non-profit. Henry Iwenofu, a supporter of the petition, said the submission of signatures reflects a broader principle. “It symbolized the fact that the people run a democracy, not a few people. The people want their voices heard. That’s what today means,” Iwenofu said. “This was not a single individual operation. It was a group of people who is concerned with their community and want to do something for it.” The Ferguson city charter allows for referendum petitions, but council member Nick Kasoff said exemptions disqualify this one. “The city charter provides for a referendum, but also has specific exceptions. This bill actually falls into two of those exceptions. We don’t allow a referendum on an administrative bill, which this is, and we don’t allow a referendum on bills pertaining to the levy of taxes, which this does,” Kasoff said. Kasoff said the petition effort won’t change what was passed last month. Kasoff said the contract has already been signed and developer Jim Onder has made the first payment to the city. “This ordinance authorized the signing of a contract. The contract’s been signed. Mr. Onder’s company has actually made the first payment, and we’ve already had a council meeting appropriating the funds from Mr. Onder to give back the money that we cut from the police and fire department,” Kasoff said. “Ferguson’s already moving forward on this. Our budget has gotten some badly needed relief from this deal, and this referendum isn’t going to change or stop that,” Kasoff said. Kasoff compared the deal to winning a lottery jackpot. “When this deal was struck, our city won the Powerball. This deal is going to leave our city in better financial shape for many, many years to come. We did win the Powerball here in Ferguson, and I’m thankful that this deal is going to move forward,” Kasoff said. The city clerk has 20 days to certify the petition. If it is deemed insufficient, organizers would have 10 days to make changes and collect additional signatures. Copyright 2026 KMOV. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Congressional candidate Casey Askar previously said he would keep data centers out of Florida. But at a more recent event, Askar said he still wants the facilities built in the nation, but in rural areas far from where he lives. Florida Politics obtained audio recorded at the event where Askar hedged on data centers and said it was also important for the U.S. to lead in artificial intelligence. “We have to be realistic,” Askar said at a meet-and-greet event in Broward County. “We can’t say, ‘Oh, I don’t want data centers, but yeah, yeah, I want to be in AI.’” That’s a different position than one the Naples Republican staked out during the Republican Primary at a forum where the topic arose. In a clip posted by The Floridian, Askar argued that America needed to stay competitive with China on AI but asserted that could be accomplished without data centers anywhere in the entire state. “I don’t want them anywhere near our homes, anywhere in densely populated areas, anywhere near schools, anywhere near agriculture, anywhere near water supplies,” Askar said. “In fact, my position will be, and you can hold me to this, I don’t want them in the state of Florida. So I will fight, do everything that I can, to keep them outside of our state, and I think that there’s a lot of really good tools that we can use to do that.” Now, Askar said he supports President Donald Trump’s more bullish position about AI. Trump endorsed Askar after he won the GOP nomination in Florida’s 22nd Congressional District, where Askar now faces Democrat Pia Dandiya in a battleground race. “Do I support the President in the mission for data centers? Yes, because we have to compete,” Askar said at the Oct. 13 meet-and-greet. “We have to compete against our adversaries, primarily China. They will eat our lunch there, just like they did with manufacturing. If we lose the AI war — I can’t even tell you because I don’t fully understand it.” Trump has pushed aggressively for the construction of data centers in the U.S., saying communities in opposition would set the nation back. In August, Trump posted on Truth Social: “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.” Askar in the leaked audio acknowledges concerns and says he does support some restrictions on where data centers can be built. “Until the science is out where we’ve got it down, where there’s no negative impact from it, maybe I’ll change my tune,” he said. “But right now, I don’t know what I don’t know. And so I want them in rural areas. I don’t want them near our homes. And I don’t want them near our schools.” Of course, many homes and schools in CD 22 are in rural areas. The district, redrawn under the new congressional map to span nearly coast to coast across the Florida peninsula, runs from Marco Island in Southwest Florida to the Weston area in Broward County where Askar’s meet-and-greet was held. In between urban centers on the district’s edges are rural communities including Immokalee, Belle Glade, Clewiston and Pahokee, all with homes and schools.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich-EVE Energy held a product launch and production-line ceremony at its Chengdu base on October 20, according to a post on BYD's WeChat account, unveiling its Longquan No. 3 2.0 all-solid-state battery and a sodium-ion battery solution for electric two-wheelers. Three products—the Longquan No. 3 2.0, a polyoxygen all-solid-state battery and a solid-liquid battery—also rolled off the production line. Image source: EVE Energy All-solid-state battery targets brain-computer interfaces The Longquan No. 3 2.0 all-solid-state battery is designed for brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. The technology has the potential to help patients with paralysis or speech impairments regain certain functions through brain-controlled interactions. Non-invasive BCI systems face challenges including limited signal precision, restricted functionality and reliance on external headsets, making large-scale deployment difficult. Invasive systems can deliver stronger signals with less noise, enabling deeper human-machine interaction and the restoration of visual and auditory functions. However, batteries implanted in the skull must meet stringent requirements for biocompatibility, long-term sealing, leak prevention and minimal immune rejection, while achieving high volumetric energy density in a very small space. Conventional liquid-electrolyte lithium batteries have struggled to combine high safety with high energy density, posing a barrier to clinical adoption. The battery uses an anode-free design, a customized form factor and insulation-dam technology. In a titanium-cased button cell measuring 23 mm in diameter and 4 mm thick, it achieves a volumetric energy density of 1,045 Wh/L, 40% higher than conventional liquid-electrolyte batteries, according to EVE Energy. The company says the design can accommodate more signal-collection channels within the limited space available in the skull, extend operating time and enable smaller devices that may reduce surgical trauma. Replacing liquid electrolyte with a solid electrolyte also eliminates the risks of leakage and thermal runaway associated with liquid electrolytes, according to the company. At the event, EVE Energy signed strategic cooperation agreements with Jingyu Medical and Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital. The partners plan to connect research and development, industrialization and clinical application to support the broader clinical use of implantable BCIs. Sodium-ion batteries designed for electric two-wheelers EVE Energy has also introduced a sodium-ion battery solution specifically designed for electric two-wheelers, targeting industry challenges such as short battery life, performance degradation during storage, reduced range at low temperatures and safety limitations. The company highlights four claimed advantages of the solution: Long cycle life: Cell cycle life reaches up to 10,000 cycles. Based on one charge every two days, EVE Energy estimates a service life of more than 25 years, potentially matching the lifespan of the vehicle. Wide operating temperature range: The battery supports discharge temperatures from -40°C to 60°C. At -20°C, its discharge capacity retention rate exceeds 93%. Storage stability: After being stored for one year in a fully discharged state, the battery retains a capacity recovery rate of more than 98%, according to the company. Safety: EVE Energy says the battery does not catch fire or explode under puncture, cutting or crushing tests, and does not undergo thermal runaway under overcharging or short-circuit conditions. Multiple technology routes support product development The simultaneous production-line rollout of the three products marks a milestone in EVE Energy's development of advanced battery technologies. The company is advancing several technical approaches in parallel, including its Longquan solid-state series, polyoxygen all-solid-state batteries, in-situ solidification and solid-liquid batteries. These technologies are being developed for different applications, including vehicles, consumer electronics and implantable medical devices.

artigo.texto: A backcountry community group has filed a lawsuit to block the construction of a proposed solar and battery storage project that would industrialize about 588 acres in unincorporated East County, arguing the development’s environmental review was flawed. An association of residents of the community of Boulevard and the surrounding Mountain Empire region — dubbed the Back Country Community Alliance for Responsible Development — are objecting to the San Diego County Board of Supervisors’ recent approval of the Starlight Solar Project. First proposed by the developer in 2022, the project includes a solar farm capable of generating up to 100 megawatts and a 217-megawatt battery energy storage system, constructed in two phases. The community group last week filed a petition in San Diego Superior Court, arguing the project violated the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and failed to disclose or mitigate the risks of toxic plume exposure from a battery thermal runaway event. Residents of the unincorporated town have opposed the development, citing concerns that clean energy projects continue to put their safety at risk. The development was proposed by Empire II LLC. “The lawsuit is without merit and will be addressed going forward,” Jim Whalen, a spokesperson for the developers, said in a written statement. The project will include unprecidented setbacks from homes and public roads, no use of local groundwater and adequate onsite supply of fire protection water, Whalen added. A spokesperson for the Board of Supervisors, which unanimously approved the project in September, said “we are unable to comment on litigation.” At the time of the project’s approval, county officials cited concerns that state energy regulators could green-light the project if the county denied the proposal, noting state approval likely wouldn’t include benefits for the community. In the lawsuit, the group said they do not oppose renewable energy projects, noting the backcountry region already hosts multiple wind, transmission and solar projects, but said the proposal failed to properly analyze risks from a potential lithium-battery fire — which are notorious for burning for long periods of time. Further, their petition argues that county leaders’ approval of the renewable energy development relied on a late plume study that contradicted the environmental review process. However, Whalen noted the project’s approval included the county’s first-ever battery plume analysis. The county’s recommendations did not require the developer to relocate the project’s phase-two battery storage facility from its original northern location. Residents of Boulevard have pushed to move the battery storage farther south, primarily due to fire safety and evacuation concerns. In a letter to the Board of Supervisors, county staff said “the originally proposed location of the Phase II batteries has seven residences within 2,230 feet” while the alternative Phase II location “will have approximately two residences within 2,230 feet,” the group’s petition noted. Starlight Solar was approved with some concessions for Boulevard residents, including groundwater monitoring, community benefits and additional fire safeguards. But the backcountry group urged officials to pause the project’s approval, noting the county is actively drafting its own regulations for battery storage facilities. “The reality is, no one knows the details because this is new technology and this is an extreme risk,” said Thomas Wall, a 10-year resident of Boulevard. Boulevard has experienced three wildfires in the last 130 days, which opponents said only underscores the need for further evaluation before one of the state’s largest battery storage energy systems is added to the desert town’s landscape. County documents showed conflicting figures on battery-fire toxic-plume distances, with one claiming a maximum of 366 feet with no homes at risk, while another cited up to 2,230 feet with seven homes at risk, and that contradiction should have been resolved before the project was approved, the petitioners argued. Many backcountry groups have sued to halt construction of clean energy projects in unincorporated East County in recent years. In 2024, a pair of ranchers filed a petition to halt the construction of 60 wind turbines on the Campo Indian Reservation. In 2021, a group of Jacumba residents brought an unsuccessful lawsuit against the county and developer to block a proposed 600-acre solar and battery project. This story was updated with a comment from the developer.

artigo.texto: Two agreements for a stand-alone BESS of 250 MW/1 GWh in the Bukhara Region of Uzbekistan have been signed by AMEA Power, a UAE-based renewable energy company. The documents, a Battery Storage Services Agreement and an Investment Agreement, were signed in Tashkent on 16 October 2026. The signing took place at the first meeting of the Energy Sector Investors' Council, where Uzenergosotish JSC and the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade signed for Uzbekistan. With 1 GWh of storage behind 250 MW of output, the system will be able to run at full power for four hours. The project will therefore support Uzbekistan, which aims to raise its energy storage capacity to 4.5 GW by 2030. In Egypt, AMEA Power has already commissioned a 600 MWh BESS at its 1 GW Benban solar PV project. AMEA Power signs two agreements for 1 GWh BESS in Uzbekistan The Bukhara Region of Uzbekistan is to get a four-hour BESS of 250 MW from AMEA Power, which has signed a services agreement and an investment agreement for it. artigo.texto: A disputa pela soberania digital na América do Sul ganhou um novo capítulo e, desta vez, o movimento veio do outro lado da fronteira. Enquanto o Brasil ainda tenta transformar sua abundância de energia renovável em vantagem para atrair grandes centros de dados, o Paraguai avançou em um acordo com investidores norte-americanos para instalar infraestrutura de computação de alto desempenho abastecida pela energia de Itaipu. O anúncio representa mais um golpe na estratégia brasileira de disputar os grandes investimentos em infraestrutura digital. Brasil e Paraguai dividem a energia produzida pela hidrelétrica, mas Assunção está tentando converter diretamente sua parcela do enorme potencial energético de Itaipu em ativo para atrair data centers, justamente uma das indústrias consideradas estratégicas na corrida mundial pela inteligência artificial. O entendimento foi comemorado pelo governo de Donald Trump e anunciado durante visita ao Paraguai pelo vice-secretário de Estado dos Estados Unidos, Christopher Landau. Ele destacou tanto a importância de Itaipu quanto o tamanho potencial do investimento norte-americano. “O poder da água é impressionante. O Paraguai e o Brasil aproveitaram a força do imponente rio Paraná na Usina de Itaipu, uma das maravilhas da engenharia mundial”, escreveu Landau ao relatar a visita. Segundo ele, investidores norte-americanos chegaram a um acordo para construir um centro de dados nas proximidades da usina, aproveitando a disponibilidade de energia hidrelétrica. Landau afirmou que o empreendimento tem potencial para se tornar “o maior investimento privado estrangeiro na história do Paraguai”. Um dos movimentos concretos envolve a Crusoe, empresa norte-americana especializada em infraestrutura de computação e inteligência artificial, e a Araico, desenvolvedora paraguaia de projetos de energia e infraestrutura. As duas empresas firmaram uma parceria estratégica para desenvolver infraestrutura de computação de alto desempenho abastecida pela energia de Itaipu. O movimento paraguaio toca diretamente numa discussão que o governo brasileiro tenta enfrentar com a política de atração de data centers. Energia abundante, renovável e relativamente barata tornou-se um dos principais ativos na competição internacional pelos investimentos necessários ao funcionamento dos grandes modelos de inteligência artificial. Nesse mercado, disponibilidade elétrica deixou de ser apenas uma questão energética e passou a ser também instrumento de política industrial e de soberania digital. É justamente aí que o avanço do Paraguai chama atenção. O país vizinho está usando uma infraestrutura energética construída conjuntamente com o Brasil para atrair capital estrangeiro destinado a uma atividade que Brasília também considera estratégica. Na prática, parte do valor econômico gerado por Itaipu poderá ser transformada em capacidade computacional instalada em território paraguaio. Isso não significa que o Paraguai esteja utilizando energia pertencente ao Brasil. Cada país possui direitos sobre metade da energia produzida pela usina, conforme o arranjo binacional. A questão política é outra: quem consegue transformar primeiro essa vantagem energética em infraestrutura digital, investimentos, empregos e capacidade de processamento. E o Paraguai parece disposto a acelerar. O acordo sobre o data center integra uma aproximação mais ampla entre Assunção e Washington. Os compromissos anunciados incluem novos investimentos privados norte-americanos, ampliação da cooperação para segurança das fronteiras e do espaço aéreo paraguaio, apoio às forças de segurança, combate a fluxos financeiros ilícitos e cooperação para utilização civil da energia nuclear. A presença dos Estados Unidos dá ao movimento uma dimensão que vai além de um empreendimento empresarial. Data centers capazes de suportar computação de alto desempenho e inteligência artificial passaram a integrar a disputa geopolítica pela localização da infraestrutura digital. Energia, chips, capacidade computacional e controle sobre dados tornaram-se componentes de uma mesma corrida tecnológica. Para o Brasil, o episódio expõe uma contradição. O país possui uma das matrizes elétricas mais renováveis entre as grandes economias, participa de uma das maiores hidrelétricas do mundo e criou incentivos específicos para tentar atrair data centers. Mesmo assim, um país vizinho consegue colocar Itaipu no centro de uma negociação internacional para receber justamente esse tipo de investimento. O problema, portanto, não está apenas em quem produz a energia de Itaipu. Está em quem consegue transformar essa energia em poder econômico e tecnológico. Se o empreendimento anunciado pelos Estados Unidos avançar na escala prometida, o Paraguai poderá converter sua participação na maior hidrelétrica binacional das Américas em vantagem competitiva na corrida pela infraestrutura da inteligência artificial. E o Brasil terá de explicar por que uma das principais fontes de energia limpa que ajudou a construir está servindo de alavanca para um vizinho avançar mais rapidamente justamente no setor que Brasília diz considerar estratégico para sua soberania digital.

artigo.texto: Germany commissioned more than half a million new battery storage systems, with a combined capacity of approximately 8.2 GWh, during the first nine months of 2026. Newly installed storage capacity increased 91% compared with the same period in 2025, according to an analysis of Federal Network Agency data by the German Solar Industry Association, BSW-Solar. Large-scale battery storage led the expansion, with additions more than quadrupling to around 3.8 GWh. The segment grew approximately 350%, accounting for roughly half of the capacity installed during the period, according to BSW-Solar’s announcement. Smaller systems also recorded growth. Newly installed residential storage capacity rose 20% to 3.2 GWh, while commercial storage additions increased 67% to around 0.7 GWh. Very small systems added approximately 0.5 GWh, up 33%. The figures are based on Germany’s market master data register as of 12 October 2026. BSW-Solar noted that subsequent registrations could increase the totals. Source: BSW-Solar. Annual additions expected to exceed 10 GWh BSW-Solar expects Germany to add well over 10 GWh of storage capacity in 2026. However, the association says deployment must accelerate further to support the expansion of renewable generation. Batteries can absorb surplus solar and wind electricity and release it when needed, helping to ease pressure on electricity networks and reduce system costs. The association cites calculations by the Fraunhofer Institute for Energy Economics and Energy System Technology (IEE) indicating that an additional 80 GWh of battery storage capacity could have reduced costs for consumers and the federal budget by almost €4 billion in the previous year. This represents estimated potential savings, rather than savings already achieved. Fifteen reforms to accelerate deployment Alongside the market figures, BSW-Solar published a position paper containing 15 reform proposals aimed at removing investment barriers, improving the use of existing grids and avoiding unnecessary costs. A central proposal is to make it easier to operate batteries alongside solar and wind installations and at electricity consumption sites. The association is calling for an enforceable right to fair and flexible grid connection agreements. BSW-Solar also wants distribution system operators to be required to tender for battery storage at substations where it can support grid operation, reducing congestion and making better use of available network capacity. A third priority concerns redispatch, the adjustment of electricity generation and operation to manage grid congestion. The association proposes managing installations at the grid connection point rather than controlling each generating plant individually. This would allow surplus solar electricity to be stored during temporary network constraints instead of curtailing production. BSW-Solar is urging the federal government and parliament to incorporate the proposals into upcoming grid legislation and reforms to the Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG). Using existing networks to connect more renewables The association is also calling for clear institutional responsibilities, binding deployment targets and a coordinated national storage strategy. It points to a separate Fraunhofer IEE study examining how batteries at substations could unlock unused network capacity. Under the conditions studied, this could enable substantially more solar installations to connect to existing distribution grids, potentially allowing installed photovoltaic capacity to double. BSW-Solar managing director Carsten Körnig argues that regulatory changes must accompany market growth so batteries can help lower electricity system costs and integrate more renewable generation.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich-Shaanxi Transportation Holding Group and CATL have signed a strategic cooperation agreement to deepen collaboration in commercial vehicle electrification, charging and battery-swapping infrastructure, new energy storage, the low-altitude economy, and Automotive Aftermarket Industry, according to a post issued via CATL's WeChat account on Oct. 21. The two parties aim to develop an efficient, intelligent and green transportation and energy network. Image source: CATL Building a Battery-Swapping Network for Heavy-Duty Trucks The two parties plan to develop battery-swapping stations for heavy-duty trucks by combining Shaanxi Transportation Holding Group's highway network and roadside resources with CATL's standardized QIJI Energy battery-swapping technology and network-based operating capabilities. The vehicle-battery separation model and standardized swapping process are intended to improve energy replenishment efficiency, reduce overall logistics costs and accelerate the large-scale adoption of new energy heavy-duty trucks. Integrating Solar Power, Stored Energy and Charging Infrastructure The two parties will jointly develop photovoltaic power generation, stored energy, and charging and battery-swapping facilities along highways. The initiative aims to increase the local utilization of clean energy and support lower-carbon highway transportation operations. Expanding Collaboration Across the Value Chain The cooperation will also explore opportunities in full-lifecycle power battery services, battery dismantling and recycling, and the low-altitude economy. The companies aim to develop an integrated transportation-and-energy model combining green energy supply, intelligent battery-swapping services and smart operational management. CATL said it will continue to deepen cross-sector collaboration between transportation and energy to support the green and low-carbon transition of transportation in northwest China.

artigo.texto: From public hearings on a Cedar Creek power plant and new downtown business rules to the return of a beloved Bastrop bridge tradition, catch up on three stories drawing attention across Bastrop-Cedar Creek. - Commissioners push TCEQ for public meeting on Cedar Creek power plant The Bastrop County Commissioners Court approved a resolution Oct. 13 to request a public meeting on the natural gas-fired power plant proposed to support a 2,842-acre Cedar Creek data center campus. The request calls on the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to hear residents’ concerns about the Pacifico Energy project. - Bastrop looks to boost business in historic downtown Bastrop officials are proposing new rules to increase foot traffic and activity in the Downtown Historic District, including a requirement that at least 60% of street-facing ground-floor storefront space be used for customer-facing businesses. Residents and business owners can weigh in during the Planning & Zoning Commission's public hearing at 6 p.m. on Oct. 29 at Bastrop City Hall, 1311 Chestnut St.

artigo.texto: Global energy storage owner-operator, BW ESS, has secured debt financing for its Hams Hall battery energy storage system (BESS) in the West Midlands, a project set to become Europe’s largest operational BESS site by megawatt-hour at commercial operations date (COD). Under the agreement, international lenders OCBC, Rabobank, and Societe Generale will provide the debt facility in equal proportions. Rabobank will also act as Facility Agent. The transaction is expected to close at COD. It follows a highly competitive financing process that attracted significant interest from the global banking community, with more than 30 lenders engaged. This response reflects BW ESS’ proven development and operating track record, as well as the increasingly important role of battery storage in supporting the UK’s energy transition. Located adjacent to National Grid’s Hams Hall substation in the West Midlands, the project will initially deliver 350 MW/1243 MWh of storage capacity. This will rise to 400 MW/1424 MWh following completion of the second phase. Once fully operational, Hams Hall will be capable of supporting the electricity needs of around 1.3 million homes for up to 3.5 hours, helping to integrate renewable energy, increase grid resilience, and strengthen the UK’s energy security. Long-term revenues for the first phase of Hams Hall BESS will be underpinned by a 10-year floor and optimisation agreement signed with EDF earlier in 2026. Nick Stamp, CFO of BW ESS, commented: “Securing financing for Hams Hall is another major milestone for BW ESS and for the wider UK energy storage market. The exceptionally strong response from lenders demonstrates growing confidence in both the investment case for battery storage and BW ESS’ ability to develop and operate strategically important infrastructure assets. We are delighted to partner with OCBC, Rabobank, and Societe Generale on this landmark project. Hams Hall will provide critical infrastructure for balancing the UK’s increasingly renewable-powered electricity system, while enhancing energy security and reliability for consumers.” Elaine Lam, Head of Global Corporate Banking, OCBC, added: “We are delighted to support BW ESS in the successful financing of the Hams Hall BESS facility, a landmark project that will become the largest BESS project by megawatt-hour in Europe at completion. The project will strengthen the resilience and flexibility of the UK power network and supports the energy transition, where battery storage infrastructure is essential to enable greater integration of renewable energy and maintaining grid stability. This transaction reinforces OCBC’s commitment to supporting UK energy and infrastructure investment under our £10 billion memorandum of understanding with the UK Government.” Gijs Hofman, Executive Director, Rabobank, noted: “Rabobank is delighted to support BW ESS in financing the Hams Hall project as lender, facility agent and hedge provider. The transaction attracted strong lender interest, reflecting the project’s compelling combination of scale, strategic location, high-quality counterparties, and the proven track record of BW ESS as a leading battery storage developer and operator. We see battery storage as a fundamental building block of a flexible, reliable, and increasingly decarbonised power system. Projects such as Hams Hall help unlock greater penetration of renewable power while strengthening security of supply. We are pleased to partner with BW ESS, OCBC, and Societe Generale on this milestone financing.” Nathalie Lemarcis, Managing Director, Societe Generale, concluded: “We are pleased to support BW ESS in this landmark financing for one of Europe’s largest battery energy storage projects. This transaction highlights the increasingly important role of battery storage in enabling the energy transition, strengthening grid resilience, and supporting energy security. It reflects our commitment to financing critical infrastructure and supporting the development of innovative energy solutions.” The financing further strengthens BW ESS’ relationships with leading international lenders and supports the company’s continued growth across its global portfolio. Hams Hall is part of BW ESS’ 2.6 GWh Ardenham portfolio, which is co-owned with leading energy and decarbonisation investor, AIP Management. In the UK, BW ESS currently operates the 331 MWh Bramley BESS in Hampshire, has 1243 MWh entering operation through Phase 1 of Hams Hall, 857 MWh under construction at Berkswell, and a broader development pipeline spanning multiple gigawatt hours across the country. CMS acted as Legal Adviser to BW ESS, while WFW acted as Legal Adviser to the lenders. Everoze and Modo Energy acted as Technical Adviser and Market Adviser, respectively. artigo.texto: How regional governments determine which aspects of data centers are the most important to locally regulate is a major question for lawmakers to consider heading into the legislative session beginning in January, said Tarrant County commissioner Matt Krause. “We understand the state’s going to have to speak to the data center issue,” Krause said. “But leave a lot of regulation — of what it looks like, how it functions in each and every one of our localities — to the local government.” He pointed to the fracking ban Denton officials enacted in 2014 that quickly led to a clash between the city and state officials. The state sued, alleging the prohibition was “arbitrary, capricious and unreasonable,” according to a report from The Texas Tribune. This was one of the areas of data center regulation Krause spoke to Thursday in the first of the three panels at the Fort Worth Report 2026 Growth Summit. On that panel, Krause was joined by Fort Worth City Council member Elizabeth Beck and Public Citizen Texas director Adrian Shelley. Beck, who’s served on the Fort Worth City Council since 2021, emphasized the importance of local control. She explained that Fort Worth is a home-rule city, meaning city leaders can adopt any regulation the state hasn’t explicitly prohibited local governments from adopting. Beck said she believes business incentives for data centers in Fort Worth need to be taken off the table. “(Data centers) are not hurting for funds,” Beck said. “I’m not a huge fan of incentives anyway. As the city of Fort Worth, we have to be very careful with those.” Areas of data centers that the state is solely authorized to regulate include water supply and planning, air quality, energy and state sales taxes. “I’d like to make sure that the state handles all of the things that they explicitly have to regulate and watch,” Beck said. Local leaders have also disagreed on whether the city should pass regulations now, amid the data center development boom, or wait for the legislature to develop statewide laws. Shelley, who’s worked with Public Citizen since 2017, said local officials should engage with residents to learn more about what they want to see out of the data center industry in the future and to “send the signal” to lawmakers. Dozens of Texas counties have passed resolutions urging legislators to act in a timely manner as data centers proliferate across the state, Shelley said. Some county officials have tested the limits of their authority by proposing moratoriums and outright bans. “Cities should be working up to the limits of their authority because, as I am seeing it, that’s what their constituents want,” Shelley said. Krause disagreed. A veteran lawmaker of 10 years, Krause said local governments should take a “wait and see” approach while sending calls to lawmakers in Austin to act on data center regulation. He cited the amount of time and resources it requires for local leaders to create regulations tailored for specific developments — such as data centers — as reasons to wait for legislative action first. “You don’t want to put a lot of time … into constructing this entire framework on how to deal with data centers only for the state government to come in and say, ‘You can’t do that,’ Krause said. A call from Tarrant County that has already been made to the legislature: doing away with data center tax abatements. However, Krause cautioned that incentives for other industries should not be entirely eliminated. Beck disagreed with Krause’s recommendation. “I trust the state government like I trust gas station sushi,” she said, drawing laughter from the crowd. She said she was happy to see Gov. Greg Abbott’s audit of data centers and halt of environmental permitting for the hubs, but added unknowns still remain for data centers following the Nov. 3 midterm elections. “I don’t want to put Fort Worth in the hands of people who we don’t know what they’re going to do,” Beck said. Panelists also discussed the proposed Circle T data center in Westlake, bordering Keller, which has drawn criticism from residents and leaders of both cities. Krause said local officials in a region should stay in touch with one another on data center questions. When multiple cities are involved in a data center development, Krause said, he’d support an approach similar to the Regional Transportation Council — a body made up of North Texas officials who plan for long-term public transit. “The more you communicate and have those open conversations with each other, the less you’re gonna have situations like we saw on Westlake and Keller,” Krause said. Beck said the Westlake data center speaks to the need for amended laws on communicating with the public. Under Fort Worth code, residents living within 300 feet of a development seeking a zoning change must be notified by mail. But those laws do not apply to residents in nearby, or even bordering, cities. “That’s something that needs to change in state law to make sure that we’re notifying all impacted residents, regardless of what municipality they live in,” Beck said. Shelley agreed with both of the perspectives offered by Krause and Beck, adding that local officials should never be involved in signing nondisclosure agreements. Data center developers should accurately inform surrounding communities on issues such as whether a center has its own power sources, Shelley urged. “Transparency is of the utmost importance,” he said. artigo.texto: Bloomberg — A recuperação do setor de inteligência artificial perdeu força após a estreia desanimadora de uma empresa sul-coreana de data centers, o que reacendeu as preocupações sobre se o boom de gastos com essa tecnologia poderá perdurar. Os futuros do S&P 500 oscilaram entre ganhos e perdas, à medida que a recepção desfavorável à Elice em Seul minou o apetite pelo investimento em ativos de risco. A provedora de infraestrutura de IA despencou 32%, registrando o pior dia de estreia para uma empresa de grande porte no país. Os futuros do Nasdaq 100 caíram 0,4%, interrompendo a recuperação que vinha ocorrendo ao longo do dia. ⟶ Assine as newsletters da Bloomberg Línea e receba as notícias do dia em primeira mão no e-mail. Os títulos do Tesouro atraíram novos investidores em busca de refúgio, mesmo com a alta dos preços do petróleo, com os rendimentos dos títulos de 10 anos caindo dois pontos-base, para 5,12%. O petróleo Brent ultrapassou US$ 111 por barril pela primeira vez desde maio, à medida que os operadores avaliavam o risco de novos ataques iranianos no Estreito de Ormuz. O dólar caiu 0,2%. A recepção negativa à Elice ecoa as preocupações com o financiamento que vieram à tona de forma acentuada com o abandono da oferta pública inicial (IPO) da australiana Firmus Grid há apenas duas semanas. Essas preocupações também são evidentes nos mercados de dívida, onde a alta nos rendimentos de empresas como a CoreWeave sinaliza que os empréstimos se tornarão mais caros. “As preocupações em torno dos investimentos em data centers e infraestrutura relacionados à IA vêm se acumulando há vários dias e agora pesam fortemente sobre o sentimento do mercado”, afirmou Roger Lee, da Cavendish. “O mercado provavelmente precisa de alguma garantia de que o enorme investimento em capex está gerando retorno. Isso é difícil de perceber no momento.” Os investidores aguardam agora os resultados das empresas que mais investem em IA para obter pistas sobre por quanto tempo esses gastos vultosos poderão continuar e em que ritmo. Espera-se que a SpaceX divulgue seus resultados após o fechamento do mercado na terça-feira (20), seguida pela Meta na quarta. Estima-se que somente a Meta, a Amazon, a Microsoft e a Alphabet gastem cerca de US$ 750 bilhões neste ano. O clima de aversão ao risco na terça-feira se estendeu por todas as regiões. O índice de referência da MSCI Inc. para a Ásia atingiu seu nível mais baixo desde julho, com o índice Kospi da Coreia do Sul caindo 3,7%. O Stoxx 600 da Europa recuou 0,6%. O bitcoin retomou as perdas. Os títulos de renda fixa, por sua vez, receberam um impulso da maior demanda já registrada em um leilão de títulos japoneses de 20 anos, um sinal de que os rendimentos elevados estão atraindo investidores domésticos de volta ao mercado. Embora os títulos europeus tenham apresentado alta modesta em toda a linha, a dívida francesa permaneceu sob pressão. O rendimento adicional exigido pelos investidores para deter títulos franceses de 10 anos em vez da dívida alemã, considerada mais segura, subiu dois pontos-base, para 150 pontos-base, nível observado pela última vez em 5 de outubro. “Vemos oportunidades em que rendimentos mais elevados dos títulos soberanos compensam melhor os investidores pelo risco, sem indicar fundamentos mais fracos”, afirmou o BlackRock Investment Institute em uma nota. No entanto, a forte onda de vendas de títulos do governo francês mostra que “a seletividade é fundamental”. → Assine a newsletter matinal Breakfast, uma seleção da Bloomberg Línea com os temas de destaque em negócios e finanças no Brasil e no mundo. artigo.texto: Soluna e Applied Digital formam joint venture para data center de IA de 50 MW no Project Dorothy 3 A Soluna Holdings firmou um acordo definitivo para criar uma empresa de propriedade conjunta com a Applied Digital Corporation para desenvolver um data center de TI crítico de 50 MW planejado para inteligência artificial e computação de alto desempenho, segundo um comunicado à imprensa da Soluna datado de 21 de outubro de 2026. A instalação está prevista para o Project Dorothy 3, o site de desenvolvimento da Soluna próximo a Silverton, no condado de Briscoe, no Texas, e seria abastecida com energia da Briscoe Wind Farm. Pelo acordo, espera-se que a Soluna contribua com uma parte do site Dorothy 3, incluindo terrenos e ativos de projeto relacionados à energia, enquanto a Applied deve fornecer capital para o desenvolvimento. Após o fechamento, espera-se que a Applied detenha 51% da empresa do projeto e a Soluna os 49% restantes. O fechamento depende de várias condições, incluindo a aprovação de uma isenção fiscal para o projeto no condado de Briscoe, a obtenção de apólices de título, certas aprovações corporativas e a negociação e assinatura de um contrato de operação, contratos de locação definitivos, contratos de energia e outros contratos definitivos. As empresas esperam concluir as transações até o fim do ano civil. O diretor-presidente da Soluna, John Belizaire, afirmou que a empresa há muito sustenta que o acesso à energia, e não os chips, é a restrição para a IA, e que a parceria combina o site e a energia eólica da Soluna com um construtor e operador comprovado de data centers de IA. Ele também mencionou as etapas restantes, incluindo o processo de isenção fiscal no condado de Briscoe, e o avanço do projeto junto à comunidade local. Planos do projeto e de locação O Dorothy 3 está planejado como um data center de IA co-localizado com a Briscoe Wind, um parque eólico de 150 MW no condado de Briscoe, próximo aos projetos Dorothy 1 e Dorothy 2 da Soluna. Sujeita à documentação definitiva, a Fase 1 do Dorothy 3, com 50 MW de capacidade de TI crítica, deve ser abastecida tanto pela Briscoe Wind quanto pela rede elétrica. A ChronoScale Holdings Corporation, plataforma de computação acelerada de capital aberto majoritariamente controlada pela Applied, assinou uma carta de intenções não vinculante para locar a instalação planejada. A locação permanece sujeita à negociação e assinatura de documentação definitiva, e a Soluna alertou que não há garantia de que um contrato de locação definitivo será alcançado nos termos previstos ou em qualquer hipótese. A Soluna se descreve como desenvolvedora de data centers verdes para aplicações de computação intensiva, incluindo inteligência artificial, e projeta, desenvolve e opera infraestrutura digital co-localizada com usinas de energia eólica, solar ou hidrelétrica para atender aplicações de computação de alto desempenho.

artigo.texto: VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. — A group of residents from across Hampton Roads gathered at Virginia Beach Town Center on Tuesday, calling on state leaders to impose a statewide moratorium on new data center development. The demonstration brought together residents from multiple localities who say Virginia's rapid growth in the data center industry should be paused until lawmakers and regulators can more closely examine environmental, infrastructure and community impacts. “We don’t really want data centers anywhere in the state other than where they are now,” one protester said during the rally. According to the Pew Research Center, Virginia leads the nation in data center development, with hundreds of facilities either operating or planned across the state. Supporters of data center projects argue the facilities generate construction jobs, tax revenue and economic investment for host communities. At the local level, some governments, including Virginia Beach and Chesapeake, have taken steps to temporarily pause or limit additional data center expansion while evaluating future policies. Chesapeake resident Jeff Staples said a statewide moratorium would offer another layer of protection if local agreements change. “It would serve as a check on Chesapeake in case they back out of what we’ve already agreed to, then the state moratorium will take precedence over that,” Staples said. Others at the rally expressed concerns about potential environmental impacts and increased demands on Virginia’s electrical grid. “I’m obviously very concerned with the data centers and what they’re doing to our environment, to our electrical cost as well,” Portsmouth resident Jennifer Hughes said. “We’ve all been facing higher electrical bills here, and so really I’m just coming out to try to show support for basically pausing building of new data centers in Virginia.” Students also participated in the demonstration, saying they are worried about long-term environmental effects associated with future development. “Deforestation, getting rid of trees, is horrible,” said Logan Hickey, a ninth-grade student. Organizers emphasized they are not seeking to shut down existing facilities. Instead, they are asking state lawmakers to pause approval of new data centers while Virginia studies the industry’s broader impacts on communities, infrastructure and the environment. artigo.texto: Em Barueri, a Scala já construiu dez prédios de data centers, opera oito e planeja chegar a 17 unidades, com 600 MW de capacidade elétrica e um compromisso de investimento total de até R$ 32 bilhões para o campus. Em Barueri, na Grande São Paulo, a Scala Data Centers já construiu dez edifícios de servidores e prepara uma expansão capaz de levar o Campus Tamboré a 17 data centers verticais. O empreendimento tem oito prédios em operação e foi planejado para alcançar 600 megawatts de capacidade elétrica, com um compromisso de investimento que pode chegar a R$ 32 bilhões. O complexo reúne aproximadamente 150 mil metros quadrados já edificados em uma área total superior a 220 mil metros quadrados. Três subestações estão energizadas e a empresa pretende ativar novas fases conforme a procura por espaço de processamento de dados. Parte da estrutura já atende clientes; outra parte integra um projeto de longo prazo que ainda depende de obras e contratos. Dez prédios foram concluídos e o plano prevê outros sete em Barueri As informações divulgadas em outubro de 2026 e detalhadas pela DatacenterDynamics apontam dez edifícios construídos no Tamboré, oito deles operacionais. Os sete restantes fazem parte da configuração máxima prevista para o campus e serão implantados em etapas, segundo a evolução da demanda. - Paraná investe quase R$ 188 milhões para transformar estrada de terra em rodovia asfaltada com 12,8 km de terceiras faixas, dois contornos e nova ponte; obra da PR-160 chega a 22% - Após R$ 86 milhões em obras, estação de esgoto no Paraná troca antigas lagoas por nova tecnologia, prepara aumento de 45% na capacidade e prevê atender o crescimento da cidade por 15 anos - Torres pode ganhar bairro de R$ 800 milhões em área do tamanho de 238 campos de futebol, com 1.400 lotes, marina no Rio Mampituba e acesso a campo de golfe já existente - Depois de 30 anos abandonado em Goiânia, prédio redondo que seria um centro médico pode virar apartamentos no Airbnb; prefeitura anuncia recuperação, mas obra segue sem data para começar Em vez de um único galpão, o complexo reúne edifícios projetados para abrigar servidores, conexões de alta velocidade e sistemas elétricos e de refrigeração. Grandes provedores de computação em nuvem precisam de energia constante e condições controladas para manter máquinas funcionando durante todo o dia. A distribuição por prédios permite à Scala ampliar a instalação conforme os contratos fechados com clientes de grande porte. Cada nova unidade exige obras civis, sistemas de segurança, fornecimento elétrico e infraestrutura para dissipar o calor gerado pelos equipamentos. Compromisso de R$ 32 bilhões se soma a obras que já superaram R$ 10 bilhões Os R$ 32 bilhões são o valor potencial comprometido para a expansão, não um total já gasto. Em novembro de 2025, a Scala informou, em comunicado oficial, que o montante aplicado no campus já ultrapassava R$ 10 bilhões. O restante do investimento planejado está associado às próximas fases de implantação. Na mesma ocasião, a empresa anunciou um memorando de entendimento com a Prefeitura de Barueri para o plano diretor do complexo. O acordo envolve propostas de melhorias viárias, mobilidade e infraestrutura urbana ao redor do empreendimento, localizado próximo ao Rodoanel. O movimento já gerou um canteiro de obras de grandes proporções. Nas primeiras etapas, cerca de 3.500 trabalhadores participaram da construção, conforme reportagem da Revista O Empreiteiro. O projeto também contratou empresas de engenharia, fornecedores de equipamentos e serviços especializados. Três subestações preparam o campus para uma demanda elétrica de 600 MW A implantação dos prédios depende de uma rede capaz de entregar energia em grande escala. O plano do Tamboré considera 600 MW de capacidade elétrica total no desenvolvimento completo. A meta corresponde ao potencial previsto para o campus, enquanto os oito prédios em operação representam a fase já instalada. Uma das subestações foi construída com participação da ENGIE para conectar a área ao Sistema Interligado Nacional. Inaugurada em 2026, essa instalação possui capacidade nominal de 560 MVA, unidade utilizada no dimensionamento elétrico. Os 600 MW divulgados para o campus correspondem à potência projetada para o conjunto de instalações. A Scala liderou requisitos e etapas de desenvolvimento da subestação, enquanto a ENGIE assumiu a infraestrutura de conexão e as atividades de operação e manutenção. A construção de novos edifícios precisará acompanhar a disponibilidade de energia e de infraestrutura de transmissão. Obras usam componentes modulares e deixam espaço para resfriamento líquido Para reduzir etapas de construção e melhorar a previsibilidade dos canteiros, a empresa afirma trabalhar com engenharia própria e métodos modulares e industrializados. A estratégia permite repetir componentes de instalações elétricas e estruturas técnicas em diferentes etapas do campus, com adaptações conforme as necessidades dos clientes. A refrigeração tem papel decisivo nesse tipo de construção. O Tamboré possui operações com sistemas de resfriamento a ar e infraestrutura preparada para incorporar refrigeração líquida. A tecnologia é voltada a equipamentos de alta densidade, como servidores usados para treinar e executar modelos de inteligência artificial. A companhia também declara contratar energia de fontes renováveis, principalmente por acordos de longo prazo com projetos eólicos e solares. São soluções importantes para um empreendimento cujo crescimento exigirá mais instalações elétricas e refrigeração, além de acompanhamento do consumo de água e da eficiência energética. Empresa prepara no Rio Grande do Sul outra cidade de data centers Além de Barueri, a Scala desenvolve a Scala AI City, em Eldorado do Sul, na região metropolitana de Porto Alegre. artigo.texto: CATL's Profit Squeeze Meets a Swapping-Station Land Grab Published on 10/21/2026 at 16:41 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL is discovering that selling more batteries is not the same as keeping more of the money. The world's largest cellmaker posted revenue growth of 58.58% year on year in its latest quarter, yet profit attributable to shareholders advanced just 14.54% — and slipped 5.77% from the prior three months. That gap between the top line and the bottom line has become the central question for investors, and it drew a swift response from Wall Street on Thursday. Citi cut its price target on the stock to RMB 479 from RMB 500, citing a gross margin that came in below expectations, higher expenses and larger impairment charges. The brokerage also trimmed its earnings forecasts for the coming years, a move that goes beyond a simple re-rating of the shares and touches the expected trajectory of the business itself. CATL's stock fell 12% on the day. The downgrade follows JPMorgan's decision a day earlier to move its rating on the Hong Kong-listed shares to Neutral from Overweight, with the target lowered to HK$500 from HK$725. JPMorgan pointed to profitability in the battery sector fading faster than anticipated. Reuters added that intensifying competition in the battery market and slower growth in Chinese car sales are weighing on earnings. Both analyst moves train attention on the quality of CATL's profit rather than the pace of its sales. A Capacity Story That Outruns the Profit Line Against that backdrop, CATL is pushing hard on a business it believes can open fresh demand: battery swapping for heavy electric trucks. The company aims to more than double its swapping network to 2,000 stations by 2027, according to MT Newswires, with 900 sites in China targeted by the end of this year. Longer term, CATL and its partners have set their sights on a nationwide network of 10,000 stations. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? The hardware behind the push is the QIJI swapping system unveiled on Wednesday, which pairs a standardised swappable pack with an additional reserve battery. CATL says the exchange can be completed within five minutes, and 13,000 units were signed under agreements at the launch event. The combination is designed to raise the usable capacity of the main battery, while a rental model — rather than an outright purchase of the pack — changes how customers pay for power. CATL reckons rental costs per kilowatt-hour can come out as much as 20% lower on base tariffs. Those figures carry different weight. Signed agreements are a firmer commitment than long-range build-out targets, and the network plan is no proof of how heavily customers will use the stations once they open. The cost saving, meanwhile, is explicitly framed as a potential reduction on base tariffs. Truck Platform, Vehicle Partners and a Demand Bet The swapping drive sits alongside the Tianxing II heavy-duty truck battery platform, also presented on Wednesday, which Reuters reported on. CATL is working to tie swapping more closely to vehicle makers as well. DIGITIMES reported on an agreement between Huawei-linked Yinwang Intelligent Technology, CATL and its battery-swapping subsidiary — a partnership that broadens the infrastructure build-out with another vehicle-technology ally. CATL says swapping is gaining recognition among automakers and partners and views the technology as one of the future main forms of vehicle energy supply. No quantified earnings contribution has been attached to the arrangement. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. Underpinning the expansion is CATL's expectation of further growth in worldwide demand for powertrain and storage batteries in 2027, helped by electrification of commercial vehicles and rising demand for energy storage both inside China and abroad. The company believes the market may hold up better than feared, with utilisation staying relatively high. The truck-swapping build-out fits that view, though it remains an investment in demand that has yet to arrive. On the earnings call, CATL said it is discussing with customers how to share the impact of tax changes, and plans to ease margin pressure through new technologies and products. No relief has yet been agreed from those talks. For investors, the measure that matters is not the station count alone but whether CATL can turn the combination of battery technology, rental pricing and partnerships into a network busy enough to justify the outlay — and, just as importantly, whether it can convert its rapid growth into steadier profitability. The analyst cuts make clear that strong revenue on its own will not be enough. Ad CATL Stock: New Analysis - 21 October Fresh CATL information released. What's the impact for investors?
